The highest-priority items — frequency-dependent squeezing and improved coatings — address the two fundamental noise sources that limit the detector across its most sensitive band and are most consistent with the existing facility infrastructure described in the paper.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Dual-Phase Xenon TPC Dark Matter Detector

## Framing: What "Primary Physics Performance" Means Here

The figure of merit is **sensitivity to WIMP-nucleon cross-section**, which scales as:

$$\sigma_{\min} \propto \frac{\sqrt{B \cdot M \cdot t}}{M \cdot t \cdot \epsilon}$$

So improvements must target: **(1) background reduction**, **(2) fiducial mass increase / better self-shielding**, **(3) energy threshold reduction**, **(4) signal efficiency**, and **(5) discrimination power (S2/S1 ratio and NR/ER separation)**.

---

## Upgrade 1: Photosensor Replacement — Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) for the PMT Arrays

### Current Limitation
Standard 3-inch PMTs (e.g., R11410-23 Hamamatsu) have:
- ~35% quantum efficiency at 178 nm (VUV)
- ~2 ppm radioactivity (U/Th chains) per unit, ~200 PMTs total → dominant internal background source
- Single photoelectron resolution adequate but not excellent
- Temperature-dependent gain drift

### Specific Upgrade
Replace both top and bottom arrays with **VUV-sensitive SiPM tiles** (e.g., Fondazione Bruno Kessler NUV-HD-cryo or Hamamatsu S13370 series adapted for VUV):

- **Tile design**: 6×6 cm² tiles with ~150 µm microcell pitch, tiled to match current PMT array footprint
- **QE/PDE**: ~24–28% PDE at 175 nm currently achievable; roadmap to >35% with improved AR coatings (SiO₂/MgF₂ multilayer on silicon)
- **Radioactivity**: SiPMs can achieve <0.1 mBq/kg (²³⁸U/²³²Th) vs ~1–5 mBq/unit for PMTs — **order-of-magnitude reduction in ER background from photosensors**
- **Correlated noise**: After-pulses and optical crosstalk require dedicated mitigation — use **non-reflective trenches between microcells** and cryogenic ASIC-based correlated noise cancellation
- **Readout**: Pair with **cryogenic transimpedance amplifier ASICs** (e.g., ABALONE-style or custom 65 nm CMOS designed for 170 K operation) mounted at the cold flange, reducing trace capacitance and Johnson noise

### Physics Impact
- Lowers single-electron S2 detection threshold → access to **sub-GeV dark matter via Migdal effect and Bremsstrahlung channels**
- Reduces internal ER background from sensor radioactivity by ~10× → directly improves sensitivity at WIMP masses 10–100 GeV
- Better single-photon resolution improves S1 reconstruction and position reconstruction at low energies

---

## Upgrade 2: Electrode Grid Redesign — Tensioned Copper-Beryllium Mesh → Photolithographically-Etched Titanium Grids

### Current Limitation
Woven wire grids (typically 100–200 µm stainless steel or CuBe wire, ~2–5 mm pitch):
- Sag under differential pressure and thermal contraction → non-uniform electric field
- Wire-by-wire tension variation → field non-uniformities of several percent across TPC radius
- Electroluminescence from sharp wire tips creates spurious single-electron backgrounds
- CuBe has measurable ²²⁶Ra contamination

### Specific Upgrade
Fabricate grids via **UV photolithography and chemical etching on 50 µm titanium sheet**:

- **Hexagonal hole pattern**, 2–3 mm pitch, ~85% optical transparency (matched to current designs)
- **Radius of curvature at hole edges**: >50 µm by electropolishing → eliminates field-emission tips
- **Planarity**: ±50 µm over 1.4 m diameter achievable with Ti grade 2 sheet under controlled tension
- **Mounting**: Annular titanium frame with 12–24 radial tension adjustment screws accessible during assembly; spring-loaded retaining clips compensate for differential thermal contraction (Ti CTE ~8.6 µm/m/K vs SS ~17 µm/m/K, better matched to PTFE/copper TPC body)
- Incorporate **redundant resistive field-shaping rings** at 5 mm vertical spacing near grid (replacing 20 mm spacing) for field uniformity at liquid-gas interface

### Physics Impact
- Eliminates or greatly suppresses **single-electron emission backgrounds** that currently limit S2 threshold and mimic low-mass DM signals
- Improved field uniformity → better S2 position reconstruction → tighter fiducial cut → less background leakage from TPC walls
- Reduces cathode-region electron emission by minimizing field hot spots → lower accidental coincidence rate (AC background)

---

## Upgrade 3: Active Inner Vessel — Electroformed Copper Field Cage with Embedded Resistor Chain

### Current Limitation
PTFE-based field cage panels are the dominant source of surface ER backgrounds (radon daughters plating out on PTFE, ²¹⁰Pb → ²¹⁰Bi → ²¹⁰Po chain). PTFE also fluoresces, creating optical artifacts.

### Specific Upgrade

#### 3a: Electroformed Copper Cylinder
- Replace segmented PTFE reflector panels with a **single-piece electroformed oxygen-free copper cylinder**, inner surface coated with **evaporated tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) + MgF₂ overcoat** for VUV-to-visible wavelength shifting and reflection
- Electroformed copper achieves **<0.1 mBq/kg** (²³²Th/²³⁸U) — among the lowest of any structural material
- Surface radon daughter accumulation still occurs, but Cu can be **electropolished and re-coated** between runs
- Wall thickness: 3 mm (sufficient structural rigidity, minimal self-absorption of LXe scintillation)

#### 3b: Embedded Resistor Divider Network
- Implant a **laser-etched resistive spiral** directly in the Cu wall surface (ion-implanted Si resistor strip or thick-film nichrome on alumina tiles bonded to Cu) to replace discrete resistor-divider chains
- This eliminates discrete component solder joints (each a potential Rn emanation point) and improves field uniformity

### Physics Impact
- Reduction in surface ER events (²¹⁰Pb progeny) by >5× → directly reduces the dominant background in the WIMP search region below ~100 keV
- Improved light collection uniformity (single reflective cylinder vs. panel gaps) → better S1 energy resolution at threshold

---

## Upgrade 4: Cryogenic Purification — Continuous Electron Lifetime Monitoring + Magnetically-Coupled Gear Pump Recirculation

### Current Limitation
Electron lifetime (proportional to electronegative impurity concentration, primarily O₂/H₂O) degrades S2 signals from events near the cathode. At 2-tonne scale (~1.5 m drift length), achieving and maintaining >5 ms electron lifetime is critical. Current hot-getter purification systems have dead volume, outgassing fittings, and cannot be easily optimized in situ.

### Specific Upgrade

#### 4a: Distributed Internal Electron Lifetime Monitor Array
- Deploy **6–8 UV LED + drift cell assemblies** (miniature alpha sources or pulsed photocathodes, ~1 cm³ active volume) at multiple heights along the field cage wall
- Real-time electron lifetime map at 1-cm spatial resolution enables **position-dependent lifetime correction** of S2 signals rather than single average correction
- Communication via fiber-optic link to avoid Cu wire feedthroughs (Rn path)

#### 4b: Magnetically-Coupled Cryogenic Gear Pump
- Replace bellows-based gas recirculation with a **submerged cryogenic gear pump** (e.g., based on Kyocera ceramic gear technology, adapted for 165 K LXe) driving liquid-phase recirculation at 5–10 standard liters per minute (slpm) equivalent
- Liquid-phase recirculation avoids vaporization/re-condensation cycle → factor of 3–5 lower pump energy, more stable thermodynamics
- **No dynamic shaft seal** (magnetic coupling) → zero Rn ingress path from ambient

### Physics Impact
- Electron lifetime >10 ms uniformly → S2 threshold effectively set by photosensor noise floor rather than attenuation
- Enables reliable detection of S2 signals within 5–10 mm of cathode → **10–15% increase in fiducial volume** at full drift length
- Position-corrected S2 improves energy resolution at 1–10 keV_nr from ~15% to ~8%

---

## Upgrade 5: Muon Veto Enhancement — Gadolinium-Doped Water Cherenkov + Outer Liquid Scintillator Layer

### Current Limitation
A pure water Cherenkov muon veto efficiently tags through-going muons (>99%) but has limited sensitivity to:
- **Muon-induced fast neutrons** that don't produce visible Cherenkov (below Cherenkov threshold in water)
- **Radiogenic neutrons** from detector materials escaping inward

### Specific Upgrade

#### 5a: Gadolinium Sulfate Doping (0.1% by mass)
- Dissolve Gd₂(SO₄)₃ in water tank to **0.1 wt%** (as demonstrated in SuperK-Gd/EGADS)
- Thermal neutron capture on ¹⁵⁷Gd (σ = 255,000 barns) produces **8 MeV gamma cascade** → detected in Cherenkov within 20–30 µs of muon
- **Veto window**: extend coincidence window from 250 µs to 500 µs with Gd → tags slow neutron thermalization and capture
- Requires water purification system upgrade: Gd-compatible ion exchange + reverse osmosis to maintain <1 ppb non-Gd metal contamination (PMT corrosion mitigation)

#### 5b: Outer Gadolinium-Loaded Liquid Scintillator Ring
- Install **annular liquid scintillator detector** (e.g., LAB+PPO+bis-MSB, 0.1% Gd by mass) as 30 cm shell between outer cryostat and water tank inner wall
- ~10 tonnes LS volume, read out by 8-inch PMTs on water-side face (doubles as muon veto photosensors)
- LS provides **both scintillation (low threshold) and Cherenkov** detection, tagging neutrons that scatter in LS before reaching xenon
- This effectively creates a **3-layer veto**: LS → water Cherenkov → TPC, with 4π coverage

### Physics Impact
- Muon-induced neutron background reduced by factor ~3–5 via extended Gd-capture veto
- Radiogenic neutron background (dominant at low-mass WIMP region for NR search) reduced by >50% via LS pre-scattering detection
- Combined veto efficiency for single-scatter neutron NR events in fiducial volume: from ~60% to >90%

---

## Upgrade 6: Cathode High Voltage — Custom Cryo-Rated Cockcroft-Walton Multiplier with In-Situ HV Filtering

### Current Limitation
Achieving uniform −50 to −100 kV on cathode (required for ~1 kV/cm drift field over 1.5 m) with commercially available HV feedthroughs:
- Feedthrough failures are a leading cause of detector downtime
- HV ripple induces correlated S2-like signals (electron emission under oscillating field)
- Rn emanation from HV cable insulation (PTFE/polyimide jacket)

### Specific Upgrade
- **In-situ Cockcroft-Walton multiplier** built from cryogenic-rated ceramic capacitors (COG/NPO type, stable to 77 K) and Schottky diodes (SiC, rated to −60°C), mounted inside the xenon vessel on the cathode support structure
- Drive with a **low-voltage RF input** (~1 kV peak, 100 kHz) through a simple coaxial feedthrough → CW stack multiplies to −80 kV locally
- RF feedthrough has **100× less Rn permeation area** than a DC HV feedthrough of equivalent rating
- Final LC filter stage (cryo-rated inductor + ceramic cap) on cathode node → HV ripple <1 mV at 100 kHz

### Physics Impact
- Eliminates HV feedthrough as Rn source and failure mode
- Sub-mV HV ripple → electron emission rate from cathode reduced by >10×
- Enables operation at higher drift fields (>1 kV/cm) → improved NR/ER discrimination via charge yield (higher field suppresses recombination differently for NR vs ER)

---

## Upgrade 7: Xenon Purity — Krypton Removal via Cryogenic Distillation Column Integrated into Recirculation Loop

### Current Limitation
⁸⁵Kr (β emitter, Q = 687 keV, 10.8-year half-life) at natural Kr/Xe ratios of ~1 ppm contributes ER background throughout the WIMP search region. Current remove-before-fill charcoal trap methods achieve ~0.1 ppt Kr/Xe but cannot maintain this during operation.

### Specific Upgrade
- Integrate a **packed distillation column** (structured stainless steel packing, ~3 m height, ~10 cm diameter) into the gas-phase recirculation loop
- Operating at ~1.5 bar, 178 K (above Xe boiling point, below Kr condensation fraction at column top)
- Continuous **online krypton stripping** during detector operation: sidestream of 1% of recirculated Xe flow passes through column, Kr-enriched reject (0.1 slpm) vented through dedicated exhaust
- Column material: electropolished 316L SS with low-outgassing seals → adds minimal Rn emanation

### Physics Impact
- Maintains Kr/Xe < 0.01 ppt **during operation**, even with slow Kr outgassing from vessel materials
- Reduces ER background from ⁸⁵Kr by factor >10 vs. current approach
- Particularly important for sensitivity to low-mass WIMPs and solar neutrino floor mapping (where ER/NR discrimination is less effective)

---

## Summary Priority Matrix

| Upgrade | Primary Background Targeted | Expected Background Reduction | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| SiPM replacement | Internal ER (sensor radioactivity) | 5–10× | High |
| Etched Ti grids | Single-electron / AC backgrounds | 10–50× | Medium |
| Electroformed Cu field cage | Surface ER (²¹⁰Pb) | 5× | High |
| Cryo pump + lifetime monitor | S2 threshold / fiducial loss | N/A → +15% mass | Medium |
| Gd+LS veto | Neutron NR | 3–5× | Medium |
| In-situ CW HV | HV-induced electron emission | 10× | Medium |
| Online Kr distillation | ⁸⁵Kr ER | 10× | Medium |

---

## Most Impactful Single Upgrade

**SiPM replacement** combined with **etched titanium grids** would provide the largest physics return: the grids eliminate the dominant fake-signal background (spurious single electrons) and SiPMs reduce the dominant internal radioactive background while simultaneously lowering the energy threshold — improving sensitivity across the entire WIMP mass range from ~1 GeV to 1 TeV simultaneously.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Advanced Gravitational-Wave Detector Performance

## Framing the Problem

Performance is limited by a hierarchy of noise sources across frequency bands. I'll address each dominant limitation with specific, concrete hardware proposals rather than generic suggestions.

---

## 1. Quantum Noise (Dominates ~10 Hz – 10 kHz)

### 1.1 Frequency-Dependent Squeezing via Filter Cavity

**Current limitation:** Broadband squeezing injects 10–15 dB of squeezing but faces the shot noise / radiation pressure noise tradeoff — squeezing one quadrature amplifies the other.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Install a **300–400 m evacuated filter cavity** (e.g., LIGO-style, as implemented at LLO/LHO post-O3) with:
  - **End mirror: Ta₂O₅/SiO₂ HR coating**, T ≈ 10–20 ppm, designed to rotate the squeezing ellipse from ~100 Hz upward
  - **Cavity linewidth:** ~50 Hz half-bandwidth (set by mirror losses < 5 ppm/mirror)
  - **Optical path length stability:** ≤ 1 pm/√Hz at 10 Hz via independent suspended optics
- **Squeezing source:** Periodically-poled potassium titanyl phosphate (PPKTP) OPO pumped at 532 nm, targeting **15 dB squeezed variance** at 1064 nm
- **Impact:** Recovers up to ~6 dB effective broadband sensitivity vs. fixed-quadrature squeezing

### 1.2 Increased Circulating Power

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace current input optics with a **Nd:YAG or Yb:YAG master-oscillator power-amplifier (MOPA)** delivering **200–300 W** at the input mode cleaner
- Install **higher-damage-threshold ETM (end test mass) coatings**: Ion-beam-sputtered (IBS) alternating SiO₂/Ta₂O₅ with **Ta₂O₅ replaced by amorphous silicon (a-Si) at room temperature or crystalline Al₀.₉₂Ga₀.₀₈As (AlGaAs)** to reduce absorption-driven thermal lensing (target absorption < 0.5 ppm)
- **Power recycling mirror reflectivity adjustment** to maintain impedance matching at ~6,000 W circulating power
- **Parametric instability suppression:** Ring dampers or electrostatic drive feedback on test masses at specific mechanical mode frequencies predicted by finite-element modeling (modes between 10–100 kHz)

### 1.3 Signal Recycling / Variational Readout

**Specific upgrade:**
- Tune signal recycling cavity detuning to implement **speed meter topology or EPR (Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen) entanglement readout** between signal and idler sidebands
- Alternatively: **Quantum non-demolition (QND) readout** using a small auxiliary "speed meter" cavity — a sloshing cavity (L ~ 1 m) coupled to the signal port that measures momentum rather than position, evading radiation pressure noise below ~50 Hz

---

## 2. Thermal Noise (Dominates ~10–200 Hz)

### 2.1 Test Mass Material and Coating Replacement

**Current limitation:** Brownian thermal noise from both bulk fused silica and the HR dielectric coatings (dominant contribution is the coating, specifically the high-index Ta₂O₅ layers).

**Specific upgrades:**

**Coating:**
- Replace IBS Ta₂O₅/SiO₂ multilayer coatings with **crystalline AlGaAs (GaAs/Al₀.₉₂Ga₀.₀₈As) mirror coatings** bonded to the test mass via direct wafer bonding
  - Loss angle φ ~ 4×10⁻⁵ (vs. ~2×10⁻⁴ for Ta₂O₅) — ~5× lower coating Brownian noise power
  - Manufactured via MBE; requires 34 cm diameter bonding to fused silica or silicon substrate
  - Demonstrated at small scale (GariLock coatings, LMA work); scale-up is the engineering challenge

**Test mass substrate (longer-term):**
- Transition to **silicon test masses (160 kg, ⌀ 55 cm)** operated at **123 K or 18 K** (zero-crossing of silicon's thermal expansion coefficient)
  - Requires switching laser wavelength to **1550 nm or 2000 nm** (Si is opaque at 1064 nm)
  - Suspension fibers: **crystalline silicon ribbon fibers** (φ ~ 10⁻⁸ at 20 K) replacing fused silica
  - Requires cryogenic payload: cold finger + radiative cooling via cold shield, or conductive cooling through maraging-steel structure (Japanese KAGRA approach validated)
  - Reduces combined substrate + coating thermal noise by factor ~10 in strain noise amplitude

### 2.2 Suspension Thermal Noise

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace current **fused silica fibers (φ ~ 10⁻⁷ at room temperature)** with:
  - For near-term: **Larger-diameter monolithic fused silica fibers** (800–1000 µm diameter vs. current ~400 µm) with **hydroxy-catalysis bonded ears** — reduces violin mode frequencies but lowers suspension thermal noise in 10–30 Hz band
  - For cryogenic upgrade: **Single-crystal silicon blade springs + silicon fiber suspensions**, φ_Si ~ 10⁻⁸ at 123 K; fibers pulled from float-zone silicon rod
- **Multi-stage blade spring optimization:** Add a 5th penultimate stage specifically tuned to attenuate 10–30 Hz thermal noise coupling; use **maraging steel C300 alloy** blades with measured loss angle < 5×10⁻⁶

---

## 3. Seismic and Newtonian (Gravity Gradient) Noise (Dominates < 10–20 Hz)

### 3.1 Newtonian Noise Cancellation (NNC)

**Current limitation:** Gravity gradient noise from density fluctuations in ground and atmosphere couples directly to test masses — no passive isolation possible.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Deploy **seismometer arrays** surrounding each test mass station:
  - **60–100 seismometers** (e.g., Nanometrics Trillium Compact or custom MEMS-based, < 1 µrad/√Hz tilt noise) in a 10–40 m radius 3D array (surface + 3–5 m depth boreholes)
  - **Infrasound microphone array** (Chaparral Physics Model 25) at ~50 m radius for atmospheric NN
  - Feed signals into **Wiener filter or neural network** (deep learning demonstrated in simulation) real-time subtraction algorithm
  - **Projected performance:** Factor 10–20 reduction in NN amplitude at 10–20 Hz, opening low-frequency band
- Hardware requirement: Vibration-isolated, thermally-stabilized seismometer vaults (ΔT < 0.1 K/day) to suppress tilt-to-acceleration coupling

### 3.2 Active Seismic Isolation Enhancement

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace current HAM (horizontal access module) isolation platforms with **next-generation 6-DOF active platforms**:
  - **Inertial sensors:** Custom folded-pendulum accelerometers or **tiltmeters** (e.g., NIKHEF-style) with noise floor < 10⁻¹⁰ m/s²/√Hz at 0.1 Hz
  - **Geophones:** Sercel L-4C replaced with **low-noise broadband seismometers** (STS-2 or Nanometrics Trillium 120) with flat response 0.008–50 Hz
  - **Actuators:** Lorentz-force voice coil actuators with **eddy-current-free design** (aluminum-free coil formers) to avoid back-action coupling
  - **Control scheme:** Model-predictive control with feed-forward from external seismometer reference, achieving **10⁻¹² m/√Hz** at 1 Hz on isolated platform
- Install **horizontal tiltmeter** (resolution: 1 nrad/√Hz at 10 mHz) in the HAM chamber to decouple horizontal ground tilt from true horizontal acceleration at low frequencies — this is the single largest limiting factor in sub-Hz isolation

---

## 4. Laser Frequency and Intensity Noise

### 4.1 Pre-Stabilized Laser (PSL) Upgrade

**Specific upgrades:**
- **Reference cavity:** Replace current 20 cm ULE spacer with a **cryogenic silicon cavity (L = 21 cm, operated at 124 K)** — thermal noise floor σ_y ~ 4×10⁻¹⁷, vs. ~10⁻¹⁵ for room-temperature ULE
  - Requires vibration-isolated cryostat: 4 K pulse-tube cooler + multi-stage thermal shields
  - Cavity mounts at **vibration-insensitive point** (measured with FEA to have ∂f/∂deformation = 0 at support points)
- **Laser linewidth:** PDH-locked to cryogenic cavity → free-running linewidth < 10 mHz over 1 s
- **Intensity stabilization:** In-loop photodiode + AOM feedback, achieving **RIN < 2×10⁻⁹/√Hz** above 10 Hz; implement **out-of-loop monitor** (balanced homodyne detection) to verify and suppress loop gain limitations

---

## 5. Stray Light and Scattered Light Control

Often underestimated as a performance limiter.

**Specific upgrades:**
- **Optical baffles:** Replace current conical aluminum baffles with **deep-groove silicon carbide (SiC) baffles** machined with sawtooth profile (pitch 200 µm, depth 300 µm) — reduces forward-scatter by ~40 dB vs. polished aluminum
- **Viewport covers:** All viewports with direct line-of-sight to beam path enclosed with **vibration-isolated beam dumps** (zerodur + carbon-loaded PEEK absorber)
- **End station enclosures:** Acoustic panels (mass-spring barrier, STL > 60 dB at 100 Hz) around HAM and BSC chambers to reduce microseism-driven chamber motion coupling to intracavity fields via scatter

---

## 6. Prioritized Implementation Roadmap

| Priority | Upgrade | Frequency Band Addressed | Estimated Sensitivity Gain |
|----------|---------|--------------------------|----------------------------|
| 1 | Frequency-dependent squeezing (filter cavity) | 10 Hz – 5 kHz | 2–3× broadband range |
| 2 | AlGaAs crystalline coatings | 30–300 Hz | 2–4× at 100 Hz |
| 3 | Newtonian noise cancellation array | 5–20 Hz | Opens new band entirely |
| 4 | Cryogenic silicon test masses + suspension | 5–200 Hz | 5–10× in band |
| 5 | Cryogenic laser reference cavity | 10 Hz – 1 kHz | Removes current frequency noise floor |
| 6 | Advanced 6-DOF tilt-corrected isolation | 1–20 Hz | 3–10× below 10 Hz |

---

## Critical Cross-Cutting Issue: Parametric Instabilities

Higher circulating power excites optomechanical parametric instabilities (three-mode interactions between carrier, sideband, and mechanical modes). Hardware mitigation:
- **Acoustic mode dampers (AMDs):** Gold/niobium rings bonded to barrel of test mass with silicate bond, targeting modes 15–80 kHz (must not increase suspension point loss)
- **Electrostatic drive (ESD) ring electrode** at penultimate mass: apply resonant RF drive to damp individual mechanical modes with measured Q × φ product
- Both approaches demonstrated at Advanced LIGO; must be redesigned for mass scaling and cryogenic operation

---

## Summary

The highest-leverage near-term upgrade is **frequency-dependent squeezing via a filter cavity** (already installed at LIGO). The next tier is **crystalline AlGaAs coatings** for thermal noise, combined with **seismometer-array Newtonian noise cancellation** to open the 5–20 Hz band. The transformational long-term upgrade is the **cryogenic silicon platform** (1550 nm laser, Si test masses, Si fibers at 123 K), which is the architecture of proposed Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer low-frequency detectors, and addresses simultaneously quantum noise, thermal noise, and suspension noise with a single coherent redesign.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for LUX: Specific Proposals

## 1. PMT Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Current limitation:** The R8778 PMTs contribute the dominant background (437±37 µDRUee, ~88 events/100kg/300 days before cuts), have only 33% QE at 175nm, and each contributes measurable U/Th/K/Co-60 radioactivity.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace 122 PMTs with tiled arrays of Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) or Hamamatsu VUV4 SiPMs, specifically their low-radioactivity variants with demonstrated sensitivity at 175nm
- SiPM tiles (e.g., 6×6mm cells tiled into ~6cm modules) can achieve 40-50% photon detection efficiency at LXe wavelengths versus 33%×90% = ~30% effective efficiency for R8778
- Critical specification: require <0.1 mBq/kg for U/Th, achievable with high-purity silicon substrates - roughly 100× reduction in radioactive background per unit photosensitive area compared to Table 2 values
- Use cryogenic ASIC readout (e.g., CUBE or similar) integrated directly onto SiPM boards to eliminate the long coaxial cable runs that currently cause ~25% pulse height reduction
- This simultaneously improves light collection (better S1 threshold), reduces dominant background source, and enables finer position reconstruction granularity

## 2. Redesigned Field Cage with Lower-Background Resistor Chain

**Current limitation:** The 1GΩ resistor chain connecting field rings operates passively without active compensation; the PTFE/UHMWPE structural components introduce dielectric charging effects; the cathode HV cable routed through xenon gas creates a purification burden requiring 0.1 SLPM dedicated purge flow.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace passive resistor divider chain with individual Cockcroft-Walton voltage multiplier stages using low-radioactivity ceramic capacitors and thin-film resistors on Cirlex boards, allowing active field uniformity adjustment without mechanical access
- Implement the cathode HV feedthrough in cold xenon-compatible coaxial geometry using PTFE-insulated cable with graded resistivity termination (similar to EXO-200 approach), eliminating the warm feedthrough outside the water shield and removing the 0.1 SLPM purge requirement that represents a circulation inefficiency
- Replace UHMWPE structural panels with ultra-pure fused silica or sapphire rods as field ring spacers, which have lower intrinsic radioactivity and eliminate electrostatic charging that distorts drift fields

## 3. Upgraded Electron Extraction Region

**Current limitation:** The anode mesh has only 88% transparency (versus 96-99% for strung grids), a 130µm deflection at operating field, and the 1cm gate-anode gap limits electroluminescence gain. Single-phase heat exchanger geometry constrains liquid surface uniformity.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace woven mesh anode with a photolithographically etched titanium (CP1 grade, consistent with existing low-background cryostat material) grid using 20µm wire equivalents on 200µm pitch, achieving >97% transparency while maintaining flatness to <20µm under tension - this directly improves S2 photon yield per extracted electron
- Implement an active liquid level control system using piezoelectric actuators on three leveling points with closed-loop feedback from the parallel-plate level sensors (already installed), targeting ±50µm level uniformity versus current ±250µm - this directly reduces S2 width variation that currently limits position reconstruction at the liquid surface
- Increase gate-anode gap from 1cm to 1.5cm at the same 10kV/cm field (requiring 15kV rather than 10kV on the anode) to increase electroluminescence photon yield by ~50%, directly improving S2/S1 discrimination at low energies near threshold

## 4. Enhanced Internal Calibration System

**Current limitation:** The 83mKr system provides spatial calibration but its 1.86-hour half-life creates operational dead time; the external source tubes attenuate flux through water and cannot illuminate the full fiducial volume uniformly; tritiated methane removal efficiency of 99.9% per pass means residual tritium requires multiple circulation cycles.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Install a 220Rn (thoron) injection system using a dedicated 228Th source in a small emanation chamber connected to the xenon circulation line - thoron's 55.6-second half-life means it distributes uniformly throughout the active volume before decaying, providing both spatial calibration and electron recoil band mapping without long-lived contamination, requiring only a pneumatically operated bypass valve
- Add a deuterium-deuterium (DD) neutron generator (e.g., Adelphi Technology DD109) mounted on one of the existing external source tube positions, producing 2.45 MeV neutrons for nuclear recoil band calibration - this replaces reliance on AmBe or 252Cf sources whose broad neutron spectra complicate yield extraction, and the DD generator can be gated for coincidence measurements
- Incorporate fiber-coupled UV LEDs (175nm capable, e.g., using AlGaN deep-UV devices) routed through existing feedthroughs to illuminate the photocathode region directly, enabling in-situ absolute QE monitoring of each PMT/SiPM independently during operation

## 5. Cryogenics and Purification Upgrades

**Current limitation:** The thermosyphon system achieves ~55 kW/K/m thermal conductivity but requires external LN2 dewars with manual refilling; the getter circulation was limited to 300 kg/day during surface operations; the purity assay system requires discrete 0.5L sample collection.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace external LN2 bath condensers with a pair of Cryomech PT90 pulse tube refrigerators (90W at 77K each), providing 180W total cooling capacity without consumable LN2, enabling fully autonomous operation for extended underground runs - this eliminates the correlated background risk from LN2 delivery interruptions and removes ~2 personnel-visits/week for dewar exchange
- Add a second SAES MonoTorr getter in parallel with independent pump, allowing one getter to be regenerated while the other maintains continuous purification - current design requires full circulation stop for getter regeneration, causing electron lifetime degradation detectable as position-dependent S2 yield variation
- Install an inline cold-trap krypton removal system (activated charcoal at 190K with automated temperature cycling) upstream of the existing getter, targeting Kr/Xe below 1 part-per-trillion - the paper's Table 3 shows 85Kr contributes up to 0.13 WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days, and online removal eliminates dependence on pre-purified xenon procurement
- Implement continuous inline xenon purity monitoring using a small (10cc) electron drift monitor with its own UV LED source and SiPM detector, providing real-time electron lifetime measurement with ~1-minute time resolution rather than the discrete sampling approach currently described

## 6. Data Acquisition Modernization

**Current limitation:** The Struck SIS3301 ADCs digitize at 100MHz/14-bit with 128k sample buffers; the trigger system requires analog summing into 16 PMT groups before digital processing, losing single-PMT hit pattern information at trigger level; POD mode requires hardware threshold setting that may introduce trigger bias near threshold.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace SIS3301 with SIS3316 (250MHz/14-bit) or equivalent, doubling the sampling rate to better resolve pile-up in high S2 events and improving S1 pulse shape discrimination - the current 10ns sampling period limits separation of multiple S1 photon clusters in the bottom array that constrain fiducial volume definition
- Implement FPGA-based trigger directly on digitizer boards using the full per-channel waveform, eliminating the analog PMT summing stage (LeCroy 628 fan-ins) that currently reduces single-PMT spatial information available at trigger decision time - modern Xilinx Ultrascale FPGAs can implement real-time neural network inference for S1/S2 classification within the required <1µs trigger latency
- Add a dedicated 500MHz oscilloscope channel (one per quadrant) continuously recording summed signals for afterpulsing and spurious emission monitoring without interrupting the main DAQ stream

These upgrades prioritize the three dominant performance limiters identified in the paper: PMT radioactivity (background), light collection efficiency (threshold and discrimination), and electron lifetime stability (fiducial volume definition).

# Hardware Design Upgrades for ProtoDUNE-SP

## Preamble: Identifying the Primary Physics Bottlenecks

Before proposing upgrades, the actual performance limitations described in the paper must be identified precisely:

1. **Photon detection efficiency is severely limited** (0.08% for dip-coated, 0.21% for double-shift, 2% for ARAPUCA)
2. **HV instabilities** cause ~2-4% dead-time even with auto-recovery, tied to insulator charging in high-purity LAr
3. **Cold electronics noise floor** is limited by the ADC ASIC design and wire capacitance
4. **Single-phase charge readout** has inherent electron attachment losses over 3.6 m drift
5. **No wire-level hit finding in firmware** during the beam run, limiting self-triggering

---

## Upgrade 1: Full ARAPUCA-Based Photon Detection System

### Motivation
The paper explicitly states ARAPUCA achieves 2% photon detection efficiency versus 0.08-0.21% for light guides — roughly a factor 10-25 improvement. An extrapolation cited in the paper predicts 1.9 photons/MeV at 3.3 m drift distance with an all-ARAPUCA system, nearly 4× the DUNE specification. The dip-coated and double-shift modules are demonstrably inferior and consume identical mechanical slots.

### Specific Hardware Changes

**Replace all 60 PD modules with X-ARAPUCA supercells:**
- The X-ARAPUCA design (not yet deployed in ProtoDUNE-SP but under development within DUNE at time of writing) expands the dichroic filter acceptance window by tiling multiple filter-reflector cells across the full 209.7 cm bar length rather than using a single small cell
- Target active area per module: increase from 1223 cm² (single ARAPUCA cell) toward the full 1744 cm² available (matching light guide active area)
- Use Hamamatsu S13360-6050VE Through-Silicon-Via MPPCs exclusively, as their reduced dead-space perimeter improves packing fraction within each cell
- Increase the number of SiPM channels per ARAPUCA bar from the current configuration to 24 MPPCs per bar (12 per side), reducing passive ganging from groups of 3-4 down to pairs, thereby improving single-photon resolution and reducing correlated noise from ganging capacitance mismatch

**Dichroic filter improvements:**
- Replace the 400 nm cutoff Omega Optical filters with custom filters optimized to a 420 nm cutoff, better matched to the TPB emission peak at 425 nm and reducing re-absorption losses in the internal reflection path
- Apply PTP at 250 μg/cm² (increased from 200 μg/cm²) on external faces to improve VUV-to-350 nm conversion efficiency, based on laboratory measurements showing yield saturation above this density

**Internal reflector upgrade:**
- Replace VIKUITI 3M specular reflector with enhanced specular reflector (ESR) film laminated with a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) diffuse backing layer (combined reflectivity >99.5% at 430 nm versus ~98% for VIKUITI alone), reducing absorption probability per bounce from ~2% to ~0.5%, which substantially improves trapping efficiency for photons requiring many reflections before reaching a SiPM

**Cryogenic SiPM bias electronics:**
- Move from passive ganging with warm-side SSP bias to active cold-side transimpedance preamplifiers mounted on the ARAPUCA PCB inside the LAr
- Use SiGe BJT-based amplifier circuits (e.g., BFP740 or equivalent cryogenic-qualified SiGe device), which maintain gain and noise figure at 87 K unlike standard CMOS analog circuits
- This eliminates the 20 m Cat6 cable capacitance that currently degrades signal rise time and SNR before the SSP, reducing effective input capacitance from ~400 pF to ~10 pF
- Power dissipation budget: ~5 mW per bar, totaling 300 mW for 60 bars — acceptable within the cryostat heat load budget given the 10,500 W total measured heat load

---

## Upgrade 2: Resistive Field Cage to Suppress HV Instabilities

### Motivation
The paper documents a well-characterized instability mechanism: charge accumulates on FRP insulating support structures of the FC in high-purity LAr (where electronegative impurity quenching is absent), producing streamers localized consistently at GP#6. The paper notes the streamer rate increased when auto-recovery prevented full discharge, and decreased dramatically when streamers were allowed to self-quench. This is a classic electrostatic charging problem on insulating surfaces in a high-field, high-purity dielectric medium.

### Specific Hardware Changes

**Replace FRP FC support beams with resistive surface-coated supports:**
- Coat all FRP I-beam and box-beam surfaces facing the drift volume with a thin (50-100 μm) layer of carbon-loaded polyimide paint targeting a sheet resistance of 10⁹–10¹¹ Ω/square
- This surface resistivity is high enough to avoid significant power dissipation (~μW per beam) but low enough that accumulated surface charge drains on a timescale of seconds to minutes rather than hours to days, preventing the buildup that initiates streamers
- The specific resistivity target must avoid being so low that it creates a parallel current path competing with the resistive divider chains (which are at 0.5 GΩ per stage)

**Replace aluminum extruded FC profiles with resistive aluminum-kapton composite profiles:**
- Current aluminum profiles have sharp ends addressed only by UHMWPE caps; the caps themselves accumulate charge
- Machine UHMWPE endcaps with embedded resistive carbon-loaded PEEK inserts that provide a ~100 GΩ path from the profile tip to the adjacent profile, preventing tip charge accumulation while maintaining the required >30 kV/cm field limit at profile edges

**Ground plane redesign:**
- GP#6 (upper upstream) is consistently identified as the discharge site. Replace the perforated stainless steel GP panels adjacent to this region with resistive steel mesh (carbon-loaded stainless, ~10⁴ Ω/square) that provides distributed leakage paths, preventing localized charge accumulation while still providing adequate field shielding
- Add dedicated surface resistivity monitoring: instrument 4 GP panels with embedded current-sensing resistors (1 GΩ, Vishay VHV series, rated to 300 V) connected to the DCS, enabling real-time detection of surface charging before streamers initiate

**HV filter upgrade:**
- Replace the existing RC filter with a cascaded LC filter (3-stage, with inductors wound on ferrite cores rated for 300 kV isolation) that more aggressively attenuates the 30 kHz power supply ripple noted in the paper
- Add a large-value (10 GΩ) bleed resistor directly at the CPA HV cup to ensure complete discharge of the cathode within minutes of HV-off events, preventing the long recharging transient that currently causes the streamer rate to restart from zero after each HV-off period

---

## Upgrade 3: Cold ADC ASIC Replacement with Higher Dynamic Range Design

### Motivation
The paper states the current ADC ASIC provides 12-bit digitization at up to 2 MS/s, with measured ENC of ~400 e⁻ at cryogenic temperature. The collection wire signal from a MIP is ~10,000 e⁻, giving SNR ~25 at 87 K. However, highly ionizing particles (protons, stopping hadrons) can deposit 50-100× more charge, saturating the 12-bit ADC at the 25 mV/fC gain setting. Simultaneously, the induction plane signals from long-range wires have lower SNR and benefit from lower noise.

### Specific Hardware Changes

**New FE ASIC with dual-gain architecture:**
- Implement a 16-channel FE ASIC in 130 nm CMOS (smaller node than current 180 nm, maintaining decade-long commercial availability) with two simultaneous gain paths per channel: high-gain (25 mV/fC, as currently) and low-gain (1.5 mV/fC), providing an effective dynamic range of ~16 effective bits
- Both paths share the input charge amplifier; a passive resistive divider after the first amplification stage feeds the low-gain shaper, adding no noise
- Power dissipation target: 8 mW/channel (marginal increase from 6 mW), manageable within the FEMB thermal budget

**New ADC ASIC with 14-bit resolution at 2 MS/s:**
- Current 12-bit ADC limits the noise floor at LSB level to ~2.5 mV, which at 14 mV/fC gain corresponds to ~180 e⁻ per LSB — comparable to the 400 e⁻ ENC, meaning ~40% of noise events are quantization-limited rather than analog-limited
- A 14-bit ADC (4× finer quantization) reduces the quantization noise contribution to ~45 e⁻ LSB, making it negligible relative to analog ENC
- Implement in the same 130 nm CMOS process as the FE ASIC; demonstrated 14-bit SAR ADC architectures in 130 nm achieve <5 mW/channel at 2 MS/s

**FEMB data bandwidth upgrade:**
- The dual-gain architecture doubles the data per channel (two ADC streams), requiring FEMB output bandwidth to increase from ~5 Gbps to ~10 Gbps per FEMB
- Replace the current FPGA mezzanine with a Xilinx Kintex-7 or equivalent device supporting 10.3125 Gbps GTX transceivers; the Kintex-7 has demonstrated cryogenic operation in independent studies
- Update the cold cable specification from current multi-conductor to a shielded twin-axial cable (100 Ω differential) rated for repeated thermal cycling between 300 K and 87 K without jacket embrittlement (use PTFE jacket with SiO₂-filled compound)

---

## Upgrade 4: Wire-Level FPGA-Based Hit Finding on FEMBs

### Motivation
The paper describes the self-triggering demonstration during the 2019 run as requiring a full dedicated server per APA for hit-finding in software on raw waveforms received from FELIX. This is computationally expensive and imposes latency. The paper notes FPGA-based hit-finding is "under study." Moving this function onto the FEMB FPGA in cold eliminates the warm-side server entirely and reduces trigger latency from ~milliseconds to ~microseconds.

### Specific Hardware Changes

**Enhanced FPGA mezzanine with dedicated DSP resources:**
- Replace the current FPGA mezzanine (which primarily performs MUX and serial driver functions) with a mezzanine carrying a Xilinx Artix-7 200T or equivalent device with 740 DSP48E1 slices
- Implement a 128-channel real-time FIR matched filter (matched to the expected MIP bipolar induction or unipolar collection waveform shape) in DSP slices, consuming ~4 DSP slices per channel (512 total for 128 channels), well within the 740 available
- The matched filter output is compared against a configurable threshold; hits above threshold generate a compact primitive message (channel number, timestamp, amplitude, integral) of ~8 bytes transmitted upstream on a dedicated low-latency control fiber separate from the data fiber

**Fiber plant addition:**
- Add one dedicated 1 Gbps optical fiber per FEMB (20 per APA, 120 total for 6 APAs) for trigger primitive transmission to the CTB, using SFP modules operating at 87 K — standard 850 nm VCSEL-based SFPs have been demonstrated to operate at 77 K with modest power derating

**CTB upgrade for primitive processing:**
- Upgrade the CTB from the current MicroZed/Zynq7020 to a Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC, providing 4× the DSP resources and a dedicated real-time processing unit
- Implement coincidence logic across all 120 FEMB primitive streams to form track candidates within a configurable time window (1-10 μs), enabling topology-based triggering (e.g., requiring hits spanning >50 cm in the drift direction) that rejects isolated noise hits

---

## Upgrade 5: Purity Monitor Expansion into the TPC Volume

### Motivation
The paper explicitly states purity monitors "are placed inside the cryostat but outside of the TPC volume due to their size" and that "purity monitors have much smaller volumes than the LArTPC" making them less affected by space charge. However, the three monitors at fixed heights (1.8, 3.7, 5.6 m) cannot resolve horizontal purity gradients revealed by the temperature sensor data (Figure 61 shows a 20 mK temperature peak below the cathode plane with gradients toward the recirculation pump). Since purity and temperature are related through the LAr flow field, horizontal purity non-uniformity is expected but currently unmeasured.

### Specific Hardware Changes

**Miniaturized fiber-optic purity monitors:**
- Develop a purity monitor with a 5 cm cathode-to-anode gap (versus the current ~35-150 μs drift time design) using a xenon flash lamp source at 172 nm (Hamamatsu L11035) delivered via 10 m long optical fiber
- At 500 V/cm (matching the TPC field), the 5 cm gap gives a 33 μs drift time, sufficient for lifetime measurements down to ~100 μs (corresponding to ~15 ppt O₂ equivalent — more than adequate for DUNE purity requirements)
- The entire monitor can be constructed within a 2 cm diameter × 10 cm length stainless steel tube, small enough to be installed at multiple locations within the FC volume by mounting on FC profile supports via a non-conductive FR4 bracket

**Array deployment:**
- Install 9 miniaturized monitors in a 3×3 grid pattern (3 horizontal positions × 3 vertical heights) within the active volume, mounted on endwall FC support beams where they introduce minimal field distortion
- Each monitor requires only a 2-fiber feedthrough (illumination in, no signal fiber needed — signal is read from an anode wire connected to a dedicated charge-sensitive amplifier on the FEMB) and a 2-wire HV connection sharing the existing FC termination flange

---

## Summary and Expected Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Quantified Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| Full X-ARAPUCA PDS | Light yield and timing | ~10× photon yield; approach 20 PE/MeV |
| Resistive FC surfaces | HV stability | Eliminate streamers; increase uptime from 96% toward >99.5% |
| 14-bit dual-gain ADC | Dynamic range and noise | 4× quantization improvement; 50× dynamic range increase |
| FEMB hit-finding | Self-trigger latency | Reduce from ~ms to ~μs; eliminate dedicated trigger servers |
| In-volume purity monitors | Calibration fidelity | Resolve 3D purity maps; eliminate spatial calibration uncertainty |

These upgrades are mutually compatible and address the distinct subsystem bottlenecks explicitly documented in the paper's operational experience, rather than speculative limitations. Each builds directly on hardware already proven in ProtoDUNE-SP, making them realistic for a Phase II deployment in the same cryostat.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a 770-tonne Single-Phase LArTPC Prototype

## Context and Baseline Assessment

This instrument corresponds closely to the ProtoDUNE-SP (Single-Phase) detector at CERN. The primary physics performance metrics are: **charge collection efficiency, spatial resolution, calorimetric energy resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and neutrino interaction reconstruction fidelity**. I'll address each subsystem with specific, concrete upgrade proposals ranked by physics impact.

---

## 1. Photon Detection System (Highest Priority)

### Current Limitation
The dip-coated light-guide (ARAPUCA-style bars) embedded in the anode plane cathode gaps suffer from:
- Limited geometric coverage (~2–4% of cathode area)
- TPB (tetraphenyl butadiene) coating degradation over time
- Photon detection efficiency (PDE) of ~0.5–1% for bulk events
- Poor timing resolution for long drift distances (>3 m)

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Replace light-guide bars with X-ARAPUCA modules (immediate, validated technology)**
- X-ARAPUCA (expanded ARAPUCA) uses a dichroic filter cavity trapping mechanism with TPB-coated wavelength-shifting plates and SiPM tiles (Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or equivalent)
- Achieved PDE >3% in SBND deployment; target >5% for optimized geometry
- Replace existing dip-coated bars with 48-cell X-ARAPUCA supercells per APA frame
- Specific component: **Hamamatsu S14160-6050HS SiPMs** (6mm × 6mm, PDE ~50% at 450 nm, low dark count rate at LAr temperatures ~87K) in 4×4 tile arrays per cell

**B. Supplement cathode plane with DUNE-FD2 HD-style cathode-mounted ARAPUCA arrays**
- Embed X-ARAPUCA modules directly in the cathode plane (CPA), increasing solid angle coverage to ~15–20% total
- CPA-mounted modules require HV-isolated feedthroughs; use **ceramic-glass hermetic connectors** rated to 180 kV
- Doubles the light yield for fiducial volume events, critical for supernova neutrino triggering

**C. Replace TPB dip-coating with vacuum-deposited pTP (para-terphenyl) films**
- Physical vapor deposition of pTP at 200–400 nm thickness on polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) wavelength-shifting foils
- PEN itself has intrinsic VUV-to-visible conversion efficiency ~85% of TPB with superior long-term stability
- Supplier: **vacuum deposition through custom PVD systems (Kurt J. Lesker PVD 75)** or commercial foil from Eljen Technology (EJ-286 base material)
- Eliminates coating delamination failures observed after thermal cycling

**D. Upgrade SiPM cold electronics**
- Replace existing amplifier ASICs with **DUNE's SiPM Signal Processor (SSP) module upgrade using Struck SIS3316 ADC** at 250 MSa/s, 14-bit
- Alternatively, deploy **LArASIC-based cryogenic front-end** adapted for SiPM (trans-impedance input stage, optimized for 50 ns SiPM pulse widths)
- Target: sub-nanosecond t₀ resolution for >50 photoelectrons, enabling drift velocity corrections and cosmogenic rejection

---

## 2. Wire Readout / Charge Collection System

### Current Limitation
- Cold electronics noise: ~650 ENC (equivalent noise charge) at operating conditions using existing LArASIC v3
- Wire tension uniformity causes ~3–5% of wires with degraded SNR
- 4.67 mm wire pitch limits dE/dx resolution for low-energy tracks

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Deploy LArASIC v4 / COLDATA-integrated front-end**
- **LArASIC v4** (developed at BNL) achieves ~400 ENC at 300 pF detector capacitance, down from ~650 ENC
- Integrate with **COLDDATA serializer ASIC** for 1.28 Gbps cold-to-warm serial link, reducing feedthrough pin count by 4×
- Full cold digital chain: LArASIC → ColdADC (12-bit, 2 MSa/s) → COLDATA → warm FELIX readout
- This combination is already baseline for DUNE FD1 but not fully deployed in the prototype; retrofitting is straightforward

**B. Replace outermost induction plane (U-plane) wires with pixel readout pads (LArPix)**
- **LArPix v2b** (LBNL): 4.434 mm pitch pixelated charge readout tiles, eliminates wire ambiguities in multi-track events
- Each tile: 100 channels, cryogenic UART/SPI communication, power dissipation <0.5 mW/channel
- Deploy 2 full APA panels with LArPix tiles as the induction layer while keeping collection wires
- Eliminates the fundamental hit disambiguation problem for complex topologies (π⁰ → γγ, multi-prong vertices)
- Physics impact: improves vertex activity reconstruction efficiency by estimated 30–40% based on ArgonCube studies

**C. Wire tension monitoring and active correction**
- Install **piezoelectric wire tension sensors** (custom fabricated on APA frames) during construction
- Monitor wire resonant frequency continuously; identify wires with tension <0.5 N (below design spec of 0.7 N)
- For next prototype build: replace 316 LVM stainless steel wire with **beryllium-copper (BeCu) alloy wire** (0.152 mm diameter), which provides 20% higher yield strength and better tension retention at cryogenic temperatures
- Supplier: **California Fine Wire Company**, BeCu alloy C17200

**D. Longer drift distance with HV system upgrade**
- Current cathode HV: −180 kV, drift field 500 V/cm, drift distance 3.6 m
- Upgrade to **Heinzinger PNC 300000-1 neg power supply** capable of −300 kV with < 10 ppm ripple
- Extend cathode to achieve 5 m drift at 500 V/cm, increasing fiducial mass by ~25% without changing cryostat
- Requires upgraded HV feedthrough: replace current resistive-divider feedthrough with **oil-filled coaxial feedthrough** from Precision High Voltage (PHV) rated to 350 kV in LAr-adjacent service

---

## 3. Data Acquisition and Trigger System

### Current Limitation
- Triggerless/self-triggered readout limited by noise floor; missing low-energy Michel electrons and sub-GeV π⁰ events
- Photon detection latency causes ~100 ns timing jitter on event t₀

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. FELIX + ATCA-based readout with real-time FPGA processing**
- Deploy **FELIX (Front-End LInk eXchange) PCIe cards** (ATLAS/DUNE standard) with Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ FPGA
- Implement online **hit-finding and clustering in FPGA firmware** (currently done offline) to reduce data volume by 10× before host CPU
- Use **RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access)** over 100 GbE for lossless transfer to GPU processing farm

**B. GPU-accelerated online reconstruction for trigger primitive generation**
- Deploy **NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs** (4 units) running WireCell Toolkit in online mode
- Enable real-time 3D trajectory reconstruction for trigger decisions on Michel electrons (threshold ~20 MeV)
- Expected: reduce trigger threshold from ~100 MeV to ~15 MeV hadronic equivalent energy

**C. Precision timing with White Rabbit protocol**
- Replace current GPS-disciplined timing with **White Rabbit PTP nodes** (CERN Open Hardware Repository WR-LEN)
- Achieves <1 ns synchronization across all readout nodes
- Critical for matching TPC charge signal timing to photon detection t₀ and external beam instrumentation

---

## 4. Cryogenic and Purity System

### Current Limitation
- Electron lifetime typically 3–10 ms; at 500 V/cm drift velocity (~1.6 mm/μs), electrons crossing the full 3.6 m drift lose signal
- Residual electronegative impurities (O₂, H₂O at sub-ppb level) are primary limitation

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Active recirculation upgrade with dual-column purification**
- Install a second molecular sieve + Oxysorb purifier column (**BASF R3-11G catalyst** for O₂ removal, **Sigma-Aldrich 3Å molecular sieve** for H₂O) operating in parallel/series with existing column
- Double the LAr recirculation flow rate from ~3 kg/s to ~6 kg/s; target electron lifetime >20 ms
- Add **Hydranautics SWC5-4040 membrane filter** upstream of purifier to remove particulates that degrade catalyst performance

**B. In-situ purity monitoring with high-precision purity monitors**
- Deploy 3 additional **Brookhaven-style alpha-source purity monitors** (⁲⁴¹Am source, 5.49 MeV α) at different heights spanning the full drift volume
- Existing monitors provide single-point measurements; spatial array maps O₂ contamination gradients from outgassing
- Add **laser-based Rayleigh scattering purity monitor** (266 nm Nd:YAG, 5 ns pulses) for independent cross-check

**C. Space charge mitigation via UV laser calibration system**
- Deploy **UV laser calibration system** (266 nm, 150 mJ/pulse, Quantel Ultra CFR Nd:YAG) with steerable mirror system (4 injection ports)
- Generates straight, known-topology ionization tracks throughout the fiducial volume
- Maps space charge distortions from positive ion accumulation (dominant systematic in surface detectors with high cosmic rate)
- Used to derive **3D distortion correction maps** applied in reconstruction; demonstrated in MicroBooNE to correct >3 cm spatial distortions

---

## 5. Beam Instrumentation Interface

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Upgrade beam plug with precision TOF system**
- Install **Cherenkov threshold counters** with **Microchannel Plate PMTs** (Photonis PP0365G, 25 ps transit time spread) for beam particle identification
- Provides kaon/pion/proton separation at 1–7 GeV/c for cleaner neutrino interaction mode tagging

**B. Secondary vertex tagging with embedded silicon strip detectors**
- Place **thin silicon microstrip modules** (300 μm thick, 50 μm pitch, Hamamatsu HPK S12571-050C reticle) immediately upstream of the TPC face
- Tags μ → e decay vertices and secondary interaction points with ~50 μm resolution, complementing TPC spatial resolution

|---|---|---|---|
| X-ARAPUCA module replacement | Very High | Medium | 1 |
| LArASIC v4 + COLDATA cold chain | High | Medium | 2 |
| UV laser space charge mapping | High | Medium | 3 |

## Most Impactful Single Upgrade

**The X-ARAPUCA photon detector replacement is the highest-leverage single intervention.** The current light-guide system's ~0.5% PDE is the dominant limitation on: (1) t₀ determination for non-beam events, (2) low-energy neutrino detection efficiency, (3) supernova burst sensitivity, and (4) cosmogenic background rejection through timing. Swapping to X-ARAPUCA supercells with Hamamatsu S14160 SiPMs and PEN wavelength-shifting foils can achieve a genuine 5–10× improvement in detected photon yield with components that are commercially available and cryogenically validated, without requiring cryostat modifications.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Cubic-Kilometre Ice Cherenkov Neutrino Observatory

## Framing: What "Primary Physics Performance" Means Here

The key figures of merit are: **angular resolution** (pointing precision for multimessenger astronomy), **energy resolution and range** (from ~1 GeV to >10 PeV), **flavor identification** (νe/νμ/ντ separation), **background rejection** (muon bundle and atmospheric neutrino suppression), and **vertex resolution** (cascade containment). I address each through concrete hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Replace Single-PMT DOMs with Multi-PMT Optical Modules

### Current Limitation
A single large-area (10") PMT per DOM has no directional sensitivity, limited dynamic range, and poor rejection of dark noise and after-pulsing.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Deploy multi-PMT modules modeled on and improving beyond KM3NeT's DOM design**, but with specific enhancements:

- **24–36 × 3" Hamamatsu R14374 or SensL/OnSemi J-series SiPM-coupled small PMTs** arranged in ~4π coverage per pressure vessel
- Each sub-PMT individually digitized at the module level
- Achieves **local photon direction reconstruction** within a single module (±15° directional sensitivity per hit cluster)
- **Dynamic range improvement**: single photoelectron to ~10³ PE without saturation by coincidence logic across sub-PMTs
- **Cross-coincidence within DOM** eliminates the dominant dark noise source: require 2+ sub-PMTs within a narrow time window (~10 ns) as a valid hit — suppresses noise by factor ~100 without efficiency loss for signal

**Specific component**: Hamamatsu R12199-02 3" PMTs (already characterized for low temperature ~−40°C operation) with **individual HV bases using DC-DC converters per channel** embedded in the base electronics board.

---

## 2. Replace PMTs with Large-Area SiPMs (or SiPM Arrays)

### Current Limitation
PMTs have ~25% peak quantum efficiency, are sensitive to the local magnetic field (Earth's field at depth causes ~10–15% efficiency loss requiring μ-metal shielding), have 50–100 ns transit-time spread jitter, and cannot be densely packed.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Tile the DOM inner surface with SiPM arrays**:

- **Hamamatsu S13361-6075 series** (6×6 mm² cells, 50 μm microcell pitch, ~50% PDE at 420 nm peaking near ice Cherenkov emission)
- Array ~600 cm² total active area per DOM (matching 10" PMT) using ~260 individual 6×6 mm tiles
- **Single-photon timing resolution: <200 ps FWHM** vs. ~2 ns for standard PMTs — directly improves angular resolution
- Eliminates magnetic field sensitivity entirely
- Operates reliably at ice temperatures (−40°C) with reduced dark count rate (~10× lower than room temperature)
- No high voltage (operate at 25–27V bias)

**Critical engineering challenge**: SiPM dark noise rate (~100 kHz/mm² at room temperature, ~1 kHz/mm² at −40°C) means ~0.6 GHz total for 600 cm²; mitigated by the coincidence requirement above and on-module FPGA zero-suppression.

**Readout ASIC**: Use or adapt the **TARGET ASIC** (developed for CTA) or **MUSIC** (Multi-channel Integrated Circuit) providing 16-channel analog buffering with 1 GHz sampling before trigger decision.

---

## 3. Precision Timing Architecture Upgrade

### Current Limitation
IceCube's RAPCal (Reciprocal Active Pulsing Calibration) achieves ~3 ns absolute timing across the array. Angular resolution for through-going muons is already ~0.3°–0.5° but is ultimately limited by photon scattering in ice (~25 m scattering length) **and** residual timing systematics.

### Proposed Upgrade

#### a) White Rabbit Ethernet Timing
- Replace RAPCal with **White Rabbit PTP (Precision Time Protocol)** implementation using **SPEC (Simple PCIe FMC Carrier)** boards at surface and embedded WR nodes per string
- Achieves **<1 ns absolute synchronization** deterministically across the array
- WR is proven at km-scale (used at KM3NeT)
- Requires replacing in-ice communication from current copper twisted-pair with **single-mode fiber** (already present in IceCube but underutilized for timing)

#### b) Per-DOM GPS-Disciplined Local Oscillator
Not feasible in-ice directly, but a **surface White Rabbit grandmaster** disciplined by a **GPSDO (e.g., Trimble Resolution T)** achieving 10 ps RMS disciplining propagated down fiber achieves the goal.

#### c) In-DOM Waveform Digitization
- Replace ATWD (Analog Transient Waveform Digitizer, 300 MHz sampling) with **DRS4 chip** (Domino Ring Sampler, PSI) providing **5 GHz sampling, 1024 samples deep** per channel
- Timing precision on leading edge: **<50 ps** for bright pulses
- Enables sub-nanosecond photon arrival time extraction even within multi-PE hits

## 4. Increased String Density in a "Core" High-Energy/Starting-Event Subarray

### Current Limitation
IceCube's 125 m string spacing optimizes for ~100 GeV–PeV muon neutrinos but poorly contains cascades and cannot reconstruct sub-100 GeV events. The DeepCore infill (72 m spacing) partially addresses this.

### Proposed Upgrade: **Dense Core Array**

- Deploy a **~8 Mton fiducial subarray** with **20 m string spacing** and **3 m vertical DOM spacing** in the clearest ice region (below 2100 m, scattering length >50 m, absorption length >200 m)
- Occupying ~200 m × 200 m × 500 m volume: ~100 additional strings × 160 DOMs/string = 16,000 DOMs
- This provides:
  - **GeV-scale threshold** for atmospheric neutrino oscillation physics and supernova relic neutrino spectrum
  - **Contained vertex identification** for all-flavor neutrino cross-section measurements
  - **Tau neutrino detection** via "double cascade" topology when double-bang separation ≥ 20 m (achievable above ~1 PeV)

**Specific DOM for this core**: The multi-PMT design (point 1) is essential here; additionally deploy **"segmented" cascade DOMs** — pairs of upward- and downward-facing hemispheres independently triggerable to improve early-photon capture geometry.

## 5. Wavelength-Shifting and Light Collection Enhancement

### Current Limitation
Borosilicate glass pressure spheres absorb UV photons (<350 nm), and PMTs/SiPMs have poor response below 350 nm. Cherenkov emission spectrum peaks in the UV. Estimated 30–40% of Cherenkov photons are lost to glass absorption.

### Proposed Upgrade

#### a) UV-Transparent Pressure Vessels
- Replace borosilicate glass with **fused silica or UV-transmitting borosilicate (e.g., Schott 8337B or Vitrovex UV-grade)** pressure housings
- Transmission edge moves from ~340 nm down to **~200 nm**
- Recovers ~20–25% more Cherenkov photons in the 200–340 nm band
- Must be requalified to 700 bar pressure (2500 m depth): fused silica spheres have been prototyped; wall thickness increase of ~10% needed

#### b) Wavelength-Shifting Coatings
- Apply **p-Terphenyl (PTP) or bis-MSB** wavelength-shifting films (50–100 μm thick) to the inner pressure sphere surface
- Converts 250–350 nm photons to 420 nm (well within PMT/SiPM peak response)
- **Laboratory-demonstrated 20–30% Cherenkov light yield increase** in small-scale tests (analogous to DEAP-3600 approach)
- Thin-film deposition via spray-coating; stable at −40°C under radiation dose

#### c) Light Concentrators
- Add **compound parabolic concentrators (CPCs)** behind each SiPM or small-PMT element within the multi-PMT DOM
- Winston cone geometry, TiO₂-coated aluminum, acceptance half-angle matched to DOM port geometry
- Factor ~2–3 increase in effective area per sensor element with preserved angular response

---

## 6. Veto and Muon-Tagging Infrastructure

### Current Limitation
Cosmic-ray muon background is ~10⁶× the neutrino signal at trigger level. The existing IceTop surface array uses ice-Cherenkov tanks that are seasonally limited, have ~50% duty cycle in storms, and poor sensitivity to near-horizontal muon bundles.

### Proposed Upgrade

#### a) Scintillator + Radio Hybrid Surface Array
Replace/augment IceTop tanks with:
- **Scintillator panels**: 1.7 m² × 5 cm thick **EJ-200 plastic scintillator** tiles read out by **SiPM arrays** (Hamamatsu S14160 series) — temperature-stable, no liquid, ~100% duty cycle
- **SKALA-2 or similar log-periodic dipole antennas** for radio detection of cosmic-ray air showers (30–80 MHz Tunka-Rex / AERA band)
- Combined scintillator+radio provides **energy resolution ~10% and arrival direction ~0.1°** for cosmic rays above 10¹⁵ eV — sufficient to veto coincident in-ice muon bundles
- Array spacing: 50 m over IceCube footprint (~200 stations)

#### b) Near-Surface In-Ice Strings ("Veto Cap")
- Deploy 20 additional strings instrumented from 0–500 m depth (currently uninstrumented in IceCube) using **robust low-cost frozen-in sensors**: single SiPM + WLS fiber per module, ~2 m spacing
- Provides **hermetic veto** against downward-going muons entering the fiducial volume from the side and top with >99.9% efficiency for events above 10 TeV
- These strings can be deployed with a smaller hot-water drill (10 kW vs. 5 MW Enhanced Hot Water Drill) since only 500 m depth required

#### c) Peripheral Muon Tracker Strings
- 8 strings deployed at ~700 m radius from array center, sparsely instrumented (every 15 m) with **directional multi-PMT modules**
- Acts as an external muon track trigger providing **incoming muon direction before** it enters the main array
- Reduces through-going muon background by enabling precise prior on direction for contained vertex searches

---

## 7. Calibration Hardware Upgrades

### Current Limitation
IceCube uses LED flashers embedded in DOMs for in-situ calibration. These characterize scattering but have limited angular control and poor absolute intensity calibration.

### Proposed Upgrade

#### a) Isotropic Laser Calibration Balls
- Deploy **dedicated calibration modules** (not science DOMs) every 5th string: **diffuse-light laser balls** using **355 nm pulsed Nd:YAG laser (3rd harmonic)** with fiber delivery and integrating-sphere diffuser
- Pulse width <1 ns (mode-locked), power adjustable over 7 decades (single photon to saturation)
- Enables **precision ice model mapping** at <1% level — the dominant systematic on angular resolution
- Wavelength-tunable option: insert **OPO (optical parametric oscillator)** at surface, deliver tunable 300–600 nm light down fiber to in-ice diffuser

#### b) Precision Geometry Calibration
- **Acoustic positioning system**: embed **piezoelectric transducers** (e.g., custom 10–30 kHz broadband) in 20% of DOMs and 5 dedicated acoustic emitter modules per string
- Trilateration with <10 cm position accuracy (vs. current ~1 m from optical reconstruction)
- DOM positions are currently the **second-largest systematic** on angular resolution; 10 cm accuracy effectively eliminates this contribution

#### c) In-Situ Radioactive Sources
- Deploy **⁵⁷Co or ²⁴¹Am γ-sources** on retrectable cable within select boreholes (lowered post-freeze)
- Provides absolute photon-counting efficiency calibration independent of ice model assumptions
- Already prototyped for PINGU; requires minor deployment hardware (sealed source on Kevlar tether)

## 8. Data Acquisition and On-Ice Triggering

### Current Limitation
IceCube's surface DAQ runs software triggers on a CPU farm with ~6 μs latency. All data must be transmitted to the surface before trigger decision — limits trigger flexibility and volume of low-energy data retained.

### Proposed Upgrade

#### a) In-DOM FPGA-Based First-Level Processing
- Embed **Xilinx Artix-7 or Lattice ECP5 FPGA** in each DOM for:
  - Local coincidence trigger (require N≥2 sub-PMT coincidence within 10 ns)
  - On-the-fly waveform feature extraction (time-over-threshold, leading edge, integrated charge) rather than transmitting raw waveforms
  - Reduces per-DOM data rate from ~1 Mbps to ~10 kbps under normal conditions
  - Transmit full waveform only on global trigger request

#### b) String-Level Trigger FPGA Hub
- One **Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGA** per string (surface) aggregating all 60 DOM streams
- Implements **local cluster trigger** (nearest-neighbor coincidence) in hardware at <100 ns latency
- Enables triggering on **slow particle hypotheses** (monopoles, nuclearites) by tracking hit patterns over 10–100 μs windows without software overhead

#### c) GPU-Based Online Reconstruction at Pole
- Deploy **4× NVIDIA H100 or AMD MI300X GPU nodes** at South Pole station
- Run **machine-learning-based event reconstruction** (e.g., graph neural network as in IceCube's current GNN direction reconstructor) at full trigger rate (~3 kHz) in real time
- Enables **realtime alerts** for multimessenger follow-up with <1 minute latency and arcsecond-class pointing
- Reduces satellite bandwidth requirements by transmitting only reconstructed events above analysis threshold rather than raw data
