| White Rabbit timing | Sub-ns absolute timing | Medium | High |
| FPGA distributed trigger | Lower energy threshold | Medium | Medium |
| SoC Main Board | Onboard processing, larger buffer | Low-Medium | Medium |
| Optical fiber cable | Bandwidth, full SLC waveforms | High | Medium |

The SiPM photon detection upgrade combined with the high-speed ADC and improved calibration system would provide the largest improvement to IceCube's primary physics performance: better energy resolution for spectral measurements of the astrophysical flux, improved angular resolution for point source searches, and lower energy threshold for oscillation physics — addressing the three most significant current systematic limitations identified in the paper.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Advanced LIGO: Concrete Proposals

## 1. Quantum Noise Reduction (Highest Priority)

### Frequency-Dependent Squeezed Light Injection
The current design notes compatibility with squeezed light but doesn't implement it at design. The specific hardware required:

- **Filter cavity**: A ~300m suspended Fabry-Perot cavity (finesse ~5000) inserted between the squeezer and the interferometer's signal recycling mirror. This rotates the squeezing ellipse as a function of frequency, simultaneously reducing radiation pressure noise at low frequencies and shot noise at high frequencies. The cavity must be at sub-kelvin-level temperature stability and housed in its own vacuum enclosure with ISI-class seismic isolation.
- **Optical parametric oscillator (OPO)**: Periodically-poled KTP or PPKTP crystal in a bow-tie cavity pumped at 532nm, generating ~15dB squeezed vacuum at 1064nm. Current GEO600 demonstrations achieve ~15dB; practical injection losses limit net improvement to ~6dB but this still yields roughly a factor of 2 in high-frequency sensitivity.
- **Output Faraday isolator upgrade**: The current 30dB isolation cited in section 4.2.3 introduces loss that degrades squeezing. Replace the TGG/DKDP assembly with a next-generation design using calcium aluminate glasses (e.g. IO-3-1064-VHP series geometry) to reduce insertion loss from ~5% to ~1%, directly preserving squeezing.

**Expected gain**: Factor ~1.5-2x in shot-noise-limited band (above ~100 Hz), extending BNS range from 190 Mpc toward ~300 Mpc.

---

## 2. Test Mass Thermal Noise Reduction

This is the dominant noise source in the 30-200 Hz band per Figure 2.

### Silicon Test Masses with Cryogenic Cooling
The paper uses 40kg fused silica at room temperature. The specific upgrade path:

- **Material**: Replace Heraeus Suprasil 3001 with Czochralski-grown crystalline silicon (Si). At 123K, silicon has near-zero thermoelastic coefficient (coefficient of thermal expansion crosses zero), eliminating thermoelastic noise. Silicon mechanical Q exceeds 10^8 at cryogenic temperatures versus ~10^7 for silica at room temperature.
- **Mass geometry**: Increase to 200kg, 55cm diameter × 30cm thickness. The paper notes beam size is limited by aperture; larger masses allow larger beams (8cm spot size vs current 6.2cm on ETM), reducing coating Brownian noise which scales as 1/beam_radius.
- **Wavelength change**: Silicon is opaque at 1064nm; switch to 1550nm Nd:YAG or Er:fiber laser. This requires replacing all core optics coatings but is achievable with current ion-beam sputtering technology.
- **Cryogenic system**: Each test mass housed in a radiation shield at 120K, cooled via crystalline silicon ribbon fibers (replacing fused silica fibers—silicon conducts heat while maintaining high Q at 123K). The ribbons serve dual purpose as thermal links and suspension elements. Heat extraction rate must exceed the ~375mW absorbed per test mass surface (Table 8) while maintaining vibration isolation; this requires careful mechanical design of the cooling ribbon geometry.
- **Coating upgrade**: Replace Ti:Ta2O5/SiO2 multilayers with amorphous silicon (a-Si) / SiO2 coatings at 1550nm. Amorphous silicon at cryogenic temperatures shows mechanical loss of ~2×10^-5 compared to 2.3×10^-4 for tantala (Table 5), reducing coating Brownian noise by ~3x. Alternatively, AlGaAs crystalline coatings (already demonstrated at 10cm scale) eliminate amorphous mechanical loss entirely; scale-up to 55cm diameter is the primary challenge requiring molecular beam epitaxy deposition area expansion.

**Expected gain**: Factor ~3-5x reduction in coating thermal noise floor, which is the dominant mid-band noise source.

---

## 3. Suspension Thermal Noise and Low-Frequency Performance

The paper shows suspension thermal noise contributing near 10-30 Hz.

### Upgraded Monolithic Suspension with Larger Fibers and Better Geometry
- **Fiber upgrade**: Current fibers are 400µm diameter, 596mm long (section 4.4.2). Increase to 600µm diameter to raise violin mode frequency to ~700 Hz (moving it further from the sensitive band) while increasing the bending point loss dilution factor. Use a more aggressive necked geometry with 300µm thin section transitioning to 900µm at the ears over a 5mm transition length rather than 20mm, reducing the thermoelastic noise contribution from the bending points by ~40%.
- **Ear bonding**: Replace current hydroxide-catalysis silicate bonding of machined ears with directly laser-pulled ears integrated with the fiber, eliminating the bonding interface mechanical loss term entirely. The paper cites silicate-bonded ear loss as a component; this modification removes it.
- **Penultimate mass material**: Replace the current fused silica penultimate mass with silicon carbide (SiC), which has higher Young's modulus (450 GPa vs 72 GPa for silica), reducing thermal noise from the penultimate stage coupling into the test mass mode.

### Active Newtonian Noise Cancellation
The paper identifies gravity gradient (Newtonian) noise as a fundamental limit below ~20 Hz (section 3.4) and notes it can be several times higher than shown. This cannot be reduced by isolation:

- **Seismometer array**: Deploy a 3D array of 40-50 high-sensitivity broadband seismometers (Nanometric Trillium Compact or Streckeisen STS-2 class, noise floor ~10^-10 m/√Hz at 0.1 Hz) in a ~50m radius around each test mass vacuum chamber, both surface and borehole-deployed (3-5m depth).
- **Wiener filter cancellation**: Use real-time Wiener filtering of the seismometer array output to construct a feedforward signal that predicts the gravitational gradient force on the test mass. Apply this via the existing electrostatic drive actuators. Demonstrated cancellation of ~10dB is achievable with realistic array geometries, pushing the Newtonian noise floor below the seismic isolation noise floor at 10-15 Hz.
- **Hardware requirement**: This requires 50-100 additional ADC channels in the DAQ system (section 4.11), real-time Wiener filter computation (achievable with existing RCG infrastructure), and careful seismometer placement to avoid their own acoustic/vibrational coupling.

**Expected gain**: Factor 3-10x improvement at 10-20 Hz.

---

## 4. High-Power Operation and Parametric Instability Mitigation

The paper identifies 5-10 potentially unstable parametric modes per test mass at full power (section 2.4), currently limiting achievable circulating power.

### Electrostatic Ring Dampers
The paper mentions this as "still in research phase." Specific hardware:

- **Ring electrode geometry**: Replace the current 4-quadrant annular gold electrode pattern on the compensation plates with a 16-segment ring electrode with 2mm pitch segmentation. This allows independent excitation of specific acoustic mode shapes (breathing modes at ~15 kHz, butterfly modes at ~7 kHz) identified as most susceptible to parametric instability.
- **Signal electronics**: Add dedicated RF drive electronics (1 kHz - 50 kHz bandwidth, 1000V peak, <1 nV/√Hz noise floor) capable of applying precisely phase-tuned damping forces at the unstable mode frequencies identified by monitoring acoustic emission sensors bonded to the test mass suspension structure.
- **Acoustic emission sensors**: Bond 4 piezoelectric sensors (PZT-5H, 10mm×10mm×1mm) to each test mass penultimate mass using hydroxide-catalysis bonding, monitoring for acoustic mode amplitude buildup before instability threshold is reached. This provides early warning and enables preemptive thermal compensation actuator response.

**Expected gain**: Enables full 750 kW arm cavity power without power limitation from parametric instabilities, recovering the full quantum-noise benefit of high power.

---

## 5. Laser Source Upgrades

The current 180W Nd:YAG system (section 4.1) with 5.3% higher-order mode content requires the PMC to filter it, wasting power.

### Fiber Amplifier Pre-Stage
- Replace the current medium-power amplifier (NPRO to 35W single-pass) with a polarization-maintaining Er:Yb co-doped photonic crystal fiber amplifier. These systems demonstrate <0.5% higher-order mode content at 30W output, reducing the burden on the PMC and increasing effective power throughput by ~5%. More critically:
- **Intensity noise**: Fiber amplifiers have fundamentally lower relative intensity noise (RIN) above 1 kHz compared to solid-state amplifiers (~10^-9/√Hz vs ~10^-8/√Hz), relaxing the cascaded intensity stabilization requirements described in section 4.1. This reduces the complexity of the two-stage sensor system and the AOM actuator bandwidth requirement.
- **Injection-locked oscillator upgrade**: Replace the current 220W ring oscillator with a 400W system using larger-aperture Nd:YAG rods (6mm × 115mm) pumped by higher-brightness, wavelength-stabilized (976nm locked) fiber-coupled pump diode arrays. This provides headroom for higher input power modes without approaching thermal lensing limits in the oscillator.

---

## 6. Output Mode Cleaner and Readout

The current OMC (section 4.8.3) is a critical noise bottleneck:

### Dual OMC Configuration
- Add a second OMC cavity in series with the first. The current single OMC with finesse 400 and 1.13m round-trip achieves ~95% transmission but finite higher-order mode rejection. A second cavity (finesse 200, 0.57m round trip, temperature-tunable for orthogonal higher-order mode suppression) provides an additional ~20dB rejection of modes that accidentally align with the first OMC's transmission peaks.
- **Homodyne angle stabilization**: Add a dedicated Mach-Zehnder interferometer monitoring the DC homodyne angle (the offset from dark fringe described in section 2.3). Feed back to the arm cavity common length to stabilize the local oscillator phase to <1 mrad, reducing the technical noise from homodyne angle fluctuations which currently couples laser frequency noise.

### Balanced Homodyne Readout
The paper uses DC/homodyne with a single output port. Replace with:
- **50/50 output beamsplitter** directing half the OMC output to a second photodetector bank. Balanced homodyne subtraction cancels common-mode laser amplitude noise by >40dB, relaxing the intensity stabilization requirements throughout the entire laser chain (sections 4.1 and 4.8) and reducing the noise floor at frequencies where laser noise currently limits performance.

---

## 7. Vacuum System Improvements

Section 3.5 notes residual gas noise at H2 partial pressure of 4×10^-10 Pa.

### Getter Pump Augmentation in Beam Tubes
- Install non-evaporable getter (NEG) strips (St707 alloy, 2m length, 50mm wide) at 200m intervals along the 4km beam tubes, activated at 350°C. Current bake-out procedures achieve 4×10^-10 Pa H2; NEG augmentation can reduce this to <10^-10 Pa, pushing residual gas noise well below other noise sources even at higher sensitivity levels.
- **Test mass chamber pressure**: Install additional titanium sublimation pumps (TSP) in each BSC chamber to reduce H2 pressure from the current 7×10^-7 Pa to <2×10^-7 Pa, providing the factor-of-3 reduction in gas damping noise cited as needed in section 3.5 without requiring the ERM geometry change.

---

## Priority Summary and Expected Composite Improvement

| Upgrade | Primary Band | Sensitivity Gain |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency-dep. squeezing | >100 Hz | ~1.8x |
| Si/cryo test masses + AlGaAs coatings | 30-300 Hz | ~4x |
| Newtonian noise cancellation | 10-20 Hz | ~5x |
| Parametric instability damping | Enables full power | ~1.4x broadband |
| Balanced homodyne | 50-200 Hz | ~1.3x |

Implemented together, these upgrades constitute the core technology roadmap toward a next-generation detector with BNS range of ~1 Gpc—broadly consistent with the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer design studies—representing roughly an order-of-magnitude improvement over the nominal 190 Mpc design described in this paper.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Improved Physics Performance

## 1. PMT Array Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

The R8778 PMTs represent the dominant background source (Table 3: 0.4 ER events vs. <0.05 for all other components combined). The specific failure modes are well-characterized in the paper.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace 122 R8778 PMTs with tiled arrays of Hamamatsu VUV4 or Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD SiPM tiles, each approximately 6×6 mm², tiled to cover equivalent photocathode area
- The R8778 has 15.9 cm² minimum effective area per PMT; replace each with a ~4×4 tile array of 1 cm² SiPMs in a copper carrier frame matching existing mounting geometry
- Retain existing copper support structures and PTFE reflector geometry to minimize redesign scope

**Physics justification:**
- SiPMs contain negligible U/Th/K/Co-60 compared to the PMT values in Table 2 (9.8 mBq/PMT U, 65 mBq/PMT K-40). The dominant 0.4 ER WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days comes almost entirely from PMT radioactivity. A factor ×10-100 reduction in radioactive mass near the active volume is achievable since SiPM tiles are almost entirely silicon dioxide and trace metals rather than the steel body, glass stem, and ceramic components dominating PMT mass
- QE at 175 nm for current VUV-optimized SiPMs reaches 20-24% at LXe temperature (versus 33% for R8778), but this is partially compensated by near-unity fill factor with tiling versus ~90% collection efficiency of PMTs. Net light yield impact is modest and partially recoverable by increasing tile coverage area
- Critically, SiPMs eliminate the afterpulsing health monitoring complexity described in Section 6.2, removing an entire class of operational risk
- Dark current at 170 K drops by approximately three orders of magnitude relative to room temperature, making correlated noise negligible

**Specific hardware changes required:**
- New Cirlex bias boards with individual SiPM channel biasing at ~25-28V rather than ~1100V, eliminating high-voltage distribution risk inside xenon space
- Transimpedance preamplifier redesign since SiPM output impedance differs from PMT anode; AD8014 or similar current-feedback op-amp at the feedthrough
- Channel count increases from 61 to approximately 400-600 per array depending on tile size chosen, requiring expanded feedthrough capacity through the existing CF flanges

---

## 2. Cathode High Voltage System Redesign

The paper acknowledges the existing HV system as a significant engineering compromise: the feedthrough is placed outside the water shield at room temperature, requiring a xenon-gas-filled umbilical of substantial length.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the Heinzinger HVC100 cable-based system with a custom coaxial feedthrough designed for operation at 170 K using ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) as the dielectric, rated to 150 kV
- Place the feedthrough directly on the inner cryostat flange penetration, eliminating the umbilical entirely
- Use resistively graded field termination in liquid xenon using a polyethylene sleeve with embedded carbon-loaded UHMWPE field grading rings, a technique demonstrated by the ICARUS collaboration referenced in the paper

**Physics justification:**
- The current design limits cathode voltage to 100 kV to achieve 2 kV/cm drift field over 49 cm. Increasing to 150 kV achieves 3 kV/cm, which reduces electron diffusion during drift (transverse diffusion scales as 1/√E), improving position resolution and fiducial volume definition
- The 0.1 SLPM xenon purge flow drawn through the umbilical to prevent outgassing back-diffusion represents a continuous impurity risk. Eliminating the umbilical removes this entire pathway
- Reduced recombination at higher field increases charge yield, improving S2/S1 discrimination for electron recoils, directly improving the 99.3-99.9% ER rejection figure cited in Section 2

---

## 3. Gate-Anode Region Redesign for Improved Electron Extraction Efficiency

The paper specifies a 5 kV/cm extraction field below the liquid surface and 10 kV/cm electroluminescence field above, with an anode mesh showing 88% transparency and 130 micron deflection at operating field.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the 30-micron wire mesh anode with a photolithographically etched 50-micron-thick stainless steel foil using 200-micron holes on a 250-micron pitch, achieving >95% open area while maintaining flatness to <20 microns under tension
- Replace the gate grid (currently 50-micron wires, 5 mm pitch, 99% open area) with an indium tin oxide (ITO) coated fused silica plate with etched slots, which is optically transparent at 175 nm and eliminates the wire shadow entirely
- Reduce gate-to-anode gap from 1 cm to 5 mm, maintaining the same absolute voltages to double the electroluminescence field to 20 kV/cm

**Physics justification:**
- Extraction efficiency at the liquid surface is the single largest uncertainty in S2 signal size. The current 5 kV/cm extraction field yields approximately 85-90% extraction efficiency; increasing to 8-10 kV/cm by reducing gap while maintaining voltage would push extraction above 99%, dramatically improving S2 signal-to-noise for low-energy nuclear recoils near threshold
- The 130-micron anode deflection documented in Section 3.3 creates a position-dependent variation in electroluminescence gap, broadening S2 pulses in a spatially nonuniform way that degrades x-y position reconstruction. A rigid etched foil eliminates this
- ITO gate eliminates the ~1% optical shadow of the current wire gate from the perspective of the top PMT array imaging S2, improving position reconstruction accuracy beyond the stated ~1 cm

---

## 4. Internal Krypton Removal System

The paper lists ⁸⁵Kr as contributing up to 0.13 ER WIMP-like events (Table 3) based on projected getter removal efficiency. Natural xenon contains approximately 1-10 ppb of krypton, and ⁸⁵Kr (T½ = 10.76 yr) is a pure beta emitter at 687 keV endpoint that cannot be removed by the SAES getter.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Install a dedicated chromatographic krypton separation column using Carboxen 1000 molecular sieve adsorbent (demonstrated at XENON100 and XMASS) inline with the existing recirculation path between the getter outlet and the concentric tube heat exchanger
- Size the column for 50 SLPM flow rate matching existing system capacity: approximately 2 kg of adsorbent in a stainless steel 316L vessel, 15 cm diameter × 60 cm length, rated to 10 bar
- Add a dedicated cold trap (liquid nitrogen cooled, 316L vessel) upstream of the column to capture water and heavy organics that would saturate the molecular sieve

**Physics justification:**
- The paper acknowledges 0.13 ER events as an upper bound "estimated from projected efficiency." Chromatographic separation achieves Kr/Xe ratios below 1 part per trillion, reducing this contribution by approximately three orders of magnitude to a completely negligible level
- This is particularly important because ⁸⁵Kr beta spectrum extends from 0 to 687 keV with significant flux in the 1-8 keVee signal region, and unlike gamma events it cannot be rejected by fiducialization since it originates in the bulk xenon
- Hardware integration is straightforward since the existing xenon gas plumbing already routes through the getter at the appropriate pressure and temperature range for chromatographic operation

---

## 5. Upgraded Muon Veto Coverage

The water tank currently uses 20 ten-inch R7081 PMTs arranged in four vertical strings. The paper states >90% muon rejection efficiency.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Increase PMT count from 20 to 60 R7081 PMTs, adding two additional string positions and supplementing each string with intermediate PMTs, achieving approximately 25% photocathode coverage of the tank walls
- Add 8 upward-facing PMTs on the tank floor pointing upward to improve tagging of near-horizontal muons
- Replace the Tyvek reflector lining with ESR (Enhanced Specular Reflector) film from 3M, which provides >98% specular reflectance versus ~95% diffuse for Tyvek, improving light collection uniformity and reducing required PMT count for equivalent photoelectron yield

**Physics justification:**
- The paper states muon-induced neutron background in the fiducial volume is ~1 event per 3 years before veto, relying on >90% veto efficiency to suppress this. Improving to >99% efficiency (comparable to Super-Kamiokande's figure cited in Section 8.2) would reduce this to ~0.03 events per 3 years, providing headroom for longer exposure runs
- At 300 kg active xenon, the experiment is statistics-limited for WIMP signals at the target cross section. Any reduction in the irreducible muon-correlated neutron background directly extends the viable exposure duration
- The upgraded coverage also enables shower reconstruction sufficient to identify muons that clip the corner of the water tank and currently escape tagging due to low photoelectron yield

---

## 6. Radon Mitigation in Xenon Gas Space

The paper addresses radon in the water tank nitrogen blanket but does not explicitly quantify radon contribution to internal backgrounds.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Install an activated charcoal radon trap (5 kg Saratech charcoal, SS316L vessel cooled to -40°C with a Peltier cooler) on the xenon gas return line between the getter and the concentric tube heat exchanger
- Add two RAD7 radon detectors (Durridge) sampling continuously from the xenon gas space at 0.1 SLPM, providing real-time radon activity monitoring with sensitivity to 1 mBq/m³
- Seal all cable penetrations through the inner cryostat flange with custom glass-to-metal seals rather than the current flexible stainless steel couplings, which represent the primary radon ingress pathway

**Physics justification:**
- ²²²Rn (T½ = 3.82 days) emanates from detector surfaces, particularly from the PTFE panels and Cirlex circuit boards, and ²¹⁴Pb/²¹⁴Bi daughters plate out on surfaces and produce beta/gamma backgrounds indistinguishable from bulk ER events
- The charcoal trap at -40°C achieves a retardation factor >1000 for radon in xenon gas flow, effectively eliminating radon from recirculated xenon
- This upgrade is particularly synergistic with the SiPM replacement above, since radon emanation from the glass PMT bodies is eliminated and the remaining dominant source shifts to the PTFE panels, which can then be specifically addressed through material selection

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a ~50 kg Two-Phase LAr TPC Dark Matter Detector

## Preamble: Identifying the Limiting Physics Factors

For a detector at this scale, the primary physics performance bottlenecks are:
1. **Nuclear recoil / electron recoil discrimination** (driven by S2/S1 ratio and S1 photon statistics)
2. **S1 light collection efficiency** (dominates energy threshold and PSD quality)
3. **Surface background rejection** (cathode, field cage, and PTFE surfaces)
4. **Electron lifetime / charge collection** (governs S2 yield and fiducialization)
5. **Radon and intrinsic background levels**
6. **Neutron veto efficiency and tagging latency**

The upgrades below are ranked roughly by physics impact.

---

## 1. Photon Detection System: Replacing or Augmenting 3-inch PMTs with SiPMs

### The Problem
3-inch cryogenic PMTs (e.g., R11065 or Hamamatsu equivalents) have:
- ~35% peak quantum efficiency at 128 nm VUV (with appropriate photocathode)
- Non-negligible dark count rates at LAr temperatures (~20–40 Hz/PMT)
- Single photoelectron resolution sufficient but not exceptional
- Relatively low geometric fill factor at TPC boundaries
- Radioactive backgrounds from borosilicate glass (~mBq/kg level from ²³⁸U, ²³²Th, ⁴⁰K)

### Specific Upgrade: Silicon Photomultiplier Tile Arrays

**Replace or supplement the PMT arrays with cryogenic SiPM tiles.**

**Concrete components:**
- **Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-Cryo or LF-Cryo SiPMs**, which demonstrate:
  - Photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 50–60% at 420 nm (after WLS conversion)
  - Stable operation at 87 K with negligible dark count rate (~0.1–1 Hz/mm² at 87 K vs. kHz/mm² at room temperature)
  - Correlated avalanche (crosstalk + afterpulsing) below 15% achievable with careful bias design
- **Alternatively: Hamamatsu S13370-6050CN VUV4** SiPMs with demonstrated VUV sensitivity at LAr temperature

**Implementation architecture:**
- Replace the bottom PMT array entirely with a close-packed tile array of **6 mm × 6 mm** FBK SiPMs ganged in groups of 16–25 into readout channels, targeting >85% geometric coverage of the bottom face
- For the top array, retain 2–3 PMTs for high-level trigger and replace remaining positions with SiPM tiles
- Use **cryogenic ASICs** (e.g., CACTUS or similar developed in the DarkSide-20k program) for front-end amplification and multiplexing at cold, reducing cable count and noise pickup

**Physics impact:**
- S1 yield improvement from ~5–7 PE/keV to potentially **10–15 PE/keV** for nuclear recoils
- PSD figure of merit (FoM) improves as √(yield); this directly extends the recoil energy threshold from ~50 keVnr down toward **20–30 keVnr**
- Reduced radioactive background from glass eliminated

---

## 2. Wavelength Shifter: Replacing TPB Evaporated Coatings with Robust Alternatives

### The Problem
Tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) evaporated onto PTFE or acrylic:
- Has non-uniform coating thickness leading to spatial variation in WLS efficiency
- Can delaminate or crack under thermal cycling
- Introduces surface background channels (alpha and beta emitters adsorbed during deposition)
- Emission peak (~430 nm) is not optimally matched to SiPM PDE curves

### Specific Upgrade: pTP + Bis-MSB Wavelength Shifter System

**Replace evaporated TPB with a two-stage system:**

1. **Dip-coated or sprayed para-Terphenyl (pTP)** as primary WLS on reflector surfaces:
   - Converts 128 nm → ~340 nm
   - Demonstrated ~70–80% conversion efficiency
   - More mechanically robust than TPB; compatible with cryogenic cycling
   - Radiopurity achievable to sub-μBq/g levels

2. **Bis-MSB doped polystyrene light guide sheets** as secondary WLS:
   - Converts ~340 nm → ~420 nm
   - Matched to peak SiPM PDE
   - Can be fabricated as flat panels backed directly by SiPM arrays (as in the ARAPUCA / X-ARAPUCA architecture)

**X-ARAPUCA light trap modules** (developed for DUNE/DarkSide-20k):
- Consist of a dichroic filter window + WLS-embedded bar + SiPM array
- Trap and concentrate photons via total internal reflection
- Demonstrated effective PDE >3% per unit area using only partial SiPM coverage, extensible to **10–15%** with optimized geometry and full SiPM coverage
- Deploy these along the barrel/field cage walls to recover lateral photons currently lost

---

## 3. Field Cage and High Voltage System: Improving Uniformity and Reducing Surface Backgrounds

### The Problem
Conventional resistor-chain field cages with PTFE reflector panels:
- PTFE surfaces contribute surface electron backgrounds (⁲¹⁰Pb/²¹⁰Po from ²²²Rn daughters plating out)
- Resistor chains introduce radioactive mass near active volume
- Field distortions near edges degrade fiducialization efficiency

### Specific Upgrade A: Photolithographically Patterned ITO on Fused Silica Field Cage

**Replace copper ring + PTFE panel field cage with:**
- **Indium tin oxide (ITO) traces patterned on UV-grade fused silica cylinders**
  - ITO is transparent to VUV and visible photons → eliminates optical dead zones
  - Resistivity tunable by trace width to act as distributed resistive divider (eliminating discrete resistors in the active volume region)
  - Fused silica is radiopure and dimensionally stable
  - Demonstrated in small prototypes; manufacturable in 20–30 cm diameter sections

**Specific vendor path:** custom fabrication through companies providing ITO-on-glass for photomask blanks; total resistance of order 100 MΩ/section achievable.

### Specific Upgrade B: Dissolved ²³⁹Pu Alpha Source Removal + Electropolished Electrodes

- **Replace all copper electrodes with electropolished** (EP) **titanium or grade-1 OFHC copper** treated with the DarkSide/XENON radiopurity protocols (acid etching, nitrogen storage)
- **Cathode HV feedthrough:** Replace commercial SHV feedthroughs with a **custom cryogenic HV feedthrough using polyethylene insulator** (lower ²³⁸U content than ceramic alternatives), rated to –50 kV, modeled on the LUX/LZ design

### Specific Upgrade C: Resistor Chain → Custom Cryogenic Thick-Film Resistors

- Use **Caddock or Ohmite cryogenic-characterized metal film resistors**, individually screened for U/Th content by ICP-MS to <1 ppb
- Mount resistors **outside the field cage radius but inside the cryostat** using a spring-loaded annular PCB to maintain contact at cold

---

## 4. Electron Lifetime: Upgraded Argon Purification System

### The Problem
Trace electronegative impurities (O₂, H₂O, N₂) at ppb level limit electron lifetime. For a 50 kg detector with ~30 cm drift, a lifetime of >5 ms is needed for <10% charge loss, but achieving and maintaining this is operationally challenging.

### Specific Upgrade: Inline Cryogenic Recirculation with Dual-Stage Getter

**Hardware:**

1. **SAES PS11-MC1-R-2 or equivalent rare-gas getter** (heated to 300°C) in the gas-phase recirculation loop:
   - Reduces O₂ and H₂O to <1 ppb
   - Supplement with a **room-temperature activated alumina + molecular sieve (4Å) cold trap** upstream to extend getter lifetime

2. **Liquid-phase recirculation pump:** Replace gas-only purification with a **magnetically coupled cryogenic gear pump** (e.g., based on the Barber-Nichols or custom FNAL design) circulating liquid LAr directly through a getter cartridge:
   - Purification rate ~5–10 liquid volumes per day
   - Electron lifetime routinely exceeds **10–20 ms** with this approach (demonstrated in MicroBooNE, LArIAT)

3. **Online purity monitor:** Deploy **two** standalone LAr purity monitors (gridded ionization chambers with UV LED photocathodes) external to the TPC but in the same cryostat, for continuous real-time monitoring without disturbing the TPC field.

**Physics impact:**
- Improved electron lifetime → uniform S2 gain → better z-position reconstruction → tighter fiducial volume cut → higher effective exposure

---

## 5. Anode/Extraction Grid: Improving S2 Gain and Position Resolution

### The Problem
Standard wire grids for the extraction region and anode have:
- Limited photon position resolution for S2 (constrains x-y fiducialization)
- Wire tension instability at cold (differential thermal contraction)
- Limited optical transparency

### Specific Upgrade A: Segmented Transparent Anode with Lensed SiPM Array

**Replace top wire grid anode with:**
- **ITO-coated fused silica plate** serving as anode (as demonstrated in small LArTPCs)
  - Transparent to S2 photons → top photon detectors collect S2 without grid shadow
  - Provides uniform extraction field
  - Eliminates wire sagging/tension issues at 87 K

### Specific Upgrade B: Dedicated S2 Position Reconstruction Camera Plane

**Add a 2D position-sensitive photon detection layer immediately above the liquid surface:**
- Array of **32 × 32 = 1024 individual 6 mm SiPM pixels** on a 5 cm pitch, covering the full anode area
- Each pixel read out individually (or in 4-pixel groups) through a **cryogenic multiplexer ASIC**
- S2 position resolution improves from ~1 cm (with 7–19 PMTs) to **<3 mm σ** in x-y
- This dramatically improves surface background rejection using radial fiducialization

**Physics impact:**
- 3 mm x-y resolution + z from drift time → mm³-scale position resolution → ability to fiducialize away from all surfaces by >5 mm → surface background rejection improves by factor 3–5 in effective background rate

---

## 6. Neutron Veto Upgrade: Gadolinium-Loaded Liquid Scintillator and Improved Timing

### The Problem
Plain liquid scintillator (e.g., EJ-301, pseudocumene-based) neutron veto:
- Relies on proton recoil PSD for fast neutron tagging (good)
- Thermal neutron capture on ¹H gives 2.2 MeV γ with ~200 μs capture time (long coincidence window → high accidental rate)
- Limited efficiency for neutrons that scatter in active volume and then thermalize in LAr before reaching veto

### Specific Upgrade A: Gadolinium Loading of Liquid Scintillator

**Load the liquid scintillator to 0.1–0.5% Gd by mass using Gd-TMHA (gadolinium trimethylhexanoic acid)** or **Gd-doped PPO in LAB solvent** (as developed for SNO+ and Super-Kamiokande-Gd):
- Gd has thermal neutron capture cross-section ~49,000 barns vs. 0.3 barns for H
- Capture time reduced from ~200 μs to **~20–30 μs**
- Capture releases 8 MeV in γ cascade vs. 2.2 MeV → much higher detection efficiency
- Coincidence window shrinks by 10× → accidental coincidence rate drops by 10×

**Specific formulation:** 0.1 wt% Gd in LAB+PPO+bis-MSB (transparent to 400–500 nm), stable for >1 year demonstrated in EGADS and SK-Gd programs.

### Specific Upgrade B: Add ⁶Li-Doped ZnS(Ag) Panels as Inner Neutron Shield

Between the LAr cryostat and the liquid scintillator veto, install:
- **EJ-426 ⁶Li-ZnS(Ag) neutron capture sheets** (commercially available from Eljen Technology)
  - ⁶Li(n,α)³H reaction: 4.78 MeV Q-value, no γ emission → background-free neutron tag
  - 5 mm thick panels provide ~20% additional capture efficiency for thermalized neutrons
  - Read out by external wavelength-shifting fiber + SiPM system

---

## 7. Radon Mitigation: Cryostat Seal and Gas Handling Upgrades

### The Problem
²²²Rn (t₁/₂ = 3.8 days) emanated from detector materials and entering via gas connections deposits ²¹⁰Pb/²¹⁰Po on surfaces, creating irreducible alpha/beta surface backgrounds.

### Specific Upgrade A: Radon Trap in Argon Supply Line

**Install a cryogenic activated charcoal radon trap:**
- **1 kg of Saratech or Pica G210 coconut-shell activated charcoal** cooled to −40°C to −60°C in the gas supply line
- Reduces Rn from commercial Ar supply from ~1 Bq/m³ to **<1 mBq/m³**
- Trap dimensions: ~20 cm diameter × 50 cm column; regenerated with N₂ purge at 150°C every 3–6 months

### Specific Upgrade B: Metal O-Ring Seals Throughout

**Replace all elastomer (Viton, Buna-N) seals on the inner cryostat and gas system with:**
- **Helicoflex HNV aluminum or silver-coated stainless O-rings** for cryostat flanges
- **VCR/Swagelok metal-to-metal face seal fittings** throughout gas handling
- Elastomer permeability to Rn is a known contamination path; metal seals reduce Rn ingress by **>100×**

---

## 8. Electronics and DAQ: Cryogenic Front-End for Noise Reduction

### Specific Upgrade: Application-Specific Cryogenic Preamplifier ASICs

**Deploy front-end electronics at cold (87 K) rather than at room temperature:**

- **Custom SiPM readout ASIC** (e.g., ABACUS or LArASIC derivatives, or the cryogenic ASIC developed by INFN Genova for DarkSide-20k):
  - Charge-sensitive amplifier + shaper + discriminator integrated on chip
  - Operates reliably at 77–100 K (CMOS processes using enclosed-geometry transistors to avoid kink effect)
  - Noise equivalent charge: **<0.1 PE** achievable
  - Power dissipation: ~1 mW/channel → manageable heat load for 200–400 channel system

- **Signal multiplexing:** Use SiPM tile groups of 16 per ASIC, with 4-wire serial readout to room temperature, reducing cable feedthrough count from hundreds to tens
  - Each feedthrough penetration is a potential Rn ingress and heat leak source

**Physics impact:**
- Electronic noise

# Hardware Design Upgrades for SNO: Targeted Improvements for Primary Physics Performance

## Assessment of Primary Physics Limitations

The core physics goal is distinguishing CC, NC, and ES interactions through precise measurement of neutrino flux and flavor composition. The principal hardware limitations in the described detector are:

1. Photocathode coverage limiting energy threshold and resolution
2. PMT timing resolution constraining vertex reconstruction
3. Neutron detection efficiency and background discrimination
4. Water radiopurity monitoring sensitivity
5. Electronics dynamic range and deadtime

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. Replace PMT Array with High-Quantum-Efficiency Large-Area PMTs

**Problem:** The R1408 tubes achieve approximately 20% quantum efficiency at peak wavelength (~420 nm). The effective photocathode coverage is 54% after concentrator reflectivity losses from the nominal 59% geometric coverage. With roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV, the energy threshold is constrained to approximately 5 MeV to stay above radioactive backgrounds, leaving significant 8B spectrum inaccessible.

**Upgrade:** Replace the R1408 with Hamamatsu R3600 or equivalent 50 cm hemispherical PMTs using bialkali photocathodes with quantum efficiency of 25–30% at 400 nm, or preferably transition to newer-generation tubes such as the Hamamatsu R7081 series with platinum-doped bialkali achieving 35% peak QE. These were under development in industry at the time of SNO's construction but not yet available in production quantities suitable for large arrays.

**Concrete specifications:**
- 50 cm diameter hemispherical envelope maintaining the mushroom geometry for pressure resistance
- Peak QE ≥ 30% at 390–420 nm
- Transit time spread σ < 1.2 ns single photoelectron (versus 1.7 ns achieved)
- Maintain Schott 8246 equivalent borosilicate with <40 ppb U/Th
- Retain waterproof enclosure design but redesign connector to eliminate the TNC breakdown problem permanently by using a fully potted connector without gas-filled void spaces

**Expected physics gain:** Photoelectron yield increases from ~8 to ~12 pe/MeV. Energy resolution improves from approximately 6.5% to approximately 5% at 6 MeV. Achievable analysis threshold could be reduced from 5 MeV toward 3.5 MeV, accessing the low-energy portion of the 8B spectrum and dramatically improving sensitivity to MSW spectral distortions, particularly the upturn region below 5 MeV that distinguishes LMA from other oscillation solutions.

---

### 2. Wavelength-Shifting Light Concentrators

**Problem:** The existing aluminum/MgF2/TiO2 concentrators achieve 82% mean reflectance. Cherenkov photons peak near 350–400 nm where acrylic absorption is rising (0.04 cm⁻¹ at 360 nm versus 0.01 cm⁻¹ at 400 nm). Short-wavelength photons are disproportionately lost.

**Upgrade:** Replace the purely reflective concentrator coating with a wavelength-shifting (WLS) compound integrated into the concentrator surface. Specifically, coat the concentrator inner surface with a thin film (~50–100 μm) of polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) or deposit tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) via vacuum evaporation onto the aluminum substrate before the dielectric coating.

**Concrete specifications:**
- TPB deposition at 0.2 mg/cm² on aluminum substrate
- TPB absorption peak at 350 nm, emission peak at 430 nm matching PMT peak QE
- Radiochemical assay of TPB to verify U/Th content below 15 ng/g (TPB is an organic molecule and can be purified to very low radioactivity)
- WLS layer protected by thin SiO2 overcoat (50 nm) to prevent dissolution in ultrapure water
- Emission time constant of TPB is approximately 1.5 ns, acceptable given existing timing resolution

**Expected physics gain:** Recovery of approximately 30% of UV Cherenkov photons that are currently lost to acrylic absorption or low-reflectance in the UV. This represents an effective increase in photoelectron yield of roughly 15–20%, improving energy resolution and lowering the analysis threshold without requiring additional PMTs.

---

### 3. Upgrade NCD Array Electronics with Full Waveform Digitization

**Problem:** The described NCD system uses pulse-shape discrimination and position encoding requiring digitized ion-current profiles, but the readout is via a single 91Ω coaxial cable per string with delay-line position encoding. Background rejection relies on distinguishing neutron events from alpha particles, electrons, and microdischarges. The described system captures waveforms but the electronics bandwidth and sampling rate are not specified to the level needed for optimal discrimination.

**Upgrade:** Replace the NCD readout electronics with a dedicated high-bandwidth waveform digitizer system using switched-capacitor array (SCA) ASICs.

**Concrete specifications:**
- Deploy DRS4 chip (Paul Scherrer Institut design, 1–5 GSPS sampling, 1024 cells) or equivalent SCA
- Sampling rate: 2 GSPS per NCD string, providing 0.5 ns time bins
- Analog bandwidth: DC to 500 MHz
- 12-bit effective resolution after calibration
- 4-μs capture window covering the full ion drift time in the proportional counter (~2 μs at 2.5 atm CF4/3He mixture)
- On-board FPGA (Xilinx Spartan-3 or equivalent) for first-level pulse classification reducing data rate by factor ~50 before transmission
- Readout via fiber optic link replacing the coaxial cable where possible to eliminate ground loops

**Expected physics gain:** Improved alpha/neutron discrimination from current ~50% identification rate toward ~80% through better characterization of the Bragg peak structure in the ionization track. This directly improves the effective NCD array efficiency from the quoted 25% toward 35% and reduces the photodisintegration background subtraction uncertainty, which is the dominant systematic in the NC flux measurement. Position resolution along strings improves from approximately 10 cm to approximately 2 cm, enabling fiducial volume cuts on the NCD data itself.

---

### 4. In-Situ Online Radon Monitoring with Electrostatic Alpha Counting

**Problem:** The described radon assay requires extracting 6 tonnes of water through a vacuum degasser at 20 l/min, an offline batch process with limited spatial resolution (six sample regions each). The 3.8-day half-life of 222Rn means radon concentrations can vary significantly between measurements, and localized contamination events may be missed.

**Upgrade:** Deploy a network of miniaturized electrostatic radon detectors permanently installed within the D2O and H2O volumes for continuous real-time monitoring.

**Concrete specifications:**
- 12 detector units: 6 within D2O at different heights, 6 in H2O between AV and PSUP
- Each detector: 50 ml degassing cell with polished stainless steel electrode, silicon PIN photodiode (Hamamatsu S3590 series) operated at +1500 V for alpha collection
- Degassing loop: 1 l/min micro-pump drawing water through a thin-film degasser (Membrana Liqui-Cel mini-module) with N2 purge gas at 10 sccm
- Silicon detector area 1 cm², energy resolution <40 keV FWHM for 7.69 MeV alpha from 214Po
- All wetted materials: electropolished 316L stainless steel and PEEK, with U/Th verified below 1 ng/g by ICPMS
- Sensitivity target: 0.01 mBq/m³ (10× better than batch method) with 1-hour integration

**Expected physics gain:** Real-time radon maps enable identification and correction of localized contamination events (such as radon ingress following maintenance activities or filter changes) within hours rather than days. This reduces the systematic uncertainty on the photodisintegration background from radon daughters from approximately 20% toward 5%, directly improving the NC flux measurement precision.

---

### 5. Upgrade Front-End Electronics: Higher-Speed ADC with Deeper Analog Memory

**Problem:** The QUSN7 chip provides 16-deep analog memory with 12-bit ADCs running at 2 μs conversion time. The per-channel deadtime of ~400 ns is acceptable for solar neutrino running but limits capability during high-rate periods. More critically, the 16-deep memory limits burst capture capability and the charge measurement is performed at fixed early/late sample times rather than integrated over an optimally defined window.

**Upgrade:** Replace the QUSN7/SNOINT/SNOD chip set with a redesigned ASIC in 0.25 μm CMOS process (mature and radiation-tolerant by late 1990s standards, widely used in LHC detector development).

**Concrete specifications:**
- New discriminator ASIC: constant-fraction discrimination (CFD) rather than leading-edge, reducing timewalk from ~3 ns to <0.5 ns over the single-photoelectron to 100-photoelectron range
- New integrator: dual-gain with selectable integration windows of 20 ns, 100 ns, and 400 ns rather than fixed early/late samples
- New memory ASIC: 64-deep analog memory (versus 16-deep), enabling capture of entire 1 μs event window at 100 ns per cell
- TAC resolution: improve from current ~0.1 ns/count toward 0.025 ns/count using a 200 MHz reference oscillator
- ADC: 14-bit pipeline ADC at 40 MSPS, converting all 64 memory cells in <2 μs total rather than per-cell conversion
- Maintain GTL signaling on SNOBus but increase clock to 100 MHz for faster readout

**Expected physics gain:** CFD timing improves single-photoelectron timing resolution from 1.7 ns RMS toward 1.0 ns RMS. With better timing, vertex reconstruction resolution improves from approximately 25 cm toward 15 cm at 5 MeV, reducing the fiducial volume systematic uncertainty. Better charge resolution improves energy resolution. The 64-deep memory substantially improves supernova burst capability and reduces data loss during high-rate calibration runs.

---

### 6. Enhanced Magnetic Field Compensation System

**Problem:** The described system cancels only the vertical component of Earth's field using 14 horizontal coils embedded in cavity walls, leaving a residual maximum field of 19 μT and 2.5% average photon-detection efficiency loss. The horizontal field components (~15° off vertical implies substantial horizontal component at ~55 μT total) are uncompensated.

**Upgrade:** Install a complete 3-axis Helmholtz-configuration compensation coil system.

**Concrete specifications:**
- Add 14 vertical coils (in pairs above and below detector equator) to cancel horizontal field components
- Add 14 diagonal coils for higher-order uniformity
- Coil wire: 4 mm diameter phosphor-bronze conductor with PTFE jacket, verified to <5 ng/g U/Th by NAA
- Power supplies: four-quadrant programmable DC supplies (±10 A, 1 mA resolution) per axis
- Fluxgate magnetometer array: 12 sensors distributed within the H2O volume between AV and PSUP, providing real-time field maps at 1 Hz
- Closed-loop control: PID controller maintaining residual field below 5 μT at all PMT locations
- Compensation for time-varying fields from mine operations and seasonal variation

**Expected physics gain:** Reducing residual field from 19 μT to 5 μT increases the average PMT photon-detection efficiency from 97.5% to approximately 99.5% of the zero-field value. More importantly, the efficiency becomes spatially uniform, reducing a position-dependent systematic in energy reconstruction. The improvement is modest in absolute terms (~2%) but removes a correlated systematic that currently affects all PMTs simultaneously.

---

## Summary Table of Expected Improvements

| Upgrade | Primary Metric Improved | Estimated Gain |
|---|---|---|
| High-QE PMTs | Photoelectron yield, energy threshold | +50% pe yield, threshold to 3.5 MeV |
| WLS concentrators | UV photon recovery | +15–20% pe yield |
| NCD waveform digitization | NC flux systematic uncertainty | α/n discrimination 50%→80% |
| Online radon monitoring | Photodisintegration background uncertainty | 20%→5% systematic |
| New front-end ASICs | Vertex resolution, energy resolution | Vertex 25→15 cm, timing 1.7→1.0 ns |
| 3-axis field compensation | PMT efficiency uniformity | Removes 2.5% correlated systematic |

The highest-priority upgrades are (1) the NCD waveform digitization and (4) online radon monitoring, as these most directly reduce the systematic uncertainties on the NC flux measurement, which is SNO's unique physics contribution. The PMT and electronics upgrades provide secondary improvements in statistical precision and threshold.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Forward Heavy-Flavour Spectrometer

## Framing the Problem

The primary physics performance drivers for this class of instrument (paradigmatically LHCb) are: **vertex resolution** (to resolve displaced heavy-flavour decays), **track momentum resolution** (for mass peaks and proper-time resolution), **particle identification** (charm/beauty decay final-state separation), and **trigger efficiency and purity** (for rare/hadronic modes). I address each with concrete technology proposals.

---

## 1. Vertex Detector: The Highest-Leverage Upgrade

### 1.1 Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS) with Thinner Epitaxial Layers

**Current limitation:** Strip or hybrid pixel detectors have ~200–300 μm silicon + bump-bond assembly, limiting the closest approach to the beampipe and introducing material budget (~0.5–1% X₀ per layer) that degrades impact parameter (IP) resolution through multiple scattering.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Deploy **fully-depleted MAPS** (e.g., based on TowerJazz 180 nm or similar modified commercial CMOS processes with deep p-well implants) with **50 μm total sensor thickness** including substrate thinning
- Achieve **10 μm pixel pitch** with in-pixel amplification and discrimination, eliminating bump bonds entirely
- Target **< 0.1% X₀ per detection layer** (achievable with thinned sensors on carbon-fibre foam supports)
- Place the innermost layer at **radius ~13 mm** from the beam axis, enabled by the reduced material and a retractable RF-foil beampipe of **250 μm beryllium** or carbon-fibre composite

**Impact:** IP resolution scales roughly as σ(IP) = a ⊕ b/pT. Halving material budget and halving innermost radius improves the multiple-scattering term b by a factor ~3–4, dramatically improving B→μν separation, Bs→μμ sensitivity, and proper-time resolution for all modes.

### 1.2 4D Tracking: Precision Timing in the Vertex Detector

**Motivation:** At high luminosity, pile-up (multiple pp interactions per bunch crossing) degrades vertex reconstruction and ghost track rates. Timing separates vertices in the time domain.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Integrate **AC-coupled Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (AC-LGADs)** or **resistive silicon detectors (RSD)** as dedicated timing layers — 2 layers of 150–200 μm AC-LGAD sensors with ~35 μm pitch
- Target **30–50 ps single-hit time resolution** per layer (systematics from Landau fluctuations managed by charge-sharing in AC-coupled geometry)
- Readout ASIC: custom **65 nm CMOS** with Time-of-Arrival (ToA) and Time-over-Threshold (ToT) capability, 1 ns TDC binning with interpolation
- Place these timing layers at r ~ 20–30 mm, just outside the MAPS layers

**Impact:** Combined 4D track seeds suppress combinatorial background in vertex reconstruction by ~10× at pile-up μ > 5. Essential for operating at luminosities ≳ 10³³ cm⁻² s⁻¹.

---

## 2. Upstream Tracker: Replacing Straws or Long-Strip Detectors

**Current limitation:** Scintillating-fibre or straw-tube trackers upstream of the magnet have spatial resolution ~100–200 μm, limiting momentum resolution and ghost track suppression, and suffer occupancy at high luminosity.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- **Upstream Silicon Micro-Strip Tracker (USMT):** 4-station detector using **320 μm thick double-sided silicon microstrip sensors** with 100 μm stereo pitch (±5° stereo angle), covering the full spectrometer acceptance (~300 mrad)
- Alternatively, **short-drift Micropattern Gas Detectors (MPGDs)**: **μRWELL** or **resistive Micromegas** with 400 μm pitch strips and 50 μm position resolution — handles high multiplicity with superior rate capability (> 10 MHz/cm²) and lower material than silicon of equivalent area
- Readout: **SALT2 or APV25-successor ASIC** at 40 MHz sampling with analogue readout for charge-centre determination

**Impact:** Improves track-seed quality fed to the trigger processor, reducing ghost rate by ~2× and enabling tighter pT cuts on Level-0/hardware trigger candidates.

---

## 3. Main Tracking System: Scintillating Fibre Optimisation and Alternatives

**Current state:** SciFi detectors (250 μm SCSF-78 fibres, SiPM readout) achieve ~100 μm resolution and are radiation-hard to ~10¹³ neq/cm².

**Proposed upgrades:**

### 3.1 Radiation-Hard SiPM Arrays
- Replace current **SiPMs** with **3D-trench SiPMs** (FBK or Hamamatsu VUV4-style) featuring reduced dark current after irradiation — trench isolation suppresses cross-talk at reduced bias, maintaining signal-to-noise post-irradiation
- Operate at **−40°C** using CO₂ cooling loops (existing in the experiment) to suppress thermally generated dark counts by factor ~10 per 10°C, extending useful detector lifetime by ~3×

### 3.2 Long-Drift MPGD Alternative (Outer Tracker Replacement)
- For the **outer acceptance** (high radius, lower occupancy), replace ageing straw tubes with **GEM+μRWELL hybrid detectors**: GEM pre-amplification stage (gain ~10) feeding a resistive μRWELL (gain ~200–500), giving total gain ~2000–5000
- Achieves **50 μm spatial resolution**, rate capability > 5 MHz/cm², and very low material budget (< 0.5% X₀/layer)

---

## 4. Particle Identification: RICH Enhancement

### 4.1 Next-Generation Photon Detectors for RICH

**Current limitation:** Multi-anode PMTs (MaPMTs, e.g., R11265) are limited by single-photon detection efficiency (~25% QE), active area fraction (~77%), and magnetic field sensitivity.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace MaPMTs with **Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) with time-tagging**, specifically **digital SiPMs** (e.g., Philips/Sensl architecture) with integrated TDC: 50 ps timing enables **time-imaging RICH** — photon arrival time used to suppress out-of-time backgrounds from pile-up crossings
- Pixel size: **3 mm × 3 mm** SiPM tiles (matching Cherenkov ring photon density); 6×6 mm² microcell size for low optical cross-talk
- Radiators: retain aerogel (n ≈ 1.03, low-β threshold) + C₄F₁₀ gas; add a **thin pressurised CF₄ stage** (n−1 ≈ 5×10⁻⁴ at 1 bar) to extend kaon–pion separation to **> 100 GeV/c** without major length increase
- Focusing mirror: switch from spherical glass to **lightweight carbon-fibre mirrors** with Al+MgF₂ coating, reducing material in acceptance

**Impact:** Improves **kaon identification efficiency** from ~95% to ~97% at fixed pion misidentification, critical for hadronic B modes (Bs→Dsπ, B→hh) and for suppressing combinatorial backgrounds in charm spectroscopy.

### 4.2 Proximity-Focusing DIRC Downstream

- Add a **compact DIRC detector** (Detection of Internally Reflected Cherenkov light) in the 2–5 GeV/c momentum range gap between the two RICH detectors: **fused-silica bar radiators** (n = 1.473) with **focusing optics** onto a SiPM matrix
- 3D reconstruction of Cherenkov angle using bar position, photon angle, and photon ToA (single-photon timing resolution ~100 ps with MCP-PMTs or fast SiPMs)
- Adds **3σ K/π separation at 5 GeV/c** in a 50 cm longitudinal space

---

## 5. Calorimetry: Upgraded Preshower and ECAL

### 5.1 Sampling ECAL with SiPM Readout

**Current limitation:** Shashlik-type ECAL with WLS-fibre + PMT readout has 10–15% energy resolution (σ/E) and slow response (~100 ns); radiation damage in the innermost cells (dose > 10 Mrad) degrades resolution.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace inner ECAL region (|x|, |y| < 300 mm) with **Pb/W-fibre sampling calorimeter** ("spaghetti" or SpaCal concept): **0.5 mm diameter crystal fibres (LYSO or PWO)** embedded in a lead matrix, readout by **SiPMs at both fibre ends** for longitudinal depth measurement
- Resolution target: **σ/E ≈ 8%/√E ⊕ 1%**, radiation hardness to 100 Mrad
- Outer ECAL: retrofit with **SiPM + WLS fibre** readout replacing PMTs, enabling **1 ns timing resolution** for calorimeter clusters (pile-up rejection)

**Impact:** Critical for B→K*γ, Bs→γγ, and electron identification in semileptonic modes. Improved resolution directly translates to better signal/background in radiative decay channels.

---

## 6. Muon System: Upgrade of Innermost Stations

**Current limitation:** MWPC innermost region suffers > 2× rate saturation at design luminosity; ageing irreversible above 0.5 C/cm accumulated charge.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace **MWPC in M1 and M2 inner regions** with **GEM detectors** (triple-GEM, 70 μm Cu-clad kapton, 128 μm pitch strips)
- Rate capability: > 10⁷ Hz/cm² (vs. ~10⁵ Hz/cm² for MWPC)
- Spatial resolution: 200 μm, sufficient for muon track matching to ID tracks
- Add **RPCs with glass electrodes** in outer stations for timing: **200 ps time resolution** for muon-vertex association in pile-up

---

## 7. Trigger and DAQ: The Enabling Backbone

### 7.1 Fully Triggerless Readout (Software-Only Trigger)

**Current state:** Even with full software trigger, an upstream hardware Level-0 trigger (e.g., ECAL ET, muon pT) introduces an irreducible efficiency loss for hadronic charm and beauty modes.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Implement **fully detector-readout at 40 MHz** (or 30 MHz for 25 ns bunch spacing) for all sub-detectors using optical data aggregators at **25 Gb/s per link** (VCSEL/VTRx+ technology, radiation-hard to 100 Mrad)
- Total data bandwidth: ~40–80 Tb/s → compressed to ~4 Tb/s at front-end FPGAs (Xilinx UltraScale+ or Intel Stratix 10) using **lossless zero-suppression and cluster finding in firmware**
- First-level software trigger on **GPU farm**: ~2000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs running Allen-framework successors for real-time track reconstruction + primary vertex finding at 40 MHz
- Latency budget: **4 μs** from collision to trigger decision, within L1 buffer depth of commercial DRAM (DDR5 at 4.8 Gb/s)

**Impact:** Hadronic trigger efficiency for D→Kππ improves from ~40% (hardware-threshold-based) to **>90%** (purely topological software selection), directly multiplying physics yields for rare charm decays, CPV measurements, and charm spectroscopy.

### 7.2 FPGA-Based Real-Time Pattern Recognition

- Deploy **Associative Memory ASICs** (AMchip05 generation or successors) or **large-FPGA content-addressable memory banks** for first-pass hit-pattern matching at 40 MHz before GPU farm
- Pattern banks preloaded with ~10⁹ patterns (covering pT > 500 MeV tracks in 5D hit space); output 5% event rate reduction with < 1 μs latency
- Enables coarser GPU first pass at 2 MHz equivalent rate, reducing GPU farm size by 3×

---

## 8. Magnet and Field Measurement

**Current:** Warm dipole magnet with ~4 Tm integrated field, field mapped with Hall probes.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Deploy **in-situ field measurement** using **NMR probes** (0.1 ppm field precision) on retractable rails inside the magnet aperture, with read-back at 1 kHz — eliminates systematic in track momentum scale calibration currently limiting B-mass and charm-mixing measurements
- Explore **superconducting dipole insert coils** in the innermost aperture to increase integrated field to ~6 Tm without enlarging detector volume, improving high-momentum (> 200 GeV) momentum resolution by ~50%; technically challenging but enables better B→J/ψμμ studies at high recoil

---

## Priority Ranking by Physics Impact

| Rank | Upgrade | Primary Gain |
|------|---------|-------------|
| 1 | Thin MAPS vertex detector | IP resolution, proper-time resolution |
| 2 | Fully software trigger (40 MHz readout) | Hadronic + charm trigger efficiency |
| 3 | 4D timing layers in VELO | Pile-up suppression |
| 4 | SiPM-based time-imaging RICH | PID efficiency and purity |
| 5 | GPU/FPGA trigger farm | Rate, latency, flexibility |
| 6 | GEM/μRWELL upstream tracker | Momentum resolution, ghost suppression |
| 7 | Radiation-hard ECAL inner (PWO fibres) | Radiative and e-ID modes |
| 8 | GEM muon inner stations | Rate sustainability |

---

## Summary

The single highest-leverage investment is a **thin MAPS pixel vertex detector combined with full 40 MHz triggerless readout**. Together these address the two fundamental constraints of the instrument class: the irreducible systematic from multiple scattering in the vertex region, and the per-event trigger efficiency loss that throttles hadronic physics. Every other upgrade — 4D timing, RICH SiPM timing, GEM trackers, calorimeter — compounds the gains from these two foundational changes.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Dual-Phase Xenon TPC Dark Matter Detector

## Framing the Problem

Primary physics performance means: **lower energy threshold, better signal/background discrimination (S2/S1 ratio and pulse shape), reduced backgrounds, and improved fiducialization**. I'll address each bottleneck with specific technologies.

---

## 1. Photosensor Replacement: PMTs → Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPDs/SiPMs)

**The core limitation:** Standard 3-inch Hamamatsu R11410 PMTs have ~35% QE at 175 nm (VUV), ~1 cm² effective area per unit, non-negligible radioactivity (~1–3 mBq/PMT from ⁴⁰K, ²³²Th chain), and single-photoelectron resolution limited by after-pulsing and transit-time spread.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- **VUV-sensitive SiPMs** — specifically **Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPCs** (S13371 series, 6×6 mm²) or **FBK VUV-HD3** tiles. These achieve **~24% PDE at 175 nm** in current generation, improving toward 40%+ with anti-reflective coating optimization for LXe emission spectrum (peak ~178 nm).
- **Tile format covering full arrays:** Replace ~250 PMTs per array with tiled 50×50 mm² SiPM modules (e.g., 36 × 6mm² cells per tile) using **low-radioactivity PCBs** (PTFE substrate, electroless Ni plating instead of standard FR4) to reduce U/Th backgrounds below 0.1 mBq/tile.
- **Operating temperature compatibility:** SiPMs must be qualified to 165 K; carrier boards use **thin-film cryogenic flex circuits** (polyimide/Cu, <50 µm) routed to feedthroughs.
- **Quantitative gain:** ~2× increase in light yield (from ~8–10 PE/keV to ~16–20 PE/keV), which directly **lowers threshold from ~1 keV_nr to ~0.3 keV_nr** and improves S1 detection efficiency for sub-keV electronic recoils.
- **Radioactivity budget:** Eliminating Kovar/glass PMT bodies removes the dominant internal gamma background; SiPM tile activity can be screened to <0.01 mBq/tile (⁶⁰Co, ²²⁶Ra) using ICP-MS and HPGe assay.

**Readout electronics consequence:** SiPM dark count rate at 165 K drops to ~0.1 Hz/mm², acceptable. Use **cryogenic ASIC front-ends** (e.g., modified ATLAS LAr LTDB chip or custom 65-nm CMOS cryo-ASIC) placed inside the xenon volume near tile arrays to minimize cable count and capacitive noise, achieving **ENC < 500 e⁻** per channel.

---

## 2. Electroluminescence Region: Improved Gate–Anode Configuration

**Current limitation:** The gate–anode gap (typically 5–10 mm, ~10 kV/cm) produces S2 signals but with geometric non-uniformity, photon absorption at wires, and electrostatic instability.

**Proposed upgrades:**

### 2a. Replacement of Wire Grids with Transparent Mesh Electrodes
- Replace standard **stainless steel wire grids** (100–200 µm wire, 5 mm pitch) with **etched titanium or electroformed copper mesh** (50 µm wire, 2.5 mm pitch, >80% optical transparency vs. ~65% for wire grids).
- Alternatively: **ITO-coated fused silica plates** (for the anode) providing near-100% optical transparency and well-defined uniform field — already demonstrated in small prototypes (e.g., Columbia/UCLA groups). ITO resistivity must be controlled to prevent charge accumulation; target **~1 kΩ/□ sheet resistance**.
- **Impact:** S2 photon collection improves by ~25%, directly improving single-electron S2 resolution and lowering the S2 detection threshold toward the single-electron level.

### 2b. Dual-Anode / Segmented Anode for S2 Position Resolution
- Implement a **segmented anode** with 2D strip or pixel readout (strip pitch ~5 mm), enabling reconstruction of x-y S2 position **directly from the charge signal** rather than relying solely on PMT hit pattern.
- Use **cryogenic charge-sensitive amplifiers** (CSA based on cryo-JFET or SiGe HBT) per strip, with noise target <200 e⁻ ENC.
- **Impact:** Spatial resolution improves from ~3–5 mm (PMT-pattern based) to **<1 mm rms**, dramatically improving fiducial volume definition and enabling identification of multiple-scatter events at mm scale (critical for coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CEνNS) background rejection).

---

## 3. Cathode High Voltage and Field Uniformity

**Current limitation:** Drift fields of 100–500 V/cm over ~1 m drift length require ~50–100 kV on cathode, creating HV instability, electron attachment from trace impurities, and field non-uniformity at the ~1% level from field-shaping resistor chains.

**Proposed upgrades:**

### 3a. Graded Field-Shaping with Precision Resistor Networks
- Replace standard **discrete resistor chains** (metal film, soldered on PCB rings) with **thick-film Pd/PdO resistors on PTFE-backed alumina substrates**, screened to <0.01 mBq/cm² for U/Th. Target resistance uniformity <0.1% per stage.
- Use **4-wire cryogenic Kelvin sensing** at 10 field-shaping rings (out of ~100) for continuous in-situ monitoring of resistor drift, with active feedback via a secondary bias network. This keeps field uniformity better than **0.5% across the active volume**.

### 3b. Improved HV Feedthrough
- Replace standard ceramic HV feedthroughs with **PTFE-body feedthroughs** with **graded stress-cone geometry** (modeled on XLPE cable termination technology) for stable operation to 150 kV.
- Use **ultrapure PTFE** (Dyneon or Chemours grade, <0.1 ppb U/Th measured by GDMS) for all insulators.

### 3c. Higher Drift Field Operation
- With improved purity (see §4), increase drift field from **200 V/cm → 500 V/cm**, which reduces charge recombination, improves NR/ER discrimination by ~15% in S2/S1 ratio at low energies, and raises electron lifetime requirement to >10 ms (achievable — see §4).

---

## 4. Xenon Purification: Continuous Cryogenic Distillation + Hot Getter

**Current limitation:** Krypton (⁸⁵Kr β-emitter) at ppq level and electronegative impurities (O₂, H₂O) at ppt level limit both the electronic recoil background and the electron lifetime.

**Proposed upgrades:**

### 4a. Online Cryogenic Distillation Column
- Install a **purpose-built packed distillation column** (100-tray equivalent, ~3 m tall, 150 mm ID, structured SS packing) integrated into the xenon gas handling system for **continuous Kr/Xe separation during detector operation**.
- Target: Kr/Xe < **0.01 ppt (molar)**, vs. current state-of-art ~0.1 ppt offline. This reduces ⁸⁵Kr ER background by 10×.
- Column thermal design: condenser at 170 K (liquid Xe reflux), reboiler at 180 K, insulated cryostat, reflux ratio ~10:1 for this separation factor.
- Processing rate: ~1 kg/hr xenon throughput while keeping detector inventory stable.

### 4b. Hot Zirconium Getter Upgrade
- Replace standard **SAES MonoTorr PS4-MT15** getters with **SAES PS4-MT50 (50 slpm)** units in parallel, operated at 400°C, removing O₂/H₂O/N₂ to <0.1 ppb.
- Add **cryogenic cold trap** (liquid N₂, 77 K, molecular sieve 5Å) upstream of getter for water/CO₂ bulk removal, extending getter lifetime by 5×.
- **Target electron lifetime >20 ms** (vs. typical 5–10 ms now), meaning charge attenuation <5% over full 1 m drift length even at higher field.

### 4c. Rn Emanation Mitigation
- The next irreducible background at post-Kr level. **Plate all inner-surface components** (field rings, PTFE reflectors, cable jackets) with **electroless gold or PFA coating** to reduce Rn emanation rates. PFA heat-shrink tubing on all cable bundles provides factor ~3 reduction in cable Rn emanation (measured by Borexino group).
- Install **electrostatic Rn concentrator/monitor** inline (PIN diode + ~5 kV bias, following Heidelberg design) for continuous Rn monitoring at **<0.1 µBq/kg** sensitivity.

---

## 5. Passive and Active Shielding Upgrades

### 5a. Water Cherenkov Veto: Upgrade to Gadolinium-Loaded Water
- Dissolve **Gd₂(SO₄)₃ at 0.1% by mass** in the water shield (as demonstrated by Super-Kamiokande's EGADS and SK-Gd programs).
- Gd captures thermal neutrons with σ~49,000 barns, emitting ~8 MeV gamma cascade detectable in the Cherenkov veto with **>95% efficiency** for single neutrons (vs. ~50% for pure water at this geometry).
- **Replace existing PMTs** in the water tank with **8-inch Hamamatsu R5912 PMTs with platinum undercoating** (Gd-water resistant), or preferably **20% coverage with 8-inch LAPPDs** (Large Area Picosecond Photodetectors, MCP-based, ~50 ps timing) for improved Cherenkov ring reconstruction and muon track fitting.
- This upgrade **rejects neutron-induced NR backgrounds by ~20×**, which becomes the dominant background after Kr and Rn reduction.

### 5b. Liquid Scintillator Skin/Veto (Inner Detector Upgrade)
- Instrument the **xenon "skin" region** (2–5 cm between field cage and cryostat wall) with **additional SiPM arrays** (same VUV4 tiles as inner detector) and a separate DAQ channel.
- Xenon skin acts as an **active veto** for gammas Compton-scattering from the field cage into the fiducial volume; skin signal resolves these events with **~95% efficiency** for deposits >1 keV.
- Add a thin (~2 mm) **acrylic shell loaded with 0.1% natural boron** (as boron-10 doped polymer) between outer cryostat and water tank for additional thermal neutron capture before Cherenkov veto.

---

## 6. Data Acquisition and Trigger

**Current limitation:** Triggering on S1 at sub-keV energies with 2t LXe produces ~100 photoelectrons, requiring zero-threshold digitization but limited by ADC noise and bandwidth.

**Proposed upgrades:**

- **Replace CAEN V1724 (14-bit, 100 MSPS)** digitizers with **CAEN V2740 (16-bit, 250 MSPS)** or **Struck SIS3316 (16-bit, 250 MSPS)** to improve dynamic range (capturing both S1 and S2 without saturation on the same channel without gain switching).
- Implement **FPGA-based online pulse finding** (Xilinx UltraScale+) with sub-PE threshold triggering, using matched-filter algorithms in real time. This enables **triggerless, buffered readout** with software trigger on any S1 ≥ 2 PE in coincidence, pushing threshold to ~0.1 keV_ee.
- Deploy **cryogenic pre-amplifiers** (cryo-JFET or SiGe BJT at 77 K stage) to reduce Johnson noise contribution from cable capacitance before room-temperature ADC.

---

## 7. Cryostat and Structural Materials

- **Replace all PTFE reflector panels** with **diamond-turned, specular PTFE** (Gore Diffuse Reflector or equivalent, >99% reflectivity at 178 nm, verified by VUV spectrophotometry), vs. standard machined PTFE (~97%). Over 2t active volume this gives ~5% more photons collected.
- **Inner cryostat vessel**: Upgrade to **electropolished low-background titanium (Grade 2)** with <0.1 mBq/kg for ²³²Th/²³⁸U (achievable with GDMS screening and controlled melting in electron-beam furnace). Titanium has lower mass and activity than 304 SS for equivalent structural performance.
- All **O-rings and seals**: Replace with **all-metal knife-edge (VCR/CF) seals** or **Helicoflex Delta metal seals** everywhere feasible; where elastomer is unavoidable, use **Kalrez 6375 FFKM** screened to <0.5 mBq/kg Th.

---

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Quantitative Estimate |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM arrays (VUV4) | Light yield, threshold | +2× LY, threshold → 0.3 keV_nr |
| Transparent mesh anode + segmented charge | S2 resolution, fiducialization | Position resolution <1 mm, S2 threshold → 1 e⁻ |
| Higher drift field (500 V/cm) + long e⁻ lifetime | NR/ER discrimination | ~15% improvement in S2/S1 band separation |
| Cryogenic distillation (Kr) | ER background | 10× reduction in ⁸⁵Kr rate |
| Rn mitigation | ER/NR background | ~3–5× reduction in ²²²Rn rate |
| Gd-loaded water Cherenkov | Neutron NR background | ~20× neutron veto efficiency improvement |
| Xenon skin SiPM veto | Gamma background | ~95% rejection of peripheral Compton scatters |
