This reduces LXe temperature variation from ±0.1°C to ±5 mK, improving drift velocity stability and simplifying position reconstruction calibration

---

## Summary Prioritization

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Technical Risk | Relative Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| SiPM photosensor arrays | +2× light yield, lower threshold | High | Very High |
| Full-voltage cathode HV | +3× NR charge yield | Medium | Very High |
| Inline Rn trap | ÷10 dominant ER background | Low | High |
| Gd-LAB neutron veto | ÷5-10 NR background | Medium | High |
| Increased purification flow | τe > 1.5 ms, uniform response | Low | Medium |
| Low-threshold DAQ | Single-electron S2 sensitivity | Low | Medium |

The SiPM replacement and full-voltage operation represent the two highest-leverage improvements, each potentially transforming the experiment's sensitivity to low-mass WIMPs. The radon trap addresses the dominant measured background with relatively straightforward engineering.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for SNO

Based on the technical specifications described in the paper, I'll propose targeted upgrades addressing the primary physics goal: precise measurement of CC/NC flux ratios for solar neutrino oscillation studies.

---

## 1. Photomultiplier System Replacement

### Current Limitations
- Hamamatsu R1408 with 31% bare photocathode coverage (54% effective with concentrators)
- 1.7 ns RMS timing resolution
- ~500 Hz dark rate at operating temperature
- 850 g glass envelope contributing ~40 ppb Th/U each

### Proposed Upgrade: Large-Area Microchannel Plate PMTs

Replace R1408 tubes with **Hamamatsu R5912 or equivalent 20cm MCP-PMTs** featuring:

- **Transit time spread of ~130 ps** versus 1.7 ns, directly improving vertex reconstruction precision from roughly 25 cm to under 10 cm at solar neutrino energies
- **Bialkali photocathode quantum efficiency of 35%** versus ~25% for R1408 at 420 nm, yielding approximately 40% more photoelectrons per event
- This improves the energy resolution from roughly **6.5%/√E to below 5%/√E**, directly reducing systematic uncertainty on the CC/NC ratio

### Complementary: Replace Winston Cone Concentrators

Current dielectric-coated aluminum reflectors achieve 82% mean reflectance. Replace with:

- **Angular-selective dichroic multilayer interference coatings** (e.g., sputtered SiO₂/TiO₂ stacks) achieving >95% reflectance at 350-500 nm across the Cherenkov spectrum
- Redesign cone geometry using **compound parabolic concentrator (CPC) profiles** computed for the actual D₂O/H₂O refractive index boundary, replacing the current three-dimensional critical angle design, recovering an additional ~8% photon collection

---

## 2. Front-End Electronics Replacement

### Current Limitations
- SNOD/SNOINT bipolar ASICs in AT&T CBICU-2 process (late 1980s technology)
- QUSN7 CMOS chip in Northern Telecom CMOS4S process
- 12-bit ADCs at 2 µs conversion time
- ~400 ns per-channel deadtime window
- 16-deep analog memory limits burst handling

### Proposed Upgrade: Full Waveform Digitization

Replace the three-chip ASIC set with **direct waveform sampling electronics**:

**Per-channel frontend cards** based on:
- **DRS4 switched-capacitor array** (Paul Scherrer Institute) sampling at 5 GSPS with 11.5 effective bits, capturing the full PMT pulse shape
  - Enables offline pulse shape discrimination between Cherenkov and scintillation-like backgrounds
  - Sub-100 ps timing resolution from waveform fitting versus leading-edge discrimination
  - Distinguishes prepulses, late pulses, and after-pulses in offline analysis rather than hardware cuts
- **16k sample depth** (versus 16 cells) provides 3.2 µs capture window, sufficient for complete neutron thermalization timing correlations in the NCD phase

**Digital trigger replacement:**
- Replace the analog summation tree with **FPGA-based (Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+) digital trigger** processing full PMT hit patterns at 250 MHz
- Implement **position-sensitive triggers** reconstructing approximate event vertex in real time to reduce the threshold on the fiducial volume trigger from the current ~100-ns coincidence to topology-aware triggers, suppressing PMT-glass Cherenkov backgrounds that currently dominate near the 5 MeV threshold
- Achievable trigger threshold reduction from ~5 MeV to **~3.5 MeV**, recovering a significantly larger fraction of the ⁸B spectrum where CC/NC discrimination is most powerful

---

## 3. NCD Array Readout Electronics

### Current Limitations
- Single 91Ω coaxial cable per string carries multiplexed pulse-reflection timing
- Pulse-shape discrimination done post-digitization with limited bandwidth
- Tritium contamination in ³He requires cold-trap processing to 5 nCi/L

### Proposed Upgrade: Per-String Digitization

- Replace single-cable readout with **underwater pre-amplifier modules** (similar to those developed for KM3NeT) housing **14-bit 250 MSPS ADCs** at the top of each string
- Full waveform capture of the 3He ionization current profile enables **improved alpha/neutron discrimination** - the current analysis takes only 25% efficiency (versus 45% capture) due to alpha contamination; improved pulse shape analysis could recover this to 35-38% effective efficiency
- Use **GaN-based HV power regulators** (e.g., EPC2038 class devices) replacing the current resistor-chain dividers, reducing per-string power dissipation and thus thermal convection currents that affect D₂O optical stability

### ³He Pressure Optimization
- Current 2.5 atm at 85%/15% ³He/CF₄ was a compromise for wall-effect mitigation
- Reoptimize to **3.0 atm with 90%/10% mixture** - the higher pressure is now safely achievable with improved nickel tube CVD wall uniformity (±0.005 cm versus the ±0.012 cm specified), increasing neutron capture efficiency by approximately 4 percentage points

---

## 4. Water Purification Enhancement

### Current Limitations
- Rn specification requires <3.2×10⁻¹⁵ g/g Ra equivalent
- Process Degasser removes Rn by factor ~50
- Cover gas system uses liquid nitrogen boiloff at <10⁻⁵ pCi/L

### Proposed Upgrade: Membrane Degassing with Heated Ultrapure Nitrogen Sweep

Replace the vacuum Process Degasser with:

- **Liqui-Cel membrane contactors** (3M, 14-inch diameter) in series configuration achieving Rn removal factors exceeding 200 versus the current ~50, with no moving parts reducing failure modes
- **Electrolytic ultra-pure N₂ generation** on-site replacing liquid dewar boiloff - modern PEM electrolyzers with Pd/Ag membrane purification produce N₂ at <10⁻⁷ pCi/L Rn without cold-chain logistics

For D₂O Th/U reduction below the current 3×10⁻¹⁵ g/g Th specification:

- Add a **MnO₂-coated silica bead column** (1 m³) in the D₂O recirculation loop with demonstrated extraction efficiency >99% for Ra, Th, and Pb at flow rates of 50 L/min
- This provides continuous in-situ purification rather than the batch SUF assay process, reducing systematic uncertainty on neutron background from photodisintegration

---

## 5. Acrylic Vessel Optical Improvement

### Current Limitations
- Bulk absorption coefficient 0.04 cm⁻¹ at 360 nm limits detection of Cherenkov photons near the PMT quantum efficiency peak
- Average figure of merit 0.73 (ratio of light detected with vs. without acrylic) at 300-440 nm

### Proposed Upgrade: Surface Antireflection Treatment

While the bulk acrylic cannot be replaced without full reconstruction, the optical performance can be improved by:

- Apply **sol-gel SiO₂ antireflection coatings** (refractive index ~1.23, versus acrylic n=1.49) to the inner and outer surfaces of the acrylic vessel in accessible regions via ROV-deployed spray applicator
- This reduces the Fresnel reflection loss at each acrylic surface from ~4% to <0.5% at normal incidence, recovering approximately 7% more Cherenkov photons
- Sol-gel coatings have been demonstrated stable in ultrapure water environments (SNO+ acrylic studies) and do not leach measurable U/Th

---

## 6. Magnetic Field Compensation

### Current Limitations
- 14 horizontal compensation coils cancel only the vertical component of Earth's field (55 µT)
- Maximum residual field 19 µT causes 2.5% efficiency reduction
- Horizontal components uncompensated

### Proposed Upgrade: Three-Axis Active Compensation

- Install **6 additional vertical-field coils** (3 pairs in ±x and ±y orientations) embedded in cavity floor and deck, wound from same low-radioactivity conductor
- **Fluxgate magnetometer array** of 12 sensors distributed on the PSUP provides real-time field mapping
- Three-axis compensation reduces maximum residual field to **<5 µT**, recovering an additional ~1.5% PMT efficiency uniformly across the array
- Critically, this makes the **efficiency correction spatially uniform** rather than the current zenith-angle dependent correction, reducing systematic uncertainty in the NC/CC flux ratio

---

## Quantified Physics Impact Summary

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Estimated CC/NC Ratio Systematic Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| MCP-PMT replacement | Vertex resolution, photoelectron yield | Reduces fiducial volume uncertainty by ~40% |
| Waveform digitization | Background rejection, threshold reduction | Extends energy range, improves NC isolation |
| NCD waveform readout | Neutron detection efficiency +10 pp | Reduces NC statistical uncertainty by ~15% |
| Enhanced Rn removal | Photodisintegration background ×4 reduction | Reduces NC background subtraction systematic by ~50% |
| Three-axis B compensation | Uniform PMT efficiency | Reduces energy scale systematic by ~0.8% |

The combination of MCP-PMT replacement and full waveform digitization provides the largest single improvement, as both the CC electron energy spectrum measurement and the NC neutron detection efficiency are directly limited by photon counting statistics and vertex resolution in the current design.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for DarkSide-50 Physics Performance

## Diagnosis: What Actually Limits the Experiment

Before proposing upgrades, the paper clearly identifies the binding constraints:

1. **Dominant background is scintillation+Cherenkov events** from Teflon reflector, not ER from radioactivity
2. **PMTs are the dominant source of both radiogenic neutrons and γ-ray backgrounds** (>90% of radiogenic neutrons; largest γ contributors)
3. **x-y position reconstruction is poor** due to 3" PMT proximity to S2 emission region, limiting radial fiducialization
4. **39Ar residual activity** still contributes even in UAr
5. **PSD statistics are photoelectron-limited** at low S1

---

## Upgrade 1: Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

This addresses the single largest background source directly.

### Motivation from Paper
The paper states PMTs contribute >90% of radiogenic neutron background through their borosilicate glass stems and ceramic dynode supports. PMTs also dominate γ-ray backgrounds (Table I: 232Th at 0.277 Bq, 40K at 2.74 Bq across 38 PMTs). The paper explicitly notes they had to use R11065 instead of the planned lower-activity R11065-20s.

### Specific Implementation
- **Device:** Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPC series (S13370 series, 3×3 mm² cells at 75 µm pitch) or Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) RGB-HD SiPMs adapted for VUV/TPB emission at 420 nm
- **Configuration:** Tile arrays of ~1 cm² individual SiPM devices assembled into ~10×10 cm² modules to cover the same solid angle as the 3" PMTs
- **Radioactivity advantage:** SiPMs are fabricated from ultra-pure silicon with no borosilicate glass, ceramics, or Kovar metal. Expected specific activity of 232Th and 238U in silicon is <0.1 mBq/kg compared to the fitted PMT values — reduction by factors of 10–100 in neutron-producing materials
- **Cryogenic operation:** SiPMs operate well at LAr temperature (87 K); dark noise rate drops dramatically at cryogenic temperatures (from ~100 kcps/mm² at 300 K to ~0.1 cps/mm² at 77 K), actually improving single-photon sensitivity relative to PMT dark rate
- **Required engineering:** Custom cryogenic readout ASICs (e.g., based on the ABCD or similar low-noise charge-sensitive amplifier designs already in development for LArTPC experiments) to handle ~200 channels per tile module without the cryogenic preamp complexity currently needed for PMTs. Surface-mount on polyimide flex circuits rather than ceramic substrates to reduce radioactivity further.
- **Photon detection efficiency:** VUV4 devices achieve ~35-40% PDE at 420 nm vs. ~30% quantum efficiency for R11065, improving photoelectron yield and hence PSD at low energies

### Quantitative Impact
Eliminating >90% of the radiogenic neutron source directly reduces that background to negligible levels. The γ-ray background from PMTs (which drives the Cherenkov background that is the dominant remaining background) would be reduced proportionally, potentially reducing the ER background by a factor of 5–10.

---

## Upgrade 2: Replace Teflon Reflector with Ultra-Pure Acrylic or Sapphire Panels

### Motivation from Paper
The paper explicitly identifies **scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov** as "the dominant ER background in the experiment" after all cuts. The S1pMaxFrac cut eliminates fused-silica Cherenkov but is ineffective against Teflon Cherenkov. The S1NLL cut and RadialFid cut provide only modest additional rejection.

### Specific Implementation
- **Material option A — Ultra-pure acrylic (PMMA):** Acrylic produces Cherenkov light, but its Cherenkov threshold for electrons is ~175 keV (refractive index ~1.49), similar to Teflon. However, acrylic can be cast and machined to optical quality, enabling specular rather than diffuse reflection. More importantly, it can be produced with demonstrated radiopurity at the level of <10 ppt 238U and 232Th (as demonstrated for SNO and Borexino). **The key advantage is that acrylic does not have the millisecond-long TPB-mediated α scintillation** that complicates surface background, and its Cherenkov yield per unit length is lower than Teflon due to lower electron density.
- **Material option B — Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) with reduced TPB coating thickness:** The LongS1tail cut (Sec. V B) already exploits α-induced TPB scintillation for surface event rejection. The Cherenkov background from Teflon itself could be reduced by switching to a **specular reflector** such as 3M ESR (Enhanced Specular Reflector) film laminated onto ultra-pure aluminum panels. Specular reflection changes the photon path statistics and could allow better discrimination of Cherenkov light (which deposits near the wall) from bulk scintillation via PMT/SiPM hit pattern analysis.
- **Material option C — Single-crystal sapphire tiles:** Al2O3 has higher refractive index (~1.77) meaning higher Cherenkov threshold (~100 keV) but more light production per electron above threshold. However, sapphire can be produced with extremely low radioactivity (<0.1 ppt U/Th), eliminating the γ-ray source that produces the Cherenkov-emitting electrons in the first place. Sapphire tiles could be polished to optical quality, uncoated (reflective via total internal reflection for 420 nm light arriving at shallow angles), eliminating TPB on the barrel while using a thin TPB coating only on the windows.

### Quantitative Impact
Since scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov dominates the ER background, and the paper states that the Cherenkov model had to be scaled up by 1.5× to match data even after extensive validation, eliminating or reducing this source would be transformative. Reducing this by a factor of 5 would bring total predicted background well below 0.02 events in an equivalent exposure.

---

## Upgrade 3: Segmented Anode for Improved x-y Position Reconstruction

### Motivation from Paper
The paper explicitly states (Sec. I): "reconstruction of the x-y position of events in DarkSide-50 proved to be very difficult... believed to be due to the proximity of the top PMTs to the S2-emission region, which limits charge sharing among the 3" PMTs." The radial fiducial cut achieves only (2.3±0.5) rejection against Cherenkov background, and the position resolution is only ~0.6 cm, estimated only from 214Bi-214Po coincidences.

### Specific Implementation
- **Primary upgrade: Segmented wire grid or GEM (Gas Electron Multiplier) anode** replacing the ITO-coated fused silica window
  - A **two-plane wire anode** with X and Y wire pitch of 3–5 mm, fabricated from ultra-pure copper-beryllium wires on a ceramic frame (verified radiopure), collects the S2 charge directly rather than inferring position from scintillation light pattern
  - Wire readout provides intrinsic 2D position with resolution equal to wire pitch (~3 mm), far better than the current optical reconstruction
  - Charge signals on individual wires encode both position and S2 amplitude simultaneously
  - Requires new feedthroughs but is technically established in large LAr TPCs (MicroBooNE, ICARUS)
- **Secondary upgrade: Finer-pitch photosensor array at top**
  - If SiPMs are adopted (Upgrade 1), the top array can use 16–32 individual SiPM tiles instead of 19 3" PMTs, improving the S2 light pattern sampling and providing a cross-check on wire-based position
  - With ~20 mm tile pitch, S2 light pattern reconstruction would have better than 5 mm resolution at the S2 energies of interest (>400 PE uncorrected)
- **Gas layer optimization:** Current 1 cm gas gap limits lateral diffusion that would help position reconstruction. Increasing to 1.5–2 cm improves S2 signal size (more proportional scintillation gain) and slightly increases transverse electron diffusion (~0.3 mm per cm of drift in the gas) which softens the S2 position signal but is more than compensated by the direct wire readout

### Quantitative Impact
The paper achieves 0.848 ± 0.002 acceptance for RadialFid with the current poor reconstruction. With wire-based position resolution of 3–5 mm, the fiducial boundary could be defined to within ±3 mm of the wall, potentially recovering 3–5% of fiducial volume while simultaneously applying a tighter radial cut (the paper's Fig. 13 shows available improvement with r < 10 cm). More importantly, genuine Cherenkov events from the wall would be rejected with a much higher factor than the current 2.3.

---

## Upgrade 4: Replace Fused Silica Windows with UV-Grade Crystalline Quartz or Sapphire

### Motivation from Paper
The S1pMaxFrac cut is needed specifically to reject Cherenkov light from fused silica windows, and even after this cut the paper states fused silica Cherenkov events are eliminated "leaving Cherenkov in the Teflon... as the dominant ER background." Eliminating the fused-silica Cherenkov source would remove the need for S1pMaxFrac entirely and reduce the cut burden.

### Specific Implementation
- **Replace fused silica with crystalline α-quartz windows:** Crystalline quartz has a higher UV absorption edge and different refractive index profile. More importantly, it can be grown with far fewer fluorescent defect centers that produce the anomalous late light contributing to the background
- **Preferred alternative — thin sapphire windows:** Al2O3 single crystal windows transmit TPB-shifted 420 nm light efficiently, have very low radioactivity, and critically have a **Cherenkov threshold of ~170 keV for electrons** (same order as fused silica, n~1.77), but sapphire can be etched with fine surface relief patterns that frustrate total internal reflection and cause Cherenkov photons generated within the window to be redirected in a distinctive angular pattern detectable by the photosensor array. This would allow event-by-event tagging of fused-window Cherenkov events rather than requiring the S1pMaxFrac cut to sacrifice acceptance.
- **ITO replacement:** The ITO cathode/anode coating on the windows contributes some radioactivity and causes light loss (~10% per surface at 420 nm). Replace with **thin (5–10 nm) sputtered indium-zinc oxide (IZO)** which has higher transmission at 420 nm (~97%) and can be deposited at lower temperatures that reduce stress on the window material.

### Quantitative Impact
Eliminating fused-silica Cherenkov as a background class would allow relaxing S1pMaxFrac, recovering the ~5% acceptance loss from that cut, and would simplify the background model by removing one of its two dominant Cherenkov components. The combined impact with Upgrade 2 would likely reduce total ER background by a factor of 10–20.

---

## Upgrade 5: Active Neutron Moderator Liner Inside the Cryostat

### Motivation from Paper
The PMTs are identified as producing >90% of radiogenic neutrons. If Upgrade 1 (SiPM replacement) is not immediately feasible, a complementary approach is to moderate and capture neutrons before they reach the active LAr.

### Specific Implementation
- **6LiF-loaded polyethylene panels** (0.5–1 cm thick) laminated to the inside of the outer cryostat wall, between the cryostat and the PMT mounting structure
  - 6Li has a thermal neutron capture cross-section of 940 barns, ~5× higher than 10B
  - The 6Li(n,α)3H reaction produces no γ rays above 2.05 MeV, making captures detectable in the LSV as a distinct low-energy signal
  - Polyethylene moderates fast neutrons from PMT glass (typically 1–5 MeV) to thermal energies within ~5 cm
  - 6LiF is chemically stable and available in radiopure form with U/Th at <10 ppt level
- **Borated polyethylene alternative:** If 6LiF panels are mechanically difficult to integrate, borated polyethylene (5% 10B by mass) panels serve the same function and are commercially available, though the 10B(n,α)7Li capture produces a 478 keV γ that must be managed (same reaction used in the LSV, already understood)
- **Panel geometry:** 5 mm thick panels behind the PMT/SiPM arrays, covering the cylindrical side wall and both end caps. Total mass ~2 kg. Fabricated in segments to allow assembly around existing PMT structure.

### Quantitative Impact
Monte Carlo simulations for similar geometries in other experiments suggest that a 5–10 mm polyethylene moderator reduces fast neutron flux from enclosed PMT assemblies by factors of 3–5. Combined with the LSV efficiency already at 0.9964, this would reduce radiogenic neutron background from <0.005 to well below 0.001 events per equivalent exposure.

---

## Upgrade 6: Improved Cathode Design to Eliminate Grid-Related Backgrounds

### Motivation from Paper
The current design uses a grid 4.7 mm beneath the liquid-gas interface to separate drift and extraction regions. Surface events on the cathode and grid are rejected by tdrift cuts but represent lost fiducial volume. The 210Po surface activity on the reflector at (2.51±0.01) mBq/m² produces backgrounds requiring multiple dedicated cuts.

### Specific Implementation
- **Replace wire grid with a **micro-mesh electrode** (similar to Micromegas technology):** A 200-line-per-inch stainless steel or copper-beryllium electroformed mesh with 50 µm wire diameter provides the field-shaping function of the current grid with dramatically reduced surface area for radon daughter deposition. Surface area reduction factor: current grid wires ~several cm² vs. mesh ~few mm² of exposed surface at the active region boundary.
- **Cathode upgrade:** Replace the ITO-coated fused silica cathode with a **thin (25 µm) gold-coated copper-beryllium mesh cathode** suspended across the bottom of the active volume. This eliminates the fused-silica Cherenkov source at the bottom (currently handled by the tdrift cut) and allows recovery of some fiducial volume at the bottom of the detector.
- **Electropolished surfaces:** All metal surfaces in the drift region (field cage rings, grid, cathode) should be electropolished to reduce surface roughness from ~1 µm Ra to <0.1 µm Ra, which reduces radon daughter attachment by reducing surface area at the microscopic level by a factor of ~3–10.

---

## Priority Ranking

| Upgrade | Background Addressed | Relative Impact | Technical Readiness |
|---------|---------------------|-----------------|---------------------|
| 1: SiPM arrays | Radiogenic neutrons, γ-ray → Cherenkov | Highest | Medium (cryo ASICs needed) |
| 2: Reflector material | Dominant Teflon Cherenkov ER background | High | Medium |
| 3: Segmented anode | Radial fiducialization | High | Medium-High |
| 4: Window material | Fused-silica Cherenkov ER background | Medium-High | High |
| 5: Neutron moderator liner | Radiogenic neutrons (if PMTs retained) | Medium | High |
| 6: Grid/cathode redesign | Surface backgrounds | Low-Medium | High |

**The single highest-leverage upgrade is SiPM replacement of the PMTs**, because it simultaneously attacks the dominant neutron source, the dominant γ-ray source, improves photoelectron yield (better PSD at low energies), and enables finer-pitch position reconstruction — addressing four of the five identified limitations simultaneously.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for the LUX Detector

## 1. PMT Array Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Current limitation:** The R8778 PMTs contribute 0.4 ER WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days, dominating the background budget (Table 3). Each PMT contains Fe, Ni, Co, glass, and other radioactive materials at levels of 9.8 mBq/PMT (U), 65 mBq/PMT (K-40).

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace 122 PMTs with tiled arrays of Hamamatsu VUV4 or FBK VUV-HD SiPMs, which have demonstrated radiopurity at the μBq/cm² level — roughly 3-4 orders of magnitude cleaner than the R8778s
- SiPMs are fabricated from ultrapure silicon with no glass envelope, dynode chain, or metal body
- Modern VUV-sensitive SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13371 series) achieve >15% photon detection efficiency at 175 nm in LXe, competitive with the R8778's 33% QE × 90% collection efficiency when deployed in closely-packed tiles
- Mount SiPMs on low-radioactivity PTFE-backed PCBs using acrylic adhesive rather than copper support structures, further reducing the copper contribution (0.03 ER events/30,000 kg-days in Table 3)
- Eliminate the 12 LED calibration sources since SiPMs can be individually dark-rate monitored and gain-calibrated electronically without optical injection

**Expected improvement:** PMT-sourced ER background reduced by factor ~100-1000, making internal backgrounds negligible relative to the 85Kr and neutrino floor contributions.

---

## 2. Inline Cryogenic Krypton Removal System

**Current limitation:** 85Kr contributes <0.13 ER WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days (Table 3), and this estimate depends entirely on getter removal efficiency. Natural krypton at the ppb level in xenon produces 85Kr beta decays at ~1 Bq/kg-Xe. The existing SAES getter removes electronegative impurities but does not remove noble gas krypton.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Install a dedicated cryogenic distillation column inline with the existing gas recirculation path, between the getter output and the condenser return line
- Use a packed-column design operating at ~170 K with a 10:1 reflux ratio, as demonstrated by the XENON100/1T groups achieving Kr/Xe < 0.02 ppt
- Specify a stainless steel column, 2 m tall × 5 cm diameter, packed with structured stainless mesh packing (Sulzer EX-type), sized for the existing 50 SLPM (420 kg/day) circulation rate
- Integrate a gas chromatograph with electron capture detector on the return line for continuous ppq-level Kr monitoring rather than periodic cold-trap mass spectrometry sampling
- Add a parallel radon-removal charcoal trap (Saratech or equivalent activated charcoal at -40°C) on the gas return line to reduce Rn ingress, which produces 214Pb and 214Bi backgrounds near the detector walls

**Expected improvement:** Kr/Xe reduced from ~ppt to <0.02 ppt level, reducing 85Kr contribution to effectively zero relative to other backgrounds.

---

## 3. Upgraded Cathode High-Voltage System with Internal Feedthrough

**Current limitation:** The current HV system routes the 100 kV cable through a room-temperature feedthrough outside the water shield, through a 25 cm unshielded section in liquid xenon, with xenon drawn away at 0.1 SLPM to prevent outgassed impurity back-diffusion. This represents a continuous impurity source and limits the achievable drift field.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Design a custom low-radioactivity HV feedthrough operating at LXe temperature, following the approach demonstrated by ICARUS but adapted for the titanium cryostat geometry
- Use a coaxial design with UHMW polyethylene dielectric rated to 150 kV, with a titanium outer conductor (CP1 grade, matching cryostat material) and a single OFHC copper inner conductor
- Eliminate the HVC100 cable entirely within the xenon volume, replacing the spring-loaded pin connection with a welded or soldered joint made during TPC assembly
- Install the feedthrough through the bottom dome of the inner cryostat rather than through the top flange, allowing the full cathode-to-gate drift distance to benefit from field uniformity
- Increase operating voltage from 100 kV to 150 kV, raising drift field from 2 kV/cm to 3 kV/cm, improving electron-recoil discrimination by reducing recombination fluctuations and increasing electron lifetime sensitivity

**Expected improvement:** Elimination of the 0.1 SLPM purge flow as an impurity source; drift field increase from 2 to 3 kV/cm improves ER/NR discrimination from ~99.3% to projected ~99.7% based on XENON100 field-dependence measurements; improved electron lifetime allowing longer drift distances in future scaled-up versions.

---

## 4. Replacement of Resistive Field-Shaping Chain with Active Feedback Network

**Current limitation:** The 1 GΩ resistor chain between cathode and gate dissipates ~10 mW at 100 kV operating voltage (I = 100 nA through the chain). More critically, resistor radioactivity contributes to backgrounds near the field cage, and resistor tolerance variations produce field non-uniformities that distort 3D position reconstruction near the PTFE walls, reducing the effective fiducial volume.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the passive resistor chain with a chain of cryogenic-rated Zener diode voltage dividers, implemented with back-to-back pairs of low-leakage Zener diodes (BZX79 series equivalents selected for low-temperature operation)
- At LXe temperature (165 K), silicon Zener diodes exhibit highly stable and reproducible voltage clamping with <0.01% variation, compared to the ±1% tolerance of 1 GΩ resistors
- Mount the Zener chain on a thin PTFE ribbon PCB laminated to the inside face of the existing copper field rings, eliminating discrete resistor bodies as radioactive point sources
- Add four independent HV monitoring electrodes at 90° azimuthal positions at mid-drift height, capacitively coupled to field rings, to provide real-time field uniformity monitoring via the slow control system
- Implement active trim capability: add one DAC-controlled trim electrode per meter of drift, addressable through the existing slow control infrastructure, to compensate for space charge accumulation from high-rate calibration sources

**Expected improvement:** Field uniformity improved from ~1% variation (estimated from current design) to <0.1%, reducing position reconstruction systematic errors near the wall from ~5 mm to <1 mm, effectively increasing fiducial volume by ~5% at fixed wall-cut radius.

---

## 5. Dual-Channel Waveform Digitizer Upgrade with Zero-Suppression FPGA Processing

**Current limitation:** The Struck SIS3301 ADCs digitize at 100 MHz with 14-bit resolution. The Pulse Only Digitization (POD) mode reduces data volume, but the 30 MHz anti-aliasing filter on each channel limits timing resolution for S1 pulse shape discrimination. Single photoelectron pulses have FWHM of 7.7 ns, requiring >130 MHz Nyquist-compliant sampling for full pulse shape capture.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace SIS3301 modules with Struck SIS3316 or equivalent 250 MHz, 14-bit ADCs providing Nyquist-compliant sampling of the 7.7 ns FWHM single photoelectron pulses
- Implement on-FPGA matched filtering for single photoelectron identification, replacing the external DDC-8DSP trigger processors with on-board processing that computes running S1/S2 likelihood ratios in real time
- Add a second digitization channel per PMT operating at 10× attenuation to extend dynamic range from the current ~2 V to ~20 V, capturing large S2 pulses from calibration sources without saturation while retaining single photoelectron sensitivity on the primary channel
- Deploy FPGA firmware implementing per-channel dark rate monitoring at 1 Hz cadence, replacing the weekly LED-based afterpulse measurement schedule with continuous PMT health tracking
- Increase DAQ fiber bandwidth from 1 Gbit to 10 Gbit using SIS1100 replacement modules to accommodate the increased data rate from 250 MHz sampling across 122 channels

**Expected improvement:** S1 pulse shape discrimination using the triplet/singlet ratio of LXe scintillation (45 ns vs 22 ns time constants) becomes viable as an additional ER/NR discrimination axis, providing an independent rejection factor of ~3-5× supplementing the existing S2/S1 ratio discrimination; elimination of digitizer saturation on calibration events reduces dead time.

---

## 6. Neutron Veto System Using Gadolinium-Loaded Water

**Current limitation:** The muon veto uses 20 PMTs in pure water detecting Cherenkov radiation, achieving >90% muon rejection efficiency. However, neutrons that enter the water shield from the rock and scatter in the xenon before being captured are not vetoed — the system has no sensitivity to neutron captures that occur after the prompt LXe interaction.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Dissolve gadolinium sulfate (Gd₂(SO₄)₃) in the water shield at 0.1% mass concentration, as demonstrated in the EGADS/Super-K-Gd program
- At 0.1% Gd loading, thermal neutron capture cross-section increases by factor ~1000 over pure water (Gd thermal capture cross-section 49,000 barns vs. 0.33 barns for H)
- Neutron capture on ¹⁵⁷Gd produces a prompt 8 MeV gamma cascade detectable in the Cherenkov PMT array within ~30 μs of the LXe interaction
- Upgrade water tank PMT count from 20 to 60 Hamamatsu R7081 PMTs (20% photocathode coverage of tank walls), maintaining Cherenkov detection efficiency for muons while achieving ~70% neutron capture detection efficiency
- Install a Gd-compatible water purification system (reverse osmosis followed by ion exchange resin tolerant of Gd³⁺) to maintain the existing U/Th/K purity requirements while retaining dissolved Gd
- Add a dedicated 100 μs coincidence trigger window in the DAQ between LXe events and water tank signals to tag delayed neutron captures

**Expected improvement:** Neutron background from rock (currently ~0.03 events/30,000 kg-days) and water shield (~0.07 events/30,000 kg-days) reduced by additional factor of ~5-10 through post-scatter neutron tagging, making neutron backgrounds completely negligible; this upgrade path is directly scalable to future larger xenon detectors.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for SNO: Specific Proposals

## Framing the Problem

SNO's primary physics goal is distinguishing CC from NC neutrino interactions to measure flavor transformation. The limiting factors are: **energy threshold**, **energy resolution**, **neutron detection efficiency**, **radioactive backgrounds**, and **vertex reconstruction accuracy**. I address each with concrete hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Photomultiplier Tube Upgrades

### 1.1 Replace R1408 with Higher-Quantum-Efficiency Tubes

The R1408 operates at roughly 21–22% peak quantum efficiency at 420 nm. The photocathode coverage after concentrators reaches ~54% effective efficiency. Every improvement here directly lowers the energy threshold and improves resolution.

**Proposal:** Replace with Hamamatsu R3600 or equivalent 20-cm hemispherical tubes using bialkali photocathodes optimized for 350–420 nm, targeting QE above 25%. The hemispherical geometry captures more of the Cherenkov spectrum's blue-UV peak compared to the mushroom geometry of the R1408. The critical tradeoff is that the R1408 mushroom shape was chosen for hydraulic pressure resistance at 200 kPa — a hemispherical replacement would require either thicker glass (increasing radioactivity from the ~40 ppb Th/U in Schott 8246) or pressure housing redesign.

**Concrete specification:** Use Schott 8246 borosilicate maintained at <40 ppb Th/U but increase wall thickness in the faceplate from the current design to survive 300 kPa, providing safety margin. The photocathode area gain from hemispherical geometry at 20 cm diameter is approximately 15–20% over the R1408 at equivalent diameter, directly improving the ~8 photoelectrons/MeV figure cited in the paper. This would push the figure toward 10–11 pe/MeV, lowering the effective threshold from approximately 5 MeV toward 4 MeV and materially increasing the CC event rate in the critical 5–8 MeV solar neutrino window.

### 1.2 Improved Light Concentrators

The paper states current concentrators have mean effective reflectance of 82 ± 3% in water. The coating is specular aluminum with MgF₂ and mixed TiO₂/Pr₂O₃ dielectric layers.

**Proposal:** Replace the aluminum substrate with a silver-substrate reflector using a protective Al₂O₃ overcoat deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD). Silver has peak reflectance above 95% at 400–500 nm compared to aluminum's ~90%, and above 98% at 600 nm. The challenge is that bare silver corrodes in deionized water — the ALD Al₂O₃ overcoat at 20–30 nm thickness provides corrosion resistance while transmitting effectively at wavelengths above 300 nm. The paper describes a dielectric stack on aluminum; replacing the reflective base layer while keeping the protective dielectric architecture improves mean reflectance from 82% to approximately 90–93%, increasing effective photocathode coverage from 54% to approximately 59–62%.

**Radioactivity constraint:** Silver itself contains no significant Th or U. The ALD Al₂O₃ precursor (trimethylaluminum and water) leaves negligible metallic contamination. This upgrade is radioactively benign.

---

## 2. Neutral-Current Detector Array Improvements

The paper describes 96 strings of ³He proportional counters with 770 m total length giving ~37% neutron capture efficiency. Several specific improvements are warranted.

### 2.1 Pulse Shape Discrimination Electronics

The paper acknowledges that alpha particles can deposit the same ionization as ³He(n,p)T events, and that pulse-shape discrimination is needed but requires digitizing ion-current profiles event by event. The described implementation is not fully specified in hardware detail.

**Proposal:** Replace the single coaxial readout cable per string with a delay-line position-encoding scheme using faster digitization. Specifically, instrument each NCD string with a Flash ADC (FADC) module at 100 MHz sampling rate with 8-bit resolution, sufficient to capture the 50–500 ns risetime differences between nuclear recoil (neutron) events and alpha/electron backgrounds. The paper notes the anode wire is 50 μm copper with gas gain ~100 at 1650 V — at this gain, the ion drift time to the cathode wall (5.08 cm diameter) at 2.5 atm He/CF₄ is approximately 5–15 μs, providing adequate time structure for discrimination.

**Concrete implementation:** The FADC modules should be placed at the deck level (outside the water volume) to avoid underwater electronics reliability issues. The 91 Ω coaxial cable described (South Bay Cable, copper/polyethylene) has 4.9 ns/m delay at the specified geometry — for a 11 m string this gives ~54 ns propagation time, adequate for maintaining pulse shape integrity to the FADC. Alpha events produce longer, multi-peaked pulses from wall effects; neutron events produce characteristic single Bragg-peak profiles. With 100 MHz sampling and appropriate shaping, discrimination factors of 100:1 between alphas and neutrons are achievable in comparable proportional counter systems, directly reducing the background subtraction uncertainty.

### 2.2 Increase ³He Pressure

The paper uses 2.5 atm He/CF₄ at 85%/15% ratio. The choice is described as a compromise between gas gain, stopping power, and wall effect mitigation.

**Proposal:** Increase to 4.0 atm while increasing CF₄ fraction to 20% to maintain adequate stopping power for the triton (range ~0.5 cm at 2.5 atm, ~0.3 cm at 4 atm). The operating voltage would increase from 1650 V to approximately 2000–2100 V to maintain gas gain ~100. The benefit: neutron capture cross section in ³He scales with 1/v so thermal capture efficiency per unit length increases proportionally with pressure. The current 37% array efficiency (Table 4) could be increased toward 45–50% with the same physical string arrangement.

**Pressure vessel constraint:** The paper notes the absolute pressure at the bottom of the SNO vessel is 3.1 atm. The NCD wall thickness is 0.036 cm of CVD nickel. At 4.0 atm fill pressure plus 3.1 atm external hydrostatic pressure at the bottom, the differential pressure across the wall reverses sign at depth — the wall is in compression from external pressure, which CVD nickel handles well given its high compressive strength. The limiting case is at the top of the vessel where external pressure is ~1.3 atm and internal is 4.0 atm, giving 2.7 atm outward differential, compared to current 1.2 atm outward differential. The hoop stress scales linearly: current stress = (1.2 atm × 0.0254 m) / (0.00036 m) = ~847 kPa hoop stress in the wall material, well within CVD nickel's yield strength of approximately 300–400 MPa. A factor of 2.25 increase remains safely within structural margins.

### 2.3 Position-Sensitive Readout

The paper describes a 30 ns delay-line termination for pulse-reflection timing. This allows position determination along the string axis, useful for rejecting end-region backgrounds.

**Proposal:** Add a second readout point at the bottom termination, converting the single-ended readout to a true delay-line doublet. The current design has a 415 Ω open-ended 30 ns delay line at the bottom; adding an active low-impedance tap with a second cable up the outside of the string to deck electronics enables position determination with resolution of (cable delay × signal propagation speed) / 2 ≈ (1 ns timing resolution × 20 cm/ns effective speed) / 2 ≈ 10 cm position resolution along the string axis. This allows rejection of events within 13 cm of the endcap dead regions (already excluded from active length per the paper) with a fiducial cut, and importantly allows identification of events clustered near string ends that suggest endcap radioactivity contamination rather than genuine neutron captures.

---

## 3. Water Purification System Enhancements

The paper specifies target levels of 3 × 10⁻¹⁵ g/g Th and 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ g/g U in D₂O, driven by photodisintegration of deuterium. Achieving and verifying these levels is the central challenge.

### 3.1 Online Radium Monitor

The paper describes MnOₓ bead columns for Ra extraction run offline. The assay cycle involves removing the column and counting Ra daughters with a silicon detector electrostatic device.

**Proposal:** Install a continuous-flow MnOₓ extraction column with an in-line silicon PIN detector array (4 detectors at 90° azimuthal spacing around the flow tube) for real-time alpha counting of ²²²Rn daughters plated onto the detector surface. PIN detectors of 300 mm² area with 20 μm depletion layer in a vacuum gap of 5 mm from the flow surface, operating at 50–100 V bias, can detect alpha particles from ²¹⁸Po (6.0 MeV) and ²¹⁴Po (7.69 MeV) with efficiency of ~15% in 4π geometry. At the expected Rn concentrations (the paper quotes laboratory air at 3 pCi/L), continuous monitoring with 30-minute integration periods provides sensitivity to Rn at the 0.1 pCi/L level in the D₂O, compared to the current offline batch method which requires 6-tonne samples.

**Radioactivity impact:** The silicon PIN detectors must be located outside the water volume in a bypass loop. The relevant constraint is preventing the monitoring bypass from introducing contamination — the loop should be constructed of electropolished 316L stainless steel with electrolytic polishing to <0.1 μin Ra surface roughness.

### 3.2 Improved Process Degasser

The paper describes the Process Degasser as achieving Rn reduction by factors of ~50. The design uses 20 torr vacuum at 10°C water temperature.

**Proposal:** Add a second-stage membrane degasser in series using hydrophobic microporous polypropylene hollow-fiber membranes (Membrana Liqui-Cel type, 0.04 μm pore size, 240 m² membrane area). These operate by sweeping a counter-current pure N₂ stream on the lumen side while water flows on the shell side. At the flow rate of 150 L/min described in the paper and a membrane area of 240 m², the Rn stripping efficiency per stage is approximately 95% based on published Henry's law constants for Rn in water at 10°C (KH ≈ 0.32 atm·m³/mol). Two stages in series achieve >99.75% Rn removal compared to the current ~98% (factor 50). This is particularly important given that Rn in the D₂O is identified as a potentially serious background source for the NC measurement.

---

## 4. Electronics and Data Acquisition Improvements

### 4.1 Increase ADC Resolution from 12-bit to 14-bit

The paper describes 12-bit, 2 μs ADCs for the charge measurement. The SNOINT chip provides dual-range integration to achieve >14 bits effective dynamic range, but the ADC itself is 12-bit.

**Proposal:** Replace the four on-board 12-bit ADCs per FEC with 14-bit successive-approximation ADCs at 1 μs conversion time (available in standard CMOS processes by the late 1990s from Analog Devices and Burr-Brown). The improvement in charge resolution directly improves the single-photoelectron peak-to-valley ratio, which the paper specifies must exceed 1.25. Better ADC resolution reduces the digitization contribution to charge uncertainty, improving the effective energy resolution. With 8 pe/MeV at threshold, the Poisson fluctuation is ±2.8 pe (35% relative), so digitization noise is not dominant at high energies. However, at threshold (~16 pe for a ~2 MeV trigger), the 12-bit ADC covering a 14-bit effective range has 4 counts per pe at the high-gain setting — a 14-bit ADC would provide 16 counts per pe, reducing digitization contribution to timing walk from the current ~0.5 ns contribution to <0.1 ns.

### 4.2 Upgrade Trigger to Finer Time Binning

The paper describes a 100 ns coincidence window for the primary trigger, set to accommodate the 66 ns maximum photon transit time across the 17 m PMT array.

**Proposal:** Implement a second hardware trigger with a sliding 50 ns window using a configurable FPGA-based delay line. The current QUSN7 chip generates 100 ns and 20 ns coincidence pulses. Adding a 50 ns window implemented in the trigger formation card (which already exists on the SNOBus backplane) using a Xilinx XC4000-series FPGA with a 96-tap digital delay line would enable rejection of random coincidences at lower NHIT thresholds. At 500 Hz dark noise rate per PMT and 9438 PMTs, the expected random coincidence rate in 100 ns at NHIT ≥ 18 (approximately 5 MeV threshold) scales as the Poisson probability — reducing the window to 50 ns halves the random coincidence rate, allowing the NHIT threshold to be lowered by approximately 2 counts while maintaining the same trigger rate, effectively lowering the energy threshold by ~0.25 MeV.

---

## 5. Acrylic Vessel and Structural Improvements

### 5.1 Improved Acrylic Surface Treatment

The paper notes acrylic bulk absorption of 0.01 cm⁻¹ at 400 nm and 0.04 cm⁻¹ at 360 nm. The surface cleanliness at water fill was ~0.1 μg/cm² dust.

**Proposal:** Apply a UV-ozone surface treatment to acrylic panels before final installation. UV-ozone cleaning (185 nm and 254 nm radiation, 10–30 minute exposure) removes surface hydrocarbons and oxidizes organic contamination to CO₂ and H₂O without introducing radioactive contamination. This reduces the surface absorption coefficient and improves D₂O wettability, reducing bubble nucleation on the acrylic surface — bubbles scatter Cherenkov light and degrade vertex reconstruction. The UV-ozone system can be portable, operating on panels before installation in the clean room environment already described.

---

## 6. Priority Ranking

Ordered by expected impact on primary physics (NC/CC separation):

1. **NCD FADC pulse-shape discrimination** — directly reduces the dominant background systematic in the NC measurement, which the paper identifies as photodisintegration neutrons indistinguishable from signal. Expected improvement: factor of 2–3 reduction in background contamination of NC sample.

2. **Higher-QE PMTs** — improves energy threshold from ~5 MeV toward ~4 MeV, increasing CC event statistics by approximately 25% (given the steeply falling ⁸B spectrum) and improving vertex resolution for all event types.

3. **Silver/ALD concentrators** — 10% increase in light collection with no radioactivity penalty, equivalent to adding ~900 PMT channels worth of sensitivity.

4. **Second-stage membrane degasser** — reduces the largest non-detector-material background source (Rn in D₂O) by an additional factor of ~40, relaxing the systematic uncertainty on the NC rate measurement.

5. **14-bit ADCs** — modest improvement in charge resolution and timing walk, primarily beneficial for low-energy threshold operation.

The NCD and PMT upgrades address opposite ends of the measurement: the NCD improvements reduce NC background, while the PMT improvements increase CC statistics. Together they would significantly improve the statistical significance of the CC/NC comparison that is SNO's defining measurement.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for EXO-200

## Critical Performance Limitations Identified from the Paper

The paper explicitly identifies several performance bottlenecks: HV instability limiting drift field to 8 kV (vs. 75 kV design), LAAPD noise limiting scintillation threshold, wire plane material budget, and radon backgrounds exceeding targets. I address each with concrete hardware solutions.

---

## 1. High Voltage System Replacement

**Current limitation:** Corona discharge on photoetched edges limits operation to 8 kV vs. 75 kV design maximum, directly reducing charge collection efficiency and position resolution via electron drift lifetime.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Replace photoetched phosphor bronze cathode and field-shaping components with **laser-cut or electropolished OFHC copper components** with controlled edge radii ≥500 μm. Laser cutting (e.g., fiber laser at 1064 nm) followed by tumble deburring and electropolishing in phosphoric acid solution eliminates the sharp photoetch-induced edges identified as the corona source.

Replace the RG217 coaxial feedthrough with a **custom feedthrough using PTFE-machined standoffs and a solid copper conductor with hemispherical terminations**, following designs demonstrated in nEXO R&D (Jeong et al., 2021). The Swagelok compression seal around polyethylene should be replaced with a **metal-to-metal indium wire seal** at the cold flange, with the conductor transitioning through a PTFE-machined cone rated to 150 kV in LXe. This is demonstrated technology from the ICARUS and MicroBooNE HV systems.

Operating at the design 75 kV (3.7 kV/cm drift field) would increase electron lifetime requirements but provides:
- Factor ~4 improvement in drift velocity, reducing diffusion-limited spatial resolution
- Improved ionization/scintillation anti-correlation at higher fields, directly improving energy resolution toward the theoretical optimum demonstrated in Conti et al. (2003)

---

## 2. Photosensor Replacement: SiPM Arrays

**Current limitation:** LAAPDs have gain ~10–50, noise 2 e⁻/pF at 170 K, capacitance 125 pF per device, and 48% packing fraction. The paper explicitly states LAAPD noise limits the scintillation threshold.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Replace 468 LAAPDs with **cryogenic silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)**, specifically the **Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) RGB-HD or NUV-HD-Cryo series**, which have been characterized extensively at 87–165 K. Relevant demonstrated parameters at LXe temperature:

- Photon detection efficiency (PDE): 24–35% at 175 nm with appropriate AR coating vs. ~15% quantum efficiency × gain for LAAPDs
- Single-photon resolution capability vs. LAAPD multi-photon threshold limitation
- Capacitance: ~50 pF/mm² but addressable in small tiles (e.g., 6×6 mm²)
- Gain: 10⁵–10⁶ vs. 10–50 for LAAPDs

**Specific implementation:**
- Tile the LAAPD platter positions with **6×6 mm² FBK NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs** in a hexagonal close-pack pattern achieving >70% geometric coverage vs. 48% current
- Read out in gangs of 9–16 devices using **transimpedance amplifiers based on the CREMAT CR-110 architecture** adapted for cryogenic operation, or the custom ASIC developed for DarkSide-20k (SiPM signal processor chip)
- Apply **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) wavelength-shifting coating** (evaporated, 0.2 mg/cm²) to shift 178 nm Xe scintillation to ~430 nm where SiPM PDE peaks, recovering an additional factor of ~2 in photon detection

Expected improvement: light yield increase by factor 3–5, directly improving energy resolution from σ/E ~1.6% toward ~1.0% at Q_ββ, and enabling single-photon counting that allows topological use of scintillation timing.

**Radioactivity concern mitigation:** FBK SiPMs on silicon substrates with minimal packaging can be screened; demonstrated contamination levels in GERDA and DarkSide programs are <1 μBq/unit for ²³²Th and ²³⁸U, comparable to or better than the LAAPD limits quoted in Table 3.

---

## 3. Charge Readout: Replacement of Wire Planes with Pixel or Charge-Induction Tile Array

**Current limitation:** The 3mm wire pitch with 9mm readout groupings provides limited topological discrimination. Single-site vs. multi-site separation using track length >2 cm is coarse. V-wire inductive readout provides ambiguous 2D information requiring pattern recognition.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Replace crossed wire planes with a **pixelated charge readout based on the Q-Pix or LArPix architecture**, adapted for LXe. Specifically:

- **LArPix ASIC** (developed for DUNE, operates at 77 K, characterized at LXe temperatures by the nEXO collaboration) with 3.8×3.8 mm² pixel pitch
- Each pixel provides independent charge integration with charge-integrate/reset readout, giving unambiguous 3D hit maps
- ASIC self-triggering at ~100 e⁻ threshold eliminates the need for external trigger from wire channels

Alternatively, implement **segmented anode tiles** using the **Topmetal-II⁻ CMOS pixel sensor** (demonstrated in gaseous detectors) adapted for LXe: 72×72 pixel array on 1 cm² die with 83 μm pitch, reading directly via cryo-compatible CMOS process (SMIC 130 nm).

The nEXO collaboration has already demonstrated this path; adapting their **charge tile design** (6×6 cm² tiles with embedded ASIC) for EXO-200's geometry would provide:
- Full 3D event reconstruction without drift-time ambiguity in coordinate assignment
- Multi-site discrimination at the ~3 mm scale rather than ~20 mm
- Elimination of the inductive V-wire plane entirely, reducing material budget by ~50% for that component

**Wiring reduction:** Replace 18 μm copper trace polyimide flex cables with **cryogenic-qualified micro-coaxial ribbon cables** (Axon' Cable Cryo series, rated to 4 K) with integrated ground planes, reducing microphonic pickup that necessitated the complex multi-layer cable design described in Section 3.3.

---

## 4. Field Cage Resistor Chain: Active Voltage Divider

**Current limitation:** 900 MΩ thick-film resistors on sapphire substrates dissipate 0.6 W at design field, creating thermal gradients in LXe. Custom fabrication at Piconics introduces radioactivity screening complexity.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Replace passive resistor chain with an **active Cockcroft-Walton voltage multiplier** implemented in a cryo-CMOS process (e.g., AMS 350 nm HV CMOS, demonstrated to 77 K). This approach:

- Eliminates ~200 resistors of heterogeneous material
- Reduces power dissipation to <50 mW total
- Provides programmable field uniformity adjustment without hardware changes
- Reduces the total exotic-material mass inside the field cage

Alternatively, use **bulk silicon high-voltage resistors** (Ohmcraft series, SiCr thin film on alumina-free substrate) which have been screened to <0.1 mBq/kg for Th and U, superior to the thick-film DuPont paste process.

---

## 5. Radon Exclusion: Active Charcoal Trap and N₂ Purge System

**Current limitation:** Paper states measured radon in cleanroom air is ~3× the 2 mBq/L design limit, and the stainless steel Rn enclosure is described as "for future use."

**Proposed upgrade:**

Implement the already-designed radon enclosure with an active **liquid nitrogen-cooled activated charcoal trap** (following Borexino/SNO+ design: 1 kg Saratech charcoal at 190 K providing Rn reduction factor >10⁴) plumbed to the volume inside the lead shield. Use **mass flow controllers** (MKS Instruments GE50A series) to maintain slight positive pressure of Rn-stripped air or N₂ inside the shield volume.

Add **continuous online radon monitoring** using an **AlphaGUARD PQ2000 PRO** electrostatic radon counter in a closed-loop feedback arrangement to verify and adjust purge flow rate. This directly addresses the identified 3× excess radon background.

---

## 6. Front-End Electronics: Cryogenic ASIC Preamplifiers

**Current limitation:** Warm discrete-component electronics located 1 m from detector introduces substantial cable capacitance (30 pF measured between signal and guard traces, 60–80 pF total for wire channels, 1000 pF for LAAPD channels), degrading noise figure. The paper acknowledges this explicitly as a trade-off.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Deploy **cryogenic front-end ASICs** at the cold flange location inside the HFE-7000 volume (170 K operating point is well within the range of standard CMOS processes).

Specifically: **CUBE ASIC** (developed for LEGEND-200 germanium detectors, operates at 77–300 K, 0.35 μm AMS CMOS, noise <10 e⁻ ENC at 1 pF input capacitance) or the **IDE3160 ASIC** (Ideas AS, Norway, used in several LXe experiments). Placing preamplifiers at the cold end reduces effective input capacitance by eliminating the 1 m cable contribution:

- Wire channel noise: from 1 e⁻/pF × 70 pF = 70 e⁻ ENC → ~15 e⁻ ENC with 1 pF parasitic at ASIC input
- Energy threshold reduction by factor ~5, opening sensitivity to low-energy solar neutrino and dark matter physics as secondary science goals

The cable plant is then replaced by simple **differential current-mode serial links** over the same polyimide substrate, reducing conductor count by 4× and associated radioactivity.

---

## Priority Ranking by Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Impact | Estimated Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| HV system (laser-cut, new feedthrough) | Energy resolution, charge yield | σ/E: 1.6% → 1.1% |
| SiPM replacement with TPB | Light yield, scintillation threshold | Factor 3–5 light yield |
| Pixel charge readout | Background rejection | Multi-site discrimination scale: 20mm → 3mm |
| Cryo ASIC preamplifiers | Noise, threshold | ENC factor ~5 improvement |
| Active radon suppression | Background rate | Factor 3 reduction in Rn background |
| Active field cage | Thermal/radioactivity | Incremental |

The HV system and photosensor upgrades would most directly improve the 0νββ sensitivity by improving energy resolution and the ionization-scintillation anti-correlation weighting that is the core innovation of EXO-200's energy estimator.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for LHCb Performance Improvement

## Identification of Primary Performance Limitations

Before proposing upgrades, the critical bottlenecks identified in the paper must be established:

1. Hardware L0 trigger limits readout to 1 MHz, creating irreducible efficiency losses especially for hadronic charm modes (D∗+→D⁰π⁺ achieves only 22-30% TOS efficiency)
2. VELO operates outside vacuum with aluminum foil separation, limiting IP resolution at low pT
3. RICH1 aerogel Npe yield (5.0 measured vs 8.0 simulated) and C₄F₁₀ angle resolution degraded by magnetic field distortions
4. OT straw tubes reach ~17-25% occupancy, degrading pattern recognition
5. Calorimeter PMT aging causes gain drift requiring frequent recalibration
6. Muon system dead-time effects in inner regions (M1R1 reaching 2.5%)

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. VELO Replacement: Silicon Pixel Detector with RF-Foil Vacuum Enclosure

**Current limitation:** Strip-based VELO with 38-102 µm pitch and aluminum foil boundary introduces multiple scattering. IP resolution at high pT saturates at ~13 µm.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Replace the strip sensors with **55 µm pitch hybrid silicon pixel sensors** based on Timepix3/Medipix3 ASIC technology:

- Pixel geometry eliminates the strip ambiguity problem in high-occupancy regions, reducing fake hit rates
- Per-pixel ToT (Time-over-Threshold) readout at 40 MHz clock enables 1.56 ns timing resolution per hit, providing direct bunch crossing assignment without requiring external timing
- **RF-foil redesign:** Replace the 300 µm aluminum foil with a corrugated 250 µm thick aluminum-beryllium (AlBeMet) composite foil, reducing material from ~0.5% X₀ to ~0.3% X₀ per foil. Beryllium's higher radiation length (35.3 g/cm²  vs 24.0 g/cm² for Al) provides equivalent mechanical rigidity at reduced thickness
- Sensor thickness reduction from 300 µm to 200 µm active layer on 500 µm substrate using epitaxial silicon, reducing material per station from ~0.8% X₀ to ~0.5% X₀
- Extend inner radius from 8.2 mm to 5.0 mm by using radiation-hard LGAD (Low Gain Avalanche Detector) sensors in the innermost zone, tolerating fluences exceeding 10¹⁶ neq/cm²

**Expected improvement:** IP resolution improvement from 13 µm to approximately 8-9 µm at high pT, propagating directly to decay time resolution improvement of ~15-20% for B⁰s oscillation measurements. Ghost rate reduction of approximately 30% from pixel vs strip ambiguity elimination.

---

### 2. Upstream Tracker Replacement: AC-LGAD Silicon Strip Detector

**Current limitation:** TT silicon microstrips show 52.6 µm hit resolution with significant occupancy in beam-proximate sectors (1.9%). More critically, TT provides no timing information, limiting pile-up rejection.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Replace TT with an **AC-coupled LGAD (AC-LGAD) strip detector**:

- Strip pitch reduced to 100 µm with AC-LGAD internal gain layer (~10-20 gain), improving S/N from ~15:1 to ~50:1
- Intrinsic timing resolution of 30-50 ps per strip hit from the fast signal rise time characteristic of LGAD devices
- Four-layer configuration retained (x-u-v-x stereo geometry) but with **two-layer timing planes** inserted between the stereo layers using 300 µm pitch strips optimized for timing rather than position
- ASIC readout using ALTIROC-derived chip capable of simultaneous amplitude and timing digitization at 40 MHz
- Active cooling via microfluidic silicon channels integrated into the module support structure, maintaining sensors at -20°C to minimize radiation damage effects (beneficial since LGAD gain degrades with radiation damage)
- Segmentation into five radial zones with pitches from 80 µm (inner) to 200 µm (outer) rather than uniform 183 µm, reducing inner occupancy by approximately 40%

**Expected improvement:** Hit resolution improvement to ~25-30 µm in inner zones. Timing capability enables 4D tracking, reducing combinatorial fake track rate by ~50% in high pile-up conditions. Pile-up rejection efficiency improves from ~85% to ~97% using combined IP + timing selection.

---

### 3. Scintillating Fibre Tracker Replacing IT/OT

**Current limitation:** OT straw tubes reach 17-25% occupancy at 50 ns spacing, worsening at 25 ns. The 200 µm single-hit resolution is adequate but the maximum drift time of 35 ns creates inherent ambiguities at high rates. IT silicon strips are functional but the hybrid IT/OT boundary creates track-matching discontinuities.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Replace the entire IT and OT tracking stations T1-T3 with a **uniform Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) tracker**:

- **2.5 mm diameter** round scintillating fibres (Kuraray SCSF-78MJ or equivalent) arranged in staggered double layers, providing ~130 µm position resolution from cluster centroiding compared to 200 µm for OT straws
- Fibre mats constructed as 12-layer modules with stereo angles of 0°, +5°, -5°, 0° matching existing geometry conventions
- **Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) readout** replacing HPD/wire readout: 128-channel SiPM arrays (Hamamatsu S13615 or custom 16 µm cell pitch device) with peak PDE >40% at 450 nm emission wavelength, matched to fibre emission spectrum
- SiPM arrays cooled to -40°C using two-phase CO₂ cooling to reduce dark count rate from ~100 kcps/mm² at room temperature to ~1 kcps/mm², critical for maintaining occupancy thresholds
- Custom readout ASIC (PACIFIC-type) with 2.5 ns shaping time and 4-bit ADC per channel, enabling both position and timing information per fibre cluster
- Cluster multiplicity per track reduces from ~2-3 straws (OT) to ~3-4 fibres with substantially smaller pitch, improving pattern recognition in overlapping tracks
- Uniform coverage eliminates the IT/OT boundary region (~15 cm × 120 cm) that currently requires separate alignment procedures with associated systematic uncertainties

**Expected improvement:** Occupancy reduced from 17-25% to 3-5% at equivalent luminosity conditions, tracking efficiency improvement of 1-2% per station especially in high-multiplicity events. Hit resolution improvement from 200 µm to 130 µm translates to ~8% improvement in momentum resolution for long tracks.

---

### 4. RICH System: Replacement of HPDs with MaPMT Arrays and Aerogel Upgrade

**Current limitation:** 
- HPD photoelectron yield is below simulation (C₄F₁₀: 20.4 measured vs 28.3 simulated) due to read-out inefficiency and magnetic field effects
- Aerogel Npe is particularly poor (5.0 ± 3.0) due to gas absorption
- σ(θC) for C₄F₁₀ is 1.618 mrad vs simulation 1.52 mrad, degraded by magnetic field distortions near RICH1

**Proposed upgrades:**

**RICH1 photon detector replacement:**
- Replace HPDs with **Hamamatsu R11265 Multi-Anode PMT (MaPMT)** arrays in a flat-panel geometry
- MaPMTs have 8×8 pixel anodes on 6.08 mm pitch, providing improved granularity compared to HPD pixel size
- Magnetic shielding: Install mumetal shielding cages around individual MaPMT units (permeability >100,000) rather than relying on the existing external shielding, reducing residual field at photocathode from ~2 mT to <0.1 mT
- This directly addresses the largest identified source of C₄F₁₀ angle resolution degradation

**Aerogel radiator redesign:**
- Replace current aerogel tiles (n≈1.03) with **hydrophobic aerogel** produced by supercritical CO₂ drying process, achieving porosity reduction that prevents C₄F₁₀ absorption
- Alternative: Introduce a **thin Mylar separation film** (25 µm) between aerogel volume and C₄F₁₀ gas, mechanically supported by a carbon fibre frame with 97% optical transparency
- Increase aerogel thickness from 5 cm to 7 cm to compensate for any photon loss from the separator film
- Use aerogel with refractive index gradient (n = 1.050 at entry to 1.020 at exit - "focusing aerogel") to reduce chromatic dispersion contribution to σ(θC)

**RICH2 upgrade:**
- Install **dichroic mirror coating** on existing focusing mirrors to reflect wavelengths below 300 nm, reducing the chromatic aberration contribution to σ(θC) from ~0.4 mrad to ~0.2 mrad
- Replace the CF₄ gas recirculation system with a closed-loop purification system incorporating molecular sieve filters to maintain Rayleigh scattering length >5 m, improving Npe by approximately 15%

**Expected improvement:** C₄F₁₀ σ(θC) improvement from 1.618 mrad to near simulation value of 1.52 mrad (~6% improvement). Aerogel Npe improvement from 5.0 to >6.5, expanding effective π/K separation below 5 GeV/c. Overall kaon efficiency at fixed 3% pion misID rate improves from ~85% to ~90%.

---

### 5. Calorimeter System: SiPM Replacement of PMTs and Crystal ECAL Inner Zone

**Current limitation:** PMT gain degradation requires frequent recalibration. HCAL calibration is restricted to bi-monthly technical stops. ECAL mass resolution of 93 MeV/c² for B⁰→K*⁰γ limits radiative decay sensitivity.

**Proposed upgrades:**

**PMT replacement with SiPM arrays:**
- Replace all 6016 ECAL PMTs and 1468 HCAL PMTs with **Hamamatsu S13360-6050CS SiPMs** (6 mm × 6 mm active area, 50 µm cell pitch, 4740 cells)
- SiPMs have no dynode degradation mechanism, eliminating the primary aging effect identified in the paper
- Gain stability better than 0.1%/month compared to ~5% per fb⁻¹ for current PMTs
- Operating SiPMs at -10°C using existing CO₂ cooling infrastructure reduces dark count rate to negligible levels relative to signal
- Compact form factor (3 mm package depth vs ~150 mm for PMT) allows redesign of light collection optics
- Radiation hardness certification required: inner ECAL cells receive ~10¹² neq/cm²/year, within LYSO crystal + SiPM radiation tolerance demonstrated at CMS

**Crystal ECAL inner zone:**
- Replace the innermost 1/3 of ECAL cells (inner section, 4.04 cm × 4.04 cm cells, highest rate region) with **LYSO (Lu₂(1-x)Y₂xSiO₅:Ce) scintillating crystals** read out by SiPMs
- LYSO radiation length of 1.14 cm (vs ~1 cm for Pb-scintillator sampling) provides improved shower containment in the same physical depth
- LYSO energy resolution: σ(E)/E ≈ 1-2%/√E ⊕ 0.5% (stochastic ⊕ constant term) compared to ~10%/√E ⊕ 1% for the current shashlik ECAL
- This directly improves B⁰→K*⁰γ mass resolution from 93 MeV/c² to approximately 45-55 MeV/c² for photons hitting the inner zone, where the majority of high-ET photons from B decays land given the forward geometry

**SPD/PS upgrade:**
- Replace scintillating pad SPD with a **1 mm² granularity silicon pixel layer** (reusing VELO-type sensors) providing charged particle veto with spatial resolution matched to upgraded ECAL inner granularity
- This eliminates the current ~5% SPD inefficiency that forces L0 vetoes on high-multiplicity events

**Expected improvement:** Calorimeter stability eliminates ~0.5% systematic uncertainty on photon energy scale. ECAL inner zone energy resolution improvement directly benefits B→K*γ, B→φγ, and H→γγ searches. Electron identification efficiency improves from 91.9% to approximately 94-95% due to better E/p resolution.

---

### 6. Muon System: GEM Expansion and Improved Front-End Electronics

**Current limitation:** M1R1 dead-time reaches 2.5% and M2R1 reaches 0.6% at 2×10³² cm⁻²s⁻¹. Front-end chip dead-time of 50-100 ns creates measurable inefficiency in inner regions.

**Proposed upgrades:**

**GEM detector expansion:**
- Extend GEM technology (currently only M1) to the **R1 and R2 regions of M2 and M3 stations**, where highest occupancy causes dead-time
- Use **triple-GEM with 2D strip readout** at 400 µm pitch replacing MWPCs, providing ~50 µm position resolution vs ~2 mm for MWPC pads while maintaining 99.5% efficiency up to 10⁷ Hz/cm² rate capability
- The improved spatial resolution in M2-M3 directly improves pT measurement accuracy in the L0 muon trigger from ~25% to ~15% resolution

**Front-end ASIC redesign:**
- Replace current front-end chips with **GEMROC-type ASICs** featuring 25 ns peaking time and dead-time reduced from 50-100 ns to <12 ns per channel
- Implement time-stamping at 1.25 ns precision per channel, enabling bunch-crossing disambiguation in high pile-up conditions
- Increase on-chip buffer depth from 4 to 16 events to reduce the dead-time from finite digital output signal length identified in M5

**Shielding against back-scattering:**
- Install 20 cm polyethylene moderator panels behind M5 to reduce neutron back-scattering from downstream beam elements, which currently causes spurious hits increasing M5 occupancy
- This addresses the specific dead-time issue identified for M5 in the paper

**Expected improvement:** M1R1 dead-time reduction from 2.5% to <0.5%, M2R1 from 0.6% to <0.2%. Overall muon trigger efficiency improvement of ~1.5%, with the largest gain in di-muon triggers for B⁰s→µ⁺µ⁻ searches. L0 muon pT resolution improvement from ~25% to ~15% reduces threshold turn-on width, improving trigger efficiency at low pT by approximately 5%.

---
