## 1. Vertex Locator (VELO) Replacement

### Current Limitations
- Silicon strip sensors with minimum 8.2 mm beam proximity
- 38–102 µm pitch strips limiting hit resolution to ~4 µm best case
- Radiation damage reaching 1.8×10¹⁴ n_eq/cm² during Run I, approaching operational limits
- 210-second closing time after stable beam declaration represents dead time
- Analogue readout architecture limits trigger integration

### Proposed Upgrade: Hybrid Pixel VELO
**Technology:** 55 µm pitch hybrid silicon pixel detectors using TimePix4 or VeloPix ASIC architecture

**Specific components:**
- **Sensor material:** n-on-p silicon pixel sensors, 200 µm thick, bump-bonded to readout ASICs
- **Pixel pitch:** 55×55 µm² providing true 2D hit information without strip ambiguities
- **Radiation hardness:** Sensors qualified to >10¹⁶ n_eq/cm² using MCz (Magnetic Czochralski) or LGAD (Low Gain Avalanche Detector) technology for innermost rows
- **RF foil thickness:** Reduce from current aluminium foil to 250 µm thick corrugated beryllium foil, reducing material budget from ~0.3% X₀ to ~0.1% X₀ per module
- **Geometry:** Retractable blade geometry with sensors at 3.5 mm from beam axis during physics (vs. 8.2 mm current), enabled by the superior radiation hardness
- **Readout:** 40 MHz continuous readout eliminating the hardware L0 trigger dependency, with timestamps at 1 ns precision per hit
- **Closing mechanism:** Electromagnetic actuators replacing stepper motors, reducing closing time from 210 s to <30 s

**Expected performance gains:**
- IP resolution improvement from ~13 µm to ~8 µm at high pT due to reduced material and closer beam approach
- Elimination of ghost hit ambiguities present in strip geometry
- Decay time resolution improvement from ~50 fs to ~35 fs for B⁰_s→J/ψφ

## 2. Upstream Tracker (UT) Replacing Tracker Turicensis

### Current Limitations
- TT hit resolution of 52–54 µm with 183 µm strip pitch
- High occupancy near beam pipe (1.9%) limiting pattern recognition
- No timing information, vulnerable to spillover at 25 ns bunch spacing
- Central region resolution degraded by minimal charge sharing at small track angles

### Proposed Upgrade: Four-Layer Silicon Microstrip with AC-LGAD Central Region
**Technology:** Combination of improved microstrip sensors peripherally and AC-coupled LGAD sensors centrally

**Specific components:**
- **Central region (r < 10 cm):** AC-LGAD sensors with 500 µm pitch and intrinsic gain layer providing 20× signal amplification, achieving 100 µm position resolution with ~500 ps timing resolution to reject out-of-time hits
- **Peripheral region:** p-on-n microstrip sensors, 150 µm pitch (down from 183 µm), 300 µm thick on n-type FZ silicon
- **ASIC:** SALT-2 readout chip with 40 MHz sampling rate and zero-suppressed digital output at 320 Mbps per chip
- **Stereo angle:** Increase from ±5° to ±10° in u/v layers to improve z-hit resolution from ~1 mm to ~500 µm, improving downstream tracking seed quality
- **Module thinning:** Reduce support structure material using carbon fibre honeycomb core at 1.5% X₀ total per station (from current ~2% X₀)

**Expected performance gains:**
- Ghost track rate reduction by ~40% due to timing rejection of pile-up hits
- IT/OT matching efficiency improvement at boundaries

## 3. Scintillating Fibre Tracker Replacing IT/OT

### Current Limitations
- OT maximum drift time of 35 ns limits operation at 25 ns bunch spacing
- OT occupancy reaching 25% at 25 ns spacing causing pattern recognition degradation
- IT/OT boundary region creates inefficiencies in track reconstruction

- MWPC-based system cannot operate at 40 MHz readout

### Proposed Upgrade: Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) Tracker
**Technology:** 250 µm diameter polystyrene scintillating fibres read out by Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPM)

**Specific components:**
- **Fibre specification:** Kuraray SCSF-78MJ multiclad fibres, 250 µm core diameter, 2.5 m active length, arranged in 6-layer mats per detection plane
- **SiPM arrays:** Custom 128-channel SiPM arrays with 55 µm microcell pitch, quantum efficiency >40% at 450 nm emission peak, operating at -40°C to reduce dark count rate from ~1 MHz/mm² to ~10 kHz/mm²
- **ASIC:** PACIFIC readout chip with 4-bit ADC at 40 MHz, integrated discriminator and cluster finding, 12.8 Gbps output per chip

- **Geometry:** Maintain x-u-v-x arrangement with stereo angles of ±5°, 12 detection planes per tracking station replacing 4 OT layers + IT, eliminating the geometrical boundary
- **Hit resolution:** 100 µm single-hit resolution (factor 2 improvement over OT) from cluster centroid of typically 2–3 fibres

**Expected performance gains:**
- Uniform coverage eliminating IT/OT boundary inefficiency
- Full 40 MHz operation enabling trigger-less readout

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Heavy-Water Cherenkov Solar Neutrino Detector

## Framing the Performance Problem

The primary physics performance metrics are: **energy threshold, energy resolution, directional resolution, flavor discrimination (CC/NC/ES separation), and systematic uncertainty on flux normalization**. I'll address each with concrete hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Photomultiplier Tube Upgrades

### Replace Standard 8" PMTs with High-QE HPDs or LAPPDs

**Current limitation:** Conventional Hamamatsu R1408 or R3600 PMTs achieve ~21-23% peak quantum efficiency with ~1.5 ns single-photoelectron (SPE) timing resolution.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- **Large-Area Picosecond Photodetectors (LAPPDs)** — microchannel plate-based detectors from Incom Inc., 20×20 cm² active area, achieving **~30% QE** and **~65 ps single-photon timing resolution** (vs. ~1.5 ns for standard PMTs)
- Alternatively, **Hamamatsu R12860 HQE PMTs** (already deployed in SK-Gd): 31% QE at 390 nm, improved from ~23%, achievable at scale today
- **Hybrid Photo-Detectors (HPDs)** with avalanche diode readout: near-Poissonian single-electron response (excess noise factor ~1.02 vs. ~1.3 for dynode PMTs), dramatically improving energy resolution at low photoelectron counts

**Physics impact:** Going from 23% to 31% QE increases detected photons by ~35%, improving energy resolution as √N and lowering effective threshold. The 65 ps LAPPD timing enables sub-degree directional reconstruction critical for pp-chain neutrino separation.

### Increase Coverage Fraction

- Current SNO-type geometry: ~54% photocoverage with 9456 PMTs
- Add **Winston cone light concentrators** (already used in SNO) but redesign for the HQE PMT angular acceptance — HQE PMTs have narrower angular response, requiring reoptimized cone geometry to maintain effective coverage
- Alternatively, pack **smaller-diameter (5") PMTs** at higher density on the same geodesic structure, trading individual area for better spatial granularity — improves vertex resolution and reduces PMT shadowing artifacts

---

## 2. Water/Heavy-Water Optical Quality and Purification

### Ultra-High-Purity D₂O Recirculation with Online Monitoring

**Current limitation:** Rayleigh scattering and absorption from trace impurities set the effective photon attenuation length; dissolved metals (especially Th, U, Ra) create radioactive backgrounds.

**Proposed upgrades:**
- **Continuous reverse osmosis + ion exchange resin loop** with sub-ppq (parts-per-quadrillion) U/Th removal — SNO achieved ~10⁻¹⁴ g/g; next generation should target 10⁻¹⁶ g/g using **electrodeionization modules** (continuous EDI, e.g., from SnowPure/Evoqua) avoiding resin regeneration dead time
- **Inline laser attenuation monitors** at 337 nm and 500 nm using pulsed nitrogen laser + SPAD detectors to track absorption length in real time without removing D₂O from the active volume
- **Dissolved oxygen removal** via membrane degasser (Membrana Liqui-Cel) to <1 ppb O₂, eliminating quenching of Cherenkov photons in the UV tail

### Wavelength-Shifting Additive

- Add **1,4-bis(2-methylstyryl)benzene (bis-MSB)** at ~1 mg/L — shifts UV Cherenkov photons (250-350 nm) where PMT QE is poor to ~420 nm where QE peaks
- This recovers roughly 40% more detected photons from the UV component of the Cherenkov spectrum
- **Critical constraint:** Must be compatible with D₂O chemistry and not introduce radioactive impurities — requires specific deuterated synthesis or demonstrated compatibility testing

---

## 3. Electronics and DAQ Upgrades

### Replace Discriminator-Based Triggering with Full Waveform Digitization

**Current limitation:** SNO-era electronics used zero-crossing discriminators with TAC/ADC readout, losing sub-PMT timing structure and charge information.

**Proposed upgrades:**
- **DRS4-based (Paul Scherrer Institute) switched capacitor arrays** at 5 Gsps per channel, sampling full PMT waveforms — allows offline discrimination of real Cherenkov hits from PMT prepulsing, late pulsing, and after-pulsing at the waveform level
- **WaveCatcher or CAEN V1742 modules** for 32-channel simultaneous digitization at 3.2 Gsps, 12-bit resolution
- Implement **FPGA-based online triggering** (Xilinx UltraScale+) performing real-time hit clustering and vertex prefit, enabling hardware trigger thresholds at **~0.5 MeV effective electron energy** vs. the ~3.5 MeV SNO threshold for NC neutrons

**Physics impact:** Lowering threshold accesses the **pp neutrino flux** (endpoint 420 keV) for the first time in heavy water — a transformative measurement.

### Precision Timing Distribution

- Replace NIM-based timing with **White Rabbit (WR) protocol** over fiber — achieves sub-nanosecond synchronization across all ~10,000 channels with hardware timestamps at 1 ps resolution
- Enables **in-situ PMT timing calibration** using laser diffusion balls without dedicated calibration runs, improving live time

---

## 4. Calibration Hardware

### Deployed Radioactive and Optical Sources

**Current SNO approach:** Periodic deployment of ²⁵²Cf (neutrons), ¹⁶N (6.1 MeV γ), and laser diffuser balls — limited by deployment dead time and position coverage.

**Proposed upgrades:**
- **Fixed fiber-optic network** with 50-100 injection points distributed throughout the D₂O volume, fed by a pulsed 405 nm diode laser (PicoQuant PDL 800-D, 70 ps pulses) — enables continuous in-situ optical calibration without source deployment
- **Tagged ⁵⁸Co source** (produces 811 keV γ near solar neutrino energies) on a remotely-actuated positioning system with ±1 cm reproducibility — specifically calibrates detector response in the critical 0.5-2 MeV range
- **Embedded ²²²Rn injection system** with controlled micro-injections into defined volume elements for PMT gain and position reconstruction verification — requires active removal loop afterward

### PMT-Level Gain Monitoring

- Install **single-LED flasher circuits** (one per 10 PMTs) on the geodesic support, pulsing at 1 Hz with ~1 photoelectron illumination — continuous gain tracking at <0.1% precision without external calibration

---

## 5. Neutron Capture Enhancement

### Gadolinium Loading of the Light-Water Shield

**Current limitation:** NC events (νₓ + d → p + n + νₓ) are detected via neutron capture on deuterium producing a 6.25 MeV γ — only ~25% detection efficiency due to the 2.2 m capture length in D₂O.

**Proposed upgrades:**
- **Load the outer light-water shield region with 0.1% GdCl₃ or Gd₂(SO₄)₃** (as demonstrated in Super-K Gd / EGADS experiment) — captures escaping neutrons that would otherwise be lost, increasing effective NC efficiency by ~15-20%
- More aggressively: **Gd-doped acrylic panels** lining the inner vessel surface, avoiding Gd contamination of the D₂O while presenting a high-capture-cross-section surface (~49,000 barns vs. 0.5 mb for deuterium) to thermalized neutrons
- **Boron-loaded scintillator panels** (⁶Li-enriched ZnS:Ag sheets, as used in SNO+) as an alternative — the 6Li(n,α)t reaction produces a scintillation burst detectable by PMTs without gamma emission, reducing systematic uncertainty from γ escape

---

## 6. Vessel and Structural Upgrades

### Inner Acrylic Vessel Replacement with Lower-Background Material

- Replace standard PMMA with **deuterated PMMA (d-PMMA)** — reduces the 2.2 MeV γ background from ¹H(n,γ) reactions on acrylic hydrogen, critical for NC event counting
- Use **radio-assayed acrylic** with U/Th <10⁻¹³ g/g (measured by ICP-MS with preconcentration), achievable from select Evonik or Mitsubishi Chemical acrylic batches with appropriate screening
- **Increase vessel diameter by 10-15%** (within cavity constraints) — the fiducial volume scales as r³, and a 10% radius increase gives 33% more target mass without adding D₂O cost proportionally (if D₂O is the limiting cost)

### Geodesic Structure Material

- Replace stainless steel geodesic support with **carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) frame** — eliminates ~500 kg of structural steel whose trace radioactivity contributes to external γ background
- CFRP has measured U/Th at ~10⁻¹² g/g vs. ~10⁻⁹ g/g for typical stainless steel — a 1000× improvement — and is now available in structural quantities from aerospace suppliers (Toray, Hexcel)

---

## 7. Veto and Shielding Upgrades

### Active Muon Veto Enhancement

- Add **scintillator panels** (EJ-200 or equivalent) on the outer water tank walls in a hermetic configuration — current water Cherenkov muon veto achieves ~99.5% efficiency; scintillator layer would push this to **>99.99%**
- This reduces spallation backgrounds (⁸He, ⁹Li, ¹²B produced by muons) that are the dominant systematic for sub-10 MeV solar neutrino measurements
- **Segmented design** using 5 cm thick panels with WLS fiber readout (Y-11 fiber, Kuraray) feeding SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13360 series) — SiPMs are more radiation-hard and compact than PMTs for this peripheral application

### Radon Exclusion

- Install **radon-stripped nitrogen blanket** at all D₂O-air interfaces and cable penetrations — ²²²Rn (T½ = 3.8 d) emanating from rock is a critical background for low-energy solar neutrinos
- Use **radon-impermeable PVDC film** (Saran wrap equivalent, commercial Dow product) at inner vessel interfaces; achieves >10× reduction in Rn emanation compared to standard polyethylene

---

## Single Highest-Impact Recommendation

If forced to choose one: **replace PMTs with Hamamatsu R12860 HQE variants and simultaneously deploy full waveform digitization**. The combination of ~35% more detected photons plus waveform-level hit cleaning reduces the effective energy threshold from ~3.5 MeV to potentially ~0.8-1.0 MeV, opening access to the **⁷Be (862 keV) and potentially pep neutrino lines** — a qualitative expansion of the physics program, not merely an incremental improvement.

## Identification of Primary Physics Limitations

The paper reveals several concrete performance constraints worth addressing systematically:

- 31% bare photocathode coverage (54% effective with concentrators)
- PMT timing resolution σ ≈ 1.7 ns
- Energy threshold limited by PMT dark noise (~500 Hz at 10°C) and radioactive backgrounds
- NC detection efficiency ~37% with NCD array, ~25% usable after alpha discrimination
- Vertex resolution limited by photon statistics and timing

---

## Upgrade 1: Photosensor Replacement with High-Quantum-Efficiency Large-Area PMTs

**Current limitation:** The Hamamatsu R1408 has standard bialkali photocathode quantum efficiency of approximately 20-22% at peak wavelength (~420 nm). The paper states roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV, which directly sets energy threshold and resolution.

**Proposed upgrade:** Replace R1408 tubes with Hamamatsu R7081-20 or equivalent 20-cm hemispherical PMTs featuring high-quantum-efficiency (HQE) bialkali photocathodes achieving 34-36% peak QE. These were subsequently developed and deployed in KamLAND-Zen and DEAP-3600.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Same 20-cm diameter form factor fits existing ABS hexagonal cells with minor modification to the retaining geometry
- Operating voltage would shift to approximately 1500-1800V range, compatible with existing HV distribution
- Expected photoelectron yield increases from ~8 pe/MeV to ~13-14 pe/MeV
- Dark noise rate for HQE variants is approximately 3-4 kHz at 20°C, reducing to ~300 Hz at 10°C, improving on the 500 Hz stated in the paper
- Radioactivity specifications for the new glass must be maintained below the 40 ppb Th/U level; Hamamatsu demonstrated this is achievable in the same borosilicate glass family

**Physics impact:** Energy threshold reduction from approximately 5 MeV to below 4 MeV, opening sensitivity to pep and CNO neutrinos. Energy resolution improvement scales as √(N_pe), giving roughly 30% improvement.

---

## Upgrade 2: Replacement of Winston Cone Reflectors with Wavelength-Shifting Light Concentrators

**Current limitation:** The paper states the dielectric-coated aluminum concentrators achieve mean effective reflectance of 82±3% in water over the Cherenkov spectrum (300-500 nm). The 18-piece aluminum construction with MgF₂/TiO₂-PrO₂ coating loses significant UV photons below 350 nm where Cherenkov emission is substantial.

**Proposed upgrade:** Replace the aluminum reflector concentrators with acrylic light guides doped with wavelength-shifting fluor, specifically bis-MSB dissolved in UVT acrylic at approximately 50 ppm concentration. This approach was validated in the Borexino Counting Test Facility and later refined for nEXO and OSIRIS.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Machine replacement concentrators from the same UVT acrylic sheet stock already qualified for the AV (radioactivity already measured at <1.1 pg/g Th/U)
- Dope with bis-MSB fluor: absorbs 300-380 nm Cherenkov photons, re-emits isotropically at 420-430 nm where PMT QE peaks
- Internal reflective surface coated with enhanced specular aluminum (>95% reflectance at 420 nm in water), simpler and more reliable than the current 3-layer dielectric stack
- The 56.4° critical angle acceptance geometry is preserved in the new machined profile
- Fluor concentration at 50 ppm contributes negligible radioactivity: bis-MSB is a pure hydrocarbon with no heavy metal content

**Physics impact:** Effective light collection improvement of 15-20% from UV photon recovery. Critically, this improves the uniformity of detector response as a function of event position, reducing systematic uncertainties in the CC/NC flux ratio measurement, which is the primary physics observable.

---

## Upgrade 3: Upgraded Front-End Electronics with Waveform Digitization

**Current limitation:** The SNOD/SNOINT/QUSN7 ASIC chain provides only integrated charge in two gain ranges plus a single TAC per channel. The paper explicitly notes the TAC starts on PMT leading edge and stops on global trigger, giving single time measurement per event with ~1.7 ns RMS resolution. Late pulses, prepulses, and afterpulses (specified <1.5%) cannot be characterized on an event-by-event basis.

**Proposed upgrade:** Replace the three-ASIC chain with a per-channel waveform digitizer based on the DRS4 (Domino Ring Sampler version 4) switched-capacitor array chip developed at PSI, operating at 2-5 GSPS sampling rate.

**Concrete implementation:**
- DRS4 chip provides 1024 capacitor cells per channel, sampling at 1-5 GSPS, with 11.5-bit effective resolution
- Single chip handles 8 channels, matching the existing daughter board organization (4 DBs × 8 channels = 32 channels per FEC)
- DRS4 operates at 3.3V, compatible with existing low-voltage power distribution
- Dead time per channel: ~130 μs for readout at 5 GSPS, acceptable given the ~8 pe/event solar neutrino signal and low event rate
- 1024 samples at 2 GSPS provides 512 ns waveform capture window, sufficient to capture the full Cherenkov wavefront arrival distribution across the 17.8 m PSUP diameter (maximum photon travel time ~90 ns in water)
- Existing SNOBus backplane bandwidth of >8 MB/s becomes the bottleneck; upgrade the XL1/XL2 translator pair to optical fiber links at 1 Gb/s using SFP modules, which is straightforward given the existing fiber infrastructure running to surface

**Physics impact:**
- Pulse shape discrimination separates Cherenkov photons from PMT dark noise hits on a statistical basis per event, reducing effective noise contribution
- Afterpulse identification and rejection improves energy resolution
- Multi-photon pile-up correction becomes possible for high-energy events (supernova, cosmic muon calibration)
- Early/late hit separation improves vertex reconstruction from ~25 cm to potentially ~15 cm, directly improving fiducial volume definition and hence signal-to-background

---

## Upgrade 4: NCD Array Signal Readout with Flash ADCs and Improved Shaping

**Current limitation:** The paper describes pulse-shape discrimination for the NCD array to separate neutron capture events from alpha backgrounds, but the readout uses a single 91Ω coaxial cable per string with analog pulse transmission. The 30 ns open-ended delay line for position encoding by pulse-reflection timing implies the digitization occurs after significant cable dispersion over the ~11 m maximum string length plus the AV neck traversal.

**Proposed upgrade:** Install preampifier/digitizer modules at the top of each NCD string, within the AV chimney volume, using custom low-radioactivity electronics.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Design a preamp module housed in electropolished nickel (consistent with NCD body material and radioactivity requirements) mounted at the cable endcap
- Use a 14-bit, 100 MSPS flash ADC (e.g., AD9644 or equivalent) for full pulse digitization at the source before cable dispersion
- Power and data transmission via the existing South Bay Cable coaxial run, using a bias-T arrangement to superimpose DC power on the signal line
- The module must operate submerged in D₂O at 3.1 atm absolute pressure; hermetic packaging in the nickel housing using the same Sn:Ag solder seal technique already developed for the NCD endcaps
- Maximum component radioactivity: the ADC package (ceramic or plastic QFP) must be screened; ceramic packages with alumina substrates have been measured at <100 pg/g Th/U in the KamLAND-Zen electronics program

**Physics impact:** 
- Pulse-shape discrimination efficiency for neutron/alpha separation improves from the paper's stated ~55% (giving effective efficiency 25% vs. nominal 45%) to >80%, potentially recovering the full nominal neutron capture efficiency
- Position resolution along string improves from the reflection-timing method (limited by cable dispersion) to direct time-of-arrival comparison between digitized pulse features, reducing position uncertainty from ~10 cm to ~2 cm
- This directly improves the NC event rate measurement accuracy and reduces the dominant systematic uncertainty in the CC/NC ratio

---

## Upgrade 5: Active Radon Barrier Using Electrostatic Precipitation in the Water Volumes

**Current limitation:** The paper identifies radon as a critical background, with the cavity rock contributing at the design maximum of 12 Rn atoms/m²/hour through the Urylon coating. The cover gas system and water degassing reduce radon but do not eliminate it. The paper states the process degasser achieves only a factor of 50 reduction in Rn.

**Proposed upgrade:** Install an electrostatic radon removal system within the H₂O recirculation loop, exploiting the fact that ²²²Rn daughters (²¹⁸Po⁺ and ²¹⁴Pb⁺) are positively charged ions immediately following alpha decay and can be collected on a negatively biased electrode.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Insert a cylindrical electrostatic precipitator vessel (2 m diameter, 3 m length, electropolished SS316L) in the H₂O recirculation loop between the process degasser output and the N₂ regassing unit
- Central anode wire (100 μm diameter Pt, low radioactivity) held at +50 kV relative to grounded outer cylinder
- Water flow rate of 150 L/min gives residence time ~40 seconds, sufficient for >95% collection of positively charged Rn daughters before they can decay further in the bulk water
- This is distinct from removing dissolved Rn gas (which the degasser handles) - it addresses the progeny already in the water from residual Rn
- Power supply: 50 kV at <1 mA, standard laboratory HV supply external to the water system
- The technique was demonstrated in the Borexino water shield system achieving additional factor of 10 reduction in ²¹⁴Bi backgrounds

**Physics impact:** Reduction of ²¹⁴Bi background in the H₂O volume reduces the photodisintegration neutron background entering the D₂O through the AV, and reduces the gamma background contributing to the Cherenkov trigger. The paper states the primary radioactivity requirement derives from the 2.2 MeV photodisintegration threshold; reducing this background directly lowers the achievable energy threshold and improves NC measurement purity.

---

## Summary of Expected Combined Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Metric | Expected Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| HQE PMTs | pe/MeV yield | +60% → threshold ~3.5 MeV |
| WLS concentrators | UV photon recovery | +15-20% light yield, improved uniformity |
| Waveform digitization | Vertex resolution | ~25 cm → ~15 cm |
| NCD digitization at source | NC neutron efficiency | 25% → ~40% usable |
| Electrostatic Rn removal | ²¹⁴Bi background | Factor ~10 reduction |

The most impactful single upgrade is the HQE PMT replacement, as photoelectron yield enters every figure of merit quadratically through energy and position resolution. The waveform digitization upgrade is the most enabling for future analysis techniques, as it preserves full information rather than requiring hardware decisions at trigger time. These two upgrades are mutually reinforcing and would substantially improve the precision of the CC/NC flux ratio measurement that is SNO's primary physics observable.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Improved Physics Performance

## Preamble: Identifying Performance-Limiting Hardware

The paper reveals several concrete hardware bottlenecks. I'll address each with specific technology proposals, prioritizing impact on primary physics goals: astrophysical neutrino detection, source identification, and low-energy neutrino physics.

---

## 1. Photon Detection: Replace PMT with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

### Current Limitation
The Hamamatsu R7081-02 achieves ~25% peak quantum efficiency (34% HQE variant), has poor single-photon timing resolution (~13 ns digitized SPE FWHM), requires ~2000V bias, consumes significant power, and is sensitive to the ambient 550 mG magnetic field requiring a mu-metal cage that blocks ~4% of incident light.

### Proposed Upgrade
Deploy large-area SiPM arrays tiling the lower hemisphere, specifically using **Hamamatsu S13360-series or FBK NUV-HD-SF devices** in a segmented mosaic of ~100–200 individual 6×6 mm² cells, sum-coupled in analog clusters of ~10 cells each.

**Specific performance gains:**
- Peak photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 50–60% at 420 nm, roughly doubling photon yield over standard DOMs and exceeding even HQE PMTs by ~50%
- Single-photon timing resolution of 100–200 ps (vs. ~2 ns for the PMT), dramatically improving vertex and direction reconstruction
- Operating voltage of 30–70V eliminates the 2 kV supply, reducing power consumption from ~300 mW (HV alone) to under 50 mW for bias circuitry
- No magnetic field sensitivity, eliminating the mu-metal cage and recovering the blocked 4% solid angle while simplifying mechanical assembly
- Intrinsic dark count rates of ~100 kHz/mm² at −30°C, which at deep-ice temperatures (−30°C to −9°C) would be suppressed further; the total SiPM dark rate would be comparable to or below the current ~560 Hz DOM dark noise dominated by glass scintillation
- No dynode chain means no afterpulsing at the ~6 µs timescale currently parameterized

**Implementation detail:** A segmented readout retains directional information within a single DOM. Grouping the hemisphere into 12–16 independently read azimuthal/polar segments enables per-DOM photon direction reconstruction, improving shower vertex resolution. The analog sum of each segment feeds a dedicated front-end channel. Total channel count per DOM increases from 1 PMT to ~16 SiPM segments, requiring a redesigned Main Board.

**Impact on physics:** Angular resolution for muon tracks improves with better photon timing. The ~0.6° angular resolution is currently limited partly by ice scattering but also by PMT timing; sub-nanosecond photon timestamps would reduce the electronics contribution to near zero, shifting the bottleneck entirely to ice optics. For cascade events, improved vertex resolution directly benefits energy reconstruction and flavor identification.

---

## 2. Front-End Digitization: Replace ATWD+fADC with High-Speed FADC

### Current Limitation
The ATWD architecture samples at 300 Msps but records only 427 ns, requiring a second slow fADC (40 Msps, 6.4 µs) for late photons. The two-chip alternating scheme introduces deadtime of up to ~32 µs per HLC hit. The architecture was designed in the early 2000s and reflects the technology of that era.

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace both ATWD chips and the fADC with a single **12-bit, 500 Msps continuous-sampling ADC** such as the **Texas Instruments ADC12DJ500** or **Analog Devices AD9625** (1 GSPS, 12-bit), combined with a large **on-chip ring buffer in an updated FPGA** (e.g., Xilinx Ultrascale+ or Intel Arria 10).

**Specific gains:**
- Continuous sampling eliminates deadtime entirely; back-to-back hits separated by any interval are captured without gaps, removing the ~32 µs deadtime that currently affects ~6.6×10⁻⁵ fractional loss for in-ice DOMs (and 3.2×10⁻³ for IceTop high-gain DOMs)
- 500 Msps at 12 bits gives 2 ns sampling with 4× better voltage resolution than the current 10-bit ATWD, improving charge resolution for small pulses near the SPE threshold
- A single digitizer path eliminates the need for post-hoc waveform stitching between ATWD and fADC records, removing a systematic calibration step
- The 6.4 µs fADC window becomes a software-configurable parameter; for [REDACTED] strings where 7 m DOM spacing means scattered photons arrive quickly, the window can be shortened to reduce data volume
- Continuous sampling with FPGA-based zero-suppression and digital triggering eliminates the analog discriminator as the sole trigger mechanism, enabling digital constant-fraction discrimination that improves timing accuracy for small pulses

**Power consideration:** Modern high-speed ADCs consume 1–2 W, comparable to current ATWD+fADC power, so thermal budget is preserved.

---

## 3. Timing System: White Rabbit Precision Timing Protocol

### Current Limitation
RAPCal achieves ~1.2 ns timing accuracy (measured via flasher cross-checks) with a standard deviation of 0.6 ns per measurement. The system requires pausing data communications once per second per DOM, and relies on a single GPS master clock (Symmetricom ET6000) with a hot spare. The 20 MHz DOR clock is phase-locked to the 10 MHz GPS output distributed via analog fanout through multiple tiers.

### Proposed Upgrade
Implement the **White Rabbit (WR) precision timing protocol** (developed at CERN, now an IEEE 1588 extension standard) on the DOR cards and a new surface timing distribution network.

**Specific components:**
- Replace the Symmetricom ET6000 with a **GNSS-disciplined oscillator with internal Cs or Rb atomic clock holdover**, such as the **Microsemi 4380A**, providing sub-nanosecond UTC traceability with holdover stability of <1 µs/day
- Replace the analog fanout tree with a **fiber-based White Rabbit network**, deploying WR switches (commercially available from Seven Solutions, CERN partner) at each rack, with WR endpoint cards in each DOMHub
- WR achieves sub-nanosecond synchronization (<200 ps) across fiber links by combining Synchronous Ethernet with IEEE 1588v2 and a precise phase measurement, eliminating the multi-tier analog fanout delay-matching requirement
- The digital timing path removes sensitivity to temperature-dependent cable propagation delays that currently limit RAPCal repeatability

**Impact:** Improving inter-DOM timing from ~1.2 ns to <300 ps would directly improve muon track angular resolution. The pointing accuracy scales roughly as σ_θ ∝ σ_t·c/L where L is the baseline; at 125 m string spacing, reducing timing error from 1.2 ns to 0.3 ns would reduce the timing contribution to angular error by a factor of 4, potentially pushing overall track angular resolution below 0.3° for high-energy muons where ice scattering is subdominant.

---

## 4. Local Coincidence: Replace Wired LC with Optical Fiber Inter-DOM Links

### Current Limitation
Local coincidence signals are transmitted via dedicated copper wire pairs to nearest and next-to-nearest neighbors (±2 DOMs), carrying simple digital pulses. The LC wiring is fixed at deployment and the ±1 µs coincidence window is conservative. Dead DOMs interrupt the LC chain, requiring modified LC settings for neighbors. The current scheme transmits only a binary coincidence flag, not timing or charge information.

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace the dedicated LC copper pairs with **short-haul optical fiber transceivers** using **850 nm VCSEL-based SFP modules** (e.g., Finisar FTLX8574D3BCL), embedded in the cable at each breakout, connecting adjacent DOMs bidirectionally.

**Specific gains:**
- Bandwidth of 10 Gbps per fiber link (vs. ~720 kbps for the current copper pair shared with power/comms) enables transmission of full hit timestamps and charge estimates between neighboring DOMs in real time
- DOMs can implement **on-string first-level trigger logic**: rather than simply flagging coincidence, adjacent DOMs exchange digitized hit times and charges, enabling on-DOM rejection of isolated dark noise hits without surface computer involvement, reducing data volume before transmission
- Optical links are immune to the RF interference (from COBRA radar, etc.) that has affected copper-based communications
- Fiber eliminates crosstalk between LC and power/communications signals that requires careful electrical design in the current system
- Extending the neighbor reach to ±3 or ±4 DOMs in software becomes trivial without additional wiring

**Implementation note:** Power for VCSEL transceivers (~150 mW each) must be supplied from the DOM's DC/DC converter. The optical fiber runs within the in-ice cable jacket as a separate bundled sub-cable, terminating at each breakout connector alongside existing copper pairs.

---

## 5. In-Situ Calibration: Integrated Picosecond Laser Source

### Current Limitation
The flasher board LEDs have a minimum pulse width of ~6 ns FWHM with 10–15% afterglow persisting 15–20 ns, limiting timing calibration precision. The LED wavelength (399 nm) is fixed and does not allow probing wavelength-dependent ice absorption and scattering. Only 16 "color DOMs" provide multi-wavelength capability, deployed on just 2 strings.

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace or supplement the standard flasher board with an **integrated pulsed laser diode module** using **PicoQuant LDH-series** or equivalent gain-switched laser diodes at multiple wavelengths.

**Specific implementation:**
- A single TO-56 package gain-switched laser diode at **405 nm** (primary) with pulse widths of **50–100 ps FWHM** achievable with 3–5 A peak drive current using a dedicated GaAs driver IC (e.g., IXYS IXDN604)
- A second laser diode at **530 nm** provides sensitivity to the absorption minimum of South Pole ice (~450–500 nm), improving ice model constraints
- Average optical power of ~1 nJ/pulse at 1 kHz repetition rate is sufficient for cross-DOM calibration at 125 m
- Integrate a **fiber beam splitter with a reference photodiode** (silicon PIN, e.g., Hamamatsu S5971) to record the exact emission time of each pulse to <100 ps, providing absolute timing reference without relying on ATWD channel 3 current monitoring

**Impact on ice model:** The current uncertainty on ice optical properties propagates to ~10% systematic on DOM efficiency and contributes to angular reconstruction error. Picosecond-resolution calibration pulses at multiple wavelengths, deployed in every DOM rather than 16, would overconstrain the ice model by ~100× in terms of measurement points, reducing ice systematics substantially.

---

## 6. Pressure Sphere: Low-Radioactivity Ultra-Clear Fused Silica

### Current Limitation
The borosilicate glass sphere (Kopp Glass) with K₂O concentration of 0.03% by weight contributes ~100 Bq of ⁴⁰K beta decays per sphere, generating Cherenkov light that contributes significantly to the ~250 Hz uncorrelated dark noise component. The correlated noise (280–340 Hz) from glass luminescence/scintillation also originates primarily from the sphere. Total dark noise (~560 Hz standard, ~780 Hz HQE) is dominated by sphere-related processes rather than PMT thermionic emission.

### Proposed Upgrade
Fabricate pressure spheres from **Suprasil-grade synthetic fused silica** (Heraeus Suprasil 300 or equivalent) with radioactive impurity levels <1 ppb U/Th (vs. ~100 ppm equivalent for borosilicate) and essentially zero potassium.

**Specific material properties:**
- Suprasil 300: U < 0.1 ppb, Th < 0.1 ppb, K < 1 ppb, yielding radioactive decay rate < 0.1 Bq per sphere vs. ~100 Bq for borosilicate
- Transmission of >95% from 170–2500 nm, improving photon collection efficiency for the UV portion of the Cherenkov spectrum (currently 50% transmission at 340 nm for borosilicate)
- No intrinsic scintillation/luminescence from cerium contamination (identified as the candidate correlated noise source)
- Refractive index of 1.46 (vs. ~1.47 for borosilicate) gives similar Fresnel reflection at the ice interface

**Engineering challenge and solution:** Fused silica is more brittle than borosilicate and machining hemispheres to 690 bar specifications requires modified fabrication. Use **chemical-strengthening via ion exchange** (replacing Na⁺ with K⁺ at the surface, standard in optical fabrication) to achieve equivalent pressure resistance. Benthos (current manufacturer) has produced fused silica spheres for ocean research.

**Physics impact:** Reducing dark noise from ~560 Hz to potentially <50 Hz (dominated by PMT thermionic emission if SiPMs are used, potentially <10 Hz) dramatically improves sensitivity to low-energy neutrino signatures. The supernova detection threshold scales inversely with noise rate; a 10× noise reduction would improve the supernova detection distance by ~3× for the same false alert rate. Low-energy solar and reactor neutrino physics would become accessible.

---

## 7. Cable System: Hybrid Copper-Fiber with Increased Bandwidth

### Current Limitation
The current in-ice cable uses 20 copper quad pairs providing 720 kbps per DOM pair, totaling ~11 Mbps aggregate per string. With 60 DOMs per string averaging ~560 Hz dark noise hits at ~500 bytes per SLC hit, the current bandwidth is already near capacity during high-rate periods. Two DOMs share one wire pair, meaning a failed DOM interrupts communication with its partner.

### Proposed Upgrade
Deploy a hybrid cable incorporating both **power-over-copper** (for DOM DC supply, retaining existing 96V architecture) and **multimode optical fiber** for data communications, using **OM4 50/125 µm fiber** with **10GBASE-SR transceivers**.

**Specific design:**
- Retain 4 copper quads per string for 96V DOM power distribution (2 per DOM pair)
- Replace all data communication quads with 8 OM4 fiber pairs (one pair per 7–8 DOMs), using on-string optical multiplexers at each breakout
- Each fiber pair provides 10 Gbps bidirectional, giving ~1.25 Gbps per DOM vs. current 720 kbps — a factor of ~1700 improvement
- One fiber per DOM (rather than shared pairs) eliminates the partner-DOM dependency; a failed DOM no longer disrupts its neighbor's communications
- Separate power and data paths eliminate the modulated power-supply communication scheme, removing a source of cross-talk and enabling cleaner power delivery

**Impact:** Sufficient bandwidth to transmit all hits without LC-based compression, enabling reconstruction-quality SLC hits from every DOM. The current SLC truncation (timestamp + minimal charge only) limits reconstruction for low-multiplicity events; full SLC waveforms would improve [REDACTED] sub-array performance for 10–100 GeV neutrino physics.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for DarkSide-50 Performance Improvement

## Analysis of Primary Limitations

Before proposing upgrades, the paper itself identifies the key performance bottlenecks:

1. **Dominant background**: scintillation+Cherenkov events from Teflon reflector, surviving all ER cuts
2. **Position reconstruction**: poor x-y resolution due to 3" PMT proximity to S2 emission region
3. **PSD at low S1**: photoelectron statistics limit rejection at low energies
4. **PMT radioactivity**: R11065 PMTs are the dominant source of radiogenic neutrons (>90%) and gamma backgrounds
5. **Light yield**: 8.0 PE/keV at zero field is modest, limiting low-energy threshold

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**This is the highest-priority upgrade**, as PMTs are simultaneously the dominant neutron source, the dominant gamma source, and a limiting factor in light collection geometry.

**Specific implementation:**

- **Device**: Cryogenic SiPMs such as Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) RGB-HD or similar devices with demonstrated operation at LAr temperature (87 K), with photon detection efficiency (PDE) of ~50% at 420 nm (TPB emission peak) compared to ~30% quantum efficiency for R11065
- **Geometry**: Tile the full top and bottom windows with close-packed SiPM arrays on fused silica carrier boards, eliminating the 19-PMT sparse array. A 7 cm² tile format with ~100 individual 6mm×6mm SiPMs per tile would provide near-hermetic coverage
- **Radioactivity benefit**: SiPMs fabricated from ultrapure silicon have intrinsic U/Th activities orders of magnitude lower than borosilicate glass PMT stems and ceramic dynode plates. The paper identifies these PMT components as the source of >90% of radiogenic neutron background. Eliminating them directly attacks this dominant neutron source
- **Electronics**: Cryogenic ASIC front-end electronics (e.g., based on CMOS processes validated at 77 K) mounted directly behind the SiPM tiles, replacing the cryogenic PMT preamplifiers. This eliminates the gain instability issues requiring preamplifiers to tame PMT breakdown
- **Light yield impact**: Higher PDE (~50% vs ~30%) combined with improved coverage fraction would approximately double photoelectron yield, improving PSD at all energies and extending the low-energy threshold

**Tradeoff**: SiPMs have higher dark count rates at room temperature, but at 87 K thermal noise is suppressed to ~0.1 Hz/mm², making this manageable. Correlated avalanche noise (optical crosstalk) requires characterization but is typically <15% for modern devices.

---

### 2. Replace Teflon Reflector with Acrylic or Pure PTFE with Wavelength-Shifting Coating Optimization

The Teflon reflector is identified as the **primary surviving ER background source** through Cherenkov light generation. Two complementary approaches:

**Option A – Cherenkov-suppressed reflector material:**
- Replace the bulk Teflon cylindrical reflector with **ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE)** panels. UHMWPE has similar VUV reflectivity characteristics when TPB-coated but a lower refractive index (n ≈ 1.50 vs 1.35 for PTFE at optical wavelengths), reducing the Cherenkov yield for electrons produced by gamma Compton scatters in the material
- More concretely: the Cherenkov threshold for electrons in PTFE is ~175 keV. Selecting reflector materials with lower refractive index raises this threshold, reducing the rate of scintillation+Cherenkov coincidences

**Option B – Thinner TPB layer with gradient deposition:**
- The paper notes that TPB itself produces millisecond-duration scintillation from alpha particles. Controlled TPB layer thickness (targeting ~200 nm rather than thick evaporated layers) would reduce the effective solid angle for Cherenkov photon generation in the bulk Teflon by reducing photon penetration depth, while maintaining adequate wavelength-shifting efficiency
- Achieve this via **atomic layer deposition (ALD)-assisted TPB coating** for better thickness uniformity and control compared to thermal evaporation

**Option C – Segmented veto layer:**
- Instrument the outer face of the Teflon reflector with a thin (2-3 mm) **acrylic light guide** coupled to dedicated SiPM sensors. Cherenkov photons generated in the Teflon and propagating outward would be detected in coincidence with the main TPC signal. This converts the reflector from a passive background source into an active veto, potentially rejecting scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov events with high efficiency without fiducial volume loss

---

### 3. Redesign the Anode/Cathode Windows to Reduce Cherenkov Background

**Current problem**: The fused silica windows (refractive index n ≈ 1.46 at 420 nm) generate Cherenkov light from gamma-scattered electrons, handled by the S1pMaxFrac cut but still contributing background.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace fused silica windows with **synthetic sapphire (Al₂O₃)** windows of equal or reduced thickness. Sapphire has n ≈ 1.77, which actually increases Cherenkov yield—this is the wrong direction. Instead:
- Use **thin (3 mm) fused silica** windows (reduced from current thickness) combined with **ITO cathode/anode on the inner LAr-facing surface only**, minimizing the total radiating material thickness. Thinner windows reduce Cherenkov photon production proportionally
- Alternative: **Crystalline quartz windows** ground to R10 surface finish, which can be made thinner while maintaining structural integrity under the differential pressure of the liquid-gas argon system

---

### 4. Upgrade S2 Detection Geometry for Improved x-y Position Reconstruction

The paper explicitly states that x-y reconstruction is "very difficult" due to 3" PMT proximity to the S2 emission region limiting charge sharing. This directly affects the effectiveness of the RadialFid cut, which achieves only a factor of 2.3 rejection.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- **Replace the top PMT array with a finely segmented SiPM array** (as in point 1) with individual readout channels. Using 6mm×6mm individual SiPM pixels across the full ~28 cm diameter top window gives ~175 independent channels versus 19 PMTs currently. The smaller pixel size dramatically improves S2 light sharing
- **Add a resistive anode readout layer**: A thin resistive coating on the inner face of the top window, read out at the periphery by 4-8 electrodes, provides a fast charge centroid measurement of S2 independent of the optical reconstruction. This technique is established in gaseous TPCs and can be adapted to the liquid-argon gas-pocket geometry
- **Quantitative expectation**: Position resolution scales approximately as (pitch)/√(N_PE). With 10× more channels and 2× higher PDE, position resolution should improve from the stated ~6 mm to ~1-2 mm, enabling a tighter radial fiducial cut that could increase background rejection by an additional factor of 3-5 while maintaining better-characterized acceptance

---

### 5. Improve the Liquid Scintillator Veto with Gadolinium Loading

**Current system**: Boron-loaded liquid scintillator achieves 99.64% neutron veto efficiency, already excellent.

**Limitation**: The 22 µs neutron capture lifetime on ¹⁰B requires a 189.5 µs delayed veto window, generating substantial deadtime and afterpulse contamination in the veto analysis.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- **Add gadolinium loading** (0.1% by mass GdCl₃ or Gd-organic complex) to the borated scintillator. Gadolinium has a neutron capture cross section of 49,000 barns (vs 3,840 barns for ¹⁰B) and a capture lifetime of ~2 µs at 0.1% loading. The resulting ~8 MeV gamma cascade is highly distinctive
- **Benefit**: The LSVdelayed window could be reduced from 189.5 µs to ~20 µs, reducing accidental coincidence rates and allowing a tighter (higher-threshold) veto cut with maintained efficiency. The high capture energy also improves signal-to-noise for the delayed signal
- **Compatibility**: Gadolinium loading has been validated in similar liquid scintillator systems. The existing LSV infrastructure (PMT arrays, data acquisition) requires no modification

---

### 6. Underground Argon Purification Enhancement for ⁸⁵Kr Removal

The paper identifies ¹.⁹ mBq/kg of ⁸⁵Kr as a significant ER background contributor alongside ³⁹Ar.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- **In-line cryogenic distillation column** integrated into the argon recirculation loop, specifically designed to exploit the argon-krypton boiling point difference (87.3 K for Ar vs 119.9 K for Kr). A packed-column distillation unit with ~20 theoretical plates, operating continuously at ~0.5 L/min throughput, could reduce ⁸⁵Kr by a factor of 100-1000 over several months of operation
- **Specification**: Column constructed from electropolished 316L stainless steel with PTFE packing, operating between the existing recirculation pump and the detector inlet. Similar systems have achieved Kr/Ar ratios below 0.1 ppt in xenon experiments (EXO-200, XENON)
- **Impact**: Reducing ⁸⁵Kr from 1.9 mBq/kg to <0.02 mBq/kg would reduce the ER background contribution from krypton to negligibility, and the freed "background budget" could be reallocated to allow a looser (higher-acceptance) f90 cut boundary

---

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Difficulty | Impact on σ_limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| SiPM arrays replacing PMTs | Eliminates >90% radiogenic neutron source; doubles light yield | High | Factor ~3-5 improvement |
| Segmented top array for x-y reconstruction | RadialFid rejection from 2.3× to ~10× | Medium | Factor ~2 improvement |
| Reflector Cherenkov mitigation (Option C active veto) | Removes dominant ER background | Medium | Factor ~2 improvement |
| Gadolinium-loaded LSV | Tighter neutron veto window | Low | <10% improvement |
| ⁸⁵Kr distillation | Reduces one ER background component | Low-Medium | <20% improvement |
| Window thinning | Reduces fused-silica Cherenkov | Low | <20% improvement |

The SiPM replacement is transformative because it simultaneously addresses the three largest hardware-driven backgrounds (radiogenic neutrons, PMT gammas, and indirectly the light yield limitation on PSD) with a single architectural change, at the cost of significant engineering effort for cryogenic tiling and readout integration.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Bare HPGe Array in Liquid Argon

This describes an instrument closely resembling **GERDA Phase II / LEGEND-200**, so I'll focus on upgrades that address the actual limiting factors in physics performance with specific, concrete technology proposals.

---

## 1. Detector Segmentation and Topology Discrimination

### Current Limitation
Bare point-contact or BEGe detectors provide pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) based on single-channel current pulse shape, but have limited spatial resolution for multi-site event rejection.

### Proposed Upgrades

**True Coaxial Segmentation → Small-Pixel Inverted-Coaxial Point Contact (ICPC) Arrays**
- Replace cylindrical coaxial geometry with **inverted-coaxial point-contact (ICPC)** detectors of larger mass (≥ 2 kg each) with segmented outer electrodes — specifically, **6–8 azimuthal + 2 axial segments** on the n+ surface
- Each segment read out individually via dedicated charge-sensitive preamplifiers
- Enables true 3D fiducialization within each crystal, rejecting surface events and multiple-scatter Compton backgrounds at the single-crystal level
- Expected background improvement: **factor ~3–5** in background index over unsegmented ICPCs

**Specific component:** Canberra/Mirion or ORTEC custom segmented ICPC fabrication, with evaporated Li-diffused contacts on segmented outer surfaces; segment boundaries defined by guard-ring implant structures ~0.5 mm wide.

---

## 2. Front-End Electronics: Low-Noise Cryogenic Preamplifiers

### Current Limitation
GERDA uses commercial or semi-custom JFETs at the cold end with significant series noise contribution, limiting energy resolution and PSD figure of merit.

### Proposed Upgrades

**Transition Edge Sensor (TES) or HEMT-based front ends — specifically SiGe HEMTs**
- Deploy **SiGe heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs)** (e.g., IBM 8HP SiGe process, fT ~200 GHz) as the input device of custom charge-sensitive amplifiers operating at 87 K (LAr temperature)
- SiGe HBTs outperform Si JFETs at cryogenic temperatures: noise current spectral density ~1 fA/√Hz, input capacitance well-matched to HPGe electrode capacitance (~1–5 pF for point-contact detectors)
- Alternative: **GaAs or InGaAs HEMTs** (e.g., Fujitsu FHX35X type), which achieve noise temperatures of a few Kelvin at 4 K and remain excellent at 87 K

**Concrete implementation:**
- Custom ASIC in SiGe BiCMOS (IHP SG25H5 or IBM 8HP process) integrating charge-sensitive amplifier + shaper in a single die
- Mount directly on detector contact PCB with 3 cm trace length maximum to point contact
- Target: **FWHM energy resolution ≤ 1.7 keV at Qββ = 2039 keV** (compared to ~2.5 keV typical in GERDA Phase II)
- This directly narrows the signal window, reducing background counts proportionally

---

## 3. Liquid Argon Scintillation Readout: Wavelength Shifter + SiPM Upgrade

### Current Limitation
GERDA Phase II used an instrumented LAr veto with wavelength-shifting fibers + PMTs and a copper shroud coated with tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB). Light collection efficiency was ~5–10 photoelectrons per MeV deposited in LAr, limiting veto efficiency for low-energy Compton scatter tags.

### Proposed Upgrades

**Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) Tile Arrays with Evaporated TPB + PEN Substrates**

**3a. SiPM tiles replacing all PMTs**
- Deploy **Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPC (S13370 series)** or **FBK VUV-HD3** SiPMs directly sensitive to 128 nm VUV argon scintillation without wavelength shifter (QE ~20% at 128 nm for VUV-optimized devices)
- Arrange as close-packed tiles on the inner surface of the detector array shroud: target coverage **> 20% geometric solid angle** facing LAr volume
- Operating at 87 K: SiPM dark count rate drops to < 0.1 cps/mm², negligible compared to scintillation signals

**3b. Wavelength-shifting reflector foils**
- Line all inner surfaces with **polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) foil** (natural scintillator + WLS, emission ~440 nm) or **VM2000 reflector + evaporated TPB** (conversion efficiency ~1.2 photons/photon at 128 nm)
- PEN foil is a deployable, self-supporting WLS scintillator; combined with SiPMs at 440 nm (QE ~40%), effectively multiplies detected photon yield

**3c. Expected performance:**
- Achieve **≥ 50 PE/MeV** detected yield in LAr (vs ~5 PE/MeV in GERDA fiber system)
- LAr veto efficiency for 2039 keV Compton-scatter coincidences: **> 99.5%** (currently ~95% in GERDA)
- Pulse-shape discrimination of LAr triplet/singlet ratio enables **neutron vs. gamma tagging** in the veto

---

## 4. Background Rejection: Active Muon Veto Integration and Neutron Moderation

### Current Limitation
The water Cherenkov shield tags muons, but hadronic showers and secondary neutron capture in Ge (producing ⁷⁷Ge or high-energy gammas near Qββ) represent a residual background.

### Proposed Upgrades

**4a. Gadolinium-loaded water shield**
- Dissolve **gadolinium sulfate Gd₂(SO₄)₃ at 0.1% by mass** in the water shield (as demonstrated by Super-Kamiokande-Gd / EGADS)
- ¹⁵⁷Gd thermal neutron capture cross-section: 254,000 barns; emits ~8 MeV gamma cascade, detected with >90% efficiency by the water Cherenkov PMT array
- Tags neutrons thermalized within ~200 μs of a muon event, enabling extended veto windows that reject muon-induced neutron backgrounds
- **Specific hardware:** Add Gd dissolution/filtration system (precipitation risk mitigated by sulfate over chloride salt); recoat PMTs with Bialkali photocathodes tolerant to Gd-water pH (~5.5)

**4b. Polyethylene neutron moderator layer**
- Insert a **20 cm thick HDPE shell** between the LAr cryostat outer vacuum jacket and the water tank inner wall
- Thermalizes fast neutrons (En > 1 MeV) from rock/concrete before they reach the LAr volume
- Specific geometry: segmented panels of reactor-grade HDPE, bolted to stainless cryostat exterior

---

## 5. Detector-Level Surface Passivation and Contact Technology

### Current Limitation
Incomplete charge collection in the "transition layer" near the p+ point contact (B-implanted, ~300 nm deep) and surface channels cause low-energy tailing into the Qββ region. Alpha and beta surface events are a known background source.

### Proposed Upgrades

**Amorphous Germanium (a-Ge) Contacts**
- Replace conventional boron-implanted p+ contacts with **sputtered amorphous germanium (a-Ge) blocking contacts** (~500 nm thick)
- a-Ge contacts demonstrated by the MAJORANA experiment to provide: dead layer < 10 nm (vs ~0.3 μm for implanted contacts), complete charge collection to the surface, and intrinsic alpha rejection via surface event topology
- Fabrication: RF magnetron sputtering of intrinsic Ge target in Ar atmosphere at room temperature, post-deposition anneal at 150°C
- **Result:** Eliminates the primary alpha background source (radon daughters depositing on detector surfaces), expected to reduce surface-background contribution by **> 10×**

**Aluminum wire bonding → Parylene-coated spring-loaded contact pins**
- Replace wire bonds (which can fracture with thermal cycling) with **PTFE-jacketed BeCu spring contacts** pressing on metalized detector surfaces
- Reduces mechanical stress and risk of detector damage during assembly in LAr

---

## 6. Radiopure Structural Components

### Current Limitation
Copper holders, signal cables, and HV cables near detectors contribute U/Th/K radioactive backgrounds.

### Proposed Upgrades

**6a. Electroformed underground copper (UG-Cu)**
- All structural parts within 5 cm of any detector: replace with **KURF or WIPP underground electroformed copper**, achieving U/Th contamination < 0.1 μBq/kg (vs. 1–10 μBq/kg for OFHC surface copper)
- Specific: detector mounting rings, signal carrier boards, ground straps

**6b. Flat kapton flex cables with low-radioactivity adhesive**
- Replace coaxial signal cables (inner conductor, dielectric, shield—each contributing background) with **custom Kapton flex circuits** (25 μm Kapton base, 18 μm Cu traces, no adhesive layer or low-activity acrylic adhesive)
- Route outside active LAr volume where possible
- Target: < 0.1 mBq/m total ²²⁶Ra equivalent for all cabling within the detector array

**6c. Sintered PTFE or PEN structural spacers**
- Replace any nylon or Delrin components with **sintered PTFE** (low U/Th, no K, low H content to reduce neutron moderation near detector)

---

## 7. Slow Control and Data Acquisition: Upgraded FADC System

### Current Limitation
Standard 100 MHz / 14-bit FADCs limit pulse-shape analysis bandwidth and dynamic range.

### Proposed Upgrades

**Digitizer: 250 MHz / 16-bit FADCs**
- Deploy **CAEN V1730** (250 MS/s, 14-bit, now available in 16-bit variant) or **Struck SIS3316** (250 MS/s, 16-bit ADC)
- 250 MHz sampling captures the ~10–100 ns rise-time structure of HPGe current pulses in full detail, enabling:
  - **Maximum-gradient PSD** with higher figure-of-merit
  - **Phonon-ionization correlation** if bolometric mode explored
  - Better reconstruction of pulse onset for LAr-coincidence timing (< 50 ns resolution)

**Online FPGA-based PSD trigger**
- Implement **Arria 10 or Xilinx Ultrascale+ FPGA** in the DAQ crate performing real-time A/E (amplitude-to-energy) calculation, firing the LAr veto readout only when a germanium event is detected in the RoI
- Reduces data rate by ~100× and enables zero-suppression with guaranteed < 1 μs deadtime

---

## Priority Ranking by Expected Background Index Improvement

| Upgrade | Expected BI Reduction Factor | Technical Readiness |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM LAr veto (item 3) | ~5× | TRL 7 (LEGEND-200 deployed) |
| a-Ge contacts (item 5) | ~5–10× | TRL 6 (MAJORANA demonstrated) |
| Segmented ICPC (item 1) | ~3–5× | TRL 5–6 |
| SiGe HBT preamps → better resolution (item 2) | ~1.5× (resolution) | TRL 5 |
| Gd-water + HDPE neutron shield (item 4) | ~2× for n-induced | TRL 7 |
| UG-Cu + low-BG cables (item 6) | ~2× for intrinsic BG | TRL 8 |

---

## Summary

The highest-leverage single upgrade is the **SiPM-based LAr veto with PEN/TPB wavelength shifting**, since it directly attacks the dominant remaining background (Compton-scattered gammas from external sources surviving the current veto). The second highest-leverage upgrade is **a-Ge surface contacts**, eliminating the alpha/surface-event background floor. Together with **segmented ICPCs** and **SiGe HBT front ends** improving energy resolution and multi-site rejection, these four upgrades could plausibly reduce the background index from the GERDA Phase II level of ~2×10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr) toward the **10⁻⁵ cts/(keV·kg·yr)** regime targeted by LEGEND-1000 for a tonne-scale experiment.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for LHCb Performance Improvement

## 1. Vertex Locator (VELO) Replacement

### Current Limitations
The silicon microstrip VELO operates at 8.2 mm from the beam, with strip pitches of 38–102 µm, achieving ~4 µm best-case hit resolution. Radiation damage reaches 1.8×10¹⁴ n_eq/cm² by Run I end, with depletion voltage approaching 100 V.

### Proposed Upgrade: VELO with Hybrid Pixel Detector
**Replace microstrip sensors with 55×55 µm² hybrid pixel sensors** (similar to Timepix/Medipix architecture):

- **Technology**: 150–200 µm thick n-on-p silicon pixel sensors bump-bonded to 65 nm CMOS ASICs, providing genuine 2D hit information per sensor plane rather than requiring R/Φ sensor pairs
- **Radiation hardness**: n-on-p sensors maintain charge collection efficiency to >10¹⁵ n_eq/cm² without type inversion issues that affect current n-on-n sensors; eliminate the space-charge-sign inversion problem observed at ~15×10¹² n_eq fluence
- **Position resolution improvement**: 2D pixel geometry achieves ~8–10 µm resolution in both coordinates simultaneously without the geometric complications of R-Φ strip pairing; combined with track angle optimization this approaches ~3 µm for optimal incidence angles
- **Reduced material budget**: Monolithic readout removes need for double-sided hybrid construction; target <0.5% X₀ per station versus current ~0.8% X₀, directly improving IP resolution through reduced multiple scattering
- **RF foil**: Replace current aluminum RF foil with 250 µm corrugated beryllium foil, reducing material from ~0.003X₀ to ~0.001X₀ at the critical inner radius

**Quantitative impact on IP resolution**: The asymptotic (high-pT) IP resolution scales as σ_IP ∝ σ_hit × (extrapolation distance). Reducing material budget by 40% and improving first-hit radius from 8.2 mm to ~5.1 mm (feasible with improved RF foil engineering) would improve the asymptotic IP resolution from the current ~13 µm to approximately ~7–8 µm, directly translating to improved decay time resolution.

---

## 2. Tracker Turicensis and Inner Tracker: Replace with LHCb-Scifi Tracker

### Current Limitations
TT silicon microstrips achieve 52.6 µm resolution with 183 µm pitch. IT silicon hits show 50.3 µm resolution. Both face occupancy challenges at high luminosity (up to 1.9% in inner sectors).

### Proposed Upgrade: Scintillating Fiber (SciFi) Tracker
**Deploy multi-layer scintillating fiber mats with SiPM readout** across the entire downstream tracking volume, eliminating the IT/OT boundary:

- **Fiber specification**: 250 µm diameter polystyrene scintillating fibers (Saint-Gobain BCF-12 or KURARAY SCSF-78MJ), arranged in staggered mats of 6 layers per plane, achieving an effective hit resolution of ~100 µm per mat while maintaining full efficiency
- **Photodetector**: Multi-channel Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) with 32-channel arrays at 250 µm pitch, operated at −40°C to suppress dark count rate to <100 kcps/mm², enabling single-photon sensitivity. Use SiPMs with 15–20 µm microcell pitch to maintain good linearity at the expected photon flux
- **Radiation tolerance**: SiPMs require cooling to compensate radiation-induced dark current increase; NIEL damage at inner radii up to ~10¹² 1 MeV n_eq/cm² manageable with cooling. Fibers maintain >80% light yield to this fluence
- **Readout ASIC**: Develop a dedicated 128-channel ASIC with 1 ns timing resolution and analog pulse-height information, enabling time-of-arrival corrections that effectively improve hit resolution below 100 µm through cluster position interpolation
- **Segmentation**: Active fiber mat area of 600 cm × 500 cm replacing the full OT volume, with additional short fiber modules in the inner region replacing IT, eliminating the OT's inherent 35 ns maximum drift time limitation

**Key performance gain**: Elimination of the drift time ambiguity that affects OT straws (±200 µm left-right ambiguity requires pattern recognition to resolve). SciFi provides unambiguous hit positions, reducing fake track rate from ~6.5% to an estimated ~2% in minimum bias events at equivalent occupancy.

---

## 3. RICH System: Upgraded Photon Detectors

### Current Limitations
Hybrid Photon Detectors (HPDs) show photoelectron yield deficits versus simulation (C₄F₁₀: 20.4 vs. predicted 28.3; CF₄: 15.8 vs. 22.7). Read-out inefficiency identified at high trigger rates. Aerogel yields highly variable (5.0 ± 3.0).

### Proposed Upgrade A: Replace HPDs with Multi-Anode Photomultiplier Tubes (MaPMTs)
**Install Hamamatsu R11265 or equivalent 64-anode MaPMTs** in the focal plane of both RICH detectors:

- **Quantum efficiency**: MaPMTs achieve 28–35% peak QE at 270–400 nm versus ~20% for current HPDs; directly increases photoelectron yield by ~40–60%, recovering and exceeding simulation predictions
- **Pixel size**: 6.5×6.5 mm² anode pixels, adequate for RICH1 (which requires ~2.5 mm granularity at the focal plane); RICH2 requires demagnification via proximity-focused lens coupling
- **Magnetic shielding**: MaPMTs require µ-metal shielding to operate in the residual field near RICH1; design compound shields achieving B < 1 mT at the photocathode, addressing the dominant systematic causing the 6% σ(θ_C) discrepancy in C₄F₁₀ attributed to magnetic distortions
- **Timing**: MaPMT transit time spread of ~300 ps enables background rejection using timing cuts, reducing accidental photon hits that currently degrade σ(θ_C)
- **Operational benefit**: Elimination of the cross-focusing HPD optics removes the photon image distortion that currently limits C₄F₁₀ resolution to 1.618 mrad versus the simulated 1.52 mrad

### Proposed Upgrade B: RICH1 Aerogel Replacement
**Replace aerogel with C₂F₆ gas radiator** in RICH1 low-momentum section:

- The aerogel Cherenkov angle resolution of 5.6 mrad (1.8× worse than simulation) is partly caused by C₄F₁₀ absorption into porous aerogel tiles. Removing aerogel and reconfiguring RICH1 optics for dual-gas operation (C₂F₆ at low momentum, C₄F₁₀ for medium range) eliminates this systematic entirely
- Refractive index of C₂F₆ (n-1 ≈ 5×10⁻³ at STP) provides threshold coverage from ~2 GeV/c for kaons, maintaining the π/K separation at low momentum that aerogel currently provides but with resolution ~2× better

---

## 4. Calorimeter System: Upgraded Photodetectors and Segmentation

### Current Limitations
ECAL and HCAL PMTs show progressive gain degradation due to dynode fatigue at high integrated anode current, requiring continuous voltage compensation. Cell-to-cell intercalibration is ~2% for ECAL, ~5% for HCAL. SPD multiplicity veto limits efficiency.

### Proposed Upgrade A: Replace PMTs with SiPMs in ECAL
**Install Hamamatsu S13360 series SiPMs** (or equivalent) coupled to ECAL scintillator tiles:

- **No gain degradation**: SiPMs have no dynode structure; gain is determined by bias voltage and microcell capacitance, stable to >100 Mrad integrated dose if temperature-stabilized. Eliminates the systematic gain-drift correction currently required, which introduces the ~5% luminosity-correlated rate variation visible in HCAL trigger rates
- **Improved energy resolution**: SiPM excess noise factor of ~1.1 versus ~1.3 for PMTs improves stochastic term by ~8%, giving ECAL energy resolution improvement from current ~10%/√E to approximately ~9%/√E; this directly narrows the B→K*γ mass resolution below current 93 MeV/c²
- **Segmentation**: The compact SiPM format (1–3 mm²) enables finer ECAL inner segmentation—replace the current 4.04 cm inner cells with 2.02 cm cells in the highest-occupancy region, reducing pile-up of neutral clusters and improving π⁰/γ separation

### Proposed Upgrade B: HCAL Scintillator Tile Replacement
**Replace existing HCAL tiles with radiation-hard polystyrene + PPO + POPOP tiles** using SiPM readout:

- Current HCAL calibration with ¹³⁷Cs sources only feasible bimonthly during technical stops. With LED+SiPM monitoring (SiPM response is absolutely stable under LED illumination unlike PMTs), intercalibration can be maintained continuously during physics running
- Target HCAL cell-to-cell uniformity improvement from 5% to 2%, directly improving the L0-hadron ET threshold precision and reducing fake triggers

---

## 5. Muon System: Upgrade M1 and Inner Regions

### Current Limitations
M1R1 dead-time reaches 2.5% at 2012 luminosity (double design). Front-end chip dead-time of 50–100 ns is the primary driver. Triple-GEM detectors already deployed in M1 highest-rate region, but read-out electronics limit performance.

### Proposed Upgrade: Micro-Pattern Gaseous Detector (MPGD) with Fast Readout

**Replace MWPCs in M2R1, M3R1 with thick-GEM (THGEM) or µ-RWELL detectors** with new-generation electronics:

- **THGEM geometry**: 0.4 mm holes at 0.7 mm pitch in 0.8 mm FR4, providing gain of 10⁴ in Ar/CO₂ 70/30 with rate capability >10⁷ Hz/cm² versus MWPC limit of ~10⁶ Hz/cm²; directly addresses M1R1 occupancy driving dead-time
- **Readout ASIC**: Deploy SAMPA chip (developed for ALICE TPC upgrade) with 10 MHz continuous digitization and zero-suppression; eliminates the 18–25 ns digital output signal length that causes logical channel occupancy problems in M5. Timing resolution of <1 ns per hit versus current 2.5–4 ns
- **Specific M5 back-scattering fix**: Install 5 cm iron absorber plates behind M5 to reduce beam-line back-scatter hits that artificially inflate M5 logical channel occupancy. This is a low-cost modification with immediate impact on M5 dead-time

**Quantitative impact**: Reducing M1R1 dead-time from 2.5% to <0.3% and M2R1 from 0.6% to <0.1% would recover the full muon trigger efficiency, improving combined 5-station muon ID efficiency from 95% to the design target of >97%.

---

## 6. Trigger System: Online Reconstruction Acceleration

### Current Limitations
HLT1 forward tracking requires p > 3–6 GeV/c minimum momentum cut due to CPU constraints, causing 1–2% per-track efficiency loss versus offline. Deferred trigger achieves only 20–30% effective farm size increase.

### Proposed Upgrade: GPU-Accelerated Online Reconstruction

**Deploy NVIDIA A100 or equivalent GPU accelerators** at rate 1 GPU per 4 CPU nodes in the Event Filter Farm:

- **VELO tracking on GPU**: The VELO pattern recognition (FastVelo algorithm) is inherently parallelizable over track seeds; GPU implementation achieves ~100× speedup over single CPU core, enabling full 3D VELO reconstruction including the second-pass unused-hit recovery at the HLT1 rate. This recovers the ~1% tracking efficiency loss from the disabled second pass
- **PID in HLT1**: GPU-accelerated RICH reconstruction enables RICH PID in HLT1 for the first time; currently RICH information is unavailable at HLT1, meaning hadronic triggers must rely on pT/IP alone. RICH PID in HLT1 would reduce fake rate by ~50% for hadronic lines, allowing lower pT thresholds and improving charm trigger efficiency
- **Forward tracking threshold**: With GPU acceleration enabling 5× faster track finding, the minimum momentum requirement in forward tracking can be reduced from 3 GeV/c to 1.5 GeV/c without exceeding per-event processing time budget. This alone is estimated to improve D⁰→K⁻π⁺ HLT1 efficiency from current ~89% to approximately ~93%

---
