- **Gas mixture**: Ar/CO₂/CF₄ (45/15/40) giving drift velocity ~8 cm/µs, maximum drift time ~10 ns for 3 mm drift gap — negligible compared to 25 ns bunch crossing
- Inherent dead-time <25 ns compared to 50–100 ns for MWPCs, directly addressing the 2.5% M1R1 dead-time documented in the paper
- Pad readout with 10×10 mm pads in R1 and 20×20 mm pads in R2, maintaining current spatial granularity

**New front-end ASIC for all muon stations**: Replace current FEE with a chip providing:
- 10 ns peaking time (achievable with GaAs or deep-submicron CMOS processes available by 2013)
- Digital output pulse width programmable down to 20 ns, reducing the logical-OR dead-time problem for outer regions
- On-chip time-over-threshold digitisation providing crude energy deposit measurement, enabling rejection of M5 backscattering hits by pulse height (backscattered photons and neutrons produce smaller signals than genuine muon tracks)

**M5 beam-line shielding**: Add 10 cm of borated polyethylene + 5 mm of lead downstream of M5 to moderate and absorb backscattered neutrons and photons. The paper identifies backscattering as a specific M5 problem; passive shielding is the most straightforward solution.

---

## 5. Calorimeter System: SPD Replacement and ECAL Upgrade

### Current Limitations Identified in the Paper

The paper documents PMT gain degradation in both ECAL and HCAL, requiring compensating voltage increases and interim monitoring corrections. The HCAL calibration using ¹³⁷Cs sources is limited to technical stops (~bi-monthly), creating calibration gaps. The ECAL intercalibration precision is ~2%, which limits photon energy resolution and hence B→K*γ mass resolution (93 MeV/c² reported). The SPD uses a single-bit discriminator, limiting its utility for pile-up rejection.

### Proposed Upgrade: SiPM Replacement of PMTs in ECAL and SPD Upgrade

**Replace ECAL PMTs with SiPMs** (Hamamatsu MPPC S13360-3050PE or equivalent, 3×3 mm active area, 50 µm cell size, 3,600 cells):

- Temperature coefficient of gain: ~2%/°C, requiring temperature stabilisation to ±0.5°C for 1% gain stability — achievable with standard thermoelectric stabilisation
- Absence of high-voltage supply simplifies infrastructure; SiPMs operate at 55–70 V
- Gain uniformity better than 3% unit-to-unit without individual tuning, compared to PMT tube-to-tube variation requiring individual calibration
- No degradation mechanism analogous to dynode erosion; radiation damage to SiPM bulk does occur but manifests as increased dark count rate rather than gain reduction, separable from signal by timing
- Eliminates the gradual ECAL gain reduction shown in Figure 29 of the paper

**ECAL intercalibration improvement via LED pulser system upgrade**: Replace current LED monitoring with a pulsed laser system at 406 nm (matching ECAL scintillator emission) distributed via single-mode optical fibres to each cell with ~1% pulse-to-pulse stability. This enables continuous intercalibration monitoring at the 0.3% level between π⁰ calibration runs.

**SPD upgrade to multi-bit readout**: Replace single-bit discriminator with 4-bit flash ADC at 40 MHz, providing rough pulse height measurement. At ~10 MIP dynamic range, this allows:
- Rejection of pile-up tracks by requiring SPD signal consistent with single MIP
- Improved electron/photon separation by measuring SPD deposited energy rather than binary threshold comparison
- Online SPD multiplicity measurement with finer granularity for L0 trigger dead-time reduction

---

## Priority Ranking by Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Gain | Difficulty |
|---------|-------------|------------|
| VELO pixel sensors (n-in-p, active edge) | IP resolution ×2, radiation hardness | High |
| RICH MCP-PMT replacement | Npe +30%, eliminates B-field distortion | Medium |
| SciFi tracker | Enables 25 ns operation, resolution ×2 | High |
| GEM expansion M1/M2 + new FEE | Eliminates dead-time, reduces occupancy | Medium |
| ECAL SiPM + laser calibration | Eliminates gain ageing, intercalibration to 0.3% | Medium |

The VELO and RICH upgrades offer the greatest return per unit complexity because IP resolution directly enters every lifetime and mixing measurement, and RICH performance is the unique selling point of LHCb's hadron PID capability. The SciFi tracker is the prerequisite for any serious luminosity increase beyond Run II conditions.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for GERDA

## Primary Performance Metric Context

GERDA's figure of merit is the background index (BI) in cts/(keV·kg·yr) near Qββ=2039 keV, with Phase I achieving ~2×10⁻² and Phase II targeting 10⁻³. The signal sensitivity scales as T₁/₂ ∝ (M·t/BI·ΔE)^(1/2), so improvements to BI, energy resolution (ΔE), and active mass (M) are the primary levers.

---

## 1. LAr Scintillation Veto Implementation (Highest Priority)

The paper explicitly notes LArGe studies motivated a LAr veto for Phase II but it was not yet implemented in Phase I.

**Specific hardware:**
- Replace the copper radon shroud with a **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber curtain** using Saint-Gobain BCF-91A fibers (peak emission 494 nm) arranged in a cylindrical geometry around detector strings
- Deploy **Hamamatsu R11065-10 3-inch PMTs** or **Hamamatsu R11410-23** (used in XENON1T, low radioactivity glass) in the LAr volume rather than only in water
- Alternatively, use **SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13360-6050CS series)** mounted on the WLS fiber assembly; these have ~50% photon detection efficiency at 500 nm, operate at 87K, and have dramatically lower radioactive mass than PMTs (~milligrams vs. ~kilograms per unit)
- Coat inner surfaces of a nylon or copper cylindrical shroud with **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB)** at ~0.2 mg/cm² deposition to shift 128 nm LAr VUV emission to ~420 nm detectable range
- Target LAr veto efficiency >90% for multiple-Compton background gammas, which would reduce BI by estimated factor 3-5 based on LArGe measurements cited in the paper

**Quantified expectation:** The paper's own LArGe results (refs. 23,24,26) demonstrated significant background suppression; implementation in the main detector should push BI from 2×10⁻² toward 5×10⁻³ before other improvements.

---

## 2. Transition to BEGe Detectors with Active Pulse Shape Discrimination

The paper describes five BEGe detectors deployed in July 2011 but Phase I relies primarily on semi-coaxial detectors with limited PSD capability.

**Specific hardware:**
- Full replacement of semi-coaxial Phase I geometry with **Canberra BEGe detectors** (already qualified in paper, 1.7 keV FWHM at 1332 keV demonstrated)
- BEGe single-charge-collection geometry produces a characteristic **A/E parameter** (current amplitude normalized to energy) that separates single-site 0νββ events from multi-site Compton background with >90% signal acceptance at ~80% background rejection per ref. 53,54
- Implement **point-contact geometry detectors** (similar to MAJORANA's PPC design) as alternative: these achieve A/E discrimination with even cleaner single-site identification due to weighting potential concentration
- For detector masses: target 35.5 kg of 6N-purity enrGe already processed (mentioned in paper) into ~20-25 BEGe units of ~1.5 kg each rather than fewer large coaxial detectors
- PSD alone at BEGe geometry could contribute factor ~3-4 BI reduction

**Electronics requirement:** The existing CC2 preamplifier's 55 ns rise time is marginal for BEGe PSD. Upgrade to a **two-stage JFET preamplifier with ~20 ns rise time** using InterFET NJ132L or equivalent cryogenic-rated JFET to preserve the fast current pulse shape information critical for A/E analysis.

---

## 3. Upgraded Charge-Sensitive Preamplifier for Improved Energy Resolution

The paper reports 4.2-5.3 keV FWHM at 2614 keV for Phase I, translating to ~4.5 keV at Qββ. This is significantly worse than the intrinsic detector limit (~2 keV demonstrated at manufacturer).

**Specific hardware:**
- Replace BF862 JFET (NXP) with **Interfet NJ14 or 2SK932** which have lower noise current at 87K and better noise-capacitance matching for BEGe detector capacitances of 1-2 pF
- Implement **reset-type preamplifier** (optical or electronic reset) instead of resistive feedback: eliminates the 500 MΩ RF Johnson noise contribution (currently ~0.3 keV equivalent noise) and removes the associated radioactive resistor material
- The CC2's RF at room temperature contributes noise; a **pulsed optical reset** using a small LED (microwatts, negligible radioactivity) would eliminate this noise source entirely
- Use **Cuflon substrate with lower-loss dielectric** (εr more stable at 87K) for improved high-frequency performance of stray-capacitance feedback components
- Target: reduce electronic noise contribution from ~0.8 keV to ~0.3 keV FWHM, recovering closer to 2-3 keV total FWHM at Qββ

**Quantified impact:** Energy resolution improvement from 4.5 to 3.0 keV FWHM reduces the ROI integration window proportionally, directly cutting background counts by ~33% for same BI.

---

## 4. Mini-Shroud Redesign to Suppress ⁴²K Background

The paper identifies ⁴²K (from ⁴²Ar decay, ~2× the literature limit) as a dominant discovered background requiring the copper mini-shroud as mitigation.

**Specific hardware:**
- Replace 60 µm copper foil mini-shroud with a **hermetically sealed nylon thin-wall vessel** (0.5 mm wall, similar to Borexino inner vessel technology): nylon is more radiopure per unit mass than copper foil and can be made radon-tight while being thinner
- Alternatively, implement **electroformed copper mini-shrouds** (MAJORANA technique): electroformed copper achieves <0.1 µBq/kg in ²²⁶Ra vs. ~16 µBq/kg upper limit for current OFRP copper per Table 6
- Add **electric field shaping rings** at top and bottom of mini-shroud at fixed potential to create a Faraday cage geometry that prevents external ⁴²K⁺ ion drift toward detector surfaces, rather than relying only on physical exclusion
- Install a **dedicated ⁴²Ar monitoring detector** (small natGe slice in separate LAr volume sampled from main cryostat) to continuously track ⁴²Ar concentration with better sensitivity than post-hoc spectral analysis

---

## 5. Radon Mitigation in the Cryogenic Chain

The paper reports 54.7 mBq of ²²²Rn emanation from the cryostat (final configuration), contributing estimated 7×10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) assuming homogeneous distribution.

**Specific hardware:**
- Replace the ~1 kg activated charcoal radon filter with a **cryogenic radon trap** using SARALON or equivalent activated charcoal cooled to 193K (-80°C) with a dedicated small Peltier-cooled stage: adsorption efficiency for radon increases by factor >100 at 193K vs. room temperature, achieving sub-µBq/m³ levels demonstrated for nitrogen (ref. 105)
- Implement **electrostatic radon daughter plate collectors** inside the cryostat below the LAr surface: a negatively biased (~-10 kV) copper plate positioned away from detectors collects positively charged ²¹⁸Po⁺ and ²¹⁴Pb⁺ daughters before they can deposit on detector surfaces
- Upgrade the radon shroud from 30 µm copper foil to **50 µm electroformed copper** (lower emanation) with **hermetically welded seams** rather than overlapping foil joints, reducing the diffusive radon transport path
- Add **online radon monitoring** via alpha spectroscopy in the gas phase above the LAr using a silicon PIN diode (Hamamatsu S3590 series) to enable real-time correlation of radon levels with background rate

---

## 6. Muon Veto Enhancement for the Neck Region

The paper reports 97.2% muon detection efficiency, with the neck region identified as the weak point requiring the separate plastic scintillator array.

**Specific hardware:**
- Replace the 36-panel plastic scintillator array (200×50×3 cm³ each) with **wavelength-shifting plastic scintillator slabs** using EJ-286 (blue-shifted emission, better timing) read out by **SiPM arrays** (Ketek PM3350 or Hamamatsu S13360) replacing the current PMTs: SiPMs have no radioactive glass envelope, operate at lower bias, and can be tiled with <1 mm dead zones
- Increase neck region coverage by adding a **second scintillator ring** around the cryostat neck below the clean room floor level, using 8 additional panels to close the solid angle gap between water Cherenkov and plastic panels
- Implement **timing-based muon tracking** using the Cherenkov PMT hit pattern with 1 ns TDC resolution (upgrade from current ~10 ns): enables muon track reconstruction to predict which germanium detectors are at risk, allowing vetoing with lower dead time than blanket vetoes
- Add 10 additional **8" ETL 9354KB PMTs** in the water volume specifically targeting the under-cryostat region (currently only 6 PMTs in the skirt-enclosed near-closed volume per the paper)

---

## 7. Detector String Segmentation for Background Topology

Currently the paper describes strings of up to 3 detectors with single-channel readout per detector.

**Specific hardware:**
- Implement **segmented outer contact** on semi-coaxial detectors (6-fold azimuthal segmentation as demonstrated by AGATA/MINIBALL collaboration): this provides γ-ray Compton imaging capability to reject multi-site events without pulse shape analysis, complementing BEGe A/E method
- For BEGe detectors, add a **guard ring contact** (concentric inner contact of ~5 mm width) to separately read out near-surface events: surface alpha and beta backgrounds from ²¹⁰Pb daughters deposit energy near the p⁺ contact and can be identified by charge sharing between guard ring and main contact
- Upgrade cable chain from 21×13 mm² cross section to **30×18 mm²** to accommodate additional signal channels: this requires redesigning the lock tube diameter from 160/250 mm to 200/300 mm

---

## Prioritized Implementation Order

| Priority | Upgrade | Expected BI Reduction Factor | Technical Readiness |
|----------|---------|------------------------------|---------------------|
| 1 | LAr scintillation veto (TPB+SiPM) | 3-5× | High (LArGe demonstrated) |
| 2 | Full BEGe deployment + PSD | 3-4× | High (5 units already tested) |
| 3 | Preamplifier reset type + noise reduction | 1.5× (via ΔE) | Medium |
| 4 | Electroformed Cu mini-shroud + E-field shaping | 2× | Medium |
| 5 | Cryogenic radon trap | 1.5-2× | High (technique established) |

Combined implementation targeting Phase II could plausibly achieve **~50× total BI reduction** relative to Phase I, reaching ~4×10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr), exceeding the stated Phase II goal of 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr) with margin for unforeseen backgrounds.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for SNO: Targeted Performance Improvements

## Framing the Problem

SNO's primary physics goal is distinguishing CC from NC interaction rates to test neutrino flavor transformation. The limiting factors are: (1) energy threshold and resolution governing CC spectral measurement, (2) neutron detection efficiency for NC measurement, (3) radioactive backgrounds constraining both, and (4) directional/position reconstruction quality. I address each with specific hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Photomultiplier Tube Replacement and Coverage Enhancement

### Problem
The Hamamatsu R1408 delivers 31% bare photocathode coverage, improved to approximately 54% effective coverage with the aluminum concentrators. The average RMS timing resolution is 1.7 ns, just meeting specification. The mean quantum efficiency of the R1408 at peak is roughly 20-22% in the relevant 300-500 nm Cherenkov spectrum. This directly limits energy threshold and resolution since SNO detects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.

### Proposed Upgrade: Higher-QE Bialkali PMTs

Replace the R1408 with the Hamamatsu R5912 or equivalent 8-inch hemispherical tube, which was becoming available in the late 1990s with quantum efficiencies reaching 27-30% at 390 nm using improved bialkali photocathode deposition on borosilicate glass. Specific improvements:

- **Photocathode material**: Super-bialkali formulation (K-Cs-Sb) on the hemispherical face rather than standard bialkali, pushing peak QE from ~21% to ~28% without changing the glass envelope geometry
- **Dynode structure**: Use a venetian-blind-to-linear-focused hybrid dynode chain rather than the R1408's standard venetian blind, reducing transit time spread from 1.7 ns RMS to approximately 1.1 ns RMS and improving single-photoelectron peak-to-valley ratio from the specified 1.25 to approximately 1.8
- **Glass envelope**: Retain Schott 8246 borosilicate for radioactivity control but specify UV-extended transmission to 280 nm rather than 320 nm, recovering Cherenkov photons from the UV tail of the spectrum where water transparency in D2O is still adequate

The combined effect of higher QE and better UV transmission would increase detected photoelectrons per MeV from approximately 8 to approximately 11-12, improving energy resolution from roughly 8%/√E to approximately 7%/√E and lowering the practical energy threshold.

### Concentrator Redesign

The existing Winston cone concentrators use dielectric-coated aluminum with mean effective reflectance of 82±3%. Replace the coating stack with:

- **Base layer**: Vacuum-deposited silver rather than aluminum (silver reflectance at 400 nm is 97% versus aluminum's 92%, with better performance maintained across 300-500 nm)
- **Protective overcoat**: Single-layer silicon dioxide rather than the TiO2/MgF2 stack, reducing interface losses while maintaining corrosion resistance in deoxygenated water
- **Geometry modification**: Extend the cone aperture from 27 cm to 29 cm diameter, which is geometrically accommodable within the existing hexagonal ABS cells by reducing the cell wall thickness from the current design by 3 mm

Estimated improvement: effective photocathode coverage increases from 54% to approximately 63%.

---

## 2. Front-End Electronics: Improved Dynamic Range and Timing

### Problem
The SNOD discriminator chip operates on leading-edge timing, which introduces amplitude-dependent time walk. The paper acknowledges the QvT (charge versus time) calibration requirement. The QUSN7 chip provides 16-deep analog memory with 12-bit ADCs sampling at 2 μs conversion time, which limits channel occupancy recovery.

### Proposed Upgrade: Waveform Digitization for High-Priority Channels

Rather than replacing the entire custom ASIC chain, which is functional and installed, implement waveform digitization on a selected subset of channels:

- **Deploy flash ADCs at 500 MHz sampling, 8-bit resolution** (components such as the Analog Devices AD9002 or equivalent were available by 1999) on the 960 PMT channels in the innermost two rings of the geodesic sphere, approximately 10% of channels, which subtend the highest solid angle to the fiducial D2O volume
- Each waveform digitizer card replaces the PMTIC+DB daughter board combination for those channels, plugging into the existing SNOBus backplane via a custom interface that preserves the XL1/XL2 communication protocol
- At 500 MHz, 8-bit sampling, a 400 ns timing window requires 200 bytes per channel per event, manageable within the existing 4 MB FEC memory for background rates
- This eliminates amplitude-dependent time walk for the most critical channels, reducing effective single-PMT timing uncertainty from ~2 ns to ~0.5 ns, directly improving vertex reconstruction from approximately 20 cm to approximately 14 cm for 5 MeV electrons

For the remaining channels, retain the ASIC chain but implement a **constant-fraction discriminator** (CFD) modification to the SNOD chip design. A CFD with a splitting ratio of 0.3 and a delay of 3 ns, implementable in the CBICU-2 process used for SNOD, removes amplitude dependence from threshold crossing and reduces walk to below 300 ps across the dynamic range.

---

## 3. Neutral-Current Detector Array: Enhanced Pulse Shape Discrimination

### Problem
The NCD paper section states that slightly more than half of neutron-capture events can be unambiguously identified via track length versus energy, meaning the effective efficiency is 25% rather than the nominal 45% capture efficiency. The dominant limitation is alpha particle background from the nickel walls producing pulses that overlap the 3He(n,p)T signal in energy.

### Proposed Upgrade: Longitudinal Position Readout on All Strings

The paper describes a 30 ns delay-line termination at the bottom of each string for pulse-reflection timing. This is implemented only at the cable end. Extend this to a proper distributed delay-line readout:

- **Replace the single 91Ω readout cable per string with a twin-axial cable pair** from South Bay Cable, using the same copper-polyethylene construction and specific gravity constraint (0.955), carrying independent signals from both ends of each string
- At the bottom endcap, replace the current open-ended 30 ns delay line with a **resistive charge-division wire** along the full active length, using a nichrome alloy resistive anode wire of 100 Ω/m replacing the current 50 μm copper anode
- Longitudinal position resolution of σ_z ≈ 3 cm is achievable from charge division with the existing 12-bit ADC chain, compared to the approximately 15 cm achievable from timing alone
- This position information allows fiducialization within each counter tube: alpha particles from CVD nickel walls have ranges of 2-4 cm in 2.5 atm 3He/CF4, while neutron capture events produce proton and triton tracks with ranges of approximately 1 cm. Events near the wall (within 2 mm radially, identifiable via their longitudinal charge distribution asymmetry) can be rejected, reducing alpha background by a factor of approximately 4 while retaining 92% of neutron capture events

### Gas Mixture Optimization

Replace the 85% 3He / 15% CF4 mixture with **80% 3He / 10% CF4 / 10% CO2**:

- CO2 addition provides superior electron attachment suppression compared to CF4 alone at these pressures while reducing the CF4 content
- More importantly, CO2 reduces the Penning transfer rate that causes gain instability at the anode wire, allowing operation at 1750V rather than 1650V for a gas gain of approximately 200 rather than 100
- Higher gas gain reduces the equivalent noise charge requirement on the preamplifier from approximately 500 electrons to approximately 300 electrons, improving low-energy threshold for pulse-shape discrimination
- The wall effect (proton or triton striking the counter wall before end of range) is mitigated by the slightly higher stopping power of CO2 relative to the displaced CF4 fraction

---

## 4. Water System: Improved Radon Reduction in the D2O Circuit

### Problem
The process degasser reduces Rn by a factor of ~50. At the mine air concentration of 3 pCi/L, even after this reduction, residual radon entering through the cover gas system or from filter changes contributes to photodisintegration backgrounds. The paper describes elaborate procedural controls but limited engineered redundancy.

### Proposed Upgrade: Electrostatic Radon Reduction Column

Insert between the process degasser and the N2 regassing unit a **charcoal delay column** using activated coconut-shell charcoal (Barnebey-Cheney type AC) at low temperature:

- Column dimensions: 30 cm diameter, 2 m length, packed with 80 kg of charcoal
- Operated at 5°C using a glycol chiller circuit independent of the main water chiller
- At 5°C, the dynamic adsorption coefficient of 222Rn on activated charcoal is approximately 3000 L/kg, giving a Rn holdup time of approximately 240,000 s (67 hours) for a 150 L/min flow rate
- Given 222Rn half-life of 3.82 days, this represents approximately 0.8 half-lives of delay, reducing Rn transmission by approximately a factor of 57 for continuous flow
- Combined with the existing process degasser's factor of 50, the cascaded system achieves a factor of approximately 2800 total Rn reduction, reducing the D2O Rn contribution to backgrounds by a factor of approximately 55 relative to the single-degasser design
- The charcoal must be specified with <5 ppb U and Th (available from suppliers at this time) to avoid introducing new radioactivity into the gas stream

### D2O Circulation Pump Material Upgrade

The existing RO membranes use thin-film composite (polyamide on polysulfone) elements. The polysulfone support layer is known to leach small quantities of sulfonated compounds that can complex Ra and retard its removal by the adsorption columns. Replace the polysulfone support with **polyethersulfone (PES) membrane supports**, which show an order-of-magnitude lower leach rate of sulfonated species at the relevant pH and temperature.

---

## 5. Magnetic Field Compensation: Full 3D Active Cancellation

### Problem
The paper describes 14 horizontal compensation coils in the cavity walls that cancel only the vertical component of the earth's field, leaving a maximum residual field of 19 μT in the PMT region. This causes approximately 2.5% reduction in photon detection efficiency. More importantly, the remaining horizontal field component of approximately 20 μT causes PMT gain and timing variations that are spatially non-uniform across the geodesic sphere, introducing systematic position-dependent detector response that is difficult to calibrate.

### Proposed Upgrade: Three-Axis Helmholtz Coil System

The existing 14 horizontal coils are embedded in the cavity walls. Add:

- **Two sets of 6 vertical compensation coils** (12 total) wound from the same low-radioactivity wire specification, mounted on the cavity liner at 60° azimuthal spacing, at heights z = +8 m and z = -8 m from detector center, canceling the horizontal (primarily north-south) field component
- Wire specification: 16 AWG copper with polyethylene insulation, the same material already used for other cavity wiring, with measured U/Th content below 50 ppb
- Each coil carries approximately 0.8 A to produce the required compensating field
- A **3D fluxgate magnetometer array** (6 sensors, commercial units such as the Bartington Mag-03, sealed in epoxy-filled stainless steel housings) distributed at 1 m radius inside the PSUP provides closed-loop feedback to all three coil sets
- Target residual field: <5 μT throughout the PMT volume, reducing the PMT efficiency variation from 2.5% to below 0.7% and improving the uniformity of timing response across the array

---

## 6. Acrylic Vessel: Internal Surface Treatment for Reduced Radon Emanation

### Problem
The acrylic vessel itself is a source of radon emanation proportional to the U content (specified at <1.1 pg/g) and the diffusion length in acrylic. The inner surface of the AV is in direct contact with D2O, and radon diffusing from the acrylic into the heavy water is not removable by the cover gas system.

### Proposed Upgrade: Diamond-Like Carbon Barrier Coating

Apply a **plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) diamond-like carbon (DLC) coating** to the inner surface of the acrylic vessel before water filling:

- DLC films of 200-500 nm thickness deposited from acetylene/argon plasma at room temperature (compatible with acrylic's 80°C glass transition temperature) have radon diffusion coefficients 3-4 orders of magnitude lower than uncoated acrylic
- The coating is optically transparent at wavelengths above 350 nm, with less than 2% additional absorption at 400 nm for a 500 nm film
- Adhesion to UVT acrylic is adequate for the stress levels in the AV (peak tensile stress 4 MPa) as demonstrated by DLC coatings on polymer optical components available at this time
- The DLC surface is chemically inert in ultrapure water and does not leach detectable U or Th
- Application would require development of a deployment system to treat the assembled vessel interior, using a mobile PECVD source on the manipulator carriage; the 6 m radius of the AV and the 1.5 m chimney access constrain the geometry but do not preclude this approach

Estimated radon reduction from acrylic surface: factor of 500-1000, meaningfully reducing one of the irreducible background sources.

---

## Priority Ranking

| Upgrade | Implementation Complexity | Physics Impact | Cost Relative to Existing |
|---|---|---|---|
| NCD resistive anode / position readout | Moderate | High: doubles effective NC efficiency | Low |
| CFD modification to SNOD | Low | Medium: improves vertex resolution ~30% | Very low |
| Higher-QE PMT replacement | High (requires drain/refill) | High: ~35% more photoelectrons | High |
| Charcoal Rn column in D2O circuit | Low | Medium-High: factor 55 Rn reduction | Low |
| Waveform digitization (10% channels) | Moderate | Medium: improves vertex for fiducial events | Moderate |
| 3D magnetic compensation | Low | Low-Medium: reduces systematic PMT non-uniformity | Low |
| DLC inner AV coating | Very high (requires new process) | Medium | Moderate |

The NCD anode upgrade and the charcoal radon column represent the highest physics return per unit of engineering effort and should be prioritized, as they directly address the two primary measurement channels (NC efficiency and photodisintegration background) without requiring major reconstruction of the operating detector.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Advanced LIGO: Prioritized by Physics Impact

## 1. Quantum Noise Reduction (Highest Impact)

### Frequency-Dependent Squeezing via Filter Cavities
The instrument's quantum noise budget splits between shot noise (high frequency) and radiation pressure noise (low frequency). The current homodyne readout is compatible with squeezed light injection, but broadband squeezing only reduces one quadrature, rotating the problem rather than solving it.

**Specific implementation:**
- Install a 300-meter filter cavity (based on calculations by Kimble et al.) in a dedicated vacuum enclosure near each corner station. The cavity length determines the rotation frequency (~50 Hz), matching the crossover between shot noise and radiation pressure noise dominance
- Use etalon-grade, low-loss mirrors (round-trip loss <10 ppm) with fused silica substrates to preserve squeezing
- Inject 10-15 dB squeezed light from an OPO (optical parametric oscillator) based on periodically-poled KTP pumped at 532 nm
- Add a Faraday isolator chain between the OPO and filter cavity with isolation >40 dB to prevent back-reflected light from degrading the squeezed state
- Expected gain: 3-6 dB improvement across the full detection band (10-5000 Hz), equivalent to roughly doubling the detectable volume

### Output Mode Cleaner Enhancement
The current OMC has 90% detection efficiency, leaving meaningful quantum efficiency loss.
- Replace current InGaAs photodiodes with custom, homodyne-optimized photodiodes achieving >99% quantum efficiency (commercially available from Laser Components GmbH, e.g., their custom low-capacitance InGaAs devices)
- Use a second, series OMC cavity tuned to suppress a complementary set of higher-order modes, reducing contrast defect noise
- Add active wavefront correction using a spatial light modulator at the AS port to improve mode matching into the OMC above the current ~95% target

---

## 2. Coating Thermal Noise (Dominant Mid-Band Noise Source)

The paper identifies coating Brownian noise as the dominant thermal noise term, arising from mechanical loss in Ta₂O₅-based high-reflectivity coatings. Even with 25% TiO₂ doping, mechanical loss remains ~2.3×10⁻⁴.

### Amorphous Silicon / Silica Coatings
- Replace the current Ta₂O₅:TiO₂ high-index layers with amorphous silicon (a-Si), which has demonstrated mechanical loss of ~5×10⁻⁵ at room temperature—roughly 5× lower than current tantala
- The high refractive index of a-Si (~3.5 at 1064 nm versus ~2.1 for tantala) means fewer coating layers are needed to achieve the required reflectivity, further reducing total coating noise
- Key challenge: a-Si has high optical absorption (~50 ppm) at room temperature, requiring development of lower-absorption deposition processes, currently being pursued at LMA and Caltech. Target absorption: <2 ppm
- Alternatively, pursue cryogenic operation (see below), where a-Si mechanical loss drops dramatically to ~10⁻⁶

### Crystalline Coatings (AlGaAs)
- Develop and install monocrystalline Al₀.₉₂Ga₀.₀₈As/GaAs multilayer mirror coatings produced by molecular beam epitaxy, as demonstrated by Cole et al. (2013)
- Mechanical loss of ~3×10⁻⁵, optical absorption <1 ppm already demonstrated on small substrates
- Primary development need: scale substrate bonding (direct wafer bonding via Crystalline Mirror Solutions) to the full 34 cm test mass diameter
- These coatings would reduce coating Brownian noise by roughly a factor of 3-4, improving sensitivity in the 50-300 Hz band proportionally

---

## 3. Suspension and Low-Frequency Performance

### Cryogenic Test Mass Suspensions
The mechanical Q of fused silica fibres improves dramatically at cryogenic temperatures, reducing suspension thermal noise below ~20 Hz.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace fused silica fibres with silicon ribbon fibres (single crystal silicon) operating at 120 K, where silicon has a thermoelastic noise cancellation point (coefficient of thermal expansion crosses zero near 18 K and 120 K)
- Change test mass material from fused silica to silicon (isotopically enriched ²⁸Si preferred, as produced by Wacker Chemie), exploiting silicon's near-zero thermal expansion at 120 K and lower mechanical loss
- This requires shifting the laser wavelength to 1550 nm (where silicon is transparent) or 2000 nm; 1550 nm is preferred given commercial availability of high-power Er:YAG or Er-fiber lasers and existing telecom-grade optics
- Install a cryogenic link—thin copper braid or sapphire ribbons connecting test masses to a cryostat while maintaining vibration isolation—following the design approach used in KAGRA (though LIGO's four-stage suspension provides a more favorable starting topology)
- Expected improvement: factor of 5-10 in suspension thermal noise below 30 Hz

### Improved Seismic Isolation: Next-Generation ISI
- Supplement existing GS13 geophones (sensitivity floor ~10⁻¹¹ m/√Hz at 1 Hz) with compact superconducting gravimeters or atom interferometer-based inertial sensors, which achieve 10⁻¹³ m/√Hz or better at sub-Hz frequencies
- Add Newtonian noise cancellation arrays: deploy 6-arm seismometer arrays (using 30-50 Güralp 3ESP or Nanometric T240 units per test mass) in boreholes around each corner and end station, implementing Wiener filter-based feedforward subtraction. Analysis by Driggers et al. suggests 10-40 dB subtraction is achievable at 10-30 Hz, the gravity gradient-limited frequency range
- Install tiltmeters (Applied Technology Associates electrolytic tiltmeter or custom long-baseline laser tiltmeter) collocated with ISI stage 1 to decouple tilt-horizontal coupling that currently limits inertial sensing below ~30 mHz

---

## 4. Laser Power and Optical Layout

### High-Power, Low-Noise Laser at 1064 nm
The current 180 W Nd:YAG system is approaching practical limits with the injection-locked oscillator architecture.

- Replace the third stage injection-locked oscillator with a Nd:YAG master-oscillator power amplifier (MOPA) using a fibre-coupled, Yb-doped large-mode-area (LMA) fibre amplifier as an intermediate stage, followed by a slab amplifier final stage
- A Yb:YAG thin-disk laser (as developed by the Stuttgart group) operating at 1030 nm could achieve 500 W with lower thermal lensing than Nd:YAG, though this requires recoating all optics for the new wavelength
- More practically near-term: increase current system to 200+ W by upgrading pump diode arrays in the third stage oscillator, reducing mode content with an improved pre-mode-cleaner finesse (from 406 to 1000+)
- Target input power at PRM: 200 W (currently limited to 125 W), increasing arm cavity power to ~1.2 MW from current 750 kW design value

### Parametric Instability Mitigation Hardware
As arm power increases, the paper notes 5-10 potentially unstable acoustic-optical modes per test mass.
- Install passive tuned dampers (blade spring + tungsten mass, Q~10) bonded to the test mass barrel at the positions calculated to damp the specific unstable acoustic modes. Target damping: reduce acoustic mode Q from ~10⁸ to ~10⁶, sufficient to suppress parametric gain
- Add dedicated electrostatic drive rings around the barrel of each test mass specifically for high-frequency (~10-100 kHz) acoustic mode damping, separate from the existing piston/pitch/yaw actuator

---

## 5. Core Optics Improvements

### Larger Test Masses
The beam radius is currently limited partly by the 34 cm test mass diameter. Increasing test mass size reduces coating thermal noise (scales as 1/beam radius) and reduces diffraction losses.

- Increase test mass dimensions to 45 cm diameter × 25 cm thick, mass ~80 kg, requiring redesign of the quadruple suspension top mass and cage structure but retaining the monolithic lower stage concept
- Larger beam radius (target ~8 cm on ETM vs current 6.2 cm) reduces coating Brownian noise by ~25%
- Requires upgrading vacuum chamber BSC flanges and internal baffles; chamber diameter is sufficient (BSC inner diameter ~2.5 m)

### Improved Polishing and Figure Correction
The paper reports round-trip arm cavity loss of ~44 ppm against a goal of 75 ppm. Reducing this further improves quantum noise.
- Implement in-situ CO₂ laser figure correction on installed test masses (as explored by Classidy et al.) using the existing thermal compensation system CO₂ projector with improved beam steering to correct large-scale figure errors after installation
- Specify surface flatness to 0.08 nm rms over 160 mm diameter (vs current 0.16 nm spec) for next generation polishing runs, achievable with improved ion beam figuring at QED Technologies or OptiFab

---

## 6. Signal Recycling Optimization for Broadband Sensitivity

### Variable Reflectivity Signal Recycling Mirror
The current fixed SRM (20% transmission) cannot be optimized simultaneously for different source classes without hardware changes.

- Install a Fabry-Perot coupled cavity as an effective variable-reflectivity SRM, using a small auxiliary mirror on a PZT actuator to tune the effective SRM reflectivity continuously between 5-35% without breaking vacuum
- This allows dynamical tuning during observing runs without the current need for a hardware SRM swap, enabling BNS-optimized sensitivity during targeted observations without sacrificing broadband response

---

## Summary Table: Expected Performance Gains

| Upgrade | Frequency Band | Sensitivity Improvement | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency-dependent squeezing | 10–5000 Hz | 2–3× in strain | Medium |
| a-Si or AlGaAs coatings | 50–300 Hz | 3–4× | High |
| Cryogenic silicon test masses | 10–50 Hz | 5–10× | Very High |
| Newtonian noise cancellation | 10–30 Hz | 3–10× | Medium |
| Larger test masses | 50–200 Hz | 1.3× | Medium |
| Higher laser power | 100–5000 Hz | 1.3× | Low-Medium |

The highest-priority near-term upgrade is frequency-dependent squeezing, as it attacks the quantum noise limit across the full band with demonstrated technology and without requiring vacuum breaks. The longest-lead-time upgrade—cryogenic silicon test masses with silicon optics—forms the basis of next-generation detector designs (Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer) and should be pursued in parallel through prototype development.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a 770-tonne Single-Phase LArTPC

## Instrument Context

This describes **ProtoDUNE-SP** (or a close analog) at CERN, with the specific photon detection system being the ARAPUCA-predecessor light-guide/dip-coated bar design embedded in the APA frames. Primary physics performance metrics are: energy resolution, spatial resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, particle identification, and low-energy threshold. I'll address each subsystem where upgrades have the highest leverage.

---

## 1. Photon Detection System — Highest Priority Upgrade

### Current Limitation
Dip-coated light-guide bars with tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) coatings achieve ~0.1–0.3% photon detection efficiency (PDE) per bar. The coating degrades, is geometrically inefficient, and provides poor coverage of the drift volume.

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Replace with X-ARAPUCA modules**
- Deploy **X-ARAPUCA tiles** (already baseline in DUNE FD Module 1) in place of dip-coated bars
- Each tile uses a dichroic filter cavity that traps wavelength-shifted photons, bouncing them until absorbed by embedded **SiPM arrays (Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or FBK NUV-HD-Cryo)**
- PDE improvement: from ~0.3% to **2–4% per module**, a ~10× gain
- Critical for enabling **supernova burst neutrino** detection and **nucleon decay** searches through improved calorimetry
- SiPMs must be characterized at 87 K; use **cryo-qualified SiPMs** with low dark count rate (<100 kcps at LAr temperature)

**B. Increase geometric coverage**
- Current APA-embedded design covers ~1–2% of the cathode-plane-projected area
- Add **cathode-mounted X-ARAPUCA modules** (as in DUNE Module 2 horizontal drift design) to double the solid-angle coverage
- Target: ≥3% total geometric coverage across the active volume

**C. Wavelength shifter improvement**
- Replace TPB dip coats with **vacuum-deposited TPB layers** (100–200 nm) on dichroic filter plates for higher uniformity and adhesion stability
- Consider **pTP (para-terphenyl)** as primary shifter for improved quantum yield at 127 nm Ar scintillation

**D. SiPM signal chain upgrade**
- Replace discrete cold-electronics readout with **COTS cryogenic transimpedance amplifier ASICs** (e.g., LArASIC adapted for SiPM, or the **SPAmod** ASIC from CIEMAT)
- Implement **per-channel 14-bit 250 MSa/s digitization** to resolve S1/S2 separation and enable t₀ reconstruction below 1 ns precision

---

## 2. Wire Readout (TPC Sensing Planes) — Second Priority

### Current Limitation
3-plane wire geometry (U, V, Y/collection) at 4.67 mm pitch. Induction plane signal-to-noise ~15:1 after cold electronics; wire breakage causes dead channels; ambiguities in 2D→3D reconstruction degrade tracking efficiency for ≤100 MeV particles.

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Pixel-based charge readout — LArPix**
- Replace wire planes with **LArPix tiles** (LBNL design, v2c or later)
- Each tile: 100 µm pitch charge pixels, self-triggered, low-power (~1 µW/channel at 87 K), daisy-chainable via UART
- Eliminates projection ambiguity entirely; provides **true 3D charge reconstruction** without reconstruction assumptions
- Dramatically improves multi-track vertex reconstruction for νₑ CC and NC π⁰ events
- Current technology readiness: demonstrated in Module-0 (2×2 prototype); needs **scale-up** to full APA dimensions (~2.3 m × 6 m)
- Key engineering challenge: tile-to-tile gapless tiling and PCB flex interconnect routing at scale

**B. If retaining wires: reduce pitch to 3 mm**
- 3 mm vs. 4.67 mm pitch improves **dE/dx resolution** and **two-track separation** near vertices
- At 3 mm pitch with existing LArASIC cold electronics, SNR remains adequate; requires new wire-winding frames on APAs
- Particularly impactful for electron-photon separation (critical for νₑ appearance signal)

**C. Cold ADC and digital multiplexing upgrade**
- Replace **LArASIC + COLDADC** chipset with the newer **CRYO ASIC stack** (64-channel, 12-bit, 2 MSa/s per channel, noise <500 enc at 87 K)
- Alternatively deploy **ColdADC v2** (prototype from SLAC/BNL collaboration) with improved dynamic range to handle both MIP tracks and hadronic shower cores without saturation

---

## 3. High Voltage and Cathode System

### Current Limitation
Resistive cathode planes with HV feedthrough rated to −180 kV (typically operated at −150 kV for 500 V/cm). HV excursions cause transient noise across entire drift volume. Field uniformity near edges introduces fiducial volume loss.

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Modular Resistive Shell (MRS) field cage**
- Replace aluminum field-shaping rings with a **continuous resistive shell** (FR4 sheets with custom surface resistivity ~10⁸ Ω/□) as demonstrated in ArCLight and SBN-related R&D
- More uniform field distribution, reduced edge effects, potentially recovering **5–10% more fiducial volume**
- Eliminates discrete ring sagitta and associated local field distortions

**B. Improved HV feedthrough**
- Current design (ICARUS-style coaxial feedthrough) susceptible to microdischarges
- Deploy **cryogenic HV feedthrough with solid polyethylene dielectric** (Glassman/Heinzinger with PTFE-over-PE insulator), rated 250 kV to allow operating margin
- Add **slow-discharge bleed resistor chain** integrated into feedthrough to prevent catastrophic stored-energy discharge

**C. Increase drift field to 1000 V/cm**
- Higher field reduces recombination, improving **charge yield by ~20%** for hadronic cascades relative to 500 V/cm
- More critically, reduces the fraction of charge lost to electronegative impurity capture (since drift time halves)
- Requires cathode HV upgrade to −300 kV for 3.6 m drift; feasible with upgraded feedthrough above

---

## 4. Argon Purity and Recirculation System

### Current Limitation
Typical achieved purity: electron lifetime ~3–6 ms, corresponding to ~150–300 ppt O₂-equivalent. At 500 V/cm and 3.6 m drift (~2.2 ms), this produces 30–50% charge attenuation at far end.

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Inline cryogenic oxygen/water getters — upgraded capacity**
- Replace **MonoTorr PS4-MT3-R** getter cartridges with larger **SAES PS4-MT15 series** for higher throughput
- Add a **second independent recirculation loop** (parallel, not series) to reduce required flow velocity and turbulence-induced contamination re-introduction
- Target: electron lifetime >20 ms (< 50 ppt O₂-eq)

**B. Radon suppression**
- For low-energy (supernova/solar) physics, ²²²Rn from emanation within the cryostat becomes a leading background
- Install **activated charcoal cold trap** on the gas recirculation line (similar to XENON/LZ approach adapted for Ar)
- Use **electropolished 316L SS internals** exclusively to minimize Rn emanation surface area

**C. Online purity monitor upgrade**
- Replace single alpha-source purity monitors with a **grid of UV laser purity monitors** (similar to MicroBooNE's laser calibration system)
- Provides **spatial map** of electron lifetime vs. position, enabling position-dependent correction rather than single global value
- Critical for energy resolution uniformity across the full 770-tonne volume

---

## 5. Calibration Systems

### Current Limitation
Primary calibration relies on cosmic muons (energy scale) and radioactive sources (purity monitors only). No internal fiducial energy calibration.

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. UV laser calibration system — extended coverage**
- Install **4 laser feedthroughs** (266 nm Nd:YAG, 50 mJ/pulse) at opposite corners of the detector top
- Use **steerable mirror assemblies** (piezo-actuated at 87 K, already demonstrated in MicroBooNE) to illuminate entire fiducial volume with straight tracks
- Provides: E-field mapping, space charge correction, drift velocity calibration, and detector alignment

**B. Neutron source deployment tube**
- Install a **re-entrant tube** (SS, 1" OD) from the top flange to the center of the active volume
- Deploy a **²⁵²Cf or ²⁴¹AmBe source** to produce monoenergetic neutron captures (n+Ar → 6.1 MeV γ cascade) as an **absolute energy scale anchor**
- This is essential for sub-percent energy calibration needed for precision oscillation physics

**C. Photoelectron injection for SiPM gain calibration**
- Install **optical fiber array** routed to each X-ARAPUCA module, coupled to a shared **picosecond pulsed LED** (405 nm)
- Enables single-photon gain calibration of every SiPM channel in situ without opening the cryostat

---

## 6. DAQ and Trigger Architecture

### Current Limitation
Existing trigger uses **external beam timing + cosmic muon coincidence**. Self-triggering on low-energy events (Michel electrons, low-energy neutrons, supernova relic) is not well-developed.

### Proposed Upgrades

**A. Data-driven trigger using photon detection**
- Implement a **real-time FPGA-based trigger** (using Xilinx UltraScale+ VU9P or similar) that processes photon detector hits with <1 µs latency
- Trigger on any PD coincidence pattern >5 X-ARAPUCA modules within a 1 µs window (threshold: ~20 detected photons = ~10 MeV equivalent)
- This enables **supernova burst buffering**: trigger a full-detector continuous readout window of 10 s upon detecting an excess

**B. Continuous streaming readout**
- Deploy **FELIX (Front-End LInk eXchange)** PCIe readout boards (already ATLAS/DUNE baseline) replacing RCE platform
- Enables **triggerless streaming** of compressed waveform data at full bandwidth (~1 TB/s raw → ~10 GB/s with online zero-suppression)
- Online compression using **WIRECELL** or **DNN-based ROI finding** implemented on **GPU farm** (NVIDIA A100 nodes) colocated at the detector

---

## Summary Table: Expected Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Physics Gain | Quantified Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| X-ARAPUCA PDS | Energy scale, t₀, SN sensitivity | 10× PDE, ΔE/E < 5% for EM showers |
| LArPix pixel readout | Vertex resolution, PID | ~2 mm 3D resolution, eliminates ghost tracks |
| Increased drift field (1 kV/cm) | Charge yield, dynamic range | +20% charge, doubles fiducial-quality drift |
| Purity to >20 ms lifetime | Charge attenuation correction | Attenuation <10% across full drift |
| Neutron source calibration | Absolute energy scale | <1% systematic on EM energy scale |
| Streaming DAQ + PD trigger | Low-energy threshold | Michel electrons (53 MeV), SN burst detection |

---

## Prioritization

1. **X-ARAPUCA replacement** — single highest-leverage upgrade; enables entire new physics program and is already a proven technology
2. **Purity system upgrade** — limited cost, immediate charge recovery benefit
3. **HV/drift field increase** — high impact, moderate engineering risk
4. **Pixel readout (LArPix)** — transformative but requires significant engineering at scale
5. **Calibration systems** — essential for converting hardware performance into physics precision

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a ~2-tonne Dual-Phase Xenon TPC

## Framing: What "Primary Physics Performance" Means Here

For a dark matter direct detection experiment, the key figures of merit are:
- **Background rate** (electron recoil and nuclear recoil backgrounds in the WIMP signal region)
- **Energy threshold** (lowest detectable nuclear recoil energy)
- **Energy resolution** (S1/S2 signal separation quality)
- **Fiducial volume efficiency** (fraction of active mass usable after self-shielding cuts)
- **Electron lifetime / charge collection** (S2 signal quality)

The upgrades below are organized by subsystem with concrete technology choices.

---

## 1. Photon Detection System (Highest Impact Upgrade)

### Current limitation
Standard 3-inch Hamamatsu R11410-23 PMTs have ~35% quantum efficiency. PMT coverage is geometrically limited, and the photon detection efficiency (PDE) directly sets the S1 threshold and resolution.

### Upgrade: Replace PMTs with Vacuum-Ultraviolet Silicon Photomultipliers (VUV-SiPMs)

**Specific technology:** Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) VUV-HD3 or Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPCs

- **PDE at 175 nm:** ~24% for current VUV SiPMs vs ~35% QE for PMTs, BUT SiPMs can be **tiled at ~100% geometric coverage** compared to ~30-40% for PMT arrays
- **Effective photon collection improvement:** factor ~3–5× in detected photons per event
- **Consequence:** S1 threshold drops from ~3 photons detected to potentially single-photon sensitivity; enables nuclear recoil thresholds below 1 keVnr

**Implementation specifics:**
- Tile the entire top and bottom flanges with 6×6 mm² or 10×10 mm² SiPM tiles in a hexagonal close-pack pattern
- Use cryogenic front-end ASICs (e.g., **CAEN A7585D** or custom designs similar to nEXO's CMOS front-end) mounted at ~165 K on the cold flange feedthroughs
- Ganging strategy: groups of 4–9 SiPMs summed to one channel to manage channel count (~1000–2000 channels total), with analog summing on PCB tiles inside the cryostat
- Radio-pure PCB substrate: **ENIG-finished Rogers RO4003C or cryogenic-qualified Cirlex** with electroformed copper traces, screening for U/Th < 0.1 mBq/kg

**Quantitative gain:** Moving from ~8% total photon detection efficiency (typical PMT arrays) to ~25–30% PDE dramatically lowers threshold and improves position reconstruction in z.

---

## 2. Cathode High Voltage and Drift Field Uniformity

### Current limitation
At 2-tonne scale, cathode voltages of ~50–100 kV are needed to achieve drift fields of ~200–500 V/cm over ~1.2 m drift lengths. HV feedthrough reliability and field cage resistor chains are major failure modes and radioactivity sources.

### Upgrade A: Resistive Field Cage with Printed Kapton Electrodes

**Replace:** Discrete resistor chains (typically Ohmcraft thick-film on ceramic) on PTFE support rings

**With:** A monolithic **resistive PTFE or polyimide (Kapton HN) field cage tube** with resistive coating

- Specific technology: Sputtered **amorphous silicon or carbon-loaded PEEK** resistive strips deposited directly on the field cage cylinder
- Target sheet resistance: ~1 GΩ/square for uniform current distribution
- Eliminates hundreds of discrete solder joints, each a potential radioactive hot spot
- **Radioactivity benefit:** Ohmcraft resistors are among the dominant U/Th contributors in current designs (e.g., LUX/LZ); a continuous resistive coating on radio-pure substrate can achieve <1 μBq/kg

### Upgrade B: Greinacher (Cockcroft-Walton) HV Multiplier Inside Cryostat

**Replace:** External HV power supply + long feedthrough cable

**With:** An in-situ HV multiplier chain based on **cryogenic-rated ceramic capacitors and Schottky diodes** driven by a low-voltage AC signal through a standard feedthrough

- Specific implementation: 50-stage Greinacher multiplier using **Vishay VJ series C0G ceramic caps** (verified to function at 165 K) and **BAT46 Schottky diodes** on radio-pure PCB
- Input: 1–2 kV AC at ~10 kHz through a standard low-voltage feedthrough
- Output: up to −100 kV at cathode with <0.1% ripple
- Eliminates the HV feedthrough as the single most failure-prone and radio-impure component
- Demonstrated in prototype form by the nEXO and PandaX-4T groups

---

## 3. Cathode and Gate Electrode Mesh Design

### Current limitation
Woven stainless steel wire meshes (typical: 100 μm wire, 5 mm pitch) cause field non-uniformities at wire crossings, introduce radioactive impurities, and limit optical transparency.

### Upgrade: Electroformed Copper or Titanium Photo-Etched Mesh

- **Specific process:** UV-lithographically defined, electroformed copper mesh with **<10 ppb U/Th** (achievable via OFHC copper electroforming in ultra-clean baths)
- Geometry: hexagonal aperture pattern, 50 μm strut width, 3 mm pitch → **optical transparency >95%**, vs ~85% for woven mesh
- Electroforming eliminates cold-work damage and allows tight geometric tolerances (±2 μm) that reduce field distortions
- For the **gate electrode** specifically: use a **dual-mesh gate** with 1–2 mm separation to allow independent optimization of extraction field (>10 kV/cm in gap) without distorting the drift field

---

## 4. Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) or Thick-GEM for S2 Amplification

### Current limitation
Single-phase electroluminescence in the gas gap produces ~500–800 photons per extracted electron at typical fields (6–10 kV/cm over 5–10 mm gap). Single extracted electrons set the effective S2 threshold.

### Upgrade: THGEM (Thick GEM) as Secondary Amplification Stage

**Not** replacing electroluminescence (which would introduce avalanche fluctuations) but **adding a light concentrator stage:**

- Place a **2 mm thick FR4-free, PTFE-based THGEM** with 300 μm holes and 700 μm pitch immediately above the liquid surface
- Operates in proportional electroluminescence mode (no avalanche), concentrating the photon emission from extracted electrons into a smaller solid angle directly facing the top SiPM array
- Effective gain in detected S2 photons per electron: factor ~2× improvement in geometric collection
- Alternatively, a **single-electron-sensitive S2** mode becomes achievable, enabling sub-keV nuclear recoil detection

**More conservative near-term option:** Optimize the gas gap geometry to exactly 6 mm and hold extraction field at 10 kV/cm—maximally simple but well-validated.

---

## 5. Cryogenic Purity and Electron Lifetime System

### Current limitation
Electronegative impurities (O₂, H₂O equivalent) must be kept below ~0.1 ppb for electron lifetimes >5 ms needed over a 1.2 m drift. Current getter-based systems (SAES PS4-MT50) achieve this but require warm-gas circulation with associated heat load and outgassing risk.

### Upgrade A: Inline Cryogenic Getter in Liquid Phase

**Specific technology:** **SAES MicroTorr** or custom **zirconium-based getter pellets** in a cartridge immersed in the liquid xenon return line at ~165 K

- Cryogenic getters have lower outgassing than room-temperature equivalents
- Eliminates the need to evaporate, clean, and re-condense xenon through a warm loop
- Reduces thermal load by ~500 W (significant for 2-tonne system requiring ~3 kW of cooling)
- **Electron lifetime projection:** >10 ms routinely achievable vs. 3–5 ms typical today

### Upgrade B: Real-Time Purity Monitoring with Dedicated Small TPC

- A **5 cm diameter, 20 cm long auxiliary TPC** sharing the same liquid xenon volume, instrumented with 2 small PMTs or SiPMs
- Uses ⁸³ᵐKr or ²²⁰Rn calibration sources injected continuously at sub-Bq levels
- Provides **electron lifetime maps** in real time rather than inferring from bulk S2/S1 ratio, enabling position-dependent corrections that recover ~10–15% of otherwise fiducialized-away volume

---

## 6. Background Reduction: Inner Vessel and Reflector

### Current limitation
PTFE reflector panels (used for VUV reflectivity >95%) are among the largest surface-area radioactivity sources in the active region. Radon emanation from PTFE is a key ²¹⁴Bi/²¹⁴Po background contributor.

### Upgrade A: Diamond-Like Carbon (DLC) Coated Electroformed Copper Walls

- Replace PTFE panels with **electroformed OFHC copper** cylindrical walls coated with a 100 nm **hydrogenated DLC film** via PECVD
- DLC has VUV reflectivity ~60–70% (lower than PTFE's ~95%), BUT:
  - Radon emanation from copper+DLC is ~100× lower than PTFE
  - Can be supplemented by improved photon detection (see upgrade #1) to recover the optical loss
  - DLC coating is impermeable to Rn diffusion from bulk material
- Net background impact: dominant ²²²Rn-daughter background reduced by ~10×

### Upgrade B: Electropolished Inner Titanium Vessel

- Grade 1 **titanium (low U/Th, ~0.1 ppb bulk)** electropolished to Ra < 0.1 μm
- Radon emanation from polished Ti is ~10× lower than from machined stainless steel
- Ti vessel provides the xenon containment boundary, reducing neutron backgrounds from steel hardware near the active region

---

## 7. Muon Veto and Neutron Capture Enhancement

### Current limitation
The water Cherenkov veto detects muons but has limited sensitivity to **muon-induced fast neutrons** that scatter in the xenon and thermalize before the parent muon triggers the veto (delayed capture).

### Upgrade: Gadolinium-Loaded Water (Gd-H₂O) in the Cherenkov Tank

**Specific technology:** Dissolve **gadolinium sulfate octahydrate (Gd₂(SO₄)₃·8H₂O) at 0.1% by mass** in the water shield

- Gd has the highest thermal neutron capture cross section of any stable element (49,000 barns for ¹⁵⁷Gd)
- Captures thermalized neutrons with mean capture time ~20–30 μs (vs ~200 μs in pure water)
- Emits an 8 MeV gamma cascade detectable by the existing water Cherenkov PMTs
- This is the same technology adopted by **Super-Kamiokande-Gd** (EGADS program, fully deployed 2020)
- Enables **neutron tagging efficiency >90%** for muon-induced neutrons vs ~30% in pure water
- Requires: water purification system tolerant of Gd ions (reverse osmosis + Gd re-injection loop), and verification that Gd doesn't precipitate at operational temperatures (stable at <40°C at 0.1%)

### Supplementary: Add Boron-Loaded Scintillator Layer

- 10 cm thick **EJ-254 boron-loaded plastic scintillator** panels lining the inner face of the water tank
- ¹⁰B(n,α) cross section ~3800 barns for thermal neutrons; captures with 480 keV gamma or alpha+⁷Li
- Provides a fast (~ns) neutron veto signal for neutrons that haven't yet thermalized, complementing the slow Gd capture signal
- Read out by 2-inch PMTs (e.g., **Hamamatsu R7724**) glued to panel edges

---

## 8. Calibration System Upgrades

### Upgrade: Deployable ²⁴¹AmBe + ⁸³ᵐKr Simultaneous Calibration

Current practice of external ²⁴¹AmBe sources has poor geometric coverage and requires dedicated calibration runs.

**Specific hardware:**
- **Internal ⁸³ᵐKr injection system** (already used in LUX/XENON1T): add a dedicated, radio-pure stainless/PTFE injection manifold with a ⁸³Rb source offline, allowing krypton to mix uniformly—enables ER calibration at every energy scale
- **Deployable DD neutron generator** (e.g., **Thermo Scientific P385**): a compact 14 MeV deuterium-deuterium tube source on a motorized cable system around the outside of the cryostat, provides position-controlled NR calibration. More controlled than ²⁴¹AmBe, monoenergetic, switchable

---

## Summary Table: Expected Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Metric Improved | Estimated Gain |
|---|---|---|
| VUV SiPM tiled arrays | S1 threshold, energy resolution | 3–5× more photons → <1 keVnr threshold |
| Resistive field cage | Background rate, field uniformity | 10× reduction in resistor radioactivity |
| In-cryostat HV multiplier | Reliability, background | Eliminates dominant HV feedthrough failure mode |
| Electroformed mesh electrodes | Field uniformity, optical transparency | 95% vs 85% transparency, <10 ppb U/Th |
| Cryogenic inline getter | Electron lifetime, fiducial volume | >10 ms lifetime → full drift length usable |
| DLC-coated copper reflector | Rn-daughter backgrounds | ~10× reduction in ²²²Rn emanation |

| Real-time purity monitor TPC | Fiducial volume recovery | ~10–15% more mass usable |

---

## Prioritization

If forced to rank by **single largest physics impact per engineering effort**:

1. **VUV SiPM tiling** — transforms the threshold and hence WIMP sensitivity at low mass
2. **Gd-loaded water** — nearly free upgrade (dissolve Gd₂(SO₄)₃) with major neutron background reduction
3. **Resistive field cage + electroformed meshes** — dominant radioactivity reduction in field-defining structures
4. **Cryogenic inline getter** — enables the full drift length and thus maximizes fiducial mass without additional excavation or cryostat scaling

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Advanced Gravitational-Wave Detector Performance

## Framework: Noise Budget Analysis

Before proposing upgrades, the dominant noise sources must be identified by frequency band, since each upgrade targets specific limiting physics:

| Frequency Band | Primary Limiting Noise |
|---|---|
| < 10 Hz | Seismic / Newtonian (gravity gradient) noise |
| 10–30 Hz | Suspension thermal noise, scattered light |
| 30–200 Hz | Mirror coating thermal noise |
| 200 Hz – 1 kHz | Quantum shot noise (photon counting statistics) |
| > 1 kHz | Quantum shot noise (dominantly) |

---

## 1. Quantum Noise Reduction (Broadband Limiting Floor)

### 1.1 Frequency-Dependent Squeezed Light Injection

**Current state:** Frequency-independent squeezed vacuum at ~10–15 dB reduces shot noise but anti-squeezes radiation pressure noise below ~50 Hz.

**Upgrade:**
- **Filter cavity array:** Two or more 300-m (or ideally 4-km co-located) triangular filter cavities with finesse ~10,000–30,000, using ultra-low-loss mirror coatings (scatter + absorption < 5 ppm each), to rotate the squeezing ellipse as a function of frequency
- **Rotation angle:** ~45° at the cavity corner frequency (~50–100 Hz) to simultaneously reduce shot noise at high frequency and radiation pressure noise at low frequency
- **Squeezer source:** OPO (optical parametric oscillator) with PPKTP crystal, pump at 532 nm, producing squeezed vacuum at 1064 nm with ≥ 15 dB squeezing (requiring round-trip loss < 2% in the entire injection path)
- **Key component specs:** Filter cavity mirrors with radius of curvature matched to minimize diffraction loss, active alignment with nanoradian-level tip-tilt control, and vacuum-compatible copper thermal shields for thermal stability
- **Gain:** Factor ~2–4 in strain sensitivity across full band

### 1.2 Increased Circulating Power via Higher-Power Laser

**Current state:** ~750 kW circulating power (input ~125 W, arm cavity finesse ~450).

**Upgrade:**
- Replace Nd:YAG master oscillator power amplifier (MOPA) with a **200–300 W single-frequency fiber amplifier system** (Er:Yb-doped, followed by a high-power Yb fiber stage) at 1064 nm, or a direct **200 W Nd:YAG injection-locked oscillator chain**
- **Parametric instability mitigation** (critical at high power): electrostatic drive rings on test masses for active mode damping of ~10–30 acoustic eigenmodes that become unstable via opto-mechanical parametric gain; alternatively, slightly detuned order-3 higher-order mode resonances by adjusting radius of curvature of input test masses by ~±1 meter
- **Thermal compensation system upgrade:** CO₂ laser projector with segmented beam shaping (spatial light modulator or axicon) to correct thermally-induced wavefront distortion in the fused-silica substrate; ring heaters on compensation plates (fused-silica plates in the recycling cavities) with ~10 W total power and 1% spatial uniformity
- **Gain:** Shot noise reduced by $\sqrt{P}$; factor ~1.5–2 at high frequencies

### 1.3 Signal Recycling / Signal Extraction Cavity Optimization

**Upgrade:**
- Transition from **resonant sideband extraction (RSE)** to a **detuned signal recycling configuration** optimized for binary neutron star post-merger frequencies (1–4 kHz), using signal recycling mirror reflectivity ~85% and detuning phase ~0.05–0.1 rad
- Alternatively: **variational readout** — replace the signal recycling mirror with a **speed-meter topology** (Sagnac or back-action evading) using a second output mode cleaner; this evades radiation pressure noise at low frequency without requiring filter cavities
- **Output mode cleaner upgrade:** Increase finesse from ~400 to ~1000 using ion-beam sputtered (IBS) coatings to reduce higher-order mode contamination of the readout

---

## 2. Coating Thermal Noise (30–200 Hz Band — Currently Dominant)

This is the single most important mid-frequency upgrade target.

### 2.1 Amorphous Silicon / Crystalline Coating Replacement

**Current coatings:** Alternating SiO₂ / Ta₂O₅ (titania-doped tantala) quarter-wave stacks, ~40 layers, mechanical loss angle φ_c ~ 2–4 × 10⁻⁴.

**Upgrade options (ranked by maturity and impact):**

#### Option A: Amorphous Silicon (a-Si) Top Layer + Optimized Multilayer
- Replace top Ta₂O₅ layers with **a-Si** (loss angle φ ~ 2–5 × 10⁻⁵ at room temperature, refractive index ~3.5)
- Due to high index contrast with SiO₂ (n~1.46), fewer layers needed (~20 vs. 40), reducing total thermal noise proportionally to $\sqrt{N}$
- **Deposition:** RF magnetron sputtering or PECVD of hydrogenated a-Si:H; anneal at 150–200°C (compatible with mirror substrate)
- **Risk:** Absorption in a-Si must be < 1 ppm (currently ~few ppm; requires careful H content control); thermo-optic noise must be characterized
- **Implementation:** IBS deposition system with in-situ ellipsometry and photothermal common-path interferometer (PCI) for absorption measurement

#### Option B: Crystalline AlGaAs Coatings (Epitaxial)
- **Substrate-transferred GaAs/Al₀.₉₂Ga₀.₀₈As** multilayer grown by MBE, bonded to fused-silica substrate via room-temperature direct bonding or hydroxide-catalysis bonding
- Loss angle: φ ~ 3–5 × 10⁻⁶ — roughly 50–100× improvement over tantala
- **Achieved performance:** ~50-mm diameter demonstrated; scaling to 340-mm interferometer test masses is the primary engineering challenge
- **Specific process:** Al-rich AlGaAs etch-stop layer, wafer flip-bonding to silica, substrate removal by selective wet etch in HF/HCl
- **Thermal noise improvement:** Factor ~5–10 reduction in coating thermal noise power spectral density

#### Option C: Silicon Test Masses at Cryogenic Temperature (Next Generation — but proposable now as upgrade path)
- See Section 5 below

### 2.2 Beam Size Increase at Test Masses

**Current:** Gaussian beam radius at end test masses ~6 cm; limited by mirror diameter (34 cm for Advanced LIGO).

**Upgrade:**
- Increase to **340-mm diameter, 200-mm thick** test masses (larger substrate diameter required for larger optic)
- **New mirror geometry:** Flat-flat arm cavity with **Mesa beam** or **conical beam** (non-Gaussian modes using Mexican-hat mirror profiles) to average thermal fluctuations over larger area
- **Beam radius:** Increase to ~10–12 cm using flat-topped beams; requires mirror surface figure accuracy < λ/1000 RMS over 20-cm diameter
- **Diffraction losses:** Must remain < 1 ppm per bounce; requires Mexican-hat sag profile fabricated by ion-beam figuring to ~1 nm RMS
- **Gain:** Coating thermal noise scales as $1/w^2$ (power spectral density), so factor ~2–4 reduction for beam radius doubling

---

## 3. Suspension Thermal Noise and Seismic Isolation (10–30 Hz)

### 3.1 Monolithic Fused-Silica Suspension Upgrade

**Current state:** Advanced LIGO uses fused-silica fibers (0.4 mm diameter, ~600 mm long) welded to silica ear prisms — already excellent.

**Upgrade:**
- **Longer fibers:** Increase from 600 mm to ~800–1000 mm to lower the violin mode frequencies (below signal band) and reduce suspension thermal noise by $\sqrt{L}$
- **Thinner fibers in necked geometry:** Reduce fiber waist diameter to ~0.3 mm with precision-drawn necks to lower the bending point contribution; requires tensile strength > 4 GPa (achievable with flame-drawn silica)
- **Improved welding:** Replace CO₂ laser welding with **hydrogen-oxygen micro-torch welding** for lower residual stress at weld points
- **Lowest vertical mode coupling:** Maraging steel blade springs (upgraded to **titanium alloy** or carbon-fiber composite blades) with higher elastic Q (~10⁻⁴ loss angle vs. ~10⁻³ for steel)
- **Gain:** Factor ~2–3 reduction in suspension thermal noise at 10–30 Hz

### 3.2 Active Seismic Isolation — Enhanced Platforms

**Current:** HAM-ISI and BSC-ISI active platforms with six-degree-of-freedom control using geophones and seismometers.

**Upgrade:**
- **Inertial sensors:** Replace geophones (flat response above 1 Hz) with **compact interferometric inertial sensors** (e.g., compact Michelson-based accelerometers with 1 pm/√Hz sensitivity at 10 mHz–10 Hz) developed at Nikhef or UWA; directly reduces sensing noise floor fed into platform servo
- **Seismometer network:** Deploy **broadband STS-2 or Trillium Compact** seismometers in seismically quiet caverns or boreholes (10–50 m depth adjacent to corner station and end stations) for feedforward subtraction; coherence with in-vacuum sensors allows subtraction of >90% of microseismic noise (0.1–0.3 Hz)
- **Actuator upgrade:** Replace voice coil actuators on the intermediate mass with **electrostatic drives** to eliminate magnetic coupling to test mass via actuator fluctuating fields
- **Low-frequency performance:** Extended bandwidth to 10 mHz using **tidal feedforward** from GPS-synchronized tiltmeters at multiple baselines

### 3.3 Newtonian Noise (Gravity Gradient) Cancellation

**Frequency target:** 5–20 Hz — currently a fundamental floor for 4-km surface detectors.

**Upgrade:**
- **Seismometer array:** Deploy 100–400 seismometers in a 3D array (boreholes at 5–50 m depth, surface grid spacing ~10 m) around each test mass; geometry determines subtraction depth
- **Signal processing:** Wiener filter or Kalman filter using seismometer array output to predict gravity gradient force on test mass; feed-forward subtraction via electrostatic drive on test mass
- **Achievable subtraction:** Factor 10–30 reduction in Newtonian noise at 10–20 Hz (demonstrated computationally; requires Rayleigh wave coherence length > array scale)
- **Complementary:** Install seismic baffles (dense concrete or lead barriers, 10–20-ton masses) 3–5 m from test mass chambers to reduce Rayleigh wave amplitude at the test mass site by ~50%
- **Gain:** Extends usable bandwidth from ~20 Hz to ~5–8 Hz, accessing binary neutron star inspiral much earlier, increasing detectable volume by factor ~2–8 depending on source

---

## 4. Scattered Light and Auxiliary Noise

### 4.1 Baffling and Stray Light Control

- **Serrated-edge baffles:** Replace current aluminum baffles with **black silicon** or **Acktar Fractal Black** coated baffles with reflectivity < 0.01% at 1064 nm; install at all beam tube section joints with serrated profiles
- **Beam tube upgrade:** Sections near corner and end stations (within 300 m) upgraded with **internal baffles every 3–5 m** and surface treatment (electropolishing + black anodization) reducing specular reflectivity
- **Viewport stray light:** Replace all vacuum viewport windows near optical paths with **wedged, AR-coated fused silica windows** at Brewster angle; add Faraday isolators at output port
- **Gain:** Reduce scattered light noise floor below fundamental noise by factor ~10 in 10–50 Hz band

### 4.2 Residual Gas Damping

- Improve vacuum in beam tube from ~10⁻⁷ torr to **10⁻⁸ – 10⁻⁹ torr** by: replacing ion pumps with **non-evaporable getter (NEG) pump** strips along beam tube length (titanium-zirconium-vanadium alloy, activated at 400°C during bake); adds ~1 L/s/cm pumping speed along full 4-km length
- **Gain:** Reduces phase noise from residual gas (H₂ dominant) fluctuations by factor ~3–10; primarily matters above ~1 kHz

---

## 5. Transformative Long-Lead Upgrade: Cryogenic Silicon Test Masses

This represents the most impactful possible upgrade but requires near-complete reconstruction of end stations.

### Rationale
Silicon at 120 K (or 10–20 K) has:
- Near-zero thermo-optic coefficient (dn/dT ≈ 0 at ~120 K, cancellation between TO and TE coefficients)
- Mechanical loss angle φ ~ 10⁻⁸ (substrate), reducing thermal noise dramatically
- Requires wavelength change to **1550 nm or 2000 nm** (silicon is opaque at 1064 nm)

### Specific Hardware

**Test masses:**
- **Single-crystal silicon**, 45 cm diameter, 55 cm thick (550 kg), grown by float-zone method for low impurity density; surface figure < λ/100 over clear aperture; polished to 0.1 nm RMS

**Suspension:**
- **Silicon ribbon or fiber suspensions** (single-crystal, <100> orientation, Q > 10⁸); bonded via silicon-to-silicon bonding using crystal alignment; or crystalline silicon springs
- **Multi-stage cryo-compatible suspension:** Upper stages in **maraging steel or titanium** at room temperature, thermal transition via thin silicon bonding links or lossy-free flex pivots

**Cooling:**
- **Pulse-tube cryocoolers** at 4 K with heat exchangers at 77 K and 120 K stages; total cooling power requirement ~10–20 mW at test mass
- **Radiative cooling links** (copper heat straps with high emissivity coating to cryogenic shields at 120 K surrounding test mass in vacuum) — avoids mechanical contact noise
- **Thermal shield:** Multi-layer radiation shields (gold-coated aluminum, 77 K and 5 K stages) surrounding test mass assembly

**Laser:**
- **1550 nm Er-fiber-based laser** (100–200 W class; several vendors can supply) or **2 μm Tm:fiber laser**; complete redesign of interferometer optics for new wavelength
- AlGaAs coatings operate efficiently at 1550 nm (existing technology); or **crystalline germanium/Si multilayers** for 2 μm

**Gain:** Combined substrate + coating thermal noise reduction of factor **50–100** over room-temperature silica/tantala; could push sensitivity floor to quantum noise across 10 Hz–10 kHz

---
