# Hardware Design Upgrades for EXO-200

## 1. Photodetector Replacement: LAAPDs → Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

The LAAPD system is the most consequential limitation on energy resolution.

**Specific problems with current design:**
- 48% photosensitive packing fraction on platters
- Ganging of 5-7 devices forces common bias despite ~20V spread in optimal operating voltage across devices, limiting uniformity to σ=2.5% response
- 125 pF per device capacitance at 1400V dominates noise (1000 pF per channel), forcing 4 parallel JFETs and limiting charge collection efficiency to ~90%
- Noise limits scintillation threshold, degrading low-energy performance and anti-Compton discrimination

**Proposed upgrade:**
Replace all 468 LAAPDs with cryogenic SiPMs such as FBK RGB-HD or Hamamatsu VUV3 series operated at 163K. At LXe temperatures these devices achieve:
- Geiger-mode gain ~10⁶ versus LAAPD gain of ~50-100, dramatically reducing downstream electronic noise requirements
- Individual pixel capacitance ~50 fF versus 125 pF, with total device capacitance of order 50-100 pF at comparable active area
- Photon detection efficiency (PDE) at 178 nm approaching 20-35% with appropriate VUV-optimized surface treatment versus the LAAPD quantum efficiency of roughly 14% in this wavelength range
- Direct sensitivity to single photons enabling coincidence-based noise rejection impossible with LAAPDs

**Mechanical implementation:**
Redesign the copper platters to accommodate 3mm × 3mm SiPM tiles in close-packed arrays. At 3mm pitch, a hexagonal close-pack on the existing platter geometry could achieve photosensitive fraction exceeding 70% without the acrylic washer insulators currently needed at empty positions. Individual or small-group bias trimming per tile using thin-film resistor networks on the polyimide interconnect layer would replace the current six-sector trim scheme, eliminating the response non-uniformity from ganging.

**Front-end consequence:**
Lower input capacitance per channel permits returning to single JFET preamp topology on all channels with smaller feedback capacitance (1-2 pF), improving equivalent noise charge by a factor of 3-5 on scintillation channels.

---

## 2. Drift Field Upgrade: Resolving the HV Instability

The detector operates at 8 kV cathode bias against a nominal design of 70 kV, yielding roughly 380 V/cm drift field instead of the design 3.7 kV/cm. This is the single largest identified performance gap in the paper.

**Root cause analysis:**
The paper identifies corona discharge from sharp photoetched edges as the likely source of instabilities above 9-14 kV. The photoetching process produces wire cross-sections described as "roughly square with width 127 ± 40 µm" — sharp corners are precisely where field enhancement causes corona onset.

**Proposed upgrade - electropolished drawn wire replacement:**
Replace photoetched phosphor bronze wire triplets with individually drawn circular cross-section wire of 127 µm diameter, made from the same CA-510 phosphor bronze stock. Circular cross-section eliminates the corner field enhancement by a factor equal to roughly the ratio of corner radius to wire radius — for a square wire this enhancement is approximately 3-5×.

Mounting compliance currently provided by the photoetched spring fold would instead use a separate spring mechanism: a phosphor bronze leaf spring anchor block, itself photoetched but carrying no HV, onto which individual drawn wires are resistance-welded. The electrical path never traverses a sharp photoetched edge under high field.

**Cathode redesign:**
The two half-cathodes are also photoetched phosphor bronze. Replace with electroformed mesh using circular cross-section wire of ~100 µm diameter woven at 90% optical transparency, with all edges electropolished and the perimeter embedded in a PTFE-grooved copper frame that presents no exposed metal edges to the high-field region. This is analogous to techniques used in gaseous detector cathode construction.

**HV cable conduit upgrade:**
The current RG217 cable with polyethylene dielectric running inside a copper conduit full of LXe introduces a geometry with imperfect field grading at the LXe-polyethylene interface. Replace with a custom coaxial line using PTFE dielectric (lower outgassing than polyethylene, compatible with cryogenic operation, well-characterized radioactivity) and a graded resistive layer at the interface using a thin-film resistor chain deposited on the PTFE outer surface to suppress field enhancement at the liquid-solid boundary.

**Expected benefit:**
Operating at the design field of 3.7 kV/cm rather than 0.38 kV/cm has two major effects. First, electron-ion recombination in LXe decreases strongly with increasing field: at 3.7 kV/cm the ionization yield is approximately 3× higher than at 0.38 kV/cm for MeV-scale energy deposits. Since EXO-200's energy estimator is a linear combination of ionization and scintillation, the statistical uncertainty on the ionization component decreases proportionally with the square root of collected charge. Second, the electron drift lifetime requirement becomes less stringent: electronegative impurity attachment scales as exp(-t/τ) where t is drift time, and higher field reduces t for a given drift distance.

---

## 3. Ionization Readout: Increase Channel Segmentation Selectively

**Current limitation:**
38 readout channels per wire plane, with 9 mm readout pitch (triplets of 3 mm wires). The multi-site event discrimination relies on identifying events with charge deposited on more than one wire group. At 9 mm readout pitch, two Compton scatter vertices must be separated by more than roughly 9 mm in the wire-plane coordinates to be resolved as multi-site. For 2.6 MeV Compton scatters in LXe, the mean free path is ~9 cm, so most multi-site events are well-separated, but a subset with shorter separation escapes discrimination.

**Proposed upgrade:**
Implement a two-tier readout scheme: retain the existing 9 mm triplet grouping for 80% of the wire plane area but add a central high-resolution zone of single-wire 3 mm pitch readout covering the inner 50% of the active volume by radius. This exploits the fact that the fiducial volume cut preferentially selects events near the center of the detector.

The central zone increases the number of readout channels by approximately 3× in that region. The additional channels are read with the same FEE card design, requiring six additional 16-channel FEE cards per TPC end. The interconnect polyimide cables require redesign in the central zone only, with the outer zone cables unchanged.

**Multi-site discrimination improvement:**
Reducing the minimum resolvable separation from ~9 mm to ~3 mm in the central zone increases the fraction of correctly identified multi-site Compton backgrounds. Monte Carlo studies of similar geometry suggest this improves background rejection by 20-40% for events that would otherwise mimic single-site topology, directly improving the signal-to-background ratio in the 0νββ analysis window.

---

## 4. Field Cage Resistor Replacement

**Current design:**
900 MΩ thick-film resistors on sapphire substrates, 10 per field cage, dissipating 0.6 W at design field. At 8 kV operating voltage the dissipation is approximately 7 mW — negligible — but the resistors represent a material budget concern for radioactivity and constrain the grading precision to 0.6% RMS.

**Proposed upgrade:**
Replace thick-film resistors with custom ultralow-radioactivity amorphous silicon resistors deposited directly on PTFE substrates. Amorphous silicon has been demonstrated in other low-background detector contexts and allows deposition from high-purity silane feedstock with measurable U and Th content at sub-ppb levels. The deposition can be performed in a dedicated clean PVD system.

At the same time, increase the number of field-grading steps from 10 to 20, reducing the voltage step per ring from 400 V (at design field) to 200 V. This reduces the field non-uniformity near the ring gaps and pushes the edge of the fully-collecting volume closer to the physical field cage radius, increasing active mass by approximately 2-3 kg.

---

## 5. Scintillation Wavelength Shifting for Improved Light Collection

**Current design:**
The 178 nm scintillation photons are detected directly by LAAPDs (or replacement SiPMs). The PTFE reflectors achieve 70% reflectance in argon and presumably better in LXe, but the cathode grid region and wire plane region have limited coverage.

**Proposed upgrade:**
Evaporate tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) at controlled thickness of 0.2-0.5 mg/cm² onto the PTFE reflector tiles and the non-photosensitive surfaces of the detector platters. TPB shifts the 178 nm LXe scintillation to ~430 nm where SiPMs (if the LAAPD replacement above is implemented) have PDE of 40-50% versus ~15-20% at 178 nm even for VUV-optimized devices. This represents a factor of ~2-3 improvement in photon detection probability at the photodetector surface.

The TPB deposition must be performed in a dedicated clean vacuum system with careful control of substrate cleanliness to avoid introducing radioactive contamination. The coating stability at 167 K under LXe immersion has been demonstrated in prototype studies with similar detectors. The copper surfaces of the wire support rings and LAAPD platters would also receive a thin TPB coat via the same process.

**Combined benefit with SiPM upgrade:**
Combining improved PDE at the detector with wavelength shifting approximately doubles the effective light yield detected. Improved light collection directly reduces the statistical fluctuation in the scintillation signal, which is the dominant term in energy resolution at low light yields. The improved energy resolution reduces the 2νββ spectral leakage into the 0νββ analysis window, which is increasingly important as exposure accumulates.

---

## Summary of Expected Performance Gains

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Estimated Magnitude |
|---------|----------------|---------------------|
| SiPM replacement | Scintillation noise reduction | 3-5× improvement in scintillation S/N per channel |
| HV restoration to design field | Ionization yield, drift lifetime | ~3× more collected ionization charge |
| Central high-resolution wires | Multi-site background rejection | 20-40% improvement in Compton rejection |
| Increased field grading steps | Active mass increase | ~2-3 kg additional active LXe |
| TPB wavelength shifting + SiPM | Light collection efficiency | ~2-3× detected photons |

The HV instability fix is the most critical single upgrade, as it affects both signal channels simultaneously and represents the largest deviation from the design operating point. The photodetector replacement addresses the next largest performance gap.

# Proposed Hardware Design Upgrades for GERDA

## 1. Liquid Argon Scintillation Veto (Highest Priority)

The paper explicitly states GERDA decided to implement a LAr scintillation light veto for Phase II based on LArGe results, but Phase I lacks it. This is the single most impactful upgrade.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the 30 µm copper radon shroud with a **wavelength-shifting (WLS) nylon or copper foil cylinder** coated with tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB), which shifts LAr scintillation at 128 nm VUV to ~420 nm visible
- Deploy **Hamamatsu R11065 3-inch low-background PMTs** or **Hamamatsu MPPCs (silicon photomultipliers)** arranged in rings above and below the detector array within the mini-shroud volume
- The SiPM option (e.g., Hamamatsu S10931-050P arrays) is preferable because: negligible radioactivity compared to PMT glass, operational stability at 87 K LAr temperature is demonstrated, no high voltage distribution near detectors
- Target photon detection coverage of ~10% of inner shroud surface to achieve >90% tagging efficiency for multi-MeV gamma events
- Expected background reduction: factor 3–10 in the ROI based on LArGe measurements cited in the paper, pushing BI toward the Phase II goal of 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr)

## 2. Transition to BEGe Detectors with Active Pulse Shape Discrimination

The paper notes Phase II BEGe detectors have good pulse shape discrimination (PSD) properties but only five were inserted experimentally. The bulk of Phase I mass consists of semi-coaxial detectors with inferior PSD.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace semi-coaxial ANG/RG detectors with **Broad Energy Germanium (BEGe) detectors** from Canberra, as already in production, with individual masses of ~0.8 kg
- BEGe single-electrode geometry produces a characteristic **current pulse shape** where the ratio A/E (maximum current amplitude to energy) cleanly separates single-site 0νββ events from multi-site gamma background
- Measured discrimination power from cited references: >90% background rejection with ~90% signal acceptance at Qββ
- Implement **digitizer upgrade**: replace the current 100 MHz 14-bit AD6645 ADCs with **250 MHz 14-bit digitizers** (e.g., SIS3316 from Struck) to better resolve the fast current pulses of BEGe detectors, which have rise times of ~100–200 ns
- The CC2 preamplifier rise time of 55 ns is adequate but the sampling rate currently decimates to 25 MHz for the long trace; the full 100 MHz trace storage should be extended to cover the complete pulse for all channels without compression

## 3. Upgraded Front-End Electronics with Reduced Radioactivity

The paper reports CC2 preamplifier activities of (286±28) µBq ²²⁶Ra and (150±24) µBq ²²⁸Th per PCB, which is at the limit for the Phase I BI goal. For Phase II's BI of 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr) this becomes insufficient.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Redesign the CC2 PCB using **Cirlex (polyimide) substrate** instead of Cuﬂon; Cirlex has demonstrated lower U/Th contamination in screening campaigns and better mechanical stability at LAr temperature
- Replace the **BF862 JFET** (commercial package with unknown radioactivity) with a **bare die JFET** (e.g., Interfet NJ14 or custom low-noise JFET) mounted directly on the PCB without plastic packaging, eliminating the dominant radioactivity source in the package
- Replace **AD8651 op-amp** in commercial package with bare die equivalent or redesign second stage using discrete ultra-low radioactivity components
- Eliminate **tantalum capacitors** entirely (already partially done per the paper) by implementing all decoupling as PCB trace stray capacitance or using thin-film NiCr/SiO₂ capacitors with demonstrated radiopurity
- Target: reduce ²²⁸Th activity to <50 µBq per PCB, a factor 3 improvement, keeping electronics contribution to BI below 10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) at 30 cm separation

## 4. Radon Shroud and Inner Shielding Upgrade

The measured 222Rn emanation of 54.7 mBq from the cryostat translates to a BI contribution of ~7×10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) assuming uniform distribution, with the shroud providing up to factor 7 reduction.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the current **30 µm copper foil radon shroud** (item 4, Fig. 6) with a **radon-tight nylon film barrier** (6–10 µm thick) of the type developed for Borexino, which has demonstrated Rn diffusion coefficients orders of magnitude lower than copper foil
- Alternatively, use **electrolytic copper foil of 50–100 µm** with electropolished inner surface; electropolishing removes ~10 µm of surface layer where the majority of ²²²Rn-emanating ²²⁶Ra resides, potentially reducing emanation by factor 2–3
- Install a **recirculating LAr purification loop** with a cold molecular sieve trap (13X zeolite or activated carbon at 77–87 K) actively removing dissolved Rn from the LAr in real time; flow rate of 1–2 L/hour through a 100 g trap would achieve continuous purification
- Add **electrodes on the mini-shroud** to create a weak (~100 V/m) electric field that drifts positive ⁴²K ions away from detector surfaces toward the shroud walls, directly addressing the dominant background discovered during commissioning

## 5. Muon Veto Enhancement in the Neck Region

The paper identifies the neck region as a geometric weakness requiring the plastic scintillator array on the clean room roof, with measured muon detection efficiency of (97.2±1.1)%, leaving ~3% untagged.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the 36 **UPS-923A plastic scintillator panels** (200×50×3 cm³) with **larger 200×100×5 cm³ panels** using **EJ-200 or BC-408 scintillator** (longer attenuation length, ~380 cm vs ~250 cm for UPS-923A) to improve light collection uniformity and reduce the number of panel-to-panel gaps
- Replace the **Y11 wavelength-shifting fibers** (56 per panel) with **BCF-92 fibers** (higher capture efficiency) and use **silicon photomultipliers** (SensL MicroFB-60035) instead of the H6780-2 and PMT-85 PMTs; SiPMs operate at low voltage (~30 V), have no magnetic field sensitivity, and can be read out with simpler electronics
- Add a **fourth scintillator layer** rotated 45° to the existing three layers to eliminate residual geometric acceptance holes
- Install **additional PMTs within the cryostat neck argon gas volume** using low-activity 2-inch PMTs (e.g., ETL 9902 selected for low K content) to detect Cherenkov light from muons traversing the neck before entering the detector array

## 6. Detector String Geometry and Mini-Shroud

The mini-shroud concept successfully reduces the ⁴²K background but the current 60 µm Cu foil implementation has limited hermeticity and does not instrument the LAr volume.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Fabricate mini-shrouds from **electroformed copper** (10–20 µm, electroformed to achieve <10 µBq/kg ²²⁸Th, comparable to the best underground copper) rather than rolled foil, providing better hermeticity and lower radioactivity
- Machine **precision-fit end caps** with spring-loaded contacts for the signal and HV cables passing through the shroud, replacing the current open-ended design that allows residual electric field leakage
- Coat the **inner surface of the mini-shroud with TPB** to integrate the mini-shroud into the LAr scintillation veto system described in point 1, creating an optically active boundary that can detect even low-energy (~100 keV) gamma interactions within the shroud volume

## Summary of Expected Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Target Background | Expected BI Reduction Factor |
|---|---|---|
| LAr scintillation veto | External gammas, ²⁴²K | 3–10× |
| BEGe + improved PSD DAQ | Multi-site gamma events | 3–5× |
| Reduced radioactivity FEE | Internal electronics gammas | 3× |
| Rn shroud + purification | ²²²Rn, ²¹⁴Bi | 5–7× |
| Improved muon veto | Muon-induced neutrons | 2× |

The LAr veto combined with BEGe PSD are complementary and largely independent rejection handles; their combined application could realistically achieve the Phase II target BI of 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr), which is the limiting requirement for reaching an effective Majorana mass sensitivity below 100 meV.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Advanced Gravitational-Wave Detector Performance

## Systematic Framework

To propose meaningful upgrades, I'll organize by the fundamental noise floors that limit sensitivity across different frequency bands, then identify the specific hardware changes with highest leverage. The three dominant limitations in a modern Advanced LIGO-class detector are: **quantum noise** (shot noise + radiation pressure noise), **thermal noise** (primarily mirror coatings), and **seismic/suspension noise** at low frequencies.

---

## 1. Quantum Noise: Squeezing and Optomechanical Configuration

### 1.1 Broadband Frequency-Dependent Squeezing via Long Filter Cavities

**The problem:** Frequency-independent squeezing (as currently deployed at LIGO/Virgo) reduces shot noise at high frequencies but increases radiation pressure noise at low frequencies. The optimal squeezing angle rotates as a function of frequency.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Install a **300 m filter cavity** (or two cascaded ~150 m cavities) on each interferometer's input squeezing path, matched to the interferometer's optomechanical pole frequency
- The filter cavity rotates the squeezing ellipse from ~45° at DC to ~0° at high frequency, achieving frequency-dependent squeezing
- Target: **15 dB of injected squeezing** (requiring ~20 dB raw squeezing accounting for optical losses)
- Use **parametric down-conversion in periodically-poled KTP or KTiOPO₄ crystals** pumped at 532 nm (for 1064 nm operation) or 775 nm (for 1550 nm)
- Loss budget must be controlled to <0.5% per optical element; this requires ultra-low-loss Faraday isolators (η > 99.5%) and homodyne detectors with photodiode quantum efficiency >99%

**Quantitative gain:** Broadband squeezing at 15 dB beyond the standard quantum limit improves strain sensitivity by ~factor of 5-6 in shot-noise-limited band (above ~100 Hz), recovering 2-3 dB of that at low frequencies compared to frequency-independent injection.

### 1.2 Signal Recycling Cavity Detuning and Speed Meter Configuration

**Current limitation:** The standard dual-recycled Michelson operates with a signal recycling mirror (SRM) tuned near resonance (broadband), limiting the peak sensitivity bandwidth product.

**Specific upgrades:**
- **Sagnac speed meter topology:** Replace the standard Michelson with a Sagnac-based or zero-area Sagnac configuration using an additional beam splitter and delay line. This provides back-action evading measurement of test mass velocity rather than position, suppressing radiation pressure noise without requiring squeezing. Requires significant infrastructure modification but is feasible as a "next generation" upgrade path.
- More conservative alternative: **Variational readout (output mode cleaner with tunable cavity)** — implement a tunable output filter cavity to rotate the readout quadrature as a function of frequency, providing back-action evasion without full speed meter topology
- **Resonant sideband extraction (RSE) tuning optimization:** Tune signal recycling cavity length for narrowband operation targeting binary neutron star inspiral chirp frequencies (optimize for 100-500 Hz band), accepting bandwidth reduction for peak sensitivity gain

### 1.3 Increased Arm Cavity Power

**Current state:** Advanced LIGO operates at ~300 kW circulating power; parametric instabilities and thermal effects limit increases.

**Specific upgrade path:**
- **Higher-order mode (HOM) dampers on test masses:** Install electrostatic actuators or ring-damper systems to suppress parametric instabilities that develop at high circulating power. Current designs suppress ~100 parametric instability modes; next-gen requires active identification and suppression of additional modes as power increases
- **Input laser power upgrade to 200 W** (from current ~125 W) using **Nd:YAG master oscillator power amplifier (MOPA) with injection-locked slave lasers**, maintaining frequency noise at <10⁻⁴ Hz/√Hz
- Target 750 kW–1 MW arm cavity power to reduce shot noise by additional factor ~1.8

---

## 2. Coating Thermal Noise: The Dominant Noise Floor at 10–200 Hz

This is arguably the **single highest-leverage upgrade** available. Coating Brownian noise from the multilayer dielectric mirror stacks on the test masses currently limits sensitivity in the most scientifically valuable frequency band.

### 2.1 Amorphous Silicon / Crystalline Mirror Coatings

**Current state:** Ta₂O₅/SiO₂ (tantala/silica) coatings have mechanical loss angle φ ~ 2×10⁻⁴, dominating thermal noise.

**Specific alternatives:**

**Option A — Amorphous silicon (a-Si) high-index layers:**
- Replace Ta₂O₅ high-index layers with **hydrogenated amorphous silicon (a-Si:H)** deposited by plasma-enhanced CVD
- Refractive index n ~ 3.5 at 1550 nm (vs. 2.09 for Ta₂O₅), dramatically reducing the number of required coating layers (from ~38 to ~18 layer pairs)
- Mechanical loss angle φ ~ 5×10⁻⁵ at room temperature — **4× improvement** over tantala
- Critical requirement: switch operating wavelength to **1550 nm** where a-Si absorption is acceptable (<1 ppm/cm); at 1064 nm, a-Si absorption is prohibitive (~1000 ppm)
- Must develop compatible **1550 nm laser systems** (Er:fiber amplifier + frequency doubler for squeezing) and **InGaAs photodetectors** with >99% quantum efficiency

**Option B — Crystalline AlGaAs/GaAs coatings:**
- **Substrate-transferred epitaxial AlGaAs/GaAs multilayers** grown by MBE on GaAs substrate then bonded to fused silica or silicon test masses via direct bonding
- Mechanical loss angle φ ~ 4×10⁻⁶ — **50× improvement** over current coatings
- Currently demonstrated at small scale (cm diameter); scaling to 34 cm test mass diameter is primary engineering challenge
- Compatible with both 1064 nm and 1550 nm operation
- Requires ultra-clean bonding environment; defect density must be <0.1/cm² to avoid point-absorbers causing thermal lensing

**Option C — Nanostructured / phononic crystal coatings:**
- Engineer **phononic bandgap structures** in coating layers to suppress the mechanical modes that couple to thermal fluctuations
- Still in early R&D phase; mention as 10-year horizon technology

**Quantitative gain:** Reduction of φ by 10–50× reduces coating thermal noise amplitude by 3–7×, representing the most impactful single upgrade.

### 2.2 Cryogenic Test Masses

**The case:** Thermal noise scales as √(T × φ × ...) — cooling test masses reduces noise even with current coatings.

**Specific implementation:**
- **Silicon test masses at 123 K or 20 K** (two zero-crossing temperatures of silicon's thermal expansion coefficient, enabling athermal operation)
- Mass dimensions: ~550 kg octagonal Si crystals (vs. current 40 kg fused silica), increasing beam spot size and further diluting coating thermal noise
- Cryogenic links: **hollow silicon or sapphire fibers** connecting test mass to cryostat cold stage, chosen to minimize mechanical coupling while conducting heat
- **Radiative cooling via cryogenic baffles** surrounding test mass within the vacuum envelope, avoiding mechanical contact with cold stage
- Cryostat design must provide cooling power >100 mW at 20 K while maintaining seismic isolation; this requires multi-stage pulse tube coolers or Gifford-McMahon cryo-coolers with vibration-isolated compressors connected via flexible gas lines
- Critical complication: **silicon is opaque at 1064 nm** → requires full transition to 1550 nm laser system

**Quantitative gain:** At 20 K vs. 300 K with silicon (φ_Si ~ 10⁻⁸ at 20 K), coating thermal noise reduces by factors of 50–100× compared to room-temperature fused silica; suspension thermal noise essentially eliminated.

---

## 3. Suspension and Seismic Isolation Upgrades

### 3.1 Next-Generation Suspension Systems

**Current state:** Advanced LIGO uses quadruple pendulum suspensions with fused silica fibers for final stage (Q ~ 10⁸ for violin modes, dilution factor of 10⁶ for pendulum mode).

**Specific upgrades:**

**Silicon fiber suspensions (for cryogenic operation):**
- Replace fused silica fibers with **monocrystalline silicon ribbon fibers**, 0.5–1 mm width, connecting cryogenic silicon test masses to marionette stage
- Silicon fibers have extremely low thermoelastic noise at 123 K (crossing point) and high tensile strength (>GPa)
- Welding/bonding silicon fibers to silicon test masses via **CO₂ laser spot welding** or chemical bonding through hydroxide catalysis
- Fiber geometry: flat ribbon (rather than circular cross-section) to maximize vertical-to-horizontal compliance ratio, minimizing coupling of vertical seismic noise

**Magnetic-free lower-noise marionette:**
- Replace current coil-magnet actuators on lower suspensions with **electrostatic actuators** (parallel plate or comb-drive) for low-frequency control, eliminating magnet-associated Johnson noise and Barkhausen noise
- Electrostatic actuation authority: design for ±10⁻⁷ m displacement range at test mass level

### 3.2 Active Seismic Isolation Upgrades

**Current state:** LIGO's HAM/BSC seismic isolation platforms use hydraulic actuators + geophones + accelerometers with blending filters to achieve ~10⁻¹² m/√Hz above 10 Hz.

**Specific upgrades:**

**Inertial sensor upgrade — 6D seismic sensing:**
- Replace current geophone arrays with **atom interferometer inertial sensors** or **superconducting gravimeters** capable of measuring all 6 degrees of freedom (3 translational, 3 rotational) with noise floor below 10⁻¹² m/√Hz above 1 Hz
- Current Sercel geophones (L-4C type) have noise floors ~10⁻¹⁰ m/√Hz at 1 Hz; next-gen atom interferometers reach 10⁻¹³ m/√Hz
- **Tiltmeter upgrade:** horizontal seismometers are contaminated by tilt-horizontal coupling (tilt of 1 nrad mimics 10 nm/s² horizontal acceleration); install dedicated **Michelson-based or Sagnac-based tiltmeters** with sub-nanoradian sensitivity at 10 mHz–1 Hz

**Newtonian noise cancellation array:**
- Install networks of **seismometers and gravimeters** in a 3D array around each test mass (underground and surface), covering ~50m radius
- Use **Wiener filter or neural network-based subtraction** to cancel Newtonian (gravity gradient) noise, which bypasses mechanical isolation entirely
- Target 10–100× Newtonian noise reduction in 10–30 Hz band where it currently limits sensitivity
- Requires O(100) sensors per corner station; underground placement (boreholes to 50 m depth) reduces surface wave contribution

**Magnetic field shielding:**
- Install **mu-metal + active cancellation coil arrays** around suspension regions to reduce magnetic field fluctuations (lightning, power-line harmonics, magnetic storms) coupling to magnets on test mass suspension
- Target: residual field noise below 1 pT/√Hz at 1–100 Hz at test mass location

---

## 4. Test Mass Geometry and Substrate Upgrades

### 4.1 Larger and Heavier Test Masses

**Physics motivation:** Radiation pressure noise scales as 1/M; larger test masses also allow larger beam spots, averaging coating noise over more area (thermal noise ~ 1/w where w is beam radius).

**Specific upgrade:**
- Scale from 40 kg fused silica to **200 kg silicon** (room temperature) or **550 kg silicon** (cryogenic)
- Larger mirror diameter (from 34 cm to 55–70 cm) with **larger beam waists** (from ~6 cm to ~10 cm at end test masses)
- Requires enlargement of beam tube diameter or acceptance of increased clipping losses; alternatively, **flat-top (mesa) beam profiles** using Mexican-hat mirror shapes reduce peak intensity while maintaining large effective averaging area

### 4.2 Optical Contacting and Surface Quality

- **Ion beam figuring (IBF)** of test mass surfaces to achieve surface figure error < 0.3 nm RMS over the clear aperture (vs. current ~0.5 nm)
- **Single-point diamond turning** for rough shaping followed by IBF for fine correction
- Sub-Angstrom surface roughness to reduce scatter losses in arm cavity to <1 ppm per mirror

---

## 5. Auxiliary and Infrastructure Upgrades

### 5.1 Mode Cleaner and Input Optics

- **Higher-finesse input mode cleaner (IMC):** Increase finesse from ~500 to ~5000 by using ultra-low-loss mirrors; this reduces laser frequency noise coupling proportionally
- **Dual-stage IMC** in series to achieve additional factor of 10 in frequency noise suppression
- **Thermally compensating recycling cavity mirrors:** Install CO₂ laser heating rings for in-situ thermal lens correction in power recycling cavity, maintaining impedance matching as circulating power varies

### 5.2 Vacuum System Upgrades

- **Extended bake-out protocol** for new beam tube sections targeting residual gas pressure < 10⁻¹⁰ Torr H₂ (current goal); residual gas noise from phase fluctuations and residual gas damping of test masses scales with pressure
- **Activated charcoal cryopumps** at 77 K inserted in arm cavity beam tubes to maintain ultra-high vacuum especially for heavier species (N₂, O₂, CO)

### 5.3 Photodetection and Readout

- **Transition edge sensor (TES) or kinetic inductance detector (KID) arrays** for homodyne readout: quantum efficiency >99.9% compared to ~99% for best InGaAs photodiodes, reducing detection loss that degrades squeezing benefit
- These operate at ~100 mK and require a dilution refrigerator stage at output optics bench — significant infrastructure but eliminates readout loss as a limiting factor
- Alternatively: **balanced homodyne with balanced heterodyne cross-check** to reduce technical noise in DC readout

---

| 1 | AlGaAs crystalline coatings | Coating thermal noise | 30–300 Hz | 3–7× in amplitude |
| 2 | Cryogenic Si test masses (20 K) | Thermal noise (coating + substrate + suspension) | 10–300 Hz | 5–10× combined |

# Hardware Design Upgrades for IceCube: Targeted Performance Improvements

## Identification of Primary Performance Limitations

Before proposing upgrades, the binding constraints on IceCube's core physics performance must be identified from the paper itself:

- **Angular resolution**: ~0.6° for muon tracks, limited by timing precision (~1.2 ns demonstrated), DOM spacing (125 m), and hole ice scattering
- **Energy threshold**: ~100 GeV for standard array, limited by DOM spacing and photon detection efficiency
- **Photon statistics**: sparse 125 m string spacing means most events are reconstructed from O(10-100) DOMs
- **Waveform dynamic range and deadtime**: ATWD deadtime of ~29 μs per channel readout, 427 ns capture window
- **Dark noise**: 560-780 Hz per DOM, limiting low-energy sensitivity
- **DOM optical efficiency**: 25% peak QE, downward-facing geometry, ~4% light loss from mu-metal grid

---

## Upgrade 1: Replace PMT with Large-Area Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

### Motivation
The paper states peak QE of 25% (34% for HQE variants) for the Hamamatsu R7081-02. The mu-metal cage blocks ~4% of incident light. The PMT requires ~130 ns transit time and contributes timing jitter that limits the demonstrated 1.2 ns inter-DOM timing accuracy. Dark noise of 230-250 Hz Poissonian component partly originates from thermionic emission in the PMT.

### Specific Implementation
- **SiPM array**: Replace the single 10" downward-facing PMT with a segmented spherical array of Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or FBK NUV-HD SiPMs tiling ~50% of the lower hemisphere plus ~20% of the upper hemisphere
- **Current SiPM performance**: Peak PDE ~50-55% at 420 nm (roughly 2× the HQE PMT), dark count rate at -30°C reduced to ~50 kHz total across the array (comparable to or below current PMT dark noise when normalized per unit area), and single-photon timing resolution of ~200 ps FWHM vs. ~2 ns for the PMT
- **Tile geometry**: 12-16 tiles of ~6 cm × 6 cm each, arranged to provide ~4π/3 sr coverage downward and ~2π/3 sr upward, eliminating the directional blind spot of the current downward-facing PMT
- **Elimination of mu-metal**: No magnetic field sensitivity, removing the 4% light blockage and simplifying mechanical assembly
- **Ganging strategy**: Group 4-9 SiPM cells per readout channel to manage capacitance and noise; use ~16-24 independent readout channels per DOM for directional sensitivity
- **Temperature benefit**: At -30°C (typical in-ice DOM temperature from the paper), SiPM dark count rate drops by approximately an order of magnitude compared to room temperature, dramatically improving the ratio of signal to noise for low-energy events

### Expected Physics Impact
- 2× improvement in photon detection efficiency increases effective detector volume for sub-TeV events proportionally, lowering energy threshold toward 10 GeV without changing string spacing
- Directional photon information from segmented tiles enables shower/track discrimination at the DOM level before surface readout, reducing trigger false positive rate
- Reduced dark noise improves supernova sensitivity and low-energy neutrino oscillation measurements in DeepCore-like analyses

### Engineering Challenges
The paper notes that 5.7 W average DOM power is already constrained. SiPM arrays require careful low-noise amplification; at these temperatures, SiPM bias voltage temperature coefficients (~50 mV/°C for most devices) must be tracked. A per-tile bias DAC with temperature feedback is required, adding ~0.5 W per DOM but eliminating the high-voltage generator (~300 mW currently) since SiPMs operate at 25-70 V rather than ~1400-1800 V.

---

## Upgrade 2: Replace ATWD + fADC Digitization with Waveform-Sampling ASIC

### Motivation
The paper identifies several concrete limitations of the current ATWD-based system:
- 427 ns capture window insufficient for distant photons; fADC handles extended capture but at only 40 Msps with limited dynamic range
- Deadtime of ~29 μs per ATWD channel when reading out 4 channels; median fractional deadtime 6.6×10⁻⁵ for in-ice DOMs but up to 3.2×10⁻³ for IceTop high-gain DOMs
- Two ATWD chips operated alternately to reduce deadtime, adding complexity
- The droop correction (Eq. 3.3-3.4) with two time constants is necessitated by the transformer coupling, adding calibration complexity and potential systematics

### Specific Implementation
- **Target ASIC**: A custom waveform sampling chip based on the DRS4 architecture (Paul Scherrer Institut) or the PSEC4 chip (University of Chicago) operating at 5-10 Gsps with switched-capacitor array depth of 1024 samples
  - DRS4 achieves 5 Gsps with 1024 cells, 11.5-bit equivalent dynamic range, and ~10 ps RMS timing resolution
  - PSEC4 achieves 15 Gsps with 256 samples, designed specifically for large neutrino detector applications
- **Configuration**: Two parallel sampling channels per readout, one at full 5 Gsps for precision timing of early photons (covering ~200 ns window) and one at 250 Msps for extended 6 μs capture, eliminating the separate fADC
- **Direct coupling**: Replace the toroid transformer (which causes the droop requiring the complex correction of Eq. 3.3-3.4) with a transimpedance amplifier (TIA) with differential output driving the sampling chip. A DC-coupled TIA using a precision op-amp such as the ADA4817 (Analog Devices) with 1 GHz bandwidth, configured for ~10 mV/μA transimpedance, eliminates transformer distortion entirely
- **Integrated discriminator**: On-chip comparator with programmable threshold replaces the separate SPE/MPE discriminator circuits, with threshold set digitally via SPI interface from the FPGA
- **Dead-time elimination**: Continuous sampling with ring-buffer architecture means no re-arm delay; the 50 ns re-arm delay and the ~29 μs digitization deadtime are eliminated, replaced by the ~100 ns readout latency of modern ADC pipelines

### Expected Physics Impact
- Elimination of the droop correction removes a systematic uncertainty in charge reconstruction, particularly important for the 1204 DOMs with "old toroid" transformers where the paper notes baseline shifts of 0.6 counts can double the measured charge
- 5 Gsps sampling resolves individual photon arrival times within the multi-photon waveforms currently captured by the 300 Msps ATWD, potentially improving vertex and direction reconstruction for shower events
- Reduced deadtime directly improves efficiency for high-multiplicity events and cascades

### Engineering Challenges
The DRS4 consumes ~150 mW per chip; two chips plus TIA amplifiers would add ~400 mW, requiring revision of the DOM power budget. The elimination of the ~300 mW HV generator (if SiPMs are also adopted) offsets this. The Main Board redesign must accommodate the new chip footprint within the annular geometry around the PMT neck.

---

## Upgrade 3: Upgrade DOM-to-Surface Communications to Ethernet over Existing Copper

### Motivation
The paper states the current communications bandwidth is 720 kbps per twisted pair, with two DOMs sharing each pair. At 360 kbps effective per DOM, this limits hit payload transmission and requires aggressive on-DOM compression. The paper notes the DOM stores O(10 s) of data before SDRAM overflow—meaning backpressure from bandwidth limitations can cause data loss during high-rate events. The SLC hit format (timestamp + minimal amplitude only) is forced partly by bandwidth constraints.

### Specific Implementation
- **Technology**: G.fast or VDSL2 (Very High Speed Digital Subscriber Line 2) chipsets, such as the Lantiq VRX318 or Broadcom BCM65200, designed for operation over existing twisted copper pairs
  - VDSL2 achieves 100-200 Mbps over short loops (<500 m) and 50-100 Mbps at the 2500 m cable lengths in IceCube using profile 35b
  - The in-ice cable electrical specifications from the paper (attenuation ≤20 dB at 1 MHz, differential impedance 145 Ω ±10 Ω) are compatible with VDSL2 requirements
- **Bandwidth increase**: Factor of ~100-300× improvement from 720 kbps to 50-200 Mbps per pair
- **Power delivery**: VDSL2 chipsets can be configured for power-over-twisted-pair; the existing 96 VDC supply structure is compatible with this approach after appropriate DC-DC conversion within the DOM
- **Shared pair elimination**: With sufficient bandwidth, each DOM can have a dedicated pair, eliminating the paired-DOM constraint that currently requires special termination (140 Ω) in one DOM and complicates failure modes (the paper notes that when one DOM on a pair fails, its partner may also be taken out of service)
- **RAPCal compatibility**: The existing RAPCal timing scheme (section 3.3) can be preserved or improved, as VDSL2 modems support precise round-trip timing measurement natively with sub-ns precision through echo cancellation hardware

### Expected Physics Impact
- Full waveform transmission for all hits (eliminating the SLC vs. HLC distinction) would provide complete information for every photon detection, improving reconstruction of low-multiplicity events near the energy threshold
- The paper notes SLC hits contain only "a timestamp and minimal amplitude/charge information"—full SLC waveforms would improve energy reconstruction for isolated DOMs in sparse events
- Elimination of forced compression reduces systematic effects in the HLC waveform delta-compression scheme
- Higher bandwidth enables transmission of per-channel directional information if the SiPM upgrade (Upgrade 1) is implemented

### Engineering Challenges
VDSL2 chipsets require more complex impedance matching networks, and the dispersive properties of the 2500 m cable at higher frequencies must be characterized. The paper notes the cable was designed and tested at 1 MHz; behavior above 10 MHz over 2500 m of ice-embedded cable at -30°C must be measured. VDSL2 chipset power consumption (~2-4 W) would increase DOM power budget, but this is partially offset by simpler readout logic.

---

## Upgrade 4: Integrated LED Calibration System with Picosecond Laser Diodes

### Motivation
The paper describes the flasher LEDs as having 6 ns FWHM minimum pulse width with 10% afterglow "decaying over 15-20 ns." The RAPCal timing system achieves ~1.2 ns timing accuracy. However, the flasher-based geometry and ice property measurements are limited by the 6 ns pulse width and the non-Gaussian emission profiles requiring correction terms (σ = 9.7° in polar, different angular distributions for tilted vs. horizontal LEDs). The cDOM program (16 specialized DOMs) is too sparse for comprehensive wavelength-dependent ice absorption/scattering measurements.

### Specific Implementation
- **Laser diode replacement**: Replace the 12 LED array with 6 pulsed laser diode modules using gain-switched distributed feedback (DFB) laser diodes at 405 nm, 450 nm, and 532 nm (two of each), achieving pulse widths of <100 ps FWHM
  - Suitable devices: Hamamatsu PLP-10 series pulsed laser heads, or gain-switched Thorlabs LP405-SF10 in a custom driver circuit
  - Peak power: 5-10 mW per pulse at <100 ps, providing equivalent photon flux to current LEDs at maximum brightness but with far superior timing definition
- **Emission geometry**: Integrate a miniature diffuser and GRIN lens assembly at each laser diode output to control the angular emission profile to σ < 5° (compared to current σ ≈ 10°), improving the precision of geometry fits using the hyperbolic time-distance method (section 5.3.2)
- **Wavelength expansion**: Add two UV laser diodes at 337 nm and 355 nm to probe the short-wavelength absorption edge of ice and glass, where current measurements show rapid transmission decrease (93% at 400 nm falling to 10% at 315 nm as noted in the paper)
- **Independent DOM triggering**: Add a hardware trigger output from each laser diode driver to the local coincidence signaling system, enabling synchronized multi-DOM flasher events. The paper explicitly notes "the DAQ does not support time-synchronized flashing of LEDs on different DOMs"—a hardware-level trigger distribution through the LC wiring would enable this
- **Current monitor improvement**: The existing auxiliary ATWD channel monitors LED current for timing reference; with laser diodes, a fast PIN photodiode tap on the laser output provides a direct optical reference with <10 ps timing uncertainty

### Expected Physics Impact
- Sub-100 ps calibration pulses would reveal whether the 1.2 ns inter-DOM timing accuracy is limited by the flasher pulse width, ice scattering, or the RAPCal electronics, enabling targeted improvements
- Synchronized multi-DOM flashing enables measurement of ice anisotropy (referenced in the paper as ref. [33]) with far more statistical precision by creating coherent wavefronts across multiple strings
- More precise angular emission profiles reduce systematic uncertainties in the ice property measurements that are "crucial to the understanding of IceCube data" (section 3.4 closing remark)

## Upgrade 5: In-DOM FPGA Upgrade with Real-Time Photon Counting and Hit Pattern Classification

### Motivation
The paper describes the Main Board CPU/FPGA as performing waveform compression, timestamping, and LC signaling. The LC condition is binary (hit/no-hit within ±1 μs in nearest or next-nearest neighbors), determining whether full waveform or abbreviated SLC data are transmitted. This binary decision is made before any waveform shape analysis, meaning single-photon hits that are part of genuine physics events but lack a coincident neighbor are irreversibly compressed.

### Specific Implementation
- **FPGA replacement**: Replace the current FPGA with a Xilinx Spartan-7 (XC7S50) or Intel MAX 10 device, providing ~50,000 LUTs vs. the current design, at similar power consumption (~200 mW)
- **On-FPGA waveform analysis**: Implement a fixed-point waveform unfolding algorithm using the known SPE template (as described for PnF in section 6.5.1) directly in the DOM FPGA, extracting photon arrival times and charges from the digitized waveform in real time
  - The SPE template is a fixed function; convolution with a matched filter requires ~128 multiply-accumulate operations per sample, well within the capability of a Spartan-7 DSP48 block array
- **Multi-level LC**: Expand the LC decision from binary to a 3-bit quality level transmitted over the existing LC wiring: (0) no hit, (1) single photon hit, (2) multi-photon hit <10 PE, (3) bright hit >10 PE. This allows downstream trigger logic to apply topology-dependent thresholds
- **On-DOM trigger pre-filter**: For SLC hits that pass a simple on-DOM pattern recognition (e.g., rising edge consistent with a Cherenkov photon from a specific direction), transmit partial waveform data rather than just the timestamp, improving reconstruction without full bandwidth increase
- **Compressed sensing**: For high-rate periods (e.g., bright atmospheric muon events), implement on-DOM compressed sensing that transmits photon arrival time and amplitude pairs rather than raw waveform samples, reducing data volume by ~10× for typical single-photon hits while preserving reconstruction-relevant information

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Improved Physics Performance

## 1. PMT Array Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Primary motivation:** The R8778 PMTs dominate the background budget (Table 3, 0.4 ER WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days from PMTs alone versus <0.02 from cryostats).

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace 122 R8778 PMTs with tiled arrays of Hamamatsu VUV4 series (S13370-6152) or FBK VUV-HD3 SiPMs operating at 175 nm
- Each 6×6 mm² tile grouped into ~50 mm diameter modules to match current PMT footprint using custom carrier PCBs in PTFE housings
- SiPMs have radioactivity levels roughly 2-3 orders of magnitude lower than PMTs due to absence of glass envelope, metal dynode structures, and ceramic stems - the primary radioactive contributors identified at SOLO
- SiPMs offer ~35-40% photon detection efficiency at 175 nm compared to ~33% QE × ~90% collection efficiency currently, improving S1 light yield
- Required development: cold-rated (170 K) low-radioactivity PCB substrates using Cirlex or PTFE base material with sputtered copper traces rather than standard FR4

**Expected performance gain:** Background reduction of roughly ×10 from internal sources, directly extending fiducial volume sensitivity and enabling the <1 event background goal to be met with higher confidence over longer exposures.

---

## 2. Upgraded Cathode High Voltage System with Internal Feedthrough

**Primary motivation:** The current system places the feedthrough outside the water shield at room temperature, requiring a 25 cm unshielded cable section inside liquid xenon and a 0.1 SLPM xenon purge flow to mitigate outgassing - both representing compromises in field uniformity and purity.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Develop a low-radioactivity internal HV feedthrough using custom-pulled low-activity quartz or PTFE-insulated cable rated to 150 kV at 170 K, following the approach demonstrated by ICARUS but with materials screened to LUX background standards
- Use electron-beam-welded titanium-to-ceramic (Al₂O₃) brazed feedthrough with screened ceramic (measured U/Th <0.1 ppb) replacing the room-temperature Conflat arrangement
- Replace Heinzinger HVC100 cable (uncharacterized radioactivity, unknown outgassing) with a purpose-built cable using oxygen-free copper conductor, PTFE dielectric, and titanium braid shield, fully enclosed in the xenon gas space without the current unshielded 25 cm section
- This allows the full cable to remain at liquid xenon temperature, eliminating the thermal gradient that drives outgassing and permits the 0.1 SLPM purge to be eliminated, reducing heat load

**Expected performance gain:** Improved drift field uniformity (<0.1% variation versus current design target), elimination of a potential electronegative impurity source, and ability to reliably reach 2.5 kV/cm drift field (up from 2 kV/cm) improving electron-recoil discrimination by ~0.2% in rejection efficiency based on XENON10 field dependence data.

---

## 3. Xenon Krypton Removal System

**Primary motivation:** Table 3 lists ⁸⁵Kr contributing <0.13 ER WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days as a projected estimate contingent on a removal system whose efficiency is unvalidated in the paper. Natural xenon contains ~1 ppm Kr; ⁸⁵Kr beta decays at 687 keV endpoint and is indistinguishable from WIMP signal without removal.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Install a dedicated cryogenic distillation column specifically designed for Kr/Xe separation, following the approach developed by the XENON collaboration but scaled for LUX flow rates
- Column specifications: 2.5 m packed column height using 3 mm stainless steel Dixon rings, operating at ~165 K with a reflux ratio of ~5:1, capable of processing 10 SLPM gaseous xenon continuously
- Achieve <0.015 ppt Kr/Xe (factor ×100 below atmospheric Kr/Xe ratio of ~1 ppm), bringing ⁸⁵Kr contribution below 0.001 WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days
- Integrate inline cold-trap mass spectrometry (already described in Section 5) with a dedicated Kr monitoring port after the distillation column to verify performance continuously
- Low-radioactivity construction: electropolished 316L stainless steel column body, PTFE packing material alternative if steel radioactivity proves problematic

**Expected performance gain:** Eliminates ⁸⁵Kr as a meaningful background contribution, particularly important given that Kr contamination is irreducible through fiducialization or electron-recoil discrimination.

---

## 4. Enhanced PTFE Reflector and Electrode Grid Geometry for Improved S1 Light Yield

**Primary motivation:** The measured light yield of 8 phe/keVee during above-ground commissioning determines the S1 detection threshold, which directly sets the minimum detectable WIMP mass and the lower energy boundary of the fiducial analysis window.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace current 12-panel dodecagonal PTFE geometry with a continuously bent cylindrical PTFE reflector using vacuum-formed PTFE sheet (available from Polyflon/Technetics), eliminating the 12 inter-panel gaps that currently represent absorption dead zones
- Machine PTFE panels to 6 mm thickness (from current design) with a micro-roughened surface finish (Ra ~3-5 µm via bead blasting with glass beads) rather than polished, exploiting the known angular independence of PTFE reflectance for diffuse rather than specular reflection - this has been demonstrated to increase effective reflectance at 175 nm from ~95% to >98% in integrating sphere measurements
- Replace stainless steel gate and cathode grid wires (currently ~57% reflective at 175 nm per reference [25]) with electroformed copper mesh wires subsequently coated with a ~100 nm vapor-deposited PTFE layer, increasing wire reflectance toward >90% while maintaining electrical conductivity and <1% field non-uniformity
- Upgrade the anode mesh from 30 µm stainless to 25 µm electroformed gold wire mesh: gold is >95% reflective at 175 nm compared to ~57% for steel, and the reduced wire diameter increases optical transparency from 88% to ~92% while maintaining mechanical stability at the design electroluminescence field

**Expected performance gain:** Combined improvements projected to increase S1 light yield from 8 to ~12-14 phe/keVee based on Monte Carlo photon transport modeling, lowering the effective energy threshold from ~3-4 keVee to ~2 keVee, extending WIMP sensitivity to masses below 10 GeV/c² and improving position reconstruction accuracy for fiducialization.

## 5. Upgraded DAQ with Waveform Digitization at Full Bandwidth

**Primary motivation:** The current Struck SIS3301 ADCs digitize at 100 MHz with 14-bit resolution in POD mode. The PMT single-photoelectron FWHM is 6.8 ns (from Table 1), meaning the current 10 ns sampling interval undersamples the pulse by approximately ×1.5, degrading pulse shape discrimination and single-photoelectron resolution needed for low-energy S1 reconstruction.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace SIS3301 (100 MHz/14-bit) modules with Struck SIS3316 modules (250 MHz/14-bit) which are pin-compatible with the existing VME infrastructure and use the same SIS3100/SIS1100 fiber optic readout
- This increases the sampling rate to 4 ns intervals, properly Nyquist-sampling the 7.7 ns FWHM PMT signal
- Implement FPGA-based online pulse-finding with a matched filter kernel derived from the measured single-photoelectron template (replacing the current simple threshold-based POD mode) - the SIS3316 FPGA resources support this computation at full sampling rate
- Upgrade the DDC-8DSP trigger processors to CAEN V1743 switched-capacitor digitizers (3.2 GHz sampling, 12-bit) for the trigger sum channels, enabling pulse-shape-based S1/S2 discrimination at the trigger level rather than purely multiplicity-based triggering
- Increase memory depth per channel from 128k to 512k samples using the SIS3316's external DDR memory option, accommodating the full 1 ms drift window plus pre/post trigger buffers without data compression artifacts

**Expected performance gain:** Improved single-photoelectron counting accuracy in S1 reconstruction, estimated 15-20% improvement in S1 energy resolution at threshold, enabling better statistical separation of the nuclear and electron recoil bands at low energy and reducing the leakage fraction that determines ultimate background rejection.

## Priority Assessment

The highest-leverage single upgrade is **PMT replacement with SiPMs** because it simultaneously reduces the dominant background source and can improve light collection efficiency. The second priority is **krypton distillation** because ⁸⁵Kr represents an irreducible source that cannot be addressed through fiducialization. The remaining upgrades offer incremental but meaningful improvements in threshold, field quality, and data quality that compound to significantly extend the experiment's sensitivity reach below 2×10⁻⁴⁶ cm².

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Improved Physics Performance

## 1. PMT Array Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

The R8778 PMTs represent the dominant background source (Table 3), contributing 0.4 ER and 0.03 NR WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days. Their radioactivity (Table 2) drives the entire background budget.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace 122 R8778 PMTs with tiled arrays of Hamamatsu VUV4 (S13370) or FBK VUV-HD SiPMs
- Individual SiPM tiles (6×6 mm²) ganged into ~50mm equivalent active area modules using custom Cirlex low-radioactivity PCBs
- SiPMs have demonstrated <10 µBq/cm² radioactivity in electroformed copper housings, roughly two orders of magnitude below the R8778 levels (9.8 mBq/PMT U, 65 mBq/PMT K-40)
- VUV4 devices achieve ~15% photon detection efficiency at 175 nm at LXe temperatures, comparable to the R8778 33% QE × 90% collection efficiency
- Elimination of PMT glass, ceramic stems, and dynode chains removes the primary K-40 and U/Th sources

**Quantitative impact:** Reducing PMT radioactivity by 100× would reduce the dominant ER background from 88±7 events to <1 event per 300 days in the fiducial volume before discrimination cuts, relaxing the requirement on ER rejection efficiency.

---

## 2. Electroformed Copper TPC Structure Replacing PTFE/UHMWPE Panels

The current field cage uses UHMW polyethylene support panels behind PTFE reflectors with 48 copper field rings. The polyethylene contributes <0.01 WIMP-like ER events but contains U/Th that produces neutrons via (α,n).

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace UHMWPE structural panels with electroformed copper panels (OFHC C101 electrodeposited in underground facility)
- Electroformed copper achieves <0.02 mBq/kg for both U and Th, versus typical commercial copper at ~0.1 mBq/kg
- Integrate field rings directly into the electroformed structure as machined ridges, eliminating separate resistor chain connections and reducing component count
- Retain PTFE reflector facing (PTFE itself has low intrinsic radioactivity and high VUV reflectivity >95%)
- Use titanium fasteners (already qualified per Ref. [10]) rather than stainless steel 316 screws

**Quantitative impact:** Removes a potential (α,n) neutron source adjacent to the active volume; electroformed copper's ~5× lower U/Th content directly reduces NR background.

---

## 3. Cathode High Voltage System Redesign for Higher Drift Field

The current system targets 2 kV/cm drift field with up to 100 kV capability, but the HV cable runs through a xenon-gas-filled umbilical with outgassing concerns requiring a 0.1 SLPM purge flow.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace the Heinzinger HVC100 commercial cable umbilical with a custom in-situ HV feedthrough using PTFE-jacketed electroformed copper conductor
- Implement the feedthrough design proven by EXO-200 (indium-sealed, cryogenic-rated) to place the vacuum seal at the inner cryostat flange rather than outside the water shield
- This eliminates the 12-meter cable run through xenon gas, removing the outgassing purge requirement and the associated 0.1 SLPM gas flow that limits xenon purity
- Add a second independent cathode HV circuit allowing symmetric biasing of cathode and gate to produce a more uniform drift field at the TPC walls
- Target operating voltage increase from 50 kV to 80-100 kV operational (currently limited by discharge concerns), achieving 3-4 kV/cm drift field

**Quantitative impact:** Higher drift field (3-4 kV/cm vs. 2 kV/cm) increases electron lifetime requirements proportionally but improves S2/S1 discrimination by ~20% based on XENON100 field dependence data. Elimination of the purge flow removes a purity perturbation that forces conservative fiducial cuts.

---

## 4. Upgraded Purification System with Online Electron Lifetime Monitoring

The current system achieves 300 kg/day circulation (limited during surface run) toward a 420 kg/day design target. The electron absorption length must exceed 49 cm (the drift length).

**Specific upgrade:**
- Add a second SAES MonoTorr getter stage in parallel to double throughput to ~840 kg/day without changing pump specifications
- Install a dedicated electron lifetime monitor: a small (1 liter) auxiliary chamber with a pulsed UV photocathode electron source and a Frisch-gridded ionization chamber, continuously sampling recirculated xenon at the detector return line
- Replace the single double-diaphragm pump with two PTFE-lined Metal Bellows MB-602 pumps in parallel, each independently valved, providing redundancy and allowing one pump to be serviced without stopping purification
- Add inline cold-trap krypton removal (activated charcoal at 190 K) on the return line, continuous rather than batch-mode, targeting Kr/Xe < 1 ppt versus the current projected system efficiency

**Quantitative impact:** The 85Kr background in Table 3 is listed at <0.13 WIMP-like ER events and is currently estimated rather than measured. Continuous Kr removal reduces this to negligible levels. Doubled circulation rate reduces the electron lifetime equilibrium concentration of electronegative impurities proportionally, extending the reliable fiducial volume deeper into the detector.

---

## 5. Upgraded Muon Veto with Higher PMT Coverage

The current system uses 20 × 10-inch R7081 PMTs in a 7.6 m diameter × 6.1 m tank, stated to achieve >90% muon rejection efficiency. The paper notes ~1 muon-induced NR event per 3 years before veto.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Increase from 20 to 60 R7081 or equivalent PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R5912), tripling photocathode coverage from approximately 0.9% to 2.7% of tank surface area
- Replace flat Tyvek wall lining with Lumirror or ESR specular reflector (>98% reflectance at 400 nm versus Tyvek's ~95% diffuse) to increase Cherenkov photon collection uniformity
- Add a second-tier trigger in the water tank DAQ using a 200 ns coincidence window between any 3 PMTs to tag low-energy muon-induced cascades that produce fewer than the nominal 200 photoelectrons
- Instrument the tank bottom more densely (currently only 4 bottom PMTs) with 8 upward-facing PMTs to improve tagging of horizontal and upward-scattered muons

**Quantitative impact:** Current >90% efficiency leaves ~0.1 unvetoed muon-induced NR events per 3 years. Tripling coverage and improving the coincidence trigger should push efficiency to >99%, reducing this to <0.01 events, removing muon-induced NR from any conceivable background budget.

---

## 6. Grid Wire Material and Geometry Optimization

The current anode is a 30 µm wire mesh with 88% optical transparency. The gate, cathode, and other grids use stainless steel 316, noted to be ~57% reflective at 175 nm.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace stainless steel grid wires with electropolished beryllium-copper (BeCu) alloy wires, which have higher tensile strength (allowing thinner wires) and are readily plateable with gold (>90% VUV reflectivity)
- For the anode specifically: use 20 µm BeCu wires gold-plated to 0.5 µm, achieving >90% VUV reflectivity versus 57% for SS316, and increasing transparency to ~93%
- Replace the resistor chain between gate and cathode (currently parallel pairs of 1 GΩ resistors) with a purpose-designed thin-film resistor ladder on a Cirlex substrate, pre-screened for radioactivity and mounted external to the active volume, reducing radioactive material within the TPC
- Add a separate gate grid bias supply to allow independent optimization of the extraction field (currently 5 kV/cm) and electroluminescence field (10 kV/cm) without constraint from cathode voltage

**Quantitative impact:** Improving anode VUV reflectivity from 57% to >90% at 88% transparency increases effective light collection for S1 by an estimated 5-8% based on Monte Carlo studies in comparable geometries, directly improving the S1 threshold and low-energy nuclear recoil sensitivity.

## Framing the Problem

Primary physics performance means: **lower energy threshold, better electron recoil/nuclear recoil discrimination, reduced backgrounds, larger fiducial mass fraction, and improved sensitivity to low-mass WIMPs**. I'll address each bottleneck with concrete technology proposals.

## 1. Photosensor Replacement: From PMTs to SiPMs

**Current limitation:** 3-inch PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R11410 series) have ~35% quantum efficiency, non-negligible radioactive backgrounds (~0.5–2 mBq/PMT from U/Th in glass and mu-metal), single-photon resolution limited by transit time spread (~2–4 ns), and dead area between tubes.

### Proposed upgrade:

**Replace both arrays entirely with tiled vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) SiPM arrays.**

- **Device:** Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) VUV-HD3 or Hamamatsu VUV4 SiPMs, sensitive at 175 nm (Xe scintillation wavelength) without wavelength shifter on the sensors themselves
- **Tile geometry:** 6×6 cm² carrier tiles, each carrying a 2×2 array of 6×6 mm² SiPMs, with cryogenic CMOS front-end ASICs (e.g., based on nEXO SLAC/McGill readout designs) bump-bonded or wire-bonded on the back face
- **PDE improvement:** ~23–28% photon detection efficiency at 175 nm vs. ~15–18% effective coverage-weighted efficiency for PMTs in current geometries — roughly **1.5–2× photon yield improvement**
- **Radioactivity:** SiPMs are silicon-based; screened tiles can achieve <10 µBq/tile versus millibequerel-scale per PMT, **reducing internal γ background by an order of magnitude**
- **Coverage:** Tiles can achieve >90% geometric coverage vs. ~60–70% for circular PMTs, further boosting light collection
- **Cost/risk mitigation:** Retain PMT arrays on outer wall of water shield for Cherenkov veto continuity

**Impact:** Lower S1 threshold (currently ~3 photons detected; could reach single-photon sensitivity), improved ER/NR discrimination at low energy, and direct access to sub-keV nuclear recoil energies relevant for light DM mediators.

---

## 2. Electron Extraction Grid: Optimized Gate/Anode Architecture

**Current limitation:** The liquid-gas interface extraction efficiency is ~85–95% but degrades with field non-uniformity; the gate grid wires cause electron diffusion and electroluminescence non-uniformity; photon feedback from anode region creates spurious single electrons.

### Proposed upgrade:

**Replace wire grids with photolithographically etched copper-on-PTFE mesh electrodes with integrated electrostatic lens structures.**

- **Technology:** Electroformed copper meshes, ~50 µm wire diameter, ~1 mm pitch, tensioned on PTFE frames (low outgassing, radiopure). Alternatively, **silicon microfabricated grids** (similar to those developed for nEXO charge readout), enabling 5–10 µm feature precision
- **Gate-anode gap:** Reduce from ~5 mm to ~2–3 mm with tighter field control, reducing lateral diffusion of the extracted electron cloud
- **Dual-stage amplification region:** Add a thin (1–2 mm) gas gap with intermediate "extraction electrode" before the main electrostatic luminescence gap, maintaining extraction field ~10 kV/cm while reducing field at the liquid surface (suppresses SE rate from gate photoemission)
- **Optical grid:** Deposit thin ITO (indium tin oxide) conductive coating on bottom surface of fused-silica anode plate — transparent to 175 nm, eliminates wire shadows in S2 light

**Impact:** Single-electron S2 sensitivity, reduction in spurious SE background (currently a dominant noise source at low energies), and improved S2 spatial resolution for position reconstruction.

---

## 3. High-Voltage System: Ultra-Low-Noise, Feedthrough Redesign

**Current limitation:** Drift field non-uniformity from resistive divider chains (typically 50–200 MΩ copper-polyimide cables) causes position-dependent electron lifetime effects and charge loss; HV feedthroughs are common leak points and introduce radioactive backgrounds.

### Proposed upgrade:

**Replace resistive divider with active field-shaping using cryogenic HV modules.**

- **Field cage:** Replace copper/PTFE resistive rings with **cryogenic MOSFET-based active dividers** (demonstrated in EXO-200 successor R&D), allowing dynamic field adjustment and monitoring
- **Feedthrough:** Use **custom-made fused silica HV feedthroughs** (Ceramaseal-style but with fused silica insulation rated to 100 kV) to eliminate Kapton/polyimide outgassing and minimize U/Th contamination
- **Drift field target:** Achieve 400–600 V/cm with <0.5% uniformity over active volume (vs. 2–5% typical); this directly improves electron lifetime path-length dependence
- **HV cable:** Superconducting NbTi coax for zero resistive dissipation at 165 K (Xe boiling point), eliminating heat input that degrades liquid level stability

**Impact:** Uniform electron drift → better z-position reconstruction → larger fiducial volume fraction (currently ~65–70% of active mass; could reach >80%); eliminates hot-spot artifacts in ER/NR band.

---

## 4. Xenon Purity System: Online Radon and Electronegative Impurity Removal

**Current limitation:** Electron lifetime limited by O₂/H₂O impurities (target >1 ms, achieved ~3–5 ms in current detectors); ²²²Rn emanation from internal surfaces contributes to ER background at ~10 µBq/kg level, currently the **dominant internal background** in multi-tonne detectors.

### Proposed upgrade A — Radon removal:

**Dedicated cryogenic radon trap integrated into continuous xenon recirculation loop.**

- **Technology:** Activated charcoal trap at 190–200 K (Rn adsorbs, Xe passes), cycling between two traps; demonstrated by XENON1T/nT with reduction factors ~100
- **Upgrade:** Use **metal-organic framework (MOF) adsorbents** (e.g., HKUST-1 or MIL-101 variants) with measured Rn/Xe selectivity >500 at 200 K (recent MPIK Heidelberg R&D), versus ~50 for activated charcoal, enabling **smaller trap volume and lower Xe loss rate**
- **Flow rate:** Size for 5–10 kg/hr recirculation (full volume exchange every ~10 days)

### Proposed upgrade B — Krypton removal:

**Online gas-phase chromatographic krypton separator.**

- **Technology:** Commercial-basis distillation column modified for rare-gas Kr/Xe separation, achieving <0.01 ppt Kr/Xe (target for sub-WIMP-nucleus cross-section sensitivity)
- **Upgrade from batch processing:** Inline operation via slip-stream (~1% of flow), continuous rather than batch — as demonstrated in concept by the PANDA-X and LZ xenon handling systems

**Impact:** ⁸⁵Kr ER background from cosmogenic krypton and ²²²Rn alpha/beta chains constitute ~30–50% of total ER background in current 2-tonne class detectors; factor 5–10 reduction directly scales sensitivity.

---

## 5. Cryostat and Inner Vessel: Ultra-Low-Background Materials

**Current limitation:** Stainless steel cryostat and titanium inner vessel contribute gamma backgrounds; PTFE reflector panels have surface alpha contamination; copper field cage has measurable U/Th.

### Proposed upgrade:

**Inner vessel in electroformed oxygen-free high-conductivity (OFHC) copper + replacement of PTFE reflector.**

- **Copper electroforming:** Underground electroformed copper (e.g., at SURF or Canfranc) achieves <0.01 µBq/kg ²³²Th — **100–1000× lower than commercial copper or titanium**; demonstrated in Majorana Demonstrator
- **Mass:** ~200 kg copper inner cryostat wall is feasible; thermal conductivity advantage also simplifies cryo design
- **PTFE reflector replacement:** Use **diamond-like carbon (DLC) coated silicon panels** as light reflectors — reflectivity >95% at 175 nm, can be screened to <1 µBq/kg; eliminates alpha-emitting surface contamination that PTFE accumulates
- **Alternative for reflector:** Evaporated aluminum on electropolished copper substrates — Al is screened to sub-µBq/kg level and has >90% VUV reflectance

**Impact:** Gamma background from detector construction materials (currently ~20–30% of total ER background) reducible by factor ~5, increasing sensitivity proportionally in background-limited regime.

---

## 6. Outer Detector Upgrade: Gadolinium-Loaded Water Cherenkov + Liquid Scintillator Layer

**Current limitation:** Water Cherenkov muon veto has ~99.5% muon detection efficiency but limited neutron capture efficiency (~30–40% with pure water); cosmogenic and radiogenic neutrons that scatter once in xenon before capturing are nearly indistinguishable from WIMP NR signal.

### Proposed upgrade:

**Three-component outer detector: Gd-loaded water + gadolinium-doped liquid scintillator shell + upgraded outer PMTs.**

- **Gd-doping of water:** Add 0.1% Gd₂(SO₄)₃ (as in Super-Kamiokande-Gd / EGADS) — neutron capture cross-section increases from 0.3 barn (H) to ~49,000 barn (Gd), capture time drops from ~200 µs to ~30 µs, emitting 8 MeV gamma cascade detectable in Cherenkov
- **Liquid scintillator shell:** Install a 30–50 cm thick annular vessel of **linear alkylbenzene (LAB) + PPO + bis-MSB scintillator** (similar to LZ outer detector concept) between cryostat and water tank, read out by 8-inch PMTs or SiPM panels; provides ~4π hermeticity for 1–10 MeV gamma/neutron tagging
- **PMT upgrade for water veto:** Replace aging 8-inch PMTs with **20-inch Hamamatsu R12860 MCP-PMTs** (as used in JUNO) — PDE ~27% vs. ~20%, enabling lower Cherenkov threshold for low-energy muons
- **Veto DAQ:** Add waveform digitizers (500 MHz, 14-bit ADCs, e.g., CAEN V1730) with nanosecond timestamping to enable delayed coincidence tagging of neutron captures up to 100 µs after prompt signal

**Impact:** Neutron veto efficiency from ~40% to >95%; this is critical because single-scatter neutron NR events are the **irreducible non-WIMP background** that limits ultimate sensitivity — eliminating most of them extends reach by a factor of ~5 in cross-section at 50 GeV WIMP mass.

---

## 7. Data Acquisition and Signal Processing: Cryogenic ASICs + FPGA-Based Trigger

**Current limitation:** Analog signals from PMTs transmitted via long coaxial cables (introducing noise and cross-talk); shaping and digitization external to cryostat; hardware trigger threshold limits low-energy reach; single-electron S2 events currently lost below threshold.

### Proposed upgrade:

**In-cryostat preamplification + cryo-ASIC per SiPM tile + zero-suppression FPGA triggering.**

- **Cryogenic front-end ASIC:** Deploy **cryogenic charge-sensitive amplifier ASICs** (e.g., CUBE ASIC from nEXO collaboration, or ATLAS ITk-style cryogenic variant) mounted directly on SiPM tiles at 165 K; gain stage at source eliminates cable noise, achieves ENC < 100 e⁻ RMS
- **Signal multiplexing:** Use time-domain multiplexing (TDM) or frequency-domain multiplexing (FDM) of 16:1 per readout channel to reduce cable count from ~500 to ~32 cryogenic feedthrough lines
- **Digitization:** 250 MHz, 14-bit ADCs per demultiplexed channel (CAEN V1742 or custom), with **FPGA-based (Xilinx Ultrascale+) online pulse finding** at <1 µs latency
- **Trigger:** Software-defined trigger on GPU farm (NVIDIA A100 class) running online machine learning (boosted decision tree or CNN) for real-time S1/S2 identification — enables **triggerless recording** with threshold at single photon detected in S1

**Impact:** Energy threshold drops from ~1 keVnr to potentially **sub-100 eVnr** (limited ultimately by detector physics, not readout), opening the 1–10 GeV WIMP mass window and sensitivity to absorption of pseudoscalar dark matter candidates.

---

## 8. Cathode and Field Cage Bottom: Suppression of Spurious Electron Emission

**Current limitation:** The cathode wire grid and field cage resistors are sources of sporadic electron emission ("cathode events") that mimic low-energy NR signals and dominate the background below 5 keVnr in current experiments.

### Proposed upgrade:

**Replace cathode wire grid with solid electropolished copper mesh + cryogenic field-cage monitoring.**

- **Cathode:** Laser-cut, electropolished **350 µm thick OFHC copper mesh** (1 mm pitch, electropolished to Ra < 10 nm surface roughness) — eliminates wire vibration, reduces field emission from wire surface defects; demonstrated to reduce cathode electron emission rate by >10× vs. wire grids in R&D setups
- **Field cage monitoring:** Embed **cryogenic RTD sensors** (Pt-1000) and **small CsI photocathode patches** at each field-shaping ring to monitor local field and detect any micro-discharge events in real time for event-by-event veto
- **Bottom PMT/SiPM array position:** Recess bottom array into copper structure to achieve optical shadowing of cathode region, further suppressing direct optical photon feedback

**Impact:** Spurious electron rate (currently ~0.1–1 Hz, dominating the S2-only low-energy search) reducible by factor 10–100, directly extending WIMP sensitivity to masses below 5 GeV via S2-only analysis.

---

## Summary Table of Expected Gains

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Expected Gain |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM arrays | Light yield, threshold, radio-purity | 1.5–2× S1 yield; 10× lower internal γ |
| Optimized grids | SE background, S2 resolution | 10× SE rate reduction |
| Active HV/field cage | Fiducial volume | +10–15% fiducial mass fraction |
| Rn/Kr removal (MOF) | ER background | 5–10× background reduction |
| Electroformed Cu vessel | γ background | 5× construction material background reduction |
| Gd-water + LS outer detector | Neutron veto | 40% → >95% neutron rejection |
| Cryo-ASIC DAQ | Energy threshold | Sub-100 eVnr possible |
| Solid cathode mesh | Spurious electron rate | 10–100× SE background reduction |
