# Hardware Design Upgrades for Improved Physics Performance

## 1. Photosensor Replacement: Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

The R8778 PMTs are the dominant background source (Table 3), contribute 0.4 ER and 0.03 NR WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days, and occupy significant passive volume near the fiducial region.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace 122 R8778 PMTs with Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPC arrays (S13370-6152CN series) or FBK-NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs tiled into modular 5.7 cm hexagonal assemblies matching existing PMT footprint geometry
- SiPMs achieve comparable QE (~35%) at 175 nm in LXe while containing orders of magnitude less U/Th/K per unit photosensitive area due to absence of glass envelope, metal dynode chains, and ceramic stem
- The R8778 dominates K-40 activity at 65±2 mBq/PMT (Table 2); SiPM arrays of equivalent area measured at <0.1 mBq/cm² at LNGS
- Operate arrays at modest reverse bias (~30V) using low-noise JFET-based cryogenic front-end ASICs (e.g., ABBA chip developed for nEXO) mounted directly on cold copper support structure, eliminating 10m internal cable runs that currently produce ~25% signal attenuation
- Expected consequence: ER background from photosensors reduced by factor >10×, permitting fiducial volume expansion toward detector walls

## 2. Cathode High Voltage Feedthrough Redesign

The current system routes HV cable through xenon gas umbilical from outside the water shield, introduces outgassing risk requiring active purge at 0.1 SLPM, and limits maximum cathode voltage by cable insulation properties in LXe.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Implement a custom coaxial feedthrough using ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) as insulator, with the feedthrough penetrating only the outer vacuum vessel flange and terminating at the inner vessel wall in transformer oil
- Replace HVC100 commercial cable inside the xenon space with a purpose-drawn coaxial conductor using PTFE dielectric and bare copper center conductor, verified to <1 ppb U/Th
- Add a graded-potential field shaper around the cable terminus using resistively-loaded PTFE sleeves to suppress local field enhancement, permitting reliable operation at 150 kV (3 kV/cm drift field vs. current 2 kV/cm design target)
- Higher drift field reduces electron-ion recombination, directly increasing S1/S2 discrimination power and improving nuclear recoil energy resolution; at 3 kV/cm the electron-recoil rejection efficiency improves from the stated 99.3-99.9% to >99.9% based on XENON100 field-dependence measurements

## 3. Anode/Gate Grid Replacement with Electroformed Copper Mesh

The current anode uses 30 µm stainless steel mesh at 88% optical transparency, introducing ~12% light loss and electroluminescence field non-uniformity. Stainless steel (alloy 316) has higher intrinsic radioactivity than ultra-pure copper.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace anode mesh with electroformed oxygen-free copper (C10100) mesh with 25 µm wire diameter at 0.4 mm pitch, achieving >93% optical transparency
- Electroforming onto precision mandrels achieves wire position uniformity of ±5 µm, reducing electroluminescence field variation across liquid surface from current ~1% to <0.3%, directly improving S2 position reconstruction resolution
- Replace gate grid (50 µm SS wire, 5 mm pitch) with 40 µm OFHC copper wire at 4 mm pitch; 99.4% transparency vs. current 99%, with measured U/Th activity <5 µBq/kg compared to ~50 µBq/kg for 316 SS
- Improved anode flatness reduces S2 pulse width variation, tightening the position-dependent corrections in z-reconstruction and recovering ~5% fiducial volume at the liquid surface

## 4. PTFE Reflector Surface Treatment

Current PTFE panels achieve >95% reflectivity in LXe (measured during surface run, Ref. [19]), but photon absorption length in LXe was measured as ≥5 m with significant uncertainty.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Machine PTFE panels with controlled micro-roughness surface finish (Ra = 0.8 µm) using diamond-tipped tooling to achieve specular-diffuse reflectivity ratio optimized by Monte Carlo for the specific dodecagonal geometry; Neves et al. (2017) demonstrated this increases effective light collection by 8-12% over standard machined PTFE in comparable geometries
- Add single monolayer of tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) wavelength shifter deposited by vacuum evaporation at 0.2 mg/cm² surface density onto all PTFE panels and PMT/SiPM window surfaces
- TPB shifts 175 nm Xe scintillation to 430 nm where SiPM and PMT quantum efficiency is higher (~40-45% vs. 33% at 175 nm) and PTFE reflectivity exceeds 99%
- Expected light yield improvement from 8 phe/keVee to ~14-18 phe/keVee, lowering the effective S1 threshold from ~2 keVee to ~1 keVee and extending WIMP sensitivity to masses below 10 GeV/c²

## 5. Cryogenic System: Pulse Tube Refrigerator Replacement of Thermosyphons

The thermosyphon system depends on external liquid nitrogen supply, introducing operational risk and requiring continuous LN2 delivery logistics at 4850 ft depth.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace the four thermosyphon cold heads with two Cryomech PT90 pulse tube refrigerators (90W at 77K), mounted on the outer vessel dome with thermal straps of annealed copper braid (99.99% Cu, 500 cm² cross-section) connecting to existing cold head attachment points on the inner vessel
- PT90 units consume 3 kW wall power each, operate continuously without consumables, and provide stable ±0.1 K temperature control through integral PID with Lakeshore 336 controllers
- Elimination of LN2 supply requirement removes a primary operational risk for extended underground runs; LN2 delivery failures currently require xenon recovery within hours
- Integrate a Cryomech LN2 liquefier (model L70) as backup, capable of producing 70 L/day from nitrogen gas for emergency thermosyphon operation, providing redundancy without cavern-level LN2 storage

## 6. Krypton Removal System Integration

Table 3 estimates <0.13 ER WIMP-like events from ⁸⁵Kr per 30,000 kg-days, with this number depending entirely on projected Kr removal efficiency. No dedicated Kr removal hardware is described.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Install a dedicated cryogenic distillation column in the xenon gas handling path, based on the design developed by Aprile et al. for XENON100, scaled for 420 kg/day throughput
- Column specifications: 3 m height, 5 cm inner diameter, structured Sulzer DX packing, operating at 165-170 K with a reflux ratio of 10:1 using a Cryomech AL300 coldhead
- Achieves Kr/Xe separation factor of >10⁵ per pass; processing full 370 kg inventory twice reduces Kr concentration from typical commercial xenon levels (~10 ppb) to <0.01 ppt
- At <0.01 ppt Kr/Xe, ⁸⁵Kr contribution drops below 0.001 ER events per 30,000 kg-days, effectively eliminating this background term entirely
- Online monitoring via the existing cold-trap mass spectrometry system (Sec. 5) with modified inlet valve timing to sample post-distillation xenon

## 7. Digital Trigger and Readout Modernization

The current DAQ uses Struck SIS3301 ADCs at 100 MHz/14-bit with POD firmware, and the trigger system uses DDC-8DSP processors operating on analog-summed PMT groups, losing per-channel timing information at the trigger level.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace SIS3301 boards with Struck SIS3316 250 MHz/16-bit ADCs with on-board FPGA processing; these are pin-compatible with existing VME crates and provide 2× improvement in single-photoelectron timing resolution (4 ns → 2 ns) directly improving S1 hit pattern reconstruction
- Implement per-channel digital trigger using the SIS3316 internal FPGA with configurable matched-filter templates for S1 (narrow, ~100 ns) and S2 (broad, ~10 µs) pulse shapes, replacing the analog DDC-8DSP sum approach
- Per-channel triggering eliminates the ~15% trigger threshold penalty from summing PMT groups with varying gains, lowering the effective S1 trigger threshold from ~2 photons detected to ~1 photon detected
- Add CAEN V1495 FPGA-based coincidence unit between inner and outer detector PMT channels to implement hardware-level fiducial triggering, reducing DAQ deadtime from accidental coincidences at the expected underground background rate

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a ~250 kg Dual-Phase Xenon TPC

## Framing the Problem

Primary physics performance in a dual-phase xenon TPC is determined by:
1. **Background rejection** (nuclear recoil vs. electron recoil discrimination)
2. **Energy threshold** (minimum detectable recoil energy)
3. **Fiducial mass fraction** (active-to-total xenon ratio)
4. **Absolute light/charge yield** (S1/S2 signal quality)
5. **Radioactive background rate** in the fiducial volume

I'll address each with concrete hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Photosensor Replacement: Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) over PMTs

### The Problem with Current PMTs
Standard 3-inch PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R11410-23 used in LUX-ZEPLIN/PandaX) have:
- Quantum efficiency ~35% at 175 nm VUV
- Significant radioactivity (~1–3 mBq/PMT from U/Th chains in glass/metal)
- 3-inch diameter creates dead gaps in the array geometry
- Operating HV (~1–1.5 kV) near high-field regions

### Proposed Upgrade: VUV-Sensitive SiPM Tile Arrays

**Specific technology:** Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) VUV-HD3 or Hamamatsu S13370 series SiPMs, wavelength-shifted or operated bare at 175 nm

- **Photon detection efficiency (PDE):** 24–28% at 175 nm *bare*; with wavelength shifter (tetraphenyl butadiene, TPB) coating, effective PDE reaches 40–50%
- **Tile format:** 6×6 mm² cells tiled into 10×10 cm² modules, enabling near-hermetic coverage
- **Radioactivity:** SiPM modules with ultra-low-background PCBs (ENIG-finish, screened copper) achieve <0.1 mBq per 100 cm² — roughly **10–20× lower** than PMTs per unit area
- **Physical tiling:** Eliminates inter-PMT gaps; bottom array can cover >95% geometric area vs. ~65–70% with 3-inch PMTs

**Quantitative gain:** Doubling photon detection efficiency directly improves S1 light collection. For a 250 kg detector, current PMT arrays may collect ~5–8 photoelectrons per keVee at low energies. SiPM arrays could push this to 10–15 PE/keVee, lowering the *software* threshold from ~1–2 keVee to ~0.3–0.5 keVee, and improving the S1-based position resolution needed for fiducialization.

**Caveats requiring engineering:** SiPM dark noise (~100 Hz/mm² at 77 K, dropping to ~10 Hz/mm² at 165 K for LXe temperature) must be handled; correlated avalanche noise (afterpulsing, crosstalk) needs characterization. Cryogenic ASIC readout (e.g., CUBE or nEXO's custom ASIC) should be co-designed.

---

## 2. Cryogenic ASIC Front-End Readout

### Motivation
PMT-based systems route signals via long cables to room-temperature electronics, introducing:
- Capacitive signal degradation (~1 ns risetime worsening)
- Thermal noise from cable impedance
- Mass/material budget (feedthroughs = background sources)

### Proposed Upgrade: In-Vessel Cryogenic ASICs

**Specific technology:** Adapt the nEXO ASIC (65 nm CMOS, validated to 77 K) or the DUNE cold electronics (LARASIC8) for xenon detector parameters.

- **Noise floor:** ~50 e⁻ ENC (equivalent noise charge) achievable at 165 K vs. ~500 e⁻ from room-temperature amplifiers with cable parasitics
- **Architecture:** Charge-sensitive amplifier + shaper + 12-bit ADC per channel, multiplexed over 4-wire cryogenic twisted pair to surface DAQ
- **Placement:** ASIC dies mounted directly on SiPM tile PCBs inside the cold volume; reduces capacitance from cm-scale traces vs. meter-scale cables
- **Feedthrough reduction:** From potentially 500+ individual coax feedthroughs (one per PMT) to ~20 low-mass differential signal pairs (LVDS) serving multiplexed ASIC clusters

**Quantitative impact on threshold:** Reduced electronic noise directly improves S2 single-electron detection efficiency. Current detectors lose efficiency below ~5 extracted electrons; improved front-end could achieve clean detection at 1–2 extracted electrons, critically improving nuclear recoil detection at sub-keV energies.

---

## 3. Field Cage Redesign: Resistive Field Cage with Reduced Material

### Current Limitation
Copper or stainless steel ring field cages with PTFE structural elements contribute:
- Radioactivity from trace U/Th in metals (PTFE is relatively clean but bulk is large)
- Electric field non-uniformities near rings causing position reconstruction errors
- Fiducial volume loss from edge effects (typically 10–15% of active mass cut)

### Proposed Upgrades

**3a. Resistive Film Field Cage**
Replace discrete metal rings with a continuous resistive coating on the PTFE cylindrical wall:
- **Material:** Diamond-Like Carbon (DLC) coating or amorphous silicon sputtered onto PTFE panels — resistivity tunable to 10⁸–10¹¹ Ω/sq
- **Advantage:** Eliminates all metal rings; single continuous graded potential creates a more uniform drift field with fewer local distortions
- **Radioactivity:** DLC coatings are ~10–100 nm thick; negligible mass, essentially zero radioactive contribution
- **Heritage:** Demonstrated in ArDM, prototyped for liquid argon TPCs; directly transferable to xenon at 165 K

**3b. Reduced-Thickness PTFE Reflector Panels**
- Replace 5–10 mm thick PTFE structural rings+reflector with 1–2 mm thin PTFE panels with internal aluminum frame (electropolished, screened)
- Optical reflectivity of PTFE for VUV maintained; structural mass of PTFE (which has ~0.3 mBq/kg from ²¹⁰Pb daughters) reduced by factor 3–5

**Quantitative fiducial gain:** Better field uniformity allows reconstructed position uncertainty to drop from ~3–5 mm σ to <2 mm σ in radius; this directly converts to ~5–8% more fiducial mass at fixed background requirement.

---

## 4. Cathode and Gate Electrode Upgrade

### Current Limitation
Woven stainless steel mesh electrodes (cathode, gate, anode) have:
- Optical opacity reducing S1 light collection below the cathode
- Non-uniform electric field near wires causing position-dependent electron extraction efficiency
- Surface radioactivity from electropolishing residuals

### Proposed Upgrade: Photolithographically Etched Copper-on-Kapton or Etched Silicon Electrodes

**Specific technology:** 
- **Silicon wafer electrodes** etched by DRIE (Deep Reactive Ion Etching) into hexagonal or circular aperture patterns at wafer fabs — achievable at 250 mm wafer diameter, tiled if needed
- Aperture fraction: 95%+ optical transmission achievable vs. 85–90% for best meshes
- Wire pitch uniformity: photolithographic precision (±1 µm) vs. woven mesh (±50–100 µm)
- **Surface finish:** HF-passivated silicon has minimal surface radioactivity

**Alternative:** Chemically etched copper-clad Kapton (PCB process) with 200 µm pitch hexagonal grid, gold-flashed to prevent oxidation; validated in small-scale detectors

**Quantitative gain:** 
- Improved gate electrode uniformity increases mean electron extraction efficiency from ~85% (typical for woven mesh) toward 92–95%; this directly scales S2 signal by ~10%, improving energy resolution and lowering threshold
- Improved optical transparency adds ~3–5% more S1 photons reaching bottom PMT/SiPM array

---

## 5. Liquid-Gas Interface Monitoring and Stabilization

### Current Limitation
The liquid surface position determines the extraction field geometry and S2 width uniformity. Typical level control via capacitive sensors achieves ±0.5–1 mm stability; tilt across a ~70 cm diameter detector can be several mm.

### Proposed Upgrade: Multi-Point Precision Level Monitoring + Active Tilt Correction

**5a. Distributed Capacitive/Optical Level Sensors**
- **Technology:** 8–12 miniature parallel-plate capacitive sensors distributed around the circumference of the gate electrode, each resolving ±50 µm
- Combined with 2-axis tilt readout (MEMS accelerometer at 4K compatible: Murata SCC2230 screened for cryogenic use)
- **Active correction:** Small cryogenic stepper motors (FAULHABER series, cryogenic-rated) adjusting three support points of the inner vessel provide <0.1 mm tilt correction

**5b. Transparent ITO-Coated Anode**
- Replace opaque metal anode with indium tin oxide (ITO)-coated fused silica or sapphire plate
- Enables **optical monitoring of the liquid surface** via camera or photodiode array looking down from gas phase
- ITO sheet resistance ~100 Ω/sq — sufficient to define anode potential; capacitively coupled to HV supply to avoid DC resistance heating issues
- Silica/sapphire is radiologically clean compared to metal electrodes

**Quantitative gain:** Improved surface uniformity reduces S2 width variance, which is used for depth (z-position) reconstruction. Current detectors see 10–20% S2 width non-uniformity from surface tilt/ripple; halving this improves z-resolution from ~3 mm to ~1.5 mm, improving fiducialization and background rejection in the surface/bulk discrimination analysis.

---

## 6. Outer Detector Upgrade: Gadolinium-Loaded Liquid Scintillator in Place of Pure Water

### Current Limitation
A water Cherenkov shield detects muons and high-energy neutrons efficiently but has low efficiency for **thermal neutron capture** (critical for radiogenic neutron background rejection). Water's thermal neutron capture cross-section is 0.33 barn on hydrogen with a 2.2 MeV gamma — detectable but with low multiplicity.

### Proposed Upgrade: Gadolinium Sulfate (Gd₂(SO₄)₃) Dissolved in Water Scintillator

**Specific technology:** 0.1% by mass Gd₂(SO₄)₃ in linear alkylbenzene (LAB) + PPO + bis-MSB water-based liquid scintillator (WbLS), as demonstrated by SNO+ and Theia R&D

- **Thermal neutron capture cross-section of Gd:** 49,000 barn (Gd-157) — ~150,000× better than hydrogen
- **Capture gamma cascade:** 8 MeV total gamma energy in ~4-gamma cascade — high detection efficiency with scintillation readout
- **Efficiency:** >95% neutron tagging efficiency for neutrons thermalizing within 50 cm of fiducial volume

**PMT upgrade for outer detector:** Replace water Cherenkov PMTs with 8-inch high-QE PMTs (Hamamatsu R5912 with ~35% QE) or low-cost large-area SiPM modules; scintillation photon yield of WbLS (~100 photons/MeV) requires higher photosensor coverage than pure water

**Quantitative background impact:** Radiogenic neutron backgrounds from PMT/structure U/Th typically dominate at ~250 kg scale (LUX, XENON1T experience). Gd-loaded veto can tag neutron-induced nuclear recoils with ~95% efficiency vs. ~40–60% for pure water veto, directly reducing this background by ~10× in the WIMP signal region.

---

## 7. Cathode High Voltage: Increased Drift Field via SF₆-Passivated Feedthrough

### Current Limitation
At 250 kg scale (~70 cm drift length), achieving uniform 1–2 kV/cm drift field requires cathode voltages of 70–140 kV. Current PTFE-insulated HV feedthroughs begin to fail above 50–80 kV in xenon-compatible configurations (XENON1T reached 12 kV/cm locally but with sparking issues).

### Proposed Upgrade: Pressurized SF₆ HV Feedthrough + Tapered Field Shaping

**Specific technology:**
- **Feedthrough:** Custom coaxial feedthrough with SF₆ gas pressurized to 3–4 bar in the intermediate region between vacuum and xenon — SF₆ dielectric strength ~3× that of N₂; enables 150 kV in a compact geometry
- **Manufacturer heritage:** HVTG GmbH (Germany) and Ceramaseal produce SF₆-insulated feedthroughs to 200 kV for physics experiments
- **Inner vessel side:** Graded field shaping with DLC-coated resistive ring on the feedthrough stem prevents local field enhancements

**Why higher drift field matters:**
- At 1 kV/cm: electron lifetime requirement ~1–2 ms (achievable with current purification)
- At 3 kV/cm: electron drift velocity increases ~2×; required electron lifetime *relaxes* to ~0.5 ms while maintaining same charge collection; OR same lifetime yields better charge yield
- Higher drift field improves electron-nuclear recoil discrimination (log(S2/S1) separation) by reducing recombination variance — critical for sub-10 keV nuclear recoil detection

---

## 8. Xenon Purity System: Cryogenic Recirculation with Metal-Sealed Hot Getter

### Current Limitation
Electronegative impurities (O₂, H₂O, N₂) must be maintained at <1 ppb O₂-equivalent for electron lifetimes >1 ms over the full drift length. Current systems using gas-phase recirculation through SAES PS4-MT15 hot getters achieve this but introduce heat load and outgassing from elastomer/VCR fittings.

### Proposed Upgrade: All-Metal-Seal Liquid-Phase Recirculation Loop

**Specific components:**
- **Cryogenic liquid pump:** Barber-Nichols BNCP-32 (or equivalent) magnetically coupled cryogenic centrifugal pump — no shaft seal, zero xenon leak; demonstrated in XENON100 upgrade studies
- **Liquid-phase getter:** SAES MicroTorr MC1000 configured for cold operation, or custom hot-getter cartridge with all-metal ConFlat (CF) flange connections — eliminates all elastomer O-rings from the purification loop
- **Inline purity monitor:** UV-transparent fused silica electron drift cell (as used in LUXe R&D) providing real-time electron lifetime measurement on diverted ~10 g/day xenon stream

**Quantitative gain:** Liquid-phase recirculation achieves 10× faster effective purification than gas-phase for the same pump throughput, since liquid density is ~3× and flow rate is naturally higher. Expected electron lifetime: >10 ms routinely achievable, enabling drift field reduction (lower electron diffusion) or longer drift lengths in future scaling.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for LHCb Performance Improvement

## Analysis of Primary Performance Limitations

Based on the paper's reported deficiencies, I identify the binding constraints on physics performance and propose targeted hardware solutions.

---

## 1. Vertex Locator (VELO) Replacement

### Current Limitations
- Silicon strip sensors approaching radiation damage limits (1.8×10¹⁴ neq/cm² at innermost strips)
- Minimum approach distance of 8.2 mm from beam during physics running
- 38 µm minimum pitch limits ultimate IP resolution (~13 µm asymptotic)
- Analog strip readout constrains occupancy handling at higher luminosity

### Proposed Upgrade
**Replace silicon strip sensors with hybrid pixel detectors using 55 µm × 55 µm pixels (Timepix3/Velopix ASIC architecture)**

- **Sensor material:** Switch from n-on-p bulk silicon to 200 µm thin active-edge silicon pixel sensors, allowing placement at 5.1 mm from beam axis rather than 8.2 mm, reducing the extrapolation lever arm and directly improving IP resolution by approximately 20-30%
- **Pixel geometry:** 55 µm pixels with per-pixel ToT (Time-over-Threshold) and timestamp readout at 40 MHz eliminates analog multiplexing dead time and reduces cluster ambiguities in high-occupancy regions near beam pipe
- **Radiation hardness:** MAPS (Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors) using CMOS 180 nm technology with deep n-well collection nodes demonstrate tolerance to >10¹⁶ neq/cm², extending detector lifetime through full Run III/IV
- **RF foil:** Replace current aluminum RF foil (200 µm equivalent material) with corrugated 100 µm beryllium foil, reducing material budget by factor ~2 at small radii, directly reducing multiple scattering contribution to IP resolution
- **Expected gain:** IP resolution improvement from ~13 µm to ~8 µm asymptotically at high pT, and improved two-track separation enabling better charm vertex reconstruction

---

## 2. RICH Detector Photon Detection System

### Current Limitations
- Hybrid Photon Detectors (HPDs) show read-out inefficiency at high trigger rates (explicitly noted in paper)
- Photoelectron yields 25-30% below simulation predictions for all three radiators
- Cherenkov angle resolution for C₄F₁₀ (1.618 mrad) exceeds simulation (1.52 mrad) due to residual magnetic field distortions on HPD images
- Aerogel resolution factor 1.8× worse than simulation due to C₄F₁₀ absorption

### Proposed Upgrades

**Replace HPDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) in RICH1 and Multi-anode PMTs (MaPMTs) in RICH2**

**RICH1:**
- Deploy 3×3 mm² SiPM arrays (Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD, 50 µm microcell pitch, PDE >40% at 420 nm) coupled to wavelength-shifting fibers matching Cherenkov emission spectrum
- SiPMs are inherently immune to magnetic fields, eliminating the dominant contribution to excess Cherenkov angle resolution in RICH1 from HPD image distortion
- Integrate SiPM arrays with 65 nm CMOS readout ASICs providing per-pixel timestamps at 1 ns resolution, enabling time-based background rejection
- Expected improvement: C₄F₁₀ resolution recovering toward simulation value of 1.52 mrad, improving π/K separation by ~15% at high momentum

**RICH2:**
- Replace HPDs with Hamamatsu R13742 64-channel MaPMTs (8×8 pixel array, 6×6 mm² effective area per pixel), already demonstrated in NA62 and characterised for LHCb geometry
- MaPMTs tolerate the lower residual field environment of RICH2, provide quantum efficiency >25% at 300 nm, and have negligible dead-time issues at LHCb rates
- Repackage photodetector planes to increase geometric efficiency from ~65% to >80% by eliminating HPD cylindrical dead zones

**Aerogel radiator:**
- Replace current aerogel tiles with hydrophobic aerogel produced by supercritical drying (Matsushita/NOVAOL type, refractive index n=1.05, transmittance >90% at 400 nm over 20 mm thickness)
- Install hermetic aerogel enclosure with silica gel desiccant to prevent C₄F₁₀ absorption, directly addressing the identified cause of resolution degradation
- Expected gain: Aerogel Npe recovering from 5.0 toward simulation value of 8.0, providing meaningful low-momentum PID below 10 GeV/c that the current system cannot deliver reliably

---

## 3. Upstream Tracker (UT) Replacing TT

### Current Limitations
- TT hit resolution of 52-54 µm is adequate but sensor geometry creates dead zones near beam pipe with highest occupancy
- Single-sensor sectors near beam pipe reach 1.9% occupancy at design luminosity; at 2× design luminosity this becomes problematic for pattern recognition
- Limited momentum kick measurement upstream of magnet degrades ghost track rejection

### Proposed Upgrade
**Replace TT with four-layer silicon microstrip detector (UT) using 100 µm pitch sensors in inner region transitioning to 200 µm in outer region**

- **Inner region (r < 10 cm):** Deploy 320 µm thick p-on-n silicon sensors with 100 µm readout pitch, AC-coupled to APV25-based 40 MHz readout, reducing occupancy by factor ~2 relative to TT
- **Intermediate region:** 100 µm pitch with 2:1 analog multiplexing using SALT ASIC (specifically developed for LHCb upgrade), providing zero-suppressed data at 40 MHz bunch crossing rate
- **Stereo angle optimization:** Change stereo layers from ±5° to ±8.5° to improve z-coordinate reconstruction of track segments upstream of magnet, reducing ghost rate in forward tracking by ~30%
- **Active-edge sensors:** Eliminate inactive guard ring regions (currently ~1 mm) using active-edge technology, increasing geometric efficiency near beam pipe acceptance boundary
- **Expected gain:** Ghost track rate reduction from 6.5% to ~4% in minimum bias events; improved momentum estimate for upstream tracks used in RICH1 background subtraction

---

## 4. Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) Tracker Replacing OT+IT

### Current Limitations
- OT straw occupancy reaches 17% at 50 ns spacing and 25% at 25 ns spacing — functionally limiting operation at higher luminosity or shorter bunch spacing
- Maximum drift time of 35 ns is fundamentally incompatible with 25 ns bunch spacing without severe efficiency loss
- IT silicon modules show sensitivity to magnetic field, displacing by up to 5 mm when field is ramped
- Combined OT+IT system requires two different technologies with separate readout and alignment

### Proposed Upgrade
**Deploy monolithic Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) tracker: 2.5 mm diameter polystyrene scintillating fibers read out by SiPM arrays**

- **Fiber specification:** 250 µm diameter multiclad scintillating fibers (Kuraray SCSF-78MJ), arranged in mats of 6 layers, providing >99% geometric efficiency per mat with <1 ns signal rise time
- **Readout:** 128-channel SiPM arrays (Hamamatsu S12571-010C, 10 µm microcell pitch, 2500 cells/mm²) mounted at fiber ends, with PACIFIC ASIC providing 40 MHz digitisation and on-chip sparsification
- **Hit resolution:** Single fiber resolution of ~100 µm (binary) improving to ~70 µm with charge sharing between adjacent fibers, compared to OT's 205 µm — this directly improves momentum resolution for long tracks
- **Occupancy:** At 50 ns bunch spacing and 2× design luminosity, SciFi occupancy remains <5% even in innermost region, compared to OT's 17-25%
- **Radiation tolerance:** Scintillating fibers demonstrate acceptable light yield after 10¹⁴ p/cm² at innermost station positions; SiPMs at fiber ends remain outside high-radiation zone
- **Structural rigidity:** Carbon fiber support frames eliminate magnetic-field-induced displacements seen in IT aluminum structures
- **Expected gain:** Momentum resolution improvement from δp/p ~ 5×10⁻³ to ~3.5×10⁻³ for p < 20 GeV/c, improving mass resolution for key B decay modes by ~30% and reducing combinatorial background accordingly

---

## 5. Calorimeter System Improvements

### Current Limitations
- PMT dynode degradation causes progressive gain loss requiring frequent recalibration (documented in Figure 29)
- ECAL cell-to-cell intercalibration precision of ~2% limits photon energy resolution
- HCAL calibration using ¹³⁷Cs sources restricted to technical stops (bi-monthly), creating extended periods of degraded performance
- SPD uses single-bit readout, losing energy information useful for electron/photon discrimination

### Proposed Upgrades

**PMT replacement with radiation-hard fine-mesh dynode PMTs (Hamamatsu R7400U series)**
- Fine-mesh dynodes show <5% gain variation up to 5×10³ integrated anode charge (vs. standard dynode failure at ~500 C), extending calibration intervals from bi-monthly to annual
- Retain existing optical fiber light collection system, requiring only photodetector replacement at ECAL/HCAL

**Online ECAL calibration using laser monitoring system**
- Install pulsed 355 nm UV laser (Nd:YAG third harmonic) with optical fiber distribution to all 6016 ECAL cells, providing continuous gain monitoring at 10 Hz between bunch crossings
- Demonstrated in CMS ECAL to maintain intercalibration at 0.3% level continuously, versus current LHCb ~2% π⁰-based calibration requiring 10⁵ events per cell
- Expected improvement: ECAL energy resolution constant term reduced from ~1.5% to ~0.8%, improving B→K*γ mass resolution from 93 MeV/c² toward ~65 MeV/c²

**SPD upgrade to 2-bit encoding**
- Modify SPD discriminator circuit to provide three thresholds (0, 0.5, 1.5 MIP), encoded in 2 bits per channel
- Hardware modification to front-end boards only; no sensor replacement required
- Provides coarse energy measurement enabling better separation of single electrons from γ→e⁺e⁻ conversions in SPD material, improving L0 electron trigger purity by estimated 15%

---

## 6. Muon System Readout Electronics

### Current Limitations
- Front-end chip dead time of 50-100 ns causes measurable efficiency loss at 2× design luminosity, reaching 2.5% in M1R1
- Digital output signals of 18-25 ns duration create occupancy buildup through logical OR channels
- M5 station affected by beam-line backscattering creating spurious hits

### Proposed Upgrades

**Replace DIALOG/CARIOCA front-end chips with FEERIC ASICs**
- FEERIC (Front-End Electronics for Resistive Plate Chambers, Improvements for Compactness) implements current-to-voltage amplification with 20 ns peaking time and monostable output of configurable width 8-20 ns
- Dead time reduced to <20 ns, eliminating the dominant inefficiency source in inner regions at high luminosity
- Fabricated in 130 nm CMOS, providing radiation hardness to >100 Mrad

**M5 shielding upgrade**
- Install 10 cm iron + 5 cm polyethylene neutron moderator downstream of M5 station to reduce backscattered hadron flux by factor ~3
- Coordinate with beam-line group to optimize collimator placement at ~z=22 m reducing albedo muon flux

**Timing resolution improvement for M1**
- Replace GEM detectors in M1 with microRWELL (resistive Well) detectors using 50 µm amplification gap, achieving <3 ns time resolution versus current 2.5-4 ns
- microRWELL provides same rate capability as GEM (>10⁶ Hz/cm²) with simpler construction and better timing from faster signal induction

# Hardware Design Upgrades for IceCube Physics Performance

## Framing the Problem

The paper identifies several concrete performance limitations that constrain physics reach. I will address each with specific hardware proposals, grounded in technologies available by 2017 and the quantitative deficiencies described in the paper.

---

## 1. Photon Detection: Replace PMTs with Large-Area Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

### Current Limitation
The Hamamatsu R7081-02 PMT achieves ~25% peak quantum efficiency (34% for HQE variants), has transit time spread contributing ~1.2 ns timing uncertainty, requires ~1000V bias, and exhibits correlated dark noise at 560–780 Hz total rate dominated by glass scintillation. The mu-metal shield blocks ~4% of incident light.

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace or augment the PMT with a **mosaic of large-area SiPM tiles** covering the lower hemisphere:

- **Device**: Hamamatsu S13360-6075PE or SensL J-series 60035 tiles, tiled to cover approximately the same photocathode area as the 10" PMT. Individual tile dimensions ~6×6 mm, requiring a mosaic of roughly 100–150 tiles for equivalent coverage.
- **Photon detection efficiency (PDE)**: 40–50% at 420 nm versus 25% for standard PMT, directly increasing detected photon statistics and lowering energy threshold.
- **Single-photon timing resolution**: ~100–150 ps FWHM versus ~2–3 ns for the PMT, improving directional reconstruction for track events beyond the current 1.2 ns array-level calibration floor.
- **Dark noise**: SiPM intrinsic dark count rate at −30°C (the DOM operating temperature) drops to ~10–50 kHz per cm², but given the total photocathode area equivalent (~500 cm²), this would need careful tiling geometry to keep total noise manageable. Crucially, the dominant noise source in current DOMs is glass scintillation (~500 Hz correlated component), not PMT dark current, so the noise budget is not dominated by the sensor itself.
- **Bias voltage**: 25–75 V versus ~1300–1700 V, eliminating the EMCO high-voltage generator (300 mW power draw) and the associated reliability concern.
- **No magnetic shielding required**: eliminates the mu-metal cage, recovering the ~4% photon detection loss and simplifying mechanical assembly.
- **Tradeoff**: SiPM optical cross-talk (1–5%) introduces correlated noise within a single tile that must be characterized. Temperature coefficient of gain (~2–5%/°C) requires precise temperature monitoring, though in-ice temperature is exceptionally stable at a given depth.

### Implementation Detail
Tile the lower hemisphere interior surface using a flexible PCB carrier conforming to the sphere geometry. Each tile connects to a local transimpedance amplifier (e.g., Texas Instruments OPA657) before signal summing or individual readout. For a first-generation upgrade, sum tiles into 4–6 sectors for directional sensitivity within a single DOM, a capability the current single-downward-facing PMT lacks entirely.

---

## 2. Front-End Digitization: Replace ATWD with High-Speed ADC

### Current Limitation
The ATWD captures 128 samples at 300 Msps with 10-bit resolution and a 427 ns window, followed by a slow digitization step taking up to 29 µs per channel readout. This creates significant deadtime for back-to-back hits. Two ATWD chips alternate to reduce deadtime but the median fractional deadtime reaches 3.2×10⁻³ for IceTop high-gain DOMs. The fADC runs at only 40 Msps with pulse shaping that limits timing precision.

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace the ATWD+fADC combination with a **continuously sampling pipeline ADC**:

- **Device**: Texas Instruments ADC12D1800RF (12-bit, 1.8 Gsps dual-channel) or Linear Technology LTC2387 (18-bit, 15 Msps) depending on application, or more practically for this bandwidth range, the AD9625 (12-bit, 2.5 Gsps) from Analog Devices.
- For the primary waveform capture replacing the ATWD: a 12-bit, 500 Msps pipeline ADC (e.g., AD9434) with continuous sampling eliminates the analog storage + sequential digitization architecture entirely. This removes the 29 µs per channel digitization latency.
- **Window depth**: With modern SDRAM and FPGA buffering, store a continuous 10 µs ring buffer at 500 Msps (5000 samples) versus the current 128 samples at 300 Msps. This captures the full photon arrival time distribution for highly scattered photons from distant sources without relying on the fADC's lower-resolution pulse-shaped output.
- **Deadtime**: A pipeline ADC is inherently deadtime-free during conversion, reducing the deadtime contribution from digitization to near zero. Deadtime would then be dominated only by memory transfer and FPGA processing.
- **Dynamic range**: The current multi-gain ATWD (×16, ×2, ×0.25) compensates for the ADC's limited dynamic range. With a 14-bit pipeline ADC (e.g., AD9648), the dynamic range increases to ~84 dB, potentially eliminating the need for three separate gain channels and simplifying the analog front end. A single programmable-gain amplifier (PGA) stage (e.g., AD8336) could replace the fixed three-channel gain structure.
- **Power**: Modern pipeline ADCs at 500 Msps consume ~500 mW, comparable to or slightly above the current ATWD pair, but the elimination of separate fADC circuitry partially offsets this.

---

## 3. Main Board: Upgrade FPGA and Processor

### Current Limitation
The paper describes the Main Board CPU handling waveform compression, calibration, and data packaging. The DOM stores O(10 s) of data before overflowing 16 MB SDRAM. The delta-compression scheme is explicitly described as operating on fixed word lengths of 1–11 bits.

### Proposed Upgrade
- **FPGA**: Replace the current FPGA (generation not explicitly stated but implied to be early-2000s era given the 2009 design publication) with a **Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A200T** or **Lattice iCE40HX** (for lower power). The Artix-7 provides ~200k logic cells, embedded DSP blocks for real-time pulse finding, and supports DDR3 memory interfaces.
- **Memory**: Upgrade from 16 MB SDRAM to **256 MB DDR3** (e.g., Micron MT41K128M16), extending the local hit buffer from ~10 s to ~160 s at equivalent hit rates, dramatically improving HitSpool capability and resilience to communication interruptions.
- **On-board pulse finding**: Implement real-time leading-edge discrimination and Gaussian pulse fitting in FPGA fabric. This allows the DOM to transmit compact pulse descriptors (time, amplitude, width) rather than raw waveforms for SLC hits, reducing uplink bandwidth by a factor of ~5 for the dominant noise-rate hit population.
- **Processor**: Replace the current embedded CPU with an **ARM Cortex-M4** (e.g., STM32F4 series), which provides hardware floating-point for on-board RAPCal computation and DOMCal routines, reducing calibration run time.

---

## 4. Local Coincidence: Optical or Wireless Inter-DOM Signaling

### Current Limitation
LC signaling uses dedicated copper wire pairs, with a software-configurable span of two DOMs in each direction. The LC time window is ±1 µs. The wiring adds complexity to the cable breakout (16.3 mm penetrator assembly with three wire pairs) and limits LC topology to nearest and next-to-nearest neighbors on the same string.

### Proposed Upgrade
Implement **capacitive or inductive through-hull signaling** to eliminate dedicated LC wire pairs:

- Use the existing power/communications copper pair to multiplex LC pulses using **out-of-band frequency signaling** above the current 720 kbps communications band. A simple LC pulse encoded as a short-duration (< 100 ns) burst at 10–50 MHz would be detectable with a simple bandpass filter and comparator at the receiving DOM without interfering with baseband data.
- This eliminates 2 of the 3 wire pairs in the penetrator assembly, reducing the penetrator hole from 16.3 mm to ~10 mm and decreasing mechanical failure risk during freeze-in.
- Alternatively, implement **inter-string LC** between DOMs on adjacent strings at the same depth using ultrasonic acoustic pulse signaling through the ice — a novel capability. A piezoelectric transducer (e.g., PZT-5A disk, 10 mm diameter) mounted on the DOM exterior could transmit a coded pulse detectable at ~125 m separation, enabling cross-string coincidence at the hardware level rather than only in software triggers.

---

## 5. Timing System: Chip-Scale Atomic Clock per DOM

### Current Limitation
The RAPCal system achieves ~1.2 ns relative timing accuracy by sending calibration pulses once per second. The DOM uses a 20 MHz TCXO (Vectron C2560A) with stability of ~1×10⁻¹¹ over 5 seconds. Between RAPCal pulses, the DOM clock drifts freely, and the linear interpolation in equation 3.7 assumes constant drift rate, which introduces timing errors during temperature transients or mechanical events.

### Proposed Upgrade
- **Chip-Scale Atomic Clock (CSAC)**: Microsemi SA.45s CSAC provides stability of 3×10⁻¹⁰ per day in a 17×35×9 mm package consuming only 120 mW at steady state.
- Replacing the TCXO with a CSAC reduces inter-RAPCal clock drift from potentially hundreds of picoseconds to < 30 ps over one second, allowing RAPCal rate to be reduced (saving bandwidth) or timing accuracy to be improved to < 200 ps relative DOM-to-DOM timing.
- At 200 ps timing resolution, angular reconstruction of muon tracks would improve, though the current limiting factor at the array level is photon scattering in ice (~few ns), so the benefit applies primarily to DeepCore where strings are 40–70 m apart and scattering is less dominant.
- **Cost/power tradeoff**: The CSAC consumes 120 mW continuously versus ~negligible power for the TCXO, adding ~4% to the per-DOM power budget of ~3.3 W (excluding HV and transmission). This is acceptable given the timing benefit.

---

## 6. Calibration Hardware: Broadband In-DOM Light Source

### Current Limitation
The standard flasher board uses 405 nm LEDs exclusively (with 16 cDOMs providing additional wavelengths). Ice optical properties depend strongly on wavelength (absorption length varies from ~10 m at 300 nm to > 200 m at 400 nm), so single-wavelength calibration cannot separately constrain scattering and absorption across the full relevant spectrum. The paper explicitly notes that 16 cDOMs on two strings is insufficient for comprehensive ice property mapping.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Equip every DOM with a multi-wavelength LED array**:

- Replace the 12-LED single-wavelength flasher board with a board carrying **4 LEDs at each of 4 wavelengths**: 340 nm (UV, near absorption edge of ice), 405 nm (current standard, near peak PMT QE), 470 nm (blue, long absorption length in ice), and 530 nm (green, sensitive to different ice layer properties).
- Use LEDs already characterized for cDOMs (UVTOP335-FW-TO39 at 340 nm, LED450-01 at 450 nm, B5-433-B505 at 505 nm) with demonstrated DOM compatibility.
- The LED driver circuit (figure 8 in the paper) is already capable of driving individual LEDs independently; extension to four wavelength groups requires only additional MOSFET driver channels, which fit within the existing Flasher Board form factor if using compact drivers like the Microchip MIC4420.
- **Physics impact**: Multi-wavelength in-situ calibration on every string transforms ice property measurement from a sparse (2 strings out of 86) to a comprehensive 3D tomographic measurement, directly improving photon propagation simulation accuracy and thus energy and angular reconstruction systematics.

---

## 7. Pressure Sphere: Low-Radioactivity Borosilicate with UV-Extended Transmission

### Current Limitation
The current Kopp Glass borosilicate spheres transmit 93% at 400 nm but only 10% at 315 nm. The K₂O concentration of 0.03% by weight contributes ~100 Bq of ⁴⁰K beta decay per sphere, producing ~250 Hz of uncorrelated dark noise. The correlated noise component (~300 Hz) is attributed to glass scintillation from ⁴⁰K and other radioactive elements stimulating cerium luminescence.

### Proposed Upgrade
- **Ultra-low-radioactivity glass**: Schott 8337B borosilicate glass or Ohara S-BSL7 provide K₂O < 0.001% by weight, reducing ⁴⁰K-induced noise by a factor of ~30. This would reduce the uncorrelated noise floor to ~100 Hz and the correlated (scintillation) component potentially by a similar factor, since the primary candidate scintillator is cerium excited by ⁴⁰K decays.
- **Extended UV transmission**: Fused silica pressure spheres (Heraeus Suprasil grade) transmit > 90% down to 200 nm but require significant engineering for pressure ratings to 690 bar, as fused silica is more brittle than borosilicate. A practical compromise is UV-enhanced borosilicate (Schott Borofloat 33 with UV coating) achieving > 80% transmission at 350 nm, opening sensitivity to Cherenkov photons currently lost in the glass.
- **Physics impact**: Reducing dark noise by a factor of ~3–5 directly improves the signal-to-noise ratio for supernova detection (which relies on a collective rise in individual DOM rates), low-energy neutrino analyses in DeepCore, and the SNDAQ sensitivity threshold.

---

## 8. Cable System: Fiber-Optic Data + Copper Power Hybrid

### Current Limitation
The in-ice cable uses copper twisted pairs carrying both power (96 V DC) and bidirectional digital communications at 720 kbps per pair. Attenuation ≤ 20 dB at 1 MHz end-to-end limits bandwidth. The cable diameter is 46 mm and mass is 2 kg/m. Communications bandwidth is a constraint noted implicitly in the one-DOM-per-pair data transmission protocol.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Hybrid optical fiber + copper power cable**:

- Replace the 20 copper quad data pairs with **4 single-mode optical fibers** (e.g., Corning SMF-28) for data, retaining 4 copper quads solely for DC power delivery and LC signaling.
- Each optical fiber supports > 10 Gbps bidirectional data using standard telecom transceivers (SFP+ modules), versus 720 kbps per copper pair today — a factor of > 10,000 bandwidth increase per fiber.
- Fiber survivability in freeze-in has been a concern (the paper notes copper was chosen over fiber for this reason, citing AMANDA experience), but **loose-tube fiber construction** with individual fiber buffers floating within a gel-filled tube has demonstrated survival of freeze-in in Antarctic ice in more recent deployments.
- The bandwidth increase enables: (1) transmission of full waveform data for all hits including SLC hits, eliminating the compressed chargestamp approximation; (2) higher RAPCal rate (100 Hz instead of 1 Hz) for better clock monitoring; (3) real-time streaming of raw ADC samples for offline pulse finding rather than on-board processing.
- Cable outer diameter could be reduced from 46 mm to ~30 mm, decreasing hole diameter requirements and drilling time/fuel by roughly the square of the diameter ratio.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for IceCube Physics Performance

## Framing the Problem

The primary physics performance limitations identifiable from the paper are:

- **Angular resolution** bounded by timing precision (~1.2 ns demonstrated via flashers)
- **Energy threshold** limited by DOM spacing and PMT quantum efficiency
- **Photon detection efficiency** with ~10% systematic uncertainty on absolute calibration
- **Dark noise** at 560–780 Hz per DOM contaminating low-energy analyses
- **Waveform digitization** dynamic range and deadtime constraints
- **Hole ice** creating poorly characterized near-DOM optical environment

---

## 1. Photomultiplier Tube Replacement

### Problem
The Hamamatsu R7081-02 achieves ~25% peak quantum efficiency (34% for HQE variants). The paper notes a 10% systematic uncertainty on absolute DOM efficiency, and the angular emission profile of Cherenkov photons is poorly sampled by a single downward-facing PMT per DOM.

### Proposed Upgrade: Multi-PMT Module Architecture

Replace the single 10″ PMT with an arrangement of multiple smaller-diameter PMTs distributed across the full sphere interior, following the general concept already being explored for KM3NeT.

**Specific implementation:**
- Use 31× Hamamatsu R12199-02 3″ PMTs arranged to provide nearly 4π steradian coverage, or equivalently use ~19× Hamamatsu R14374 3″ HQE tubes
- The R14374 achieves approximately 35% peak quantum efficiency at 390 nm in production units available by 2017, comparable to the existing DeepCore HQE PMTs but in a much smaller package allowing multi-PMT tiling
- Total photocathode area with 19× 3″ tubes: approximately 19 × 45 cm² = 855 cm², compared to the single 10″ PMT photocathode area of ~500 cm², representing roughly 70% increase in effective collection area
- Distributed geometry provides intrinsic directional information per DOM, reducing reliance on inter-DOM timing for photon direction reconstruction

**Specific advantages over the current design:**
- Coincidences between PMTs within the same DOM provide a hardware-level noise rejection mechanism, directly addressing the 560 Hz dark noise problem; requiring 2-fold coincidence within a ~10 ns window reduces accidental coincidence rate to approximately (560 Hz)² × 10 ns ≈ 0.003 Hz per DOM, a reduction of ~5 orders of magnitude for uncorrelated noise
- The directional sensitivity per DOM improves cascade vertex reconstruction, reducing the 15% energy resolution quoted in the paper
- Individual PMT gain of ~10⁶ rather than 10⁷ reduces space charge effects and improves linearity at high photon flux, directly addressing the saturation problem described for the ATWD at ~2 V

**Key engineering constraint:** The existing 13″ glass sphere accommodates this geometry; the paper confirms the sphere inner volume is sufficient since current boards plus a 10″ PMT already fit within it.

---

## 2. Front-End Digitization Electronics

### Problem
The paper describes two fundamental digitizer limitations:

1. The ATWD samples at 300 Msps for 128 samples, giving only 427 ns recording window; photons from scattering arrive over ~6.4 μs requiring the lower-resolution 40 Msps fADC
2. The two-ATWD alternating scheme still produces deadtime, with median fractional deadtime of 6.6×10⁻⁵ for in-ice DOMs, and the timing sequence shows ~32 μs total cycle time for back-to-back HLC hits
3. The transformer coupling introduces temperature-dependent droop requiring complex correction (equations 3.3–3.4 in the paper), with old-toroid DOMs particularly susceptible to baseline errors creating >2 PE apparent charge from 1 PE deposits

### Proposed Upgrade: Continuous Sampling ADC with Deep Pipeline

Replace the ATWD + fADC combination with a single continuous-sampling pipeline ADC architecture.

**Specific components:**
- **Texas Instruments ADS5409** or equivalent: dual-channel 12-bit ADC at 900 Msps, consuming approximately 1.5 W per channel, available in production quantities by 2016–2017
- Alternatively, **Analog Devices AD9625**: 12-bit, 2.5 Gsps, though at higher power (~2 W)
- A more practical choice balancing speed and power: **Texas Instruments ADS5281** operating at 65 Msps with 8 channels on a single chip, allowing parallel sampling of multiple gain channels without switching

**Specific implementation:**
- Three parallel gain channels (matching current 16×, 2×, 0.25× structure) each fed into a separate ADC pipeline running at 250–500 Msps continuously
- Deep FIFO buffer of 65,536 samples per channel (implementable in the FPGA fabric using Xilinx Spartan-7 block RAM totaling ~4.5 Mb) stores approximately 130 μs of continuous data at 500 Msps
- Trigger-on-threshold causes the FPGA to freeze the relevant portion of the ring buffer rather than initiating a separate capture sequence
- Eliminates the re-arm delay of 50 ns and the ~32 μs digitization cycle entirely; deadtime becomes only the time to transfer data from FIFO to SDRAM via DMA

**Droop correction:** Eliminating the transformer coupling by using a DC-coupled front end with a transimpedance amplifier (TIA) directly on the PMT anode removes the droop problem entirely. A suitable TIA using the **Analog Devices ADA4817** (1.2 GHz bandwidth, 4 nV/√Hz noise) provides adequate bandwidth for the 7–8 ns FWHM SPE pulse while maintaining DC coupling. This removes equations 3.3 and 3.4 from the calibration chain entirely.

**Quantitative improvement:** Current ATWD timing resolution is limited to ~3.3 ns by the 300 Msps sampling (one sample period). A 1 Gsps ADC reduces this to ~1 ns, and with interpolation to the zero-crossing the effective timing resolution approaches 0.3–0.5 ns, improving upon the 1.2 ns demonstrated with RAPCal.

---

## 3. FPGA Upgrade and Local Processing

### Problem
The current Main Board uses an FPGA for local processing of waveforms and LC signaling, but the described functionality is relatively limited: delta-compression, LC forwarding, and DMA transfer. The paper notes that waveform deconvolution to extract photon arrival times is performed offline in the Processing and Filtering system, not at the DOM level.

### Proposed Upgrade: Xilinx Spartan-7 or Intel MAX 10 FPGA with Onboard Feature Extraction

**Specific component:** Replace the current FPGA (not explicitly named in the paper but implied to be a mid-2000s vintage device given the 2009 DAQ paper reference) with a **Xilinx Spartan-7 XC7S50**, which provides:
- 52,160 logic cells
- 2,700 Kb block RAM
- 120 DSP slices
- 3.3 W typical power consumption
- Available in commercial production by 2015–2016

**Specific onboard algorithms to implement in FPGA fabric:**

1. **Leading-edge time extraction:** Implement a linear interpolation across the threshold crossing using DSP slices, extracting photon arrival time to sub-sample precision (0.3 ns at 1 Gsps) without surface processing. This moves the core timing computation to the DOM, reducing surface DAQ load.

2. **Charge integration:** Integrate waveform samples over a configurable window in real time, transmitting a charge value rather than raw samples for SLC hits. The paper notes SLC hits currently transmit only 3 fADC samples as a chargestamp; a proper integration over the full pulse reduces charge uncertainty.

3. **Multi-PMT coincidence logic** (in conjunction with upgrade 1): If multiple PMTs are present, the FPGA implements configurable coincidence windows between PMT channels within the DOM, providing the hardware noise rejection described above without surface processing.

4. **Waveform feature vector compression:** Rather than transmitting losslessly compressed raw waveform samples (the current delta-compression scheme), extract {time, charge, width} triplets for each identified pulse in the ATWD/fADC waveform. This could reduce HLC payload size by a factor of 3–5 for typical multi-photon events, increasing effective bandwidth and allowing higher trigger rates.

---

## 4. RAPCal Timing System Upgrade

### Problem
The paper demonstrates 1.2 ns timing accuracy via flasher measurements, limited by the 20 MHz communications ADC used to digitize the returning RAPCal pulse (50 ns per sample), with fine-delay correction via zero-crossing interpolation. The cable delay distribution has 0.6 ns standard deviation per DOM per measurement, and individual outliers beyond 10 ns are discarded.

### Proposed Upgrade: Higher-Rate RAPCal with Dedicated Timing ADC

**Specific implementation:**
- Add a dedicated **Texas Instruments ADS8860** 16-bit, 1 Msps ADC (or the ADS8861 at 2 Msps) solely for RAPCal pulse digitization, at a cost of approximately $5–8 per chip
- Increase RAPCal pulse transmission rate from 1 Hz to 10 Hz per DOM; at 720 kbps total channel bandwidth shared between two DOMs, RAPCal pulses consume approximately 2–3 ms of bandwidth each, meaning 10 Hz requires ~2–3% of channel capacity, leaving >97% for data — acceptable given current data rates
- With 10 measurements per second, the uncertainty on the clock offset estimate (currently ~0.6 ns/√1 = 0.6 ns per second) improves to 0.6/√10 ≈ 0.19 ns per second
- The dedicated higher-resolution ADC improves the zero-crossing interpolation, targeting sub-nanosecond systematic uncertainty in the fine-delay correction

**Alternative approach — White Rabbit Protocol:**
Implement the White Rabbit precision timing protocol (developed at CERN, publicly available hardware designs by 2017) using the existing copper pairs. White Rabbit achieves sub-nanosecond synchronization over standard Ethernet using a combination of PTP (IEEE 1588) and SyncE, with demonstrated performance of ~100 ps synchronization over copper links. This would require replacing the DOR card's timing circuitry but could use the existing cable plant.

---

## 5. In-Situ Calibration Hardware

### Problem
The paper identifies several calibration limitations:
- Absolute DOM optical efficiency has 10% systematic uncertainty, described as the dominant nuisance parameter in physics analyses
- The hole ice (16 cm diameter central column with anomalous scattering) has poorly characterized optical properties
- Ice optical property measurements depend on the flasher LEDs, which have ~30° FWHM emission profile and fixed 405 nm wavelength for standard DOMs (only 16 cDOMs have multi-wavelength capability)

### Proposed Upgrade A: Expanded Multi-Wavelength Calibration DOMs

**Specific implementation:**
- Equip every 5th DOM (rather than only 16 cDOMs total) with the multi-wavelength flasher board
- Add a **375 nm** LED (e.g., Nichia NVSU233A) to each standard flasher board; this wavelength sits between existing 340 nm and 405 nm LEDs and corresponds to a region of strong wavelength dependence in the ice absorption coefficient
- Add **265 nm** deep-UV LEDs (e.g., SETi UVTOP265) to probe wavelengths near the PMT quantum efficiency cutoff and the glass transmission edge, providing better constraint on the wavelength-dependent efficiency model
- Total additional cost: approximately $30–50 per DOM in LED components, negligible relative to total DOM cost

**Specific physics impact:** The 10% efficiency uncertainty directly propagates to 10% uncertainty in reconstructed neutrino energy, which currently limits the precision of the astrophysical neutrino spectral index measurement. Reducing this to 3–4% would substantially improve spectral analyses.

### Proposed Upgrade B: Isotropic Light Source per DOM

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace or supplement one LED pair per flasher board with a **pulsed isotropic source**: a small integrating sphere (5 mm diameter, PTFE-coated interior) with an embedded LED, providing <5° angular variation in output intensity
- The **Hamamatsu L12194** pulsed LED module with fiber output, coupled to a ground-glass diffuser, provides approximately isotropic emission with pulse widths of 1–3 ns
- This enables direct measurement of the absorption length at each DOM location independent of the scattering model, since isotropic emission produces a well-defined geometric dilution factor R⁻² for distant receivers

---

## 6. DOM Glass Sphere and Pressure Housing

### Problem
The paper identifies the glass pressure sphere as the dominant source of dark noise (560 Hz uncorrelated, 280–340 Hz correlated), with the correlated component attributed to luminescence from radioactive decays in the borosilicate glass. The K₂O concentration of 0.03% by weight corresponds to ~100 Bq per sphere, driving the 250 Hz uncorrelated component via ⁴⁰K beta decays and Cherenkov emission.

### Proposed Upgrade: Low-Radioactivity Glass or Acrylic Housing

**Option B — Acrylic pressure housing:**
Cast acrylic (PMMA) can be produced with substantially lower intrinsic radioactivity than borosilicate glass, as demonstrated in neutrino experiments including SNO and KamLAND. The mechanical challenge is accommodating 250 bar sustained pressure and 690 bar transient; this requires a thicker wall (~15 mm versus 12.7 mm glass) and a different geometry. Acrylic has superior UV transmission (>90% at 300 nm versus ~10% for borosilicate glass at 315 nm), directly expanding the detectable photon spectrum and improving sensitivity to Cherenkov emission at shorter wavelengths where PMT quantum efficiency is still appreciable.

**Quantitative impact:** Halving the dark noise rate from 560 Hz to ~280 Hz per DOM would reduce the accidental coincidence rate in DeepCore analyses quadratically, improving the sensitivity of low-energy oscillation and dark matter analyses by reducing the effective energy threshold from ~10 GeV toward ~5 GeV.

---

## 7. Local Coincidence Wiring Extension

### Problem
The current LC system uses dedicated wire pairs to signal only the immediately adjacent DOM above and below, with configurable forwarding span (currently set to 2, meaning the signal propagates to nearest and next-to-nearest neighbors). The ±1 μs LC window is set by the light travel time in ice. SLC hits transmit only timestamp and 3-sample chargestamp, discarding waveform information for isolated hits.

- The additional fiber strands add <0.5 mm to cable diameter, within the existing design margins

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Forward Heavy-Flavour Spectrometer

## Context and Performance Drivers

Before proposing upgrades, I'll identify the binding constraints for this class of instrument (canonical example: LHCb). Heavy-flavour physics performance is ultimately limited by:

1. **Decay-time resolution** → vertex/impact-parameter resolution
2. **Mass resolution** → momentum resolution + particle identification
3. **Background rejection** → trigger efficiency × purity, PID
4. **Luminosity reach** → occupancy handling, radiation hardness, readout bandwidth
5. **Acceptance** → geometric coverage and threshold effects

Each upgrade below is tied directly to one or more of these.

---

## 1. Vertex Detector: The Highest-Priority Upgrade

### Current limitation
Silicon strip or hybrid pixel detectors ~5–8 mm from the beam axis, with ~50–200 μm pitch, deliver IP resolution of order 15–20 μm in the transverse plane. This limits *B*–*D* separation and τ physics.

### Proposed upgrade: **Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS) in a RF-foil-retracted geometry**

**Technology:** Tower Semiconductor (formerly TowerJazz) 180 nm or TSMC 65 nm CMOS imaging process with in-pixel amplification, discriminator, and sparse readout logic (similar to ALICE ITS3 or LHCb Upgrade II VELO concept).

**Specific choices:**
- **Pixel pitch:** 20–25 μm (achievable in 65 nm node) vs. 55 μm for hybrid pixels → direct improvement in single-hit resolution from ~16 μm to ~5–7 μm
- **Sensor thickness:** 50 μm epitaxial layer on high-resistivity substrate; thin to 100 μm total (vs. 300 μm for hybrids) → radiation length X/X₀ per layer drops from ~1% to ~0.3%
- **Material budget impact:** IP resolution scales as σ_IP ∝ (X/X₀)^(1/2)/p_T; halving X/X₀ gives ~30% improvement in IP resolution at low momentum, which is critical for charm tagging
- **Retraction mechanism:** Motorized RF-foil halves retracted to r = 3.5 mm during stable beams (vs. typical 8 mm), reducing the lever arm effect; foil made from 100 μm Be or 25 μm Al-coated Kapton
- **Radiation hardness:** MAPS in 65 nm node tolerate >10^15 n_eq/cm² with proper design (n-type collection electrode in p-type substrate, or pixel-level HV bias); adequate for 50 fb⁻¹ at high luminosity
- **Readout:** Column-drain binary architecture at 40 MHz bunch crossing rate; on-chip zero suppression reduces bandwidth to ~1 Gb/s per sector

**Expected gain:** σ_IP(transverse) from ~18 μm → ~8 μm at p = 1 GeV/c; B-meson decay-time resolution improves by factor ~1.5, opening sensitivity to CP asymmetries in ΔΓ-suppressed modes and very short-lived charm states.

---

## 2. Upstream Tracker / Scintillating Fibre Replacement

### Current limitation
Outer tracker drift-time chambers or coarse-pitch silicon strips have single-hit resolution ~200 μm and relatively slow response (25–50 ns drift), creating occupancy problems at high luminosity (pp interaction rates > 30 MHz).

### Proposed upgrade: **Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) tracker with SiPM readout + LGAD time layer**

**SciFi tracker:**
- **Fibre diameter:** 250 μm multiclad polystyrene fibres, 6 layers per station, mat thickness 2.4 mm → single-hit resolution ~70 μm, radiation length ~0.8% X/X₀ per station
- **SiPM array:** Custom 128-channel SiPM arrays (Hamamatsu S13552 or KETEK) with 250 μm pitch, operated at −30°C to mitigate radiation damage (dark count rate); SPAD size 57 μm, fill factor >60%
- **Readout ASIC:** Dedicated 128-channel front-end (e.g., PACIFIC ASIC at LHCb) with 4-sample pipeline at 40 MHz, cluster finding on FPGA
- **Why better than drift chambers:** 25 ns time resolution (one bunch crossing) eliminates ghost hits from adjacent crossings; hit rate capacity >2 MHz/cm² vs. ~100 kHz/cm² for straws

**LGAD (Low-Gain Avalanche Detector) timing plane:**
- **Position:** One station immediately downstream of the vertex detector
- **Technology:** AC-coupled LGAD (AC-LGAD or RSD) from FBK/CNM in 50 μm active layer; gain ~10–20
- **Timing resolution:** 30–50 ps per hit → 4D tracking (x, y, z, t)
- **Key physics benefit:** At 30 MHz pp rate with ~2–3 interactions per crossing, vertex association ambiguity is a leading systematic. With 50 ps timing, vertices separated by >150 μm in z that overlap in time (Δt < 200 ps) can be disambiguated using track timing → effective pile-up rejection without increasing ghost rate
- **Segmentation:** 1.0 mm × 3.0 mm strips (trapezoidal geometry matching forward acceptance), 500 μm pitch in precision direction

---

## 3. RICH Particle Identification: Photon Detector Upgrade

### Current limitation
Multi-anode PMTs (MaPMTs, e.g., Hamamatsu R11265) with ~6 mm pixel size and quantum efficiency ~28% at 200 nm limit Cherenkov angle resolution, especially at high occupancy.

### Proposed upgrade: **Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) for RICH-1 near-IP; lifetime-extended MaPMT for RICH-2**

**RICH-1 SiPM upgrade:**
- **Device:** 1 mm × 1 mm SiPM pixels (Hamamatsu VUV4 or SensL J-series with UV-enhanced coating), PDE >40% at 300–400 nm, operated in moderate magnetic field (compensated by magnetic shielding or field-free region)
- **Advantage over MaPMT:** Factor ~1.5 in PDE → more Cherenkov photons detected per ring → Cherenkov angle resolution improves from ~0.4 mrad → ~0.3 mrad → π/K separation extended from ~100 GeV/c → ~130 GeV/c (for RICH-2 geometry)
- **Pixel size reduction:** 1 mm vs. 6 mm → reduced occupancy at high luminosity, enabling operation at 5× nominal luminosity
- **Challenge:** SiPM dark count rate at room temperature ~100 kHz/mm²; mitigated by cooling to +5°C and tight timing cuts (2 ns coincidence window with tracking)
- **Readout:** TOFPET2 ASIC (PETsys) adapted for Cherenkov application: 64 channels, 50 ps TDC, triggerless streaming

**Aerogel radiator optimisation:**
- Replace current n = 1.03 silica aerogel with **dual-layer focusing aerogel** (n₁ = 1.05 upstream, n₂ = 1.02 downstream), same concept as Belle II ARICH but adapted for forward geometry
- Achieves constructive interference of Cherenkov rings, recovering angular resolution degraded by chromatic dispersion
- Net effect: >3σ π/K separation maintained down to **~2 GeV/c** (vs. current ~3 GeV/c threshold)

---

## 4. Calorimeter System: Longitudinal Segmentation and Timing

### Current limitation
Shashlik ECAL with sparse longitudinal sampling cannot distinguish π⁰ Dalitz and prompt photons from hadronic backgrounds; energy resolution ~10%/√E limits *B*→*Kγ* mass resolution.

### Proposed upgrade: **Dual-readout crystal calorimeter front section + W/Si sampling for high-rate region**

**Crystal preshower + front ECAL section:**
- **Material:** PWO-II (lead tungstate with improved light yield via La/Mo co-doping, as used in CMS ECAL) or LYSO:Ce crystals (5× higher light yield, radiation hard to 10^6 Gy)
- **Geometry:** 4 radiation lengths of crystals (segmented 20 × 20 mm²) in front of existing shashlik, acting as electromagnetic preshower with precision energy measurement
- **Dual readout:** Each crystal read by both a SiPM (scintillation, ns timescale) and a UV-enhanced SiPM or photodiode (Cherenkov, faster component) → event-by-event electromagnetic fraction correction → hadronic energy resolution improvement from ~60%/√E → ~30%/√E
- **Key physics:** Improves *B*→*K*(*)*γ radiative decay signal-to-background by factor ~2 via better π⁰ rejection and γ energy resolution

**High-granularity forward region (innermost 1 m² around beam):**
- **Technology:** Tungsten-Silicon sampling calorimeter (W-Si), 30 layers, inspired by CMS HGCAL
- **Cell size:** 1 cm² hexagonal silicon pads in first 20 layers (EM section), 5 cm² in last 10 layers (HAD)
- **Benefit:** At η > 4, particle density is extreme; granularity replaces inefficient clustering; pion rejection via shower shape improves by factor ~3

---

## 5. Muon System: Timing and Rate Capability

### Current limitation
MWPC-based muon stations have ~5 ns timing resolution and <1 MHz/cm² rate capability; at high luminosity, fake muon rates from punchthrough degrade trigger purity.

### Proposed upgrade: **MicroRPC (thin-gap RPC) + GEM hybrid stations**

**Micro-RPC for timing:**
- **Technology:** 2-gap glass RPC with 0.3 mm gas gap, operated in avalanche mode (vs. streamer in standard RPC)
- **Timing resolution:** ~300 ps per station (vs. ~2 ns for MWPC)
- **Rate capability:** ~10 kHz/cm² sustained (vs. ~1 kHz/cm² for standard RPC), adequate for luminosity up to 2×10³³ cm⁻²s⁻¹
- **Strip pitch:** 1 cm × 10 cm strips read by low-power front-end (FEERIC ASIC or equivalent)

**GEM (Gas Electron Multiplier) for high-rate innermost regions:**
- **Technology:** Triple-GEM detectors (CERN GEM technology, as in CMS ME0), 140 μm pitch copper strips
- **Rate capability:** >10 MHz/cm² — handles innermost acceptance near beam pipe where rates are highest
- **Single-hit resolution:** ~70 μm (strip direction) → improves muon momentum measurement via better track extrapolation to the magnet region
- **Cluster-time:** ~10 ns with fast gas mixture (Ar/CO₂/CF₄ 45/15/40)

**Physics benefit:** Muon trigger fake rate (from π/K decay-in-flight and punchthrough) reduced by factor ~5 via timing cuts and improved pattern recognition → *B*→*μμ* and *B*→*J/ψ X* trigger efficiency/purity improved, enabling operation at 3–5× higher luminosity

---

## 6. Trigger and DAQ: Full Online Reconstruction

### Current limitation
A hardware Level-0 trigger using calorimeter/muon primitives applies a transverse-energy or p_T threshold that biases the hadronic event sample, particularly rejecting low-p_T charm decays (D⁰→*Kπ*, hadronic *B* decays) and introducing acceptance distortions that are the dominant systematic in many branching-fraction measurements.

### Proposed upgrade: **Triggerless readout with GPU-accelerated real-time reconstruction (Allen framework extended)**

**Readout architecture:**
- Eliminate hardware L0 entirely; all sub-detectors run at full 30–40 MHz collision rate in continuous readout mode
- **Front-end links:** lpGBT (low-power GBT) at 10.24 Gb/s per link, aggregated via FELIX (Front-End Link eXchange) PCIe cards with Xilinx Ultrascale+ FPGAs
- **Aggregate bandwidth:** ~40 Tb/s raw detector data → requires O(1000) 100GbE links to GPU farm

**GPU first-level trigger (High-Level Trigger 1):**
- **Hardware:** 500 NVIDIA A100 (80 GB HBM2e) or H100 GPUs in a dedicated GPU farm, interconnected via NVLink + InfiniBand HDR (200 Gb/s)
- **Algorithm:** Allen (already demonstrated at LHCb) runs full VELO Kalman track finding, primary vertex reconstruction, secondary vertex finding, and RICH pattern recognition on GPU in <10 ms latency
- **Key addition:** **Displaced-vertex trigger** without p_T bias — select events with any track with IP > 100 μm relative to the best primary vertex, regardless of p_T → recovers ~40% more hadronic charm events vs. L0 calorimeter trigger
- **Throughput:** Reduce 40 MHz input to ~1 MHz output for HLT2

**HLT2 CPU+GPU farm:**
- Full offline-quality reconstruction (Kalman filter on all tracks, full RICH reconstruction, full calorimeter clustering) at 1 MHz input
- **Machine learning inference:** Graph Neural Network (GNN) for *b*-tagging and decay-topology classification, deployed via ONNX runtime on GPU; adds ~0.5 ms per event but provides >95% *B*-hadron tagging efficiency with <1% fake rate
- **Output:** ~10 GB/s to permanent storage (physics-selected candidates only)

**Specific physics gain:** An unbiased displaced-vertex trigger enables first measurements of absolute hadronic charm branching fractions, extends sensitivity to *B*→ purely hadronic final states (e.g., *B*→*DK*, *D*→*Kππ* for γ measurement) with factor ~3 more signal candidates, and enables fully inclusive *b*-hadron lifetime measurements without p_T bias.

---

## 7. Upstream Magnet Tracking (Upstream Tracker/UT)

### Proposed upgrade: **Silicon strip micro-strip detector with AC-LGAD strip layer for time-stamping**

- **Sensor:** 75 μm pitch single-sided silicon microstrip (p-on-n, 300 μm thick, radiation hard to 5×10^14 n_eq/cm²), four measurement layers in XYUV stereo geometry
- **ASIC:** SALT (Silicon ASIC for LHCb Tracker) with 12.5 ns peaking time, zero-suppressed output at 40 MHz
- **Added layer:** One 500 μm-pitch AC-LGAD strip layer (50 μm active, FBK production) providing 50 ps time stamp
- **Benefit:** Momentum measurement of tracks *before* the magnet allows RICH-1 hypothesis to be formed early in the trigger chain; rejects ~60% of clone/ghost tracks in HLT1 before GPU reconstruction of downstream tracker, reducing CPU load by ~25%
- **Ghost-track reduction physics impact:** Fake displaced-vertex rate falls by factor ~3, enabling lower IP threshold in the trigger and recovering low-lifetime charm states (D⁰ proper time < 0.1 ps)
