# Hardware Design Upgrades for LHCb Performance Improvement

Based on careful analysis of the performance limitations documented in this paper, I propose the following concrete hardware upgrades targeting the primary physics bottlenecks.

---

## 1. Vertex Locator (VELO) Replacement

### Identified Limitations
- Silicon sensors approaching radiation damage limits (~1.8×10¹⁴ neq/cm² by Run I end)
- Effective depletion voltage rising toward 100V, approaching 500V operational limit
- 210-second average closing time after stable beams declaration
- IP resolution plateau of ~13 µm at high pT

### Proposed Upgrade: VELO Pixel Detector

**Replace silicon microstrip R/Φ sensors with hybrid pixel sensors:**

- **Sensor technology:** 55×55 µm² pixel pitch VeloPix ASICs based on Timepix3 architecture, providing per-pixel time-of-arrival with ~1 ns resolution alongside charge measurement
- **Sensor material:** n-on-p float zone silicon, 200 µm active thickness (down from 300 µm), reducing multiple scattering contribution to IP resolution
- **Radiation hardness:** Adopt 3D columnar electrode geometry (as developed at FBK/CNM) for innermost pixel columns within 5-8 mm of beam axis, providing radiation tolerance exceeding 10¹⁶ neq/cm² through lateral charge collection that is geometrically insensitive to bulk trapping
- **Thinned sensor periphery:** Reduce inactive edge to <200 µm using active-edge processing, allowing closer approach to beam without geometric acceptance loss
- **Mechanical closure:** Replace stepper motor resolver system with linear optical encoders providing <1 µm reproducibility, eliminating the ~5 µm uncertainty currently limiting half-station relative alignment and reducing closing time to <60 seconds through improved position feedback

**Expected performance gain:**
- IP resolution improvement from 13 µm to ~8 µm asymptotic value through reduced scintillator material and improved hit resolution
- Radiation lifetime extension by factor ~3-5 beyond current silicon strip design
- 4D tracking capability (x, y, z, t) enabling pile-up rejection through timing

---

## 2. RICH Detector Photon Detector Replacement

### Identified Limitations
- Hybrid Photon Detectors (HPDs) yield lower Npe than simulation: C₄F₁₀ shows 20.4 vs predicted 28.3 (28% deficit), CF₄ shows 15.8 vs 22.7 (30% deficit)
- Residual magnetic field distortions in RICH1 causing σ(θC) = 1.618 mrad vs simulated 1.52 mrad
- HPD read-out inefficiency identified during high trigger rate running
- Aerogel Npe of only 5.0 with large uncertainty, partly from C₄F₁₀ absorption

### Proposed Upgrade A: Replace HPDs with Multi-Anode Microchannel Plate PMTs (MaPMT)

**RICH1 and RICH2 photon detectors:**

- **Device:** Hamamatsu R11265 or equivalent 64-channel MaPMT arrays with 2×2 mm² pixel size
- **Key advantage:** MaPMTs operate effectively in magnetic fields up to ~1.5 mT without demagnification electrodes, eliminating the image distortion currently degrading C₄F₁₀ resolution
- **Quantum efficiency:** Bialkali photocathode with peak QE ~28% versus HPD silicon sensor QE of ~18% at 300 nm, directly recovering ~40% of the photoelectron deficit
- **Gain uniformity:** MaPMT pixel-to-pixel gain variation <1:3, allowing simpler equalization than HPD electron optics
- **Read-out ASIC:** Pair with CLARO or NINO front-end chips providing 25 ns time resolution per channel, enabling bunch crossing disambiguation

**Expected performance gain:**
- σ(θC) for C₄F₁₀ improving from 1.618 to ~1.55 mrad, approaching simulation
- Npe recovery to ~25 for C₄F₁₀, improving kaon/pion separation significance by ~√(25/20) ≈ 12%
- Kaon efficiency at fixed 3% pion misID rate improving from ~85% to ~90%

### Proposed Upgrade B: RICH1 Aerogel Replacement

- **Remove aerogel radiator** (contributing only Npe ~5 with large uncertainty) and replace with additional **C₄F₁₀ gas volume** extending RICH1 upstream
- **Alternatively:** Replace with **silica aerogel tiles** of n=1.03 refractive index manufactured by Matsushita with hydrophobic surface treatment, physically isolated from C₄F₁₀ gas volume by thin Mylar window (25 µm) to prevent gas absorption that currently degrades performance
- Low-momentum particle identification below 10 GeV/c recovered through improved aerogel Npe (~15 expected with isolation)

---

## 3. Upstream Tracker (UT) Replacing Tracker Turicensis

### Identified Limitations
- TT hit resolution of 52-53 µm with significant variation across sectors
- Occupancy reaching 1.9% near beam pipe, limiting pattern recognition
- Only 4 detection layers with limited standalone momentum resolution

### Proposed Upgrade: Silicon Microstrip UT with Reduced Material

**Replace TT with higher-granularity silicon tracker:**

- **Sensor geometry:** Four stereo layers (x-u-v-x at ±5°) retained but with **strip pitch reduced from 183 µm to 100 µm** in innermost sectors using AC-coupled p-on-n microstrips
- **Sensor thickness:** Reduce from 500 µm to 320 µm for innermost modules, reducing material budget from ~4% X₀ to ~2.5% X₀ per layer
- **Read-out:** Replace BEETLE ASIC with **SALT ASIC** providing 40 MHz sampling rate with 4-bit ADC per channel, enabling bunch-crossing-precise hit timing that reduces effective occupancy by factor ~2
- **Module segmentation:** Increase from 280 to ~900 read-out sectors using shorter strip lengths (maximum 5 cm), reducing occupancy in high-flux inner region from 1.9% to <0.5%
- **Cooling:** Replace bi-phase CO₂ cooling loops with microfluidic silicon cooling channels integrated into sensor substrate, reducing material by ~0.3% X₀ per layer

**Expected performance gain:**
- Hit resolution improvement from 53 µm to ~25 µm in inner region
- Ghost track rate reduction through improved TT-track association
- Long track momentum resolution improvement of ~15% through better upstream momentum seed

---

## 4. Scintillating Fibre Tracker Replacing IT/OT

### Identified Limitations
- OT single-hit resolution of 205 µm (design 200 µm, marginal)
- OT maximum drift time of 35 ns limits performance at 25 ns bunch spacing (occupancy rising to 25%)
- IT occupancy reaching 1.9% near beam pipe with read-out dead-time effects
- Magnetic field sensitivity causing IT box displacements of up to 5 mm requiring frequent realignment

### Proposed Upgrade: Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) Tracker

**Replace T1-T3 stations with scintillating fibre modules:**

- **Fibre specification:** 250 µm diameter round scintillating fibres (Kuraray SCSF-78MJ) arranged in staggered 6-layer mats achieving ~130 µm position resolution without drift time ambiguity
- **Photo-detector:** Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) with 50×50 µm² cell size operating at -40°C to reduce dark count rate, with custom PACIFIC ASIC providing 25 MHz read-out at 2-bit ADC resolution
- **Radiation tolerance:** SiPM radiation hardness exceeds 10¹² neq/cm² at operational temperature, adequate for T1-T3 flux levels; fibre radiation length >100 Mrad
- **Mechanical stability:** Carbon fibre composite support structures with CTE matched to fibre mat, eliminating the thermomechanical displacement seen in IT; no magnetic sensitivity
- **Timing:** SiPM + PACIFIC system achieves <1 ns per-cluster timing, enabling 25 ns bunch crossing identification and eliminating the multi-bunch-crossing OT ambiguity

**Expected performance gain:**
- Hit resolution improvement from 205 µm (OT) to ~130 µm
- Elimination of 25 ns bunch spacing occupancy degradation (25% → <5%)
- Tracking efficiency improvement of 1-2% through elimination of drift-time-based inefficiencies at cell edges
- Mass resolution improvement ~10% for hadronic decay modes through improved T-station hits

**For ECAL inner region (highest radiation/rate):**

- Replace conventional PMTs with **radiation-hard SiPMs** (Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent), 3×3 mm² active area with 50 µm cell pitch

- Replace voltage divider chain with **individual SiPM bias voltage DACs** (12-bit, 0.1V resolution) per channel, enabling continuous online gain correction without PMT high-voltage ramping
- Implement online gain monitoring via **blue LED pulser** with reference PIN diode, enabling gain correction at 1 Hz rate versus current bi-monthly cadence

**Expected performance gain:**

- Reduce ECAL intercalibration uncertainty from 2% to ~0.8% through continuous correction

- This enables 4D calorimeter clustering, rejecting pile-up neutral particles from secondary vertices by >2 ns timing cut

# Hardware Design Upgrades for LUX: Specific Proposals

## 1. PMT Array Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

### Motivation
The R8778 PMTs dominate the background budget (Table 3: 0.4 ER and 0.03 NR WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days), primarily due to radioactive contamination in their glass, steel body, and the aluminum ring flagged by XMASS. The PMTs also define the minimum fiducial volume through their proximity to the active region.

### Specific Implementation
- **Replace 122 R8778 PMTs with tiled arrays of Hamamatsu VUV4 (S13370) or FBK VUV-HD SiPMs**, which have demonstrated >20% photon detection efficiency at 175 nm in LXe
- SiPM tile assemblies using 6mm × 6mm cells mounted on **low-radioactivity PTFE-backed PCBs with copper traces**, eliminating the borosilicate glass and steel PMT body entirely
- Each tile (~25mm × 25mm) would contain a 4×4 array of cells, with tiles ganged to match current PMT channel count or increased granularity
- **Radioactivity advantage**: Modern SiPM arrays achieve <1 µBq/cm² of U/Th contamination versus the measured 9.8 mBq/PMT U and 2.3 mBq/PMT Th (Table 2), representing roughly a **factor 100 reduction** in the dominant background source
- **Geometrical advantage**: Flat tile arrays can be positioned with the active silicon layer closer to the TPC boundary than the R8778 photocathode, allowing the bottom buffer region to shrink from 5 cm toward ~1 cm, directly increasing fiducial mass
- **Cryogenic operation**: VUV4 devices are qualified to 87K (LXe temperature ~165K in LUX), requiring only modest bias (~25-30V) supplied through existing cable infrastructure

### Tradeoffs to Engineer
- SiPMs have higher dark count rate (~100 kcps/mm² at 165K, though strongly suppressed versus room temperature) requiring coincidence logic thresholds to be revisited
- Correlated avalanche noise (optical crosstalk ~10-15% for current devices) degrades S1 single-photon counting; this requires careful threshold setting in the trigger system described in Sec. 7.3
- Individual cell capacitance summing across a large tile increases output pulse rise time; a **transimpedance amplifier (TIA) using an OPA657 or similar cryogenic-compatible op-amp** co-located on the tile PCB would replace the current two-stage preamplifier/postamplifier chain

---

## 2. Upgraded Cathode High-Voltage System

### Motivation
The paper notes the cathode HV system targets 100 kV to produce a 2 kV/cm drift field, but explicitly acknowledges difficulty due to xenon discharge susceptibility and places the feedthrough outside the water shield, creating a 25 cm unshielded cable section inside LXe (Sec. 3.4). This compromises both field uniformity and potential outgassing.

### Specific Implementation
- **Replace the HVC100 cable with a custom coaxial line using PTFE dielectric and ultra-pure copper conductor**, with radioassayed PTFE verified to <0.1 ppb U/Th, eliminating the identified outgassing concern requiring the 0.1 SLPM purge flow
- **Implement a Greinacher (Cockcroft-Walton) multiplier cascade inside the xenon space** using surface-mount capacitors and diodes on a Cirlex PCB, fed by a lower-voltage (~10 kV) input cable — this keeps high fields entirely within LXe where Paschen breakdown is suppressed, rather than at the liquid-gas interface near the feedthrough
- Alternatively, adopt the **triaxial feedthrough geometry used in EXO-200**, where a grounded guard electrode surrounds the HV conductor throughout the umbilical, eliminating unshielded regions and field distortions near the cathode connection point
- Add **field-shaping electrodes at the cathode connection point** (replacing the current spring-pin/polyethylene arrangement) using a geometry modeled to keep E < 50 kV/cm everywhere in LXe, suppressing electroluminescence from field non-uniformities that generate spurious S2-like signals

---

## 3. Replacement of Copper Field Rings with Etched Kapton/Cirlex Resistive Divider

### Motivation
The 48 copper field rings (3.2 mm thick, 12.7 mm wide, 1 cm spacing per Sec. 3.3) connected by a discrete resistor chain of 1 GΩ pairs represent a significant mass of material within the active region boundary. Copper exposed at the Sanford Surface Laboratory accumulates cosmogenic radionuclides (specifically ⁶⁰Co, noted in Table 3 as pending measurement), and the discrete resistor connections represent potential failure points.

### Specific Implementation
- **Replace the copper ring/discrete resistor architecture with a monolithic resistive Cirlex cylinder** — a single machined Cirlex (polyimide) tube with **carbon-loaded PTFE resistive traces** photolithographically patterned to provide the voltage gradient, eliminating all discrete resistors and copper rings
- Target bulk resistivity of ~10¹⁰ Ω·cm achievable in carbon-doped PTFE composites, dimensioned to provide the same 500 MΩ total cathode-to-gate resistance as the current 1 GΩ parallel pairs
- This approach was later adopted in LZ (LUX-ZEPLIN) and demonstrated mechanically stable performance; the LUX geometry is directly compatible
- **Radioactivity benefit**: Cirlex (polyimide) has been measured at <0.1 ppb U/Th, and the eliminated copper mass (~2 kg) removes the cosmogenic activation concern entirely
- The UHMW polyethylene support panels behind the PTFE reflectors would be replaced with **machined PTFE panels serving dual function** as both field-ring support and optical reflector, reducing total component count

---

## 4. Enhanced S1 Light Collection via Wavelength-Shifting Reflector Coating

### Motivation
The paper reports 8 phe/keVee light yield (Sec. 6.3), and notes PTFE reflectivity >95% in LXe. However, the gate, cathode, and bottom shield grids (96-99% transparent at normal incidence) still represent optical losses, particularly for oblique photons, and the gas phase electroluminescence region above the liquid surface has limited S1 light recovery.

### Specific Implementation
- **Apply tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) wavelength-shifting coating** (evaporated at 0.2 mg/cm²) to all PTFE reflector panels and the inner faces of the top/bottom PMT support structures — this converts 175 nm LXe scintillation to ~430 nm where PMT quantum efficiency is higher, though R8778 is already optimized for 175 nm (33% QE); more importantly it enables the use of the SiPM upgrade above at visible wavelengths where VUV4 PDE exceeds 50%
- **Replace the stainless steel grid wires** (noted as ~57% reflective at 175 nm in Sec. 6.3) with **electroformed copper wires** with a thin evaporated aluminum/MgF₂ overcoat achieving >85% UV reflectivity, recovering ~3-4% additional light per grid crossing
- Install a **secondary mirror-polished copper reflector ring** around the gas phase electroluminescence region between the gate and anode grids, directing S2 photons emitted sideways preferentially toward the top PMT array, improving S2 position reconstruction accuracy below the current ~1 cm target

---

## 5. Upgraded Xenon Krypton Removal System

### Motivation
Table 3 lists ⁸⁵Kr as contributing up to <0.13 WIMP-like ER events per 30,000 kg-days, estimated from "projected efficiency of the LUX Kr removal system" — indicating this was not yet demonstrated at the time of the paper. Natural krypton at ppb levels in xenon produces a ⁸⁵Kr beta background directly in the energy range of interest.

### Specific Implementation
- **Install a dedicated chromatographic krypton separation column** using Charcoal-CBFA activated charcoal or **13X molecular sieve** operated at 190K inside a cryostat adjacent to the detector, capable of processing the full 370 kg xenon inventory in a single pass and achieving <0.1 ppt Kr/Xe (versus the ~1 ppt ppb natural abundance starting point)
- This approach, subsequently demonstrated by XENON1T to reach 0.36 ppt Kr/Xe, would reduce the ⁸⁵Kr contribution to effectively zero in Table 3
- **Integrate a continuous online krypton assay** using the existing cold-trap mass spectrometer system (Sec. 5) with a dedicated sample line from the weir reservoir, providing real-time monitoring of Kr levels during dark matter running rather than periodic spot checks
- The existing diaphragm pump and getter circulation (50 SLPM, Sec. 5) would route a fraction (~10 SLPM) through the Kr column during normal operation, providing continuous maintenance of xenon purity against Kr outgassing from detector materials

---

## 6. Active Neutron Veto Using Gadolinium-Loaded Water

### Motivation
The muon tagging system (Sec. 8.2) uses only 20 PMTs and is designed for Cherenkov detection of through-going muons. The paper notes muon-induced neutrons remain at ~0.1 events per 30,000 kg-days (Table 4) — subdominant but non-negligible — and the veto has no sensitivity to radiogenic neutrons from internal components that don't produce a muon coincidence.

### Specific Implementation
- **Dissolve 0.1% by mass Gd₂(SO₄)₃ in the water shield**, following the Super-Kamiokande methodology — Gd has a thermal neutron capture cross-section of 49,000 barns, and the resulting 8 MeV gamma cascade is detectable in the water Cherenkov system with high efficiency
- **Increase the water tank PMT count from 20 to ~60 Hamamatsu R7081 units** (the same PMT already used), tripling photocathode coverage from the current ~0.5% to ~1.5%, sufficient to detect the Gd capture gamma cascade with >90% efficiency for neutrons thermalizing anywhere in the water volume
- This upgrade would veto radiogenic neutrons from the PMT arrays and cryostat that currently escape untagged, potentially reducing the NR background in Table 3 by the PMT-originated 0.03 events — a factor of several improvement at the level where NR backgrounds currently sit
- The existing RG-58 cable infrastructure (Sec. 8.2) and breakout box are already sized for additional PMT channels given the custom backplane design described

---

## Priority Ranking by Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Background Reduction | Complexity | Impact on Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|---|
| SiPM array replacement | ~100× on dominant ER source | High | ~3× improvement in spin-independent reach |
| Krypton removal column | Eliminates ⁸⁵Kr ER background | Medium | ~20% improvement in ER background |
| Resistive field cage | Eliminates cosmogenic Cu activation | Medium | Enables longer surface exposure |
| Gd-loaded water veto | Tags radiogenic neutrons | Low-Medium | Factor ~2 on NR background |
| HV system redesign | Reduces spurious S2 rate | Medium | Improved threshold and livetime |
| TPB coating + grid reflectivity | +20-40% light yield | Low | Lower energy threshold, better ER/NR discrimination |

The SiPM replacement represents the most transformative single upgrade, simultaneously addressing the dominant background source, improving fiducial volume, and enabling better position reconstruction — directly improving the primary WIMP sensitivity metric.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for the DarkSide-50 LAr TPC

## Identified Performance Limiters from the Paper

The paper explicitly identifies several hardware constraints limiting physics performance:

- PMT proximity causing poor x-y reconstruction (charge sharing limitation with 3" tubes)
- Scintillation+Cherenkov backgrounds as the **dominant** surviving background
- PMT radioactivity (borosilicate glass stem, ceramic dynodes) as the **dominant** radiogenic neutron source (>90%)
- 39Ar and 85Kr residual activity in UAr
- Limited radial fiducialization effectiveness (~4mm from wall at center)
- S2 resolution limiting multi-scatter rejection (4.65mm vertical merge threshold)

---

## Upgrade 1: Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**The Problem:** The R11065 3" PMTs are simultaneously the dominant radioactive background source and the cause of poor position reconstruction due to their proximity to the S2 emission region.

**Specific Implementation:**
- Deploy cryogenic SiPM tile arrays (e.g., Fondazione Bruno Kessler NUV-HD-cryo tiles, as already being developed for DarkSide-20k) with ~6mm × 6mm individual cells tiled into ~50mm × 50mm modules
- Operate at 87K LAr temperature, which SiPMs tolerate without the breakdown issues requiring the cryogenic preamplifiers currently needed
- Target photon detection efficiency (PDE) of >40% at 420nm (TPB emission peak) vs. ~30% quantum efficiency for R11065 PMTs
- Place tiles on a planar substrate rather than in protruding PMT bodies, allowing the detector geometry to move the photosensor plane farther from the active volume, directly addressing charge-sharing limitations

**Expected Impact:**
- Radioactivity in PMT borosilicate glass stems and ceramic dynode supports eliminated entirely — removes >90% of radiogenic neutron background
- 40K, 232Th, 238U, 60Co backgrounds from PMT Kovar casings and ceramics (Table I activities: 232Th ~0.277 Bq, 40K ~2.74 Bq summed across 38 PMTs) reduced by several orders of magnitude
- Higher granularity (~thousands of channels vs. 38 PMTs) directly improves x-y position reconstruction from S2 light patterns, enabling sharper radial fiducialization
- Elimination of cryogenic preamplifier boards (themselves a radioactivity source) as a secondary benefit
- Improved light yield from higher PDE improves f90 discrimination at low S1 where the WIMP search box lower boundary is currently determined by ER leakage

---

## Upgrade 2: Wavelength-Shifting Fiber or Plate Light Guides with SiPM Readout Placed Outside Active Volume

**The Problem:** The geometry requiring photosensors adjacent to the active volume causes both the radioactivity problem and the x-y reconstruction problem simultaneously.

**Specific Implementation:**
- Line the Teflon barrel reflector with wavelength-shifting (WLS) plates using polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) or polystyrene doped with bis-MSB, which shifts 420nm light to ~490nm with >80% efficiency
- Read out the WLS plates with SiPMs mounted on the outer surface of the Teflon reflector or even outside the cryostat vacuum boundary via fiber bundles
- Use acrylic light guides doped with TPB to capture 128nm VUV directly and shift to longer wavelengths transmissible through the guide to external sensors
- For the endcaps, use PTFE light guide discs coupled to SiPM arrays outside the field cage

**Expected Impact:**
- Photosensors physically separated from active argon reduce fiducial mass loss to radioactive backgrounds
- The Teflon reflector already present becomes an active component rather than passive
- Combined with higher granularity, sub-centimeter x-y reconstruction becomes achievable, enabling RadialFid cuts penetrating much closer to walls (currently limited to ~4-23mm from wall)
- Reduction in Cherenkov background from fused silica PMT windows, which the paper identifies as requiring the S1pMaxFrac cut — removing fused silica windows from proximity to active volume eliminates this background class

---

## Upgrade 3: Redesigned Field Cage with Lower-Radioactivity Electrode Materials

**The Problem:** The current grid-cathode geometry with Teflon side reflector and ITO-coated fused silica windows defines the active volume but introduces several background sources.

**Specific Implementation:**
- Replace ITO-coated fused silica cathode/anode windows with thin metallic mesh electrodes (photo-etched stainless steel or titanium mesh with >95% optical transparency) with assayed radioactivity
- Extend the drift length: increase from current ~376 µs maximum drift (implied by the acquisition window) to longer drift times by using a taller aspect ratio cylinder, improving z-position resolution and top/bottom fiducialization
- Use ultrapure copper (OFHC, electroformed if possible) for all field-shaping rings rather than stainless steel, exploiting copper's lower U/Th content
- Increase the liquid-gas interface gap and grid-to-interface distance from 4.7mm to ~10mm to improve electron extraction uniformity and S2 yield consistency, reducing S2 variability that limits the S2/S1 discrimination

**Expected Impact:**
- Improved extraction field uniformity directly increases S2 yield and reduces position-dependent corrections
- Better S2/S1 resolution enables the MaxS2/S1 cut to work at lower S1 values where it currently provides no benefit — the paper explicitly notes it is "not effective at low S1, where further rejection is most needed"
- Longer drift improves the 4.65mm S2 two-pulse resolution threshold, enabling better multi-scatter rejection
- Copper field rings reduce gamma backgrounds from steel components

---

## Upgrade 4: Enhanced Underground Argon Purification System with Cryogenic Distillation for Kr Removal

**The Problem:** The paper reports 1.9 ± 0.1 mBq/kg of 85Kr as a non-negligible ER background, and residual 39Ar at 0.73 ± 0.11 mBq/kg.

**Specific Implementation:**
- Install a dedicated cryogenic distillation column (similar to that used by XENON/LUX for xenon but designed for argon boiling point 87K) capable of processing the full detector volume recirculation flow
- Target: 85Kr/Ar ratio below 10-14 mol/mol (current best achieved ~10-13), reducing the 85Kr ER rate by factor >10
- For 39Ar: increase the depth and sealed storage time of the UAr source or source argon from deeper geological formations with longer cosmogenic isolation; Urania Argon Mine source selection to minimize exposure to cosmogenic neutrons
- Add a room-temperature gas-phase getter (SAES PS11-MC500 or equivalent) to the recirculation loop rated for argon service to remove electronegative impurities that reduce S2 yield

**Expected Impact:**
- 85Kr reduction by factor 10+ removes it as a relevant ER background, leaving only Compton scatters from detector components
- Improved electron lifetime (from getter) reduces the position-dependent S2 corrections that currently require the 83mKr calibration every few days, improving analysis stability
- Higher S2 yield improves x-y reconstruction directly

---

## Upgrade 5: Veto System Enhancement — Gadolinium-Loaded LSV

**The Problem:** The current borated liquid scintillator achieves 99.64% neutron veto efficiency (Table II), which is excellent but the ~22µs capture lifetime requires a long veto window causing deadtime.

**Specific Implementation:**
- Replace or supplement B-10 loading with gadolinium loading (0.1% by mass Gd, as used in Super-Kamiokande-Gd), exploiting Gd's thermal neutron capture cross section of ~49,000 barns vs. ~3,840 barns for 10B
- Gd capture emits ~8 MeV in gamma cascades (vs. ~2.8 MeV for B-10 channel), providing higher-energy, more easily detected capture signal
- Mean capture time on Gd at 0.1% loading: ~20µs (comparable to current system), but the higher energy cascade gives better detection efficiency per capture
- Alternatively, load with both B and Gd, using the Gd cascade as a high-confidence neutron tag and B as a fast capture channel
- Add an inner neutron moderator layer (10cm polyethylene) between the cryostat and LSV to thermalize neutrons before they reach the active volume, increasing LSV capture probability for higher-energy neutrons from PMT (α,n) sources

**Expected Impact:**
- Radiogenic neutron background, currently <0.005 events (already small), reduced further
- The prompt LSV cut threshold could be lowered by using the distinctive Gd cascade topology, reducing accidental veto rate
- Most importantly for a scaled-up detector, the Gd system scales more favorably than pure B-loading since the higher gamma energy is detectable even with lower scintillator photon yield per unit volume

---

## Priority Ranking by Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Background Addressed | Expected Improvement |
|---------|------------------------------|----------------------|
| SiPM replacement (Upgrade 1) | Radiogenic neutrons + position reconstruction | >10× neutron BG reduction; enables sharper fiducialization |
| UAr purification (Upgrade 4) | ER (85Kr, 39Ar) | Factor 10+ in ER rate |
| Field cage redesign (Upgrade 3) | S2/S1 discrimination at low S1 | Opens new rejection channel at critical low-energy boundary |
| WLS plate geometry (Upgrade 2) | Cherenkov (fused silica) | Eliminates one identified background class entirely |
| Gd-LSV (Upgrade 5) | Radiogenic neutrons | Modest improvement on already-small background |

The SiPM upgrade is the highest priority because it simultaneously attacks the dominant neutron background source, the dominant cause of poor position reconstruction, and the Cherenkov background from PMT windows — three of the paper's explicitly identified performance limitations — with a single hardware change.

# Proposed Hardware Design Upgrades for LHCb

## Diagnosis: Performance-Limiting Factors

Before proposing upgrades, the paper itself identifies the binding constraints:

1. **L0 hardware trigger at 1 MHz readout limit** caps luminosity regardless of other improvements
2. **Aerogel RICH1 radiator degradation** (factor ~1.8 worse Cherenkov resolution than simulation)
3. **OT occupancy reaching ~17-25%** at Run I conditions, degrading pattern recognition
4. **VELO radiation damage** approaching operational limits toward Run II end
5. **Calorimeter PMT aging** requiring frequent recalibration
6. **HLT CPU constraints** forcing algorithmic simplifications that cost 1-2% tracking efficiency per track

---

## Upgrade 1: Full VELO Replacement with Pixel Detector

### Problem Being Solved
The current silicon microstrip VELO has several intrinsic limitations:
- Strip geometry creates ambiguities in high-occupancy environments
- At higher luminosity, the ~0.5-1% cluster occupancy will degrade pattern recognition
- Radiation damage at 1.8×10¹⁴ n_eq/cm² is approaching the safe operating voltage ceiling (~100V effective depletion, limit ~500V)
- The 38 µm minimum pitch already gives ~4 µm best resolution, but analog interpolation becomes unreliable at high occupancy

### Proposed Technology
**55 µm pitch hybrid silicon pixel sensors** (Timepix3/VeloPix-style ASIC) arranged in a retractable RF-foil geometry:

- **Sensor material**: n-on-p planar silicon, 200 µm thick (thinner than current 300 µm to reduce material budget and multiple scattering contribution to IP resolution)
- **Pixel pitch**: 55×55 µm² giving unambiguous 2D hit coordinates, eliminating ghost hits from strip ambiguities
- **ASIC**: Custom VeloPix design with ~800 Mhits/s per chip data-driven readout, no external trigger needed
- **Module geometry**: L-shaped modules allowing closer approach to beam (target 5.1 mm vs current 8.2 mm inner radius)
- **RF foil**: 250 µm thick corrugated aluminum-beryllium alloy separating primary vacuum from detector secondary vacuum, replacing current pure aluminum foil — beryllium content reduces radiation length from ~0.3% to ~0.17% X₀ per foil crossing

### Quantitative Expected Improvement
- IP resolution at high pT: improve from 13 µm to approximately 8-9 µm (extrapolating from material reduction and closer approach)
- Ghost track rate: reduce from ~6.5% to below 2% due to elimination of strip ambiguities
- Radiation hardness: n-on-p technology with p-stop isolation handles >10¹⁶ n_eq/cm² before performance degradation, extending operational life through Run III/IV
- Decay time resolution: improve from ~50 fs toward ~35-40 fs, increasing B⁰_s oscillation dilution factor from ~0.7 toward ~0.85

---

## Upgrade 2: RICH Detector Overhaul — Replace HPDs with Multi-Anode PMTs and Remove Aerogel

### Problem Being Solved
The Hybrid Photon Detectors (HPDs) have multiple issues identified in the paper:
- Photoelectron yields in data are systematically lower than simulation (C₄F₁₀: 20.4 vs 28.3 expected; CF₄: 15.8 vs 22.7)
- Read-out inefficiency at high trigger rates identified as a contributing cause
- Residual magnetic field distortions degrade RICH1 C₄F₁₀ resolution (1.618 mrad measured vs 1.52 mrad expected)
- Aerogel resolution 1.8× worse than simulation due to C₄F₁₀ absorption into porous material
- HPD ion feedback and quantum efficiency degradation over time

### Proposed Technology

**RICH1:**
- **Remove aerogel entirely**: The paper shows aerogel Npe = 5.0±3.0 with large uncertainty, poor resolution, and unmodeled systematic effects. Low-momentum particle identification below ~2 GeV/c can be partially recovered by extending the C₄F₁₀ momentum coverage
- **Replace C₄F₁₀ with C₂F₆**: Higher refractive index (n-1 ≈ 1.5×10⁻³ vs 1.5×10⁻³ at similar pressure but different temperature tuning) allows better optimization for 2-60 GeV/c range; alternatively reduce radiator pressure to tune threshold
- **Photon detectors**: Replace HPDs with **Multi-Anode Photomultiplier Tubes (MaPMTs)**, specifically Hamamatsu H12700 style with 8×8 = 64 pixels per tube, 6×6 mm² pixel size
  - Quantum efficiency: ~35% peak vs ~20-22% for HPDs
  - No ion feedback
  - Magnetic shielding: MaPMTs are far less sensitive to fringe fields than HPDs (which use electron-optic focusing); this directly addresses the identified RICH1 image distortion problem
  - Rate capability: >10 MHz/cm² without efficiency loss
- **Flat photon detector panels**: Remove the current spherical HPD arrangement and use flat MaPMT panels with appropriate optical system adjustment

**RICH2:**
- Keep CF₄ radiator (performing well: measured 0.68 mrad matches simulation)
- Replace HPDs with same MaPMT technology
- Modify mirror tiling to correct for current spherical aberration contributions

### Quantitative Expected Improvement
- C₄F₁₀ Cherenkov angle resolution: from 1.618 mrad to near-simulation value of 1.52 mrad (~6% improvement) primarily from eliminating magnetic field distortion effects on photon detectors
- Photoelectron yields: increase Npe(C₄F₁₀) from 20.4 to approximately 28-30 (approaching simulation) due to higher QE MaPMTs
- Net kaon identification efficiency at ∆logL(K-π)>0: from ~95% with ~10% pion misID, to approximately 95% with ~6-7% pion misID at same threshold, or same misID rate with ~97% efficiency
- Elimination of aerogel systematic uncertainties removes one source of unmodeled background in RICH1

---

## Upgrade 3: Replace Outer Tracker with Scintillating Fibre Tracker

### Problem Being Solved
The straw-tube OT has fundamental occupancy limitations identified in the paper:
- Central modules reach 17% occupancy at standard Run I conditions (50 ns, µ=1.4)
- Rises to 25% at 25 ns bunch spacing
- Maximum drift time of ~35 ns requires reading out 3 bunch crossings, inherently importing hits from adjacent crossings
- 200 µm spatial resolution, while adequate, is the limiting factor for forward tracking momentum resolution at high multiplicity
- Individual straw diameter (4.9 mm) sets a granularity floor

### Proposed Technology
**Scintillating fibre (SciFi) tracker** with silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout:

- **Fibre specification**: 250 µm diameter multiclad scintillating fibres (Saint-Gobain BCF-12 or equivalent), packed in ~2.5 mm thick mats of 5 layers
- **Fibre material**: Polystyrene core, PMMA inner cladding, fluorinated polymer outer cladding; peak emission ~450 nm matching SiPM sensitivity
- **Module construction**: Fibres glued into carbon-fiber frames, 6 detection layers per station replacing current x-u-v-x arrangement with x-u-v-x-u-v for redundancy
- **Photon detectors**: Arrays of **Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)** at fibre ends, 128-channel arrays with 100 µm² microcell pitch
  - Photon detection efficiency: ~40% at 450 nm
  - Dark count rate manageable with cooling to -40°C (reduces dark current by ~factor 10 per 10°C)
  - Compact: entire readout system at detector edge rather than HPD boxes
- **Signal timing**: Fibre+SiPM combination achieves ~1 ns timing resolution, enabling **bunch-crossing discrimination** — hits from adjacent crossings can be rejected at the hit level rather than requiring 75 ns readout windows
- **Spatial resolution**: ~100 µm per layer achievable with charge-sharing between adjacent fibres (factor ~2 improvement over OT)

### Quantitative Expected Improvement
- Occupancy: reduce from ~17% to below 1% at same luminosity conditions due to finer granularity and single-bunch-crossing discrimination
- Spatial resolution: from 205 µm (OT design value) to ~100 µm per layer
- Momentum resolution: improve δp/p from ~8 per mille at 100 GeV/c toward ~5-6 per mille (combined effect of better position resolution and reduced occupancy confusion)
- Elimination of 75 ns readout window removes systematic hit-from-wrong-BX contamination entirely
- No gas system required, eliminating associated infrastructure and safety constraints

---

## Upgrade 4: Full 40 MHz Readout Electronics with Triggerless Architecture

### Problem Being Solved
This is the most impactful single change. The paper states explicitly:
- L0 trigger at 1 MHz caps luminosity regardless of detector improvements
- L0 hardware trigger causes **53% efficiency loss for B⁰→K⁺π⁻** before HLT even runs
- Calorimeter-based L0 triggers are particularly inefficient for purely hadronic final states
- The 4 Tm dipole, calorimeters, and muon stations are all needed for L0, but this forces suboptimal decisions at hardware level

### Proposed Architecture

**Remove L0 entirely; implement full 40 MHz readout:**

- **Front-end electronics redesign**: All subdetectors require new ASICs capable of continuous data output at 40 MHz bunch crossing rate rather than triggered readout
  - VELO (pixel): VeloPix ASIC already designed for data-driven operation
  - SciFi tracker: custom PACIFIC ASIC (PR-based readout at 40 MHz with 2-bit dynamic range)
  - Calorimeters: replace current 12-bit 40 MHz ADCs with pipeline-buffered versions that hold data pending software trigger decision
  - Muon system: redesign readout to handle continuous data stream

- **Data throughput**: Total raw data rate at 40 MHz: approximately 40 Tbit/s from all detectors, requiring:
  - **Optical readout links**: 10 Gbit/s per fibre, approximately 4000 fibres total
  - **Readout boards**: custom PCIe-based DAQ cards in standard servers
  - **Event building network**: 100 GbE switching fabric

- **Software High Level Trigger on GPU farm**:
  - Replace current CPU-only EFF with hybrid CPU+GPU farm
  - GPU algorithms for: VELO pattern recognition (parallelizable over hit collections), Kalman track fitting (parallelizable over track collections), primary vertex finding
  - Target: full event reconstruction equivalent to current offline quality within trigger
  - **Specific GPU implementations**: Allen framework concept — execute full track reconstruction in ~10 ms per event on GPU vs ~50× slower CPU equivalent
  - GPU hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 class (available by 2014 planning horizon) with 5120 CUDA cores, ~14 TFLOPS FP32 per card
  - Farm size: ~500 GPU cards + supporting CPU infrastructure

### Quantitative Expected Improvement
- B⁰→K⁺π⁻ total trigger efficiency: from current 53%×97%×80% = **41%** to approximately **80-85%** (removing L0 calorimeter inefficiency entirely)
- D⁰→K⁻π⁺ trigger efficiency: from 44%×89%×90% = **35%** to approximately **70%**
- For B⁰_s→µ⁺µ⁻: efficiency maintained near 89% L0 × 92% × 87% = **71%** improves to ~**90%**
- Effective luminosity increase: luminosity can be raised from 4×10³² to potentially 2×10³³ cm⁻²s⁻¹ with acceptable pile-up if fast enough reconstruction is available; combined with efficiency gains this represents an effective data collection rate increase of factor ~4-5

---

## Upgrade 5: Calorimeter System — Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers

### Problem Being Solved
The paper documents progressive PMT gain degradation requiring frequent recalibration:
- Dynode degradation at high integrated anode current
- HCAL calibration limited to bi-monthly technical stops (Cs-137 source procedure)
- ECAL cell-to-cell intercalibration only ~2% precision even after π⁰ fitting

### Proposed Technology

**Replace all PMTs with SiPMs in ECAL and HCAL:**

- **SiPM specification for ECAL**: Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent, 3×3 mm² active area, 50 µm microcell pitch, ~4×10⁴ microcells
  - Photon detection efficiency: 40% at 450 nm (comparable to good PMTs but stable over time)
  - Gain: ~10⁶, no high-voltage distribution network required
  - No aging under high photon flux (unlike dynode systems)
  - Magnetic field immunity: operate in full dipole fringe field without shielding
  - Temperature coefficient: ~2%/°C requiring ±0.1°C thermal stabilization, achievable with Peltier cooling per module

- **SiPM specification for HCAL**: Larger active area SiPMs (6×6 mm²) with higher microcell count to handle larger dynamic range of hadronic showers

- **Readout electronics**: Remove current 12-bit ADC system, replace with direct SiPM current readout with trans-impedance amplifiers and 14-bit 40 MHz ADCs (matching the new triggerless architecture)

- **Calibration**: With SiPMs, continuous gain monitoring is possible via single-photon spectrum measurement; replace current Cs-137 source with LED-based fast calibration runnable at any time

### Quantitative Expected Improvement
- Eliminate progressive gain degradation entirely: current ~10-15% rate fluctuation visible in Figure 29 disappears
- Intercalibration precision: improve from ~2% (ECAL) and ~5% (HCAL) to ~1% and ~2% respectively through more frequent and precise calibration cycles
- ECAL energy resolution: improvement of ~10-15% through better uniformity translates to B⁰→K*⁰γ mass resolution improving from 93 MeV/c² toward ~80 MeV/c²
- No maintenance downtime required for Cs-137 source procedures

---

## Upgrade 6: Muon System — Replace M1 GEM Detectors, Upgrade Inner Regions with Micro-Pattern Gas Detectors

### Problem Being Solved
- M1R1 dead-time reaches 2.5% at twice nominal luminosity due to front-end chip saturation
- M2R1 reaches 0.6% dead-time
- If L0 trigger is removed (Upgrade 4), M1 station (currently used only for L0 pT measurement) becomes redundant and can be removed, reducing material upstream of calorimeters

### Proposed Technology

**If L0 removed**: Eliminate M1 entirely, reducing material budget upstream of ECAL (currently M1 contributes ~0.3 X₀ before calorimeter shower measurement)

**For M2-M5 inner regions (R1, R2)**:
- Replace MWPCs in highest-rate regions with **Micro-Pattern Gas Detectors (MPGDs)**, specifically **MicroMegas** or **GEM** detectors with 400 µm pitch 2D readout strips

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Dual-Phase Xenon TPC (~250 kg Active Mass)

## Framing the Problem

For a detector at this scale (comparable to LUX or early XENON1T), the dominant physics performance limitations fall into several coupled categories: photon detection efficiency, electron lifetime, position reconstruction fidelity, background discrimination, and low-energy threshold. I address each with specific hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Photon Detection System

### Replace Conventional PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) on the Bottom Array

**Specific technology:** Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) RGB-HD 6×6 mm² SiPM tiles, or Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPC arrays (S13371 series), operated at ~170 nm VUV sensitivity.

**Why this matters most:**
The bottom array dominates S1 light collection because most scintillation photons travel downward toward higher solid-angle coverage. PMTs like the R11410-23 achieve ~35% QE at 175 nm; cryogenic SiPMs can reach **50–60% photon detection efficiency (PDE)** at LXe temperatures where dark current drops dramatically.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Tile the entire bottom face (roughly 50–60 cm diameter for 250 kg) with closely packed 6×6 mm² SiPM modules in a hexagonal arrangement
- Use a 4-layer PCB backplane with integrated transimpedance amplifiers (e.g., BF862 JFET front-ends) thermalized to ~170 K
- Group tiles into ~24 channels to balance readout complexity against position reconstruction granularity
- Total improvement: ~1.5–1.8× gain in S1 photon yield, directly lowering threshold from ~2 keVnr to potentially sub-keVnr

**Critical engineering challenge:** SiPM dark count rate at 170 K is negligible (<0.1 Hz/mm²), but correlated afterpulsing in photon-correlated backgrounds requires careful characterization of the cross-talk probability, which should be <3% for these devices.

### Retain R11410-23 PMTs on Top Array but Add Anti-Reflective VUV Coating

The top array primarily provides S2 position reconstruction (the xy plane) via the light pattern. Replacing top PMTs with SiPMs offers less marginal gain relative to cost and complexity.

**Specific upgrade:** Apply MgF₂ or Al₂O₃ anti-reflective coatings (quarter-wave at 175 nm, ~44 nm thickness) to PMT windows via atomic layer deposition (ALD). This recovers ~8–12% absolute efficiency lost to Fresnel reflection at the fused silica–LXe interface.

---

## 2. Reflector and Light Collection Geometry

### Replace PTFE Reflector Panels with Specular ESR Film + Diffuse PTFE Hybrid

**Current state of practice:** Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) is used universally as a diffuse VUV reflector (~95–97% reflectance at 175 nm) but multiple reflections in a tall TPC accumulate losses.

**Proposed upgrade:** Line the inner barrel with **3M Enhanced Specular Reflector (ESR) film** laminated onto PTFE backing. ESR achieves >98.5% reflectance in the visible but requires a VUV-compatible fluorescent coating—specifically a thin (few hundred nm) **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) layer** deposited via vacuum evaporation at 0.1 nm/s.

**Geometry optimization:**
- Specular sidewalls redirect photons toward detector ends more efficiently in tall-aspect-ratio geometries (height/diameter ~2 for 250 kg), reducing mean path length by ~15–20%
- Geant4/NEST simulations for similar geometries (cf. LUX TDR) indicate this recovers 10–15% additional S1 photons

**TPB coating protocol:** Evaporate onto PTFE panels before assembly at 3×10⁻⁶ Torr, target areal density 0.2 mg/cm²—thick enough for full VUV absorption, thin enough to avoid cracking under thermal cycling.

---

## 3. Electron Lifetime and Purity System

### Upgrade to Heated Zirconium Getter + Dedicated Recirculation Loop

**Current bottleneck:** Electron lifetime >5 ms is required for full drift (e.g., ~60 cm drift at 500 V/cm). Achieving this demands electronegative impurity concentrations below ~0.1 ppb O₂-equivalent.

**Specific hardware:**
- **SAES MonoTorr PS4-MT15** heated zirconium getter (or equivalent SAES PS950) operating at 400°C, flow rate 15–20 SLPM LXe equivalent
- Add a **dedicated liquid-phase recirculation pump** (Barber-Nichols cryogenic gear pump or magnetically coupled variant) creating a separate slow loop (~1–2 SLPM) that passes liquid xenon over a **cold trap** at 163 K before the getter—this removes water and heavy organics that outgas slowly from detector components and survive hot getter operation
- Install **electron lifetime monitor (ELM) tubes**: two small auxiliary drift tubes (5 cm drift, 83mKr or UV photocathode source) positioned in the xenon gas return line to provide continuous online monitoring at 1-minute cadence

**Expected improvement:** Demonstrated electron lifetime >10 ms routinely, extending fiducial volume to full drift length and improving position reconstruction at depth.

### Low-Outgassing Material Substitution

- Replace all internal O-ring seals with **metal C-seals (Helicoflex)** or **indium wire seals** to eliminate elastomer outgassing
- Substitute any internal cable insulation with **radiation-hard FEP/PTFE** rather than PVC or silicone
- Bake all internal copper and stainless components at 200°C under 10⁻⁷ Torr vacuum for 48 hours before assembly

---

## 4. Field Cage and Electrode System

### Replace Wire Meshes with Etched Photochemical Mesh Electrodes

**Problem with current wire electrode grids:** Conventionally wound wire grids (cathode, gate, anode) suffer from wire sag at cryogenic temperatures, electrostatic instability, and optical obscuration of the bottom PMT array.

**Specific upgrade:** Use **photochemically etched stainless steel mesh** (e.g., 304 SS, 100 µm wire diameter, 1 mm pitch hexagonal pattern) with electropolished surfaces:
- **Transmission:** ~82% optical transparency vs. ~70–75% for typical wound wire grids—directly translates to more S1 light reaching bottom array
- **Planarity:** Photochemical etching (acid bath through photoresist mask) produces flat panels accurate to ±25 µm, eliminating the main source of position-dependent electric field non-uniformity
- **Cathode:** Single circular mesh ring mounted in a tensioned annular support frame with Macor standoffs; apply 400–600 V/cm nominal drift field

### Resistive Divider Chain Upgrade

Replace discrete resistor chains with **thick-film resistor networks on ceramic substrates** (e.g., alumina tiles, 1 MΩ resistors, Vishay VCS series):
- Operating at 170 K maintains <0.01% field uniformity over the drift volume
- Distributed capacitance reduces field ring response time, important for pulse shape discrimination

### Electroluminescence Gap Precision

The S2 signal magnitude and position resolution depend critically on the extraction field (typically 10 kV/cm) and the gas gap (typically 2–5 mm). 

**Hardware fix:** Mount the gate and anode electrodes on a **piezo-adjustable support frame** (PICMA P-882 actuators in cryo-compatible configuration), allowing ±0.5 mm adjustment of the gas gap *in situ* after cooldown to compensate for thermal contraction—eliminates the current practice of shimming during room-temperature assembly.

---

## 5. Position Reconstruction Enhancement

### Increase Top Array Granularity

For a 250 kg detector (~60 cm diameter), the standard configuration uses ~30–50 3-inch PMTs on top. 

**Proposed upgrade:** Replace with a **mixed-pitch array**:
- Central region (r < 20 cm): 37× **1-inch Hamamatsu R8520** or equivalent low-profile PMTs at tighter pitch
- Outer region: retain 3-inch R11410s

This improves S2 position resolution from ~3–5 mm to **<2 mm σ** in the central fiducial volume by providing finer sampling of the S2 light cone (which has ~5 mm 1/e spread at the top surface for a 10 mm gas gap).

**Readout electronics:** Pair with **CAEN V1730** 500 MHz 14-bit digitizers (or the newer V2740 with 250 MHz 16-bit ADC), providing waveform capture with sufficient dynamic range for both single-photon S1 and high-S2 saturation avoidance.

---

## 6. Veto and Shielding System Upgrades

### Gadolinium-Loaded Water Cherenkov Outer Veto

**Specific implementation:** Dissolve **Gd₂(SO₄)₃ at 0.1% by mass** in the outer water shield (replacing pure water). This is the approach now standard in Super-Kamiokande-Gd and adopted by LZ.

- Gadolinium has a thermal neutron capture cross-section of 49,000 barns—captures neutrons within ~30 µs and emits an 8 MeV gamma cascade
- Photons detected in the water Cherenkov array (existing 8-inch PMTs on water tank walls) form a coincident signal with any nuclear recoil in the TPC
- Expected neutron single-scatter background reduction: **~90%** for neutrons above ~100 keV

**Complication to manage:** Gd sulfate is corrosive to some stainless alloys; water tank must use 316L SS or be lined with HDPE panels. pH must be maintained at 7.0–7.5 via continuous monitoring.

### Inner Liquid Xenon Skin Veto

For a 250 kg class detector, there is typically 20–40 kg of xenon between the TPC field cage and the cryostat wall ("skin" region). 

**Upgrade:** Instrument this skin region with **3-inch Hamamatsu R11065** low-background PMTs (6–8 units distributed around the cylindrical wall) operated as an anti-coincidence veto. Surface events that deposit energy in both the skin and the fiducial volume can be rejected with high efficiency, reducing the dominant ER background source (radon daughters plating on PTFE).

---

## 7. Low-Background PMT and Cable System

### Reduced-Radioactivity Cable Plant

PMT signal cables are a significant source of U/Th background in the inner detector.

**Specific hardware:** Replace conventional coaxial cable with **Axon' Cable cryogenic micro-coax** (0.5 mm OD, PTFE dielectric, silver-plated copper conductor) screened for U/Th at <5 ppb by ICP-MS. Route cables through a field-free region external to the TPC.

**Further improvement:** Implement **multiplexed readout** using cold front-end ASICs (e.g., adapted version of ATLAS FELIX or custom 8-channel charge-sensitive preamplifier ASIC in 130 nm CMOS, radiation-tested). Reducing cable count from 1-per-PMT to 1-per-8-PMTs cuts the cable mass inside the fiducial volume by ~85%.

---

## 8. Calibration System Hardware

### In Situ Tritiated Methane Source + Dedicated Injection Port

**Specific implementation:** A 10 Bq sealed ampoule of **tritiated methane (CH₃T)** connected via a dedicated micro-capillary (50 µm ID, 316L SS) to the xenon gas system. Tritium beta decay produces a flat spectrum to 18.6 keV—ideal for calibrating the ER/NR discrimination band and the low-energy response function.

- Injection line uses a **piezoelectric microvalve** (Lee Company INKA) for <1 nL/pulse injection precision
- Flushed out within 24 hours via normal recirculation through the getter

### Monochromatic 83mKr Calibration Line

**Hardware addition:** An **⁸³Rb getter source** (⁸³Rb adsorbed on zeolite, activity ~10 kBq) mounted in a bypass line with dedicated valve. ⁸³mKr emits 41.5 keV + 9.4 keV internal conversion electrons—providing a spatially uniform two-line calibration source for field uniformity mapping and S1/S2 calibration simultaneously. Standard in the field but should be on a dedicated recirculation loop isolated from the main purification circuit to allow rapid injection and removal.

---

## Prioritization Matrix

| Upgrade | Cost/Complexity | Physics Gain | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bottom array → SiPMs | High | Very High (threshold, S1 yield) | **1** |
| Gd-loaded water veto | Medium | High (neutron BG) | **2** |
| Etched mesh electrodes | Low-Medium | High (field uniformity, light) | **3** |
| Upgraded getter + liquid loop | Medium | High (electron lifetime) | **4** |
| Skin veto instrumentation | Low | Medium-High (surface BG) | **5** |
| Top array granularity | Medium | Medium (xy resolution) | **6** |
| Low-BG cable plant | Medium | Medium (radioactive BG) | **7** |
| In-gap piezo adjustment | Low | Medium (S2 uniformity) | **8** |

---

## Summary of Expected Composite Performance Gains

With all upgrades implemented on a 250 kg baseline instrument, the realistic physics improvements relative to a standard PMT-based design are:

- **Nuclear recoil detection threshold:** 2 keVnr → ~0.8 keVnr (SiPM + reflector gains)
- **Electron lifetime:** 3–5 ms → >10 ms (purity system)
- **ER/NR discrimination at 10 keVnr:** 99.5% → 99.8% (field uniformity + S1 yield)
- **Neutron single-scatter background:** Reduced by ~90% (Gd veto)
- **Surface ER background:** Reduced by factor ~3–5 (skin veto)
- **xy position resolution:** 5 mm → <2 mm (granular top array)

These compound into a projected **3–5× improvement in overall spin-independent WIMP-nucleon cross-section sensitivity** relative to the baseline 250 kg design, depending on exposure and dominant background regime.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for IceCube: Concrete Proposals

## Framing the Problem

The primary physics performance limitations identifiable from the paper are:

1. **Angular resolution** bounded by timing precision (~1.2 ns demonstrated) and DOM spacing
2. **Energy threshold** limited by PMT efficiency, noise, and string spacing
3. **Dark noise** at 560–780 Hz per DOM dominates isolated hits
4. **Hole ice** creates an uncontrolled scattering column around each DOM
5. **Waveform digitization** deadtime and dynamic range constraints
6. **DOM optical acceptance** is hemispherical and downward-facing only

---

## Upgrade 1: Replace Single-PMT DOM with Multi-PMT Module

### Problem
The current 10″ Hamamatsu R7081-02 faces downward, covering roughly 2π steradians. The paper notes cable shadowing and hole ice effects that are partially uncharacterized. Angular coverage is fundamentally asymmetric. The mu-metal cage blocks ~4% of incident light and only partially suppresses the ~550 mG South Pole field effect.

### Proposed Solution
Replace the single large-hemispherical PMT with **multiple smaller PMTs** distributed over the full sphere.

**Specific implementation:**
- Use **24–36 Hamamatsu R12199-02 3″ PMTs** (or equivalent) arranged in a soccer-ball-like geometry covering the full 4π steradians
- Each 3″ PMT has ~33% quantum efficiency at peak (similar to HQE type) and much lower dark noise per tube (~100–200 Hz thermally) due to smaller photocathode area
- Total photocathode area: 24 × π(3.8 cm)² ≈ 1,090 cm², compared to the current π(12.7 cm)² ≈ 507 cm² for the downward-facing hemisphere — roughly **2× increase in effective photocathode area with full angular coverage**
- Individual PMT solid angles of ~π sr mean that coincidence between adjacent PMTs provides **immediate hardware-level direction sensing per DOM**
- At the South Pole field of 550 mG, smaller 3″ tubes require no mu-metal shielding: field effects on collection efficiency for small-diameter tubes are below 1% without shielding

**Technical rationale:** The directionality information from multi-PMT coincidences within a single DOM provides a first-order photon direction estimate before inter-DOM reconstruction, directly improving vertex resolution for contained events. The reduction of per-channel dark noise from ~560 Hz total to ~100–200 Hz per small tube, with coincidence requirements between adjacent tubes, suppresses noise triggers dramatically.

**Precedent within the paper's context:** The paper notes that KM3NeT is under development — KM3NeT's DOM uses exactly this multi-PMT approach with 31 3″ PMTs, validating the technology.

---

## Upgrade 2: Waveform Digitization — Replace ATWD with Switched Capacitor Array at Higher Speed and Depth

### Problem
The paper describes the ATWD as sampling at **300 Msps with 128 sample depth**, giving a **427 ns recording window**. The fADC covers the long tail at only 40 Msps. Key limitations:
- Deadtime: after two back-to-back HLC launches, deadtime is ~32 µs per the timing diagram
- Dynamic range requires three gain channels (×16, ×2, ×0.25) with associated complexity
- The 427 ns ATWD window is insufficient for photons from DOMs more than ~30 m away before scattering extends arrival times
- Two ATWD chips per DOM (alternating) still produce measurable deadtime at ~6.6×10⁻⁵ fractional rate

### Proposed Solution
Replace the ATWD+fADC combination with a **single-chip 14-bit switched capacitor array sampling at 1–2 Gsps with 1024 sample depth**.

**Specific implementation:**
- Use the **DRS4 chip** (Paul Scherrer Institut) or equivalent: 1024 capacitor cells, 0.7–5 Gsps tunable, 11.5-bit effective resolution, designed for physics detector applications
- At 1 Gsps: 1024 ns recording window — more than doubling the ATWD window, capturing scattered photon tails from distances up to ~80 m
- At 14-bit effective resolution with proper input ranging, **eliminate the three-gain amplifier chain** in favor of a single amplifier stage covering the full 1 mV–2 V dynamic range, reducing component count and a major systematic uncertainty
- Run **two DRS4 chips alternating** as currently done with ATWDs: rearm time for DRS4 is ~100 ns, reducing deadtime by a factor of ~300 compared to the 29 µs ATWD digitization time
- The DRS4 draws ~100 mW per chip vs. the ATWD's analog storage requirements; total power impact is modest

**Technical rationale:** The paper explicitly identifies that the ATWD recording duration being "sufficient for reconstructing light produced within tens of meters" is a limitation — distant signals require the lower-resolution fADC. Eliminating this dichotomy with a single high-resolution, longer-window digitizer removes a systematic calibration uncertainty (the ATWD/fADC time offset calibration described in section 3.2) and improves reconstruction of mid-range (30–100 m) photon arrivals where the current system transitions between digitizers.

**Quantified improvement:** Deadtime reduction from ~32 µs to ~200 ns for back-to-back HLC hits reduces the fractional deadtime for high-gain IceTop DOMs from 3.2×10⁻³ to below 10⁻⁵, and eliminates the primary high-rate performance limit.

---

## Upgrade 3: SiPM-Based Calibration and Low-Threshold Detection Module

### Problem
The paper reports dark noise of **560 Hz total** for standard DOMs, dominated by glass sphere scintillation (~40K decay products and luminescence). The SPE discriminator threshold is set at 0.25 PE to suppress this noise, meaning photons depositing less charge than this are lost. For low-energy physics (GeV-scale neutrinos in DeepCore, supernova MeV neutrinos), single-photon efficiency at threshold is critical.

### Proposed Solution
For DeepCore/PINGU-region strings: deploy **Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays** as secondary sensors within the existing DOM or in a supplementary module.

**Specific implementation:**
- Hamamatsu **S13361-3050** SiPM tiles (3×3 mm cells, 50 µm pixel pitch, ~40% photon detection efficiency at 450 nm, ~70 kcps dark count rate at −20°C per mm²)
- At in-ice temperatures of −31°C to −9°C, SiPM dark count rate drops by factor ~10× compared to room temperature — approximately **7,000 cps/mm² dark rate**
- An array of 25 mm² total area (nine 3×3 mm tiles) gives ~175 kcps dark rate per array — comparable to the *correlated noise component alone* in the current PMT
- Crucially, SiPM dark counts are **Poissonian and uncorrelated between pixels**, unlike the glass-sphere-induced correlated noise bursts the paper identifies as the dominant problematic noise component
- No high-voltage supply required (SiPMs operate at 25–70 V), eliminating the 300 mW HV generator and simplifying the power budget
- Place SiPM arrays in a separate pressure module of ~5 cm diameter mountable on the existing cable harness, with dedicated readout through spare quad cable pairs

**Technical rationale:** The paper identifies correlated noise (280–340 Hz) from glass luminescence as a fundamental background for supernova detection and low-energy analyses. SiPMs have no glass envelope generating this noise. Their smaller photocathode area means any residual radioactive background produces far fewer coincident hits. The uncorrelated nature of SiPM noise makes it straightforwardly subtractable in the supernova scalar stream.

**Quantified improvement:** Reducing correlated noise from ~300 Hz to ~5 Hz (from a 25 mm² SiPM array) would improve the SNDAQ significance threshold, potentially extending Galactic supernova sensitivity distance by a factor computable from the √(background rate) scaling.

---

## Upgrade 4: In-Situ Hole Ice Optical Characterization and Correction

### Problem
The paper notes that the refrozen hole ice has "a central core of about 16 cm diameter with much smaller scattering length than bulk ice," and that "optical properties of this hole ice are still under active investigation." The systematic uncertainty from hole ice is included as a 10% normalization uncertainty on DOM efficiency — a dominant systematic for many analyses.

### Proposed Solution
Deploy a **dedicated in-hole optical tomography module** between every 4th–5th DOM pair during string deployment.

**Specific implementation:**
- A small pressure cylinder (~5 cm diameter × 20 cm length) containing:
  - One **405 nm picosecond pulsed laser** (PicoQuant LDH-P-C-405B, pulse width < 100 ps, peak power 300 mW) with a fiber-coupled diffuser for isotropic emission
  - One **single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) array** (e.g., SensL MicroFC-30035 with timing resolution < 200 ps FWHM) with a narrow-angle acceptance cone pointing radially outward
  - A **MEMS micro-mirror** (Texas Instruments DLP2000) to scan the SPAD acceptance angle azimuthally through 360° in the horizontal plane
- The module emits calibrated picosecond pulses and records the time-of-flight of backscattered photons as a function of azimuthal angle
- By measuring the photon arrival time distribution vs. angle, the scattering length profile across the hole ice column can be reconstructed with ~1 cm radial resolution

**Technical rationale:** Current hole ice characterization relies on the camera deployed on String 80 (one string, qualitative imaging) and on statistical inference from flasher data. The paper explicitly states the hole ice properties are under investigation. A per-string tomographic measurement would replace the current single 10% normalization nuisance parameter with a **string-by-string, depth-dependent scattering profile** that can be propagated into photon transport simulations. This is likely the single largest reducible systematic uncertainty in current energy reconstruction.

---

## Upgrade 5: GPS-Disciplined Oscillator with Sub-100 ps RAPCal Precision

### Problem
The paper reports RAPCal timing precision of **~1.2 ns** (from the flasher validation, 1.7 ns width divided by √2). The cable delay distribution has 0.6 ns standard deviation per measurement, and individual outliers >10 ns are discarded. The 20 MHz communications ADC limits interpolation precision.

### Proposed Solution
Upgrade the DOR card timing system with a **higher-frequency sampling ADC and a temperature-compensated crystal oscillator (TCXO) with GPS-disciplined phase-lock**.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the 20 MHz communications ADC in the DOR card with a **200 MHz, 12-bit ADC** (e.g., AD9434, Analog Devices — 12-bit, 370 Msps, available in full 200 Msps mode, 1.1 W power draw)
- The finer time sampling reduces the interpolation uncertainty in the RAPCal fine-delay correction from ~50 ns/sample (at 20 MHz) to ~5 ns/sample, with interpolation achieving **sub-100 ps precision** on the zero-crossing determination
- Upgrade the DOR card oscillator from the current 20 MHz to a **100 MHz Vectron TCXO** (e.g., Vectron C2663A, stability 5×10⁻¹² at 5s, compatible with GPS phase-lock), improving the clock stability over the current 1×10⁻¹¹ figure by a factor of ~2 at relevant timescales
- Maintain RAPCal every second per DOM (unchanged), but the improved ADC sampling reduces the per-measurement uncertainty from 0.6 ns σ to an estimated 0.15 ns σ based on the interpolation improvement ratio

**Technical rationale:** The paper's equation 3.7 shows that the UTC conversion uses linear interpolation between RAPCal measurements. The dominant uncertainty in each RAPCal measurement is the fine-delay interpolation. Improving this from ~0.6 ns to ~0.15 ns per measurement improves the inter-DOM timing calibration precision from 1.2 ns to approximately 0.3 ns — directly improving muon track angular resolution, which scales as δθ ∝ δt/L where L is lever arm distance.

**Quantified improvement:** Current angular resolution is 0.6° for muon tracks. Timing is not the only limitation (ice scattering also contributes), but for bright, high-energy tracks, a 4× timing improvement could reduce the timing-limited component of angular error by a similar factor, improving source localization for point source searches.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Primary Limitation Addressed | Key Technology | Expected Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multi-PMT DOM | Angular coverage, noise | 3″ Hamamatsu PMT array (24–36 units) | 2× photocathode area, full 4π coverage, per-DOM directional info |
| DRS4 digitizer | Deadtime, recording window, dynamic range | DRS4 switched capacitor @ 1 Gsps, 14-bit | 100× deadtime reduction, 2.4× longer window, eliminate gain-chain systematics |
| SiPM calibration module | Correlated dark noise in low-E analyses | Hamamatsu S13361 SiPM array | ~60× reduction in correlated noise background |
| Hole ice tomography | Dominant optical systematic | Picosecond laser + SPAD + MEMS mirror | Replace 10% normalization uncertainty with per-string profile |
| High-speed RAPCal ADC | Inter-DOM timing precision | AD9434 200 MHz ADC + 100 MHz TCXO | 0.6 ns → 0.15 ns per-measurement timing σ |

The highest-priority single upgrade is the **multi-PMT module**, as it simultaneously improves photon collection efficiency, angular coverage, and per-DOM noise rejection — all of which feed directly into the primary physics figures of merit for both high-energy neutrino astronomy and low-energy oscillation physics.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for EXO-200

## Framing the Problem

The primary physics goal is maximizing sensitivity to 0νββ decay, which requires improvements in three coupled areas: **energy resolution**, **background rejection**, and **fiducial mass efficiency**. The paper explicitly identifies the binding constraints.

---

## 1. Photodetector Replacement: LAAPDs → Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

### Current Limitation
The 468 LAAPDs operate at 48% packing fraction with individual capacitances of 125 pF per device. Gangs of 5–7 devices yield ~1000 pF input capacitance per channel, driving electronic noise to 2 e⁻/pF. The scintillation threshold is explicitly noise-limited. The devices require −1400 V bias and exhibit substantial spread in gain × quantum efficiency (requiring per-sector trim voltages to achieve σ = 2.5% uniformity).

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace LAAPDs with **cryogenic-qualified SiPMs** (e.g., Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPC series or FBK VUV-HD devices, which were entering development by 2012).

**Specific implementation:**
- SiPMs with 6 mm × 6 mm active area tiles tessellated to >70% geometric coverage (versus 48% current)
- Operating bias ~25–35 V with Geiger-mode gain of ~10⁶ (versus LAAPD gain of ~50–200 at LXe temperature)
- Device capacitance ~320 pF per 6×6 mm tile versus 125 pF per LAAPD die, but the dramatically higher gain means the preamplifier noise contribution to the energy measurement becomes negligible
- Individual channel readout rather than ganged readout, eliminating the gain-uniformity problem entirely
- No trim voltage network required, reducing passive component mass near the fiducial volume

**Expected benefit:** The paper states the scintillation channel is the limiting factor for energy resolution. Higher photon detection efficiency (PDE ~20–25% at 178 nm for VUV-sensitive SiPMs versus ~15% effective for the LAAPD system including packing losses) directly improves the anti-correlation measurement used for energy reconstruction. The combined ionization+scintillation energy resolution could improve from σ/E = 1.6% toward ~1.0% at Qββ, which reduces the 0νββ analysis window and therefore the background count by ~35%.

**Radioactivity concern:** SiPM substrates must be screened; silicon bulk is intrinsically low in U/Th. The elimination of the phosphor bronze spider spring contact network (which contributes to the bronze wire activity budget in Table 3) partially offsets any SiPM substrate activity.

---

## 2. Wire Plane Redesign: Elimination of Ganged Readout and Improved Position Resolution

### Current Limitation
Wire triplets with 9 mm readout pitch (three 3 mm wires per channel) were adopted to reduce channel count and material. The paper acknowledges this is larger than field-optimization requires. The photoetching process introduces surface contamination requiring aggressive HNO₃ cleaning with 15% mass loss. The square wire cross-section (127 ± 40 µm) with ±40 µm tolerance degrades field uniformity.

### Proposed Upgrade

**Individual wire readout at 3 mm pitch** using **gold-plated tungsten wire** (25–50 µm diameter):

- Tungsten wire is commercially available at 25 µm diameter with <1% diameter tolerance, yielding far superior and more predictable electric field performance than photoetched phosphor bronze
- Gold surface coating provides good electrical contact without platinum plating complexity and eliminates the 40K contamination concern from gold plating solutions (the paper specifically notes this as a reason for choosing platinum)
- Wire tension can be set mechanically with higher reproducibility; thermal expansion coefficient of tungsten (4.5 µm/m·K) is much lower than phosphor bronze (17.8 µm/m·K), drastically reducing the thermal cycling tension variation problem described in Section 3.2.1
- At 3 mm readout pitch, single-site versus multi-site discrimination improves because the position resolution of individual energy depositions narrows from ~9 mm to ~3 mm, directly improving the topological background rejection that is central to the 0νββ analysis

**Wire support frame redesign:**
- Replace acrylic support beams with **PTFE or ultra-pure quartz** to eliminate the large CTE mismatch (acrylic CTE = 73.6 µm/m·K versus copper 16.9 µm/m·K) that currently forces a complex tension analysis
- PTFE CTE (~100 µm/m·K) is larger but the spring mechanism in the wire mounting can be redesigned to accommodate this predictably; alternatively quartz (0.5 µm/m·K) nearly eliminates differential thermal stress entirely

**Channel count impact:** Moving from 38 to 114 readout channels per wire plane per end requires 304 total wire channels versus the current ~152. This is manageable with the discrete preamplifier architecture described and improves 3D event reconstruction fidelity substantially.

---

## 3. Front-End Electronics: In-Situ Cold Preamplifiers

### Current Limitation
The paper explicitly states the choice of warm electronics "trades some increased noise for the simplicity and accessibility of room temperature, conventional construction electronics." The polyimide cables carrying signals ~1 m from detector to FEE contribute 60–80 pF of capacitance per wire channel, which is the dominant noise source. The LAAPD channels see ~1000 pF total.

### Proposed Upgrade
Deploy **cold JFET preamplifiers** at the first stage of signal processing, mounted on the LAAPD platter or wire plane support ring, inside the HFE-7000 volume but outside the LXe vessel.

**Specific implementation:**
- Use **Interfet NJ132L or equivalent low-noise JFET** qualified for operation at 170–200 K (JFETs generally improve in noise performance at cryogenic temperatures due to reduced thermal carrier noise)
- Mount preamplifier boards on the outer surface of the copper TPC legs, inside the cryostat but in the HFE-7000 bath, where they are accessible for replacement without opening the LXe vessel
- This location reduces the effective input capacitance seen by the JFET to the wire or LAAPD capacitance alone (~30–125 pF) versus the current 60–80 pF cable capacitance added in series
- Power dissipation per channel must be budgeted against the cryogenic cooling capacity; at ~1 mW per channel for 300 channels, the 300 mW additional heat load is manageable within a well-designed cryogenic system

**Expected benefit:** For wire channels, reducing input capacitance from ~70 pF (cable-dominated) to ~30 pF (wire capacitance alone) reduces the electronic noise contribution by approximately a factor of 2.3, directly improving the ionization channel energy resolution.

---

## 4. High Voltage System Redesign to Achieve Design Drift Field

### Current Limitation
The HV system is limited to 8 kV operation (versus the 75 kV design goal) due to corona discharge instabilities described in Section 3.2.4. This corresponds to a drift field of roughly 0.4 kV/cm versus the design 3.7 kV/cm. At low fields, electron-ion recombination is higher, reducing both charge yield and the anti-correlation quality between charge and light signals, degrading energy resolution.

### Proposed Upgrade

**Reconfigured HV delivery with field-graded feedthrough:**
- Replace the RG217 coaxial cable feedthrough with a **purpose-designed Kapton-insulated, graded-field feedthrough** of the type used in high-voltage R&D for noble liquid detectors
- The corona problem is localized to "sharp edges of various photoetched parts" — replace all HV-connected photoetched components (cathode grid, field cage contact springs) with **electropolished machined parts** with all edges having controlled radii >0.5 mm
- Specifically, replace the photoetched half-cathode design with a **single-piece etched or wire-EDM machined cathode** from 0.1 mm phosphor bronze with laser-trimmed rounded edges, maintaining the 90% optical transparency via a hexagonal or circular perforation pattern

**Field cage resistor chain upgrade:**
- Current 900 MΩ thick-film resistors on sapphire substrates (Piconics/DuPont) are adequate in principle, but the HV instabilities prevent their use at design voltage
- Replace with **metal-film resistors on aluminum nitride substrates** (AlN has better thermal conductivity than sapphire and is available in low-radioactivity form), with explicit voltage coefficient of resistance specification at 170 K
- Add a second resistor chain in parallel to provide redundancy and reduce the voltage across individual components

**Expected benefit:** Achieving even 50% of design drift field (1.85 kV/cm) would substantially improve electron lifetime requirements and reduce recombination, potentially improving the charge channel energy resolution by 20–30% and significantly strengthening the ionization-scintillation anti-correlation that is the basis for the improved combined energy estimator.

---

## 5. Radon Exclusion: Active Emanation Suppression

### Current Limitation
Section 5.3 identifies that measured radon in the clean room air is approximately three times the 2 mBq/L allowable limit for the 0νββ analysis, with the paper noting this "favors, for the future, the purging of the volume inside the lead shield." The stainless steel enclosure around the lead is mentioned as a future-use provision.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Active radon exclusion system** using the existing stainless steel enclosure:

- Install a **dedicated boil-off nitrogen purge system** flowing through the stainless steel enclosure surrounding the lead shield, with input and exhaust ports already partially anticipated in the design
- Flow rate of ~10 L/min of boil-off nitrogen (essentially radon-free) through the ~200 L enclosed volume provides a complete volume exchange approximately every 20 minutes, reducing equilibrium radon to <0.1 mBq/L
- Add a **radon monitor** (electrostatic collection type, as already used for component screening per references [50-52]) on the exhaust line to continuously verify enclosure performance
- The nitrogen supply can be taken from the existing cryogenic infrastructure already present for the detector

**Expected benefit:** Reduction of radon-related background from the current ~3× excess to <10% of the 0νββ analysis window target rate. This is essentially a zero-cost modification relative to other hardware upgrades since the enclosure already exists.

---

## 6. Calibration System Enhancement: Internal Source Deployment

### Current Limitation
The calibration guide tube (Section 3.5) only allows external source placement in the HFE-7000 volume. This means calibration data for the fiducial volume center relies on extrapolation through the full LXe depth, with limited full-absorption efficiency for the lower-energy 137Cs source. The 228Th source at 2615 keV is essential for energy scale calibration near Qββ but produces multi-site events preferentially at the detector periphery.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Dissolved source calibration capability** using **⁸³ᵐKr injection:**

- ⁸³ᵐKr (T₁/₂ = 1.86 hr) produces a 41.5 keV conversion electron that is detectable throughout the active volume and has been demonstrated as a calibration source in noble liquid detectors
