| Charge Readout Ambiguity | 2D projected (wire) | True 3D pixel | LArPix v2b, 4 mm pitch |
| HV Uptime | 96–98% (with auto-recovery) | >99.5% (no streamers) | Resistive shell FC, DLC cathode |
| ADC Dynamic Range | 12-bit (4096 counts) | 14-bit dual-gain (~65K effective) | SAR ADC ASIC |
| Trigger Latency | ~1 µs (CTB) | <200 ns with classification | Alveo U250 FPGA |
| Timing Synchronization | ~1 ns RMS | <100 ps RMS | White Rabbit PTP |
| Purity Spatial Sampling | 3 external points | 18 in-TPC points | Miniaturized laser purity cells |

The most impactful single upgrade would be the **X-ARAPUCA photon detection replacement**, as the paper identifies photon yield as the primary limitation for non-beam physics goals (supernova detection, nucleon decay), and the efficiency improvement from 0.08–0.21% to 15–30% represents the largest fractional gain of any proposed modification.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for GERDA

## 1. Liquid Argon Scintillation Veto (Highest Priority)

The paper explicitly states GERDA decided to implement a LAr scintillation light veto for Phase II based on LArGe results, but it is absent in Phase I. This is the single most impactful upgrade.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace or supplement the copper radon shroud with a **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber curtain** surrounding the detector strings. Tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) coated fibers shift 128 nm LAr scintillation to ~430 nm for detection by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) or PMTs
- Deploy **Hamamatsu R11065-10 low-radioactivity PMTs** or equivalent, with measured activity below 5 mBq/unit for ²²⁸Th, arranged in a cylindrical array around the detector strings at roughly 40 cm radius
- Alternative: **SiPM arrays** (e.g., Hamamatsu S12572-010P or similar cryogenic-qualified devices) operating at LAr temperature (~87 K). These have essentially negligible radioactivity compared to PMTs, superior single-photon detection efficiency (~25-35%), and can be placed much closer to detectors. The primary challenge is the large capacitance at cryogenic temperatures requiring careful front-end design
- Coat inner surfaces of the mini-shroud and radon shroud with TPB via vacuum evaporation to ~0.2 mg/cm² thickness, achieving conversion efficiency of roughly 80% for VUV to visible
- Expected background rejection: factors of 3-10 in the ROI based on LArGe studies, pushing the BI from 2×10⁻² toward 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr)

---

## 2. Replacement of Phase I Coaxial Detectors with BEGe Detectors

The paper describes BEGe detectors as having "good pulse shape discrimination properties" but only five were deployed by July 2011 as a test string.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Full deployment of the 20.8 kg already-sliced enriched germanium in **BEGe geometry** from Canberra Olen, which was already in production at paper submission time
- BEGe detectors have a small p⁺ point contact geometry producing a characteristic current pulse with a single-site event (SSE) ratio A/E (amplitude over energy) that cleanly separates 0νββ signal events from multi-site Compton background. The paper cites Budjaš et al. JINST 4 P10007 (2009) demonstrating this
- The A/E parameter for BEGe detectors achieves >90% signal acceptance with ~80% Compton background rejection, compared to essentially no useful pulse shape discrimination in the existing p-type coaxial detectors
- This represents a factor of ~5 improvement in effective background index without any other changes

---

## 3. Upgraded Charge-Sensitive Preamplifier (CC3 or Equivalent)

The CC2 preamplifier achieves 0.8 keV baseline noise but the Phase I energy resolution at Qββ is 4.2–5.3 keV FWHM, substantially worse than the intrinsic detector capability of ~1.7 keV shown in vacuum cryostat tests.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the BF862 JFET input stage with a **custom low-noise JFET** optimized for operation at 87 K rather than the commercial package rated for room temperature. At LAr temperature, JFET transconductance and noise improve substantially if the device is designed for this operating point. Candidates include custom-fabricated JFETs from Moxtek or IF Electronics with gate areas optimized for ~1 pF detector capacitance
- Replace the AD8651 second stage (a CMOS op-amp not optimized for cryogenic operation) with a **cryogenic CMOS op-amp** qualified to 77 K, such as the OPA657 which maintains reasonable performance at low temperatures, or a custom differential pair stage using ALD1106 JFETs
- Implement the feedback resistor R_F (currently 500 MΩ) as a **pulsed reset scheme** rather than a resistive feedback. This eliminates the Johnson noise contribution from R_F entirely, which at 87 K contributes approximately 0.3 keV equivalent noise. The pulser reset architecture used in some bolometer experiments would be directly applicable
- Switch from the current single-layer Cuflон PCB to a **multilayer low-radioactivity substrate** allowing better noise shielding between channels and reducing cross-talk below the current 0.1% specification
- Target: reduce electronic noise contribution from ~0.8 keV to ~0.3 keV FWHM equivalent, recovering most of the gap between measured 4.5 keV and intrinsic 1.7 keV detector resolution

---

## 4. Improved Radon Shroud and Mini-Shroud Design

The measured ²²²Rn emanation of 54.7 mBq from the cryostat corresponds to BI ~7×10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) assuming uniform distribution, but the radon shroud reduces this only by up to a factor of seven.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the 30 µm copper foil radon shroud with **electroformed copper** of comparable thickness but dramatically lower ²²²Rn emanation. Electroformed copper from NUCLEC or equivalent underground electroforming facilities achieves <0.01 µBq/kg ²²⁶Ra versus the measured cryostat steel values of several mBq/kg
- Redesign the mini-shroud from 60 µm Cu foil to incorporate a **nylon film inner liner**, as demonstrated effective in Borexino, to further suppress ²²²Rn diffusion. Nylon has very low Rn permeability (~10⁻¹² cm²/s) compared to most polymers
- Add **activated charcoal cold traps** directly in the LAr recirculation path within the cryostat, exploiting the radon adsorption demonstrated at low temperature. A 1 kg charcoal column within the cold volume would maintain continuous Rn reduction rather than acting only at initial fill
- Install **electrostatic focusing electrodes** inside the mini-shroud at modest negative potential (~100 V) to repel the positively charged ⁴²K ions without creating the large external stray fields that caused the original ⁴²K problem. This requires careful field simulation to ensure containment within the shroud

---

## 5. Muon Veto Enhancement for the Neck Region

The paper identifies that muons entering through the neck region of the cryostat are insufficiently covered by the plastic scintillator array, which achieves only 97.2% efficiency from the lower bound estimate.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the current 36-panel plastic scintillator array with **larger-area panels** using Saint-Gobain BC-408 or equivalent with higher light yield (10,000 photons/MeV versus UPS-923A), covering a larger solid angle including the cryostat neck flanges
- Add a **segmented water Cherenkov ring** at the neck level using 6–8 additional ETL 9354KB PMTs mounted directly on the cryostat neck structure (the paper shows 6 mount positions already exist on the skirt), specifically to detect near-vertical muons that traverse minimal water
- Implement **time-of-flight discrimination** between the plastic panels and water Cherenkov to improve rejection of the low-multiplicity background (the unexplained bump around M=10) that currently complicates efficiency determination. This requires upgrading the muon DAQ timing resolution from the current 10 ns GPS synchronization to ~1 ns using a dedicated White Rabbit timing network
- Target: increase confirmed muon detection efficiency from 97.9% to >99.5%, reducing the unvetoed muon background contribution by a factor of ~4

---

## 6. High-Voltage Decoupling for AC-Coupled Detector Operation

The paper shows AC-coupled operation (n⁺ grounded, p⁺ biased) reduces ⁴²K background comparably to the mini-shroud, but current HV cables (Sami RG178) running through the lock contribute ²²²Rn emanation and represent a screening concern.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the Sami RG178 HV cables with **custom-drawn PTFE-insulated silver-plated copper coaxial cables** with verified radiopurity below 50 µBq/kg ²²⁸Th. The current cables show <680 µBq for 40 m length; a factor of 3 improvement is achievable with selected PTFE stock
- Replace the CAEN N1471H NIM HV modules with **custom ultra-low-noise HV supply** using the ISEG NHS series or equivalent with ripple below 1 mV peak-to-peak. Excess HV ripple at the detector bias level translates directly to gain instability and broadens the energy resolution
- Implement **on-detector HV filtering** using additional low-radioactivity tantalum capacitors (already used in the CC2) directly at the detector mount point to suppress noise conducted through the 10 m cable length

---

## Summary of Expected Impact

| Upgrade | Expected BI Improvement Factor | Implementation Complexity |
|---|---|---|
| LAr scintillation veto with SiPMs | 3–10× | High |
| Full BEGe deployment with A/E cuts | ~5× | Medium (in progress) |
| Improved preamplifier (energy resolution) | Indirect: better signal separation | Medium |
| Radon shroud/emanation reduction | 2–3× | Medium |
| Muon veto neck coverage | ~1.1× | Low |
| HV/cable improvements | ~1.2× | Low |

The LAr scintillation veto combined with BEGe pulse shape discrimination are the two upgrades with transformative impact, potentially achieving the Phase II target of 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr) without any increase in detector mass.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for EXO-200

## 1. Charge Readout System

### Replace Wire Planes with Charge-Coupled Pixel Detectors
The current crossed-wire scheme (U/V at 60°) has fundamental limitations in multi-site event discrimination. Replace with a pixelated charge readout using:

- **Topmetal-II or similar CMOS charge-sensitive pixel arrays** (pixel pitch ~1 mm, comparable to or finer than the current 3 mm wire pitch)
- Each pixel operates as an independent charge-integrating amplifier, eliminating the ambiguity inherent in the wire induction method for reconstructing 3D charge topology
- This directly improves the single-site vs. multi-site discrimination that is central to rejecting Compton-scattered gamma background near Q_bb
- The photoetched phosphor bronze triplet scheme introduces mechanical complexity and HV instabilities; monolithic silicon pixels would eliminate the corona discharge problems observed above 9-14 kV

**Concrete concern:** Radioactivity of the CMOS substrate must be verified. Use high-resistivity float-zone silicon, which has demonstrated low U/Th content, and minimize backend metal layers to reduce potassium contamination.

---

## 2. High Voltage System

### Replace Cable-Based Feedthrough with Custom Ceramic Feedthrough
The current RG217 polyethylene-dielectric coaxial cable feedthrough is identified as a source of HV instability, limiting drift field to ~0.4 kV/cm (8 kV across ~19 cm half-drift) versus the designed 3.7 kV/cm. This represents nearly a 10× shortfall in achievable drift field.

- **Replace with a graded-dielectric alumina or sapphire ceramic feedthrough** using platinum-metallized conductor, similar to designs developed for nEXO and XENON1T
- Sapphire has demonstrated excellent HV holdoff in LXe up to 100 kV with minimal surface leakage
- Specifically use a **Conflat-style titanium-sapphire brazed assembly** with field-grading electrodes to suppress triple-point discharges
- The spring-loaded receptacle contact inside the PTFE block is a mechanically unreliable interface; replace with a hard-soldered (indium-based, low-radioactivity) or compression-welded copper-sapphire contact

**Expected improvement:** Achieving the design 3.7 kV/cm drift field would improve electron lifetime requirements (longer drift distances are more tolerant at high field), improve z-position resolution via faster/cleaner drift, and sharpen ionization signal pulse shapes for better energy resolution and topology discrimination.

---

## 3. Photon Detection System

### Replace LAAPDs with Vacuum Ultraviolet Silicon Photomultipliers (VUV SiPMs)
The 468 LAAPDs operate with several significant disadvantages:
- Ganging of 5-7 devices per readout channel degrades position sensitivity of scintillation
- 125 pF device capacitance per LAAPD drives noise (2 e⁻/pF measured)
- 48% photosensitive packing fraction
- Fixed gain ~50-100 at LXe temperature limits dynamic range

**Proposed replacement:**
- **Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) VUV-HD3 SiPMs** or **Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPC series** (3mm × 3mm or 6mm × 6mm tiles) operated at ~130 K
- These devices demonstrate >20% photon detection efficiency at 175 nm without wavelength shifter, compared to ~70-80% quantum efficiency of LAAPDs but with the LAAPD's ~50 gain versus SiPM's ~10⁵ intrinsic gain
- The dramatically higher gain eliminates the noise-dominated threshold problem that currently limits the scintillation channel
- Tile the readout planes at ~85-90% packing fraction using edge-on mounting frames in oxygen-free copper
- Individual SiPM readout (rather than ganging) provides genuine 2D scintillation hit maps, enabling fiducialization using light pattern alone and improved event reconstruction

**Required R&D:** Screen FBK/Hamamatsu VUV SiPM substrates for U/Th/K. Current measurements suggest ~1 mBq/kg achievable with careful wafer selection from low-background silicon feedstock. The Kovar or ceramic packaging must be eliminated entirely—use bare die mounting as currently done for LAAPDs.

**Signal processing:** Replace the current discrete JFET preamps with **cryogenic SiPM-optimized ASICs** (e.g., PETIROC2A adapted for LXe temperature), reducing cable capacitance contribution by co-locating amplification.

---

## 4. Field Cage and Reflector System

### Replace Acrylic Structural Components with PTFE or Sapphire
The acrylic combs and spacers represent a background concern (Table 3 shows <1.6 counts/yr at 0ν from acrylic, but this is a limit, not a measurement) and have a large CTE mismatch:

- Acrylic CTE: 73.6 µm/(m·K) vs. copper 16.9 µm/(m·K) creates severe thermal stress
- Replace acrylic structural combs with **machined PTFE (TE-6472 grade, same as reflector tiles)**, which has been screened and shows acceptable radioactivity
- For high mechanical load areas, use **sapphire rods or alumina-zirconia ceramic** components, both of which have demonstrated very low U/Th content and better CTE matching to copper at cryogenic temperatures

### Increase PTFE Coverage
- Current inner radius PTFE lining covers field cage region (18.3 cm radius) but the aluminum/MgF₂-coated copper platter faces between LAAPDs provide only ~50% reflectivity at 178 nm vs. PTFE's 70%+ (likely higher in LXe)
- **Machine PTFE inserts for all inter-LAAPD gaps** on the platter faces, with precision laser-cut holes for SiPM active areas, increasing effective reflectance of the end-cap regions substantially

---

## 5. Xenon Purification Integration

### In-Vessel Getter with Low-Radioactivity Catalyst
The current SAES MonoTorr getters are external to the cryostat. Electron lifetime is limited by oxygen/water impurities, and purification requires circulation through warm external plumbing:

- Install **miniaturized zirconium getter cartridges** (custom low-radioactivity version of SAES St172) inside the HFE-7000 volume but external to the TPC vessel, connected via short-path copper tubing
- This reduces the dead volume and thermal gradient in the purification loop, improving achievable electron attenuation length from the current operational value toward the intrinsic LXe limit (~meters)
- Screen getter material specifically: SAES zirconium alloy has known but acceptable radioactivity; minimize getter mass by using higher-surface-area nanoporous zirconium powder beds

**Expected improvement:** Better electron lifetime directly improves energy resolution of the ionization channel. Combined with higher drift field (from HV upgrade), achieving >10 ms electron lifetime would make the ionization signal resolution cathode-anode symmetric and reduce position-dependent corrections.

---

## 6. Resistor Chain for Field Grading

### Replace Thick-Film Sapphire Resistors with PTFE-Encapsulated Metal Film
The current 900 MΩ thick-film resistors on sapphire substrates from Piconics use DuPont resistive paste:

- DuPont resistive pastes contain ruthenium oxide (RuO₂) as the resistive element, which is acceptable but the binder glasses may contain trace rare earth or heavy elements
- Replace with **bulk metal foil resistors on fused silica substrates** (Vishay/Caddock technology adapted for cryogenic use), which have demonstrated lower noise and better stability at cryogenic temperatures
- Alternative: **laser-trimmed thin-film resistors on sapphire** using nichrome (NiCr) resistive layer, which has established low-radioactivity content from Swiss Jewel Co. substrates already used in EXO-200
- Encapsulate in PTFE holders rather than leaving exposed, to protect from LXe flow-induced mechanical resonances

---

## 7. Electronics Architecture

### Move to Continuous Waveform Digitization at Higher Sampling Rate
The current 1 MS/s sampling with sample-and-hold architecture introduces dead time and limits pulse shape analysis:

- **Replace with 2.5 MS/s or 5 MS/s continuous streaming ADCs** (e.g., ADS5282 or similar 16-channel 14-bit pipeline ADC)
- Eliminate the sample-and-hold stage, which introduces nonlinearity and sampling jitter
- Implement **FPGA-based online pulse finding** (Xilinx Ultrascale or Intel Arria 10) with circular buffer depth of 4 ms to capture the full ²¹⁴Bi-²¹⁴Po delayed coincidence (214Po t₁/₂ = 164 µs) with greater margin
- This enables **online waveform-based multi-site discrimination** rather than relying purely on track-length estimators in offline analysis

### Reduce Cable Capacitance by Preamplifier Repositioning
The dominant noise contribution for wire channels (60-80 pF) comes from the polyimide cables traversing ~1 m from detector to FEE:

- Install **small cold preamplifier modules** in the HFE-7000 volume at the cryostat cold hatch, reducing the critical signal-carrying cable length from ~1 m to ~10 cm
- Use **cryogenic JFET arrays** (InterFET NJ14C or similar) in a compact 8-channel module potted in PTFE-encapsulated copper housing, screened for radioactivity
- The HFE-7000 at 170 K provides adequate cooling while the FEE bulk remains at room temperature outside the lead shield
- This would reduce wire channel input capacitance to ~10-15 pF, improving ENC from the current ~160 µV_rms toward ~60 µV_rms, directly improving ionization energy threshold

---

## Summary of Expected Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Estimated Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| Pixelated charge readout | Background rejection via topology | 2-3× better multi-site ID |
| HV feedthrough + higher drift field | Energy resolution, drift uniformity | Reach design 3.7 kV/cm |
| VUV SiPMs | Scintillation threshold, light yield | 2× better S/N, improved E resolution |
| Cold preamplifiers | Ionization noise floor | ~2.5× noise reduction |
| Continuous digitization | Pulse shape discrimination | Improved single/multi-site tagging |
| Improved purification | Electron lifetime | Position-correction systematics reduction |

The highest-priority single upgrade is the **HV system**, as the factor of ~9 shortfall in drift field relative to design propagates into nearly every other performance metric.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for DarkSide-50

## Critical Analysis of Performance Limiters

The paper explicitly identifies the dominant backgrounds and acceptance limitations:
1. **Scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov** events dominate the ER background
2. **PMT radioactivity** is the primary source of both γ-ray and neutron backgrounds
3. **Limited x-y position reconstruction** forces conservative radial fiducialization (losing ~15% acceptance)
4. **Low photoelectron yield** (8.0 PE/keV) limits PSD at low energies
5. **3" PMT proximity to S2 region** causes poor charge sharing, degrading reconstruction

---

## Proposed Upgrades, Ordered by Impact

### 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**The problem:** The 38 Hamamatsu R11065 PMTs contribute >90% of radiogenic neutron background (from borosilicate glass stems and ceramic dynode supports) and dominate the γ-ray-induced ER background. They are explicitly identified as the single largest background source.

**Specific implementation:**
- Deploy cryogenic SiPM tiles (e.g., Fondazione Bruno Kessler NUV-HD or Hamamatsu VUV4 series, already demonstrated at LAr temperatures ~87K) tiled directly on the fused silica windows
- Replace 38 × 3" PMTs with arrays of 6mm × 6mm SiPM cells totaling equivalent active area (~570 cm² per window)
- Use low-radioactivity substrates: high-purity silicon wafers with electroless nickel/copper traces rather than ceramic PCBs; eliminate borosilicate glass entirely
- Mount SiPMs on ultra-pure PTFE or sapphire carrier boards with photolithographed connections in electrodeposited gold on parylene-coated kapton

**Expected gains:**
- Radioactivity reduction by factor ~50-100× based on mass reduction and material purity (SiPMs have ~mg-scale active material vs. ~100g PMT assemblies including stem and dynodes)
- Radiogenic neutron background reduced from ~0.005 to <<0.001 events per exposure
- Eliminates the dominant source requiring the large LSV veto system
- SiPM dark count rates at 87K are ~0.1 Hz/mm², negligible compared to physics signals
- Higher photon detection efficiency (~40-50% PDE vs. ~30% QE × collection efficiency for PMTs) directly improves photoelectron yield

### 2. Increase Light Yield via Improved TPB Application and Reflector Geometry

**The problem:** The 8.0 PE/keV zero-field yield fundamentally limits PSD at low S1. The paper shows that the WIMP box lower boundary at low S1 is determined by ER leakage through f90. Additionally, Teflon Cherenkov is the dominant surviving background after all cuts.

**Specific implementation:**

*Replace Teflon reflector with ESR (Enhanced Specular Reflector) film or sputtered aluminum on PTFE:*
- 3M Vikuiti ESR has >98% reflectance at 420nm vs. ~95% for PTFE, but more importantly it is specular rather than diffuse, which dramatically changes the light collection geometry and reduces path lengths through the Teflon bulk, suppressing Cherenkov generation
- Alternatively: evaporate 200nm aluminum on electropolished PTFE substrate with MgF₂ protective overcoat, then vacuum-deposit TPB at controlled thickness (1-2 mg/cm²)
- Cherenkov yield in Teflon is proportional to pathlength through material; specular reflection at a metallic interface with minimal penetration depth reduces Cherenkov photon generation by estimated factor 10-20×

*TPB deposition improvements:*
- Replace vacuum evaporation with matrix-assisted pulsed laser evaporation (MAPLE) to produce uniform, crack-free TPB films at controlled 2 mg/cm² thickness
- Uniform TPB eliminates the degraded-α energy spectrum variation seen in Fig. 2, though more importantly it eliminates the correlated scintillation+Cherenkov path that contaminates f90
- Add a thin (0.5mm) deuterated polyethylene (dPE) layer behind the TPB on side walls as a Cherenkov suppressor: dPE has a higher Cherenkov threshold for electrons than standard polyethylene due to lower electron density

*Optical parameter result:* modeling (Section V E) shows scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov determines the box boundary; eliminating it allows the box lower edge to descend by ~0.05 in f90 at low S1, recovering significant NR acceptance.

### 3. Redesign the Anode/Grid/Cathode Stack for Improved S2 and Position Reconstruction

**The problem:** The 3" PMTs are too close to the S2 emission region, causing poor charge sharing and limiting x-y reconstruction to ~6mm resolution. The paper notes this explicitly as the reason radial fiducialization was not done in previous analyses.

**Specific implementation:**

*Increase gas gap thickness from 1cm to 2-3cm:*
- Larger gas gap causes S2 light cone to spread before hitting photodetectors, dramatically improving charge sharing
- Requires reoptimizing extraction field; at 3kV/cm in 3cm gas gap, electroluminescence yield increases proportionally, partially compensating for geometric acceptance
- Monte Carlo studies in similar detectors (XENON, LUX) show position resolution improves from ~6mm to ~2mm with factor 2-3 increase in gas gap at fixed detector size

*Replace ITO-coated windows with wire mesh electrodes:*
- Current ITO cathode/anode limits optical transmission; replace with 25μm diameter electroformed copper-beryllium wire mesh at 2mm pitch (>95% optical transparency)
- Positions cathode/anode as thin parallel planes rather than surface coatings, allowing independent optimization of electric field uniformity
- Eliminates ITO deposition non-uniformity that causes field distortions affecting drift and extraction

*Add dedicated position-sensitive layer:*
- Insert a single plane of 1mm pitch silicon strip detectors (operating in ionization mode at 87K, as demonstrated by the ATLAS ITk program) 5mm above the liquid surface to directly image the S2 electron cloud position
- This is technically challenging but would provide sub-mm position resolution independent of light sharing, eliminating the need for algorithmic position reconstruction and its associated systematic errors

**Expected gain:** Improved position resolution from ~6mm to ~2mm would allow radial fiducial cut to reach within ~2mm of wall rather than current 4-23mm varying with drift time, increasing fiducial mass from 31.3kg to ~38kg (~20% increase) for the same active volume.

### 4. Replace Borosilicate Fused Silica Windows with Crystalline Sapphire

**The problem:** Fused silica windows generate scintillation+fused silica Cherenkov events, which while mostly rejected by S1pMaxFrac, still contribute to backgrounds and drove development of that cut.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace 3mm thick Hamamatsu R11065-compatible fused silica windows with 5mm thick single-crystal synthetic sapphire (Al₂O₃) windows
- Sapphire has a Cherenkov threshold of ~175 keV for electrons (vs. ~20 keV for fused silica), eliminating virtually all Compton-scattered electron-induced Cherenkov from typical γ-ray backgrounds (Compton edge for 2.6 MeV ²⁰⁸Tl is ~2.4 MeV but most deposited energies are far lower)
- Sapphire transmits at 420nm (TPB emission) with >85% transmission, comparable to fused silica
- Ultra-high-purity sapphire (Rubicon Technology or Saint-Gobain Crystals) has U/Th contamination <0.1 ppt, lower than fused silica
- Thermal expansion coefficient of sapphire (5.3×10⁻⁶/K) differs from stainless steel; design indium wire gasket seal allowing differential contraction, as used in cryogenic optical systems

**Expected gain:** Essentially eliminates fused-silica Cherenkov contribution, reducing ER background category currently requiring S1pMaxFrac cut. Allows S1pMaxFrac to be relaxed, recovering ~5% NR acceptance.

### 5. Upgrade the Veto System with Gadolinium-Loaded Liquid Scintillator

**The problem:** The LSV uses boron-loaded scintillator achieving 99.64% neutron capture efficiency. The paper notes that the 10B α-only capture peak (branching ratio ~6%) and γ-escaping events reduce the efficiency of their modified delayed cut to ~79% for the VPT sample analysis.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace boron-loaded pseudocumene/TMB mixture with 0.1% Gd-loaded linear alkyl benzene (Gd-LAB), as developed for SNO+ and JUNO-TAO
- Gadolinium has neutron capture cross section of 49,000 barns (vs. ~3,800 barns for ¹⁰B), with capture lifetime reduced to ~15μs (from 22μs in current boron-loaded scintillator)
- Gd capture releases 8.0 MeV in cascaded γ rays (vs. 2.3 MeV for ¹⁰B α+γ branch), making captures unambiguous and detectable even when some γ rays escape
- Gd capture γ ray cascade has nearly 100% detection efficiency in 30 tonne LSV due to multiple γ rays at high energy
- This would increase the modified-delayed-cut efficiency from ~79% to >95%, improving the neutron counting statistics in the VPT analysis

**Secondary upgrade:** Add a thin (2cm) layer of borated polyethylene between the cryostat outer vacuum jacket and the LSV to moderate and capture neutrons from PMTs before they reach the active LAr volume, reducing the initial neutron flux by estimated factor ~5 based on neutron transport calculations.

---

## Summary Table of Expected Improvements

| Upgrade | Background Targeted | Estimated Gain |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM replacement | Radiogenic neutrons, γ-ray ER | 50-100× reduction in PMT radioactivity |
| Specular/metallic reflector | Scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov | 10-20× Cherenkov suppression |
| Enlarged gas gap + mesh electrodes | Position reconstruction | 3× better resolution, ~20% more fiducial mass |
| Sapphire windows | Fused-silica Cherenkov | Elimination of this background category |
| Gd-loaded LSV | Neutron detection efficiency | 79%→>95% modified veto efficiency |

The SiPM replacement and reflector material change together directly attack the two explicitly identified dominant backgrounds and would provide the most significant improvement in primary dark matter sensitivity.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for LUX: Targeted Improvements for Dark Matter Sensitivity

## 1. PMT System Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

### Motivation
The R8778 PMTs dominate the background budget (Table 3: 0.4 ER WIMP-like events vs. <0.05 for PTFE panels), contain radioactive U/Th/K/Co-60, and have a 5.7 cm diameter that creates dead regions requiring PTFE trifoil gap-fillers.

### Specific Upgrade
Replace both 61-PMT arrays with **Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD or Hamamatsu VUV4 SiPM tiles** in a close-packed configuration:
- Individual SiPM cells (6mm × 6mm) tiled on low-radioactivity fused silica or PTFE substrates to cover the full array area
- **Measured radioactivity of SiPM arrays** (primarily silicon, aluminum traces) is ~10-100× lower in U/Th than glass-body PMTs
- Operating voltage ~27-35V eliminates the high-voltage divider chains within the xenon space, removing resistor/capacitor radioactivity contributions
- Photon detection efficiency (PDE) of ~20-24% at 175nm for VUV-optimized devices vs. 33% QE × ~90% collection = ~30% for R8778; gap closes with improved anti-reflection coatings while dramatically reducing mass
- Eliminates ion-feedback afterpulsing entirely, removing a significant PMT health-monitoring burden
- **Eliminates the 122 PMT assemblies as dominant background source**; projected ER background from PMT equivalent drops by estimated factor of 10-50×

### Cabling Consequence
Low-voltage SiPM bias (~35V) allows substitution of thin, low-mass ribbon cables for the heavy Gore coaxial cables, reducing heat load and potential outgassing.

---

## 2. Cathode High-Voltage System Redesign

### Current Problem
The present system routes the HV cable through a xenon-gas umbilical from outside the water shield, with unshielded cable running 30 cm through liquid xenon to the cathode. The controlled 0.1 SLPM xenon purge away from the detector to prevent outgassed impurity back-diffusion represents a continuous purity perturbation. Maximum rated 100 kV limits drift field to 2 kV/cm.

### Specific Upgrade
Implement a **submerged, graded-dielectric feedthrough** modeled on the ICARUS/DarkSide-20k design philosophy but adapted for the LUX geometry:
- Use **ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) rod stock** as the primary dielectric, machined to provide controlled field grading along the feedthrough length
- Fabricate the feedthrough from **electropolished 316L stainless steel** with measured radioactivity, locating it at the bottom dome where it is furthest from the fiducial volume
- Eliminate the xenon-gas umbilical entirely, removing the 0.1 SLPM purge flow that perturbs the liquid level and adds a heat load pathway
- Target operating voltage of **150 kV** to achieve 3 kV/cm drift field, improving charge collection and electron-recoil/nuclear-recoil discrimination by ~5% based on XENON100 field-dependence measurements
- Add a **dedicated monitoring resistor** (1 GΩ, ceramic substrate, verified low-background) in series inside the xenon space for discharge current measurement

---

## 3. Upgraded Electron Extraction Region

### Current Problem
The gate-anode gap is fixed at 1 cm with a 30-micron wire mesh anode deflecting 130 microns under operating fields. This non-planarity creates spatial variation in electroluminescence gain, degrading S2 position resolution and energy resolution. The 88% transparency of the mesh anode is the lowest of any grid.

### Specific Upgrade
Replace the mesh anode with a **photo-etched stainless steel or electroformed copper grid** of the strung-wire type:
- Use **25-micron diameter wires** at 0.75 mm pitch, maintaining >97% optical transparency (vs. current 88%)
- Tension the wires to >80% of yield strength on a titanium frame with precision-machined wire-groove spacing to guarantee <20 micron deflection at operating fields
- Increase gate-anode gap to **1.5 cm** to improve electroluminescence uniformity: the field uniformity scales as (wire pitch)/(gap height), and increasing the gap reduces the fractional ripple
- Implement **independent anode voltage control** with 1V precision rather than resistive chain referencing, allowing in-situ tuning of extraction efficiency
- Add **three capacitive fringe-field sensors** (similar to the existing liquid-level sensors) at 120° azimuthal spacing between gate and anode to continuously monitor the gas gap thickness during operations

---

## 4. Internal Calibration System Enhancement

### Current Problem  
The paper describes external source tubes that require sources to penetrate the water shield, limiting fiducial-volume calibration uniformity. The 83mKr system (1.86 hour half-life) provides uniform spatial calibration but only electron-recoil response. Nuclear recoil calibration relies on external neutron sources with poor fiducial-volume penetration.

### Specific Upgrades

**A. Tritiated methane confirmed, but add a $^{220}$Rn nuclear recoil calibration source:**
- Implement a **thin-walled $^{228}$Th emanation source** (20 Bq, on a 2 cm² sintered glass bead substrate) connected via a dedicated 3mm diameter PTFE tube to the xenon recirculation line
- $^{220}$Rn daughters provide Pb-212 nuclear recoils at 101 keV, and the coincidence tagging of the alpha from $^{216}$Po (t½=0.145s) provides a clean nuclear recoil sample for in-situ NR band calibration
- Source is isolated by a pneumatic valve; secular equilibrium of the Ra-228/Th-228 source means no long-lived contamination reaches the active volume

**B. Collimated DDT (deuterium-deuterium) neutron generator:**
- Install a compact **Adelphi Technology DD109 sealed-tube generator** (2.45 MeV neutrons, ~10⁸ n/s) in a dry source tube in place of one passive tube
- The 2.45 MeV neutrons produce NR events throughout the active volume with known kinematics
- Provides absolute NR energy scale calibration without requiring external Am-Be sources that produce multiple-scatter backgrounds
- Gate the neutron pulse with the LUX trigger for coincidence rejection of accidentals

---

## 5. Improved Xenon Purity and Krypton Removal

### Current Problem
The paper notes 300 kg/day circulation rate was limited by sub-optimal surface-run plumbing, and the Kr background (Table 3: <0.13 ER WIMP-like events) depends on the projected efficiency of an unspecified removal system.

### Specific Upgrades

**A. Chromatographic krypton removal:**
- Install a dedicated **charcoal chromatography column** (2 kg activated charcoal, cooled to -80°C using a Peltier cooler array) in the recirculation path downstream of the SAES getter
- Based on published results from EXO-200 and XENON1T, this achieves Kr/Xe separation factors of >10⁶, reducing Kr to <0.01 ppt
- Column is regenerable by warming to room temperature and pumping, with Kr captured on a secondary cold trap for disposal
- **Dedicated cold-trap mass spectrometer** sampling at 5-minute intervals (vs. current grab-sample method) provides continuous purity monitoring

**B. Second-stage redundant getter:**
- Add a parallel **SAES MonoTorr PS4-MT3** getter cartridge with automated cross-over valve, enabling getter replacement without stopping xenon recirculation
- This eliminates purity degradation during getter regeneration, which currently requires detector downtime

---

## 6. Active Radon Mitigation

### Current Problem
The paper mentions nitrogen gas circulation above the water surface to prevent radon accumulation, but does not describe active radon reduction in the xenon gas space itself. Radon daughters plating out on PTFE surfaces create a low-energy background that is not listed in Table 3 but has emerged as a critical background in subsequent LXe experiments.

### Specific Upgrade
Install a **radon trap** in the xenon gas recirculation path:
- A **2-liter activated charcoal trap cooled to -40°C** using a compact mechanical refrigerator (e.g., Laird Thermal PF Series Peltier module) inserted between the getter output and the detector return line
- At -40°C, the Rn adsorption coefficient on charcoal is ~50 hours, providing ~99% single-pass Rn rejection at the 50 SLPM design flow rate
- Monitor trap performance with a dedicated **electrostatic Rn monitor** (Durridge RAD7 or equivalent) on the getter output line, providing real-time Rn activity at the sub-mBq/m³ level
- Complement with **electropolishing** of all inner-surface stainless steel plumbing components to reduce emanation at the source

---

## 7. Thermosyphon Redundancy and Precision Temperature Control

### Current Problem
Four thermosyphon cold heads provide all cooling with PID control, but the paper indicates the system operates just below N₂ vapor-pressure equilibrium (Fig. 6), meaning small perturbations in LN₂ supply can cause control excursions. Temperature offsets of 780±270 mK RMS exist in the xenon space, and thermometer failure rate was 40% before redesign.

### Specific Upgrades

**A. Redundant cooling circuit:**
- Add two additional thermosyphon lines (5 mm OD, 316L SS) connecting to an independent LN₂ dewar, selectable via pneumatic valves, providing N+1 redundancy
- Size the secondary circuit to maintain xenon temperature within ±2K of operating point during primary system maintenance

**B. Replace platinum RTD thermometers with calibrated **Cernox CX-1050** resistive sensors:**
- Cernox sensors provide 10 mK accuracy at 160-180K operating range vs. the current 170 mK post-calibration accuracy
- Their thin-film design on a sapphire substrate is less susceptible to the thermal cycling failures that caused 40% failure rate in the Omega ceramic-substrate sensors
- Use a 4-wire (Kelvin) measurement configuration throughout, replacing the current 3-wire ADAM module approach to eliminate lead-resistance errors contributing the 147±47 mK wiring systematic

---

## Summary Priority Matrix

| Upgrade | Background Reduction Factor | Technical Readiness | Cost Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| SiPM array replacement | ~10-50× ER from PMTs | High (TRL 7-8) | High |
| Radon trap | ~5-10× on Rn daughters | High (TRL 8-9) | Low |
| Kr chromatography | ~10× on ⁸⁵Kr | High (TRL 8) | Medium |
| Improved HV feedthrough | Enables higher drift field | Medium (TRL 6) | Medium |
| Anode grid upgrade | Improves S2 resolution ~20% | High (TRL 9) | Low |
| DD neutron generator | Calibration only | High (TRL 8) | Low |

The SiPM replacement and radon/krypton mitigation together address the dominant backgrounds identified in Table 3 and would move the experiment toward the background-free regime for a successor run with the same xenon mass.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for the LHCb Detector

## 1. Vertex Locator (VELO) Replacement

### Primary Limitation
The silicon strip VELO has 38–102 µm pitch strips with analogue readout, limiting impact parameter resolution at high luminosity and constraining readout to below 1 MHz (hardware trigger bottleneck).

### Proposed Upgrade
**Replace with pixel-based VELO using 55 µm × 55 µm hybrid pixel sensors (e.g., Timepix3/VeloPix ASIC architecture):**
- Pixel geometry eliminates strip ambiguities and reduces fake hit rates dramatically in high-multiplicity environments
- VeloPix ASIC capable of 40 MHz continuous readout at ~800 Mhits/s/chip, enabling triggerless operation
- Reduce inner radius from 8.2 mm to ~5 mm using RF foil thinned to ~250 µm aluminum, directly improving IP resolution at high pT toward the ~10 µm asymptotic limit
- Switch from n-on-n to n-on-p sensors to avoid type inversion issues observed at fluences above ~15×10¹² n_eq/cm²; 200 µm thick sensors with p-stop isolation between pixels
- Implement active edge technology to minimize dead area near beam axis
- Expected IP resolution improvement: ~20–25% at high pT, approximately 10 µm asymptote versus current 13 µm

---

## 2. Upstream Tracker (UT) Replacing TT

### Primary Limitation
The TT has 183 µm strip pitch, 52.6 µm hit resolution, and insufficient granularity near the beam pipe (1.9% occupancy), degrading track momentum estimates in the L0-free trigger environment.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Replace with 4-layer silicon microstrip detector using finer pitch sensors in high-occupancy regions:**
- Inner region (r < 10 cm): 100 µm pitch sensors reducing occupancy from ~2% to ~1%, reducing ghost track rate
- Use 250 µm thick sensors (versus current 500 µm TT) to reduce multiple scattering contribution to momentum resolution
- Implement APV25-derived ASICs with 40 MHz readout capability, eliminating the current 1 MHz readout constraint
- Carbon fiber support structures with embedded cooling to improve temperature stability, addressing the J/ψ mass bias (~3 MeV/c²) observed with 15°C temperature excursions
- Staggered sensor overlaps in all four layers (x-u-v-x) to enable standalone track segments for alignment constraints

---

## 3. Scintillating Fiber Tracker (SciFi) Replacing IT and OT

### Primary Limitation
The OT drift-tube system has 205 µm single-hit resolution and ~35 ns maximum drift time, making it fundamentally incompatible with 40 MHz continuous readout. At 25 ns bunch spacing the occupancy reaches ~25% in inner modules. The IT silicon strips require annual shutdown repairs.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Replace entire T1-T3 station volume with 2.5 mm diameter scintillating fiber mats read out by Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs):**
- SciFi modules: 250 µm diameter fibers (SCSF-78MJ Kuraray or equivalent) grouped in 2.5 mm ribbons, 6 layers deep per module plane
- SiPM arrays (128-channel, 55 µm cell size) at fiber ends with -40°C cooling to suppress dark count rate from radiation-induced increase
- Single-hit resolution ~100 µm (factor 2 improvement over OT's 205 µm), directly improving momentum resolution σ(p)/p at high momentum
- Maximum response time <10 ns (scintillation + SiPM), fully compatible with 40 MHz readout
- Radiation hardness: SiPMs tolerate ~10¹² n_eq/cm² with acceptable noise increase; fiber transmission degradation manageable with UV-enhanced cladding
- Eliminates gas system infrastructure (Ar/CO₂/O₂ mixture handling, gas-tightness maintenance)
- Expected improvement: track momentum resolution σ(p)/p improving from ~8‰ at 100 GeV/c toward ~5‰

---

## 4. RICH System Photodetector Replacement

### Primary Limitation
Hybrid Photon Detectors (HPDs) suffer from read-out inefficiency identified during high trigger rate running in Run I, contributing to photoelectron yields below simulation (C₄F₁₀: 20.4 measured vs. 28.3 simulated; CF₄: 15.8 vs. 22.7). HPDs require high-voltage (~15 kV) cross-focusing and are sensitive to magnetic fringe fields causing image distortions in RICH1.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Replace HPDs with Multi-Anode Photomultiplier Tubes (MaPMTs, e.g., Hamamatsu R11265) or SiPM arrays:**

**For RICH1:**
- MaPMT arrays (64-channel, 2×2 mm² pixels) with µ-metal shielding optimized for the residual fringe field environment
- Single photon detection efficiency ~35% quantum efficiency versus HPD ~20%, recovering most of the photoelectron yield deficit
- Eliminate cross-focusing voltage, simplifying HV distribution and removing a known source of image distortion
- Implement improved photon ring reconstruction using time-of-propagation correction (±0.3 ns timing resolution from MaPMT) to resolve ring overlaps

**For RICH2:**
- SiPM arrays with 25 µm microcell pitch: quantum efficiency ~45% at 420 nm, compatible with CF₄ Cherenkov spectrum peak
- Requires cooling to -30°C and active bias correction for dark count rate versus temperature
- Expected Cherenkov angle resolution improvement in C₄F₁₀: from 1.618 mrad toward simulation expectation of 1.52 mrad

---

## 5. Calorimeter System Readout and Photon Detector Replacement

### Primary Limitation
PMT gain degradation causes systematic rate drift (visible in Figure 29 as gradual L0-hadron rate reduction); HCAL calibration limited to bi-monthly technical stops using ¹³⁷Cs sources. ECAL cell-to-cell intercalibration precision of ~2% limits B→K*γ mass resolution (currently 93 MeV/c²). The 12-bit ADC dynamic range and 25 ns readout window cause spill-over requiring active subtraction.

### Proposed Upgrade
**ECAL photomultiplier replacement with radiation-hard fine-mesh PMTs plus online gain monitoring:**
- Replace aging standard dynode PMTs with fine-mesh dynode tubes (Hamamatsu R7400 series): factor ~5 higher magnetic field tolerance, significantly improved gain stability at high integrated anode current
- Install dedicated LED calibration with pulsed UV laser distributed via optical fibers for continuous gain monitoring at <0.5% relative precision (versus current ~2% intercalibration)
- Upgrade ADC to 14-bit with 12.5 ns sampling (dual-sample approach) to reduce spill-over from adjacent crossings without active subtraction, improving energy resolution by ~15%
- Add longitudinal segmentation to inner ECAL region (r < 20 cm) with 5X₀ preshower + 20X₀ main section using separate readout: enables electromagnetic shower profile fitting to distinguish merged π⁰ from photons up to 10 GeV/c (currently limited to ~5 GeV/c)

**HCAL:**
- Replace ¹³⁷Cs hydraulic calibration with embedded radioactive wire sources (e.g., ⁶⁰Co) that can be deployed remotely without full access, enabling weekly calibration cycles
- Add hadron-shower timing capability (±1 ns resolution) using fast plastic scintillator layers to reduce pile-up contribution

---

## 6. Muon System Inner Region Upgrade

### Primary Limitation
M1R1 dead-time reaches 2.5% and M2R1 reaches 0.6% at twice nominal luminosity due to 50–100 ns front-end chip dead-time. GEM detectors in M1 highest-rate region perform adequately but MWPC chambers in M2R1-M3R1 face occupancy-driven inefficiency.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Replace inner regions (R1 and R2) of M2–M4 with Micro-Pattern Gas Detectors:**
- Install thick-GEM (THGEM) or µ-RWELL detectors in M2R1, M3R1, M4R1: gain ~10⁴ with 10 ns signal collection time versus 50–100 ns MWPC
- 2 mm pitch anode strips (versus current pad size scaling 1:2:4:8) in R1 to accommodate factor ~4 higher luminosity
- Replace MWPC front-end chips in inner regions with SAMPA ASICs (originally developed for ALICE TPC): 10 ns shaping time, negligible dead-time at expected occupancies, 10 MHz sampling
- Expected improvement: M2R1 efficiency from current ~98.5% (at 2× nominal luminosity) to >99.5%
- Retain existing MWPC chambers in R3-R4 where occupancy is acceptable

---

## 7. Trigger and Online System Architecture

### Primary Limitation
The hardware L0 trigger at 1 MHz introduces irreducible inefficiency: L0 efficiency for B→K⁺π⁻ is only 53% (Table 5), and the SPD multiplicity veto rejects high-multiplicity events indiscriminately. Deferred HLT processing recovers only ~20–30% additional CPU.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Full software trigger at 40 MHz:**
- Upgrade all sub-detector front-ends to continuous 40 MHz readout (enabled by VELO pixel, SciFi, UT upgrades above)
- Deploy GPU-accelerated first-pass reconstruction: Allen framework or equivalent achieving VELO tracking at ~40 MHz on NVIDIA A100-class GPUs; estimated 100 GPU nodes replacing current hardware L0 logic
- FPGA-based (Xilinx Ultrascale+) first-level event builder assembling 40 MHz fragments across ~200 detector subsystems with <1 µs latency per event
- Increases effective L0 efficiency for B→K⁺π⁻ from 53% toward >90% by replacing calorimeter ET threshold with full track+IP selection
- Eliminates SPD multiplicity veto, recovering ~5% of currently discarded high-multiplicity events containing genuine heavy flavor decays

---

## Summary of Expected Performance Improvements

| Subsystem | Current Performance | Projected Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| IP resolution (high pT) | ~13 µm | ~10 µm |
| Momentum resolution σ(p)/p at 100 GeV/c | ~8‰ | ~5‰ |
| Cherenkov angle resolution (C₄F₁₀) | 1.62 mrad | ~1.52 mrad |
| L0 efficiency (B→Kπ) | 53% | >90% |
| Muon inner region efficiency | ~98.5% | >99.5% |
| ECAL intercalibration | ~2% | ~0.5% |

These upgrades collectively address the three fundamental constraints identified in the paper: the 1 MHz hardware trigger bottleneck, radiation damage accumulation in inner tracking, and photodetector gain instability in calorimeter and RICH systems.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for SNO: Physics-Motivated Proposals

## Framing the Problem

SNO's primary physics goal is distinguishing CC from NC interactions to measure solar neutrino flavor transformation. The limiting factors are: (1) energy resolution and threshold, (2) background rejection, (3) NC detection efficiency, and (4) vertex/direction reconstruction. I address each with concrete hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Photomultiplier System Upgrades

### 1.1 Replace R1408 with Higher Quantum Efficiency PMTs

The R1408 achieves roughly 20-22% peak quantum efficiency. The detector operates at 31% bare photocathode coverage, boosted to ~54% effective coverage with concentrators. Every improvement in QE directly improves energy resolution as σ_E/E scales as 1/√N_pe.

**Concrete proposal:** Hamamatsu was developing the R5912 and similar hemispherical dynode PMTs in the late 1990s with bialkali photocathodes achieving 25-27% QE at 390 nm. Replacing the R1408 with such tubes would increase photoelectron yield by roughly 20-25%, improving energy resolution from approximately 20% at 5 MeV toward 16-17%. This directly lowers the effective analysis threshold, critical for accessing the low-energy solar neutrino spectrum where MSW spectral distortions are most prominent.

**Secondary benefit:** Higher QE reduces the photoelectron threshold needed for triggering, potentially lowering the hardware trigger from roughly 23 PMT hits to perhaps 18 hits, extending sensitivity below 5 MeV kinetic energy for electrons.

### 1.2 Improved Light Concentrator Design

The current Winston cone-style concentrators use aluminum with MgF₂/TiO₂-PrO dielectric coating achieving 82±3% mean reflectance. The angular acceptance cutoff at 56.4° excludes photons from beyond 7 m radius.

**Concrete proposal:** Replace the 18-piece aluminum concentrator assembly with electroformed nickel substrates coated with protected silver. Protected silver (Ag + SiO₂ overcoat) achieves 95%+ reflectance across 300-600 nm in water compared to 82% for the current aluminum system. This is achievable with electroforming technology that was mature by the late 1990s. The net gain would be roughly 15% more photons detected, equivalent to adding ~1400 PMTs without any structural modification.

A secondary geometric modification: slightly reduce the critical acceptance angle to 52° to sharpen the fiducial boundary definition, improving vertex reconstruction at the acrylic vessel boundary where the primary systematic uncertainty in the fiducial volume sits.

### 1.3 Suppression of Late Pulsing and After-Pulsing

The R1408 specification allows up to 1.5% late-pulse fraction. For a 5 MeV electron event producing roughly 40 hit PMTs, this generates ~0.6 spurious hits per event on average, contributing non-Gaussian tails to the time residual distributions used for vertex fitting.

**Concrete proposal:** Implement an additional single-stage electron bombardment getter in the PMT vacuum process. More practically within an operating detector context, add a per-channel hardware discriminator delay circuit on the PMTIC cards that applies a 150 ns software-settable veto window after each primary hit, suppressing late pulses from PMT ion feedback from reaching the charge integrators. This requires only PMTIC redesign, not tube replacement.

---

## 2. Electronics Upgrades

### 2.1 Increase ADC Sampling Depth and Bandwidth

The current QUSN7 chip stores 16 analog memory samples with 12-bit ADCs running at 2 µs conversion time. The time measurement is a single TAC value per event. The charge measurement has four selectable integration windows but no pulse shape information.

**Concrete proposal:** Replace the QUSN7 analog memory architecture with a switched-capacitor array (SCA) sampling at 500 MHz (2 ns sampling interval) with a 32-sample deep buffer per channel. This is feasible using GaAs or advanced BiCMOS processes available in the late 1990s. The Domino Ring Sampler (DRS) concept being developed at PSI around this time demonstrated exactly this approach.

**Physics gain:** Full waveform capture per PMT hit enables:
- Pulse shape discrimination between single photoelectrons and multiply-coincident photons arriving within a few ns (critical for high-energy events and supernova bursts)
- Better separation of Cherenkov signal from PMT prepulses in the offline analysis
- Direct measurement of photon arrival time distributions for improved vertex reconstruction, potentially reducing vertex resolution from ~25 cm toward ~15 cm at 5 MeV

### 2.2 Multi-Threshold Trigger Architecture

The current trigger counts PMT hits within a ~100 ns coincidence window above a single programmable threshold, with a second narrower 20 ns coincidence window for a reduced fiducial volume trigger.

**Concrete proposal:** Implement a hardware trigger processor using a lookup table architecture (feasible in the Xilinx 4000-series FPGAs available by 1999) that forms a spatial hit-pattern trigger rather than a purely temporal coincidence. Specifically:

- Divide the 9438 PMTs into 12 solid-angle sectors of ~785 PMTs each
- Require that hits satisfying the time coincidence condition are distributed across at least 4 sectors (enforcing isotropy consistent with a Cherenkov ring rather than a point-like background)
- This rejects PMT-correlated noise bursts and single-PMT breakdown events at the hardware level rather than offline

**Background rejection improvement:** The dominant low-energy background is from Cherenkov light produced by beta/gamma from U/Th chain decays near or on the acrylic vessel. These events are concentrated near the vessel wall and subtend a limited solid angle in the PMT array. A spatial trigger requiring minimum angular spread would reduce this trigger rate by an estimated factor of 2-3 at threshold energies near 5 MeV, enabling a lower hardware threshold.

### 2.3 Dedicated High-Speed Muon Veto Electronics

The detector sees ~70 muons per day through the inner volume. Each muon can produce spallation products (primarily ¹²B, ¹²N, and lighter isotopes) that mimic solar neutrino signals for timescales from milliseconds to seconds. The current system handles this in offline software.

**Concrete proposal:** Add a dedicated fast muon trigger card that:
- Accepts the analog sum signal from the SNOINT chips when it exceeds a high threshold (> 500 hit PMTs, clearly a muon)
- Immediately issues a hardware deadtime gate of programmable length (1-20 seconds) selectable in 100 ms steps
- Logs the muon track direction (using the existing 20 ns coincidence sum as a crude directional primitive) to enable asymmetric deadtime zones in the offline analysis

This reduces the software complexity of muon rejection and ensures no spallation product events enter the primary data buffer, rather than requiring offline correlation.

---

## 3. Neutral Current Detector Array Improvements

The NCD array as designed achieves ~37% neutron capture efficiency, but the effective analysis efficiency is taken as ~25% due to alpha particle backgrounds from the nickel tube walls that cannot be unambiguously separated from neutron events by pulse shape alone in 45% of cases.

### 3.1 Waveform Digitization on NCD Signals

The current NCD readout uses a single coaxial cable per string with a 30 ns delay line for position encoding via pulse reflection timing. The pulse shape information is not fully exploited in hardware.

**Concrete proposal:** Replace the current preamplifier/discriminator chain at deck level with flash ADC modules sampling at 100 MHz (10 ns resolution). This was commercially achievable by 1999 with modules from companies such as Struck or Joerger. The full current pulse profile from the proportional counter (which spans roughly 20-100 µs depending on track geometry and gas gain) encodes:

- **Event type discrimination:** The ³He(n,p)T reaction produces a distinctive bipolar pulse shape as the proton and triton tracks diverge from the wire. Alpha particle wall events produce a single-ended pulse. A 100 MHz flash ADC with 1024-sample depth captures the full discrimination profile.
- **Position along string:** The existing reflection timing gives position to ~30 cm. Full waveform analysis of the rising edge shape improves this to ~10 cm, enabling fiducial cuts within individual NCD strings to reject end-cap backgrounds.

**Quantitative gain:** If the alpha discrimination efficiency improves from ~55% to ~80% through full pulse shape analysis, the effective NCD analysis efficiency rises from 25% toward 35%, improving NC statistical precision by ~18% for the same running time.

### 3.2 Substitute Enriched ⁶Li:Cs(I) Crystal Detectors for Some NCD Strings

While the full replacement of the NCD array is beyond the scope of an upgrade, the paper notes that ~5% of strings are filled with ⁴He:CF₄ as background monitors. These provide limited physics return.

**Concrete proposal:** Replace the ⁴He monitor strings (approximately 5 strings out of 96) with thin-walled tubes containing ⁶LiI(Eu) crystalline scintillator fibers read out by small PMTs. ⁶Li has a thermal neutron capture cross section of 940 b via ⁶Li(n,α)³H, producing 4.78 MeV in a highly quenched alpha signal. The scintillation pulse is readily distinguishable from gamma/beta backgrounds by pulse height and shape.

**Physics gain:** These hybrid strings would provide an independent neutron detection channel with different systematic uncertainties than the ³He proportional counters. Cross-calibration between ³He and ⁶LiI channels constrains the neutron detection systematic uncertainty, which is a primary limitation on the NC/CC ratio measurement.

---

## 4. Water System Upgrades

### 4.1 Online Radium-226 Monitor via Electrostatic Collection

The current Ra assay uses offline MnOₓ bead extraction followed by daughter counting, with a cycle time measured in days. Radon daughters from ²²⁶Ra decay enter the water continuously, and the current monitoring cadence cannot catch transient contamination events.

**Concrete proposal:** Install two continuous online electrostatic RaA (²¹⁸Po) monitors directly in the D₂O recirculation loop. These consist of a 1-liter stainless steel vessel with a central biased electrode (+500 V) in a flowing gas stream degassed from a 10 l/min D₂O sidestream. The ²²²Rn daughter ²¹⁸Po is positively charged after alpha emission and collects on the electrode with ~50% efficiency. An implanted silicon surface barrier detector measures alpha events. This provides a continuous radon monitor with ~1 hour time resolution at the design specification levels of 3×10⁻¹⁵ g/g Th equivalent.

The technology is well established in the radon monitoring literature and requires only integration engineering specific to the D₂O environment.

### 4.2 UV-Oxidation Stage for Organic Carbon Removal in D₂O

The current D₂O system uses RO filtration and ion exchange but lacks a dedicated total organic carbon (TOC) reduction stage equivalent to the 185 nm UV stage in the H₂O system. The paper notes the H₂O system uses 185 nm UV to break organics into ionic form. Organics in the D₂O are potentially problematic because they can fluoresce under Cherenkov photon irradiation, creating a broadband optical background.

**Concrete proposal:** Install a 185 nm UV unit (Trojan Technologies or equivalent, using low-pressure mercury amalgam lamps in quartz sleeves) on the D₂O recirculation return line upstream of the ion exchange columns. At 185 nm, the photon energy (6.7 eV) dissociates C-H and C-C bonds in dissolved organic molecules including residual EDTA from the H₂O system that may diffuse across the acrylic vessel. Flow rate of 20 l/min through a 2-lamp unit provides adequate UV dose. Isotope exchange of organic H for D is not a concern at the trace organic concentrations present.

---

## 5. Acrylic Vessel and Optical Improvements

### 5.1 Anti-Reflection Coating on Acrylic Inner Surface

The acrylic vessel inner surface is uncoated. At normal incidence in the D₂O/acrylic interface (n_D₂O ≈ 1.328 at 400 nm, n_acrylic ≈ 1.492), the Fresnel reflection loss is approximately 0.5% per surface. More significantly, at the acrylic/H₂O outer interface the reflection loss affects photons at shallow angles, and scattered photons arriving at non-normal incidence experience substantially higher losses.

**Concrete proposal:** For a future refurbishment of the vessel neck or any acrylic repair operations, apply a single-layer SiO₂ anti-reflection coating (quarter-wave optical thickness at 390 nm, deposited by plasma-enhanced CVD or sol-gel dip coating) to acrylic panels before bonding. Sol-gel SiO₂ on acrylic was demonstrated in the optical coating literature by the mid-1990s and is chemically compatible with ultrapure water. The refractive index of SiO₂ (1.46) is nearly ideal for matching acrylic to water. This would reduce surface reflection losses by ~factor of 5 at normal incidence, recovering approximately 1% of total photon flux, and more importantly flattening the angular response of the vessel for oblique photon incidence.

### 5.2 Wavelength-Shifting Outer Reflector

The current PSUP carries a light barrier (black ABS cells) that absorbs photons missing the PMT photocathode. Roughly 46% of photons incident on the PSUP face are not detected (since effective coverage is 54%).

**Concrete proposal:** Line the non-PMT areas of the ABS hexagonal cells with a tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) wavelength-shifting film. TPB absorbs near-UV photons (300-380 nm) where the PMT quantum efficiency is falling and re-emits at 430 nm where QE peaks. Applied as a 1 µm evaporated film on aluminum foil backing in the gaps between PMT concentrators, this converts otherwise lost UV Cherenkov photons into detectable visible photons. The radioactivity of a thin evaporated organic film is negligible. At 300-380 nm, approximately 15-20% of the total Cherenkov photon flux from a 5-10 MeV electron event is emitted; recovering even 30% of these would increase the mean photoelectron yield by ~5%, directly improving energy resolution.

---

## Priority Ranking by Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Energy Resolution Gain | Background Rejection | NC Efficiency | Implementation Difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NCD waveform digitization | None | High | +18% rel. | Low |
| Higher-QE PMTs | +20-25% N_pe | Moderate | Indirect | High (replacement) |
| Spatial trigger processor | None | Factor 2-3 at threshold | None | Moderate |
| NCD flash ADC readout | None | High (alpha discrim.) | Direct | Low |
| Online Ra monitor | None | Enables faster response | Indirect | Moderate |
| Protected-silver concentrators | +15% N_pe | Low | Indirect | Moderate |
| SCA waveform electronics | Significant | High | Indirect | High |

The single highest-leverage upgrade achievable without major structural intervention is **NCD waveform digitization via flash ADCs at deck level**, combined with a **spatial hit-pattern hardware trigger**. Together these address the two dominant systematic uncertainties: NC signal efficiency (alpha background contamination in NCD) and low-energy threshold (PMT noise triggers), which directly limit the statistical precision of the CC/NC ratio that is SNO's core measurement.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Forward Heavy-Flavour Spectrometer

## Framing: What Limits Primary Physics Performance?

For a detector like LHCb, the binding constraints on heavy-flavour physics are:
1. **Vertex resolution** (displacement significance for *b/c* separation)
2. **Trigger efficiency and rate capability** (especially for hadronic modes)
3. **Particle identification** (π/K/p separation over broad momentum range)
4. **Track reconstruction efficiency and fake rate**
5. **Luminosity / interaction rate headroom**

I'll address each with concrete hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Vertex Detector: The Highest-Leverage Upgrade

### 1a. Replace strip/hybrid-pixel sensors with **Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS)**

**Specific technology:** 65 nm or 28 nm CMOS imaging process (e.g., Tower/Jazz 180 nm was used for ALPIDE; move to 65 nm TJ-Monopix / ATLASPix style or a dedicated process like IFX 130 nm).

**Why it matters:**
- Reduce single-hit spatial resolution from ~10 µm (current hybrid pixel) to **3–5 µm** pitch pixels without increasing material
- Thinnable to **50 µm** epitaxial layer → radiation-hard, low material budget (~0.1–0.2% X₀ per layer feasible)
- Eliminates bump-bonding → thinner assemblies, better yield, lower cost per cm²

**Mechanical arrangement:**
- RF-foil shielded retractable modules sitting **5 mm from the beam axis** (matching current VELO geometry but exploiting thinner sensors)
- Add a **"Layer 0"** at r ≈ 4–5 mm from beam: a dedicated ultra-thin sensor (25 µm thick, 20 µm pitch) purely for impact-parameter constraint, read out at full bunch-crossing rate
- Use **4D tracking** (spatial + timing): integrate a fast timing layer with **~50 ps per-hit resolution** using AC-LGAD (AC-coupled Low-Gain Avalanche Diode) strips at 10–15 cm from IP to resolve pile-up vertices in z during high-luminosity running

**Expected gain:** Impact-parameter resolution improves from ~15 µm to **~8–10 µm** at high pT, directly translating to ×2 improvement in *B*–*D* decay-length significance and sensitivity in rare decays.

---

### 1b. Radiation-hard columnar 3D sensors for innermost layers

Where MAPS cannot survive flux (>10¹⁶ neq/cm²), use **3D silicon sensors** with columnar electrodes (20 µm × 20 µm cell, 150 µm active thickness). These maintain full efficiency after extreme fluence with modest bias voltage (~100 V). Source: CNM Barcelona / FBK Trento production lines.

---

## 2. Upstream Tracker: **µTPC-mode Silicon Microstrip or µ-strip MAPS**

Replace downstream scintillating-fibre or silicon strip detectors closest to the magnet with:

**Specific technology:** **HVMAPS** (High-Voltage MAPS, e.g., H35DEMO / MuPix family, 180 nm HV-CMOS) or thin silicon microstrip (50 µm pitch, 300 µm thick) with **AMS 130 nm ASICs** (VeloPix-successor style, ~800 MHz/mm² hit rate tolerance).

- Implement **µTPC (micro Time Projection Chamber) cluster analysis**: use 3–4 time samples per strip at 40 MHz sampling + TDC to reconstruct track angle within a single sensor layer, improving single-hit residuals from ~50 µm to **~15 µm** without halving strip pitch (technique demonstrated in CMS Phase-2 Outer Tracker studies)
- This directly improves momentum resolution and ghost-track rejection upstream of the magnet

---

## 3. Trigger Architecture: Full Software Trigger on Custom Hardware

### 3a. Eliminate the L0 hardware trigger — implement **Allen-style GPU trigger at full rate**

**Specific hardware:** Deploy a farm of **NVIDIA H100 or AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs** (or their successors) connected via **100 GbE / 400 GbE** optical links directly from detector front-end electronics.

- Run **full online track reconstruction** at 30–40 MHz visible interaction rate on GPU farm
- Each GPU node handles ~0.5–1 Tb/s sustained data throughput; a farm of ~500 GPUs processes the full LHC rate
- Implement **Allen framework** (or equivalent): sequence includes VELO track finding → PV reconstruction → downstream tracking → displaced-vertex selection, all in <4 ms latency per event

**Why this is critical:** An L0 hardware trigger with a calorimeter/muon seed is fundamentally inefficient for **hadronic charm modes** (D⁰→Kπ, Ds→KKπ, Λc→pKπ). A purely software trigger with full tracking can apply **decay-topology selections** at trigger level, recovering 30–50% more signal for these modes. This is the single largest physics gain for charm physics and hadronic *B* decays.

### 3b. **FPGA-based data concentrator / event builder upgrade**

- Use **Xilinx Versal / Intel Agilex FPGA SoCs** as front-end concentrators, each handling 1–5 Tb/s aggregate bandwidth
- Implement zero-suppression and cluster finding **on-chip** to reduce off-detector bandwidth by ×10–30 before GPU farm
- Deploy **Time-Division Multiplexed readout** with **GBT (GigaBit Transceiver) successors** running at 10–25 Gb/s per link (e.g., lpGBT + VTRx+ optical transceiver pairs, already qualified for LHC radiation environments)

---

## 4. RICH Detectors: Improved Cherenkov Photon Detection

### 4a. Replace current HPDs with **Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)** in RICH 2 (high-momentum PID)

**Specific technology:** **FBK RGB-HD SiPM** (35 µm cell, 57% PDE at 420 nm) or **Hamamatsu S13360 series** multi-pixel arrays in custom tiles.

- SiPM tiles: 6 × 6 mm² packages tiled into ~3 m² active area; no magnetic shielding needed unlike HPDs (HPDs require µ-metal shielding that constrains geometry)
- **Time resolution:** SiPMs provide ~200–300 ps single-photon timing → use **photon arrival time** to suppress combinatorial background in Cherenkov ring reconstruction (demonstrated in TORCH detector R&D)
- Allows **tighter ring isolation** in high-occupancy environment → improves π/K separation at 60–100 GeV/c where RICH 2 performance is marginal

### 4b. Add a **TORCH (Time Of internally Reflected CHernkov light) detector**

**Location:** 9.5 m from IP, covering 6 m² with 10 mm thick fused-silica plates + MCP-PMTs (Photek / Photonis, 64-channel multianode, 100 µm spatial resolution, <100 ps TTS).

- Provides **π/K separation up to 10 GeV/c** via time-of-flight (complementary to RICH 1 which struggles above 5 GeV/c and RICH 2 below 15 GeV/c)
- Fills the **PID gap** in 8–15 GeV/c range that limits Bs→Dsπ vs Bs→DsK separation
- Target: **15 ps per-track timing** from averaging ~30 photons per track

---

## 5. Calorimeter System: Upgrade for Neutral Particle Reconstruction

### 5a. Replace Shashlik ECAL with **lead-tungstate crystals + SiPM readout**

**Specific technology:** **PWO-II crystals** (as used in CMS ECAL barrel, 23 cm long, 2.2 × 2.2 cm² face) or, more practically, **LYSO:Ce crystals** (better light yield, faster decay time τ ≈ 40 ns) read out by **Hamamatsu S14160-3050HS SiPMs**.

- Energy resolution: improve from ~10%/√E (Shashlik) to **~2–3%/√E** (crystal)
- Critical for: π⁰ and η reconstruction in *B*→*Xγ* radiative decays, *B*→*K*ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ modes where π⁰ veto efficiency is resolution-limited, and lepton universality ratios where photon background control matters
- SiPM readout eliminates conventional PMTs (incompatible with fringe magnetic fields in forward region)

### 5b. Add **timing layer in ECAL** using **LGAD tiles** at shower maximum

- 500 µm thick LGAD with 30 ps timing, tiled behind ~6 X₀ of absorber
- Allows **pile-up cluster separation** in calorimeter at high luminosity (two *B* events in same bunch crossing overlapping in ECAL acceptance)

---

## 6. Muon System Upgrade: Increase Rate Capability and Spatial Resolution

**Replace existing MWPC stations M2–M5 with GEM (Gas Electron Multiplier) detectors:**

**Specific technology:** **Triple-GEM** with 2D strip readout (400/800 µm pitch X/Y strips), based on CMS GE1/1 production experience.

- Rate capability: >10 MHz/cm² (vs. ~1 MHz/cm² for MWPC) — critical near the beam pipe in M1
- Spatial resolution: ~120 µm (vs. ~500 µm MWPC) → better muon candidate matching to tracking, reducing fake-muon rate from punch-through
- Add **µRWELL** (resistive-strip WELL) in the highest-rate innermost region (R < 20 cm from beam) where even GEMs may saturate — these handle >50 MHz/cm²

---

## 7. Magnet and Field Volume Optimization

**Add a second dipole magnet (mini-dipole) immediately downstream of VELO:**

- A compact warm dipole (~0.3 T·m) at z ≈ 1–2 m bends tracks before they enter the tracker proper
- **Purpose:** Measure very-low-momentum tracks (p < 1 GeV/c) that curl before reaching the main magnet — improves reconstruction of soft pions from D*→D⁰π and Bs oscillation tagging via slow pions
- Practical implementation: C-type magnet from iron yoke + copper coils, 50 cm aperture, drawing ~500 kW

---

## Priority Ranking by Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Beneficiary | Estimated Gain |
|---|---|---|
| **MAPS vertex detector + Layer-0** | All heavy-flavour; IP resolution | ×2–3 in signal/background for hadronic modes |
| **Full software GPU trigger** | Hadronic charm, rare hadronic B | ×2–5 efficiency for D⁰, Ds, Λc modes |
| **TORCH PID detector** | Bs→DsK, charm CPV, hadronic B | Fills PID gap, ×1.5–2 in mode separation |
| **SiPM-RICH 2** | High-momentum PID | 15–20% improvement in π/K above 40 GeV/c |
| **Crystal ECAL** | Radiative/rare decays | ×3 improvement in energy resolution |
| **GEM muon stations** | B→J/ψX, rare muonic B decays | Eliminate rate-driven inefficiency at high L |

---

## Summary Principle

The dominant physics gains come from **earlier and more precise tracking** (MAPS sensors closer to IP) and **removing the hardware trigger bottleneck** (GPU-based full-rate reconstruction). These are complementary: you need the former to have the occupancy and resolution for the latter to work cleanly. The PID and calorimeter upgrades are necessary to maintain the full physics programme breadth but are second-order relative to the vertex/trigger combination.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for DarkSide-50 Performance Improvement

## 1. Photosensor Replacement: SiPMs Instead of PMTs

The R11065 PMTs are explicitly identified as the **dominant source of radiogenic neutron background** (>90% of radiogenic neutron background comes from PMT borosilicate glass stems and ceramic dynode plates) and the primary source of γ-ray background requiring the Cherenkov rejection machinery.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace 38 × 3" R11065 PMTs with silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) tile arrays
- Use Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs or similar cryogenic-qualified devices
- Tile arrays of ~6mm × 6mm cells covering equivalent photocathode area (~450 cm² per face)
- Mount on low-radioactivity printed circuit boards using ENIG-free trace routing to eliminate gold activation; use Cirlex or PTFE substrates with electrodeposited copper traces screened to <1 mBq/kg ²³²Th

**Quantified benefit:** Removing the PMT glass/ceramic assemblies eliminates the single largest radiogenic neutron source. The paper states PMTs produce >90% of radiogenic neutrons reaching the fiducial volume. Even partial reduction directly relaxes the neutron veto efficiency requirement and reduces the Cherenkov background that dominates the ER rejection budget.

**Additional photon detection benefit:** SiPMs achieve photon detection efficiency (PDE) of ~50% at 420 nm (post-TPB) at cryogenic temperatures versus ~35% quantum efficiency for R11065 PMTs. This improves S1 photoelectron yield from ~8 PE/keV to potentially ~12-14 PE/keV, directly improving f90 discrimination at low S1 where ER rejection is statistics-limited.

---

## 2. Improved TPB Wavelength Shifting Layer

The paper identifies the Teflon reflector TPB coating as generating the **dominant surviving ER background** (scintillation + Teflon Cherenkov events), because high-energy γ rays scatter in the Teflon and produce Cherenkov photons that mix with LAr scintillation to fake NR-like f90 values.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace evaporated TPB on Teflon with **polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) or tetraphenyl butadiene-doped polystyrene (PS:TPB) cast plates** as a self-supporting reflector/wavelength-shifter combination
- PEN has intrinsic WLS properties with ~80% efficiency shifting 128 nm VUV to ~440 nm, eliminating the separate TPB layer
- Alternatively, use **deuterated polytetrafluoroethylene (DPTFE)** reflector panels with atomic-layer-deposited (ALD) TPB coatings of precisely controlled 1-2 µm thickness
- ALD deposition provides uniform, pinhole-free coatings versus the ~200 µg/cm² evaporated layers currently used, reducing the thickness of material generating slow TPB scintillation that currently limits the LongS1tail background cut efficiency

**Quantified benefit:** The paper notes that TPB-induced millisecond-long scintillation currently provides a veto factor >100 for Type 1 surface events. More uniform TPB would sharpen this discriminant. More importantly, reducing Cherenkov yield from the side reflector directly reduces the dominant ER background that forced the current box boundaries.

---

## 3. Upgraded Field Cage and Electrode Design

The current design uses a grid 4.7 mm beneath the liquid-gas interface to separate drift and extraction regions. The paper identifies cathode and grid surface α decays as requiring z-fiducialization cuts that remove significant active volume.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace the current wire grid with **transparent indium tin oxide (ITO) mesh on fused silica substrate** for the extraction grid
- Use **electroformed copper** rather than welded stainless steel for field cage rings, reducing ²³²Th and ²³⁸U content by ~100× compared to machined stainless (achievable <0.1 mBq/kg vs. ~10 mBq/kg for stainless)
- Implement **thinner cathode geometry**: replace ITO-coated fused silica window cathode with a tensioned 10 µm stainless wire mesh at 95% optical transparency, reducing the total mass of radioactive material at the cathode boundary
- Add **sculpted field rings** using Cirlex polyimide with copper traces rather than stainless steel hoops, reducing γ-ray flux into active volume from field cage hardware

**Quantified benefit:** Reducing electrode radioactivity allows relaxing the 40 µs (≈4 cm) top and bottom z-fiducialization cuts. Recovering even 2 cm at each end on a 35 cm drift region increases fiducial mass by ~11% for the same background rejection.

---

## 4. Cryogenic Preamplifier Relocation and Redesign

The current design mounts cryogenic preamplifiers directly on the PMTs immersed in LAr. The paper notes these preamplifiers are necessary to tame PMT breakdown issues, implying the PMT gain must be run low.

**Specific upgrade:**
- For SiPM-based readout (upgrade #1), implement **cryogenic CMOS application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs)** based on 65 nm or 130 nm processes qualified for 87 K operation
