# Hardware Design Upgrades for a ~50 kg Two-Phase Liquid Argon TPC

## Framing the Problem

For a two-phase LAr TPC in this mass range, the primary physics performance metrics are:

- **S1 light collection efficiency** (sets nuclear recoil energy threshold and S1/S2 discrimination power)
- **S2 electron lifetime / charge yield** (sets low-energy threshold via S2-only analysis)
- **Nuclear recoil / electron recoil discrimination** (PSD + S1/S2 ratio)
- **Fiducialization fidelity** (3D position reconstruction)
- **Radiogenic background suppression** (detector self-shielding + veto efficiency)

Each upgrade below targets one or more of these directly.

---

## 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) Tiled Across Full Solid Angle

**Current limitation:** 3-inch cryogenic PMTs have ~30–35% quantum efficiency (QE) at 128 nm (with appropriate window/coating), finite geometric coverage due to circular packing, non-negligible radioactive contamination in the glass/dynode stack (~tens of mBq/unit), and single-photoelectron resolution that degrades at cryogenic temperatures for some models.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Replace PMT arrays with **tiled arrays of Hamamatsu VUV4 (S13370 series) or Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs**, operated at ~87 K.
- These achieve **~50–60% photon detection efficiency (PDE) at 175 nm** (LAr peak with WLS), compared to ~30% for best cryogenic PMTs.
- Use **1 cm² or 6 cm² tile format** on a custom PCB with cryogenic-rated surface-mount components (thin-film resistors, no electrolytic capacitors).
- Tile the **full cathode plane and anode plane** at close to 100% geometric fill — eliminating the ~50–60% dead area in a hexagonal-packed PMT array.
- Add **SiPM tiles on the barrel/field cage inner surface** using a cylindrical tiling approach (as demonstrated by DarkSide-20k R&D) to capture photons that currently escape laterally.

**Performance impact:**
- Light yield improvement from ~8–10 PE/keV (typical for 3-inch PMT arrays) to **~20–25 PE/keV**, directly lowering the S1 threshold to sub-keV nuclear recoil energies.
- Improved PSD figure of merit because F-prompt discrimination scales with √N_detected; doubling photon statistics improves rejection by ~√2.
- **Radioactivity reduction**: SiPMs contain no glass, no photocathode chemicals — FBK devices have been measured at <1 μBq/cm² ²²⁶Ra equivalent, vs. tens of mBq per PMT.

**Specific part numbers:** FBK NUV-HD-Cryo quad-channel modules (4×(6×6 mm²) per module), Hamamatsu S13371-6050 (6mm VUV4), cold ASIC readout via **DUNE-style COLDADC** or custom **cryogenic trans-impedance amplifier** (e.g., BF862-based discrete cryo-amp).

---

## 2. Tetraphenyl Butadiene (TPB) Coating Optimization with PTFE Reflector Replacement

**Current limitation:** Evaporated TPB films on PTFE reflector panels are the standard approach, but:
- TPB coating uniformity on large PTFE panels is difficult to control (±30% thickness variation is common).
- PTFE has ~95% reflectivity at visible wavelengths but only ~20–30% at 128 nm — the WLS must be on the first surface.
- Uncoated regions (field cage resistors, electrode frames, SiPM/PMT gaps) are dead zones that absorb 128 nm photons.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Replace PTFE reflector panels with **VM2002 (3M ESR) specular reflector laminated with vacuum-deposited TPB**, using the technique developed by the LEGEND-200 collaboration. VM2002 has >99% reflectivity at 420 nm (TPB emission peak).
- Use **dip-coating or spray-coating of TPB in toluene solution** on all interior surfaces including field cage rings (if metallic) — validated to give uniform ~200 μg/cm² films.
- Replace metallic field cage resistors with **custom cryogenic surface-mount thick-film resistors** embedded in the PTFE support structure to minimize uncoated absorbing area.
- Apply **TPB-doped polystyrene films** (PS+TPB cast films, as used in MicroBooNE light collectors) on the barrel where tiling SiPMs cannot reach.

**Performance impact:**
- Photon collection uniformity improvement reduces position-dependent light yield variation from ~15–20% to <5%, directly improving fiducialization quality and PSD uniformity across the fiducial volume.
- Net light yield increase of ~15–25% from better reflector performance.

---

## 3. Underground Argon (UAr) as Target Medium

**Current limitation:** Atmospheric argon (AAr) contains **~1 Bq/kg of ³⁹Ar** (a beta emitter, Q = 565 keV), which creates a pile-up background at the ~100 Hz/kg level. For a 50 kg detector this is ~5 kHz of ³⁹Ar events, imposing severe dead-time and leakage into the WIMP search region even with excellent PSD.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Source **depleted argon from underground gas wells** (the Urania/Aria process developed by DarkSide collaboration): CO₂ well gas contains argon with ³⁹Ar depleted by factor >1400 relative to atmospheric.
- The **Aria cryogenic isotopic separation column** (Sardinia) can further deplete to <0.1 mBq/kg.
- Procure ~100–150 kg of UAr (accounting for inactive regions) from the DarkSide/Global Argon Dark Matter Collaboration supply chain, which is now producing at scale.

**Performance impact:**
- Reduces ³⁹Ar rate from ~5 kHz to **<5 Hz total**, essentially eliminating pile-up.
- Enables lower analysis thresholds (no pile-up rejection cuts needed) and allows S2-only analysis down to single-electron sensitivity.
- Directly enables the **sub-GeV WIMP search** via S2-only threshold below 100 eV nuclear recoil energy.

**Cost/logistics note:** UAr currently costs ~$1–2M per 50 kg batch — realistic for a staged experiment but must be designed into the program from the start.

---

## 4. Charge Readout: Replace Wire Planes with Pixel or Segmented Anode

**Current limitation:** Standard two-phase LArTPCs use a single anode plane (mesh or wires) that collects charge and produces an S2 signal in the gas phase. A single-channel anode gives:
- No transverse position information from charge alone (must rely on S2 light pattern on PMT/SiPM array).
- Limited ability to identify and reject multi-site events within the active volume.
- Sensitivity to single-channel noise as a floor on S2 threshold.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Implement a **segmented anode** using a 2D strip or pixel geometry:
  - **Option A (near-term):** Two perpendicular wire planes (X and Y induction + collection), 3 mm pitch, using **30 μm gold-plated tungsten wire** with crimped/soldered termination on a G10/FR4 tensioning frame. Wire sag must be controlled to <100 μm over ~25 cm span.
  - **Option B (advanced):** **Charge-readout pixel tiles** — LArPix ASICs (developed for DUNE ND-LAr) bump-bonded to 4.434 mm² pixel pads. These self-trigger on charge at ~100 e⁻ threshold, require no external trigger, and give true 3D charge topology.

- For a 50 kg detector (~35 cm diameter active region), a **LArPix tile array of ~4 tiles (each 10×10 cm²)** covering the anode would provide full coverage with ~50 μm equivalent 3D position resolution from charge.

**Performance impact:**
- True 3D event topology enables rejection of **surface backgrounds** (events near PTFE walls reconstructed in X-Y by charge) that pure light-based z-position + light-centroid position cannot cleanly fiducialize.
- Multi-site event rejection (gamma Compton scattering) improves by identifying separated charge clusters — relevant for rejection of ²⁰⁸Tl and other gamma backgrounds.
- S2 threshold improvement: pixel readout eliminates coherent noise across a single collection wire, enabling single-electron S2 sensitivity for sub-GeV dark matter searches.

---

## 5. Electrostatic Grid Upgrade: Electroformed Mesh Replacing Woven Wire

**Current limitation:** The critical grids (cathode, gate, anode screening grid) in most detectors use **woven stainless steel wire mesh**. Weaving introduces:
- Non-uniform wire spacing (±5–10% tension variation)
- Cross-wire solder joints that are radioactive and mechanically fragile
- Optical opacity that degrades light collection
- Electric field non-uniformity at the wire crossings that distorts the extraction field

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Replace all internal wire grids with **electroformed nickel or copper mesh** (photochemically etched, then electroformed to precise thickness):
  - Wire diameter: 50 μm, pitch: 500 μm (achievable by commercial vendors, e.g., Precision Eforming LLC or Tecan)
  - Optical transparency: >95% (vs. ~85% for typical woven mesh)
  - Wire-to-wire tension uniformity: <1%
  - No crossover joints — monolithic sheet

- **Gate grid**: electroformed mesh at 5 mm above liquid surface, biased to define extraction field. Uniform mesh ensures uniform extraction efficiency across the entire liquid surface, eliminating position-dependent S2 gain that currently limits energy resolution.

- **Cathode**: large-area electroformed mesh (or sparse spoke design) to maximize light transmission from the bottom half of the detector to bottom sensors.

**Performance impact:**
- Extraction field uniformity improvement from ~±10% to **<±2%** across the liquid surface → S2 energy resolution improves from ~5% to ~2% at 100 keV, sharpening the ER/NR discrimination band separation.
- Light collection improvement from cathode transparency: ~5–10% more S1 photons detected.

---

## 6. Neutron Veto Upgrade: Gadolinium-Doped Liquid Scintillator with High-Coverage PMT Array

**Current limitation:** A standard organic liquid scintillator (e.g., EJ-301, pseudocumene+PPO) neutron veto relies on hydrogen capture (n + H → D + γ, 2.2 MeV) with a ~200 μs capture time, creating a large dead-time window and modest tagging efficiency (~60–70%) for a thin veto volume.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Dope the veto scintillator with **0.1% by mass gadolinium** using a Gd-carboxylate complex soluble in LAB (linear alkylbenzene) + PPO scintillator — the same formulation validated by EGADS and SNO+.
  - Gd has a thermal neutron capture cross-section of **49,000 barns** (vs. 0.33 barns for H).
  - Capture time drops from ~200 μs to **~30 μs**, reducing coincidence window and accidental rate by 7×.
  - Capture releases **~8 MeV in gamma cascade** (multiple gammas) vs. 2.2 MeV single gamma — much higher detection efficiency.

- Increase PMT coverage of the veto volume to **>20% solid angle** using 8-inch Hamamatsu R5912 or ET Enterprises 9372KB PMTs.
- Add a **fast digitizer (250 MHz, 14-bit, e.g., CAEN V1730)** for the veto PMTs to enable precise time-of-flight neutron tagging.
- Implement an inner **acrylic vessel** (UV-transparent, low-radioactivity) separating the Gd-doped zone from an outer unloaded scintillator buffer to prevent Gd diffusion and maintain optical clarity long-term.

**Performance impact:**
- Neutron tagging efficiency: from ~70% to **>95%** for neutrons above 0.5 MeV kinetic energy (validated by KamLAND-Zen, SNO+).
- Reduced accidentals from shorter capture window → lower veto dead time (<1% vs. ~5%).
- The remaining neutron background (the irreducible floor) drops by a factor of ~10, pushing the experiment toward a coherent neutrino scattering floor limit rather than neutron-limited.

---

## 7. Cryogenic Analog Front-End: Cold Amplifier ASICs

**Current limitation:** In most small LArTPCs, SiPM or PMT signals are transmitted on long coaxial or twisted-pair cables from the cold volume to warm front-end electronics. This introduces:
- Capacitance on the cable that smears the fast SiPM pulse (τ_rise ~1 ns) → degrading PSD
- Johnson noise from cable resistance
- Pickup from external EMI

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Deploy **cryogenic trans-impedance amplifier (TIA) ASICs** directly bonded to or within 2 cm of SiPM tiles:
  - **ABALONE/CACTUS ASIC** (developed by INFN for DarkSide-20k) or **LArASIC** (BNL, adapted for SiPM input impedance): operates at 87 K, ~1 mW/channel, gain-bandwidth product >1 GHz.
  - Integrate **14-bit ADC** at 250 MHz (either on-ASIC or co-located cryogenic ADC) to digitize in the cold and transmit serial data on twisted pairs — dramatically reducing cable count.

- Implement **SiPM signal summing in the cold** with analog summing boards: group 16–64 SiPM channels into one digitizer channel for trigger, while retaining individual channel readout for position reconstruction — reduces data bandwidth 16× for triggering purposes.

**Performance impact:**
- Single-photoelectron time resolution improves from ~5–10 ns (cable-limited) to **<1 ns (intrinsic SiPM jitter)** → F-prompt PSD window can be tightened from 90 ns to **~45 ns** integration window, improving ER/NR discrimination figure of merit by ~15–20%.
- Dark noise (thermal SiPM dark counts, ~100 Hz/mm² at 87 K for FBK NUV-HD) contributes negligible pile-up given the faster integration window.

---

## 8. Field Cage: Resistive PTFE Rings Replacing Discrete Metal Ring + Resistor Chain

**Current limitation:** Conventional field cages use copper or stainless steel rings connected by a resistor divider chain. Resistors are:
- Radioactive (SMD resistors contain ~μBq-level ²²⁶Ra from ceramic binders)

# Hardware Design Upgrades for the ProtoDUNE-SP Detector

## Identification of Primary Physics Performance Limitations

Based on the paper's own performance metrics, operational issues, and stated goals, the critical bottlenecks are:

1. High-voltage instability from charge-up of insulating FC components
2. Photon detection efficiency (measured 0.08-2% depending on technology)
3. Cold electronics noise floor and analog bandwidth
4. Limited self-triggering capability for non-beam physics
5. LAr purity dynamics and spatial non-uniformity

---

## Upgrade 1: Field Cage Insulator Replacement to Eliminate HV Instabilities

**Problem Identified:** The paper describes persistent "current streamers" at 4-6 per day, correlated with charging of FRP/UHMWPE insulating materials in high-field regions. The auto-recovery system interrupted data-taking and the underlying mechanism was never fully resolved.

**Proposed Solution:**

Replace bulk FRP I-beams and UHMWPE endcaps with **ultra-high-purity fused silica (amorphous SiO₂) structural elements** for all components in field regions exceeding 10 kV/cm.

Specific implementation:
- Fused silica has bulk resistivity >10¹⁸ Ω·cm versus ~10¹⁵ for FRP, reducing surface charge accumulation by several orders of magnitude
- Replace UHMWPE profile endcaps with **injection-molded PTFE-encapsulated alumina ceramic caps** — alumina provides superior dielectric strength (~15 kV/mm vs ~20 kV/mm for UHMWPE but with far lower charge trapping cross-section)
- Machine pultruded FRP I-beams out of **Stesalit 4411W glass-fiber/epoxy**, which has demonstrated superior charge dissipation behavior in ATLAS and CMS HV systems
- Apply **resistive surface coating** (sheet resistance ~10¹⁰–10¹² Ω/sq) to all insulating surfaces facing the drift volume using atomic layer deposition (ALD) of Al₂O₃, providing a slow bleed path that prevents charge accumulation without significant current draw at nominal field

**Expected Impact:** Elimination of current streamers would recover the ~2-4% HV uptime loss and remove correlated single-photon backgrounds observed on GP#6, directly improving PDS background rejection for low-energy physics.

---

## Upgrade 2: X-ARAPUCA Photon Detector Replacement Throughout All APA Slots

**Problem Identified:** The paper reports photon detection efficiencies of 0.08% (dip-coated), 0.21% (double-shift), and 2% (ARAPUCA single cell), with the extrapolated full-ARAPUCA system yielding 1.9 photons/MeV at 3.3 m — just barely above the 0.5 PE/MeV specification. The light guide technologies underperform by factors of 10-25× relative to ARAPUCA.

**Proposed Solution:**

Replace all 60 PD module slots with **X-ARAPUCA supercells** using second-generation dichroic filter geometry and enhanced SiPM coverage.

Specific components:
- **Dichroic filters:** Switch from 400 nm cutoff (Omega Optical) to **custom 410 nm cutoff long-pass filters** from Semrock (FF01-410/LP) with steeper transition slope (<5 nm), reducing photon leakage back through the filter by ~40%
- **External WLS:** Replace PTP (P-terphenyl) coating with **evaporated tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) at 300 μg/cm²** on all external filter faces — TPB emission at 425 nm is better matched to the filter cutoff than PTP emission at 350 nm
- **Internal reflector:** Replace VIKUITI ESR (reflectivity ~98%) with **3M Radiant Mirror Film** (reflectivity >99.5% at 430 nm) for internal cell walls, reducing per-bounce losses by factor ~2.5
- **SiPMs:** Replace SensL 35 μm pixel devices with **FBK NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs** (15 μm pixel pitch, PDE ~50% at 420 nm at 77K, dark count rate <10 cps/mm² at 77K) — these are specifically optimized for cryogenic operation unlike the SensL A/C-Series devices which were characterized primarily at room temperature
- **Ganging scheme:** Replace passive resistive ganging (which degrades SNR) with **transimpedance amplifier (TIA) based active ganging** using cryogenic SiGe HBT ASICs (e.g., derived from the LArASIC architecture) placed within the APA slot, reducing effective capacitance from ~500 pF to ~50 pF per readout channel

**Expected Impact:** Conservative projection based on published X-ARAPUCA test results suggests detection efficiency of 8-12% per module, yielding ~15-20 photons/MeV at 3.6 m drift distance — a factor of 8-10 improvement over demonstrated performance. This enables calorimetric energy reconstruction via scintillation light alone and sub-microsecond timing for supernova neutrino physics.

---

## Upgrade 3: Cryogenic Signal Processing ASIC Replacement

**Problem Identified:** The paper reports the ADC ASIC suffered from known cryogenic performance issues (the 320,000 transistor design is noted as complex). ENC of ~400 e⁻ at 77K is achieved, but the collection wire SNR of 13-16 for MIPs leaves limited margin. The paper also notes the ADC ASIC had stability concerns requiring careful transistor design rules.

**Proposed Solution:**

Replace the existing 2-ASIC (FE ASIC + ADC ASIC) architecture with a **monolithic cryogenic readout ASIC** implementing continuous-time analog signal processing followed by a noise-shaped delta-sigma ADC.

Specific implementation:
- Fabricate in **TSMC 65 nm CMOS** (demonstrated cryogenic operation by multiple groups including SLAC and KEK) rather than the current 180 nm process — smaller geometry reduces input MOSFET thermal noise by ~√(180/65) at fixed bias current
- Implement **continuous-time ΔΣ modulation** at 4th order with OSR=64, achieving effective 16-bit resolution at 2 MHz output rate without the metastability issues that plague the SAR/pipeline ADC architectures at 77K
- Integrate **per-channel baseline restoration** using correlated double sampling in the digital domain, eliminating the low-frequency 1/f noise contribution which dominates at cryogenic temperatures where the noise corner frequency shifts
- Target ENC of **150 e⁻ RMS** on collection wires with 150 pF input capacitance, improving MIP SNR from ~15 to ~40
- Reduce power from ~11 mW/channel to **~4 mW/channel** through process node scaling, reducing LAr boil-off from cold electronics heat load
- Add **on-chip 12-tap FIR filter** configurable for matched filtering to the known bipolar/unipolar pulse shapes for U/V/X planes, enabling trigger primitive generation at the FEMB level without routing raw data off-chip

**Expected Implementation Path:** Use the DUNE FD cold electronics ASIC development (COLDATA + COLDADC) as baseline, incorporating the ΔΣ ADC modification which has been prototyped in 65 nm by the LZ experiment's analog front-end group.

---

## Upgrade 4: Distributed Purity Monitoring via Laser Photoionization

**Problem Identified:** The paper notes three discrete purity monitors at fixed heights of 1.8, 3.7, and 5.6 m, which missed the spatial variation shown by the temperature sensors (20 mK horizontal gradients under recirculation). The CFD models show unexplained features ("bump at 6.2 m") not captured by the sparse purity measurement grid.

**Proposed Solution:**

Deploy a **UV laser photoionization purity monitor array** using the existing fiber penetrations, providing 3D purity mapping with O(10 cm) spatial resolution.

Specific components:
- **Laser source:** Nd:YAG pumped OPO system (Ekspla NT342) generating tunable UV output at 118 nm (10th harmonic, Xe-Ar mixing cell) or alternatively a **Kr₂ excimer source at 146 nm** — both above the ~12 eV LAr photoionization threshold of trace impurities but below the 11.6 eV LAr direct ionization threshold, enabling selective impurity detection
- **Fiber delivery:** Replace existing single quartz fibers with **Crystran UVFS (UV fused silica) step-index fibers** rated to 110 nm transmission, routed to a 5×5 grid of collimators distributed across the cathode plane surface
- **Ionization track readout:** Use existing TPC wire readout — each laser pulse creates a straight ionization column whose charge attenuation as a function of drift distance directly measures local electron lifetime with 2 cm spatial bins
- **Timing:** Synchronize to 50 MHz timing system with <1 ns jitter, enabling drift velocity measurement simultaneously with lifetime via the known laser position geometry
- **Rayleigh scatter rejection:** Implement crossed polarization filtering at fiber outputs to suppress 128 nm scintillation backgrounds from the laser-argon interaction

**Expected Impact:** Full 3D electron lifetime map updated every 10 minutes, enabling position-dependent charge calibration corrections at the percent level rather than the current ~15% uncorrected variation shown in Figure 58. Directly resolves the CFD validation puzzle and enables identification of localized contamination sources.

---

## Upgrade 5: Resistive Cathode with Integrated Charge Readout

**Problem Identified:** The paper describes the CPA as a passive resistive surface at uniform potential, with no position-resolved information from the cathode. HV breakdown events cause localized charge deposition with no diagnostic capability. The resistive Kapton D11261075 material provides slow discharge but no active sensing.

**Proposed Solution:**

Instrument the cathode plane with a **segmented resistive charge-sensing layer** using the same CPA mechanical structure.

Specific implementation:
- Replace the monolithic Kapton resistive sheets with **patterned ITO (Indium Tin Oxide) on polyimide substrate** — 5 cm × 5 cm pads at sheet resistance 1 MΩ/sq, providing the same slow-discharge protection while enabling induced charge sensing
- Each pad connects through a **2 GΩ bias resistor** (same voltage isolation function as current design) to a **cryogenic charge amplifier ASIC** mounted on the cathode frame exterior — use SiGe HBT technology (IHP SG13G2 process) demonstrated stable at 77K
- Implement **64-channel multiplexed readout** per CPA module (18 modules × 64 channels = 1152 total cathode channels) digitized at 1 MS/s — sufficient to capture cathode-side induction signals with microsecond timing
- Cathode signals provide: (a) independent measurement of track z-position via charge induction timing, resolving the left-right ambiguity in two-drift-volume geometry; (b) direct localization of HV discharge events; (c) an additional wire-independent measurement for calorimetry cross-checks

**Expected Impact:** This upgrade eliminates the fundamental position ambiguity in the two-drift-volume TPC geometry (which drift volume did the interaction occur in?), improves vertex resolution in z from ~cm to ~mm for contained events, and provides the HV diagnostic capability that the paper acknowledges was insufficient during streamer episodes.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Improved Physics Performance

## Assessment of Primary Physics Drivers

The instrument's core performance limitations derive from: photon detection efficiency (~25% QE standard PMTs), timing resolution (~1.2 ns demonstrated), DOM angular acceptance (downward-facing single PMT), dark noise (~560 Hz dominated by glass sphere radioactivity), and the 125m string spacing limiting low-energy threshold. I'll address each with concrete proposals.

---

## 1. Photon Sensor Replacement

### Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Current limitation:** Hamamatsu R7081-02 achieves 25% QE (34% HQE), with dark noise dominated by the glass sphere rather than the sensor itself. The single downward-facing geometry creates severe angular blind spots.

**Proposed upgrade:**

Deploy multi-SiPM optical modules using tiled SiPM arrays covering the full sphere surface:

- **Sensor:** Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or FBK NUV-HD-SF devices, achieving 50-55% photon detection efficiency at 420nm, roughly doubling photon yield versus standard DOMs
- **Tiling geometry:** 24 SiPM tiles of ~6cm² each arranged in a geodesic pattern across the full sphere, providing 4π angular coverage rather than the current hemispherical acceptance. This directly addresses the reconstruction degeneracy for near-horizontal tracks and improves shower energy resolution
- **Operating temperature advantage:** SiPM dark noise drops dramatically at South Pole temperatures (-30°C to -10°C in ice). At -20°C, dark count rates fall to ~50 kHz/mm², so a 6cm² tile runs at ~30 kHz total, comparable to or better than the current PMT dark noise after accounting for the elimination of glass-sphere scintillation noise since smaller pressure spheres with lower radioactivity become feasible
- **Single photon timing:** SiPMs achieve transit time spreads of ~200ps FWHM versus ~2ns for the R7081, directly improving angular resolution from the current ~0.6° toward ~0.2° for TeV muon tracks

**Specific concern to address:** SiPM correlated noise (optical crosstalk, afterpulsing) must be suppressed. Use FBK's trench-isolated "HD" series with crosstalk below 3%, combined with ASIC-level discrimination to reject correlated pulses within a 5ns window.

**Quantitative physics impact:** Doubling detected photon yield improves energy resolution (currently ~15%) by roughly √2, and the 4π coverage reduces reconstruction systematics for cascade events, potentially improving shower direction resolution from the current ~15° toward ~5°, enabling cascade-based neutrino astronomy.

---

## 2. Waveform Digitization Electronics

### Replace ATWD+fADC with High-Speed Switched-Capacitor Arrays

**Current limitation:** The ATWD samples at 300 Msps with 128 samples (427ns window) and requires ~29μs digitization time per channel, creating deadtime issues. The fADC at 40 Msps provides 6.4μs coverage but with poor timing resolution.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- **Primary digitizer:** DRS4 chip (PSI Villigen) operating at 1-5 Gsps with 1024 capacitor cells, providing 200ns-1μs capture windows at full sampling speed. At 2 Gsps, this gives 512ns coverage with 0.5ns sample spacing, improving on the ATWD's 3.3ns spacing while eliminating the separate slow fADC
- **Complementary long-range digitizer:** Replace fADC with a 250 Msps 12-bit pipeline ADC (e.g., AD9625 or equivalent), providing 6.4μs continuous coverage at 4ns sampling with 12-bit dynamic range versus current 10-bit, expanding the usable dynamic range by 4x
- **Deadtime reduction:** DRS4 ping-pong operation with two chips achieves re-arm in <5ns versus the current 50ns ATWD re-arm, essentially eliminating deadtime for double-pulse events critical for tau neutrino identification
- **FPGA upgrade:** Replace current FPGA with Xilinx Ultrascale+ with embedded ARM core, enabling onboard hit clustering and primitive track reconstruction to reduce data volume before transmission, supporting potential string spacing increases

**Quantitative impact:** The 0.5ns sampling of DRS4 versus 3.3ns ATWD improves the leading-edge photon arrival time determination from ~1ns to ~0.3ns per hit, propagating directly to angular resolution improvement.

---

## 3. Pressure Sphere and Dark Noise Reduction

### Ultra-Low-Background Glass with Integrated Light Guide

**Current limitation:** Dark noise of 560 Hz per DOM is dominated by Cherenkov emission and scintillation from 40K and other radioactive elements in the Benthos borosilicate glass sphere. The 0.03% K₂O concentration contributes ~100 Bq/sphere beta decays.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- **Glass composition:** Switch to Ohara S-FPM2 or equivalent low-radioactivity synthetic silica with K₂O below 0.001% (30x reduction). This material is available from Nikon/Ohara and is used in astronomical optics requiring low radioactivity backgrounds. The higher cost (~5x per sphere) is justified by the science impact
- **Sphere geometry optimization:** Reduce sphere diameter from 13" to 10" for non-PMT sensors or for SiPM-based modules where the PMT bulb no longer constrains minimum diameter. Smaller volume reduces total radioactive mass proportionally
- **Correlated noise elimination:** The current correlated noise burst structure (3-4 hits per burst from glass luminescence) creates false local coincidences that contaminate low-energy analyses. Ultra-low-K glass eliminates this component entirely, improving supernova neutrino detection sensitivity and low-energy dark matter searches
- **Anti-reflective gel reformulation:** Replace current RTV6136-D1 with custom sol-gel coating achieving 99.5% transmission at 340-500nm, particularly improving UV photon collection relevant for shower energy reconstruction

**Quantitative impact:** Reducing dark noise from 560 Hz to ~100 Hz (Poissonian component from PMT thermionic emission only) reduces accidental coincidence rates in low-multiplicity triggers by 5x, enabling the SMT threshold to be reduced from 8 hits to potentially 5 hits, lowering the energy threshold from ~100 GeV to ~30 GeV for standard array strings.

---

## 4. Local Coincidence and Communications Upgrade

### Fiber Optic Intra-String Network

**Current limitation:** Local coincidence uses dedicated copper wire pairs with digital pulse signaling, limited to nearest and next-to-nearest neighbor coincidences within ±1μs. The 720 kbps per twisted pair communications bandwidth constrains data volume and forces aggressive hit compression.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- **Optical fiber backbone:** Deploy hybrid copper-fiber cable replacing current all-copper design. Use 4-fiber bundle (2 working, 2 spare) of radiation-hard pure-silica-core fiber (Fujikura Ultra-Low-Loss or equivalent). Each fiber supports 10 Gbps wavelength-division multiplexed channels using VCSEL transceivers qualified for low-temperature operation
- **Bandwidth impact:** Increase per-string bandwidth from 720 kbps to 10 Gbps, enabling transmission of all waveforms (not just HLC hits) to surface. This eliminates the current SLC hit compression that loses waveform information for isolated photons, which are particularly important for low-energy events where few DOMs trigger
- **Extended local coincidence:** With 10 Gbps fiber, implement software-defined coincidence windows at surface rather than hardware-defined ±1μs in DOM. This allows retrospective application of different coincidence criteria for different physics analyses and extends coincidence checking across the full string in <15μs (string light travel time)
- **Connector technology:** SEACON connectors have historically contributed to deployment failures. Replace with Diamond ODVA underwater fiber connectors qualified to 700 bar, with O-ring and epoxy double-seal

**Mechanical considerations:** Pure silica fiber withstands the freeze-in pressure (690 bar demonstrated for copper) but requires careful jacketing. Use tight-buffered fiber with Kevlar strength member in a 3mm outer diameter unit, incorporated into the cable quad structure replacing one copper pair.

**Quantitative impact:** Full waveform readout of all 5160 DOMs at current hit rates requires ~5 Gbps per string at peak atmospheric muon rates, accommodated by the 10 Gbps fiber. This eliminates the information loss in ~40% of hits that currently carry only SLC charge stamps.

---

## 5. In-Ice Calibration System Enhancement

### Deployable Isotropic Nanosecond Pulsed Light Sources

**Current limitation:** The flasher board LEDs are collimated (σ=9-10° in ice) and limited to 405nm plus four additional wavelengths in cDOMs. Timing calibration achieves 1.2ns precision, but ice optical property measurements are limited by the non-isotropic LED emission profiles and sparse wavelength coverage.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- **Isotropic pulsers:** Replace directional LEDs with integrating sphere-coupled fiber pigtails from a central high-power picosecond laser diode (PicoQuant LDH series). A single 405nm laser diode with fiber splitter illuminates 12 output ports with frosted diffuser caps, achieving <1° angular variation in output intensity. Pulse width of 50ps FWHM at source (versus current 6ns) improves timing calibration precision to <0.3ns
- **Multi-wavelength coverage:** Add laser diodes at 337nm (ice absorption edge), 470nm (peak scattering sensitivity), and 532nm (low scattering reference) in addition to existing 405nm. This enables precise wavelength-dependent scattering and absorption measurement during regular operations rather than requiring dedicated calibration campaigns
- **Absolute photon counting:** Incorporate a monitor photodiode with NIST-traceable calibration directly on the flasher board to establish absolute photon output per pulse to 1% accuracy. Current system has ~10% absolute efficiency uncertainty that limits dark matter search sensitivity and point source flux measurements
- **Timing reference pulse:** Transmit a fiber-coupled reference pulse directly to an onboard SiPM monitor simultaneously with each flasher pulse, providing sub-100ps jitter reference for inter-DOM timing calibration

**Quantitative impact:** Reducing absolute photon detection efficiency uncertainty from 10% to 3% directly reduces the dominant systematic uncertainty in astrophysical neutrino flux measurements and dark matter annihilation cross-section limits.

---

## 6. RAPCal Timing System Upgrade

### White Rabbit Precision Timing Protocol

**Current limitation:** RAPCal achieves ~1.2ns timing precision using 20 MHz ADC sampling with interpolated zero-crossing. The master clock GPS receiver and fanout tree introduce correlated timing errors across the array.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- **White Rabbit protocol:** Replace the current proprietary RAPCal scheme with the White Rabbit precision timing protocol (CERN/NIKHEF), which uses Synchronous Ethernet combined with IEEE 1588v2 PTP to achieve sub-nanosecond synchronization across all nodes. White Rabbit is already deployed in KM3NeT and gravitational wave detector networks
- **Hardware:** Install White Rabbit Switch 18 (WRS18) units as timing distribution nodes in the ICL, with White Rabbit-capable DOR card replacement providing 10 MHz reference to each DOM. The DOM Main Board clock oscillator is replaced with a 125 MHz VCXO phase-locked to the distributed White Rabbit reference
- **GPS redundancy:** Add a second GPS disciplined oscillator (Microsemi XLi or equivalent) with independent antenna, combined with a hydrogen maser reference for the ~3 hour daily satellite communication gap, maintaining <1ns absolute timing accuracy continuously
- **In-DOM precision:** Replace the current 20 MHz RAPCal ADC with a 1 Gsps TDC-equivalent measurement using a Cyclone V SoC FPGA with tapped delay line interpolation, achieving 50ps timing precision per RAPCal measurement versus current 1ns

**Quantitative impact:** Improving timing from 1.2ns to 0.3ns per DOM improves muon track angular resolution from 0.6° toward 0.3° at 10 TeV, directly doubling the point source sensitivity for neutrino astronomy by reducing the angular search bin area by 4x.

---

## 7. DOM Power System Redesign

### Resonant Inductive Power Transfer with DC-DC Optimization

**Current limitation:** DOMs receive 96VDC from series-connected Acopian supplies over copper pairs with 160Ω loop resistance specification, consuming 5.7W average per DOM with significant transmission losses. The 96V requirement constrains cable design and represents a single-point failure mode.

**Proposed upgrade:**

- **Higher voltage DC bus:** Increase DOM supply voltage from 96V to 400VDC, reducing cable I²R losses by 17x for the same power delivery. This allows use of thinner conductor gauge in new cables (0.5mm versus current 0.9mm), reducing cable weight and diameter
- **DC-DC converter efficiency:** Replace current DOM internal power converter with a GaN-based converter (Efficient Power Conversion EPC2045 series), achieving 95% efficiency versus estimated 85% current efficiency, reducing heat dissipation in the DOM from ~0.8W to ~0.3W thermal, which is relevant for dark noise reduction
- **Per-string current monitoring:** Upgrade DOR card current monitoring from current simple threshold fuse to a high-resolution 16-bit ADC monitoring each twisted pair at 100Hz, enabling early detection of insulation degradation before catastrophic failure and improved diagnosis of intermittent connection issues responsible for some of the 55 deployment/freeze-in failures observed

---

## Priority Ranking and Implementation Path

| Upgrade | Physics Impact | Technical Risk | Deployment Complexity |
|---------|---------------|----------------|----------------------|
| SiPM multi-PMT module | Very High | Medium | High (new DOM design) |
| DRS4 digitization | High | Low | Medium (electronics swap) |
| Low-background glass | High | Low | Low (drop-in replacement) |
| Fiber optic cable | High | Medium | High (new cable design) |
| Isotropic calibration sources | Medium | Low | Low (flasher board swap) |

The highest immediate return would come from the **low-background glass sphere** combined with **SiPM-based multi-PMT modules** in new string deployments, as these address the two most fundamental limitations: dark noise floor and photon collection efficiency. The **White Rabbit timing upgrade** is deployable in existing infrastructure and would immediately improve angular resolution for all ongoing analyses. For IceCube-Gen2, all of these upgrades should be incorporated into the baseline design from the outset rather than retrofitted.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for GERDA

## 1. Detector Technology: Transition to All-BEGe or Point-Contact Geometry

The Phase I coaxial detectors achieve only modest pulse shape discrimination (PSD). The paper notes BEGe detectors have "good pulse shape discrimination properties" but only five were deployed.

**Specific upgrades:**
- Replace all remaining coaxial HPGe diodes with **BEGe or inverted-coaxial point-contact (ICPC) geometry** detectors from the Phase II enriched material
- Point-contact geometry produces a highly non-uniform weighting potential, giving A/E (current amplitude to energy ratio) parameters with clean single-site versus multi-site separation; signal acceptance ~90% with background rejection ~80% for surface alpha events
- Target detector mass per unit: 0.8–1.0 kg per BEGe, fabricated from the 35.5 kg of 6N-purity enriched Ge already zone-refined at Canberra Oak Ridge
- Specify crystal dislocation density <5000 cm⁻², net carrier concentration 10⁹–10¹⁰ cm⁻³ to maximize charge collection uniformity

**Expected gain:** PSD alone suppresses the background index by a factor of ~3–5 within the ROI, directly attacking the 2.0×10⁻² cts/(keV·kg·yr) Phase I result.

---

## 2. LAr Scintillation Veto: Full Implementation for Phase II

The paper describes LArGe R&D demonstrating LAr scintillation light veto feasibility, and states "Gerda decided to implement a LAr scintillation light veto for Phase II" but it is absent from Phase I. This is the single highest-impact missing subsystem.

**Specific upgrades:**

### Wavelength Shifting and Light Guides
- Coat all inner surfaces of the mini-shroud and detector string support structures with **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB)** at 0.2–0.5 mg/cm² surface density, shifting LAr scintillation from 128 nm VUV to ~420 nm visible
- Use **VM2000 reflector foil** (already deployed in the water tank, reflectivity >99% at 400–775 nm) as an inner barrel around the detector array, coated with TPB on the LAr-facing side
- Implement **wavelength-shifting fibers** (Kuraray Y11, already used in plastic scintillator panels) running vertically along the inner radon shroud to channel shifted photons upward toward photosensors

### Photosensors
- Deploy **Hamamatsu R11065 3-inch low-radioactivity PMTs** in the LAr volume, mounted on the top and bottom flanges of the radon shroud
  - Specified radioactivity: <5 mBq/unit ²²⁶Ra, <2 mBq/unit ²²⁸Th — already achievable with selected Hamamatsu low-background glass
  - Target: 16–20 PMTs giving ~15% geometric coverage of the instrumented LAr volume
- Alternative/supplement: **SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu MPPC S10931-050P or equivalent)** operated at LAr temperature (87 K)
  - These were not mature enough for large-area deployment at the time of Phase I design, but by the Phase II deployment window offer: no radioactive glass envelope, <0.1 g mass per unit, operation at 87 K demonstrated in test stands
  - Array of ~100 SiPMs with 6×6 mm² active area each, mounted on low-radioactivity PCB (Cuflon substrate, already used for CC2) arranged in rings inside the radon shroud
  - Require bias voltage of ~70 V at 87 K; noise dominated by dark counts (~10⁻² Hz/mm² at 87 K vs. MHz/mm² at room temperature)

### Integration with DAQ
- Add dedicated VME FADCs (SIS3301 type, already used for muon veto) with 100 MHz sampling for LAr PMT/SiPM channels
- Hardware coincidence: LAr veto signal within ±1 µs of Ge trigger suppresses Compton-scattered gamma events that deposit partial energy in Ge and remainder in LAr

**Expected gain:** LAr veto provides additional background suppression factor ~3 beyond PSD alone for the dominant gamma-ray backgrounds, particularly ²⁰⁸Tl and ²¹⁴Bi lines visible in Table 8.

---

## 3. Front-End Electronics: Replace CC2 with Lower-Noise Cold ASIC

The CC2 preamplifier uses commercial components (BF862 JFET, AD8651 op-amp) in commercial packages not optimized for LAr operation or radiopurity. Energy resolution of 4.2–5.1 keV FWHM at 2614 keV is above the theoretical limit.

**Specific upgrades:**
- Develop a **custom CMOS or BiCMOS charge-sensitive preamplifier ASIC** for operation at 87 K
  - Input transistor: **custom n-channel JFET in 0.35 µm or 0.5 µm CMOS process**, sized for optimal noise at detector capacitance of 15–40 pF (BEGe detectors have ~2–5 pF, coaxial ~30–40 pF)
  - Target: equivalent noise charge (ENC) of 50–80 electrons RMS at BEGe capacitance, versus current ~150 electrons
  - Eliminate the AD8651 second-stage op-amp (SOIC package, non-trivial radioactivity contribution from package leads) by integrating full CSP on single die
  - Fabricate on **high-resistivity silicon substrate** to minimize substrate leakage at cryogenic temperature
- Replace tantalum filter capacitors with **silicon-based integrated capacitors** on ASIC to eliminate the dominant radioactive component (Ta: ¹⁸⁰Ta cosmogenic activation)
- PCB substrate: retain Cuflon (already qualified) but reduce board area by factor ~3 through ASIC integration
- Power consumption target: <15 mW/channel (vs. current <45 mW/channel) to reduce thermal load on LAr and microphonics

**Expected gain:** Energy resolution improvement to 2.0–2.5 keV FWHM at Qββ for BEGe detectors (from current 4.5 keV mass-weighted average), directly narrowing the ROI and reducing background events counted proportionally.

---

## 4. Radon Mitigation: Active Radon Barrier System

The paper reports final cryostat ²²²Rn emanation of (54.7±3.5) mBq, contributing ~7×10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) if uniformly distributed. The radon shroud provides passive mitigation but its effectiveness depends on its tightness.

**Specific upgrades:**
- Replace the 30 µm copper foil radon shroud with a **double-walled electroformed copper cylinder** (electroformed copper achieves <0.01 mBq/kg ²²⁶Ra vs. rolled copper foil)
  - Inner diameter: 750 mm (same as current shroud)
  - Wall thickness: 0.5 mm electroformed + 0.5 mm electroformed with 2 mm gap between walls
  - Gap continuously purged with **radon-depleted argon gas** at slight overpressure (100 Pa)
- Install a dedicated **radon-trapping column** specifically for the gas phase above the LAr surface inside the radon shroud
  - Use activated charcoal (Carbo-Act International, already qualified) at controlled temperature of -40°C to -60°C where radon adsorption coefficient is maximized
  - Column mass: 500 g, integrated into the manifold feedthrough path
  - Expected radon reduction factor: >100 for the inner volume based on results cited (>1000 reduction demonstrated in gas phase with 150 g trap)
- Upgrade all O-ring seals in the lock system from Kalrez to **metal C-seal or Helicoflex delta-seal** wherever geometry permits, eliminating the remaining ~1 mBq contribution from elastomer seals

---

## 5. Mini-Shroud Redesign: Hermetic Electroformed Copper with Integrated Fiber Veto

The current 60 µm Cu foil mini-shroud effectively suppresses ⁴²K collection but is a mechanical compromise.

**Specific upgrades:**
- Fabricate mini-shrouds from **electroformed copper** (0.3 mm wall, OFHC grade, <0.01 mBq/kg ²²⁸Th demonstrated at MPIK)
  - Hermetically welded top and bottom caps with single-point LAr fill holes (1 mm diameter) to equilibrate pressure while blocking ion drift
  - Mass per shroud: ~150 g (comparable to current foil approach but with better radiopurity)
- Integrate **TPB-coated inner surface** on the mini-shroud to serve simultaneously as the near-field LAr scintillation light collector
- Add **light-tight feed-throughs** at the top cap for 4–6 wavelength-shifting fibers (Y11 type) routing scintillation light to SiPMs above the LAr surface, outside the high-radioactivity zone near detectors

---

## 6. Calibration System: Replace ²²⁸Th with ⁵⁶Co or ²²⁸Th at Reduced Activity

The paper notes a dropped source contributing ≤1.1×10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr) as a permanent background. The steel band rupture demonstrated a reliability concern.

**Specific upgrades:**

- Reduce source activity from ~22 kBq to ~5 kBq ²²⁸Tl equivalent by using sources with thicker tantalum self-absorption, maintaining calibration statistics within acceptable weekly run time (~2 hours vs. current ~1 hour)
- Add a **fourth calibration source port** on the cluster flange specifically for a ²²⁸Th source deployable to the bottom of the detector array, improving energy calibration uniformity for extended Phase II array

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Advanced Gravitational-Wave Interferometer Performance

## Framing the Problem

Primary physics performance means **strain sensitivity** across the detection band (~10 Hz – 10 kHz), which is limited by a well-characterized noise hierarchy. I'll address each dominant noise floor systematically, proposing concrete upgrades with realistic technology specifications.

---

## 1. Quantum Noise: The Dominant Broadband Limitation

### 1a. Frequency-Dependent Squeezing via Filter Cavities

**Current state:** Injection of ~10–15 dB frequency-independent squeezed light trades shot noise for radiation pressure noise at a fixed rotation angle.

**Upgrade:**
- Install a **300–400 m suspended filter cavity** (or two cascaded ~100 m cavities) with finesse ~5,000–10,000 in a dedicated vacuum enclosure adjacent to each main interferometer
- Use **EPR (Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen) entanglement-based squeezing** as an alternative: two bright beams in a two-mode squeezed state, eliminating the separate filter cavity and its round-trip losses
- Target: 10 dB effective squeezing across the full band by rotating the squeezing ellipse from ~10 Hz to ~10 kHz

**Specific components:**
- Periodically-poled KTP (PPKTP) or periodically-poled RTP nonlinear crystals in bow-tie optical parametric oscillators, pumped at 532 nm (for 1064 nm signal)
- Low-loss Faraday isolators with terbium gallium garnet (TGG) crystals, AR-coated to <50 ppm per surface
- Output mode cleaner cavities with finesse >2,000 to reduce higher-order mode content before homodyne detection

**Expected gain:** 6–8 dB improvement in shot-noise-limited high-frequency sensitivity (>200 Hz)

---

### 1b. Signal Recycling Cavity Detuning and Variational Readout

**Upgrade:**
- Transition from resonant sideband extraction to **detuned signal recycling** with tunable signal recycling mirror (SRM) reflectivity (R ~ 0.93) to create an optomechanical resonance near 50–100 Hz
- Implement **variational readout** (frequency-dependent homodyne angle) using the filter cavity output to measure the back-action-evading quadrature below the SQL
- Install a **speed meter topology** variant: a sloshing cavity between the two arm cavities couples the output to velocity rather than position, reducing radiation pressure noise without sacrificing shot noise

**Specific hardware:**
- SRM with *in-situ* adjustable tilt via piezo-actuated tip-tilt suspension stage
- Balanced homodyne detector with quantum efficiency η > 99% (custom InGaAs photodiodes with anti-reflection coating)
- Output Faraday isolator with <0.3 dB insertion loss

---

## 2. Thermal Noise: The Mid-Band Floor (~30–300 Hz)

### 2a. Test Mass Material Upgrade to Crystalline Silicon

**Why:** Fused silica at room temperature has mechanical loss angle φ ~ 10⁻⁷; crystalline silicon at 123 K has φ ~ 10⁻⁹, a ~100× improvement. Thermoelastic noise also vanishes at 123 K where the CTE of silicon crosses zero.

**Upgrade:**
- Replace 40 kg fused silica test masses with **200 kg octagonal silicon test masses** (e.g., 55 cm diameter × 55 cm thick), grown by the float-zone method for <10¹² oxygen atoms/cm³
- Optical path: switch from 1064 nm Nd:YAG to **2 µm Tm:fiber laser** or **1550 nm Er:fiber laser** (silicon is transparent at both; 2 µm preferred for lower quantum noise at equivalent power due to lower photon energy)
- Cool test masses to **123 K** via conductive cooling through the suspension fibers

**Specific components:**
- Silicon ribbon or **crystalline silicon fiber** suspensions replacing fused-silica fibers (silicon fibers drawn from float-zone boules, ~1.5 mm diameter, ~60 cm length per stage)
- Cryogenic baffles and cold shields around test masses: multi-layer insulation blankets, liquid nitrogen pre-cooling stage, pulse-tube cryocoolers thermally isolated from mirror suspension
- 2 µm high-power laser: cryogenically cooled Tm:YAG or Ho:YAG master oscillator with fiber power amplifier to 200 W CW, then power-recycled to ~2 MW intracavity

**Expected gain:** ~10–30× reduction in coating and substrate thermal noise in 30–300 Hz band

---

### 2b. Amorphous vs. Crystalline Optical Coatings

**Current limitation:** Ion-beam-sputtered (IBS) Ta₂O₅/SiO₂ coatings dominate thermal noise; loss angle φcoating ~ 4 × 10⁻⁴.

**Upgrade options (in priority order):**

**Option A – Amorphous silicon (a-Si) / SiO₂ coatings:**
- a-Si has refractive index ~3.5 at 2 µm, enabling fewer layers (lower total coating thickness) for the same reflectivity
- Deposit by plasma-enhanced CVD or IBS; anneal at 400–600°C to reduce network defect density
- Loss angle at 120 K: φ ~ 5×10⁻⁵ (estimated), ~8× better than room-temperature Ta₂O₅

**Option B – Epitaxial AlGaAs/GaAs crystalline mirror coatings:**
- Grow by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) on GaAs substrates, bond to silicon test mass via room-temperature direct bonding or adhesive-free hydroxide-catalysis bonding
- Loss angle φ < 4×10⁻⁶ (measured at room temperature), potentially ~100× better than IBS coatings
- Demonstrated at small apertures (75 mm); scale-up to 350 mm diameter requires novel MBE chamber design
- Challenge: GaAs/AlGaAs transparent only at wavelengths >870 nm; compatible with 1550 nm or 2 µm operation

**Option C – LPCVD silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) coatings:**
- Loss angle ~1×10⁻⁵ at room temperature; stoichiometry tunable via N₂/SiH₄ ratio
- Suitable for near-IR wavelengths

**Recommended path:** AlGaAs crystalline coatings bonded to silicon substrates, operated at 123 K, for ~30–100× improvement in coating thermal noise

---

### 2c. Suspension Thermal Noise Reduction

**Current:** Fused-silica fiber suspension (last stage), loss angle limited by surface contamination and weld joints.

**Upgrade:**
- Replace with **single-crystal silicon blade springs + silicon fiber** suspension at the last two stages, all operating at 123 K
- Use **geometric anti-spring (GAS) blades** in MARAGING steel (upper stages) or silicon at intermediate stages to lower effective vertical resonance from ~10 Hz to ~0.1 Hz, moving suspension thermal noise out of detection band
- Implement **negative stiffness Euler spring** assemblies for horizontal isolation at each stage

**Specific hardware:**
- Silicon fibers welded by CO₂ laser (10.6 µm) to silicon ears bonded to test mass via hydroxide-catalysis bonding
- Blade springs with tunable tilt compensation (feedback via low-noise piezostacks, noise < 10⁻¹⁴ m/√Hz above 10 Hz)

---

## 3. Seismic and Newtonian (Gravity Gradient) Noise

### 3a. Newtonian Noise Subtraction Array

**Newtonian noise** (gravity gradient from seismic density fluctuations in local ground) is a fundamental floor below ~20 Hz that is **not attenuated by seismic isolation**.

**Upgrade:**
- Deploy an array of **seismometers in a 3D arrangement** around each test mass: 6–8 seismometers in boreholes at depths 5–30 m and on the surface within ~30 m radius
- Use **tiltmeters** (Nanometrics Titan or custom vertical-axis atom interferometer sensors) to separate tilt from translation
- Real-time **Wiener filter or neural-network-based subtraction** of the estimated gravity gradient signal from the differential arm length readout

**Specific instruments:**
- Nanometrics Trillium Compact or Guralp CMG-3T broadband seismometers (self-noise < −170 dB rel. 1 m²/s³/Hz at 0.1 Hz)
- Custom 6-axis rotation sensors (ring laser gyroscopes or fiber optic gyroscopes) at each corner station
- 100-channel real-time DSP system with latency <1 ms for feedforward subtraction

**Expected gain:** Factor of 3–10 reduction in noise floor below 20 Hz (unlocking the 10–30 Hz band significantly)

---

### 3b. Seismic Isolation Platform Upgrade

**Current:** Hydraulic external pre-isolator (HAM-ISI, BSC-ISI) + multi-stage pendulum in LIGO Advanced design.

**Upgrade:**
- Add a **6-DOF active platform** stage using inertial sensors with lower noise floor:
  - Replace current L4C geophones with **broadband seismometers** (noise floor ~10⁻¹¹ m/√Hz at 1 Hz) or **cold-atom inertial sensors** (no mechanical resonance, flat response 0.1 mHz – 10 Hz)
  - Use voice-coil / Lorentz actuators with bias-field magnets outside vacuum for low-noise actuation
- Install **nested Euler spring isolation tables** at room temperature stages to provide passive attenuation of ~100 dB/decade above ~0.1 Hz before active stages
- Consider **cryogenic seismic isolation platforms** co-located with cryogenic test masses, using **phononic crystal vibration isolators** machined from silicon or aluminum with periodic mass-in-mass structures tuned to block transmission at 1–10 Hz

**Expected gain:** 10–100× improvement in transmitted seismic noise at 5–30 Hz

## 4. Laser Noise and Optical Power

### 4a. High-Power, Low-Noise 2 µm Laser Source

**Upgrade (for silicon test mass scenario):**
- **Master oscillator:** CW Tm:YAG or Tm-doped fiber ring laser at 2090 nm, linewidth <1 Hz via Pound-Drever-Hall lock to a reference cavity
- **Power amplifier chain:** Tm:fiber MOPA (Master Oscillator Power Amplifier) to 200 W, then Tm:YAG rod amplifier to 500 W
- **Intensity noise:** Two-stage AOM (acousto-optic modulator) pre-stabilization + in-loop intensity servo to achieve RIN < 10⁻⁹/√Hz above 10 Hz
- **Frequency stabilization:** Pre-stabilized to a rigid reference cavity (finesse > 50,000, mounted on a seismically isolated platform), then length-and-frequency servo to the common-mode arm

**For near-term 1064 nm operation:**
- Upgrade to Nd:YAG **master oscillator + Yb:fiber power amplifier** to 500 W pre-input-mode-cleaner power
- Power recycling gain × arm finesse → ~4 MW intracavity arm power (limited by parametric instability and coating absorption)

---

### 4b. Parametric Instability Control

Higher intracavity power excites **opto-mechanical parametric instabilities** (3-mode interactions between TEM₀₀ carrier, higher-order optical modes, and acoustic modes of test masses).

**Upgrade:**
- **Ring dampers:** Annular lossy coatings (e.g., silicone rubber rings) bonded to the barrel of test masses to damp mechanical Q without affecting mirror surface
- **Electrostatic drive (ESD) ring:** Low-noise electrostatic actuator for active damping of specific acoustic modes identified by an acoustic mode monitor
- **Active mode tuning:** Thermally tune the radius of curvature of input test masses via CO₂ laser spot heating of the mirror surface (0.5–5 W CW at mirror center), shifting higher-order mode spacing away from mechanical resonances

---

## 5. Photodetection Upgrades

### 5a. High-Quantum-Efficiency Homodyne Detectors

**Upgrade:**
- Replace RF-readout (heterodyne) with **DC balanced homodyne** detection (eliminates carrier-frequency photon shot noise from LO fringe)
- Use custom **large-area InGaAs photodiodes** (2 mm diameter) with quantum efficiency η > 99.5% at 1064 nm or η > 95% at 2 µm (InGaAs or extended-InGaAs)
- Transimpedance amplifier using JFET input stage (e.g., IF3602 or similar) with input-referred current noise < 2 pA/√Hz and voltage noise < 1 nV/√Hz

**Upgrade:**
- Extend arm length from 4 km to **10–20 km** (or build underground to reduce seismic and Newtonian noise baseline)
- Underground site (e.g., ~200 m depth): reduces surface seismic noise by ~10–100× and gravity gradient noise by reduced soil density fluctuation coupling
- The Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer designs formalize this: 10 km triangular underground (ET-D) or 20–40 km L-shape surface (CE)

# Hardware Design Upgrades for DarkSide-50 Physics Performance

## 1. Photomultiplier Tube Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Primary motivation:** The PMTs are identified as the dominant source of radiogenic neutron background (>90%) and the primary source of Cherenkov background contamination.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the 38 Hamamatsu R11065 PMTs with cryogenic SiPM tiles, specifically devices like the Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-Cryo series or Hamamatsu S13370 cryogenic-grade SiPMs
- The borosilicate glass stems and ceramic dynode supports in the PMTs are the identified radioactive culprits; SiPMs contain essentially no borosilicate glass and eliminate ceramic dynode structures entirely
- Array geometry: tile the top and bottom windows with ~1 cm² SiPM cells in a hexagonal close-packed configuration, achieving ~85% photon detection efficiency coverage versus the current sparse PMT arrays
- Key specification target: <1 μBq/kg of ²³²Th and ²³⁸U in the SiPM substrate and packaging, achievable with silicon-based devices versus the current PMT activities of ~0.277 Bq total ²³²Th
- Eliminates the fused silica PMT windows as Cherenkov radiators simultaneously, removing one of the two identified Cherenkov background channels
- Expected impact: >10× reduction in radiogenic neutron background, >5× reduction in Cherenkov background, enabling a much larger fiducial volume

**Tradeoffs to manage:** SiPM dark count rates at LAr temperatures (~87K) are manageable (~0.1 Hz/mm² at 87K for modern devices), correlated noise (optical crosstalk ~3-5%) requires careful signal processing, and the preamplifier architecture described in the paper would need redesign for the higher channel count.

---

## 2. Replacement of Teflon Reflector with Radiopure Polytetrafluoroethylene + Elimination of Cherenkov-Active Materials

**Primary motivation:** The paper explicitly identifies scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov events as "the dominant background in the experiment" after all cuts, and the cylindrical side wall as the primary remaining Cherenkov source after the S1pMaxFrac cut removes fused-silica Cherenkov events.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the current Teflon (PTFE) cylindrical reflector with **deuterated polyethylene (dPE) or ultra-pure PTFE** sintered under cleanroom conditions with verified low-radioactivity feedstock, but more importantly address the Cherenkov yield
- The fundamental issue is that PTFE has a refractive index of ~1.35 at 420 nm; the Cherenkov threshold for electrons in PTFE is ~0.4 MeV, directly accessible from the ²⁰⁸Tl 2.6 MeV γ-ray Compton continuum
- **Primary upgrade:** Line the inner Teflon surface with a thin (~1 mm) layer of **specular reflector material with refractive index <1.05**, such as an aerogel-based coating or a multilayer dielectric coating on a low-Z substrate, to raise the Cherenkov threshold above the energies accessible from dominant γ-ray backgrounds
- Alternative approach: Replace the side-wall TPB coating application with a **thin evaporated TPB layer on a deuterated polystyrene substrate**, which has a higher Cherenkov threshold due to lower electron density, combined with a wavelength-shifting efficiency >90%
- Implement **active tagging** of the Teflon region by embedding wavelength-shifting fibers read out by dedicated SiPMs in the outer Teflon structure, providing coincidence rejection of Cherenkov-producing events
- Expected impact: The paper's analysis required a 1.5× upward scaling factor on the model and a 2.3× rejection penalty from radial fiducialization specifically because of Teflon Cherenkov; eliminating this background relaxes both corrections and recovers ~3.5× in effective exposure

---

## 3. Upgraded Liquid Scintillator Veto with Higher Light Yield and Gadolinium Loading

**Primary motivation:** The current boron-loaded LSV achieves 99.64% neutron veto efficiency, which is excellent, but the remaining neutron budget (<0.005 events) could be further reduced, and the ER rejection efficiency (~1/3 of γ-rays) is modest.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the current borated liquid scintillator (30 t) with **gadolinium-loaded liquid scintillator at 0.1% Gd by mass**, using the chemical formulation developed for CHOOZ/Double Chooz (Gd-β-diketonate in pseudocumene/dodecane)
- Gadolinium's thermal neutron capture cross section is 49,000 barns versus ¹⁰B's 3,840 barns, and the Gd capture releases 8 MeV in γ-rays versus the ¹⁰B α+γ at 2.79 MeV total, providing a much higher-energy, cleaner capture signal above the γ-ray background
- Capture time in 0.1% Gd-LS is ~30 μs, comparable to the current boron system's 22 μs, preserving the delayed-capture search window
- Increase the LSV photomultiplier coverage from the current configuration to achieve >25% photocathode coverage using high-QE bialkali PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R7081-20), improving the γ-ray detection efficiency from ~33% toward ~60%
- Install a **segmented inner veto** of 5 cm thickness of Gd-loaded plastic scintillator panels directly surrounding the TPC cryostat, read out by SiPMs, providing a 4π active veto layer with sub-100 ns timing for coincidence rejection of Compton scatters
- Expected impact: Neutron veto efficiency >99.99%, γ-ray veto efficiency doubling, allowing the LSV prompt threshold to be lowered, substantially reducing the ER background that relies on the veto for rejection

---

## 4. Improved Electric Field Cage and Cathode Design for Enhanced Electron Lifetime and S2 Quality

**Primary motivation:** The paper notes that S2/S1 discrimination is ineffective at low S1 (where it is most needed) partly due to electron collection efficiency issues; surface events show heavily suppressed S2; and the 200 V/cm drift field leaves room for improvement in charge yield.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the current ITO-coated fused silica cathode with a **fine-mesh wire grid cathode** (100 μm diameter electropolished copper-beryllium wires at 1 mm pitch), eliminating the fused silica as a Cherenkov radiator at the bottom of the active volume
- This directly removes one of the Cherenkov-producing surfaces while improving field uniformity
- Upgrade from 200 V/cm to **400-600 V/cm drift field**: at 400 V/cm, the argon ionization yield increases by ~30% and the recombination fraction decreases, improving the S2/S1 discrimination power at all energies; the SCENE measurements referenced in the paper extend to this range
- Install **field-shaping rings** of higher radiopurity copper (OFHC grade, <1 ppb U/Th) at 5 mm spacing along the side wall, replacing or supplementing whatever current field cage exists, to achieve <1% field non-uniformity across the active volume
- Add a **liquid-level monitoring system** using capacitive sensors at the liquid-gas interface accurate to ±0.1 mm, stabilizing the gas pocket thickness and thus S2 gain to <0.1% variation
- Increase extraction field from the current unspecified value to >3 kV/cm in the gas phase, improving single-electron detection efficiency and S2 light yield per extracted electron
- Expected impact: 30-50% improvement in S2/S1 discrimination at low energies, better radial position reconstruction (since S2 size improves), enabling the MaxS2/S1 cut to be effective at lower S1 where the paper identifies it as currently insufficient

---

## 5. Cryogenic Preamplifier and Digitizer Upgrade for Improved Single-Photoelectron Resolution

**Primary motivation:** The paper's PSD performance is fundamentally limited by photoelectron statistics at low S1; the current 8.0 PE/keV light yield and single-photon detection chain determine the minimum achievable WIMP mass threshold and the ER rejection at low energies.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the current cryogenic preamplifiers [Ref. 5 in the paper] with **cryogenic CMOS amplifiers** operating at 87K using a 180 nm CMOS process (demonstrated by the nEXO collaboration), achieving noise equivalent charge of <0.1 electrons RMS versus the current system
- The paper states preamplifiers were needed to tame PMT breakdown issues; with SiPMs (upgrade #1) this constraint is removed and the amplifier can be optimized purely for noise performance
- Upgrade digitizers from the current 250 MHz (4 ns sampling) to **1 GHz, 14-bit digitizers** for TPC channels (matching the current veto digitizer rate); the 90 ns f90 integration window contains only ~22 samples at 250 MHz, limiting the accuracy of f90 determination; at 1 GHz this becomes 90 samples
- Implement **online FPGA-based pulse fitting** using template matching for real-time f90 computation, replacing threshold-crossing-based timing; this reduces the f90 resolution from ~0.02 to ~0.005 at the relevant S1 range of 50-200 PE
- Deploy **charge-integration ASICs** (similar to those developed for DarkSide-20k) with dual-gain inputs to handle the dynamic range from single-PE to saturating S2 pulses without the current need for separate saturation correction
- Expected impact: Improved f90 resolution directly translates to lower NR/ER overlap, extending the effective WIMP mass threshold downward by ~30% (from ~30 GeV/c² toward ~20 GeV/c²) and improving sensitivity at low masses by potentially one order of magnitude

---

## Summary of Expected Performance Improvements

| Upgrade | Primary Background Addressed | Expected Improvement Factor |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM replacement | Radiogenic neutrons, Cherenkov | >10× neutron reduction |
| Cherenkov-suppressing reflector | Scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov | ~3.5× effective exposure recovery |
| Gd-loaded LSV + inner veto | Neutrons + γ-ray ER | Neutron efficiency >99.99% |
| Wire cathode + higher drift field | Surface events, S2/S1 discrimination | 30-50% S2/S1 improvement |
| SiPM/digitizer upgrade | f90 resolution, low-mass threshold | ~30% lower mass threshold |

The combination of upgrades 1 and 2 addresses the two dominant backgrounds identified in the paper; the paper explicitly states the experiment is limited by scintillation+Cherenkov and that the PMTs are the dominant radioactivity source, making these the highest-priority hardware changes for a successor instrument.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Improved Physics Performance

## Assessment of Primary Limitations

Based on the paper's own stated constraints, the binding performance limitations are:

1. **Energy resolution** limited by LAAPD noise and light collection efficiency (~48% packing fraction)
2. **High voltage instability** capping drift field at 8 kV vs. designed 3.7 kV/cm (implying ~14 kV nominal)
3. **Background rate** from internal components, particularly flat cables and bronze hardware
4. **Fiducial mass inefficiency** (110 kg active of 175 kg total LXe)

---

## Upgrade 1: Replace LAAPDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

### Specific Implementation
- **Device**: Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPC S13370-6050CN or FBK VUV-HD3 series, both with demonstrated sensitivity at 175 nm in LXe
- **Configuration**: Tile arrays replacing the current hexagonal LAAPD platters, using 6mm × 6mm SiPM cells in close-packed arrays
- **Packing fraction**: Achievable >80% photosensitive coverage vs. current 48%, directly doubling photon statistics

### Performance Impact
- SiPMs at LXe temperature (~165K) achieve single-photon resolution with gain ~10⁶, compared to LAAPD gain of ~100 at equivalent bias
- Correlated avalanche noise (the dominant SiPM noise source) is suppressed at cryogenic temperatures by approximately one order of magnitude relative to room temperature operation
- The current paper explicitly states LAAPD noise **limits the scintillation threshold** — eliminating this constraint directly improves the anti-Compton single-site/multi-site discrimination at low energies
- Expected improvement in combined energy resolution: from σ/E = 1.6% toward ~1.0% at Q_ββ, based on light yield scaling arguments and demonstrated LXe SiPM results from nEXO R&D
- Individual SiPM cells have been measured at <1 mBq/kg for U and Th in dedicated radiopurity campaigns, comparable to or better than the LAAPDs quoted in Table 3

### Engineering Considerations
- Each SiPM requires individual bias trimming — implement via custom ASIC (e.g., modified ATLAS ITk-style per-channel bias trim) rather than the current sector-level trim, reducing the response spread below the current σ = 2.5%
- Flat polyimide cables servicing SiPMs can carry lower bias voltages (~25-50V vs. ~1400V), substantially reducing the microphonics problem explicitly mentioned in Section 6.3
- Wire bonding to polyimide flex circuits eliminates the phosphor bronze spider spring contact system, removing a radioactive component

---

## Upgrade 2: Replacement of Wire Readout with a Charge-Readout Tile System

### Specific Implementation
- **Technology**: Segmented copper charge-collection pads on low-radioactivity ceramic (alumina or sapphire substrate) or directly machined PTFE tiles with thin-film copper traces
- **Pitch**: 3mm × 3mm pixels matching the current wire pitch, but providing genuine 2D charge collection without the inductive V-wire ambiguity
- **Substrate**: Sapphire (Al₂O₃) has been measured at <0.1 mBq/kg for ²³²Th — the same material used for the field cage resistors in the current design, confirming radiopurity viability

### Performance Impact
- Eliminates the 60° stereo-angle reconstruction ambiguity inherent in the current U/V wire crossed-plane geometry, which creates ghost hits for multi-cluster events
- Direct 2D charge measurement rather than inductive pickup on V-wires removes the deconvolution step that degrades position resolution
- Improved transverse position resolution from ~9mm (current readout pitch) to ~3mm genuine spatial resolution improves multi-site event rejection — the primary handle against Compton γ-ray background
- The current design explicitly notes that readout pitch was made coarser than optimal (9mm vs. 3mm field-optimization pitch) due to electronics channel count concerns; a tiled ASIC readout removes this constraint

### Engineering Considerations
- Readout ASIC: adapt the ATLAS MAPS-style or the nEXO charge readout ASIC designs, implementing 64-channel charge-sensitive amplifier arrays in 0.18μm CMOS
- CMOS at LXe temperature (167K) is well-characterized; sub-threshold current freezeout is manageable with appropriate transistor sizing
- Tile edges must be managed with guard rings biased to prevent charge loss between tiles — standard in silicon strip detector design

---

## Upgrade 3: Elimination of the HV Instability via Resistive HVFT Redesign

### Specific Implementation
- **Replace the RG217 coaxial cable feedthrough** with a custom-drawn ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) rod feedthrough
- Inner conductor: 4mm diameter oxygen-free copper rod, electropolished and then coated with a 1μm thick layer of parylene-C to passivate sharp edges identified as the probable corona source
- Dielectric: UHMWPE tube, which has lower gas permeability than polyethylene and has been used in LZ and PandaX at comparable voltages
- **Corona suppression**: Replace all photoetched parts in the HV circuit (cathode grid, leaf springs) with electroformed or diamond-turned parts having controlled edge radii >500μm — photoetching inherently produces burrs and sharp edges that the paper itself implicates in the instability

### Performance Impact
- Current operation at 8 kV vs. designed 14 kV represents a **factor of ~1.75 reduction in drift field**, directly degrading charge collection efficiency and electron-ion recombination suppression
- At the design field of 3.7 kV/cm, recombination is suppressed sufficiently that the anti-correlation between charge and light signals is stronger, improving the combined energy estimator resolution
- Published LXe data shows charge yield increases by approximately 40% going from 8 kV to the design voltage, with corresponding improvement in the charge/light combined resolution
- Stable HV also eliminates the ~mV glitches on the cathode line that create spurious triggers and dead time

### Engineering Considerations
- All sharp metallic surfaces in the HV circuit should be replaced with electroformed copper components (achievable via standard electroforming over wax mandrels), providing naturally smooth surfaces
- A resistive voltage divider along the HV cable using thin-film surface-mount resistors (same sapphire substrate technology already used for field cage resistors) allows intermediate voltage monitoring and provides a soft discharge path

---

## Upgrade 4: Replacement of Flat Polyimide Cables with Coaxial Ribbon Cable Arrays

### Specific Implementation
- **Technology**: Round or rectangular coaxial ribbon arrays with individual shields per signal line, using copper center conductors (25μm) in PTFE dielectric with copper braid shield, following the construction approach of Axon Cable's low-radioactivity cryogenic cable lines
- **Geometry**: Bundle format retained for the existing leg geometry, but with per-channel shielding
- The PTFE dielectric satisfies the existing radiopurity requirements (PTFE already used extensively in the detector)

### Performance Impact
- Table 3 shows flat cables inside the TPC contribute **4.6 ± 0.7 counts/yr** in the 0νββ window from ²³⁸U alone — the second largest single identified background source after the bronze cathode
- Per-channel shielding eliminates the crosstalk between high-voltage V-wire bias lines and signal lines that requires the complex multi-layer conducting plane mitigation currently employed
- Individual shielding removes the microphonics coupling mechanism (vibrating unshielded conductor near ground plane) without requiring the high-voltage bias planes that add radioactive material

### Engineering Considerations
- The leg cross-section geometry must be slightly enlarged or cables rerouted — this is a manageable mechanical change for a next-generation version
- Feedthrough sealing: replace the current epoxy cup feedthrough with an indium-wire compression seal around individual coaxial cables, similar to the cold flange gasket technology already used elsewhere in the detector

---

## Upgrade 5: Active Radon Mitigation Inside Lead Shield

### Specific Implementation
- **Install a sealed, low-emanation inner volume** using 3mm electrolytic copper sheet forming a hermetic enclosure inside the existing lead shield volume
- Continuously flush with boil-off nitrogen from the LXe cryogenic system at ~1 L/min, passing first through a commercially available activated charcoal radon trap (Durridge RAD7 trap technology) cooled to -40°C
- Install four alpha-counting PIN diode monitors (Hamamatsu S3590-09) at representative locations to provide real-time Rn monitoring
- Add a 1mm thick low-radioactivity copper mesh at all cable penetrations serving as a Faraday shield while allowing cable passage with convoluted path Rn suppression

### Performance Impact
- Section 5.3 explicitly states measured radon is **~3× above the 2 mBq/L limit** for <0.3 counts/yr in the 0νββ window
- At 3× the limit, radon alone contributes ~0.9 counts/yr, roughly comparable to all the internal bronze hardware combined
- This is an immediate and relatively low-cost improvement with no detector opening required

---
