**Wire pre-tension improvement:** Implement wire tensioning with in-situ force measurement using strain gauges on the wire support frame before cool-down. The paper notes elastic deformation is already a concern (a single perpendicular wire was added to the bottom screen to minimize deformation). Pre-tensioning wires to 80% of yield stress at room temperature, accounting for differential thermal contraction between Au-plated stainless steel and the OFHC copper frame, would maintain wire sag below 0.1 mm at −96°C versus the current unconstrained condition.

---

## 4. Neutron Veto Addition Between Cryostat and Water Shield

### Identified Problem
The paper reports radiogenic neutron background at **0.55 (t·y)⁻¹** NR events in 1 t fiducial (table 2). While below the CNNS floor of 0.6 (t·y)⁻¹, both backgrounds together constitute a ~1.15 (t·y)⁻¹ irreducible NR floor approaching signal sensitivity for a 2 t·y exposure. The muon-induced neutron tagging efficiency is only 43% with the current coincidence threshold of Npmt=8, and the paper acknowledges the plan to reduce to Npmt=5. More critically, radiogenic neutrons from PMT glass and cryostat steel cannot be vetoed by the muon veto.

### Proposed Upgrade: Gadolinium-Doped Water or Boron-Loaded Liquid Scintillator Neutron Capture Veto

**Specific technology:** Fill the annular region between the outer cryostat wall (diameter 1.62 m) and a new inner cylindrical acrylic vessel (diameter 2.2 m, height 2.5 m) with **gadolinium sulfate (Gd₂(SO₄)₃) dissolved in water at 0.1% by mass**. This is the same technology demonstrated by Super-Kamiokande-Gd and proposed for WATCHMAN.

Gd has a thermal neutron capture cross section of 49,000 barns (compared to 0.33 barns for ¹H), with capture gamma cascades totaling 8 MeV. At 0.1% Gd loading, the mean capture time drops from ~200 µs (pure water) to ~30 µs. The 8 MeV gamma cascade is detectable by the existing 84 water Cherenkov PMTs, which have adequate sensitivity down to ~1 MeV given their 30% QE in the 300-600 nm range.

**Alternatively:** A 40 cm thick layer of **boron-loaded liquid scintillator** (e.g., BC-525 with 5% natural boron by mass, as used by Borexino CTF) would provide >99% neutron capture efficiency within 50 µs for neutrons entering from the cryostat. The scintillator layer would be contained in an acrylic vessel between the cryostat outer vessel and the water shield, instrumented with 20 additional 8-inch PMTs mounted on the inner acrylic surface.

**Expected performance:** Gadolinium-water at 0.1% loading provides >95% neutron capture tagging efficiency for neutrons with energies below 10 MeV, improving radiogenic neutron rejection from the current ~50% (multiple scatter rejection only) to >95%. This reduces the effective radiogenic neutron background from 0.55 to <0.03 (t·y)⁻¹, pushing total NR background below the CNNS floor.

**Engineering constraint:** The Gd-loaded water must be isolated from the primary deionized water volume to prevent Gd precipitation on PMT surfaces and to allow separate circulation and purification. The acrylic barrier vessel must be optically transparent to allow Cherenkov light from the outer water volume to reach the lateral PMTs.

---

## 5. Purification Flow Rate Upgrade

### Identified Problem
The paper explicitly states: *"The purity was limited by detector outgassing and a purification flow of 50 slpm (≈425 kg/d), above which the QDrive gas pumps could not operate reliably given the flow impedance in the circuit."* Electron lifetime τₑ averaged only 452 µs during Science Run 0, limiting the S2 signal collection for events near the cathode (drift time up to 673 µs means roughly 22% signal loss at the cathode).

### Proposed Upgrade: LXe Phase Liquid Circulation Pump

**Specific technology:** Replace gas-phase purification with direct **LXe-phase circulation** using a cryogenic centrifugal pump, specifically a magnetically-coupled cryogenic gear pump (as developed by Iwatani for liquid helium and adapted for LXe by the group at Columbia/XENON100 described in reference [40]).

Direct liquid-phase pumping at 50-200 slpm equivalent (corresponding to liquid flows of ~0.5-2 L/min) bypasses the need to evaporate and re-condense xenon in the heat exchanger loop, reducing the heat load into the cryostat. The SAES getter operates efficiently in gas phase, so a small side-stream evaporator feeds the getter while the main flow circulates as liquid through a liquid-phase purification membrane (e.g., metallic membrane getter operating at room temperature under 10 bar LXe pressure).

**Quantitative improvement:** Increasing effective purification throughput from 425 kg/day to >1000 kg/day would bring the outgassing equilibrium electron lifetime above 1 ms, reducing signal loss at the cathode from 22% to <10%. This improves energy resolution and extends the effective fiducial volume to regions closer to the cathode, potentially increasing the fiducial mass from 1.0 t to 1.3-1.5 t without any changes to the TPC itself.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Target Limitation | Technology | Expected Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| SiPM top array | g₁ = 12.5% PDE, PMT failures | FBK VUV-HD SiPM tiles | g₁ → 0.25 PE/γ, threshold lowered to <5 GeV WIMP mass |
| Rn cold trap + pump replacement | 620 (t·y)⁻¹ Rn ER background | Charcoal cold trap at 183 K, piezo pumps | Rn background reduced 10× |
| Cathode HV upgrade | 0.125 kV/cm drift field | Thicker W wires, resistive divider | Field → 0.31 kV/cm, position bias <20 mm |
| Gd-water neutron veto | 0.55 (t·y)⁻¹ radiogenic NR background | 0.1% Gd₂(SO₄)₃ in annular vessel | NR background reduced to <0.03 (t·y)⁻¹ |
| LXe-phase circulation pump | τₑ limited to 452 µs | Cryogenic magnetically-coupled gear pump | τₑ → >1 ms, fiducial mass increase to ~1.4 t |

The highest-priority single upgrade is the radon cold trap, as it addresses the dominant background (Rn ER at 620 (t·y)⁻¹) with established technology at modest engineering risk. The SiPM array upgrade offers the most transformative long-term physics gain by opening the low-mass WIMP parameter space.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a ~250 kg Dual-Phase Xenon TPC

## Framing the Problem

Primary physics performance means: **lower energy threshold, better electron recoil/nuclear recoil discrimination, reduced backgrounds, and improved fiducial volume efficiency**. I'll address each with specific hardware solutions.

---

## 1. Photodetector Upgrade: Replace 3-inch PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

### Current limitation
Standard instruments at this scale (LUX-era, early XENON1T) used Hamamatsu R11410-23 or similar 3-inch PMTs. These have:
- Single photoelectron (SPE) detection efficiency ~90% at room temperature, but quantum efficiency (QE) ~35% at 175 nm
- Dark count rate ~50 Hz/PMT at LXe temperature, but afterpulsing ~0.1% introduces correlated noise
- Bulky geometry leaves dead regions and limits packing fraction

### Proposed upgrade
**VUV-sensitive SiPMs** — specifically Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) VUV-HD3 or Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPCs (3mm × 3mm or 6mm × 6mm tiles)

- **Photon detection efficiency (PDE):** 24–28% at 175 nm (vs ~15–18% effective for PMTs accounting for geometry), improving light yield by ~40–60%
- **Sub-single-photon resolution:** SiPMs resolve individual photon peaks far more cleanly; the excess noise factor is ~1.1 vs ~1.25 for PMTs
- **Zero afterpulsing** from ionization of residual gas (no vacuum tube); correlated noise from optical crosstalk can be suppressed with trenched cell designs (FBK's "RGB-HD" trench isolation)
- **Tile the cathode and anode planes at ~95% coverage** using 6×6 mm² tiles on low-radioactivity PTFE-backed PCBs

### Critical engineering requirement
Cold readout ASICs (e.g., **ABCD-style or the NEXUS ASIC developed for nEXO**, operating at 77–165 K) must be located inside the cryostat to avoid signal degradation over long cables. Use **low-radioactivity ceramic or silicon interposers** screened to <1 mBq/kg U/Th.

---

## 2. Electroluminescence Gap Engineering: Segmented or Optimized Extraction Region

### Current limitation
The gas gap thickness and electric field uniformity in the gas phase directly control S2 photon yield and spatial resolution. Typical uniform-field gaps (~5 mm, ~10 kV/cm in gas) yield ~25 photons/electron, but field non-uniformities at the edge of the active region reduce S2/S1 resolution at large radii.

### Proposed upgrade A: Transparent resistive anode (THGEM-style or ITO-coated mesh)

Replace the standard wire anode with a **photolithographically patterned indium tin oxide (ITO) anode on a fused silica plate**:
- Achieves <1% field uniformity across the full aperture (demonstrated by XENOSCOPE/DARWIN prototyping)
- ITO transmittance >90% at 175 nm for optimized thickness (~10 nm)
- Eliminates wire sag and electrostatic deflection that distort fields at the ~0.5 mm level in large-diameter grids

### Proposed upgrade B: Active charge readout with pixel or strip anode

**Pixelated charge-sensitive anode** (e.g., 3 mm pitch pads read out by ATLAS-style cryogenic charge amplifiers):
- Provides direct (x,y) localization of S2 with ~1 mm resolution without relying on PMT hit-pattern reconstruction
- Eliminates the S2 position reconstruction bias near array edges — a significant systematic for fiducial volume definition
- Technology: **Topmetal-II- style CMOS pixel sensors** adapted for LXe (tested by PandaX-III for gaseous Xe; adaptation needed for cold LXe environment)

---

## 3. Field Cage Redesign: Eliminate Field Non-Uniformity and Radioactive Sources

### Current limitation
Resistive divider chains on copper or Kapton-clad rings introduce radioactive contamination (⁶⁰Co from copper, ²³⁸U/²³²Th from Kapton) and cause field distortions from charge buildup on PTFE walls.

### Proposed upgrade: Amorphous silicon (a-Si) or diamond-like carbon (DLC) resistive cylinder

Replace discrete ring electrodes with a **single-piece cylindrical resistor** made from:
- **Diamond-like carbon film** (resistivity tunable 10⁶–10¹² Ω/sq by deposition conditions, sputtered onto PTFE or fused silica substrate)
- Demonstrated in concept by EXO-200 and currently pursued for nEXO
- Provides a **perfectly continuous, uniform axial field** — no discrete ring spacing artifacts
- Material is carbon-based, intrinsically low in U/Th (<0.1 ppb achievable with DLC on cleaned substrate)
- Eliminates all metal from the active region walls

**Quantitative gain:** Field uniformity improves from typical ~2–5% variation to <0.5%, reducing position-dependent S1/S2 biases that smear the nuclear recoil band.

---

## 4. Cathode High Voltage Delivery: In-Xenon HV Feedthrough

### Current limitation
Standard HV feedthroughs (ceramic-metal brazed or PEEK/Kapton) are the dominant source of radon emanation and can limit cathode voltage to –50 to –100 kV, capping drift field at ~200–500 V/cm over ~1 m drift.

### Proposed upgrade: Cryogenic coaxial cable with polyethylene (PE) dielectric

- Use **Habia or Axon ultra-pure PTFE-dielectric coaxial cable** with electropolished stainless steel inner conductor, mass-selected for low Rn emanation (<1 µBq/m)
- Alternative: **Warm-to-cold HV feedthrough using graded dielectric geometry** (stacked UHMW-PE plugs with geometry optimized via COMSOL to suppress triple-point field enhancement), enabling stable –200 kV operation demonstrated by nEXO feedthrough R&D
- Higher drift field (600–1000 V/cm) improves **electron lifetime sensitivity** (reduces attachment to O₂/H₂O impurities), effectively increasing fiducial volume efficiency and S2/S1 energy resolution

---

## 5. Xenon Purity System: Cryogenic Molecular Sieve + Heated Getter Loop

### Current limitation
Electron lifetime in typical 250 kg instruments is 1–3 ms, limiting drift length efficiency. The dominant impurities are O₂ and H₂O outgassing from internal surfaces.

### Proposed upgrade: In-line cryogenic charcoal trap + high-throughput hot getter

- **SAES MonoTorr PS4-MT15** (or equivalent) heated Zr-based getter rated at 15–50 slpm, with a **bypass loop** that recirculates through liquid phase via a submerged heat exchanger to avoid gas-phase thermal gradients
- Add a **cryogenic activated charcoal trap at 77 K** upstream of the getter to remove krypton (⁸⁵Kr is a dominant beta background): achieves Kr/Xe < 0.01 ppt (vs ~0.1 ppt with room-temperature charcoal column chromatography), improving beta background by ~10×
- Supplement with **online krypton monitoring** using a dedicated small-volume residual gas analyzer + cold trap pre-concentrator, allowing real-time purity feedback

---

## 6. Neutron Veto Upgrade: Gadolinium-Doped Water or Liquid Scintillator Shell

### Current limitation
A pure water Cherenkov shield is effective for muon veto but has low efficiency for neutron capture tagging — neutrons from rock/cavern or detector materials that scatter once in xenon (mimicking WIMP signal) may escape without triggering the water veto.

### Proposed upgrade: 0.1% GdCl₃ or Gd₂(SO₄)₃ loaded water + expanded PMT coverage

- **Gadolinium doping at 0.1% by mass** raises thermal neutron capture cross-section to ~49,000 barn (vs 0.3 barn for H), producing an 8 MeV gamma cascade after capture (~20 µs after scatter)
- Water-soluble Gd sulfate is chemically stable; demonstrated at large scale by **Super-Kamiokande-Gd (SKGD)** since 2020
- Add **Wavelength-shifting plates (EJ-286 or bis-MSB doped acrylic)** on the inner tank wall to boost Cherenkov photon collection to >20% coverage with 8-inch PMTs (Hamamatsu R7081), sufficient for ~90% neutron tagging efficiency
- This directly improves **nuclear recoil signal purity** by tagging coincident neutron scatters that would otherwise fake WIMP candidates

---

## 7. Radon Mitigation: Electropolished Radon-Barrier Inner Vessel + Active Radon Removal

### Current limitation
²²²Rn daughters (²¹⁴Pb, ²¹⁴Bi betas) plate onto cathode and PTFE surfaces, creating surface background that limits sensitivity at low energies. Emanation from weaker internal components (cables, seals, welds) is the dominant source.

### Proposed upgrade

**A. Electropolished 316LN stainless steel inner cryostat** with Ra-screened welds (tested by XENON1T to ~0.5 mBq/kg Ra, achievable to ~0.1 mBq/kg with material selection + acid passivation)

**B. Cryogenic radon trap in the recirculation loop:**
- A **1-liter activated charcoal cold trap at –40°C to –60°C** in the gas-phase recirculation line has a Rn retention time of >1 hour, effectively removing Rn before it enters the active volume
- Demonstrated to reduce Rn activity by factor ~10–50 in XENON1T offline analysis; integrating it continuously into the loop rather than as a batch purification step is the key upgrade
- Target: Rn activity in LXe <1 µBq/kg (vs ~10 µBq/kg in XENON1T)

---

## 8. Bottom PMT Array / Light Collection: Wavelength-Shifting Reflector Panels

### Current limitation
PTFE reflectivity at 175 nm is ~95–97% per bounce but degrades with surface contamination; photon collection for S1 (which directly sets energy threshold) is typically ~8–12 photoelectrons per keV_ee.

### Proposed upgrade: Tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) + enhanced specular reflector

- Coat all PTFE internal surfaces with **evaporated TPB at ~200 µg/cm²**: converts 175 nm VUV to ~430 nm visible, where SiPM PDE is >40% (vs 24% at VUV)
- Use **3M Vikuiti ESR (Enhanced Specular Reflector) film** laminated behind TPB on field cage walls: reflectivity >99% at 430 nm vs 96% for raw PTFE at 175 nm
- Monte Carlo estimates (based on LZ optical simulations) suggest this combination can increase S1 light yield from ~8 to **~15 phd/keV_ee**, reducing threshold from ~2 keVnr to approximately **1 keVnr** — directly extending dark matter sensitivity to sub-GeV masses

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Quantitative Gain |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM arrays + cryo-ASICs | Light yield, threshold | +40–60% PDE, ~1 keVnr threshold |
| ITO/pixel anode | S2 resolution, fiducial volume | <1 mm x,y reconstruction |
| DLC resistive cylinder | Field uniformity, backgrounds | <0.5% field variation |
| HV feedthrough / high-E field | Electron lifetime, resolution | Drift field up to 1 kV/cm |
| Cryo charcoal + hot getter | Kr/Rn purity | ⁸⁵Kr to <0.01 ppt |
| Gd-loaded water veto | Neutron background | ~90% neutron tagging |
| Cryogenic Rn trap | Rn background | <1 µBq/kg Rn in LXe |
| TPB + ESR reflectors | S1 yield, threshold | ~15 phd/keV_ee |

The **highest-leverage single upgrade** for physics reach is the **SiPM + cryogenic ASIC readout combined with TPB-coated ESR reflectors**, as these together address the fundamental light collection limit that sets energy threshold and therefore the WIMP mass range accessible.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for ProtoDUNE-SP / DUNE-SP

## Analysis of Primary Performance Limitations

Based on the paper's documented performance metrics and identified weaknesses, I identify the following principal physics performance bottlenecks warranting hardware intervention:

---

## 1. High Voltage System Stability

**Documented Problem:** Current streamers at 4-6 events/day, localized to GP#6, correlated with LAr purity. HV instabilities require auto-recovery interrupting data taking, reducing uptime. The charging-up of FRP insulating surfaces drives partial discharges.

**Proposed Upgrades:**

**A. Resistive Field Cage Profiles**
- Replace extruded aluminum profiles with resistively coated aluminum or carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer profiles having bulk resistivity ~10⁹–10¹⁰ Ω·cm
- Resistive surfaces prevent charge accumulation on insulating supports by providing slow bleed-off paths without compromising field uniformity
- Precedent: MicroBooNE and SBND resistive cathode work demonstrates viability
- Specifically coat FRP I-beams and box beams with loaded epoxy (carbon black loaded, ~10⁸ Ω/square) to eliminate the dominant charging mechanism

**B. Improved FC Profile End Caps**
- Replace UHMWPE caps with field-graded resistive caps using stacked resistor networks embedded in cast epoxy
- Grade the resistivity from ~10⁸ Ω·cm at the profile contact to ~10¹⁰ Ω·cm at the outer tip
- Eliminates discrete voltage steps at profile terminations identified as discharge initiation points
- Target: reduce peak E-field at profile ends from current ~30 kV/cm to below 15 kV/cm in LAr

**C. HV Feedthrough Upgrade**
- Replace the single UHMWPE-insulated feedthrough with a segmented design incorporating intermediate guard electrodes biased through an external resistive divider
- Add capacitive voltage monitors at each guard electrode for real-time field distribution measurement
- Implement SF₆-insulated warm section to increase standoff voltage margin from 300 kV demonstrated to 400 kV operational

---

## 2. Photon Detection System Efficiency

**Documented Problem:** Photon detection efficiencies of 0.08% (dip-coated), 0.21% (double-shift), and 2% (ARAPUCA single cell) are dramatically unequal. The minimum spec of 0.5 PE/MeV at 3.6 m is marginally met. Total APA surface active coverage is only 12.5%.

**Proposed Upgrades:**

**A. X-ARAPUCA Modules as Standard**
- Replace all light guide modules with X-ARAPUCA geometry, which extends the dichroic filter acceptance window to cover the full APA slot width (8.6 cm → full slot aperture)
- X-ARAPUCA replaces the single-cell geometry with a series of cells sharing a common reflective cavity, increasing geometric acceptance by ~4×
- Use pTP (p-terphenyl, 200 µg/cm²) on exterior dichroic filters (cutoff 400 nm) with polysiloxane-based TPB on interior surfaces for improved cryogenic adhesion over the resistive evaporation technique currently used
- Target: 8% detection efficiency per module, yielding >4 PE/MeV at maximum drift distance

**B. SiPM Upgrade to 3×3 mm² Tile Arrays with Through-Silicon Via Packaging**
- Replace current 6×6 mm² discrete SiPMs with tiled 3×3 mm² Hamamatsu S14160-3050HS or FBK NUV-HD-SF devices
- Smaller pixel pitch (50 µm → 35 µm or 25 µm) reduces correlated noise (dark count rate scales with area while photon detection efficiency maintained)
- NUV-HD-SF devices achieve PDE >50% at 420 nm at 77K vs ~38% for current SensL devices
- TSV packaging (already partially adopted) enables dense tiling achieving >90% fill factor vs ~65% current
- Passive ganging replaced with active transimpedance amplification at the SiPM tile using cryo-qualified SiGe BiCMOS amplifiers (IHP SG13G2 process demonstrated to 77K), eliminating the capacitance penalty of passive ganging 12 devices

**C. Wavelength-Shifting Reflector Foils on Cathode and Field Cage**
- Line cathode CPA surfaces and FC inner faces with tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB)-coated Vikuiti™ ESR foils (3M), converting 128 nm VUV photons isotropically emitted away from APAs into 425 nm photons that reach the APA-mounted PDS
- Expected 1.5-2× increase in detected photon yield without APA modification
- Requires verification that foil outgassing does not degrade LAr purity beyond 10 ppt O₂ equivalent; initial measurements from DarkSide-20k R&D suggest <2 ppt contribution with proper bake-out at 60°C under vacuum for 48 hours

---

## 3. TPC Cold Electronics

**Documented Problem:** ENC of ~400 e⁻ at cryogenic temperature for collection plane, ~600 e⁻ for induction. ADC ASIC exhibited instabilities at cryogenic temperatures (320,000 transistors at 77K). SNR of 13-16 for MIPs is adequate but limits low-energy physics.

**Proposed Upgrades:**

**A. 65 nm CMOS FE and ADC ASICs**
- Replace 180 nm CMOS FE and ADC ASICs with designs in TSMC 65 nm LP process
- Demonstrated cryogenic performance with lower threshold voltage variation (VT shift ~15% vs ~40% in 180 nm at 77K)
- Lower input-referred noise achievable: target ENC <200 e⁻ at 150 pF input capacitance
- Increased transistor density allows on-chip zero suppression and hit-finding, reducing data bandwidth by 50× for DUNE while preserving full waveform for triggered windows
- Integrate 16-channel FE + 16-channel 12-bit ADC in single ASIC die, eliminating inter-chip connections that currently contribute noise and reliability concerns

**B. 2 MHz → 4 MHz Sampling Rate**
- Upgrade ADC ASICs to 4 MS/s sampling
- Improves Landau peak position resolution on induction planes and enables better separation of overlapping tracks
- Requires corresponding WIB upgrade to 2× fiber bandwidth (already feasible with FELIX architecture using 25G links)

**C. FEMB Substrate**
- Replace current FR4 mother board with Rogers 4350B high-frequency laminate
- Reduces dielectric loss and inter-channel crosstalk at cryogenic temperatures
- FR4 has highly variable cryogenic dielectric properties; Rogers material is stable 77K–300K
- Implement copper coplanar waveguide signal routing rather than microstrip to improve ground reference continuity

---

## 4. Wire Plane and APA Mechanical Design

**Documented Problem:** 4.669 mm wire pitch limits spatial resolution on induction planes. Wire breakage during transport is a known risk (acceptance testing upon arrival at CERN). The 3.9 m unsupported diagonal wire length requires combs introducing dead zones.

**Proposed Upgrades:**

**A. Reduced Wire Pitch on Collection Plane**
- Reduce X-plane wire pitch from 4.790 mm to 3.0 mm using same 150 µm CuBe wire
- Improves 𝑦-𝑧 vertex resolution from ~1.5 cm toward ~1.0 cm
- Increases channel count per APA from 2560 to ~3500, requiring FEMB count increase from 20 to 28 per APA
- Wire tension maintained at 5 N; breaking tension unchanged at 25.6 N

**B. Pixel or Pad Readout for High-Occupancy Region**
- Instrument the central 10% of each APA (facing beam direction) with 5 mm × 5 mm charge-collecting pad array using LArPix ASIC (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)
- LArPix 2.0 achieves <1000 e⁻ ENC at 77K with self-triggered readout
- Eliminates track reconstruction ambiguities in the highest-multiplicity beam interaction region
- Pad array connects to dedicated feedthrough without displacing wire channels

**C. Wire Tension Monitoring**
- Embed piezoelectric resonance sensors (PZT-5H, cryogenic grade) at APA frame corners
- Continuously monitor wire tension via acoustic resonance frequency measurement
- Detect wire breaks in situ without opening detector, enabling targeted maintenance scheduling
- Resolution: detects single wire break among 3520 wires per APA within 10 minute integration

---

## 5. Purity and Cryogenics Instrumentation

**Documented Problem:** Three purity monitors cannot sample within TPC volume. Bottom monitor shows systematically lower lifetime measurements (~30 ms vs >70 ms for upper monitors). CFD models show unexplained temperature bumps at 6.2 m. LAr recirculation pump failures caused significant purity disruptions.

**Proposed Upgrades:**

**A. Distributed Inline Purity Monitors**
- Install 6 miniaturized purity monitors (10 cm cathode-anode gap, 5 cm diameter) directly on APA frames at 1 m vertical intervals
- Use UV LED sources (265 nm AlGaN LED, Thorlabs or similar) rather than external xenon lamp + fiber to eliminate fiber-related signal attenuation variability
- Each monitor communicates via existing CE data pathway, requiring no additional feedthroughs
- Provides real-time 3D electron lifetime map with ~1 m spatial resolution

**B. Redundant Gear Pump with Magnetic Coupling**
- Replace single centrifugal LAr pump with parallel pair of magnetically coupled gear pumps (Barber-Nichols or Nikkiso cryogenic series)
- Magnetic coupling eliminates shaft seal as failure mode (current pump replacement April 2019 caused extended purity loss)
- Gear pump provides precise flow control at 1-10 t/hr range vs centrifugal pump's narrow efficiency band
- Hot-swap capability: second pump comes online before first is taken offline, maintaining continuous recirculation

**C. Radon Emanation Monitoring**
- Install electrostatic radon monitor (Durridge RAD7 adapted for LAr service) on recirculation return line
- Radon from ²²²Rn decay chain produces ²¹⁰Pb surface contamination on detector components, contributing long-term electronegative impurity loading not captured by standard O₂-equivalent measurements
- Target: detect >0.1 mBq/m³ radon activity before it deposits on wire surfaces

---

## 6. Cosmic Ray Tagger Upgrade

**Documented Problem:** CRT covers only upstream and downstream faces, leaving ~60% of cosmic muons untagged. Timing resolution <60 ns limits track matching. The split upstream geometry due to beampipe creates a dead zone.

**Proposed Upgrades:**

**A. Full 6-Face Coverage with Plastic Scintillator Tiles**
- Add top, bottom, and side CRT panels using SiPM-readout plastic scintillator tiles (CAEN DT5702 readout)
- Use 30 cm × 30 cm × 1 cm EJ-200 tiles with SiPM readout (Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE) replacing wavelength-shifting fiber + M64 PMT
- SiPM readout achieves <1 ns timing resolution vs current 20 ns, enabling track matching with <5 cm position resolution
- Top panel particularly valuable: tags downward-going cosmics that mimic beam neutrino topology

**B. Beam Plug Instrumentation**
- Instrument nitrogen-filled beam plug with small scintillator paddle (3 cm × 3 cm EJ-228 fast plastic) read by SiPM
- Provides beam particle crossing time with <0.5 ns resolution for improved t₀ determination
- Replaces reliance on upstream beam instrumentation with 600 m propagation delay and timing jitter

---

## Summary Prioritization

| Upgrade | Physics Impact | Implementation Complexity | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| X-ARAPUCA + WLS foils | High: 10-20× PDS efficiency | Medium | 1 |
| Resistive FC surfaces | High: eliminates HV downtime | Medium | 2 |
| 65 nm CE ASICs | Medium: 2× SNR improvement | High | 3 |
| Redundant cryogenic pump | High: eliminates purity crises | Low | 4 |
| Full CRT coverage | Medium: improves calibration | Low | 5 |
| Reduced wire pitch | Low-Medium: marginal resolution gain | Medium | 6 |

The X-ARAPUCA photon detector upgrade combined with TPB-coated reflector foils and the resistive field cage surface treatment represent the highest-leverage interventions, directly addressing the two most operationally disruptive limitations documented in the paper while substantially exceeding DUNE far detector physics specifications.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for the LUX Detector

## 1. PMT Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Current limitation:** The R8778 PMTs dominate the background budget (Table 3), contributing 0.4 ER and 0.03 NR WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days. They also have significant radioactivity (Table 2: 9.8 mBq/PMT U, 65 mBq/PMT K-40) and only 33% QE at 175 nm.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace both 61-PMT arrays with tiled arrays of Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD or Hamamatsu VUV4 SiPMs, specifically the 6mm × 6mm tiles optimized for 175 nm VUV detection
- SiPMs have demonstrated >20% photon detection efficiency at 175 nm in recent LXe detectors (nEXO R&D), with potential to reach 30-40%
- Radioactive contamination per unit active area is reduced by >2 orders of magnitude versus PMTs, since SiPMs are fabricated from ultrapure silicon wafers without glass envelopes, mu-metal bodies, or ceramic stems
- Tile into 3-inch modular units on PTFE-backed copper carrier boards with individual bias trimming to compensate gain variation at LXe temperatures
- This directly attacks the dominant background source while simultaneously improving S1 light yield, lowering the energy threshold, and improving position reconstruction

**Expected impact:** S1 yield improvement from ~8 phe/keVee toward 15-20 phe/keVee, enabling threshold reduction from ~3 keVnr to ~1 keVnr, opening sensitivity to low-mass WIMPs below 10 GeV/c²

---

## 2. Upgraded Cathode High Voltage System

**Current limitation:** The HV feedthrough is placed outside the water shield at room temperature, requiring a 25 cm unshielded cable section inside the LXe. The system is limited to 100 kV, producing a 2 kV/cm drift field over 49 cm. Electron attachment to impurities scales with drift time, so higher fields directly improve charge collection at any given purity level.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Design a custom low-radioactivity in-situ HV feedthrough operating at LXe temperature, following the approach developed for the EXO-200 experiment (using custom PTFE-insulated coaxial feedthroughs with electropolished 316L stainless steel center conductors)
- Use a Kapton-insulated, low-outgassing coaxial cable (similar to the COMET cable used in nEXO R&D) rather than commercial HVC100, reducing outgassing into the xenon volume and eliminating the need for the 0.1 SLPM purge flow that currently draws impurities toward the active volume
- Upgrade the power supply to deliver up to 200 kV, increasing the drift field to 4 kV/cm
- At 4 kV/cm versus 2 kV/cm, electron-ion recombination is substantially reduced, increasing the S2/S1 ratio and improving ER/NR discrimination. Based on XENON100 measurements, the ER discrimination efficiency improves from ~99.3% toward ~99.7% at 4 kV/cm at 50% NR acceptance
- Install a dedicated HV monitoring resistor chain inside the xenon with picoammeter readout to detect micro-discharge events in real time

---

## 3. Upgraded Electron Extraction Region

**Current limitation:** The anode mesh uses 30 µm wires at 0.5 mm pitch with 88% transparency, the lowest of all grids. The gate-anode gap is 1 cm with a 10 kV/cm electroluminescence field. The anode deflection of 130 µm at operating field introduces position-dependent S2 width variations.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the woven stainless steel anode mesh with a photolithographically etched 100 µm thick silicon wafer with 50 µm hexagonal holes at 75 µm pitch, achieving >95% optical transparency while maintaining flatness to <10 µm across the full 50 cm aperture
- This approach was demonstrated in the EL-region development for NEXT-100 and eliminates the mechanical tensioning problem entirely
- Coat the silicon surface with a 100 nm sputtered layer of aluminum or gold to provide electrical conductivity and ~57% UV reflectivity (matching stainless steel) or higher with gold (~85%)
- Reduce the gate-anode gap to 5 mm while increasing the electroluminescence field to 15 kV/cm, increasing the number of electroluminescence photons per extracted electron from ~820 to ~1230, directly improving S2 single-electron detection efficiency
- Install three capacitive planarity sensors (replacing the current parallel-plate liquid level sensors) with sub-10 µm resolution to actively servo the gate voltage on three independent sectors, maintaining liquid surface parallelism with the anode to <50 µm, ensuring uniform extraction efficiency across the full aperture

---

## 4. Krypton Removal and Online Radon Reduction

**Current limitation:** The 85Kr background is estimated at <0.13 WIMP-like ER events (Table 3), with the estimate depending on getter removal efficiency. Natural xenon contains ~1 ppm krypton. No dedicated online radon mitigation is described beyond nitrogen blanket on the water surface.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Install a dedicated cryogenic krypton distillation column directly inline with the xenon recirculation loop, between the getter output and the concentric tube heat exchanger. A packed column with 25 mm Pro-Pak stainless steel packing, 2 m tall operating at 165 K, can reduce Kr/Xe from 1 ppm to <0.015 ppt in a single pass at 50 SLPM flow rates based on the XENON1T distillation column performance
- Replace the diaphragm pump with a magnetically coupled metal bellows pump (LEWA EK series or equivalent), which has demonstrated radon emanation rates below 0.5 mBq versus ~5 mBq for typical diaphragm pumps, since bellows pumps eliminate the elastomer diaphragm that is the primary radon source in the current design
- Add a radon trap consisting of a 2-liter activated charcoal volume (Saratech 207C grade, 0.1 mBq/kg Rn emanation) cooled to -40°C inline after the getter, reducing radon concentration in returning xenon by >10⁴ before it re-enters the active volume
- Install a dedicated online radon monitor (electrostatic collection type, sensitivity <0.1 mBq/m³) at the gas return line to provide continuous radon assay rather than periodic mass spectrometry sampling

---

## 5. Enhanced Position Reconstruction and Fiducialization

**Current limitation:** The top PMT array achieves ~1 cm x-y position reconstruction using likelihood methods. The drift time provides z position. No independent x-y position measurement exists to cross-check or improve resolution at the ~1 cm level, which directly limits the sharpness of the fiducial boundary and the self-shielding effectiveness.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Install a single layer of 2 mm pitch wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber ribbons (Kuraray Y-11 double-clad, coated with tetraphenyl butadiene at 1 mg/cm²) in an x-y crossed grid pattern at the gas-liquid interface, 2 mm above the liquid surface, read out by SiPM arrays at the perimeter outside the active volume
- The fiber layer intercepts a fraction (~5%) of the S2 electroluminescence light before it reaches the top PMT array, providing an independent measurement of x-y interaction position with ~0.5 mm resolution from the fiber hit pattern, substantially sharper than PMT-array-based reconstruction
- This second independent position measurement enables a precise in-situ calibration of the PMT-based position reconstruction using the full ⁸³ᵐKr calibration dataset, tightening the fiducial volume boundary uncertainty from the current ~5 mm to <2 mm, directly increasing the usable fiducial mass for a given background target
- The fiber layer also provides a fast coincidence veto for surface events (gate grid interactions) that produce S2 without S1, suppressing a class of accidental coincidence backgrounds

---

## 6. Thermosyphon Replacement with Pulse Tube Refrigerators

**Current limitation:** The thermosyphon system requires continuous liquid nitrogen supply and delivery logistics underground. The LN2 bath introduces a vibration-free but operationally complex cryogenic infrastructure. Temperature control relies on heater-based PID loops working against the fixed LN2 condensation point.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the LN2-bath condensers with two Cryomech PT415 pulse tube refrigerators (PTRs), each providing 40W at 77K and 1.5W at 4K, mounted at the top flange of the outer cryostat vacuum space
- PTRs eliminate all liquid cryogen handling underground, removing a significant operational risk and logistical burden. They have demonstrated continuous operation for >2 years between maintenance intervals in similar noble liquid detectors (DarkSide-50, MiniCLEAN)
- The PTR cold heads couple to the existing copper thermal shields via flexible high-conductivity copper braid links (99.99% OFHC, 200 mm² cross-section), maintaining thermal isolation from PTR vibration while providing the required ~400W cooling capacity
- Add a 10-liter LN2 buffer dewar as emergency backup, sufficient to maintain detector temperature for 48 hours during a PTR maintenance interval without warming the xenon
- PID control loops with 100 mK setpoint stability become more straightforward since the PTR cooling power is electronically adjustable via helium compressor speed control, rather than requiring heater opposition against a fixed LN2 bath temperature

---

## Summary of Expected Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Quantitative Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM arrays | Background reduction, lower threshold | ER background from PMTs reduced >100×; threshold ~1 keVnr |
| Higher drift field | Improved ER discrimination | Discrimination efficiency 99.3% → 99.7% |
| Flat anode | Uniform S2, improved single-electron detection | S2 yield +50%, position uniformity <1 mm |
| Kr/Rn removal | Reduced ER rate | 85Kr contribution negligible; Rn below 0.1 mBq/kg |
| Fiber position layer | Sharper fiducialization | Fiducial boundary uncertainty <2 mm, ~10% more usable mass |
| PTR cryogenics | Operational reliability | Continuous operation without LN2 logistics; reduced downtime |

The SiPM upgrade and cathode HV upgrade represent the highest-priority interventions as they attack the dominant background source and directly improve the core ER/NR discrimination that is the experiment's primary WIMP sensitivity lever.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for LUX: Specific Proposals

## 1. PMT Array Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

The R8778 PMTs are the dominant background source (Table 3), contributing 0.4 ER and 0.03 NR WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days. They are also physically large, limiting fiducial volume fraction.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace 122 R8778 PMTs with arrays of Hamamatsu S10931-050P SiPMs (3mm × 3mm tiles), tiled into ~5cm × 5cm modules mounted on low-radioactivity printed circuit boards using PTFE substrates
- SiPMs have demonstrated operation at LXe temperatures (~170K) with acceptable dark count rates
- Radioactivity per unit photosensitive area is orders of magnitude lower than PMT glass/metal assemblies; the ceramic/silicon construction eliminates the dominant U/Th/K contributors (Table 2 shows 9.8 mBq/PMT uranium)
- Thinner profile allows expanding the active xenon volume within the same cryostat diameter, increasing fiducial mass
- QE of SiPMs at 175nm with appropriate anti-reflection coating on the entrance window can reach 15-25%, competitive with the R8778's 33% QE but without correlated radioactivity penalty
- Eliminates the afterpulsing monitoring program entirely, simplifying operations

**Quantitative impact:** If PMT radioactivity is reduced by factor ×100 (conservative for SiPMs vs. glass PMTs), the ER background drops from 0.4 to ~0.004 WIMP-like events per 30,000 kg-days, making PMTs a negligible contributor and enabling a substantially larger fiducial volume cut to be relaxed.

---

## 2. Anode Grid Replacement to Improve S2 Resolution

The current anode uses a 30-micron wire mesh with 88% optical transparency and measured 130-micron deflection at operating field. This is the worst-performing optical element in the detector.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace the woven stainless steel mesh anode with a photo-etched electroformed copper or gold-plated tungsten grid using 25-micron wires on a 250-micron pitch
- Achieved transparency: ~90% versus current 88%, but more importantly the electroformed construction produces a geometrically flat surface with <10-micron deflection under tension, eliminating field non-uniformity
- Apply a thin (50nm) evaporated gold coating to achieve ~70% reflectivity at 175nm (versus ~57% for bare stainless steel per Ref. [25]), improving S2 light collection
- The gate-to-anode gap is only 1 cm; the 130-micron sag creates measurable electroluminescence field variation that degrades S2 pulse width uniformity and hence z-position reconstruction
- Alternative: replace gate and anode with a single Frisch grid using 10-micron diameter electro-polished tungsten wires at 200-micron pitch, achieving 95% transparency

**Quantitative impact:** Improved S2 uniformity directly improves z-position resolution. Current drift distance is 49 cm; improving position resolution from ~1mm to ~0.3mm in z would allow tighter fiducial cuts on the top and bottom faces, reducing the MSSI background fraction currently projected at 4×10⁻³ toward the 6×10⁻³ goal with margin to spare.

---

## 3. Upgraded Cathode HV System with Internal Feedthrough

The current system routes the HV cable through a room-temperature feedthrough outside the water shield, running 25 cm through unshielded LXe before reaching the cathode. The design explicitly draws 0.1 SLPM of xenon away from the detector to prevent outgassing contamination, representing a permanent purity cost.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Design a cold, low-radioactivity HV feedthrough using an ultrahigh-purity alumina (Al₂O₃) ceramic insulator with a titanium (CP1 grade, matching the cryostat material, per Ref. [10]) metal seal, operating at LXe temperature
- Alumina has demonstrated radioactivity levels of <0.1 ppb U/Th, comparable to the titanium cryostat
- The feedthrough penetrates the outer vacuum jacket at the bottom dome, keeping the entire HV cable within the cold xenon environment, eliminating the warm xenon umbilical and the associated outgassing purge flow
- Use a coaxial geometry with graded resistive coating on the ceramic surface (using a fired platinum-palladium thick-film resistor) to grade the electric field and prevent surface discharge
- This approach was successfully demonstrated for ICARUS at comparable voltages (referenced in the paper); adapt their design with lower-radioactivity materials

**Quantitative impact:** Elimination of the 0.1 SLPM purge flow increases net purification throughput available for the main active volume. The outgassing from the warm HV cable represents an uncontrolled impurity source; removing it would extend achievable electron lifetime, directly improving charge collection and S2 yield, and thus improving nuclear/electron recoil discrimination at low energies where S2/S1 separation is most critical.

---

## 4. Replacement of the Dual-Phase Heat Exchanger with a Pulse Tube Refrigerator

The current thermosyphon + external LN₂ bath system requires continuous LN₂ replenishment and operates at ~55 kW/K/m effective thermal conductivity. The LN₂ consumption is an operational overhead and a potential source of thermal instability.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Install a Cryomech PT415 pulse tube refrigerator (PTR) providing 40W of cooling at 77K, with a cold head insertable through the existing top flange penetration
- The PT415 cold head is 5.7cm in diameter, compatible with existing feedthrough geometry, and requires only electrical power and room-temperature helium supply lines
- Cooling power regulation via a resistive heater (as currently done for the thermosyphon cold heads) remains unchanged operationally
- PTR has no moving parts at low temperature, eliminating vibration-induced microphonic noise in PMT signals—a known issue in large LXe detectors with mechanical coolers
- Measured vibration from PT415 cold head is <5 microns amplitude at the cold tip; isolate mechanically from the TPC structure with a flexible copper braid thermal link
- The PTR cooling temperature is actively controlled by the drive electronics (Cryomech compressor unit), providing ±10 mK stability versus the vapor-pressure-regulated thermosyphon which depends on LN₂ bath temperature stability

**Quantitative impact:** Microphonic noise couples into baseline noise of PMT channels. The paper states 155 µV_RMS baseline noise; reducing microphonics by even 20% increases the signal-to-noise margin for single photoelectrons, lowering the effective S1 detection threshold from ~2 phe toward 1 phe, extending sensitivity to lower WIMP masses below ~10 GeV/c².

---

## 5. Replacement of Struck SIS3301 ADCs with Higher-Resolution Digitizers

The current DAQ uses 14-bit, 100 MHz flash ADCs. The single-photoelectron peak must be placed at 30 ADC counts to achieve 5σ separation from noise (Sec. 7.2), consuming dynamic range headroom unnecessarily.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace Struck SIS3301 boards with 14-bit, 250 MHz digitizers (e.g., Struck SIS3316, which uses the same VME interface already deployed, preserving DAQ infrastructure)
- The 250 MHz sampling rate (4 ns sample interval versus current 10 ns) better resolves the R8778 single-photoelectron FWHM of 6.8 ns, improving pulse area reconstruction accuracy
- At 250 MHz sampling, the anti-aliasing filter can be raised from 30 MHz to 80 MHz, passing more of the fast output bandwidth and recovering pulse shape information currently lost
- Implement FPGA-based online pulse area integration within the SIS3316 firmware, replacing the current POD compression scheme with a zero-suppressed area+timestamp format, reducing data volume by ~3× and enabling higher trigger rates
- Add a parallel 12-bit, 1 GSPS digitizer channel (e.g., one channel of a DRS4 evaluation board) per PMT group to capture the fast S1 pulse shape with sufficient time resolution to implement photon-counting-based S1/S2 discrimination in firmware

**Quantitative impact:** Improved S1 pulse area resolution directly improves energy resolution at threshold. The current threshold of ~2 phe in S1 corresponds to ~3 keVnr; with better pulse shape reconstruction and lower noise floor, threshold can approach 1 phe (~1.5 keVnr), improving sensitivity to light WIMPs (<10 GeV/c²) by extending the detectable recoil spectrum.

---

## 6. Addition of a Gadolinium-Doped Water Cherenkov Veto

The current muon veto uses 20 R7081 PMTs in a bare water tank, achieving >90% muon rejection efficiency. Neutrons from muon spallation that enter the LXe without an accompanying muon signal are the residual concern.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Dissolve gadolinium sulfate [Gd₂(SO₄)₃] in the water tank to a concentration of 0.1% by mass
- Gadolinium has a thermal neutron capture cross-section of 49,000 barns, ~5 orders of magnitude larger than hydrogen; neutron capture on Gd releases an 8 MeV gamma cascade detectable in the water Cherenkov system
- At 0.1% Gd concentration, mean neutron capture time drops from ~200 µs in pure water to ~30 µs, within the coincidence window of the existing trigger system
- The existing 20 R7081 PMTs provide ~0.5% photocathode coverage; add 20 additional R7081 PMTs (doubling coverage to ~1%) to ensure efficient detection of the 8 MeV gamma cascade, which produces ~200 Cherenkov photons per PMT at 1% coverage
- The Gd sulfate solution is chemically stable, non-corrosive to stainless steel and PVC at these concentrations, and does not affect water transparency at relevant wavelengths
- This technique was demonstrated effective at Super-Kamiokande (referenced as Ref. [31] in the paper) and in dedicated neutron veto prototypes

**Quantitative impact:** The paper projects ~0.1 NR events per 30,000 kg-days from muon-induced neutrons in both rock and water (Table 4). With Gd doping and doubled PMT coverage, neutrons that do not accompany a prompt muon signal (delayed or multiply-scattered neutrons) would be tagged with ~90% efficiency by the capture gamma cascade, reducing the muon-induced neutron NR background by approximately one order of magnitude.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a ~50 kg Two-Phase LAr TPC Dark Matter Detector

## Framing: What "Primary Physics Performance" Means Here

For a LAr TPC dark matter detector, the figures of merit are:
- **Nuclear recoil energy threshold** (determines low-mass WIMP reach)
- **Electronic/nuclear recoil discrimination** (S2/S1 ratio, pulse shape discrimination)
- **Fiducial mass fraction** (self-shielding efficiency)
- **Background rejection efficiency** (neutron, gamma, radon, surface events)
- **S1 and S2 light/charge collection efficiency**

The upgrades below are ranked roughly by physics impact.

---

## 1. Replace 3-Inch PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**The problem:** 3-inch cryogenic PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R11065 or similar) have several fundamental limitations:
- Quantum efficiency ~30–35% at 128 nm (with TPB wavelength shifter)
- Each PMT covers a relatively small solid angle, with dead area between units
- Radioactive contamination in glass/metal bodies contributes internal backgrounds (~few mBq/PMT from ²³⁸U, ²³²Th, ⁴⁰K)
- PMT bodies displace argon and reduce geometric coverage

**Proposed upgrade:** Tile the top and bottom planes entirely with **Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs** or **Hamamatsu VUV4 MPPC arrays** in a close-packed mosaic geometry.

Specific implementation:
- Use **FBK NUV-HD-Cryo 6×6 mm² cells** operated at ~77–87 K; these achieve photon detection efficiency (PDE) of ~50–55% at 420 nm (post-TPB conversion) at liquid argon temperature, compared to ~30% for PMTs
- Tile into **50 mm × 50 mm quad-SiPM modules** with individual readout channels ganged in groups of 4–9 depending on required channel count and noise budget
- Coat SiPM active surfaces directly with **evaporated TPB (tetraphenyl butadiene)** at ~0.2 mg/cm² — eliminates the separate wavelength-shifting foil boundary reflection losses
- Mount on **low-radioactivity PTFE-backed PCBs** with radioassayed copper traces; target <0.1 mBq/kg ²²⁶Ra equivalent in the sensor plane
- Expected improvement: **light yield increase from ~7–8 PE/keVee to 14–18 PE/keVee**, directly lowering the S1 detection threshold from ~4–5 keV to ~1–2 keV nuclear recoil equivalent — critical for sub-10 GeV WIMP sensitivity

**Why this matters most:** S1 threshold is the single biggest limiter of low-mass reach. Every factor of 2 in light yield lowers the threshold approximately proportionally.

---

## 2. Redesign the Field Cage for High, Uniform Drift Field with Reduced Radioactive Mass

**The problem:** Conventional resistor-chain field cages using standard resistors and metal rings introduce:
- Radioactive contamination (resistor ceramic, solder)
- Field non-uniformities at the few-percent level that smear S2 position reconstruction
- Electroluminescence hot spots that mimic signal

**Proposed upgrade: Polyimide/copper PCB field cage with custom thick-film resistors**

- Replace discrete resistor chain with a **continuous resistive Kapton (polyimide) strip** — a single helical or segmented resistive Kapton film (surface resistivity ~500 MΩ/square) eliminates thousands of solder joints and discrete resistor bodies
- Use **laser-etched copper field-shaping rings on 125 μm Kapton substrate**, 5 mm pitch; rings are <0.1 mm wide to minimize solid angle subtended from fiducial volume
- Implement **gradient-doped amorphous silicon or carbon-loaded PEEK** as the resistive element, with bulk radioactivity <10 μBq/kg ²²⁶Ra (achievable by material selection and radioassay screening)
- Target drift field: **1.0 kV/cm** (vs. typical 200–500 V/cm in existing detectors) — higher field dramatically reduces electron-ion recombination, boosting S2 yield and improving S2/S1 discrimination at low energies
- Field uniformity goal: **<0.1% variation** across fiducial volume, validated by UV laser calibration tracks

**Physics impact:** At 1 kV/cm vs. 200 V/cm, the charge yield at 20 keVnr improves by roughly a factor of 3–4, qualitatively transforming discrimination capability at threshold.

---

## 3. Replace the Gas Electron Multiplier or Wire Grid S2 Amplification with a Thick-GEM or LEM Stage

**The problem:** Standard extraction grids (woven wire meshes, typically 100–150 μm stainless steel wire at 3–5 mm pitch) have:
- Limited and variable optical transparency (~80–85%)
- Wire sag under electrostatic tension causing field non-uniformities
- Photon feedback from electroluminescence creating correlated backgrounds

**Proposed upgrade: Single-sided Large Electron Multiplier (LEM) or THick GEM (THGEM)**

- Install a **1–2 mm thick G10/FR4 or Kapton THGEM** with 0.5 mm diameter holes at 0.8 mm pitch, operated in the gas phase between liquid surface and anode
- THGEMs can provide intrinsic gain of 10–20× in addition to standard electroluminescence, effectively creating a **hybrid S2 amplification** stage — useful for single-electron detection
- Alternatively: use a **biconical electron lens grid** made from **electroformed copper mesh** (10 μm wire, 97% optical transparency) to minimize the shadow on the photosensor plane below
- Critical addition: a **PTFE reflector collar** at the liquid-gas interface to redirect sideward-emitted electroluminescence photons toward the top photosensor array

**Physics impact:** Single-electron S2 detection capability would allow sensitivity to ~0.1 keVnr via the ionization-only (S2-only) channel, opening the detector to WIMP masses below 1 GeV where S1 signals are undetectable.

---

## 4. Implement ³⁹Ar-Depleted Argon (Underground Argon) Combined with Active Online Pulse Shape Discrimination Electronics

**The problem:** Atmospheric argon contains ³⁹Ar at ~1 Bq/kg (cosmogenic activation), producing ~1 MHz singles rate in 50 kg — overwhelming trigger systems and creating pile-up that degrades discrimination.

**Proposed upgrade: Underground argon + FPGA-based real-time PSD**

- Source argon from the **Urania/Aria plant** (DarkSide-20k supply chain) providing **³⁹Ar depletion factor ≥1400×** — reduces ³⁹Ar rate from ~50 kBq total to ~35 Bq total, transforming the trigger environment
- Simultaneously deploy **custom 14-bit, 250 MSa/s waveform digitizers** (e.g., based on CAEN V1730 or custom ASIC) with **on-FPGA pulse shape discrimination** running in real-time:
  - Compute the **F-prompt parameter** (fraction of light in first 90 ns vs. total 7 μs window) event-by-event in firmware
  - Apply hardware trigger veto for F-prompt > 0.3 (electron recoil rejection) with <10 μs latency
  - This allows **zero-suppression trigger** without losing nuclear recoil candidates
- Add a **64-channel multiplexed slow control** ASIC for SiPM bias voltage trimming (±50 mV per channel) to maintain uniform gain across temperature gradients

**Physics impact:** Even with SiPM upgrade, ³⁹Ar rate with atmospheric Ar would produce trigger rates of hundreds of kHz — underground argon is arguably a prerequisite, not an upgrade. The electronics upgrade enables discrimination at the hardware level with **electron recoil rejection >10⁸** at 50% NR acceptance, as demonstrated by DarkSide-50.

---

## 5. Upgrade the Neutron Veto: Replace Passive Liquid Scintillator with Gd-Loaded or B-Loaded Scintillator with SiPM Readout

**The problem:** Plain liquid scintillator neutron vetoes have:
- Neutron capture on H producing 2.2 MeV γ (long 200 μs capture time, large coincidence window)
- PMT-based readout with radioactive glass bodies close to TPC
- Limited segmentation, poor vertex reconstruction

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Replace standard mineral oil/pseudocumene scintillator with **0.1% Gd-loaded LAB (linear alkylbenzene) scintillator** — Gd has σ_capture ~ 49,000 barns, reducing mean capture time from ~200 μs to ~30 μs and producing 8 MeV γ cascade (vs. 2.2 MeV), far above typical PMT noise threshold
- Alternatively: **¹⁰B-loaded scintillator** (boron carbide nanoparticle suspension) with capture time ~1 μs and 480 keV γ + α signature — allows 2 μs coincidence window, drastically reducing accidental coincidence rate
- Read out veto scintillator with **3×3 mm² SiPMs on low-radioactivity PCBs mounted outside the veto vessel** viewing through a thin acrylic window — eliminates PMT radioactivity from the veto region
- Add **active muon veto segmentation**: divide veto into 8–12 optically isolated segments to enable neutron directionality reconstruction, tagging spallation neutrons associated with muon tracks

**Physics impact:** Neutron veto efficiency improves from typical ~95% to **>99.5%** for single-scatter neutrons, while accidental coincidence rate drops by >10× with the reduced capture time window. This is especially important as the experiment accumulates exposure and neutron backgrounds become limiting.

---

## 6. Anode and Cathode Electrode Redesign for Reduced Radioactivity and Improved Optical Performance

**The problem:** Wire-wound or etched metallic anodes and cathodes contribute:
- Radioactive surface contamination (radon daughters plating out on metal)
- Reflection losses (bare metal is a poor reflector at 128 nm / 420 nm)
- Field emission at high voltage from wire surfaces

**Proposed upgrade:**

- Replace stainless steel cathode ring with a **single-crystal silicon or pyrolytic graphite cathode disc** — both have extremely low intrinsic radioactivity and very smooth surfaces minimizing field emission
- Coat all PTFE reflector panels with **enhanced specular reflector (ESR) multilayer film** (3M Vikuiti) overcoated with evaporated TPB — reflectivity >98% at 420 nm vs. ~95% for bare PTFE, increasing light collection by ~5–10% marginally but more importantly creating a **defined optical cavity** that improves S1 position reconstruction uniformity
- Implement **radon-reduced argon gas purge** of the gas phase above the liquid using a charcoal trap cooled to −50°C in the argon supply line, targeting <0.1 μBq/m³ ²²²Rn in the gas phase

---

## Summary Table: Expected Physics Gains

| Upgrade | Primary Metric Improved | Expected Quantitative Gain |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM photosensor array | S1 threshold, light yield | Threshold: 4 keVnr → 1–2 keVnr |
| High-field resistive field cage | S2 yield, discrimination | Charge yield ×3–4 at threshold |
| THGEM/LEM S2 amplification | S2-only analysis, low-mass reach | Single-electron sensitivity → sub-GeV WIMPs |
| Underground Ar + real-time PSD electronics | Trigger rate, ER rejection | ER rejection >10⁸; trigger rate kHz→Hz |
| Gd-loaded scintillator veto + SiPM readout | Neutron background | Veto efficiency 95%→99.5% |
| Cathode/anode/reflector redesign | Surface backgrounds, light collection | Radon backgrounds ×5–10 reduction |

---

## Priority Ordering for a Fixed Upgrade Budget

1. **SiPMs** — largest single impact on threshold and thus discovery potential for low-mass WIMPs
2. **Underground argon** — without this, SiPMs don't help because ³⁹Ar pile-up is disqualifying
3. **High drift field field cage** — transforms discrimination at threshold energies
4. **Real-time FPGA PSD** — needed to exploit PSD at high statistics
5. **Gd-loaded veto** — becomes critical once signal-region sensitivity reaches neutron-background-limited regime
6. **S2 amplification stage** — opens new physics channel but is an R&D risk

The SiPM + underground argon combination is the minimum viable upgrade set for a qualitative physics performance improvement.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for GERDA

## 1. Liquid Argon Scintillation Veto (Highest Priority)

The paper explicitly states GERDA decided to implement a LAr scintillation light veto for Phase II based on LArGe results, but it is absent in Phase I. This is the single highest-leverage upgrade.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the 30 µm copper radon shroud with a **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber curtain** surrounding the detector array. Specific candidate: Kuraray Y-11 fibers (already used in the plastic scintillator panels, reference [80]), arranged in a cylindrical geometry around each mini-shroud
- Deploy **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** rather than conventional PMTs for light readout, because they are far more compact, operate stably at 87 K LAr temperature, and have dramatically lower intrinsic radioactivity than glass PMTs. The ETL 9357 PMTs used in LArGe introduce significant mass near detectors
- Coat inner surfaces of the radon shroud with **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB)** as wavelength shifter to convert 128 nm LAr VUV scintillation to ~420 nm visible light detectable by SiPMs
- Target veto efficiency >90% for multi-Compton backgrounds based on pulse shape differences between nuclear recoils and electron recoils in LAr

This directly attacks the dominant remaining background from 42K and from multi-Compton gamma scattering, which pulse shape discrimination in germanium alone cannot fully reject.

---

## 2. Replacement of Coaxial Detectors with BEGe Detectors

The paper notes only five BEGe detectors were inserted in July 2011, with the bulk of the active mass remaining as legacy coaxial detectors (ANG and RG series) with substantially worse pulse shape discrimination (PSD) capability.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Complete transition to **Broad Energy Germanium (BEGe) detectors** (Canberra product referenced as [52], with PSD properties demonstrated in [53,54])
- BEGe detectors have a single small p+ contact producing a characteristic single-site event pulse shape parameter A/E (ratio of current amplitude to energy) that cleanly separates 0νββ point-like events from multi-site Compton scattering backgrounds
- The achieved energy resolution of **1.7 keV FWHM at 1332 keV** for the first seven BEGes is significantly better than the 4.2–5.3 keV range quoted for the legacy coaxial detectors at 2614 keV
- At Qββ = 2039 keV, improved resolution directly reduces the background window linearly. Moving from ~4.5 keV to ~2.5 keV FWHM reduces background counts in the ROI by approximately a factor of 1.8 for fixed BI
- The 20.8 kg of crystal slices already at Canberra Olen should be prioritized for detector production and deployment

---

## 3. Upgraded Front-End Electronics with Reduced Radioactivity

The CC2 preamplifier contributes (286±28) µBq in 226Ra and (150±24) µBq in 228Th per PCB board, which is close to the stated Phase I limit. For Phase II with BI target of 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr), this budget is unacceptably tight.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the **Cuﬂon PCB substrate** with a custom PCB fabricated from **oxygen-free high-conductivity (OFHC) copper traces on PTFE substrate**, eliminating the PCB dielectric material almost entirely as a radioactivity source
- Replace the **BF862 JFET** (NXP, standard commercial package) with a bare die JFET mounted without ceramic packaging, since ceramic packages contain significant 226Ra/228Th. Candidate: IF3602 bare die
- Replace **tantalum filter capacitors** entirely with stray capacitance implementation already partially used in CC2, but extend this to all decoupling functions. Tantalum is a significant source of radioactive contamination
- Move to a **cold ASIC design** specifically engineered for 87 K operation in place of discrete components, integrating the JFET input stage and feedback network monolithically. This reduces the total component count and associated radioactivity while improving noise performance. The noise specification of 0.8 keV + 0.024 keV/pF should be improvable to below 0.5 keV baseline with a dedicated cryogenic ASIC
- Relocate preampliﬁers **further from detectors** (currently ~30 cm) to ~50 cm using lower-capacitance signal interconnects, reducing solid angle subtended by electronics

---

## 4. Improved Radon Mitigation in the Cryostat

The paper reports a final 222Rn emanation rate of 54.7±3.5 mBq from the cryostat, contributing ~7×10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) assuming homogeneous distribution. The radon shroud provides up to a factor of seven reduction but this is not guaranteed.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the **30 µm copper foil radon shroud** with an **electroformed copper cylinder** of 500 µm thickness. Electroformed copper has demonstrated 222Rn emanation rates below 1 µBq/kg, roughly 100× lower than rolled copper foil, due to absence of grain boundaries and surface defects that trap 226Ra
- Install an **electrostatic 42K ion collector** — a grounded copper mesh cylinder at larger radius than the mini-shroud, biased at -100 V to -300 V to attract positive 42K ions before they drift toward the detector electric field. This directly addresses the leading observed background mechanism identified during commissioning
- Upgrade the activated charcoal radon filter on the LAr supply line from ~1 kg to **10 kg of Carbo-Act charcoal** cooled to liquid nitrogen temperature, achieving the demonstrated gas-phase reduction factor of >1000 referenced in [106] rather than the factor ~100 for the liquid-phase column
- Implement **continuous LAr recirculation** through a cold radon trap during operations rather than only during filling

---

## 5. Upgraded Muon Veto Coverage for the Neck Region

The paper acknowledges that muons entering through the cryostat neck receive only minimal water coverage, requiring plastic scintillators. The current 36-panel plastic array covers only 4×3 m² and has efficiency estimated at 97.9%.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Add a **second layer of 3 m water shielding above the cryostat neck** by extending the water tank roof geometry, or alternatively install a dedicated **small water Cherenkov detector** surrounding the neck region of diameter ~1 m with 6–8 ETL 9354KB PMTs (same type already qualified for water operation)
- Replace the current **H6780-2 and PMT-85 plastic scintillator readout PMTs** with **SiPM arrays**, which offer higher quantum efficiency (~40% vs ~20%), lower operating voltage, and compatibility with more compact panel geometries enabling finer segmentation
- Increase plastic scintillator panel thickness from **3 cm to 5 cm** using the same UPS-923A scintillator material to improve the muon/gamma discrimination and increase light yield per muon track, reducing the probability of misidentification at the plastic panel trigger level

---

## 6. Replacement of Signal Cable Chain with Lower-Mass Alternative

The stainless steel cable chain (21×13 mm² cross section) supporting detector strings is a significant mass of metal near the detectors and contributes to the radioactivity budget through activated isotopes.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the stainless steel cable chain with a **PTFE-jacketed Kevlar load-bearing cable bundle**, using the same Habia SM50 coaxial cables for signals already qualified for radiopurity (Table 5 shows 273±50 µBq for 508 m)
- Use **electroformed copper signal strips** with PTFE insulation for the final 30 cm detector connection rather than wire-erosion cut copper strips, reducing surface contamination from machining
- Replace the **Teledyne Reynolds 167-2896 HV cables** (10 required per 3-string lock) with custom HV cables on Kapton substrate with lower dielectric radioactivity; screen each candidate cable batch with ICP-MS before deployment given the cable mass is significant (Table 5 shows HV TR 18 kV cables contribute <11.1 mBq, the single largest lock component contribution)

---

## Summary of Expected Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Background Addressed | Expected BI Reduction Factor |
|---|---|---|
| LAr scintillation veto with SiPMs | 42K, multi-site Compton | 3–10× |
| Full BEGe deployment + PSD | Multi-site events | 3–5× |
| Improved front-end electronics | Internal radioactivity | ~2× |
| Electroformed Cu shroud + electrostatic collector | 42Ar/42K ions | 5–10× |
| Enhanced neck muon veto | Muon-induced neutrons | ~2× |

The LAr veto and BEGe PSD are complementary and largely independent rejection handles; combined they could plausibly reach the Phase II target of 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr) even without the other improvements.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for GERDA

## Analysis of Primary Performance Limitations

Based on the paper, the dominant constraints on physics performance are:
1. Background index of 2.0×10⁻² cts/(keV·kg·yr) — target for Phase II is 10⁻³
2. Energy resolution of 4.5 keV FWHM at Qββ — limiting signal-to-background discrimination
3. ⁴²K ion collection on detector surfaces — dominant commissioning background
4. ²²²Rn in LAr — contributes ~7×10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) even with shroud
5. No active LAr scintillation veto in Phase I — identified as needed for Phase II

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. LAr Scintillation Veto Implementation

The paper explicitly states LArGe studies motivated this for Phase II, but it is absent from Phase I. This is the highest-priority upgrade.

**Specific implementation:**

- **Wavelength shifter coating:** Deposit tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) at ~0.2 mg/cm² onto the inner surface of a new nylon or VM2000 curtain surrounding the detector array. TPB shifts LAr scintillation from 128 nm VUV to ~420 nm, within PMT quantum efficiency range. The existing VM2000 foil already shifts some UV but is not optimized for 128 nm conversion.

- **Photosensor array:** Replace or supplement the existing 8" ETL PMTs in the water tank neck region with Hamamatsu R11065 3" low-radioactivity PMTs (metal channel dynode structure, ~35% quantum efficiency at 420 nm, <10 mBq/kg ²²⁶Ra) mounted on the inner surface of the radon shroud or a new inner nylon vessel. Target ~20 PMTs viewing the LAr volume directly. These PMTs have substantially lower radioactivity than standard tubes and were already being characterized for similar applications within the community by 2012.

- **Alternative photosensor:** Cryogenic silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) such as Hamamatsu MPPC S10931-100P, which operate at LAr temperature (87 K) with adequate gain (~10⁶) and low dark count rate when cold (~10 Hz/mm² at 87 K versus MHz at room temperature). Mount in a sparse array on the mini-shroud exterior. The low mass (~milligrams per device) minimizes radioactivity contribution. A tiled array of 1 cm² devices covering ~500 cm² would provide sufficient solid angle at <1 g total silicon mass.

- **Expected gain:** LArGe studies cited in the paper showed background rejection factors of ~3–10× for surface alpha and beta events using combined pulse shape discrimination and scintillation detection. This alone could close most of the gap to the 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr) Phase II target.

---

### 2. Replacement of Coaxial Detectors with BEGe Detectors for Enhanced Pulse Shape Discrimination

The paper mentions BEGe detectors are in production for Phase II with "good pulse shape discrimination properties," but Phase I operates entirely with coaxial detectors.

**Specific implementation:**

- **BEGe geometry rationale:** The point-contact geometry of BEGe detectors produces a single-site vs. multi-site discrimination parameter A/E (ratio of current pulse maximum to energy) with separation power that coaxial detectors cannot match. Published results from Budjaš et al. (cited as reference 53) demonstrate >90% signal survival with ~80% background rejection for surface events.

- **Detector specification:** Canberra BEGe detectors of ~700–800 g mass (larger masses degrade the weighting potential uniformity needed for PSD). The first seven produced for GERDA already achieved 1.7 keV FWHM at 1332 keV — superior to the 4.5 keV average of Phase I coaxial detectors at Qββ. Deploying a full array of ~35 such detectors reaching ~25 kg total enriched mass while maintaining PSD capability is the concrete path.

- **Energy resolution improvement:** Moving from 4.5 keV to ~2.5 keV FWHM at Qββ reduces the effective ROI width by ~45%, directly reducing background counts proportionally without changing the BI, effectively improving sensitivity by the same factor.

---

### 3. Upgraded Preamplifier with Lower Noise and Reduced Radioactivity

The CC2 preamplifier achieves ~0.8 keV + 0.024 keV/pF noise floor. For BEGe detectors with ~1–2 pF capacitance, this is acceptable, but the PCB radioactivity (286±28 µBq ²²⁶Ra, 150±24 µBq ²²⁸Th per board) pushes against the Phase II budget.

**Specific implementation:**

- **Substrate:** Replace Cuflon PCB with a crystalline quartz substrate or sapphire substrate. Both have demonstrated <1 µBq/kg in ²²⁸Th — roughly three orders of magnitude below Cuflon. Sapphire is machinable and available in sheets suitable for trace deposition. This requires adapting trace layout for different dielectric constant (~9.9 for sapphire vs ~2.1 for Cuflon) but the reduced radioactivity (~0.1–1 µBq total per board versus 150–286 µBq currently) would provide substantial margin.

- **Input JFET replacement:** The BF862 in a commercial SOT23 package has an uncharacterized plastic package contributing unknown radioactivity. Substitute a bare die JFET (InterFET NJ132L or equivalent) bonded directly to the substrate, eliminating the plastic package. Bare silicon die has negligible ²²⁶Ra and ²²⁸Th content.

- **Feedback resistor:** The 500 MΩ feedback resistor is a known radioactivity concern in low-background electronics. Replace with a "transistor reset" or pulsed-reset scheme eliminating the physical resistor entirely, as demonstrated in several low-background germanium detector systems. This also removes a common source of excess low-frequency noise.

- **Tantalum capacitors:** The paper notes these are used and are a radioactivity source. Replace with vacuum-gap or air-gap capacitors implemented as precision-machined copper structures — effectively zero radioactivity, compatible with LAr operation, and appropriate for the small capacitance values (0.35 pF) needed.

---

### 4. Improved Radon Shroud and Active Radon Suppression

The paper reports 54.7 mBq ²²²Rn emanation from the cryostat, giving ~7×10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) if uniformly distributed, with the shroud providing up to 7× reduction.

**Specific implementation:**

- **Upgraded mini-shroud material:** Replace the 60 µm copper foil mini-shroud with electroformed copper of ~200 µm thickness. Electroformed copper achieves <0.1 µBq/kg ²²⁶Ra (compared to ~16 µBq/kg upper limit for the rolled copper currently used, per Table 6). The electroforming process inherently excludes ²³²Th and ²³⁸U at the ppq level. The increased thickness also better suppresses electric field leakage — directly addressing the ⁴²K ion collection problem.

- **Nylon radon barrier:** Install a 125 µm thick nylon-6 vessel (as used successfully in Borexino, cited in the paper) coaxially between the radon shroud and the copper mini-shroud. Nylon-6 has a ²²²Rn diffusion coefficient of ~3×10⁻¹¹ cm²/s at room temperature, substantially lower at 87 K, providing additional passive radon suppression without introducing significant mass or radioactivity.

- **Online radon monitoring with closed-loop feedback:** Install a continuous electrostatic radon monitor (based on the MoREx technology already in the collaboration's possession) on the LAr boil-off gas. Connect its output to the LN₂ cooling rate controller. Elevated radon triggers increased cooling, suppressing convective transport toward the detectors. This is a controls upgrade but requires a dedicated gas-phase radon sensor calibrated to ~1 µBq/m³ sensitivity.

---

### 5. Replacement of the DAQ with Continuous Digitization

The current Phase I DAQ uses a trapezoidal filter trigger with a 40 µs window at 25 MHz (downsampled) plus a 5 µs full-rate trace. This discards waveform information before any software selection.

**Specific implementation:**

- **Full waveform digitization:** Replace the custom NIM-based Phase I DAQ with struck SIS3316 16-bit, 250 MHz ADCs (the same manufacturer as the muon DAQ's SIS3301, ensuring familiarity). At 250 MHz with 16-bit depth, each 160 µs trace requires ~640 kB. At the GERDA event rate of <1 Hz per detector, this is ~10 MB/detector/day — entirely manageable with 2012-era storage.

- **Zero-suppression firmware:** Implement FPGA-based online zero-suppression keeping only the 20 µs around any trigger plus a 100 µs pretrigger baseline region. This reduces data volume by ~5× while preserving all pulse shape information.

- **Benefit for PSD:** The full 250 MHz bandwidth preserves the <100 ns rise-time features of BEGe detector signals that carry multi-site vs. single-site discrimination information. The current 100 MHz / 25 MHz architecture marginally resolves these features. Monte Carlo studies of BEGe PSD show that bandwidth above 100 MHz improves A/E separation by ~15–20%.

---

### 6. Underground Crystal Growing for Phase II Material

The paper identifies cosmogenic ⁶⁰Co as contributing (1–2)×10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr) from above-ground exposure during previous HdM/IGEX operation, and notes minimization to ~5 days above ground for reprocessing.

**Specific implementation:**

- **Underground zone refinement:** Establish a dedicated zone-refinement furnace at LNGS or HADES (500 m w.e.) rather than at surface facilities. A commercial Leybold-Heraeus or equivalent zone refiner requires ~20 kW power and ~10 m² floor space — both available at LNGS. At 500 m w.e., ⁶⁰Co production rate is suppressed by ~10⁴ relative to surface, essentially eliminating this background source for Phase II material.

- **Underground crystal pulling:** Similarly relocate the Czochralski puller underground. This is more demanding (vibration isolation, clean room requirements, ~50 kW power) but the LNGS Hall A infrastructure demonstrated for GERDA itself shows this scale of installation is feasible. The payoff is elimination of the dominant internal background for detectors produced from new enriched material.

---

## Summary of Expected Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Effect | Estimated BI Reduction Factor |
|---|---|---|
| LAr scintillation veto (TPB + SiPMs) | Reject surface/beta events | 3–5× |
| Full BEGe array with PSD | Reject multi-site backgrounds | 3–4× |
| Electroformed Cu mini-shroud + nylon vessel | Suppress ⁴²K and Rn | 2–3× |
| Improved CC2 on sapphire/quartz | Reduce near-detector radioactivity | ~2× |
| Underground crystal production | Eliminate ⁶⁰Co internal background | removes ~10⁻³ contribution |
| Full-bandwidth DAQ | Enable optimal PSD algorithms | 1.5× (complementary to BEGe) |

Combined, these upgrades are multiplicative in background suppression and could realistically reach the Phase II target of 10⁻³ cts/(keV·kg·yr), while the BEGe energy resolution improvement simultaneously reduces the effective ROI background by ~45% independent of the BI reduction.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Liquid Xenon TPC Searching for 0νββ

## Context and Performance Priorities

The primary physics performance metric is **energy resolution at Q_ββ = 2458 keV**, since 0νββ appears as a peak above a continuous background. Secondary metrics are **background rejection** (primarily from 2νββ, γ backgrounds, and radon daughters) and **fiducial mass efficiency**. I'll address each bottleneck concretely.

---

## 1. Replace Avalanche Photodiodes with Vacuum Ultraviolet Silicon Photomultipliers (VUV-SiPMs)

**The problem:** APDs operated in liquid xenon at ~165 nm have single-photon detection efficiency of roughly 15–20%, high bias voltage requirements (~1400 V), non-trivial excess noise factor (F ≈ 2), and relatively large capacitance that degrades timing.

**The upgrade:**
- Deploy **Hamamatsu VUV4 SiPMs** (S13370-6050CN series) or **FBK VUV-HD3 SiPMs**, which achieve photon detection efficiency of **24–27% at 178 nm** (the LXe emission peak) at cryogenic temperatures.
