- Same mass in Ti-Grade2 from select stock: <0.002 mBq — factor 1000
- At 250 kg scale operating at 10⁻⁴⁷ cm² WIMP cross-section sensitivity, the ER background budget from internal components can be held below **0.01 events/tonne/year/keV_ee** only with this substitution

### PTFE Reflector Panels: Ultra-low background custom formulation

Standard PTFE has ~1–10 ppb U/Th. **Manufacturer-specific low-background PTFE** (e.g., Daikin Polyflon M-12 with pre-screening, used in XENON1T) achieves <0.1 ppb. For 250 kg TPC requiring ~5 kg of PTFE panels, this reduces contribution by factor 10–100.

Alternatively: replace PTFE panels with **sputtered aluminum-on-copper reflector** (99.999% purity aluminum, 200 nm thick) — near-UV reflectivity >95% at 178 nm, radioactivity negligible. Demonstrated in NEXT experiment electrodes.

---

## 6. Neutron Veto Upgrade: Gadolinium-Loaded Water vs. Liquid Scintillator Shell

If using a water Cherenkov outer detector (baseline), the single most impactful upgrade is adding **0.1% GdSO₄ by mass** to the water shield.

- Thermal neutron capture on natural Gd releases **~8 MeV in gamma rays** with ~20–30 µs capture time
- Detection efficiency for neutrons reaching the inner vessel increases from ~40% (pure water) to **>95%** with Gd-loading and standard 8" PMT coverage of ~20%
- **Specific implementation:** Use Gd₂(SO₄)₃ dissolved at 0.1 g/L (SK-Gd demonstrated at SuperKamiokande since 2020), with 50% coverage by 8" Hamamatsu R5912 or equivalent PMTs, plus a UV-transparent acrylic containment barrier at 50 cm radius separating Gd-water from pure water to protect optical surfaces

**Alternative for maximum neutron rejection:** A 5 cm thick **EJ-335 Gd-loaded liquid scintillator** shell between the inner cryostat and water tank, read out by 3" R11065 PMTs — increases neutron tagging to ~98% and also tags gammas from cryostat materials.

---

## 7. Cryogenic System: Pulse Tube Refrigerator Vibration Isolation

### Decouple PTR mechanically and acoustically

**The underappreciated problem:** 1–2 Hz vibration from pulse tube refrigerators (e.g., Cryomech PT90 or PT415) couples into the liquid surface, creating surface waves that vary the liquid level by ±50–200 µm at the gate electrode. This modulates S2 gain by ~1–5% with a periodic signature.

**Specific fix:** 
- Mount PTR on **metal bellows isolation flange** (e.g., Senior Flexonics Pathway series, stainless, rated to 10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s He leak rate) with 6-degree-of-freedom passive isolation
- Add a **fast capacitive liquid level sensor** (resolution 10 µm, 100 Hz bandwidth) with feedback to a **small piezoelectric liquid level actuator** (small heater coil under xenon injection point corrects level to ±10 µm)
- Net effect: S2 gain stability improves from ~2% RMS to ~0.1% RMS → directly improves ER/NR band separation at low energy (the bands overlap more when S2 resolution is degraded)

---

## Summary Priority Ranking

| Upgrade | Primary Metric Improved | Difficulty | Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| SiPM bottom array | S1 threshold, position resolution | High | Very High |
| Extraction grid / gate redesign | S2 yield, single-electron threshold | Medium | Very High |
| Resistive field cage panel | Fiducialization, ER/NR discrimination | Medium | High |
| Gd-loaded water veto | Neutron background rejection | Low-Medium | High |
| Graded HV feedthrough | Spurious electron background | Medium | High |
| Ti/Al electrodes | ER background rate | Low | Medium-High |
| PTR vibration isolation | S2 gain stability | Low | Medium |

The **single highest-leverage upgrade** for a detector at this scale is the **bottom SiPM array with cryogenic ASIC readout**, because it simultaneously improves photon detection efficiency, single-photon resolution, position reconstruction, and eliminates a major radioactivity source — all of which feed into every primary physics observable simultaneously.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Bare HPGe Array in Liquid Argon

## Context and Performance Drivers

The primary physics performance metric is **background index** (BI, counts/keV/kg/yr at Q_ββ = 2039 keV) and **energy resolution** (FWHM at Q_ββ), which together determine the half-life sensitivity. I'll address each major background source and resolution limitation with concrete technology proposals.

---

## 1. Germanium Detector Upgrades

### 1.1 Detector Geometry: Inverted Coaxial Point Contact (ICPC)

**Current limitation:** Standard BEGe or coaxial geometries either limit mass per detector or have suboptimal pulse shape discrimination (PSD).

**Upgrade:** Deploy **inverted coaxial point contact (ICPC) detectors** at large mass (≥1 kg per crystal, targeting 2–3 kg).

- Single small readout electrode (point contact, ~5 mm diameter) gives low capacitance (~1 pF), hence low electronic noise
- Full depletion at modest bias (~3–5 kV)
- Weighting potential strongly peaked at point contact → excellent A/E (amplitude-over-energy) discrimination between single-site events (signal) and multi-site events (γ background)
- Demonstrated by GERDA Phase II upgrade; LEGEND-200 uses these with BI ~5×10⁻⁴ cts/keV/kg/yr

**Concrete spec target:** FWHM < 2.5 keV at 2039 keV, A/E survival fraction >90% for signal with >99% rejection of Compton-scattered γ events.

### 1.2 Detector Surface Passivation and Groove Geometry

**Current limitation:** Incomplete charge collection near surfaces, especially the passivated groove around the point contact, creates a "surface event" background from α and β particles.

**Upgrade:**
- **Amorphous germanium (a-Ge) contacts** replacing boron-implanted or lithium-diffused contacts on the n+ side — thinner dead layer (<1 μm vs. ~0.3 mm for Li-diffused), reducing α and β energy degradation and improving surface event rejection
- **Optimized groove geometry** with etched and re-passivated silicon oxide/nitride layer to minimize leakage current (target <5 pA at operating temperature)
- **Detector-holder interface:** use PTFE-free, ultra-low-background holders (electroformed copper or silicon carbide) to minimize radon progeny deposition on detector surfaces

### 1.3 Signal Readout: Low-Noise Front-End Electronics

**Current limitation:** Johnson noise and 1/f noise in front-end ASICs limit resolution, especially at the low-capacitance point contact.

**Upgrade:**
- **Cryo-compatible charge-sensitive preamplifiers** based on **SiGe HBT ASICs** (e.g., developed for LEGEND) operating at 87 K (LAr temperature) — eliminates the warm cable capacitance penalty
- Place the first-stage FET or HBT within 1–2 cm of the detector contact using a compact flex-PCB assembly in LAr
- Target equivalent noise charge (ENC) < 30 e⁻ RMS at 87 K → contributes <0.5 keV FWHM noise term
- **Fully differential signal routing** on twisted-pair PTFE-insulated cables to suppress microphonic pickup from LAr boiling
- **Dual-gain readout:** one channel optimized for the 2039 keV ROI (12-bit, ~0.25 keV/ADC bin), one for high-energy γ tagging (for veto coincidences)

---

## 2. Liquid Argon Instrumentation Upgrades

### 2.1 LAr Scintillation: Wavelength-Shifting Fiber + SiPM System

**Current limitation:** Bare LAr emits at 128 nm (VUV), requiring either VUV-transparent photodetectors or wavelength shifters. Coverage and photon detection efficiency (PDE) are typically limited.

**Upgrade:** Deploy a **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber curtain + SiPM array** system surrounding the detector array.

- Coat inner nylon or copper shroud with **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB)** via vacuum evaporation (coating density ~0.2 mg/cm²) — shifts 128 nm → 420 nm with ~1.2 photon/photon efficiency
- Route **BCF-91A or Y-11 WLS fibers** (Saint-Gobain, 1 mm diameter, double-clad) in a dense curtain (pitch ~5 mm) capturing re-emitted blue photons
- Read fibers with **Hamamatsu S13360-series SiPMs** (PDE ~50% at 420 nm, dark count rate ~100 kcps/mm² at 87 K — significantly reduced from room temperature)
- Target: **≥3% overall photon detection efficiency** for 128 nm LAr photons, enabling detection of ~150 photons per MeV deposited
- This enables **LAr veto efficiency >99.9%** for events with any energy deposition in LAr outside germanium

**Alternative/complement:** **ARAPUCA or X-ARAPUCA light traps** — dichroic filter cavities that trap shifted photons and read with embedded SiPMs. X-ARAPUCA demonstrated ~3× higher effective PDE than flat TPB+PMT schemes; concrete implementation uses 6×6 cm² tiles tiled on the inner shroud surface.

### 2.2 LAr Purity and Recirculation

**Current limitation:** Electronegative impurities (O₂, H₂O, N₂) quench LAr scintillation and can affect charge transport in Ge (though Ge is self-shielded).

**Upgrade:**
- **Inline Oxisorb + molecular sieve (13X) purification loop** with cryogenic pump, maintaining O₂ equivalent <0.1 ppb in LAr
- **Radon-suppressed argon supply**: use **underground argon** (e.g., from CO₂ well sources, as developed for DarkSide-20k) with ³⁹Ar activity ~0.73 mBq/kg vs. 1 Bq/kg for atmospheric argon — this is perhaps the single most impactful LAr upgrade
  - ³⁹Ar (β⁻, endpoint 565 keV) at atmospheric abundance creates ~10⁶ events/day/tonne in LAr; these require vetoing and cause pile-up/deadtime issues
  - Underground argon reduces this by factor ~1400
- **LAr level and temperature stabilization** to <1 mK fluctuation to prevent microphonic noise on Ge contacts from boiling

### 2.3 Radon Mitigation in LAr

**Current limitation:** ²²²Rn emanated from surfaces dissolves in LAr, producing ²¹⁰Pb→²¹⁰Bi→²¹⁰Po decay chain; ²¹⁰Po α decays (5.3 MeV) on or near Ge detector surfaces create tail events in the ROI via degraded α energy.

**Upgrade:**
- **Electroformed copper inner shroud** with measured Rn emanation <1 μBq/m² (requires electroforming in Rn-free environment underground)
- **Rn-suppressed argon blanket** on all surfaces exposed to warm gas phase
- **Rn trap on LAr recirculation loop**: activated charcoal trap at ~190 K achieves Rn retention factor >10⁴
- **α tagging from ²¹⁰Po:** use the LAr scintillation veto — α particles produce high scintillation/ionization ratio (quenching factor ~0.25 for nuclear recoils in LAr but α particles detectable) — combined with the Ge detector's own charge-pulse shape (α events near surface show characteristic slow collection)

---

## 3. Passive Shielding and Muon Veto Upgrades

### 3.1 Water Cherenkov Muon Veto Enhancement

**Current limitation:** Standard water shield with PMTs may have geometric gaps and limited muon tagging efficiency; muon-induced neutrons can capture and emit 2.2 MeV γ (¹H capture) or higher-energy γ from Ge activation, contributing backgrounds.

**Upgrade:**
- **Replace PMTs with large-area SiPM modules or LAPPDs** (Large Area Picosecond Photodetectors, 20×20 cm², Incom Inc.) — improved PDE (30–40% vs. 20–25% for PMTs), no high-voltage distribution risk, faster timing (σ_t ~50 ps) for muon track reconstruction
- **Gd-doped water** (0.1% Gd₂(SO₄)₃ by mass): thermal neutrons capture on Gd with 8 MeV γ cascade (σ_capture = 49,000 barn vs. 0.3 barn for H) within ~20 μs — enables tagging of muon-induced neutrons with ~90% efficiency
  - Requires corrosion-resistant liner (HDPE or stainless with epoxy coating)
  - Water transparency maintained with Gd at 0.1% for >10 m attenuation length at 420 nm
- **Muon veto efficiency target: >99.9%** with <500 μs coincidence window
- **Active muon tracker panels** above the water tank: 2 layers of scintillator strips (e.g., extruded plastic scintillator from Fermilab, 4 cm × 1 cm cross section) with WLS fiber readout and SiPM, providing muon direction reconstruction to identify candidate spallation neutron trajectories

### 3.2 Inner Copper Shield

**Current limitation:** External γ flux from surrounding rock/water shield contributes at some level; more critically, the support structure and front-end electronics emit γ radiation.

**Upgrade:**
- **Electroformed copper inner vessel** (10–15 cm thick) surrounding the LAr volume containing the detector array
- Electroformed copper achieves **<0.1 μBq/kg of ²²⁶Ra** and **<0.5 μBq/kg of ²³²Th** — 10–100× lower than OFHC copper
- This attenuates external γ below ~100 keV by >10 orders of magnitude and reduces the flux from electronics by ~3 orders of magnitude at 2039 keV
- Fabricated underground at SURF or LNGS electroforming facilities to avoid cosmogenic activation

---

## 4. Electronics and Data Acquisition

### 4.1 Full Waveform Digitization

**Current limitation:** Triggered DAQ systems can miss pileup events or apply suboptimal shaping.

**Upgrade:**
- **Flash ADCs at 250 MS/s, 14–16 bit** (e.g., SIS3316 or Struck equivalents, or custom ASICs) for all Ge channels — enables **offline pulse shape analysis** without committing to online trigger decisions
- **Zero-suppression firmware in FPGA** (Xilinx Ultrascale or equivalent) storing only windows around candidate events (±50 μs) with full trace
- **Multi-site event rejection via current pulse analysis:** rise-time analysis, A/E parameter, and **time-coincidence between Ge detectors** (coincident events in two crystals = γ background, rejected) — all done offline with full waveforms
- **Trigger-less (streaming) readout** synchronized with SiPM LAr veto — no deadtime from veto processing

### 4.2 SiPM Readout Electronics

- **Cryogenic SiPM signal summing** at 87 K using low-noise transimpedance amplifiers (JFET-input op-amps) before routing to warm electronics
- **Nanosecond timing** on LAr pulses to exploit **triplet/singlet ratio** in LAr (τ_singlet = 6 ns, τ_triplet = 1.6 μs) for particle identification — α vs. γ vs. neutron discrimination in the LAr itself provides additional veto handles

---

## 5. Radiopurity and Assembly Upgrades

### 5.1 Underground Detector Fabrication and Storage

- **Zone-refine and grow crystals underground** (or transport in Rn-free containers with cosmogenic exposure time <1 week) — Ge cosmogenic isotopes (⁶⁸Ge, t₁/₂=271 d; ⁶⁰Co, t₁/₂=5.27 yr) produce backgrounds in the ROI; minimizing surface exposure is critical
- **⁶⁸Ge veto strategy:** 271-day half-life means after ~3 years underground, activity falls 8×; design experiment for phased operation with improving BI over time
- **Detector underground storage** in LAr or liquid nitrogen from the moment of fabrication

### 5.2 Material Screening and Component Selection

- **ICP-MS screening** of all construction materials to <μBq/kg levels for U/Th chains before use; **HPGe counting** (ironic but effective) for cosmogenic and anthropogenic isotopes
- **Electroformed copper detector holders** with no solder joints, no plastics within 5 cm of detectors; use only **Cirlex (polyimide) or MACOR** if insulators are needed
- **Underground cable production:** PTFE-insulated copper signal cables with measured ²²⁶Ra < 0.1 μBq/m

---

## 6. Prioritized Impact Summary

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Expected BI Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| Underground (low-³⁹Ar) argon | Eliminate pile-up, reduce accidental coincidences | Factor ~10 in LAr veto efficiency |
| ICPC detectors with a-Ge contacts | PSD for multi-site rejection; surface α/β rejection | Factor ~5–10 in BI |
| X-ARAPUCA + SiPM LAr veto | LAr anti-coincidence efficiency 99.9%+ | Factor ~5 in γ background |
| Gd-doped water + muon tracking | Spallation neutron tagging | Factor ~2–3 in muon-induced background |
| Electroformed Cu inner vessel + Rn trap | Reduce ²¹⁰Po α tails and external γ | Factor ~2–5 in surface/external backgrounds |
| Cryo-ASIC front-end at 87 K | FWHM from ~2.5 → <2.0 keV | Directly improves signal/background ratio |
| Full waveform streaming DAQ | Optimal offline PSD, no trigger bias | Factor ~2 in analysis efficiency |

**The highest single-impact upgrade** is the deployment of **underground argon combined with the X-ARAPUCA/SiPM LAr veto system**, as the LAr anti-coincidence veto is the defining discriminator for this detector concept and its efficiency is directly tied to photon detection efficiency and the intrinsic ³⁹Ar activity driving accidental coincidence rates.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for ProtoDUNE-SP / DUNE-SP

## Framing the Problem

The paper identifies specific, quantified performance limitations. I'll target upgrades to the components where the physics constraints are most clearly documented, avoiding speculation about post-2021 developments.

---

## 1. Anode Plane Assembly Wire Readout → Pixel or Strip Charge Readout

### Current Limitation
The wrapped-wire geometry (U/V at ±35.7°) creates inherent ambiguities in 3D reconstruction. The paper notes the angle was specifically chosen so "each induction wire only crosses a given collection wire one time, reducing the ambiguities that the reconstruction must address" — acknowledging this remains a problem rather than solving it. Induction plane signals are bipolar and harder to interpret. ENC at room temperature is 1100 e⁻, dropping to ~400 e⁻ in LAr.

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace wrapped-wire APAs with **pixelated charge readout** using LArPix-style CMOS ASICs directly bump-bonded to tiled pixel pads.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Tile the APA face with 3–4 mm pitch pixel pads on a polyimide flex circuit
- Each pixel connects directly to a cryogenic CMOS charge amplifier (0.18 μm process, same as current FE ASIC) bonded to the back of the PCB tile
- Target pixel capacitance: ~5–15 fF versus ~150 pF per wire currently, reducing Johnson noise contribution proportionally
- Expected ENC improvement: from ~400 e⁻ to below 100 e⁻ in LAr, given the roughly 10× capacitance reduction
- Eliminates wire tension, combs, and soldering infrastructure entirely
- Removes reconstruction ambiguity — every pixel gives an unambiguous 3D space point

**Tradeoffs to engineer:**
- Channel count increases from 2,560 per APA to approximately 150,000 per APA (at 4 mm pitch over 5.984 m × 2.3 m active area), requiring aggressive zero-suppression in-pixel
- Heat dissipation must be budgeted: at 6 mW/channel × 150k channels = 900 W per APA, requiring a radical redesign of the power delivery and cooling scheme; power must be reduced to ~0.1 mW/channel through aggressive duty cycling or continuous operation at very low supply voltage (sub-threshold regime)
- The wrapped-wire design's advantage of covering both drift faces becomes moot with pixels since each face is read out independently

---

## 2. Cold Electronics Architecture → Cryogenic Signal Processing with Local Zero-Suppression

### Current Limitation
The paper states TPC data streams at **430 Gb/s** continuously with no zero-suppression, explicitly because "this allows for the acquisition of an unbiased dataset to be used offline to study data reduction methods." The FE ASIC dissipates 6 mW/channel and the ADC ASIC below 5 mW/channel. The FPGA mezzanine on each FEMB is performing only 4:1 multiplexing, not signal processing.

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace the FPGA mezzanine with a **cryogenic ASIC trigger primitive extractor** capable of hit-finding in-situ, reducing output bandwidth by a factor of ~50–100.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Design a 128-channel digital signal processing ASIC in the same 0.18 μm CMOS process used for FE and ADC ASICs (demonstrated cryogenic-capable)
- Functions to implement on-ASIC: baseline subtraction using a running median filter, hit detection via configurable threshold (in multiples of RMS noise), hit parameter extraction (start time, peak ADC, integral, width)
- Output only hit primitives: at 2 MHz sampling, a 500 μs drift window contains 1000 samples; a typical MIP produces ~200 hit samples across ~10 wires per APA face, so trigger primitive output is O(10 kb/s) per APA versus 430 Gb/s
- Include a 13 μs deep circular buffer (matching the SSP design already used in PDS) so that upon an external trigger, the full raw waveform can be shipped — preserving the unbiased dataset option during calibration runs
- Power target: <1 mW/channel for the digital processing ASIC, achievable by running at reduced voltage (0.9 V) at 77 K where leakage current is suppressed

**Quantified benefit:**
The paper describes retrofitting self-triggering to ProtoDUNE-SP using warm servers performing software hit-finding on raw 430 Gb/s data from a single APA. Moving this to cold ASICs eliminates the need for O(10) high-end warm servers per APA and reduces optical fiber count from 30 WIBs (5 per APA × 6 APAs) by a factor proportional to the compression ratio.

---

## 3. High Voltage System → Segmented Cathode with Active Discharge Suppression

### Current Limitation
The paper devotes extensive discussion to HV instabilities: "current blips" and "current streamers" originating specifically from GP#6, reaching rates of 4–6 streamers/day. The root cause is identified as "a slow discharge process of charged-up insulating materials present in the high-field region outside of the FC." The auto-recovery script cycles HV down and back up in under 4 minutes, causing dead time. The correlation with LAr purity is explicitly noted: higher purity worsens streamers because electronegative impurities had been acting as quenchers.

### Proposed Upgrade A: Replace FR4/Kapton Resistive Sheet with Embedded Resistor Network Cathode

**Current design:** 3 mm FR4 sheet laminated with Kapton D11261075 resistive film (bulk resistivity provides slow discharge).

**Proposed design:**
- Replace monolithic resistive sheet with a grid of discrete surface-mount thick-film resistors (1 GΩ each, same value as FC divider chain resistors, rated for cryogenic use) connecting a copper mesh in a ladder network
- Each node of the copper mesh is held within a controlled voltage range by the resistor network
- In the event of a discharge at any node, only the local capacitance (~pF) discharges rather than the full cathode capacitance
- Use Rogers RO4003C laminate for the cathode PCB substrate instead of FR4 — lower dielectric loss at cryogenic temperatures, less outgassing, and better dimensional stability (CTE closer to copper)

### Proposed Upgrade B: Active Streamer Quench Using Fast Current-Sense and Local MOSFET Switch

**Concrete implementation:**
- Install a current-sensing resistor (10 kΩ) in series between HV bus and each CPA panel's local connection
- Monitor voltage across sensing resistor with a fast comparator circuit (LM339 equivalent rated for cryogenic operation, demonstrated to function at 77 K in existing literature)
- When current exceeds threshold (indicating streamer onset), a high-voltage MOSFET (SiC JFET type, operational at cryogenic temperatures) momentarily disconnects that CPA panel for <100 μs — orders of magnitude faster than the 4-minute auto-recovery currently used
- The localized disconnection means 5/6 CPA panels remain at nominal voltage; physics data loss is reduced from minutes to microseconds

---

## 4. Photon Detection System → Replace Light Guides with Tiled SiPM + TPB-Coated Reflector Panels

### Current Limitation
The paper reports photon detection efficiencies of:
- ARAPUCA: 2.0% (2 modules)
- Double-shift light guides: 0.21% (29 modules)
- Dip-coated light guides: 0.08% (29 modules)

The requirement is ≥0.5 PE/MeV at 3.6 m drift distance. The paper states ARAPUCA extrapolation gives 1.9 photons/MeV, "exceeding specifications by almost a factor of four," but only 2 ARAPUCA modules were deployed versus 58 light-guide modules. The light-guide approach is severely photon-starved.

### Proposed Upgrade: Full-Coverage ARAPUCA Array with 6×6 mm² SiPM Tiles

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace all 10 PD slots per APA with ARAPUCA modules (removing dip-coated and double-shift designs, which the paper's own data show are ~10–25× less efficient)
- Increase the number of SiPMs per ARAPUCA cell: current design uses 12 Hamamatsu S13360-6050 MPPCs (6×6 mm² each); increase to a 4×4 array (16 devices) per cell by reducing cell internal geometry
- Use the VE (Through-Silicon Via) MPPC variant throughout — the paper notes this variant allows "better packaging" due to reduced dead area around the active region
- Add a second ARAPUCA cell on the opposite face of the APA (the wall-facing side currently has the G-plane wire grid acting as a light block) — install ARAPUCA modules behind the G-plane using the existing mechanical slots, targeting cosmic ray events from the non-beam side

**Wavelength shifter improvement:**
- Replace hand-sprayed TPB on dichroic filter interior surfaces with vapor-deposited TPB at controlled 200 μg/cm² surface density (already used for external filter coating per the paper) applied to all internal reflector surfaces
- The paper already uses VIKUITI 3M specular reflector (>98% reflectivity); replace with **enhanced specular reflector (ESR) film** from 3M specifically cut to fit the cell geometry with no seams, eliminating reflection loss at joints

**Quantified expected improvement:**
- Current: 2 ARAPUCA + 58 light guides → effective average efficiency ~0.13% weighted by module count
- Proposed: 60 ARAPUCA modules → extrapolating from paper's 2.0% per module → ~2% average, a factor of ~15 improvement in average light yield
- This would yield approximately 15× the current photon statistics for supernova burst timing and nucleon decay event 𝑡₀ determination

---

## 5. Field Cage → Replace Extruded Aluminum Profiles with Resistive Kapton Strip Panels

### Current Limitation
The paper identifies that the aluminum FC profiles, particularly at their ends and corners, are "the most likely candidates for HV discharges to ground" due to high local electric fields. Custom UHMWPE caps are required for every profile end. The FC divider chain uses 0.5 GΩ per stage and varistors for protection. The current streamers correlate with charging of insulating FRP support structures.

### Proposed Upgrade: Continuous Resistive Panel FC

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace 57 discrete aluminum profiles per FC module with a continuous resistive panel made from **Kapton HN polyimide film** with screen-printed carbon-loaded resistive ink
- Panel dimensions match the existing FC module face: 2.3 m × 3.5 m per top/bottom module
- Resistive ink sheet resistance: 10–100 GΩ/square, selected to give the same 0.5 GΩ per 6 cm stage as the current discrete resistor chain, but distributed continuously
- Eliminates all profile end-field enhancement (no sharp aluminum edges), removing the primary streamer initiation sites
- The FRP I-beam and box beam support structure is retained for mechanical rigidity, but the Kapton panels attach to them with no electrical connection (panels are self-grading)
- Voltage uniformity: continuous resistive grading is inherently more uniform than a discrete 57-step approximation; E-field uniformity improvement of approximately one part in 57 (1.8%) at each step location

**Kapton at cryogenic temperatures:** already demonstrated in the CPA design (Kapton D11261075 film used for resistive cathode sheets), confirming the material survives thermal cycling to 87 K.

**Tradeoff:** if the Kapton panel develops a local defect (pinhole, crack), the resistive continuity is broken in a way that a discrete resistor failure is not. Mitigation: use double-layer laminated panels with offset resistive layers so that a single defect in either layer is bridged by the other.

---

## 6. Cryogenics Purification → Continuous Electrostatic Oxygen Getter Inside Cryostat

### Current Limitation
The paper reports the liquid recirculation rate is 7.0 t/h giving a full volume turnover in 4.6 days. Impurities are controlled by external molecular sieve and copper-based chemical filters. The paper reports pump outages cause sudden purity drops visible in purity monitor data (the "dips" in Figures 56 and 57). The electron lifetime requirement is >10 ms; ProtoDUNE-SP achieved >70 ms at nominal operation but is vulnerable to recirculation system failures.

### Proposed Upgrade: In-Cryostat Electrostatic Ion-Drift Getter

**Concrete implementation:**
- Install a set of alternating high-voltage wire planes (±5 kV, well below the 30 kV/cm breakdown threshold in LAr) spanning the ullage space at the top of the cryostat, using the same CuBe wire and PCB termination technology already developed for the APA
- Electronegative impurity molecules (O₂, H₂O) in the LAr vapor phase above the liquid surface have small but nonzero electron affinities; they form negative ions in the gas phase under UV or cosmic-ray ionization
- The electrostatic planes drift these negative ions to a collection electrode coated with activated copper (same material as the external filter) for neutralization
- This operates continuously regardless of recirculation pump status, providing a baseline purification floor

**Sizing estimate:**
- Ullage volume: 0.45 m height × 8.5 m × 8.5 m = ~32 m³ of argon gas
- At 1050 mbar and ~87 K, gas density ~7 kg/m³ → ~225 kg of argon gas in ullage
- Even a collection efficiency of 10% of impurities in the gas phase would supplement the liquid-phase filtration meaningfully during pump-off periods
- The design uses no moving parts and requires only two HV feedthroughs, which are already available as spares per the paper (five spare penetrations noted in Section 3.1.3)

---

## Summary Priority Table

| Upgrade | Primary Metric Improved | Complexity | Estimated Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pixel charge readout | 3D reconstruction, ENC | Very High | Factor 10+ in noise; eliminates ambiguity |
| Cold signal processing ASIC | Data bandwidth, self-trigger | High | Factor 50–100 bandwidth reduction |
| Segmented cathode + fast HV switch | HV uptime, dead time | Medium | Dead time from minutes → microseconds |
| Full ARAPUCA PDS | Light yield, timing resolution | Medium | Factor ~15 in average photon efficiency |
| Resistive Kapton FC panels | Field uniformity, streamer rate | Medium | Eliminates primary streamer sites |
| Electrostatic in-cryostat getter | Purity resilience during pump faults | Low-Medium | Baseline purity floor during outages |

The highest-leverage single upgrade is the **full ARAPUCA photon detector replacement**, because the current light-guide system is demonstrated in the paper's own data to be severely underperforming relative to available technology already tested in the same detector, and photon detection is the enabling capability for supernova neutrino detection and nucleon decay searches — the core physics goals of DUNE that the TPC charge readout alone cannot address.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for XENON1T

## 1. Photosensor System

### Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)
The R11410-21 PMTs represent the most significant performance bottleneck. Specifically:

- **Deploy 6mm × 6mm VUV4 Hamamatsu MPPC arrays** (or FBK VUV-HD series) tiled across both arrays. These achieve ~20% photon detection efficiency (PDE) at 175nm versus the ~12.5% photon detection efficiency measured in XENON1T, directly improving g1 from 0.144 PE/γ to potentially ~0.23 PE/γ
- **Critical consequence**: Lower S1 detection threshold, enabling sensitivity to lighter WIMPs below 10 GeV/c² and improved nuclear/electronic recoil discrimination at low energies
- **Radioactivity advantage**: Modern SiPM tiles can be fabricated on radiopure silicon substrates achieving <1 µBq/kg in ²³⁸U/²³²Th, substantially below the PMT contributions documented in reference [33]
- **Correlated noise mitigation**: Implement coincidence-based optical crosstalk rejection in firmware, requiring ≥2 SiPM pixels firing within 10ns to constitute a valid hit, suppressing the dark count rate contribution that currently limits S1 threshold
- **Retain the 6 R8520 PMTs** in the outer LXe region for calibration monitoring continuity

### Bottom Array Geometry Optimization
- Increase bottom array packing fraction from current ~70% to >90% using **hexagonally tiled 50mm × 50mm SiPM modules** with custom PCB integration
- Implement **individual SiPM segment readout** (4 segments per module) to preserve position reconstruction capability while maximizing photocathode coverage

---

## 2. Drift Field and Electrode System

### High-Voltage Upgrade
The science run 0 operated at only −12 kV cathode bias (0.125 kV/cm drift field) versus the design target, causing the field non-uniformities described in section 3.5. Specific upgrades:

- **Replace the Heinzinger PNC 150000-1** with a **Spellman SL150 series** capable of sustained −150 kV operation, verified stable in cryogenic LXe environments. The custom UHMW polyethylene feedthrough should be replaced with a **graded-permittivity composite feedthrough** using alternating PTFE/UHMW layers to reduce field concentration at the insertion point
- **Target drift field of 0.50 kV/cm** (requiring ~−48 kV for the 97 cm drift length), which reduces electron-ion recombination, improving charge yield by ~40% based on published NEST model predictions at this field strength
- **Practical benefit**: The improved S2/S1 discrimination band separation at higher fields would reduce ER leakage into the NR signal region below the current >99.5% rejection value

### Electrode Redesign
- Replace spot-welded hex-etched meshes with **electroformed copper meshes** at 50 µm wire diameter and 1.0 mm pitch for the gate electrode, improving optical transparency from 92.7% to >97% while maintaining mechanical stability
- **Woven stainless mesh with 50 µm Au plating** for cathode and bottom screen, maintaining the 97.2% transparency while eliminating the wire pre-stretching procedure that introduces mechanical uncertainty
- Install **4-point capacitive wire tension monitors** on cathode wires to detect sag in situ, addressing the anode sagging issue identified in the S2 correction maps (figure 22)

---

## 3. Radon Reduction System

Radon at 10 µBq/kg is documented as the dominant background (620 (t×y)⁻¹ ER rate in table 2). Hardware mitigations:

### Radon-Trap Cold Finger
- Install a dedicated **activated charcoal radon trap** (2 kg of Saratech or equivalent low-emanation charcoal) at −40°C on the purification return line. At this temperature, the Rn adsorption coefficient exceeds 10⁴ L/kg, providing >10× additional radon suppression beyond material selection alone
- **Dual-trap configuration** with thermal bypass allows one trap to be regenerated at 200°C while the other operates, maintaining continuous purification flow

### Electropolishing and Surface Treatment Extension
- Apply **UV/ozone surface treatment** (254 nm, 10 mW/cm²) to all inner cryostat surfaces after electropolishing. This technique has demonstrated 3-5× reduction in ²²²Rn emanation from stainless steel by oxidizing surface Ra deposits, complementing the existing electropolishing described in section 2.2.2

### Purification Loop Redesign
- Replace the QDrive magnetic-resonance pumps with **metal-bellows pumps** (e.g., Senior Flexonics MB-602 series). These eliminate the polymer diaphragm components present in the QDrive that contribute to Rn emanation, and can operate reliably at >75 slpm, breaking the 50 slpm limitation described in section 3.4 that constrained electron lifetime to 350-500 µs
- **Target electron lifetime >2 ms** at 75 slpm flow, reducing the S2 correction uncertainty that currently dominates position-dependent systematic errors

---

## 4. Distillation and Krypton Removal

The measured ⁸⁵Kr concentration of 0.36 ppt was a factor ~2 above the design goal:

- **Extend the distillation column packing from 2.8 m to 5.0 m** of Sulzer EX structured packing within the existing 5.5 m column housing (replacing insulation and support structures in the upper section). HETP measurements from reference [52] indicate this would increase the separation factor from 6.4×10⁵ to >4×10⁶, enabling online Kr removal to reach <0.05 ppt in weeks rather than 70 days
- **Add a second reboiler** with independent temperature control to enable staged reflux ratios, improving throughput to 25 slpm without sacrificing separation efficiency

---

## 5. Muon Veto Enhancement

The documented 43% efficiency for tagging muon-induced neutrons from external showers is a clear limitation:

- **Add 20 additional 8-inch PMTs** (Hamamatsu R5912) to the three middle rings (currently only 12 PMTs each at z = 2.5, 5.0, 7.5 m), increasing to 20 PMTs per ring. Optical simulation indicates this raises neutron shower tagging efficiency from 43% to >70%, reaching the design goal stated in section 3.1 without the trigger coincidence reduction risk
- **Replace 3M DF2000MA reflective foil** on the bottom hemisphere with **Lumirror E60L** (DuPont), which maintains >98% reflectivity down to 280 nm versus the 400 nm cutoff of DF2000MA, better matching the Cherenkov emission spectrum at these muon energies and reducing the required coincidence threshold

---

## 6. Data Acquisition and Trigger

The current 200 PE (≈7 electrons) S2 trigger threshold limits sensitivity to sub-GeV dark matter:

- **Replace CAEN V1724 (100 MHz, 14-bit) ADCs with CAEN V1730 (500 MHz, 14-bit)** digitizers. The 5× improvement in sampling rate resolves individual electron S2 pulses (width ~1 µs) from the waveform baseline, enabling a **single electron S2 trigger** at ~11.5 PE (from the measured g2b value) versus 200 PE currently
- **Implement FPGA-based matched filter** in the V1730 firmware using a pre-computed single-electron S2 template, achieving >95% single electron detection efficiency while maintaining <1 Hz dark-matter-search trigger rate
- **Practical impact**: Sensitivity to dark matter-electron scattering signals and sub-GeV nuclear recoils requiring only 1-3 extracted electrons

---

## 7. Internal Calibration System

The 83mKr system (T½ = 1.83 h) requires periodic injection disrupting dark matter running:

- **Install a ³⁷Ar source** (T½ = 35 days, 2.82 keV electron capture) via a dedicated **cold finger injection port** on the purification system return line. Unlike ⁸³mKr, the 35-day half-life allows a single injection to provide calibration data throughout a science run without repeated interventions, and the 2.82 keV energy directly calibrates the detector response in the most critical low-energy WIMP region
- **Add a UV photon injection system** using 172 nm Xe excimer lamps (Hamamatsu L11035) fiber-coupled to 4 additional PTFE-jacketed VUV fibers routed alongside existing LED fibers, enabling direct photon detection efficiency mapping without radioactive sources

---

## Prioritized Impact Assessment

| Upgrade | Primary Metric Improved | Estimated Gain |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM replacement | g1, low-energy threshold | ~2× improvement in PDE |
| HV/drift field upgrade | ER/NR discrimination | ~40% better charge yield |
| Metal-bellows pumps + Rn trap | ²²²Rn background | ~10× reduction |
| Additional muon veto PMTs | Neutron veto efficiency | 43% → >70% |
| V1730 ADCs + matched filter | S2 threshold | 200 PE → ~12 PE |

The SiPM conversion and radon reduction represent the highest-leverage modifications, as they directly attack the two dominant limitations identified in the paper: photon detection efficiency and the leading background source.

# Proposed Hardware Design Upgrades for LHCb

## Framing the Analysis

The paper identifies several concrete performance limitations during Run I. I will map each limitation to specific hardware solutions, drawing only on technologies demonstrable by 2014.

---

## 1. Vertex Locator (VELO) Replacement

### Identified Limitations
- Silicon strip sensors accumulating up to 1.8×10¹⁴ neq/cm² fluence, approaching operational limits
- 29 mm retraction requirement wastes ~210 seconds per fill (~750 fills in Run I)
- Minimum inner radius of 8.2 mm limits impact parameter resolution
- Analogue strip readout constrains pattern recognition in high-multiplicity events

### Proposed Upgrade: Pixel-Based VELO

**Sensor technology:** Replace R/Φ strip sensors with hybrid silicon pixel detectors based on the Timepix/Medipix ASIC family, which by 2014 had demonstrated radiation-hard operation. Pixel cells of approximately 55×55 µm² provide two-dimensional hit information per layer, eliminating the geometric ambiguity inherent in the separate R and Φ strip architecture.

**Specific improvements:**
- Pixel sensors eliminate ghost hits from strip combinatorics at high track multiplicity, directly improving pattern recognition efficiency which the paper notes degrades to below 96% above Ntrack > 200
- Through-silicon via (TSV) interconnect technology, demonstrated by 2014 at several foundries, enables thinning of the sensor-ASIC stack to below 200 µm total thickness, reducing material budget and thus multiple scattering contribution to the IP resolution floor of ~13 µm at high pT
- A retraction mechanism redesign exploiting the smaller pixel sensor geometry could reduce the beam-clearance gap from 8.2 mm to approximately 5 mm under stable beams, improving IP resolution intercept directly since σ(IP) ∝ (first measurement radius)

**Radiation hardness:** The paper notes depletion voltage reached ~100 V at end of Run I and predicts acceptable operation through Run II below 500 V. n-in-p pixel sensors with p-spray isolation, available from vendors including CiS and Micron by 2014, maintain charge collection efficiency to fluences of 10¹⁵ neq/cm² without type inversion complications observed in the current n-bulk strips.

**Readout:** Replace the Beetle ASIC with a pixel readout chip capable of 40 MHz continuous readout with on-chip zero suppression, eliminating the hardware trigger gating that forces the current architecture.

---

## 2. RICH Detector Photon Detector Replacement

### Identified Limitations
- Hybrid Photon Detectors (HPDs) show a read-out inefficiency identified during high trigger rate running, reducing photoelectron yield below simulation predictions (C₄F₁₀: 20.4 measured vs 28.3 simulated; CF₄: 15.8 vs 22.7)
- HPD response is distorted by residual magnetic field near RICH1, causing σ(θC) for C₄F₁₀ of 1.618 mrad versus simulated 1.52 mrad
- HPD ion feedback and aging under high photon flux limits long-term stability

### Proposed Upgrade: Multi-Anode Microchannel Plate Photomultipliers (MaPMTs)

**Technology:** Replace HPDs with Hamamatsu R11265 multi-anode PMTs or equivalent devices. By 2014 these had been extensively characterized for Cherenkov applications. Key parameters: ~25% quantum efficiency at 270 nm, pixel pitch of 6×6 mm², and critically, substantially lower sensitivity to magnetic fields than HPDs due to the short electron transit path in the MCP structure.

**Specific improvements:**
- Elimination of the magnetic distortion correction, which the paper explicitly identifies as the dominant source of the C₄F₁₀ resolution discrepancy, would recover the ~0.1 mrad gap between data and simulation
- Higher photon detection efficiency directly increases Npe, improving the single-track Cherenkov angle resolution as σ(θC,single) ∝ 1/√Npe
- Faster timing response of MaPMTs (~300 ps transit time spread versus ~1 ns for HPDs) would allow time-based photon association to reduce ring overlap confusion in high-multiplicity events

**Magnetic shielding redesign:** Pair the MaPMT installation with redesigned local μ-metal shielding. Since MaPMTs require lower field suppression than HPDs, the shielding geometry can be optimized without compromising photon transmission paths.

**Aerogel radiator:** The paper notes aerogel Npe has large uncertainty (5.0±3.0 from D* data) and attributes part of the resolution degradation to C₄F₁₀ gas absorption by porous aerogel. Replace current aerogel tiles with hydrophobic aerogel produced by the Matsushita/Panasonic process with controlled porosity below 50 nm pore diameter, substantially reducing gas absorption while maintaining refractive index n≈1.03.

---

## 3. Upstream Tracker (TT) Replacement

### Identified Limitations
- Hit resolution of 52.6–53.4 µm is dominated by binary charge sharing in the central regions closest to the beam pipe
- Average occupancy reaches 1.9% in sectors nearest the beam pipe, degrading pattern recognition
- The paper notes remaining misalignment contributes to hit resolution being worse than the 47.8 µm Monte Carlo expectation
- TT temperature sensitivity creates curvature bias in J/ψ mass requiring dedicated re-alignment per temperature period

### Proposed Upgrade: Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) Tracker Station

**Technology:** Replace TT silicon strip detectors with a scintillating fibre tracker using 250 µm diameter polystyrene fibres doped with para-terphenyl and POPOP wavelength shifter, read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). By 2014, SiPM technology from Hamamatsu, SensL and KETEK had achieved photon detection efficiency above 40% at 450 nm with dark count rates manageable at -40°C operation.

**Specific improvements:**
- Fibre pitch of 250 µm provides intrinsic spatial resolution of ~75 µm, comparable to current TT, but the continuous sensitive volume eliminates the binary-readout degradation at small track angles
- Critically, SiPM readout with fast timing (~1 ns) enables bunch-crossing identification at 40 MHz, supporting the removal of the hardware Level-0 trigger
- The monolithic fibre mat construction eliminates the module boundary effects and temperature-sensitive support structures responsible for the curvature bias documented in the paper
- Radiation length of the fibre plane (~0.5% X₀ per layer) is competitive with silicon strip detectors at equivalent granularity

**SiPM operating point:** The paper notes occupancy concerns at 25 ns bunch spacing. SiPM integration windows of 25 ns with appropriate threshold suppress dark count noise while maintaining efficiency above 99% for minimum-ionising particles demonstrated in beam tests at CERN by 2013-2014.

---

## 4. Calorimeter Trigger Readout Electronics

### Identified Limitations
- L0 hadron trigger efficiency for two-body beauty decays is only 40% (TOS), representing the single largest efficiency bottleneck in the trigger chain (Table 5 shows L0 at 53% for B⁰→K⁺π⁻ combined with TIS, but pure TOS is lower)
- PMT gain degradation requires manual intervention: the paper shows gradual HCAL trigger rate decrease with intermittent step corrections
- SPD multiplicity veto introduces dead time that the paper implicitly accepts as unavoidable within current architecture
- ECAL calibration requires several hundred thousand events and the π⁰ mass fit procedure, limiting calibration frequency

### Proposed Upgrade: Full-Granularity Digital Calorimeter Readout

**Electronics:** Replace the current 12-bit ADC readout operating at 40 MHz with a continuous digitization scheme using pipelined ADCs sampling at 160 MHz with 14-bit precision per channel. By 2014 this was achievable with standard FADC technology from e2v and Analog Devices within the power budget constraints of the calorimeter front-end crates.

**Specific improvements:**
- Four-sample digitization per bunch crossing enables digital pile-up subtraction, replacing the current analog signal clipping that introduces nonlinearity in the ECAL energy measurement
- Online gain monitoring using injected LED pulses on every beam-empty bunch crossing, rather than the current periodic LED runs, would allow continuous PMT gain tracking and eliminate the step-function corrections visible in Figure 29
- Full-granularity cluster transmission to the HLT farm eliminates the fixed 2×2 cluster ET threshold of L0, permitting software-defined cluster algorithms that recover the ~15% absolute L0 hadron efficiency loss from threshold effects

**PMT replacement in HCAL inner region:** Install multi-dynode PMTs with higher linear dynamic range (10⁷ electrons vs current ~10⁶) in the inner HCAL cells experiencing the most severe gain degradation. The Hamamatsu R7899 series, available by 2014, demonstrated substantially reduced gain droop at high integrated anode current.

---

## 5. Muon System Inner Region Detector Replacement

### Identified Limitations
- Dead-time of front-end readout chips reaches 2.5% in M1R1 and remains non-negligible in M2R1 at twice nominal luminosity
- The paper states operation at 2×10³² cm⁻²s⁻¹ causes larger dead time than originally expected
- M5 station suffers spurious hits from beam-line back-scattering, creating logical OR dead time in outer regions
- Time resolution of 2.5–4 ns approaches the 4.5 ns budget, leaving little margin

### Proposed Upgrade: GEM Detector Extension to M2R1

**Technology:** The paper already notes triple-GEM detectors are used in M1 highest-rate region. Extend GEM technology from M1 to M2R1 and M3R1, the two regions showing the most significant dead-time effects. The COMPASS triple-GEM design with 3 mm drift gap and Ar/CO₂ (70/30) operating gas, well-characterized by 2014, provides rate capability exceeding 10⁷ Hz/cm² with dead time below 100 ns.

**Specific improvements:**
- GEM intrinsic gain ~10⁴ with reduced sensitivity to space charge at high rates compared to MWPC, directly addressing the front-end chip dead time which the paper attributes to high occupancy in inner regions
- GEM timing resolution of ~5 ns with optimized gas mixture is achievable, comparable to current MWPC performance, maintaining the trigger time budget
- Reduced ion backflow in GEM geometry (~1% vs ~10% in MWPC) suppresses the space-charge buildup that contributes to gain sag at high luminosity

**M5 shielding:** Install additional iron absorber segments of ~10 cm thickness immediately behind M5 to attenuate beam-line back-scattered particles. Geant4 simulations available by 2014 would establish the optimal geometry without compromising forward acceptance.

---

## 6. Trigger Farm Architecture: Online Tracking Processor

### Identified Limitations
- HLT1 must limit forward tracking to VELO tracks with significant IP or muon matches, creating 1–2% per-track efficiency loss in HLT2 relative to offline
- Deferred trigger stores ~20% of L0 events to disk with modest (~60 MB/s) I/O requirements, demonstrating CPU is the binding constraint
- Processing time forces simplified Kalman filter geometry in HLT1, causing 3% worse J/ψ mass resolution online vs offline

### Proposed Upgrade: FPGA-Based Fast Track Finder as HLT1 Preprocessor

**Technology:** Deploy a dedicated fast track processor based on Xilinx Virtex-7 or Altera Stratix V FPGAs (both available and characterized for HEP use by 2014) implementing the Hough transform track finding in hardware. The ATLAS Fast TracKer (FTK) project, well-documented by 2014, demonstrated the feasibility of FPGA-based full-event tracking at 100 kHz input rates using associative memory chips.

**Specific implementation for LHCb:**
- Implement pattern recognition for VELO+TT track segments in FPGA using stored hit patterns from a content-addressable memory bank, providing track candidates at full L0 rate of 1 MHz with ~1 µs latency
- This eliminates the IP significance pre-selection in HLT1 that currently biases the track sample against prompt charm and introduces the per-track efficiency loss
- The hardware tracker output feeds the existing CPU farm for Kalman filter fitting, which is computationally less demanding than pattern recognition and parallelizes efficiently

**Quantified benefit:** The paper shows HLT2 charm trigger efficiency for D⁰→K⁻π⁺ is 90% but drops to 26% for four-body D*+ decays. A hardware track finder providing complete track lists at HLT1 input would recover a significant fraction of this efficiency by enabling HLT2 to use downstream tracks and looser pT thresholds within the same CPU budget.

---

## Priority Ranking

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Relative Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Pixel VELO | IP resolution, high-multiplicity tracking | Highest — affects all analyses |
| MaPMT RICH readout | Cherenkov angle resolution, PID performance | High — core to flavour ID |
| Full calorimeter digitization | L0 hadron efficiency recovery | High — largest single trigger loss |
| SciFi upstream tracker | Occupancy, temperature stability | Medium — targets specific systematics |
| GEM inner muon stations | Dead-time at high luminosity | Medium — future-proofs for Run II |
| FPGA track processor | HLT charm efficiency | Medium — recoverable by deferred trigger |

The pixel VELO and calorimeter readout upgrades address the two largest identified performance gaps: the IP resolution floor set by sensor geometry and material, and the 40–50% absolute L0 hadron trigger efficiency that dominates the hadronic physics programme efficiency budget shown in Table 5.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for DarkSide-50

## Analysis of Primary Performance Limitations

Before proposing upgrades, the dominant limitations identified in this paper are:

1. **Scintillation+Cherenkov background** from Teflon reflector (dominant ER background)
2. **Poor x-y position reconstruction** due to PMT proximity to S2 emission region
3. **Surface backgrounds** from ²¹⁰Po on Teflon reflector
4. **PMT radioactivity** (dominant radiogenic neutron source, >90% of background)
5. **Limited fiducial mass fraction** due to radial cut reaching ~23mm from wall at TPC top/bottom
6. **PSD statistics limited at low S1** by photoelectron yield of 8.0 PE/keV

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**The problem:** The 38 Hamamatsu R11065 PMTs are explicitly identified as the source of >90% of radiogenic neutron background, contributing through their borosilicate glass stems and ceramic dynode supports. PMT activities include 0.277 Bq of ²³²Th and 0.84 Bq of ²³⁸U lower chain.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace all PMTs with cryogenic SiPM tiles based on the Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) RGB-HD or NUV-HD technology, which demonstrated operation at LAr temperature (~87K)
- SiPMs are fabricated from ultra-pure silicon with negligible U/Th content, eliminating the borosilicate glass stem and ceramic dynode plate radioactivity entirely
- Tile the top and bottom windows with ~3mm × 3mm SiPM cells in a close-packed array, achieving comparable or better photon detection efficiency (PDE >40% at 420nm for NUV-HD vs. ~30% quantum efficiency for R11065)
- Use cryogenic front-end ASICs (e.g., based on the ABCD chip architecture adapted for SiPM) mounted outside the active volume to reduce radioactive mass inside the cryostat
- SiPM arrays also eliminate the need for cryogenic preamplifiers currently required to manage PMT breakdown issues

**Expected impact:** >90% reduction in radiogenic neutron background; improved photoelectron yield directly improves PSD at low S1

---

### 2. Redesign the Teflon Reflector to Eliminate Cherenkov Background

**The problem:** Scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov is explicitly identified as the dominant surviving ER background after all cuts. The paper states this is the primary motivation for the radial fiducial cut, which costs 15.2% acceptance. Teflon generates Cherenkov radiation because its refractive index (~1.35 at 420nm) exceeds 1.0.

**Proposed upgrade option A — Segmented reflector with optical isolation:**
- Replace the monolithic Teflon cylinder with a segmented reflector incorporating thin black polyethylene light-absorbing gaps between segments oriented parallel to the drift field
- Each segment (e.g., 5cm tall) is read out optically in isolation via dedicated SiPM strips on the outer surface, allowing identification and rejection of events where Cherenkov photons originate from a segment spatially inconsistent with the reconstructed event position
- The TPB wavelength-shifting coating is retained on the inner Teflon surfaces

**Proposed upgrade option B — Replace Teflon with polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) foam or aerogel composite:**
- Use PTFE foam with ~50% void fraction, reducing the effective refractive index toward 1.0 and dramatically suppressing Cherenkov yield while maintaining high diffuse reflectivity (>95%)
- The TPB coating is applied directly to the foam surface; the reduced density also lowers the ²¹⁰Po surface activity per unit volume

**Proposed upgrade option C — Active veto layer:**
- Line the inner Teflon surface with a 2-3mm layer of gadolinium-loaded silicone rubber instrumented with a sparse SiPM layer (1 SiPM per ~100 cm²)
- Gadolinium captures thermal neutrons with high cross section (49,000 barns for ¹⁵⁷Gd), emitting ~8 MeV in γ cascades detectable in the LSV, supplementing the boron-loaded LSV neutron veto
- The silicone layer simultaneously acts as a light guide for Cherenkov photons generated in the Teflon, allowing tagging of surface Cherenkov events

**Expected impact (option A or B):** Factor of ~5-10 reduction in ER background, allowing the box boundary to be lowered in f90, improving sensitivity at low WIMP masses and potentially eliminating the radial acceptance penalty

---

### 3. Upgrade the Photon Detection Array Geometry to Improve x-y Reconstruction

**The problem:** The paper explicitly notes x-y reconstruction is "very difficult" due to proximity of top PMTs to the S2 emission region, limiting charge sharing among 3" PMTs. This forces reliance on a coarse radial cut with poorly calibrated acceptance.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the 19-PMT top array with a finer-granularity SiPM array of ~200 individual 6mm × 6mm cells arranged in a hexagonal grid covering the full window area
- The smaller cell pitch (~6-8mm vs. ~76mm PMT pitch) dramatically increases the number of cells illuminated per S2 event, improving spatial sampling
- The proximity issue is addressed by the intrinsically smaller cell size rather than by moving the array: with ~200 cells vs. 19 PMTs, light sharing becomes effective even at small drift distances
- Implement a maximum likelihood position reconstruction using the known S2 electroluminescence point-spread function, trained on ⁸³ᵐKr calibration data which is already used for other calibrations
- Expected position resolution improvement: from ~6mm (current) to ~2-3mm based on photon statistics scaling, enabling a sharper radial fiducial cut that recovers ~5-8% acceptance currently lost in the transition region near the wall

**Expected impact:** Improved fiducial mass fraction; sharper radial cut allows better rejection of Teflon Cherenkov events concentrated near the wall; potentially recovers 5-8% signal acceptance

---

### 4. Replace Fused Silica Windows with Crystalline Quartz or MgF₂

**The problem:** Fused silica PMT and TPC windows generate scintillation+Cherenkov background. The S1pMaxFrac cut is effective against fused-silica Cherenkov but at the cost of efficiency, and residual fused-silica Cherenkov events still contribute.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the fused silica top and bottom TPC windows with crystalline MgF₂ windows
- MgF₂ has a refractive index of ~1.38 at 420nm (lower than fused silica at ~1.46), raising the Cherenkov threshold: minimum electron energy for Cherenkov production scales as 1/(n²-1), so the ~6% lower n reduces Cherenkov yield approximately proportionally
- More importantly, MgF₂ has substantially lower radioactivity than fused silica (which contains trace U/Th at ~1-10 ppb levels) due to its simpler crystal growth process
- MgF₂ is transparent down to 120nm, potentially allowing direct detection of some 128nm LAr scintillation without wavelength shifting, which could be exploited for additional PSD information
- For the PMT entrance windows, if retaining PMTs, replace with low-activity borosilicate variants or switch to UV-transparent polymer windows with SiPMs

**Expected impact:** Reduction in fused-silica Cherenkov background by factor of ~2-3; small improvement in photoelectron yield from UV transparency

---

### 5. Upgrade the Inner Cathode and Grid to Reduce Surface Activity

**The problem:** ²¹⁰Po surface activity of 2.51 mBq/m² on the ~0.4 m² Teflon reflector drives surface background design requirements. The cathode and grid α backgrounds are handled by z-fiducialization, but this costs active volume.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the ITO-coated fused silica cathode with a thin stainless steel mesh cathode electropolished and passivated using the same protocols developed for xenon TPC electrodes (electropolishing removes surface-embedded ²¹⁰Pb by removing ~20 µm of surface material)
- Replace the extraction grid wire material from its current composition to be electroformed copper or electropolished stainless steel with measured ²¹⁰Pb content <0.1 mBq/m²
- Coat cathode and grid with a thin (~100nm) layer of amorphous carbon or diamond-like carbon (DLC) by CVD, which has demonstrated resistance to radon daughter plate-out and allows electropolishing of the underlying metal
- Implement a dedicated radon-suppressed glove box protocol for all final assembly steps, with radon concentration monitored at <1 Bq/m³ using an electrostatic radon monitor
- Reduce z-fiducialization dead region from 40 µs (~4 cm) to 20 µs (~2 cm) at top and bottom, recovering ~10% of the active volume currently sacrificed

**Expected impact:** Reduction in cathode/grid surface events; potential recovery of ~10% of active volume; reduced Type 1 surface background

---

### 6. Upgrade the Liquid Scintillator Veto Photon Detection

**The problem:** The LSV achieves 99.64% neutron veto efficiency. However, γ-ray veto efficiency is only ~33%, and the LSV contributes to the accidental veto rate through PMT afterpulsing (noted in the paper as complicating the delayed neutron capture analysis).

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace the current LSV PMTs with high-quantum-efficiency, low-afterpulse-rate PMTs such as the Hamamatsu R5912 MOD with reduced afterpulse specification, or with 8" SiPMs arrays
- Increase LSV light yield by replacing the current borated pseudocumene/trimethylborate scintillator with a higher-light-yield formulation: linear alkylbenzene (LAB) + PPO at 2 g/L + bis-MSB at 15 mg/L + natural boron loading at 3 g/L provides ~8000 photons/MeV vs. ~5000 photons/MeV for pseudocumene-based scintillators at comparable boron loading
- Higher light yield improves γ-ray detection efficiency above ~200 keV, increasing the γ-veto efficiency from ~33% toward ~50%, providing additional rejection of γ-induced ER events that Compton scatter in the TPC

**Expected impact:** Improved γ-ray veto efficiency reduces ER background contribution from external γ rays; reduced afterpulsing simplifies neutron capture analysis and may allow tightening the LSVdelayed threshold

---

## Summary of Expected Combined Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Background Addressed | Expected Improvement |
|---------|------------------------------|---------------------|
| SiPM replacement | Radiogenic neutrons (PMT-sourced) | >90% reduction |
| Teflon reflector redesign | Scintillation+Teflon Cherenkov (dominant ER) | Factor 5-10 reduction |
| Fine-pitch SiPM top array | x-y reconstruction fidelity | ~5-8% acceptance recovery |
| MgF₂ windows | Fused-silica Cherenkov | Factor 2-3 reduction |
| Cathode/grid passivation | Surface backgrounds | ~10% volume recovery |
| LSV photosensor upgrade | γ-ray veto efficiency | ~50% improvement in γ veto |

The most impactful single upgrade is the SiPM replacement combined with Teflon reflector redesign, as these address the two explicitly identified dominant background sources in the paper. These changes together could plausibly reduce total background from 0.09 events per 532 days to below 0.01 events per 532 days, enabling a factor of ~3 improvement in cross-section sensitivity at fixed exposure, or allowing a substantial reduction in the radial fiducial cut that would increase effective exposure.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Ge-76 0νββ Experiment in Liquid Argon

This describes an experiment like **GERDA/LEGEND**, so I'll focus on upgrades that address the actual limiting factors in physics performance: background rate in the region of interest (ROI) near Q_ββ = 2039 keV, energy resolution, detection efficiency, and signal-to-noise discrimination.

---

## 1. Detector Array Upgrades

### 1.1 Inverted-Coaxial Point-Contact (ICPC) Geometry Optimization

**Current state:** Point-contact detectors (PPC/BEGe) already give good A/E discrimination, but charge collection non-uniformities limit performance.

**Upgrade:**
- Fabricate ICPCs with **lithographically patterned passivation layers** (silicon nitride or amorphous germanium) to suppress surface-channel leakage currents at the groove between p+ contact and passivated surface
- Implement **sub-millimeter point contact geometry** (contact diameter < 2 mm) to maximize the gradient in the weighting potential, sharpening A/E separation between single-site (0νββ signal) and multi-site (Compton background) events
- Use **segmented outer n+ contacts** with individual readout channels — even 6-fold azimuthal segmentation dramatically improves multi-site event rejection without introducing passive material

**Physics impact:** Improves multi-site rejection factor by ~3–5×, directly reducing the γ background index.

### 1.2 Detector Surface Treatment

- Replace conventional Li-diffused n+ contact (dead layer ~0.5–1 mm) with **phosphorus-implanted n+ contacts** at ~100 μm thickness, reducing the dead-layer contribution to incomplete charge collection events that populate the ROI as a continuous background
- Apply **amorphous germanium (a-Ge) contacts** on the p+ side for better surface passivation and lower leakage current at LAr temperatures, reducing electronic noise floor

**Physics impact:** Improves energy resolution by reducing ballistic deficit from incomplete charge collection; reduces degraded-energy background.

---

## 2. Signal Readout Electronics

### 2.1 Cryogenic Front-End ASICs

**Current state:** Charge-sensitive preamplifiers based on discrete SiGe transistors (e.g., Canberra/Mirion or custom BJTs) operating at ~90 K in LAr.

**Upgrade:**
- Deploy **purpose-designed cryogenic ASICs in 65 nm CMOS** (following work by groups at LBNL/MIT for CMB/rare event experiments) integrated directly on the detector mounting structure — eliminates long cables which degrade noise performance
- Target **equivalent noise charge (ENC) < 30 e⁻ RMS** at 90 K, compared to ~50–80 e⁻ for current discrete front-ends
- Implement **on-chip digital filtering** with trapezoidal shaping and pile-up detection at the ASIC level

**Physics impact:** Improves FWHM energy resolution from ~2.5 keV to **< 1.5 keV at 2039 keV**. For a Gaussian peak, the signal-to-background ratio scales as 1/FWHM, so this directly improves sensitivity.

### 2.2 Full Waveform Digitization at Higher Bandwidth

- Upgrade to **250 MHz, 16-bit flash ADCs** per channel (from ~100 MHz, 14-bit)
- Implement **FPGA-based real-time pulse shape discrimination** including:
  - Rise-time analysis
  - Current pulse reconstruction
  - Multi-site hit detection on microsecond timescale
- Store **full 100 μs waveform windows** to enable offline machine-learning-based event classification

**Physics impact:** Enables ML-based PSA (see Section 5) and improves multi-site rejection efficiency.

---

## 3. Liquid Argon Instrumentation Upgrades

### 3.1 High-Coverage SiPM-Based LAr Scintillation Veto

**Current state:** GERDA used wavelength-shifting fibers + PMTs; LEGEND-200 uses a curtain of WLS fibers + SiPMs.

**Upgrade:**
- Replace fiber-based light collection with **direct-view tiled SiPM arrays** (Hamamatsu VUV4 or FBK VUV-HD series, sensitive at 128 nm) surrounding the detector array
- Tile the inner cylindrical surface at **> 40% geometric coverage** with cryogenic SiPMs arranged in **4π geometry**
- Use **3M Vikuiti ESR specular reflector foil** or **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB)-coated PTFE diffuse reflector panels** between SiPM panels to maximize photon collection efficiency
- Implement **individual SiPM channel readout** rather than ganged readout to enable topological reconstruction of LAr scintillation light

**Physics impact:**
- Achieves **LAr veto efficiency > 99.5%** for events with any LAr energy deposition (Compton scatters, α events, muon-induced activity)
- Allows **position reconstruction** of veto events to distinguish correlated backgrounds

### 3.2 LAr Purity Monitoring and Active Purification

- Install **in-situ alpha-source purity monitors** (using ²¹⁰Po on thin wires) to continuously monitor electron lifetime
- Deploy a **recirculating LAr purification system** with molecular sieve + OXISORB cartridges to maintain electron lifetime > 5 ms and optical attenuation length > 3 m at 128 nm
- Monitor **LAr nitrogen contamination** with parts-per-billion optical sensors (N₂ quenches Ar scintillation significantly)

**Physics impact:** Maintains LAr veto efficiency; degraded purity is a major failure mode of the veto system.

---

## 4. Passive Shielding and Material Selection

### 4.1 Ultra-Low-Background Detector Hardware

**Current state:** Copper holders, signal cables with ≤ 100 μBq/kg ²²⁸Ra.

**Upgrade:**
- Machine detector holders from **underground-sourced copper** (NOSV copper from Aurubis, stored underground to minimize cosmogenic activation of ⁶⁰Co)
- Replace any remaining PTFE components near detectors with **electroformed copper** or **high-purity sapphire** structural pieces
- Use **parylene-C coated** Kapton signal cables to eliminate surface ²²⁶Ra contamination while maintaining flexibility at 90 K
- Validate all components by **ICP-MS screening** to < 10 μBq/kg for U/Th chains and **gamma spectrometry** in dedicated underground HPGe screening facilities before deployment

**Physics impact:** Directly reduces the irreducible β/γ background contribution from near-detector materials.

### 4.2 Muon Veto Enhancement

- Instrument the outer **water tank with additional 8" PMTs** (Hamamatsu R5912) to achieve > 99.98% muon detection efficiency via Cherenkov light
- Add **water Cherenkov tracking capability** by segmenting PMT timing to reconstruct muon track direction, enabling rejection of **muon-induced spallation neutrons** even when the muon itself misses the fiducial volume
- Implement a **10 ms veto window** post-muon for delayed neutron capture signatures

---

## 5. Machine Learning-Based Event Classification

This is now a hardware-relevant design choice because it determines the ADC and FPGA specifications.

### 5.1 Real-Time Neural Network Inference on FPGA

- Implement **hls4ml-compiled graph neural networks** on Xilinx Ultrascale+ FPGAs for real-time pulse shape analysis
- Train on **simulated charge drift waveforms** (using Siggen/ICPC field maps) augmented with calibration data from ²²⁸Th sources
- Input features: full digitized current pulse I(t), integrated charge Q(t), LAr coincident light signal amplitude and timing

**Key classifiers to implement in hardware:**
| Classifier | Target Background | Expected Rejection |
|---|---|---|
| A/E (current amplitude/energy) | Multi-site Compton | 80% at 90% signal efficiency |
| LAr anti-coincidence | Any particle leaving LAr signal | 99%+ |
| Waveform ML (CNN on I(t)) | Surface α, degraded β | ~5× over cut-based |
| Multi-detector coincidence | Compton cascade | >99% at 2039 keV |

---

## 6. Calibration System Upgrades

### 6.1 Automated Precision Calibration Deployment

- Replace current source-on-wire deployment with a **precision robotic source positioner** allowing reproducible positioning to < 1 mm, enabling systematic studies of position-dependent energy response
- Use **⁵⁶Co sources** (in addition to ²²⁸Th) for high-energy calibration lines at 1771 and 2599 keV bracketing the ROI more tightly
- Implement **continuous low-activity ²¹⁰Pb/⁵⁷Co pin sources** permanently mounted at the periphery of the array for real-time gain monitoring between calibration campaigns

**Physics impact:** Corrects for gain drift from radon, temperature, and electronics aging; critical for maintaining sub-keV energy scale systematic uncertainty.

---

## 7. Summary: Expected Performance Gains

| Upgrade | Current Performance | Upgraded Performance | Background Reduction Factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cryogenic ASIC readout | FWHM ~2.5 keV | FWHM ~1.5 keV | ~1.7× (ROI narrower) |
| Segmented ICPC detectors | A/E rejection ~85% | ~95% multi-site rejection | ~3× |
| SiPM LAr veto (4π) | ~98% veto efficiency | >99.5% | ~5× on Compton backgrounds |
| Ultra-pure near-detector materials | BI ~10⁻⁴ cts/(keV·kg·yr) | < 3×10⁻⁵ | ~3× |
| ML pulse shape classification | Cut-based A/E | Full waveform NN | ~2× additional |
| **Combined** | BI ~10⁻⁴ | **~10⁻⁶ cts/(keV·kg·yr)** | **~100×** |

The **sensitivity to the 0νββ half-life** scales as T_{1/2}^{sens} ∝ √(M·t / BI·FWHM), so a combined ~100× background reduction and 40% resolution improvement translates to roughly a **10–15× improvement in half-life sensitivity** for a fixed exposure — pushing from the current ~10²⁶ yr into the **10²⁷–10²⁸ yr regime** needed to cover the inverted neutrino mass ordering.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for SNO

## Assessment of Primary Physics Limitations

SNO's core measurement is the CC/NC ratio for solar neutrino flavor transformation. The binding constraints are:

1. **Photon detection efficiency** (31% bare photocathode coverage, ~54% effective)
2. **Energy threshold** (~5 MeV, limiting accessible flux)
3. **Neutron detection efficiency** (~37% with NCD array, ~25% effective after cuts)
4. **Radioactive backgrounds** limiting fiducial volume and threshold
5. **Energy resolution** (~14% at 6.13 MeV) blurring spectral measurements

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. Replace PMTs with High-Quantum-Efficiency Devices

**Problem:** Hamamatsu R1408 has ~20% peak quantum efficiency (QE). With 54% geometric coverage, the effective photoelectron yield is ~8 pe/MeV, limiting energy resolution and threshold.

**Upgrade:** Replace with **Hamamatsu R12860 HQE dynode PMTs** or **R7081-100 HQE variants** achieving 35-40% peak QE at 390 nm, the peak Cherenkov emission wavelength in water. These are commercially available and were adopted by SNO+ as the direct successor experiment.

- Concrete improvement: photoelectron yield increases from ~8 pe/MeV to ~13-14 pe/MeV
- Energy resolution improves from ~14% to ~11% at 6 MeV (scaling as √N)
- Energy threshold potentially reducible from 5 MeV toward 3.5 MeV, accessing the full ⁸B spectrum above the 2.2 MeV NC threshold
- Same physical envelope (same PSUP mounting hardware, same HV cables), reducing installation complexity

**Alternative path:** Deploy **Large Area Picosecond Photodetectors (LAPPDs)** from Incom Inc. in a subset of positions. These 20×20 cm microchannel plate devices achieve 25-30% QE with **~50 ps transit time spread** versus 1.7 ns RMS for the R1408. Even deploying 500 LAPPDs (replacing ~5% of PMTs) would dramatically improve vertex resolution for high-energy events and muon tracking through improved timing. The challenge is pressure housing design for 200 kPa deployment.

---

### 2. Wavelength-Shifting Light Concentrators

**Problem:** The existing Winston cone concentrators use aluminum/MgF₂/TiO₂ dielectric stacks with 82% mean reflectance, dropping sharply below 350 nm where Cherenkov emission is significant.

**Upgrade:** Coat the interior of the ABS concentrator cells with **bis-MSB wavelength-shifting paint** (used in Borexino and reactor antineutrino detectors), absorbing UV Cherenkov photons (300-380 nm) and re-emitting at 420 nm where PMT QE is maximal and water attenuation length is long (~50 m in SNO heavy water).

- The existing acrylic vessel already uses UVT-grade material transmitting to ~300 nm
- Bis-MSB dissolved in polyvinyltoluene can be spray-applied to concentrator surfaces at ~0.1 mg/cm² loading
- Estimated additional photon collection: 15-20% increase in detected pe/MeV
- Combined with HQE PMTs above: total improvement ~35-40% in light yield
- Requires accelerated aging tests in D₂O/H₂O environment to verify chemical compatibility and leaching rates below the 3×10⁻¹⁵ g/g Th / 4.5×10⁻¹⁴ g/g U radioactivity limits

---

### 3. Upgraded NCD Array with ⁴He Pressure Vessels and Digital Pulse Readout

**Problem:** The 3He proportional counters achieve only ~25% effective neutron detection efficiency after alpha/background cuts. The 50 µm anode wire and analog readout limit pulse-shape discrimination capability. Additionally, post-2009 global ³He shortages make replacement counters expensive.

**Upgrade A - Digital waveform readout:** Replace the existing resistive-coupler analog readout with **flash ADC digitizers at 500 MHz sampling** (e.g., SIS3316 from Struck Innovative Systeme, 250 MHz 16-bit) deployed at the deck level with low-radioactivity coaxial cable to each string. Full waveform capture enables:

- Improved pulse-shape discrimination between neutron capture tracks (~4 cm) and alpha particles (~1 cm) using rise time and track-length-to-energy ratio simultaneously in feature space rather than 1D cuts
- Machine-learning classifiers trained on Monte Carlo waveforms can push effective efficiency from 25% toward 35% by recovering events currently cut on ambiguous topology
- Position reconstruction along string axis via pulse reflection timing improves from the current ~15 cm to ~5 cm resolution, enabling spatial correlation with Cherenkov events

**Upgrade B - Boron-loaded fiber neutron detectors:** For a future phase, replace ³He strings with **⁶Li-doped ZnS(Ag) scintillator fibers** read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) at string ends. The ⁶Li(n,t)α reaction (Q=4.78 MeV, σ=940 b thermal) provides excellent n/γ discrimination from pulse shape. Fibers can be fabricated from ultra-low-radioactivity materials (fused silica cladding, ZnS with measured Th/U). This eliminates dependence on scarce ³He entirely.

---

### 4. Electronics Chain Modernization

**Problem:** The SNOD/SNOINT/QUSN7 ASIC chain was designed in AT&T CBICU-2 and Northern Telecom CMOS4S processes from the early 1990s. The 12-bit 2 µs ADCs, 16-deep analog memory, and ~400 ns per-channel deadtime are significant limitations.

**Specific upgrade - Replace with CATIROC or TARGET ASICs:**

- **CATIROC** (developed for KM3NeT): 16-channel ASIC with 12-bit charge measurement, 1 ns TDC resolution, 0.3 fC charge threshold, and onboard zero-suppression. Directly drop-in replaceable on redesigned FEC daughter boards
- **TARGET-7** (developed for CTA): 16-channel switched capacitor array achieving 1 GSa/s sampling with 96 deep analog memory, enabling full waveform capture of PMT pulses
- Reduces per-channel deadtime from 400 ns to <50 ns, important for supernova burst capability
- 1 ns TDC resolution versus current ~1.7 ns RMS timing improves vertex reconstruction by ~10 cm
- Eliminates obsolescence risk from 1990s processes with no current fabrication line

**Trigger upgrade:** Replace the analog summing tree with a **Field Programmable Gate Array-based trigger** using Xilinx Ultrascale+ devices. Enables software-defined trigger algorithms including directional Cherenkov ring triggers (rejecting isotropic radioactive backgrounds), multiplicity triggers with spatial clustering, and online neutron-capture coincidence tagging. This directly reduces threshold by rejecting backgrounds the hardware trigger cannot discriminate.

---

### 5. Ultra-Low-Background Acrylic Vessel Neck Seal and Cover Gas

**Problem:** The paper notes radon at 3 pCi/L in laboratory air and the need for N₂ cover gas from liquid nitrogen boiloff (measured <10⁻⁵ pCi/L Rn). The chimney interface is a primary radon ingress point during calibration operations.

**Upgrade:** Install a **radon trap cold finger system** integrated directly into the glove box at the deck interface, using activated charcoal at -40°C (achievable with a two-stage Peltier cooler, no liquid nitrogen required). This provides:

- Inline radon removal from cover gas flow to <10⁻⁶ pCi/L 
- Eliminates periodic liquid nitrogen dewar handling reducing personnel access frequency and associated dust generation
