# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Bare HPGe Array in Liquid Argon

## Context and Performance Baseline

This describes an instrument in the GERDA/LEGEND family. The primary physics figure of merit is:

**S/√B** (or more precisely, the half-life sensitivity) ∝ **a · ε · M · t / √(B · M · t)** = **a · ε · √(M · t / B)**

where background index B [counts/(keV·kg·yr)] is the dominant limiting factor. Upgrades must attack B, improve energy resolution (signal acceptance ε), or scale M.

---

## 1. Germanium Detector Upgrades

### 1.1 Inverted-Coaxial Point-Contact (ICPC) Geometry — Extend and Optimize

**Current state:** LEGEND-200 uses ICPCs up to ~2 kg/detector.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- **Larger-diameter ICPC crystals**: Push boule diameter from ~100 mm toward **130–140 mm**, increasing mass per detector to **3–4 kg**
- This reduces the surface-to-volume ratio, decreasing the fractional contribution of surface alpha/beta backgrounds
- Requires advances in zone-refining and crystal pulling (Czochralski) for 76Ge-enriched material at larger diameter without dislocation density increase (target: <500 dislocations/cm²)
- **Benefit**: Fewer detector-detector interfaces (less inert material), fewer electronics channels per kg, reduced cosmic activation per enriched mass unit

### 1.2 Detector Passivation and Surface Treatment

**Specific technology:** Replace conventional **amorphous germanium (a-Ge) contacts** with **ion-implanted contacts** on the n+ side and investigate **hydrogenated amorphous germanium (a-Ge:H)** passivation layers on the groove/surface regions

- Ion-implanted boron (p+) contact: achieve <1 μm dead layer vs. ~0.3–1 mm for lithium-diffused — directly reduces α and β surface background by minimizing the transition layer where charge collection is incomplete and events mimic the 2039 keV ROI
- **Laser ablation groove passivation**: replace mechanical grinding with laser-defined groove + plasma-cleaned passivation to reduce microfracture-induced surface leakage current (improves noise floor → better energy resolution)

### 1.3 Detector Operating Point and Bias Stability

- Implement **individual bias voltage fine-tuning per detector** via ultra-low-noise, low-power HV supplies (e.g., custom ASIC-based, <10 μW/channel) with **DAC resolution of 1 mV** to maintain each detector at optimal depletion without over-bias risk
- Use **temperature-compensated bias ramping algorithms** to handle LAr temperature fluctuations (±0.5 K affects depletion voltage by ~1–2 V for typical HPGe)

---

## 2. Front-End Electronics and Energy Resolution

### 2.1 Charge-Sensitive Amplifier ASIC

**Current state:** Discrete JFET-based (e.g., Moxtek MPF-102 or IF9030) at the detector contact.

**Proposed upgrade:** Replace discrete JFETs with a **fully custom deep-cryogenic ASIC** (65 nm or 130 nm CMOS, characterized for 87 K operation)

- Target: **equivalent noise charge (ENC) < 15 e⁻ RMS** at 87 K with detector capacitance of ~1 pF (ICPC point contact)
- Key design: **dual-channel per ASIC** (one per detector face), with integrated **continuous reset** (resistive feedback using sub-threshold PMOS, avoiding discharge transients from LED-reset schemes)
- Shaping: integrate a **4-pole semi-Gaussian shaper** on-chip with programmable peaking time (3–10 μs) to optimize for the LAr noise environment
- **Benefit**: FWHM at 2039 keV improved from current ~2.5 keV toward **1.8–2.0 keV FWHM** — directly improves signal-to-background ratio since ROI width can be tightened

### 2.2 Digital Signal Processing Upgrade

- Replace analog shapers with **on-detector 16-bit ADC at 100 MHz** (low-power pipeline ADC, e.g., derived from ATLAS/CMS strip detector readout ASICs adapted for 87 K)
- Implement **on-FPGA (or on-ASIC) real-time multi-site event (MSE) tagging** using a **time-domain current pulse shape library** matched filter — reject Compton-scattered coincident energy depositions with >99% efficiency while retaining >90% of true 0νββ signal
- **Pole-zero cancellation** and **baseline restoration** implemented digitally with adaptive algorithms tracking slow drifts from LAr bubbling/vibration noise

### 2.3 Cabling and Grounding

- Replace copper signal cables with **superconducting NbTi coaxial cables** (Tc = 9.2 K, well below 87 K LAr operating temp) from detector to feedthrough — eliminates Johnson noise from cable resistance, reduces microphonic pickup
- **Benefit**: ~30% noise reduction on long cable runs (>1 m) within the LAr volume

---

## 3. Liquid Argon Instrumentation and Veto

### 3.1 LAr Scintillation Light Readout — Wavelength Shifter Upgrade

**Current state (LEGEND-200):** Tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) coated wavelength-shifting fibers + SiPM readout.

**Proposed upgrade — dual-component LAr veto:**

#### a) Fiber Barrel with New WLS
- Replace TPB fibers with **polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) scintillating fibers** — PEN is itself a scintillator (emission ~425 nm) AND a WLS (absorbs 128 nm LAr VUV, re-emits at 425 nm), eliminating the deposition step and improving long-term stability of the WLS coating
- PEN is radiopure (<1 mBq/kg ²²⁶Ra demonstrated) — critical since fibers are close to detectors
- Target: **2× improvement in light collection efficiency** over TPB-on-nylon

#### b) SiPM Array Upgrade
- Replace current SiPMs with **cryogenic-optimized SiPMs** (e.g., Hamamatsu VUV4 Multi-Pixel Photon Counters, or FBK LF-series) with:
  - **Direct VUV sensitivity** (no WLS needed at SiPM face) — photon detection efficiency >20% at 128 nm at 87 K
  - **Low dark count rate at 87 K**: <0.1 Hz/mm² (thermal noise suppressed at cryogenic temps)
  - **Large active area**: tile the inner nylon mini-shroud surface and the outer copper cylinder with SiPM tiles at ~30% geometric coverage
- Implement **SiPM signal summing at 87 K** via analog summing PCBs with low-noise transimpedance amplifiers (cryogenic GaAs or SiGe BJT), reducing cable count

#### c) Add a Second LAr Volume (Outer LAr Veto)
- Instrument the **outer LAr** (between copper shroud array and water tank inner wall) with an independent SiPM+WLS-plate system
- Use large-area **PEN plates** (300 × 300 mm) coated on both faces with TPB, read out by SiPM strips on edges — provides **hermetic veto of external gamma rays** entering the inner volume and tagging of muon-induced events in LAr

**Combined LAr veto target:** Achieve **>99.9% tagging efficiency** for events depositing >200 keV in LAr within a ±1 μs coincidence window (vs. ~99.5% currently)

### 3.2 LAr Purity Monitoring and Active Purification

- Install **inline cryogenic argon purification**: recirculating LAr through a **cold getter (SAES MonoTorr PS4-MT3)** cartridge rated for cryogenic temperatures, removing O₂, N₂, H₂O to <0.1 ppb level — oxygen quenches LAr scintillation; achieving <0.1 ppb O₂ extends attenuation length to >1 m
- Deploy **3–4 two-phase argon purity monitors** (gridded ionization chambers with α sources, e.g., ²⁴¹Am) at different heights/radii to map electron lifetime; target **>5 ms electron lifetime** (not critical for LAr veto but important if drift signal is used for topology)
- **Radon suppression**: Replace all polymer O-rings in contact with LAr volume with metal-seal feedthroughs; implement **radon-emanation monitoring** of all materials with <0.1 mBq/m³ ²²²Rn target in LAr — radon daughters on detector surfaces are a leading background

---

## 4. Detector Support Structure and Materials

### 4.1 String Hardware

- Replace current copper string hardware (detector holders, spacers, contact springs) with **electroformed copper** (OFHC electroformed in underground lab, ~0.01 mBq/kg ²²⁶Ra) rather than commercially machined OFHC copper
- Design **spring contacts** from **CuBe alloy replaced by pure Cu with sapphire ball contact** — eliminates beryllium (potential activation product) and reduces contact resistance variability

### 4.2 Mini-Shroud Material

- Replace nylon mini-shrouds with **PEN mini-shrouds** — PEN is both radiopure AND acts as a scintillation light guide, increasing light collection from the immediate vicinity of each detector string
- Add **wavelength-shifting coating (TPB)** on inner PEN surface facing detectors — photons from 0νββ-correlated Bremsstrahlung or photoelectrons in the argon immediately around the detector are captured and veto-tagged

### 4.3 Close-in Radioactive Background Mitigation

- Implement **underground electroforming of all copper parts** in the underground laboratory to avoid cosmogenic activation (⁶⁰Co in copper: t₁/₂ = 5.27 yr, Eγ = 1173 + 1332 keV — potentially summing into ROI)
- Use **low-radioactivity silicon** for detector spacers (instead of PTFE or similar polymers with higher U/Th)

---

## 5. Water Cherenkov Shield Upgrade

### 5.1 Muon Veto Enhancement

- **Replace PMTs** in the water tank with **large-area flat-panel PMTs** (e.g., Hamamatsu R7081HQE or equivalent 8" low-background PMTs with borosilicate glass containing <2 ppm Th equivalent) or transition to **20" Hamamatsu R3600** equivalents, increasing photocathode coverage from ~25% to **>40%**
- Install **Gd-loaded water** (0.1% Gd₂(SO₄)₃ by weight) — gadolinium has enormous neutron capture cross-section (49,000 barn for thermal neutrons), with capture gamma cascade at 8 MeV (detectable in water Cherenkov) — this tags muon-induced neutrons that could otherwise activate ⁷⁶Ge to ⁷⁷Ge (a β-emitter with Q > 2039 keV)
  - Alternatively: add **⁶Li-loaded scintillator panels** on the inside face of the water tank wall as a dedicated thermal neutron catcher

### 5.2 Neutron Moderation Layer

- Add a **20–30 cm layer of borated polyethylene panels** (5% B by mass) between the water tank inner wall and the LAr cryostat — provides additional neutron thermalization and capture before neutrons reach the germanium array

---

## 6. Calibration System Upgrade

- Replace the current **¹³³Ba source deployment** on retractable cables with a **multi-point ²²⁸Th source system** on a motorized positioning arm capable of mapping the full detector array in 3D — ²²⁸Th provides the 2614 keV γ-line (from ²⁰⁸Tl) directly above the ROI, allowing **in-situ detector response characterization at ROI energies**
- Implement **optical calibration** (LED + fiber) for SiPM gain calibration without introducing radioactive sources — **photon number resolving capability** of cryogenic SiPMs (at 87 K, dark rate is suppressed enough to resolve single photons) enables precise gain tracking

---

## 7. Data Acquisition and Analysis Hardware

- Deploy **FPGA-based trigger-less streaming readout** (analogous to STRUCK SIS3316 or custom μTCA-based system) with **full waveform digitization** (250 MHz, 14-bit) for all channels — enables offline optimization of pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) cuts without trigger bias
- Implement **real-time coincidence processing in FPGA** between LAr SiPM signals and HPGe signals with <100 ns timing resolution — critical for identifying and rejecting 2-site events where one deposit is in LAr

---

## Priority Ranking by Background Reduction Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Mechanism | Estimated ΔB/B |
|---|---|---|
| Cryogenic ASIC + energy resolution improvement | Narrower ROI | −30 to −40% |
| PEN mini-shrouds + upgraded SiPM LAr veto | Alpha/beta/gamma tagging | −50 to −70% |
| Underground electroformed Cu hardware | Intrinsic radioactivity | −20 to −40% |
| Ion-implanted contacts (thin dead layer) | Surface alpha rejection | −30 to −50% |
| Gd-doped water + BPE neutron shield | Neutron backgrounds | −60 to −80% (of neutron component) |
| Larger ICPC crystals | Surface/volume ratio | −15 to −25% |

---

## Summary

The **single highest-leverage upgrade** is the combination of **cryogenic front-end ASICs** (improving energy resolution to ~1.9 keV FWHM at Qββ) with **PEN-based mini-shrouds and upgraded SiPM LAr veto** (closing the geometric and efficiency gaps in scintillation readout). Together these address both the energy resolution (ROI window width) and the largest remaining background sources (surface events and external gammas), and are technically achievable with demonstrated materials and fabrication processes within a near-term development program.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for EXO-200

## 1. Photon Detection System Replacement

**Current limitation:** 468 LAAPDs with 48% packing fraction, limited gain (~50 at 170K), noise floor constraining scintillation threshold, and 125 pF capacitance per device degrading electronic noise performance.

**Proposed upgrade: Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

- Replace LAAPDs with Hamamatsu VUV4 (S13370 series) or FBK VUV-HD3 SiPMs optimized for 178 nm direct detection
- These devices achieve Geiger-mode multiplication (gain ~10⁶ vs ~50 for LAAPDs), dramatically reducing the contribution of electronic noise to energy resolution
- Modern VUV-sensitive SiPMs achieve photon detection efficiency >20% at 178 nm in LXe, comparable or superior to LAAPDs
- Much lower operating voltage (~25-40V vs 1400V) simplifies biasing infrastructure and reduces risk of electrical breakdown
- Tile the entire end-cap and field cage barrel region with 6mm × 6mm SiPM dies in custom copper-backed PCB arrays, targeting >70% geometric coverage vs current 48%
- Critical caveat: SiPM dark count rate increases dramatically below ~100K but remains manageable at 167K operating temperature; correlated avalanche noise must be characterized and subtracted
- Ganging strategy: group 4×4 tiles (16 devices) per readout channel to maintain manageable channel count while improving spatial resolution for position-dependent light yield corrections

**Expected impact:** Combined improvement in light collection efficiency (~factor 2 geometric) and gain (~factor 20) would reduce scintillation threshold by roughly an order of magnitude and improve combined energy resolution by reducing the Fano-limited scintillation noise term significantly.

---

## 2. Wire Plane Replacement with Charge-Coupled Pixel Readout

**Current limitation:** 3mm wire pitch with 9mm readout grouping in triplets, 60° stereo geometry providing only 2D ionization position reconstruction with inherent ghost hit ambiguities, and ~127μm square cross-section wires with non-ideal field uniformity.

**Proposed upgrade: Pixelated charge readout using application-specific integrated circuits**

- Replace photoetched phosphor bronze wire triplets with a pixelated anode plane using 3mm × 3mm copper pixels on low-radioactivity polyimide substrate (similar to the existing flexible cable technology already proven in EXO-200)
- Each pixel read out individually using a cryogenic ASIC (e.g., adapted from DUNE cold electronics COLDATA/COLDADC architecture) bump-bonded or wire-bonded to the pixel board
- True 3D ionization cluster reconstruction eliminates stereo ghost ambiguities and dramatically improves multi-site event rejection
- Key radioactivity concern: ASIC must be fabricated on high-resistivity silicon with verified low U/Th content; die area minimized; back-end material (underfill, substrate) screened rigorously - silicon itself has well-characterized and acceptable radioactivity
- Alternative lower-risk approach: retain wire geometry but implement charge induction readout on both collection and induction planes using low-noise ASIC (e.g., LARASIC4 or custom cryogenic JFET-input design) to improve signal-to-noise on induction signals, enabling better event topology reconstruction without introducing new materials

**Expected impact:** Genuine 3D single-site/multi-site discrimination with <1mm position resolution would reduce γ-ray Compton scatter backgrounds by an estimated factor of 3-5 based on topological discrimination studies in nEXO simulations.

---

## 3. High Voltage System Redesign

**Current limitation:** HV instabilities above 9-14 kV limit operating field to ~0.4 kV/cm (8 kV across 19.2 cm half-drift) vs design capability of 3.7 kV/cm, severely degrading charge collection efficiency and electron-ion recombination rejection.

**Proposed upgrade: Segmented resistive field cage with improved HV delivery**

- Replace sharp photoetched edges on cathode and field-shaping components with electropolished, rounded copper rings (minimum edge radius >1mm) machined by CNC from bulk stock rather than photoetched, eliminating corona initiation sites identified as the probable instability source
- Replace the RG217 coaxial cable feedthrough with a custom feedthrough using ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) rod as dielectric, machined to eliminate voids and surface irregularities; UHMWPE has superior dielectric strength and lower outgassing than the current polyethylene cable extrusion
- Implement a Heinzinger PNC-70000 or equivalent ultra-low-noise power supply (noise <1ppm of output) with multi-stage LC filtering using copper inductors and polypropylene film capacitors replacing current RC filter design, reducing noise injection into ionization channels
- Add a graded resistor chain using higher-value (10 GΩ) resistors fabricated on alumina substrate to reduce power dissipation and thermal gradients that may contribute to LXe convection and electron drift lifetime degradation
- Install field uniformity monitoring via small embedded capacitive pickups on field shaping rings to detect ring potential deviations in real time

**Expected impact:** Operating at 2 kV/cm vs current ~0.4 kV/cm would reduce electron-ion recombination by roughly a factor of 5 at the double beta decay energy, substantially improving the anti-correlation between charge and light signals and hence the combined energy resolution from the current σ/E ~1.5% toward the ~0.8% fundamental limit.

---

## 4. Radon Mitigation in Internal Volumes

**Current limitation:** Radon emanation from internal surfaces (particularly PTFE, acrylic, and flexible cables) deposits ²¹⁴Bi daughters on detector surfaces, and the measured cleanroom Rn level exceeds the 2 mBq/L design limit by factor ~3.

**Proposed upgrade: Active Rn removal and surface treatment**

- Install a cryogenic radon trap (activated charcoal at 200K) on the HFE-7000 recirculation loop using a Entegris ChromaGas or custom charcoal bed in a PTFE-lined copper vessel, achieving >99% Rn reduction with demonstrated technology from Super-Kamiokande and XENON100
- Coat all internal acrylic and PTFE surfaces with a 50nm ALD (atomic layer deposition) aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) barrier layer - ALD Al₂O₃ has been demonstrated to reduce Rn emanation by factors of 10-100 from polymer surfaces while maintaining optical properties and is deposited at temperatures compatible with PTFE and acrylic (80°C process)
- Replace the stainless steel Rn enclosure shell (0.8mm) with a sealed Rn-barrier aluminum enclosure with continuous purge using electro-negative-filtered boil-off N₂, maintaining positive pressure to prevent in-leakage
- Critical implementation note: ALD coating must be verified for radioactivity content (Al₂O₃ itself is ultra-pure, but the trimethylaluminum precursor residuals must be measured) and LXe compatibility

**Expected impact:** Reduction of internal ²²²Rn by factor 10-30 would reduce the ²¹⁴Bi surface background contribution from the current dominant ~few counts/yr in the 0νββ window to sub-dominant levels.

---

## 5. Scintillation Wavelength Shifting for Barrel Coverage

**Current limitation:** PTFE reflectors on the barrel achieve only 70% reflectance at 178nm (measured in Ar gas; actual LXe value uncertain), and photons undergo multiple reflections losing efficiency, while the field cage geometry prevents direct LAAPD/SiPM placement on the barrel.

**Proposed upgrade: Tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) wavelength shifting coating with dichroic filter system**

- Vacuum-evaporate 300 μg/cm² TPB onto the PTFE barrel tiles in situ using a portable evaporator deployed before final vessel closure
- TPB shifts 178nm LXe scintillation to ~430nm where reflectance of PTFE exceeds 95% and SiPMs have PDE >40%, effectively converting the barrel into an efficient secondary reflector with much reduced multi-reflection losses
- Add dichroic long-pass optical filters (cutoff at 380nm, fabricated from low-radioactivity fused silica with dielectric coating) in front of the SiPM end-cap arrays to reject any residual 178nm photons and pass only TPB-shifted light, eliminating the wavelength mismatch between direct and shifted photons
- Screen TPB for radioactivity: anthracene-based materials have historically shown acceptable U/Th content at the sub-ppt level; batch screening by ICP-MS required
- Verify TPB stability in LXe at 167K (literature shows stable performance over multi-year timescales in similar noble liquid detectors including MiniCLEAN and DEAP-3600)

**Expected impact:** Modeling suggests improvement in total photon collection efficiency from ~8% (estimated current) to ~15-20%, directly improving scintillation energy resolution and lowering the effective detection threshold.

---

## 6. Cryogenic Preamplifier Relocation

**Current limitation:** Front-end electronics located ~1m outside lead shielding connected via 25μm polyimide cables contributes dominant noise from cable capacitance (60-80 pF for wire channels), and the long cable runs introduce microphonic susceptibility from HV-biased conductors.

**Proposed upgrade: Cold preamplifiers at the TPC end-caps**

- Mount first-stage JFET preamplifiers (single JFET per wire channel, 4-parallel for LAAPD gangs) directly on the copper support ring at LXe temperature using 2SK932 or improved NXP BF862 JFETs verified operational at 170K
- At 170K, JFET drain current noise is reduced, transconductance increases ~30% relative to room temperature, and thermal noise of resistors in feedback networks decreases - all improving noise figure
- JFETs package in hermetic TO-71 cans (gold-plated Kovar) with U/Th screened by NAA; typical commercial JFETs contain <0.1 mBq/kg of combined U+Th
- Connect preamp output (low impedance, ~50Ω) to room-temperature shaping electronics via existing polyimide cable infrastructure - now carrying voltage signals rather than charge, eliminating the dominant cable capacitance noise term
- Feedback resistor implemented as a cold FET operated in linear region to avoid introducing radioactive resistor materials; alternatively use capacitor reset with periodic discharge
- Total additional radioactive mass: ~50 JFETs × ~0.5g each = ~25g of screened silicon/Kovar, acceptable given current internal component masses

**Expected impact:** Reduction of effective input noise from current 2e⁻/pF to approaching 0.5e⁻/pF based on demonstrated cryogenic JFET performance, improving wire channel energy threshold and enabling reconstruction of smaller ionization clusters for enhanced multi-site discrimination.

---

## Summary of Expected Performance Improvements

| Upgrade | Primary Metric | Expected Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM replacement | Light yield, scintillation threshold | ×5-10 improvement in scintillation S/N |
| Pixel charge readout | Multi-site rejection | Factor 3-5 background reduction |
| HV system | Operating field, charge resolution | 5× improvement in recombination rejection |
| Rn mitigation | Surface background | Factor 10-30 reduction in ²¹⁴Bi |
| TPB + cold optics | Photon collection efficiency | ~2× improvement |
| Cold preamplifiers | Electronic noise | Factor 3-4 noise reduction |

The combined effect of improved energy resolution (targeting σ/E <0.8% vs current ~1.5%) and enhanced background rejection would improve the 0νββ half-life sensitivity by roughly an order of magnitude in a detector of equivalent mass, which is broadly consistent with the performance targets of the successor nEXO experiment.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Cubic-Kilometre Ice Cherenkov Neutrino Observatory

## Framing: What "Primary Physics Performance" Means Here

The dominant limitations of an IceCube-like detector are:
- **Angular resolution** (limited by PMT timing, photon scattering in ice, geometry)
- **Energy resolution** (limited by photon detection efficiency and dynamic range)
- **Flavor identification / cascade vs. track discrimination** (limited by photon angular information)
- **Low-energy threshold** (limited by noise, detection area per module)
- **Vertex resolution** (limited by string spacing ~125 m, sparse instrumentation)

Each upgrade below is evaluated against these physics goals.

---

## 1. Replace Single-PMT DOMs with Multi-PMT Optical Modules

**Specific technology:** Replace 10-inch single-Hamamatsu-R7081 DOMs with **multi-PMT modules** carrying 24–31 × 3-inch PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R12199-02 or ET Enterprises 9305KB) arranged to provide near-4π solid angle coverage, as demonstrated by KM3NeT's DOM design.

**Concrete implementation:**
- 17-inch pressure sphere (Vitrovex or Nautilus borosilicate glass)
- 24× 3-inch PMTs with individual HV bases (e.g., CAEN R11265 MAPMT bases adapted for single-channel operation)
- Per-PMT waveform digitization at 250 MHz with 12-bit ADCs
- Dedicated FPGA (Xilinx Artix-7 or Lattice ECP5) per module for local coincidence triggering

**Physics gain:**
- **4× to 6× improvement in effective photon collection area** per module at fixed sphere diameter
- **Directional photon sensitivity**: coincidence patterns across PMTs constrain photon arrival direction to ~30°, enabling local "mini-reconstruction" that dramatically improves cascade directional resolution (potentially from ~15° to ~3–5° for TeV cascades)
- **Reduced noise sensitivity**: requiring 2-fold local coincidence within ~10 ns suppresses dark noise from ~500 Hz per 10" PMT to effectively ~10 Hz equivalent, lowering energy threshold by a factor of ~3–5

---

## 2. Wavelength-Shifting Pressure Vessel Coating

**Specific technology:** Coat the inside of the pressure sphere with **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) or bis-MSB** wavelength shifter dissolved in polystyrene (1–2% by weight), applied as a ~100 µm evaporated or spin-cast film.

**Why this matters:** Glacial ice and Cherenkov emission peak in the UV (300–400 nm). Standard borosilicate glass and bialkali photocathodes have poor QE below 350 nm. TPB shifts 350 nm → 430 nm where bialkali QE peaks (~25–30%).

**Concrete alternative:** Use **SCHOTT 8337B borosilicate** spheres (better UV transmission than standard grades) combined with **wavelength-shifting gel pads** (EJ-298 or custom acrylic-TPB composite) optically coupled between sphere and PMT face.

**Physics gain:**
- ~20–30% increase in detected photon yield in the 300–380 nm band
- Improved energy resolution, especially important for sub-TeV events near threshold

---

## 3. High-Quantum-Efficiency PMTs with Extended Red Response

**Specific technology:** Replace standard bialkali Hamamatsu R7081 (QE ~25% peak) with:
- **Hamamatsu R7081-20 HQE** (QE ~35% peak) — already partially deployed in IceCube-Upgrade
- Or: **Large-area SiPM tiles** (Hamamatsu S13360-6075 or FBK NUV-HD series, 6×6 mm² cells, ~50% PDE at 420 nm)

**SiPM-specific implementation for deep-ice DOMs:**
- Tile 144 cm² of SiPM area per module using 400× 3×3 mm² cells
- Operate at –40°C (ice temperature): SiPM dark count rate drops to ~10 kHz/mm² at –40°C from ~200 kHz/mm² at +25°C, making noise manageable
- Custom transimpedance amplifier + SiPM summing board; bias at ~3V above breakdown (~27V for FBK NUV-HD)
- Challenge: correlated noise (optical crosstalk, afterpulsing) at ~15% must be characterized

**Physics gain:**
- SiPMs: up to **2× photon detection efficiency** over HQE PMTs
- Dark noise at –40°C is ~10–50 kHz total per module, comparable to PMT dark noise
- This is the highest-leverage single-component upgrade for **low-energy physics** (< 1 TeV, supernova neutrinos, indirect dark matter)

---

## 4. Precision Timing: White Rabbit Synchronization to <100 ps

**Specific technology:** Implement **White Rabbit PTP (Precision Time Protocol)** over fiber, as used in KM3NeT, replacing the IceCube LED flasher/RAPCal timing calibration system.

**Hardware specifics:**
- White Rabbit switch (e.g., CERN WR-LEN or Seven Solutions WRS) at surface
- Per-string fiber with **dedicated WR timing fiber pair** (single-mode OS2)
- Per-DOM **White Rabbit node ASIC** (SPEC board or custom FPGA implementation using WR HDL core) providing < 100 ps absolute timing synchronized across all DOMs
- Replace current 40 MHz DOM clock with **VCTCXO disciplined by WR** (e.g., ABRACON ASTX-H12)

**Physics gain:**
- Current IceCube timing: ~3 ns RMS per DOM
- WR achieves: **< 100 ps RMS** across full detector
- Angular resolution for muon tracks scales as σ_θ ∝ σ_t / baseline: improving from 3 ns to 0.1 ns on a 125 m string spacing → **angular resolution improvement from ~0.5° toward ~0.05° for well-reconstructed through-going muons**
- Critical for identifying point sources and measuring neutrino mass ordering via Earth tomography

---

## 5. Reduced String Spacing with Denser Infill Strings

**Specific technology:** Deploy **additional strings at 40 m spacing** (vs. current 125 m) in a subarray, using **narrower-gauge cable** (reduce from ~46 mm to ~30 mm diameter) to enable faster/cheaper drilling.

**Drilling technology:** Replace Enhanced Hot Water Drilling (EHWD) with **coiled-tubing hot water drilling** or **hybrid thermal-mechanical drilling** (e.g., based on IDDO intermediate drill modified for smaller boreholes, ~15 cm diameter vs. current 60 cm).

**Geometry:** A 10-string, 40 m spacing infill array at depth 1800–2600 m (optimal ice) providing a **~0.003 km³ dense subarray** within the larger detector.

**Physics gain:**
- Energy threshold drops to **~1 GeV** in the dense subarray (cf. DeepCore at 8 m Debye-screened equivalent spacing)
- Enables: atmospheric neutrino oscillations, tau neutrino appearance, core-collapse supernova burst reconstruction
- Vertex resolution: 5 m vs. current 15 m for contained events

---

## 6. Waveform Digitization Upgrade: High-Speed ADC + FPGA Edge Processing

**Specific technology:** Replace the current IceCube ATWD (Analog Transient Waveform Digitizer, 300 MHz, 10-bit, 3-channel) with:
- **16-bit, 1 GSPS ADC** (e.g., Texas Instruments ADC16DX370 or Analog Devices AD9208) operating in single-channel mode at 500 MSPS
- Paired with a **mid-range FPGA** (Xilinx Kintex Ultrascale XCKU035) for:
  - Real-time pulse fitting (template matching) on-chip
  - Local triggering with programmable coincidence logic
  - Data compression: transmit pulse parameters (t, charge, width) rather than raw waveforms

**Physics gain:**
- 16-bit ADC: **dynamic range from ~10⁴ to ~10⁶ photoelectrons** (important for tau double-bang events and near-source high-energy cascades)
- Improved **charge resolution**: σ_Q/Q from ~15% to ~3% per photoelectron → better energy resolution
- On-FPGA feature extraction reduces per-DOM data rate by ~10× enabling more aggressive triggering strategies
- 1 GSPS: resolves individual photoelectron pulses even at high occupancy, enabling **photon counting mode** at moderate fluxes

---

## 7. In-Situ Calibration: Isotropic Precision LED Light Sources

**Specific technology:** Deploy dedicated **calibration modules** (one per 3 strings) containing:
- **Picosecond pulsed laser source**: PicoQuant LDH-P-C-405 (405 nm, <70 ps FWHM pulse) coupled to isotropic diffuser ball (Spectralon-coated PTFE sphere, 5 cm diameter)
- Absolute intensity calibration using **on-board silicon photodiode** (Hamamatsu S2281) with NIST-traceable calibration
- **Polarized emission option**: liquid crystal variable retarder to probe ice birefringence

**Also:** Distribute **acoustic positioning hydrophones** (RESON TC4013 or equivalent, 1–100 kHz) on each module for triangulation-based position calibration to <10 cm accuracy.

**Physics gain:**
- Absolute timing calibration to **< 200 ps**
- Ice optical property mapping (absorption + scattering lengths) to **< 1% uncertainty** every 10 m depth
- Position calibration to **< 10 cm** (current IceCube: ~30 cm)
- Collectively, these reduce systematic uncertainties in energy and direction reconstruction by a factor of **2–3×**

---

## 8. Veto and Surface Array Integration

**Specific technology:** Deploy a **surface air shower array** (scintillator panels + radio antennas) directly above the in-ice array:
- **4 m² plastic scintillator tiles** (EJ-200, coupled to 3-inch PMT via WLS fiber) on 10 m × 10 m grid over 1 km²
- **AERA-style log-periodic dipole antennas** (30–80 MHz) for cosmic ray air shower reconstruction
- Synchronized to in-ice timing via White Rabbit

**Physics gain:**
- **Veto efficiency > 99.9%** for downgoing atmospheric muon background (currently ~10⁶ Hz background vs ~10¹ Hz signal for cosmic neutrinos)
- Enables **unvetoed Northern and Southern sky** searches for astrophysical neutrinos
- Cosmic ray energy and composition measurement cross-calibrates neutrino flux normalizations

---

## Priority Ranking by Physics Impact per Cost

| Priority | Upgrade | Primary Gain | Cost Driver |
|----------|---------|--------------|-------------|
| 1 | Multi-PMT modules (mDOM) | Angular resolution, threshold | Moderate |
| 2 | WR timing (< 100 ps) | Angular resolution for tracks | Low |
| 3 | HQE PMT / SiPM | Low-energy threshold, energy resolution | Moderate |
| 4 | 16-bit 1 GSPS ADC + FPGA | Dynamic range, energy resolution | Low |
| 5 | Dense infill strings | Threshold, oscillation physics | High (drilling) |
| 6 | Calibration module network | Systematic uncertainties | Low |
| 7 | Surface veto array | Background rejection | Moderate |
| 8 | WLS sphere coating | UV photon collection | Very Low |

---

## Most Impactful Single Upgrade

**Multi-PMT optical modules with per-PMT waveform digitization** represent the highest-leverage single hardware change because they simultaneously improve photon collection efficiency, provide local directional sensitivity, reduce noise-driven threshold, and increase dynamic range — all within the same borehole footprint and with demonstrated feasibility (KM3NeT is operating this design today). Combined with White Rabbit timing, this addresses all three primary physics limitations (angular resolution, energy resolution, flavor identification) at once.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a 770-tonne Single-Phase LArTPC Prototype

## Framing the Problem

The instrument described maps closely to ProtoDUNE-SP (DUNE 35-ton predecessor → actually the 770-tonne figure matches **ProtoDUNE-SP at CERN**). Primary physics performance metrics are: **charge collection efficiency, spatial resolution, calorimetric energy resolution, neutrino interaction reconstruction fidelity, and low-energy threshold**. I'll address each subsystem systematically with concrete technology proposals.

---

## 1. Photon Detection System (Highest Leverage Upgrade)

The dip-coated light-guide bar + ARAPUCA-style collector architecture has well-documented limitations in photon detection efficiency (PDE) and spatial uniformity.

### 1a. Replace Dip-Coated Light Guides with X-ARAPUCA Modules

**Specific components:**
- **X-ARAPUCA cells** using dichroic filter supercell geometry (already demonstrated in ProtoDUNE-SP run 2 and adopted for DUNE FD)
- Filter: long-pass dichroic filter transmitting >420 nm, reflecting <400 nm (commercially available from Omega Optical or Chroma Technology, e.g., 400 nm cutoff, ~25 mm × 25 mm tiles)
- **Wavelength shifter**: Evaporated **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB)** at 0.2 mg/cm² on the external filter face — replace dip-coating (non-uniform, ~30–50 μg/cm²) with **vacuum thermal evaporation** for ±5% thickness uniformity
- **SiPM array**: Hamamatsu **S13360-6075PE** (6×6 mm², 75 μm cell pitch, ~50% PDE at 450 nm, VUV-transparent encapsulation) or **FBK NUV-HD-Cryo** specifically characterized for 87 K operation
- **Cell multiplexing**: 48-SiPM ganged readout per X-ARAPUCA supercell to reduce channel count while maintaining ~15 cm spatial segmentation along drift direction

**Performance gain**: PDE improvement from ~0.3–0.5% (dip-coated bars) to **~3–4% geometrically averaged** across the active volume, directly improving t₀ determination for non-beam events and lowering trigger threshold.

### 1b. Add a Second Photon Detection Layer on the Cathode Plane

Currently the cathode is optically passive. Install:
- **Cathode-mounted X-ARAPUCA tiles** embedded in FR4 cathode frames, using the same SiPM + dichroic filter stack
- Requires **HV-isolated readout** via custom cryogenic transformers or fiber-optic signal transmission (e.g., **SiPM + LED pulser scheme** with Thorlabs SM400 fiber pigtails for optical data transmission)
- Adds ~50% solid-angle coverage currently lost to the cathode face

**Performance gain**: Near-uniform photon detection across the full drift volume; critical for **supernova neutrino burst detection** (MeV-scale events) and for correcting drift-velocity variations via precise t₀.

---

## 2. Wire Readout → Pixel or Stripline Upgrade

The APA wire-based readout (U/V/Z planes at 4.67 mm pitch) has **intrinsic ambiguities** from the 2D projective geometry requiring computational disambiguation.

### 2a. LArPix-Based Charge Pixel Readout (Full 3D)

**Specific components:**
- **LArPix ASIC v2b** (LBNL design, ~28,000 pixels per tile, 4.434 mm pixel pitch, 1 ke⁻ noise ENC at 87 K in demonstrated tests)
- Tile form factor: 10 cm × 10 cm modular tiles, ~2400 tiles to instrument a single APA face
- **Integrated cold multiplexing**: UART-based daisy-chain within each tile, reducing cable plant by ~100× vs. wire readout
- **Self-triggering capability** at ~100 e⁻ threshold — eliminates the beam-gate dependency for low-energy physics

**Critical enabling component**: LArPix requires **low-mass PCB** (Rogers 4350B, 0.2 mm thickness) and **micro-coaxial ribbon cables** (Axon' Cable, 50 Ω, 0.25 mm pitch) routed through the cold flange feedthroughs.

**Performance gain**: Eliminates hit disambiguation entirely; provides **4π stereo tracking** at ~4 mm³ voxel resolution; enables detection of ~5 MeV electron/gamma from neutron capture on Ar (relevant for nucleon decay background rejection).

### 2b. If Full Pixel Replacement is Infeasible: Capacitive Multiplex Strips

- Replace induction plane wires with **2D strips** (e.g., charge-sharing pads as in the ArgonCube/Module-0 design)
- Strip pitch: 3.0 mm × 3.0 mm crossed geometry
- **Cold ASIC**: LARASIC8 or **COLDADC** (both developed for DUNE, characterized to 77–89 K, 600 e⁻ ENC, 2 MHz sampling)
- Eliminates ~30% of ghost track rate from wire-based induction plane ambiguity

---

## 3. Cold Electronics Upgrade

### 3a. Replace Warm Flange Analog Readout with Full Cold Digital Chain

**Current state**: Analog signals carried ~10 m on cold cables to warm ADCs — susceptible to cable capacitance noise (~1500 e⁻ ENC total).

**Proposed system:**
- **COLDATA ASIC** (DUNE CDR design): 8-channel 12-bit ADC + serializer, characterized at 77 K, power dissipation ~7 mW/channel
- **COLDMUX** ASIC for 64:1 digital multiplexing on cold side
- Cold cable plant replaced with **twinaxial 28 AWG** differential pairs (Junkosha CF-series cryogenic-qualified) at 1.28 Gbps per line
- **Feedthrough**: Upgrade to **D-sub 78-pin hermetic** or custom **micro-HDMI-style** cryogenic flanges (as developed by BNL for SBND)

**Performance gain**: Noise reduction to **~400–500 e⁻ ENC** (from ~1000–1500 e⁻ in current warm-ADC topology); directly improves dE/dx resolution (currently ~7–8% for minimum-ionizing particles, target <5%) and low-energy threshold.

### 3b. Increase Sampling Rate

- Current: 2 MHz (500 ns/sample)
- Upgrade COLDADC to **10 MHz sampling** mode (prototype demonstrated by DUNE electronics consortium)
- Benefit: Improved **longitudinal spatial resolution** (currently ~1.5 mm along drift at 1.5 m/ms drift velocity; improves to ~0.3 mm), critical for Bragg peak resolution in proton/pion separation

---

## 4. High Voltage / Field Uniformity

### 4a. Resistive Field Shell (Replace Wire Field Cage)

- Current field cage uses a ladder of discrete resistors (~100 MΩ/stage), which introduces:
  - Localized field distortion at each resistor node (~1% E-field non-uniformity)
  - Single-point failure modes

**Proposed upgrade:**
- **Resistive Kapton (polyimide) field cage panels**: Kapton film with carbon-loaded bulk resistivity of ~10⁹ Ω/sq (custom laminate from DuPont or Duplex, achievable by carbon black loading at ~3–5% mass fraction)
- Continuous resistive divider — eliminates discrete distortion nodes
- Field uniformity improvement: <0.1% spatial variation (demonstrated in SBND-style TPC prototypes at MIT)
- **Voltage grading electrodes**: Replace bare copper profiles with **electropolished 316L stainless** strips at 6 cm pitch, laser-welded to resistive Kapton backing

### 4b. Upgrade Cathode HV Feedthrough

- Replace current SHV/Glassman cable feedthrough with **custom coaxial feedthrough** based on **UHMWPE (ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene) insulation** rated to −200 kV in LAr (demonstrated by ICARUS/WA105)
- Target operating voltage: −300 kV for full 3.6 m drift at 500 V/cm (vs. current ~−180 kV at ~430 V/cm)
- Higher drift field: reduces electron-ion recombination (improves charge yield by ~15% per the Birks-modified Box model at 500 vs. 430 V/cm), critical for calorimetry

---

## 5. Purity / Fluid Handling Upgrade

### 5a. In-Vessel Liquid Purification Loop

- Add **cryogenic circulation pump** (Barber-Nichols centrifugal, model BNCP-32, LAr-qualified) recirculating at 10 tonnes/hour through a **4-column regenerable filter** (Oxisorb + 4A molecular sieve, 200 mm diameter × 1 m per column)
- Target: reduce steady-state O₂ equivalent contamination to **<10 ppt** (from current ~30–50 ppt)
- **Electron lifetime monitor**: Install 3× **parallel-plate Purity Monitors** (BNL design, α-source photocathode, 50 cm drift length) distributed vertically in the cryostat

**Performance gain**: Electron lifetime >10 ms at 500 V/cm → <1% charge loss over 3.6 m drift (currently ~5–10% with 30 ppt contamination at 430 V/cm); directly critical for far-detector-relevant calorimetry.

### 5b. Cryostat Thermal Insulation Upgrade

- Add a second layer of **aerogel blanket** (Aspen Aerogels Cryogel Z, 25 mm) to the outer vessel
- Reduces boil-off from ~0.1%/day → ~0.05%/day, reducing argon replenishment-driven impurity ingress
- Enables **longer steady-state run periods** between purification interruptions

---

## 6. Data Acquisition and Triggering

### 6a. Streaming Readout with FELIX + artDAQ

**Specific components:**
- **FELIX v2 (Front-End LInk eXchange)** PCIe cards (ATLAS/DUNE standard, 10 Gbps optical links, Xilinx Ultrascale FPGA) replacing current RCE-based readout
- **100 GbE network fabric** (Mellanox Infiniband HDR or Arista 7060CX) for lossless streaming at full 2 MHz × 15,360 channel throughput (~80 GB/s raw)
- **GPU-accelerated online reconstruction**: NVIDIA A100 cards running **Wire-Cell toolkit** algorithms for real-time 3D image formation — enables software triggering at <100 MeV threshold for supernova candidates

### 6b. Optical Trigger Upgrade

- Deploy **fast-timing NV2 trigger boards** (BNL design, 1 ns timestamp resolution) receiving SiPM summed signals
- Enables **photon-based primary trigger** independent of wire readout — crucial for non-beam (atmospheric, supernova, nucleon decay) physics

---

## Prioritized Summary Table

| Priority | Subsystem | Specific Technology | Primary Physics Impact |
|----------|-----------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| 1 | Photon detection | X-ARAPUCA + evaporated TPB + FBK NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs | t₀ resolution, low-E threshold, SN burst detection |
| 2 | Cold electronics | COLDATA + COLDMUX full cold chain, 10 MHz sampling | ENC noise floor, dE/dx, track resolution |
| 3 | HV / drift field | UHMWPE feedthrough @ −300 kV, resistive Kapton field cage | Charge yield, field uniformity, calorimetry |
| 4 | LAr purity | In-vessel recirculation, 3× purity monitors | Electron lifetime, charge attenuation correction |
| 5 | Charge readout | LArPix v2b pixel tiles (or 3mm strip hybrid) | 3D disambiguation, low-energy vertexing |
| 6 | DAQ | FELIX v2 + GPU Wire-Cell online reco | Trigger threshold, non-beam physics |
| 7 | Cathode PDS | Cathode-embedded X-ARAPUCA | Solid-angle uniformity |

---

## Highest Single Improvement

If forced to choose one: **replace the dip-coated light-guide PDS with X-ARAPUCA supercells with vacuum-evaporated TPB and FBK NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs.** The ~10× improvement in photon detection efficiency is the single largest performance lever because it simultaneously improves: event t₀ (enabling fiducial volume definition for all non-beam events), energy resolution at the MeV scale, and the instrument's capability as a supernova observatory — which is arguably the most unique physics contribution a large LArTPC can make that no other technology matches.

# Proposed Hardware Design Upgrades for LHCb

## Preamble on Scope

The paper documents Run I performance (2010–2012) and explicitly identifies limitations. I focus on upgrades addressing the **primary physics drivers**: decay time resolution, particle identification, trigger efficiency for hadronic modes, and tracking performance. I restrict myself to technologies credibly available by 2014.

---

## 1. Vertex Locator (VELO) Replacement

### Core Problem Identified in the Paper
The paper notes radiation damage reaching 1.8×10¹⁴ neq/cm² at the innermost strips (8.2 mm radius), effective depletion voltage approaching 100 V by end of Run I, and projected operation until end of Run II only below 500 V. The strip-based R/Φ sensor geometry also forces a two-coordinate readout architecture that limits pattern recognition speed. Critically, the hardware L0 trigger forces a 1 MHz readout bottleneck: the VELO cannot contribute to the hardware trigger decision at all, since the L0 relies only on calorimeters and muon stations.

### Proposed Upgrade: Pixel-Based Silicon Detector with Thinner Sensors

**Sensor technology**: Replace the 300 µm thick single-sided silicon strip sensors with **pixel sensors** based on the Timepix/Medipix family of hybrid pixel ASICs, bump-bonded to n-in-p silicon sensors of **200 µm or thinner** (ideally 150 µm active thickness achievable with standard float-zone silicon at this era). Pixel cell size of approximately 55×55 µm² provides genuine two-dimensional hit information per sensor plane rather than requiring separate R and Φ sensors.

**Radiation hardness**: Switch from n-bulk to **p-type bulk (n-in-p)** silicon, which does not undergo the problematic space-charge sign inversion documented in Figure 6 of the paper. The paper explicitly shows n-bulk sensors inverting at ~15×10¹² neq, requiring increasing bias voltage throughout Run I. P-type bulk sensors collect electrons rather than holes after inversion, maintaining better charge collection efficiency at high fluence without sign inversion complications. This is well-established in the ATLAS IBL programme by 2014.

**Geometry change**: The current design requires the VELO to retract 29 mm during injection, taking on average 210 seconds to close after stable beams are declared (the paper notes ~750 closing procedures in Run I). A pixel geometry enables a **RF foil redesign** with thinner corrugated aluminium (reducing from the current foil to approximately 250 µm equivalent aluminium), reducing the material budget that dominates the impact parameter resolution at high pT. The paper states IP resolution at asymptotically high pT is ~13 µm; thinner material upstream of the first measurement plane could bring this toward 8–10 µm.

**Readout architecture**: Pixel sensors with column-drain or data-driven readout (as opposed to the current triggered analogue pipeline) allow operation without a hardware trigger gate. The entire VELO readout can be made continuous at 40 MHz bunch crossing rate. This eliminates the latency constraint that currently forces the L0 hardware trigger to make decisions without VELO information, which is the single largest source of hadronic trigger inefficiency documented in the paper (L0 hadron TOS efficiency of only 22–40% in Table 5 and Figure 44).

**Quantitative expectation**: With pixel sensors providing 2D hits at ~10 µm precision, removing the need for the R/Φ two-sensor-per-module architecture, the number of detector planes can be increased from 42 modules to approximately 52 planes in the same mechanical envelope, improving pattern recognition efficiency in high-multiplicity events. The paper notes fake track rates of 6.5% in minimum bias events increasing to ~20% at high multiplicity; genuine 2D pixel hits directly eliminate the left-right ambiguity in the current strip geometry that contributes to fake track formation.

---

## 2. Upstream Tracker Replacement (TT → UT)

### Core Problem
The Tracker Turicensis (TT) with 183 µm strip pitch and 500 µm sensor thickness provides hit resolutions of ~53 µm (Table 1). Its primary role is momentum determination for downstream tracks (K⁰_S, Λ) and upstream tracks, and seeding of the forward tracking algorithm. The paper notes that roughly two-thirds of K⁰_S decays use downstream tracks with significantly worse mass resolution (7 MeV/c² versus 3.5 MeV/c² for long tracks, Figure 27). Additionally, at 40 MHz readout, the TT must be completely redesigned since its current front-end electronics are designed around the 1 MHz L0 accept rate.

### Proposed Upgrade: Fine-Pitch Silicon Microstrip Upstream Tracker

**Sensor redesign**: Replace the 500 µm thick TT sensors with **320 µm thick sensors** using **100 µm strip pitch** (approximately half the current 183 µm pitch). This directly halves the single-hit resolution to approximately 25–27 µm for tracks with small projected angles (where charge sharing is minimal), improving the momentum seed quality for downstream tracking. The thinner sensors reduce multiple scattering for the low-momentum tracks that the TT intercepts.

**Geometry expansion**: The current TT active area is ~8 m². Expanding this to ~9 m² with four detection layers in x-u-v-x geometry but with reduced inactive regions near the beam pipe (achieved by moving the first active strip to a smaller radius using the reduced radiation damage from thinner sensors and better radiation-hard silicon) increases acceptance for the low-momentum particles currently lost.

**Readout**: Adopt the **LHCb Beetle successor ASIC** (in development by 2014 within the collaboration) capable of continuous data-driven readout at 40 MHz, storing hits in a digital pipeline with timestamps. This is the same technology path used in the ATLAS IBL readout chip development. The zero-suppressed data output rate per strip is manageable because strip occupancies in TT are 0.2–1.9% (documented in the paper), meaning the data volume is dominated by occupied channels only.

**Impact on physics**: Improved upstream tracker resolution directly improves the momentum resolution for downstream tracks, reducing the 7 MeV/c² K⁰_S mass resolution toward ~5 MeV/c². Since many B decay analyses involving K⁰_S use downstream tracks for approximately two-thirds of signal candidates, this has broad impact on hadronic B physics.

---

## 3. Main Tracking Stations (T1–T3): Scintillating Fibre Replacement of Outer Tracker

### Core Problem
The Outer Tracker straw tubes have a maximum drift time of ~35 ns, requiring readout of three bunch crossings (75 ns window, as documented in Section 2.1.3). At 25 ns bunch spacing (tested briefly in 2012 and the planned LHC Run II mode), the OT occupancy reaches ~25% in the innermost modules. Figure 10 shows clearly that 25 ns operation severely increases occupancy. Furthermore, the 205 µm single-hit resolution, while close to design, is limited by the 4.9 mm inner straw diameter and gas drift physics. At 40 MHz continuous readout, the OT's drift-time-based architecture is fundamentally incompatible without extensive buffering.

### Proposed Upgrade: Scintillating Fibre Tracker with SiPM Readout

**Active element**: Replace all OT straw tube modules with **250 µm diameter scintillating fibres** (such as the Kuraray SCSF-78 or Saint-Gobain BCF-12 fibres, both commercially available by 2014 and studied for LHCb upgrade purposes). Fibres are assembled into mats of several layers, with a mat thickness of approximately 2.5 mm providing ~6 fibre layers per mat. The fibre pitch of 250 µm naturally gives a single-hit resolution of approximately 250/√12 ≈ 72 µm without charge sharing, improving to ~50 µm with light sharing between adjacent fibres — comparable to or better than the OT's 205 µm while being intrinsically faster.

**Key advantage — response time**: Scintillating fibres produce light within ~2–3 ns of particle passage (SCSF-78 has a decay time of ~2.8 ns), completely eliminating the 35 ns drift time that forces the OT to read out multiple bunch crossings. The entire T1–T3 hit is contained within a single 25 ns LHC clock cycle. This is the decisive advantage for 40 MHz operation.

**Photodetector**: Read out the fibre mats using **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** with pixel pitch of ~57.5 µm, matching the fibre pitch. By 2014, SiPMs from Hamamatsu (MPPC series), SensL, and KETEK had demonstrated photon detection efficiency >30% at 450 nm (matching scintillating fibre emission peak), dark count rates manageable at the ~2.5×10⁶ hits/s/channel expected in the inner tracking regions, and radiation tolerance to ~10¹² neq (sufficient for the T1–T3 radiation environment, which is much less severe than the VELO).

**Channel count and granularity**: With 250 µm fibre pitch across the total T1–T3 active area of approximately 3×(597 cm × 485 cm), the channel count is approximately 130,000 channels per station, versus the current ~53,000 OT channels plus ~129,000 IT channels. The increased granularity directly reduces occupancy in the high-rate inner regions. The paper notes IT occupancy of up to 1.9% and OT occupancy of up to 17% at 50 ns spacing; with 250 µm fibres the occupancy in the corresponding region falls below 1% at the same luminosity.

**Elimination of IT/OT boundary**: The current detector has a problematic boundary between the Inner Tracker (silicon strips) and Outer Tracker (straws) that requires two different reconstruction algorithms and introduces inefficiency at the boundary region. Replacing both with a uniform scintillating fibre technology eliminates this boundary entirely and simplifies the tracking software substantially.

**Quantitative tracking improvement**: The improved single-hit resolution (~50 µm versus 205 µm in OT) directly improves the T-station contribution to long-track momentum resolution. The paper shows δp/p of 5 per mille below 20 GeV/c and 8 per mille near 100 GeV/c. With improved T-station hits, and assuming VELO resolution dominates at low momentum while T-station resolution dominates at high momentum, the high-momentum resolution could improve to approximately 5–6 per mille at 100 GeV/c, improving the Z⁰ mass resolution (currently 1727 MeV/c² per Table 2) and high-mass dimuon measurements.

---

## 4. RICH Detector Modifications

### Core Problem Identified
The paper reports that the RICH1 gas (C₄F₁₀) Cherenkov angle resolution of 1.618 mrad is significantly worse than the simulation prediction of 1.52 mrad, with the discrepancy "largely attributed to imperfect corrections for distortions in the RICH photon detector images caused by the residual magnetic ﬁeld in the vicinity of the RICH1 detector." The aerogel radiator Npe of only 5.0 versus 8.0 predicted (Table 3) is attributed to C₄F₁₀ absorption by porous aerogel. The HPD photodetectors also show a read-out inefficiency identified during high trigger rate running.

### Proposed Upgrade 4a: Replace Aerogel with Additional C₄F₁₀ Volume or Remove Aerogel

The aerogel radiator in RICH1 is performing significantly below specification — the standard deviation of ΔθC is 5.6 mrad versus 3.1 mrad expected, a factor of 1.8 worse. The cause (C₄F₁₀ gas absorption into porous aerogel) is a fundamental material incompatibility. **Remove the aerogel radiator entirely** and extend the C₄F₁₀ gas volume to begin at a shorter distance from the interaction region. This sacrifices particle identification for 2–10 GeV/c particles (the aerogel's designed working range) but eliminates a system performing at nearly half its design specification. The C₄F₁₀ radiator already provides good separation in the 10–60 GeV/c range; RICH2 covers 15–100 GeV/c. The gap region (2–10 GeV/c) is partially covered by dE/dx information from the silicon trackers (which the paper does not exploit but is technically feasible).

Alternatively, if aerogel PID in the 2–10 GeV/c range is essential for physics (particularly for low-momentum kaon/pion separation in charm decays), replace the silica aerogel tiles with **hydrophobic aerogel** (available from Matsushita/Panasonic by 2014) that has been treated to minimise gas absorption. Hydrophobic aerogel with refractive index n ≈ 1.03 can achieve transmission lengths above 4 cm at 400 nm, sufficient for the RICH1 geometry.

### Proposed Upgrade 4b: Replace HPDs with Multi-Anode PMTs or SiPMs

The Hybrid Photon Detectors (HPDs) used in both RICH detectors have a documented readout inefficiency at high trigger rates. HPDs require high voltage (~20 kV for the electron bombardment gain stage) and are sensitive to magnetic fields, directly causing the image distortions degrading RICH1 resolution. 

**Replace HPDs with multi-anode PMTs** (specifically Hamamatsu H8500 or H9500 series flat-panel MAPMTs, 64 or 256 anode pixels per unit, available commercially by 2014). MAPMTs operate at lower voltages (~1000 V), have demonstrated magnetic field tolerance up to ~1 mT (sufficient for the RICH1 fringe field environment with appropriate shielding), and have well-established single-photon detection efficiency of ~20–25% at 270–650 nm — comparable to HPD performance but without the complex electron optics susceptible to field distortions.

**Quantitative impact**: Eliminating the magnetic field distortion in RICH1 would bring the C₄F₁₀ resolution from 1.618 mrad toward the simulated 1.52 mrad, approximately a 6% improvement. Combined with the increased Npe from eliminating the read-out inefficiency (the paper states a few percent improvement is expected for Run II from retuning alone), the net kaon-pion separation power at 50 GeV/c improves by approximately 0.5–0.8σ in terms of Cherenkov angle pull, meaningful for the high-momentum hadron identification used in B→hh decays.

---

## 5. Calorimeter System: ECAL Front-End Electronics Upgrade

### Core Problem
The paper documents that PMT gain degradation from radiation damage is ongoing and requires bi-monthly 137Cs recalibration for HCAL and continuous monitoring/correction for ECAL (Figure 29). The SPD uses a single-bit discriminator per cell, providing no pulse-height information that would help separate pile-up contributions at 40 MHz operation.

### Proposed Upgrade: Replace SPD Single-Bit Readout with Multi-Bit ADC

**SPD**: Replace the binary discriminator with a **4-bit flash ADC** on the SPD front-end, providing 16 levels of energy measurement. At a cost of modest front-end electronics redesign (the scintillator and WLS fibre geometry remain unchanged), this transforms the SPD from a charged/neutral discriminator into a low-resolution energy sampler. In high-luminosity pile-up conditions (µ ≈ 1.8 as in 2012), the single-bit SPD cannot distinguish between one and multiple overlapping charged particles in a cell. Multi-bit information enables shower-shape discrimination at the first detector layer, improving the L0 electron/photon purity without changing the L0 rate.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a 770-tonne Single-Phase LArTPC Prototype

## Context and Performance Bottlenecks

This instrument matches the description of **ProtoDUNE-SP** (CERN, 2018). The primary physics performance metrics are: charge collection efficiency, spatial resolution, calorimetric energy resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and event triggering/timing. I'll address each systematically with concrete upgrade proposals.

---

## 1. Photon Detection System (Highest Priority)

### Current Limitation
The ARAPUCA-precursor light-guide dip-coated bars (with TPB wavelength shifter) achieve **~0.3–1% photon detection efficiency (PDE)** per bar and suffer from:
- Inefficient light trapping in the light guides
- TPB coating non-uniformity and delamination at cryogenic temperatures
- Poor geometric coverage within anode plane assemblies (APAs)

### Proposed Upgrades

#### 1a. Replace with X-ARAPUCA Supercells
- **Technology:** X-ARAPUCA modules using dichroic filter + wavelength-shifting plates (PTP or bis-MSB doped) with SiPM arrays (Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or FBK NUV-HD-Cryo series)
- **Specific configuration:** 48-cell supercell format, each cell ~10 × 8 cm², mounted in the same APA frame slots
- **Expected gain:** PDE improvement from ~1% to **~3–5%**, demonstrated in ProtoDUNE-SP-II baseline
- **Cryogenic SiPMs:** Use FBK VUV-HD3 SiPMs (dedicated VUV-sensitive, Vbr ~28V at 87K) to eliminate the wavelength-shifting step entirely for direct LAr scintillation at 127 nm
- **Impact:** Enables sub-nanosecond t₀ determination; improves absolute energy scale by anchoring it to scintillation light; enables supernova burst detection and low-energy physics below the charge-readout threshold (~10 MeV)

#### 1b. Increase Geometric Coverage with Cathode-Mounted PDS
- **Technology:** Mount ARAPUCA modules on the cathode plane (opposite face) using HV-isolated support structures with coaxial signal feedthroughs
- **Specific component:** Use Vishay Dale CRCW series HV resistors in divider chains for field shaping around cathode-mounted units; signal extraction via PEEK-jacketed coax rated to −150 kV with SHV connectors outside cryostat
- **Impact:** Doubles solid-angle coverage, improves uniformity of light yield across drift volume, critical for fiducialization of events near the cathode

---

## 2. Cold Electronics and Charge Readout (Second Priority)

### Current Limitation
The FE ASICs (LArASIC, version 4) operate at the design limit, with equivalent noise charge (ENC) of **~400–500 e⁻ RMS** for the collection wires and ~600 e⁻ for induction wires. The ADC (AD chips at 2 MHz, 12-bit) limits dynamic range, and the Cold ADC + COLDATA mux chain introduces non-linearities at ~0.1% level that degrade calorimetry.

### Proposed Upgrades

#### 2a. Next-Generation ASIC Suite: LArASIC v5 + ColdADC v2 + COLDATA v2
- **LArASIC v5:** Reduces ENC to **~250 e⁻ RMS** at 400 pF detector capacitance through improved input transistor geometry (TSMC 180nm process with optimized PMOS input stage); adds programmable baseline for induction channel bipolar signals
- **ColdADC v2 (12-bit, 2 MSPS):** Implement correlated double sampling and improved reference voltage stability using bandgap references trimmed at 77K; target INL < 0.05% for calorimetric-quality ADC response
- **COLDATA upgrade:** Replace current 1.28 Gbps serial link with a **2.56 Gbps SLVS link** using LP-CMOS drivers to reduce power dissipation in cold (target < 10 mW/channel total) and improve data throughput margin
- **Impact:** ~30% improvement in S/N ratio on induction planes; enables lower threshold for Michel electron and low-energy photon reconstruction

#### 2b. Continuous Readout with Zero-Suppression in FPGA
- **Technology:** Replace triggered readout with continuous streaming using **Xilinx UltraScale+ KU15P FPGAs** in the warm interface electronics
- **Algorithm:** Implement online hit-finding (threshold + morphological filter) at full 2 MHz rate, reducing data volume by ~50:1 while preserving waveform data within ±100 µs windows around hits
- **Impact:** Enables capture of slow neutron captures, late light, and Michel electrons without pre-trigger; critical for supernova physics in the full DUNE FD

---

## 3. Wire Plane and Field Cage Upgrades

### Current Limitation
The APA wire planes (U/V induction at ±35.7°, X collection, wire pitch 4.79 mm, wire diameter 150 µm) suffer from:
- **Broken wire inefficiency:** ~0.1–0.3% dead channels per APA from soldering failures at 87K
- **Induction plane signal ambiguity:** The bipolar induction signals require sophisticated deconvolution; field response non-uniformities near wire solder joints degrade position resolution
- **Field cage resistor chains:** Current HV divider uses surface-mount resistors that occasionally fail at cold, causing field distortions

#### 3a. Replace Induction Planes with Pixel or Strips Charge Readout (LArPix)
- **Technology:** **LArPix v2b ASIC** (LBNL) — 64-channel self-triggering pixel readout ASICs bump-bonded to PCB tiles, pixel pitch 3.8 mm
- **Configuration:** Replace one or both induction wire planes per APA with LArPix tile arrays; retain collection wire plane for energy measurement
- **Specific component:** LArPix tiles on 0.5 mm FR4 PCB with gold-plated pads; power and readout via 100 Mbps UART daisy-chained to warm interface
- **Impact:** Eliminates signal ambiguity entirely on induction planes; provides **true 3D hit position** without reconstruction ambiguity; improves vertex resolution from ~5 mm to **~2 mm** for multi-track vertices

#### 3b. Field Cage Resistor Chain Replacement
- **Current:** Ohmite/Vishay through-hole resistors at 50 MΩ per segment
- **Upgrade:** Replace with **Cernox-graded thick-film resistor arrays** on alumina substrates (designed by CCI/Cryomech practice), or alternatively use **voltage divider chains fabricated on flex-PCB** (polyimide/Kapton with Ni-Cr resistive traces) rated to operate at 87K without TCR drift
- **Specific vendor:** Minco HK series flex heaters repurposed as resistive dividers; target TCR < 50 ppm/K between 87–300 K
- **Impact:** Eliminates ~3–5 mm spatial distortions near field cage edges observed in ProtoDUNE-SP space charge map; improves fiducial volume accuracy by ~2%

---

## 4. High Voltage System

### Current Limitation
The Heinzinger/Heinzmann HV feedthrough (Stainless-Kapton design) showed HV instability and current leakage events in ProtoDUNE-SP at −180 kV, limiting the nominal drift field to 500 V/cm rather than the design 1000 V/cm. Lower drift field → longer electron lifetime requirement → more space charge distortion.

### Proposed Upgrades

#### 4a. New Feedthrough Design: Tapered Polyethylene/UHMWPE Feedthrough
- **Technology:** Replace the Kapton-based coaxial feedthrough with a **solid UHMWPE (ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene) tapered feedthrough** with graded-permittivity field shaping rings, following ICARUS-T600 upgrade experience
- **Specific design:** Rogowski-profiled geometry, 1 m insertion length, rated to −300 kV, tested at 3× safety margin; metal shield electrode at LAr surface to prevent charging of gas phase
- **HV supply:** Replace with **iseg NHQ-226M** (200 kV, 2 mA, current-limited with trip-less ramp) combined with a passive RC filter (10 GΩ, 10 nF in LAr) to suppress noise injection onto detector
- **Impact:** Allows operation at full 1000 V/cm drift field, cutting electron transit time from ~2.25 ms to ~1.1 ms, reducing space charge accumulation by ~4× and improving spatial resolution in the drift direction

#### 4b. Space Charge Mitigation: UV Laser Calibration System Upgrade
- **Current:** 4 feedthroughs with Nd:YAG 4th harmonic (266 nm) laser
- **Upgrade:** Add **8 additional laser ports** with motorized mirror assemblies (Newport AG-M100N piezo actuators, cryogenic rated) to achieve full volume coverage; implement **photocathode ionization targets** (Au-coated quartz discs) for absolute E-field mapping
- **Specific addition:** Integrate a **cosmic ray tagger (CRT)** using plastic scintillator panels (BC-408, 5 cm thick, SiPM readout) around the cryostat exterior providing ~1 ns timing for through-going muon tracks — these serve as a complementary E-field calibration tool
- **Impact:** Reduces systematic on E-field non-uniformity from ~1.5% to <0.3%, directly improving calorimetric energy resolution

---

## 5. Data Acquisition and Triggering

### Current Limitation
The RCE/FELIX-based DAQ introduces ~10 µs latency jitter and the trigger system lacks sensitivity to diffuse low-energy signals.

### Proposed Upgrades

#### 5a. FELIX v2 + ATCA Platform
- **Technology:** Replace RCE modules with **FELIX (Front-End LInk eXchange) PCIe Gen4 cards** (ATLAS/DUNE collaboration design) hosted in ATCA shelves with Intel Xeon Scalable (Ice Lake) servers
- **Bandwidth:** 48× 10 Gbps optical links per FELIX card → 480 Gbps per shelf, sufficient for continuous full-stream readout
- **Impact:** Enables triggerless operation; all trigger decisions made offline on buffered data

#### 5b. Real-Time GPU-Based Trigger
- **Technology:** Deploy **NVIDIA A100 GPUs** (4× per DAQ server) running real-time wire signal processing: noise filtering (frequency-domain Wiener filter), hit finding, and primitive clustering at full rate
- **Algorithm:** Implement Hierarchical Trigger Primitive (HTP) algorithm in CUDA, providing 3D cluster energy sums within 100 µs of readout
- **Impact:** Enables online identification of SNB candidates, beam neutrino interactions, and radiological backgrounds; reduces storage requirement from ~10 PB/year to ~1 PB/year

---

|---|---|---|
| X-ARAPUCA supercells + VUV SiPMs | Light yield / timing | 5–10× PDE improvement |
| Cathode-mounted PDS | PDS uniformity | 2× geometric coverage |
