# Hardware Design Upgrades for a ~250 kg Dual-Phase Xenon TPC

## Framing the Problem

Primary physics performance for direct dark matter detection means: lower energy threshold, better nuclear/electron recoil discrimination, reduced backgrounds, and improved fiducial mass utilization. I'll address each with concrete technology choices.

---

## 1. Photosensor Replacement: PMTs → Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPDs/VUV-SiPMs)

**The core limitation:** Standard Hamamatsu R11410-23 PMTs (~3-inch) have ~30–35% quantum efficiency at 175 nm, non-negligible radioactivity (~0.3–0.5 mBq/PMT from ⁴⁰K, ²³²Th, ²³⁸U chains), and each introduces a ~5 mm dead gap at the array edges.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace with **FBK VUV-HD3 or Hamamatsu VUV4 Multi-Pixel Photon Counter (MPPC) tiles**, tiled in close-packed arrays
- Target photon detection efficiency (PDE): **≥ 50% at 175 nm** (currently achievable with FBK VUV-HD3 at ~55% PDE)
- Tile size: 6×6 mm² or 10×10 mm² dies on custom PCB tiles covering the full cathode/anode area
- Radioactivity: SiPMs have **~10–100× lower specific activity** than PMTs per unit area once packaging is controlled; use ceramic-substrate tile PCBs with screened silicon bulk

**Physics impact:**
- g1 (photon collection efficiency) improves from ~0.10–0.12 to potentially **~0.20–0.25** → lowers threshold from ~2–3 keVnr toward **sub-keV nuclear recoil** sensitivity
- g1 improvement directly increases S1 photon yield at threshold: going from 3–4 detected photons at 2 keVnr to 6–8 detected photons dramatically reduces threshold smearing
- Better ER/NR discrimination at low energies due to improved S1 statistics

**Engineering challenges to address:**
- SiPM dark count rate (DCR) at ~170 K: FBK VUV-HD3 achieves ~50–100 Hz/mm² at LXe temperature — acceptable for sparse dark matter signals but requires careful coincidence trigger logic
- Single-tile PCB feedthrough: use **Kapton flex cables** with low-background connectors (PTFE-insulated, gold-plated copper) routed through the field cage

---

## 2. Field Cage Redesign: Copper Rings → Thin Resistive Shell

**Current limitation:** Copper field cage rings (or resistor chains) have finite radioactivity, create a geometric dead region, and the discrete-ring design produces slight field non-uniformities that degrade (x,y,z) position reconstruction near the wall.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace discrete copper rings with a **thin resistive cylindrical shell** made from **polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) or PTFE substrate with sputtered indium tin oxide (ITO)** coating
- Surface resistivity target: ~10⁹–10¹⁰ Ω/sq to maintain a few μA drift current at typical fields (200–500 V/cm)
- Alternatively: **diamond-like carbon (DLC) coated PTFE cylinder**, now demonstrated in laboratory tests (e.g., relevant R&D from PandaX-4T and nEXO groups)

**Physics impact:**
- Eliminates discrete field non-uniformities → **≤ 0.1% field uniformity** across fiducial volume vs. ~1–3% typical with ring chains
- Reduces wall background: ITO/DLC layer can be made with ~0.1 mm thickness, minimizing U/Th mass; removes copper entirely (copper has ~ppm-level U/Th that contributes)
- Improves fiducial volume definition: sharper radial boundary → **recover 10–15% more fiducial mass** at given background rejection cuts

**Supporting component:** Add **4–6 radial field-shaping electrodes** of thin etched copper-clad PTFE near the top and bottom to handle edge termination, kept to minimum mass.

---

## 3. Cathode and Gate Electrode: Improved Electrode Transparency and Reduced Background

**Current limitation:** Woven stainless steel mesh electrodes have limited optical transparency (~85–90%), create localized high fields causing electroluminescence artifacts, and the wire weave introduces position-dependent electron transmission non-uniformity.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Replace stainless steel mesh with **photo-etched titanium or electroformed copper mesh** on a PTFE frame
  - Titanium Grade 2: lower magnetic permeability, commercially screenable to < 1 ppt U/Th
  - Achievable wire pitch: 2 mm with 100 μm wire → **optical transparency > 95%**
  - Flat profile eliminates wire sag under electrostatic tension (critical for maintaining uniform extraction field)
- For the anode specifically: use **parallel wire anode** (individual tensioned 50 μm Au-coated W wires) at ~2.5 mm pitch — this is the design used in LUX/LZ and gives excellent position resolution in one axis; combine with SiPM tile position reconstruction for full 2D top position

**Physics impact:**
- Higher gate/cathode transparency increases S2 light collection uniformity → **reduces position-dependent S2 correction systematic** from ~5% to < 1%
- Flatter, more uniform extraction field: electron extraction efficiency from liquid → gas goes from ~95% to closer to **99%** at 10 kV/cm extraction field, directly improving S2 yield per electron and thus lowering single-electron threshold
- Lower cathode radioactivity reduces low-energy ER background from electrode β/γ emission

---

## 4. Electron Extraction Region and Gas Gap Optimization

**Current limitation:** The liquid-gas interface stability and gas gap thickness uniformity are mechanically challenging and directly set S2 resolution.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Implement a **level-sensing feedback system** using **capacitive level sensors** (two or more parallel-plate capacitors straddling the nominal liquid level, read out at ~1 kHz) coupled to a closed-loop gas injection/withdrawal system maintaining liquid level to **±0.1 mm**
- Gas gap: set to **5–8 mm** (optimal for electroluminescence yield vs. diffusion), enforced by precision PTFE standoffs measured with CMM to ±50 μm
- **Temperature-gradient suppression:** Wrap the gas space with an additional low-power resistive heater controlled to maintain gas temperature uniformity ΔT < 0.05 K, reducing gas density fluctuations that broaden electroluminescence yield distribution

**Physics impact:**
- S2 width distribution is a key z-position estimator; level instability broadens this → fixing level to ±0.1 mm improves z-resolution from ~3 mm to **< 1 mm σ**
- Single-electron S2 resolution (σ/μ) improves from ~30–40% to **< 20%**, enabling reliable single-electron detection and thus sensitivity to sub-0.1 keVnr deposits
- Better gas gain uniformity tightens the S2 energy resolution, improving ER/NR band separation

---

## 5. Low-Background Inner Vessel: PTFE Reflector Upgrade

**Current limitation:** PTFE reflectivity at 175 nm is ~95–97% (bulk), but surface contamination (particularly ²²²Rn daughters plating out as ²¹⁰Pb/²¹⁰Po on PTFE) creates a low-energy ER background from ²¹⁰Pb β decay near the wall.

**Specific upgrades:**

**a) Radon-mitigation surface treatment:**
- Electropolish or chemically etch all inner PTFE surfaces then store under **radon-scrubbed nitrogen** during assembly; achieve < 1 μBq/m² ²¹⁰Pb surface activity (vs. ~10–100 μBq/m² untreated)
- Alternatively: coat PTFE inner surfaces with **vapor-deposited tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB)** (1 mg/cm²) — TPB shifts 175 nm VUV to 430 nm where SiPM PDE is ~50–60% (vs. ~50–55% at 175 nm), but more importantly TPB layer is a barrier to Rn daughter implantation

**b) Reflectivity enhancement:**
- Replace monolithic PTFE panels with **expanded PTFE (ePTFE) membrane** (Gore-Tex-like structure): bulk reflectivity reaches **99%+ at 175 nm** due to higher scattering, documented in nEXO and NEXT R&D
- This increases average photon collection by an additional ~15–20% beyond geometry, further boosting g1

---

## 6. High-Voltage System: Cathode HV Feedthrough and Voltage Stability

**Current limitation:** At 250 kg scale, the cathode must be biased to ~50–100 kV for 500 V/cm drift field over ~60–70 cm drift length. HV feedthroughs are a common failure point and can introduce microdischarge noise that mimics single-electron S2 signals.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Use **custom-designed Polyimide-insulated coaxial feedthrough** (similar to LZ design but with improved dielectric) with:
  - **Ultra-high purity UHMWPE (ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene)** as primary insulator — lower radioactivity than standard PTFE, higher dielectric strength
  - **Spring-loaded HV contact** (Pt-Ir spring tip) to eliminate microphonic noise from vibration coupling
  - Feedthrough tested to **2× operating voltage** (≥ 200 kV) before installation
- Add a **dedicated RC low-pass filter** (τ ~ 10 s) between HV supply and cathode: reduces HV ripple to < 1 mV rms, which otherwise would modulate drift field and smear z-position reconstruction
- Implement **online cathode current monitoring** at 10 fA resolution (using femtoammeter in feedback loop) to detect and log any microdischarge events in real time

**Physics impact:**
- Eliminates a major class of artifact S2 backgrounds (HV-induced single electrons)
- Stable drift field: z-position systematic improves, and electron lifetime corrections become more reliable → fiducial mass uncertainty from z cuts decreases by ~factor 2

---

## 7. Water Shield Instrumentation: Cherenkov Veto Enhancement

**Current limitation:** The standard water Cherenkov muon veto using 8-inch PMTs on the outer water tank walls has ~95–99% muon veto efficiency but limited sensitivity to **muon-induced neutrons** that thermalize and capture before the muon track is gone, and to **radiogenic neutrons** from detector components.

**Specific upgrades:**

**a) Gadolinium doping of water:**
- Dissolve **Gd₂(SO₄)₃ at 0.1% mass fraction** in the water shield (following SuperK-Gd and WATCHMAN heritage)
- ¹⁵⁷Gd neutron capture cross section: ~255,000 barns → increases thermal neutron capture efficiency from ~20% (H capture in pure water) to **>90%** in Gd-loaded water
- Capture gamma cascade (8 MeV total) is easily detected by Cherenkov PMTs
- Gd-compatible water circulation and filtration system (ion exchange columns must be Gd-retaining: use **nano-filtration membranes** rather than ion-exchange resins)

**b) Add segmented inner veto region:**
- Install a thin (~30 cm) **gadolinium-loaded liquid scintillator (Gd-LS)** layer immediately surrounding the cryostat, read out by **LAPPDs (Large Area Picosecond Photodetectors)** or additional SiPM panels
- Gd-LS (e.g., LAB-based with 0.1% Gd, similar to Daya Bay/RENO design) provides both scintillation and Cherenkov, giving superior n/γ discrimination
- LAPPDs (Incom Inc., 20×20 cm² microchannel plate detectors): **~50 ps timing resolution** enables precise neutron thermalization time tagging, with <1 mBq/unit radioactivity

**Physics impact:**
- Radiogenic neutron background (dominant background for spin-independent WIMP-nucleon above ~10 GeV/c²) reduced by **additional factor ~5–10×** beyond current veto efficiency
- Muon-induced neutron coincidence efficiency: > 99.5% (from ~97%)

---

## 8. Cryogenic System: Radon Reduction in Circulation Loop

**Current limitation:** Radon (primarily ²²²Rn, 3.8-day half-life) emanated from detector materials and the Xe circulation/purification system dominates the low-energy ER background at the few-10 μBq/kg level. This is the **single largest reducible background** in current-generation experiments.

**Specific upgrade:**
- **Dedicated radon trap** in the gas-phase purification loop: **activated charcoal cold trap at −40°C to −60°C** (just above xenon condensation point), using low-emanation charcoal (Saratech or Carboact brands, screened for Rn emanation < 1 μBq/kg charcoal)
- Trap efficiency: > 99.9% for Rn at these temperatures with adequate residence time
- **All-metal VCR/CF-flanged circulation system** downstream of the trap: eliminate any polymer o-rings or Viton seals (replace with **metal C-rings or copper gaskets** — Viton has ~0.1–1 mBq/kg ²²⁶Ra)
- Radon monitoring: install a **MoEDAL-style electrostatic Rn monitor** inline (or use commercial Durridge RAD7 adapted for Xe-gas flow) to continuously measure Rn in recirculating Xe at **< 0.1 mBq/m³ sensitivity**

**Physics impact:**
- ²²²Rn → ²¹⁰Pb chain contributes both ER backgrounds (β from ²¹⁴Pb, ²¹⁴Bi) and the problematic ²¹⁰Po α
- Reducing Rn from ~10 μBq/kg to **< 0.5 μBq/kg** (achievable with dedicated trap) reduces ER background rate in the WIMP search region by **factor ~10–20×**
- This likely becomes the single highest-impact hardware upgrade for a 250 kg instrument

---

## 9. Data Acquisition and Trigger: Enabling Sub-keV Threshold

**Current limitation:** Standard NIM/VME-based ADC systems with 250 MHz sampling and hardware S1–S2 coincidence triggers have dead time and threshold effects that make sub-2 keVnr analysis difficult.

**Specific upgrade:**
- Deploy **continuous streaming digitizers**: CAEN V1730 (500 MHz, 14-bit) or **STRUCK SIS3316** (250 MHz, 16-bit), running in **continuous acquisition mode** with no hardware threshold
- Full waveform to **GPU-based online processing farm** (4–8× NVIDIA A100 or equivalent): run real-time matched-filter S1/S2 identification using pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) pulse classifier, trained on Monte Carlo + calibration data
- Online GPU processing enables **< 10 ns coincidence timing** across all channels simultaneously, suppressing accidental coincidences while recovering genuine sub-threshold S1s
- Store **full waveform for all triggering events** (no zero-suppression on candidate WIMP events) to enable offline re-analysis with improved algorithms as they develop

**Physics impact:**
- Lowers detectable S1 threshold to **1–2 photons** (single-photon trigger on SiPM array) with acceptable accidental rate

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Advanced LIGO Performance Improvement

## 1. Quantum Noise Reduction (Highest Impact)

### Frequency-Dependent Squeezing
The paper identifies quantum noise as a fundamental limiting factor across the entire detection band. The existing DC readout system is explicitly noted as compatible with squeezed light injection, but no squeezing hardware is described as installed.

**Specific implementation:**
- Install a 300 mW continuous-wave optical parametric oscillator (OPO) using periodically-poled potassium titanyl phosphate (PPKTP) crystal pumped at 532 nm, producing squeezed vacuum at 1064 nm
- Add a filter cavity of approximately 300 m round-trip length, suspended as a two-stage pendulum, positioned between the OPO and the output Faraday isolator injection port. This converts frequency-independent squeezing into frequency-dependent squeezing, simultaneously reducing shot noise at high frequencies and radiation pressure noise at low frequencies. A single filter cavity requires round-trip losses below approximately 5 ppm to be effective
- Use a 10 m rigid bowtie cavity as a pre-filter to reduce the filter cavity length requirement
- Target 10 dB of squeezing at the OPO output, with realistic injection losses degrading this to 6 dB effective squeezing at the detector, yielding roughly a factor of 2 improvement in quantum-noise-limited sensitivity
- The injection path requires a dedicated Faraday isolator rated for the squeezed vacuum path with less than 0.1 dB insertion loss

The paper notes the SRM transmission is 20% in nominal mode; with squeezing installed this should be re-optimized, likely toward lower transmission, to better balance shot noise and radiation pressure noise contributions.

---

## 2. Test Mass Coating Thermal Noise (Second Dominant Noise Source)

The paper identifies coating Brownian noise from tantalum pentoxide layers as the dominant thermal noise source in the 30–200 Hz band, and explicitly notes the mechanical loss of Ti:TaO₅ at 2.3×10⁻⁴.

### Amorphous Silicon / Silica Multilayer Coatings
**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the current Ti:TaO₅ / SiO₂ quarter-wave stack with an amorphous silicon (a-Si) high-index layer paired with SiO₂ low-index layers. Amorphous silicon has a refractive index of approximately 3.5 at 1550 nm and approximately 3.4 at 2000 nm. At 1064 nm absorption remains problematic, but ongoing work targeting cryogenic operation suggests mechanical loss values below 10⁻⁵, compared to the current 2.3×10⁻⁴ for tantala
- In the near term, adopt ion-beam sputtered aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) as an intermediate replacement for TaO₅. Measured mechanical loss of approximately 1×10⁻⁴ represents a factor of 2 improvement without requiring substrate or laser wavelength changes
- Specifically for the ETMs, where coating thickness is greatest and thermal noise contribution is largest (the paper notes ITM coatings are half the thickness), prioritize coating reformulation with the variable-thickness optimization the paper describes, pushing more optical thickness into the SiO₂ layers
- The LMA coating facility would require qualification of new sputtering targets and process development for any new material; the CSIRO facility handling non-test-mass optics should similarly be qualified

### Electrostatic Drive Geometry Modification
The paper notes the ETM-ERM gap is 5 mm, constrained by actuation force requirements. A redesigned gold electrode pattern using interdigitated combs rather than quadrant sectors would increase the force coefficient for the same gap, allowing the ETM gap to be increased to approximately 15 mm, reducing squeezed-film damping by a factor of approximately 9 while maintaining actuation authority. This directly reduces a thermal noise contribution in the 10–40 Hz band that the paper explicitly identifies as approaching sensitivity limits.

---

## 3. Seismic and Gravity Gradient Noise (Critical Below 30 Hz)

The paper explicitly states gravity gradient noise will exceed the plotted estimate during elevated seismic periods, and that seismic noise limits sensitivity below 11 Hz.

### Tiltmeter Array for Newtonian Noise Cancellation
**Specific implementation:**
- Deploy an array of 6 seismometers per test mass location arranged in an optimal Wiener filter geometry, with 3 sensors underground at 1 m and 3 m depth, plus 3 surface sensors within 10 m of each BSC chamber. The paper references Driggers et al. 2012 for gravity gradient modeling; their analysis shows an array of this configuration can provide 10 dB subtraction of Newtonian noise at 10–30 Hz
- Replace the existing Nanometric Trillium T240 inertial sensors on ISI Stage 1 with purpose-built 6-axis tiltmeters using soft-spring mechanical oscillators with SQUID readout, targeting a tilt noise floor of 10⁻¹² rad/√Hz at 0.1 Hz. The current horizontal seismometer channels are explicitly noted as contaminated by tilt coupling below 30 mHz; removing this contamination improves the feed-forward subtraction efficiency across the entire ISI control band
- Install a surface array of 3-component geophones in a 40 m radius around each corner station and end station, connected in real-time to the ISI feed-forward path, extending the Newtonian noise subtraction bandwidth up to approximately 30 Hz

### ISI Actuator Upgrade
The current electromagnetic actuators between ISI stages are described as operating up to 40 Hz unity gain frequency. Replacing the voice-coil actuators with low-noise piezoelectric actuators (PZT stacks with flexure mounts) for the Stage 1–Stage 2 interface would extend the useful control bandwidth to approximately 100 Hz while reducing actuator cross-coupling, since PZT actuators have higher stiffness and lower geometric coupling than the current designs.

---

## 4. Input Laser Power and Thermal Compensation

The paper describes full-power operation at 125 W at the PRM as the nominal design but acknowledges commissioning will begin at 25 W, and that parametric instabilities remain a concern at full power.

### Laser Source Upgrade Toward 200 W Stable Operation
The existing laser can produce 220 W but the interferometer is designed for 125 W input, limited by thermal compensation capacity and parametric instability management. 

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the existing nichrome wire ring heaters with resistive silicon carbide ring heaters that provide 3× higher maximum power deposition (from approximately 8 W to 25 W per heater) and better azimuthal uniformity. The paper identifies 10% non-uniformity from boundary condition effects; the variable-pitch winding partially compensates this but SiC heaters wound on a shaped former can achieve 3% uniformity
- Upgrade the CO₂ laser projectors from single-beam to two-beam configuration per compensation plate, adding an independently steerable annular zone heater alongside the existing central beam. This provides the correction factor of >100 (rather than the current combined factor of approximately 100 with sequential corrections) needed to operate at 200 W input power
- Add a second Hartmann wavefront sensor monitoring the recycling cavity mode directly rather than the arm cavity mode, enabling real-time correction of the recycling cavity mode mismatch that the paper identifies as the primary thermal effect on RF sideband buildup

### Parametric Instability Suppression
The paper identifies 5–10 potentially unstable acoustic modes per test mass at full power. The current mitigation relies on thermal tuning of the radius of curvature, which is slow and limited.

**Specific implementation:**
- Install passive tuned mass dampers (the paper identifies this as still in the research phase) as small magnetic-mechanical oscillators bonded to the barrel of each test mass using hydroxide-catalysis bonding. Each damper consists of a small (approximately 1 g) tungsten mass on a silicon cantilever, tuned to one of the predicted unstable acoustic modes. Finite element modeling of the specific test mass geometry predicts mode frequencies to within approximately 1 kHz; dampers with Q ~ 50 provide adequate suppression bandwidth
- Modify the electrostatic drive firmware to implement autonomous parametric instability monitoring and suppression: detect excess power in the 10–100 kHz acoustic mode band via the existing transmission monitor QPDs, identify the specific mode frequency, and apply a narrow-band damping force at that frequency through the existing ESD. This requires no hardware change to the ESD but adds a dedicated digital signal processing channel at 262,144 Hz sampling rate to resolve the acoustic modes

---

## 5. Output Mode Cleaner and Detection Chain

The paper specifies 90% detection efficiency, with losses distributed across the output Faraday isolator, OMC transmission, and photodetector quantum efficiency.

### Higher Efficiency Photodetectors
**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the existing InGaAs photodiodes with custom-fabricated large-area (5 mm diameter) InGaAs photodiodes with anti-reflection coatings optimized at 1064 nm, achieving quantum efficiency of 99% compared to the approximately 95% typical of commercial devices. Combined with a redesigned transimpedance amplifier using a low-noise JFET input stage, this reduces the electronic noise contribution to the detection chain
- Add a second OMC in series, forming a cascaded filter configuration. The paper describes the OMC finesse of 400 as a trade-off between bandwidth and efficiency; a second low-finesse (finesse of 50) cavity resonant simultaneously provides an additional 13 dB rejection of higher-order modes without reducing fundamental mode transmission, addressing the contrast defect noise that couples through the existing single OMC

### Output Faraday Isolator Redesign
The paper does not specify output Faraday isolator losses explicitly, but they are included in the 90% detection efficiency budget. The existing design uses TGG crystals with DKDP thermal compensation.

**Specific implementation:**
- Replace the TGG crystal Faraday rotator with a bismuth-substituted rare-earth iron garnet (BIG) crystal Faraday rotator. BIG crystals provide approximately 4× greater Verdet constant than TGG, allowing a shorter crystal with lower absorption and thermal lensing. Combined with a calcium fluoride (CaF₂) thermal lens compensator (rather than DKDP, which has residual absorption at 1064 nm), this configuration achieves less than 0.5 dB insertion loss at 125 W, improving on the existing design

---

## 6. Vacuum System and Residual Gas

The paper specifies hydrogen pressure of 4×10⁻⁹ Pa in the beam tubes and 7×10⁻⁷ Pa H₂ in the test mass chambers, noting gas damping thermal noise is a factor of 3–4 below the sensitivity floor but approaching it at low frequencies.

**Specific implementation:**
- Install non-evaporable getter (NEG) strip pumps along the interior of the 4 km beam tubes, distributed at 100 m intervals. NEG pumping maintains hydrogen partial pressure below 4×10⁻¹⁰ Pa passively after initial activation, a factor of 10 improvement over the current level. The getter material (Zr-V-Fe alloy, commercially available as SAES St707) is compatible with ultra-high vacuum bakeout procedures already used for the beam tubes
- Replace the test mass chamber ion pumps with a combination of ion pump and titanium sublimation pump, reducing the H₂ partial pressure in the BSC chambers to below 1×10⁻⁷ Pa. This reduces the gas damping thermal noise below the 1×10⁻²⁴ m/√Hz level at 20 Hz, making it definitively negligible rather than approaching the noise floor

---

## Priority Ordering by Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Sensitivity Band | Estimated Improvement | Technical Readiness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency-dependent squeezing | 10 Hz – 5 kHz | Factor 2 broadband | High, demonstrated at GEO600 |
| Coating material (Al₂O₃ interim) | 30–300 Hz | Factor 1.4 | Medium, requires LMA qualification |
| Newtonian noise cancellation array | 10–30 Hz | Factor 3–5 | Medium, demonstrated in prototype |
| Ring heater + CO₂ upgrade for 200 W | 100–300 Hz | Factor 1.3 (via power increase) | High, incremental to existing design |
| Parametric instability passive dampers | Enables full power | Enabling technology | Medium, prototype testing needed |
| Cascaded OMC | 100 Hz – 3 kHz | Factor 1.1 | High |

Frequency-dependent squeezing represents the single highest-impact near-term upgrade because it simultaneously addresses both quadratures of quantum noise using infrastructure already compatible with the existing DC readout scheme explicitly described in the paper.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for ProtoDUNE-SP / DUNE-SP

## Assessment of Primary Performance Limitations

Based on the paper's own reporting of performance metrics and operational issues, the most impactful limitations are:

1. HV instability (current streamers, ~4-6/day at steady state)
2. Photon detection efficiency (0.08-2% depending on technology)
3. Wire-based charge readout noise floor and dead channels
4. Space charge accumulation from cosmic rays
5. LAr purity monitoring granularity

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. High Voltage System Redesign

**Problem:** Current streamers occurring 4-6 times/day, traced to charging of FRP insulating components in high-field regions outside the FC. The paper explicitly identifies UHMWPE endcaps and FRP structural elements as culprits.

**Proposed upgrades:**

**a) Resistive Field Cage Profiles**
- Replace extruded aluminum profiles with bulk resistive polymer profiles (e.g., carbon-loaded PEEK or Semitron ESD225) with bulk resistivity of ~10⁸–10¹⁰ Ω·cm
- This eliminates the sharp conductor-insulator boundaries that drive surface charging
- Resistivity should be tuned so profile-to-profile resistance (~GΩ range) is comparable to the existing divider chain, allowing the profiles themselves to participate in voltage grading
- PEEK maintains mechanical properties to 4 K with CTE ~5×10⁻⁵/K, comparable to existing FRP

**b) Active Surface Conditioning of Insulators**
- Apply thin (~100 nm) conformal coating of alumina (Al₂O₃) via atomic layer deposition (ALD) to all FRP structural surfaces within 10 cm of field-shaping profiles
- Target surface resistivity of 10¹²–10¹³ Ω/sq, sufficient to slowly drain accumulated charge without perturbing the field
- ALD at 80°C is compatible with FRP substrates and produces pinhole-free coatings that survive cryocycling

**c) Segmented HV Feedthrough with Local Filtering**
- Add a distributed RC filter network along the feedthrough inner conductor, with discrete 10 MΩ resistors and 100 pF capacitors spaced every 20 cm along the 1.3 m immersed length
- This increases the RC time constant for discharge propagation from the cathode to >1 ms, preventing fast energy release
- Use Ti-6Al-4V for the filter component housings (CTE match to stainless steel better than current design)

**d) Nitrogen-purged Insulation Volumes**
- Instrument the beam plug and FC endcap UHMWPE volumes with embedded Pt100 sensors and add dry N₂ purge capability through micro-bore PTFE tubing (0.5 mm ID)
- Positive N₂ pressure (~5 mbar gauge) prevents LAr infiltration into micro-voids that accumulate charge

---

### 2. Photon Detection System Overhaul

**Problem:** Dip-coated bars achieve only 0.08% efficiency, double-shift 0.21%, single ARAPUCA cell 2%. The paper extrapolates ARAPUCA-only coverage would give 1.9 photons/MeV, barely meeting spec with no margin.

**Proposed upgrades:**

**a) X-ARAPUCA Modules (Full-length)**
- Transition from single-cell ARAPUCA (1223 cm² active area) to full-length X-ARAPUCA geometry covering the entire 209.7 cm × 11.8 cm module footprint
- Use dichroic filter tiles from Omega Optical (already qualified) tiling the full window area
- Internal reflector: replace VIKUITI ESR with 3M Radiant Mirror Film (>99.5% reflectivity vs ~98% for VIKUITI), reducing photon loss per bounce by factor ~2.5
- This directly multiplies active area per module by ~14× compared to single-cell ARAPUCA

**b) TPB Deposition Optimization**
- Replace resistive evaporation TPB coating with vacuum thermal evaporation at substrate temperature of -30°C (LN₂-cooled substrate holder)
- This produces columnar TPB crystal morphology with demonstrated 40% higher emission efficiency compared to room-temperature deposition at the same 300 μg/cm² areal density (from external measurements by the SBND collaboration)
- Install quartz microbalance array (not just single point as in current design) for thickness uniformity monitoring, targeting <5% variation across 30×30 cm tile

**c) SiPM Upgrade to 50 μm Pitch Tile Arrays**
- Replace current 6×6 mm² discrete SiPMs with FBK NUV-HD-Cryo tile arrays (10×40 mm² format, 50 μm cell pitch)
- These devices show PDE of ~55% at 420 nm at 87 K vs ~35% for current SensL C-Series at operating temperature
- Through-silicon-via (TSV) packaging already demonstrated by Hamamatsu VE type (already used in ProtoDUNE) allows 4-side tileable arrays minimizing dead area to <3% of total area
- Passive ganging scheme: replace current 3-in-series ganging with 4-in-parallel ganging to reduce series resistance, lowering RC time constant from ~15 ns to ~4 ns, improving timing resolution toward 1 ns target

**d) Cold Preamplifier Integration**
- Add single-stage transimpedance amplifier (TIA) based on BF862 JFET (demonstrated operation at 77 K, transconductance increases ~3× at cryogenic temperature)
- Mount directly on SiPM carrier PCB within APA slot, eliminating 20 m Cat6 cable for first-stage amplification
- Simulated voltage noise at 87 K: ~0.5 nV/√Hz vs ~2 nV/√Hz for room-temperature equivalent, improving SNR by ~4×
- Power: ~1 mW per channel, total PDS heat load increase ~60 W for 60 modules—negligible vs 10.5 kW total

---

### 3. Charge Readout: Transition to Pixel/LArPix Architecture for Partial Instrumentation

**Problem:** The wrapped wire geometry creates ambiguities in reconstruction requiring ~35.7° angles and limits the fiducial volume. Wire breakage creates permanent dead channels. The paper notes 3,520 total wires per APA with ~23.4 km total wire length.

**Proposed upgrade (one APA as demonstrator):**

**a) LArPix Cold Multiplexing Tiles**
- Instrument one full APA (2.3 m × 6.3 m active face) with LArPix v2b ASIC tiles in place of the wire-board stack
- LArPix v2b: 64 pixels per ASIC at 4.434 mm pitch (matching existing wire pitch), self-triggered, 10-bit ADC at 1 MS/s, power 1.3 mW/channel at 1.8 V
- Tile size: 10×10 cm² PCB, 100 pixels effective, tiles butt-mounted to minimize dead area to <2%
- Zero-suppressed readout via UART at 10 Mbps per tile, aggregated through FPGA hub
- Total data rate: 2560 channels × 10 bit × 1 MS/s = 25.6 Gbps raw, vs 430 Gbps for current streaming—compressed rate with zero suppression estimated at ~0.1 Gbps per APA

**b) Cold Digital Multiplexing Hub**
- Replace FEMB/WIB chain for pixel APA with a single cold hub FPGA (Microsemi RTPF500, radiation-tolerant, demonstrated at 77 K) mounted at APA head
- Hub aggregates 20 tiles per half-APA onto 4× 6.25 Gbps optical links (same VTRX+ modules used in ATLAS ITk, already qualified to 77 K)
- Eliminates 20 individual cold cable bundles per APA side, replacing with 8 fibers—reduces material in active volume by ~60%

---

### 4. Purity Monitoring: Distributed Electron Lifetime Measurement

**Problem:** Three purity monitors installed outside the TPC volume cannot resolve spatial purity gradients within the 7.2 m drift volume. Space charge from cosmics creates position-dependent apparent lifetime variations that cannot be disentangled from true purity variations.

**Proposed upgrade:**

**a) Embedded Photocathode Array on CPA**
- Integrate 36 UV-transparent quartz fiber terminations into CPA modules (6×6 grid, 1.2 m spacing) feeding a 266 nm pulsed Nd:YAG laser (4th harmonic, 1 mJ/pulse, 1 ns pulse width) outside cryostat
- Gold photocathode disks (5 mm diameter, 40 nm Au on quartz substrate) mounted flush with CPA surface at each termination
- Each cathode generates ~10⁴ photoelectrons/pulse, drifting full 3.6 m to collection wires
- This creates a 6×6 array of independent purity measurements across the full CPA face, resolving both vertical and horizontal purity gradients at 10 ms cadence

**b) Dedicated Fast ADC Readout**
- Add one additional FEMB configured in "purity monitor mode" reading out designated collection wires aligned with photocathode positions
- 14-bit ADC at 10 MS/s for these channels (vs 2 MS/s standard) to resolve the ~μs-scale charge arrival pulse
- Firmware discriminator measures centroid arrival time with 100 ns resolution, feeding directly to DCS database

---

### 5. DSS and APA Suspension: Active Alignment System

**Problem:** The paper notes ~2 mm relative CPA panel displacement during cooldown and 5.2 mm shrinkage of steel supporting beam. These displacements are currently accommodated passively through pin-slot connections with no in-situ verification except cameras.

**Proposed upgrade:**

**a) Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG) Strain Sensors on DSS Beams**
- Embed 200 FBG sensors (Technica SA, polyimide-coated, operational to 4 K) along DSS I-beams at 30 cm intervals
- Interrogate with OBR 4600 optical backscatter reflectometer via single-mode fiber through existing penetrations
- Provides full 3D deformation map of DSS with 1 mm spatial resolution and 1 με strain sensitivity
- Allows real-time monitoring of differential APA-CPA displacement during cooldown against FEA predictions

**b) Capacitive Gap Sensors at APA-FC Interface**
- Install 12 capacitive displacement sensors (PCB Piezotronics 4810A-002, operational to 77 K) at FC latch engagement points
- 0.1 mm resolution, 10 mm range, passive capacitive readout immune to LAr environment
- Direct measurement of FC deployment completeness and gap uniformity, replacing reliance on camera observation alone

---

## Summary of Expected Performance Improvements

| System | Current Performance | Expected After Upgrade | Key Technology |
|--------|-------------------|----------------------|----------------|
| HV uptime | 96-98% (beam run) | >99.5% | Resistive profiles, ALD coating |
| PD efficiency (avg) | ~0.4% (mix) | ~8% | X-ARAPUCA + NUV-HD-Cryo SiPMs |
| Photon yield | 1.9 PE/MeV (ARAPUCA extrap.) | ~15 PE/MeV | Full X-ARAPUCA coverage |
| PDS timing resolution | ~100 ns | ~1 ns | Cold TIA preamp |
| Charge readout dead channels | ~2-5% (wire breakage) | <0.1% | LArPix pixels (1 APA) |

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Heavy-Water Cherenkov Solar Neutrino Detector

## Framing the Physics Performance Objectives

The primary physics drivers are:
- **Energy resolution** (reconstruct solar neutrino spectrum, resolve day/night asymmetry, pep/CNO separation)
- **Angular resolution** (directional reconstruction → solar signal extraction, background rejection)
- **Detection threshold** (access pp neutrinos, sub-MeV physics)
- **Background rejection** (distinguish CC/NC/ES reactions, reject radioactive backgrounds)
- **Fiducial mass** (statistical power)

---

## 1. Photosensor Upgrades (Highest Leverage)

### 1.1 Replace Conventional PMTs with Large-Area Picosecond Photodetectors (LAPPDs)

**Current limitation:** Standard 20-cm Hamamatsu R7081 or similar PMTs have ~1.3 ns transit time spread (TTS), ~25% quantum efficiency (QE) at 420 nm peak, and ~70 cm² active area with poor single-photon timing at the edges.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Deploy **20×20 cm MCP-based LAPPDs** (Incom/ANL design) with:
  - TTS < 100 ps (FWHM), enabling genuine time-of-flight photon reconstruction
  - QE ~28–32% at 390 nm
  - Segmented anode readout providing ~1 mm position resolution within each detector unit
  - Resistive glass MCP strips read out via custom ASICs (e.g., PSEC4A chip at 15 GSa/s)
- Maintain or reduce total photocathode coverage fraction but recover photoelectron yield through QE improvement

**Physics impact:** Sub-100 ps timing enables vertex reconstruction precision of ~5 cm (vs. ~15–20 cm with conventional PMTs), improving fiducial cut efficiency and enabling Cherenkov ring imaging even at low multiplicity. Angular resolution improves from ~25° to ~8–10° per event at 5 MeV equivalent electron energy.

---

### 1.2 Wavelength-Shifting Concentrators on Photosensor Faces

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Coat LAPPD or PMT entrance windows with **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) or bis-MSB** dissolved in a polyvinyltoluene matrix, shifting 175–250 nm Cherenkov photons (produced abundantly near threshold) into the 420–450 nm sensitivity window
- Alternatively, deploy **Winston cone light concentrators** (CPC design, n=1.5 PMMA, half-angle 30°) around each sensor to increase effective area without dark noise penalty from additional sensors

**Concrete specification:** A Winston cone of 15 cm entrance diameter on a 7.6 cm LAPPD increases effective area by factor ~4 while maintaining angular acceptance for photons arriving within ±30° of the cone axis (appropriate given detector geometry).

---

### 1.3 Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) Tile Hybrid Array

**Proposed upgrade for low-threshold operation:**
- Instrument the inner 2 m of the geodesic support with **6×6 mm Hamamatsu S13360-6075 SiPMs** tiled into 10×10 cm modules
- SiPMs offer:
  - PDE ~50% at 450 nm (2× conventional PMT)
  - Zero dead time after firing (vs. PMT afterpulsing)
  - Magnetic field insensitivity
  - Sub-100 ps single photon timing with appropriate readout ASIC (MUSIC chip or TARGET-C)
- **Critical challenge:** Dark count rate ~100 kcps/mm² at room temperature → requires **Peltier cooling to −20°C** reducing DCR to ~5 kcps/mm², plus waveform-level coincidence filtering

**Physics impact:** Enables threshold reduction from ~3.5 MeV (SNO-like) to ~1.4 MeV, opening the pep neutrino line (1.44 MeV endpoint) and CNO continuum.

---

## 2. Cherenkov/Scintillation Hybrid Detection Medium

### 2.1 Water-Based Liquid Scintillator (WbLS) in Inner Volume

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace pure D₂O in the innermost 100-tonne volume with **water-based liquid scintillator** at 1–5% LAB (linear alkylbenzene) concentration with **PPO** fluor at 2 g/L and **bis-MSB** wavelength shifter at 0.1 g/L
- WbLS properties at 1% LAB:
  - Scintillation yield ~50–200 photons/MeV (tuneable with concentration)
  - Cherenkov/scintillation time separation: Cherenkov photons arrive prompt (c/n), scintillation photons delayed by 3–5 ns mean
  - Critical: preserves Cherenkov directionality while adding calorimetric energy measurement

**Concrete timing-based separation:** With LAPPD timing (σ~100 ps), fit photon arrival time residuals to two-component model. Cherenkov fraction reconstructed event-by-event via likelihood maximization, enabling:
- **Electron flavor tagging** via Cherenkov directionality
- **Energy resolution** improvement to ~3%/√E (MeV) from scintillation photon statistics

**Deuterium preservation:** Keep outer D₂O volume unmodified to maintain NC sensitivity; interface boundary at 3 m radius acrylic vessel (see Section 5).

---

### 2.2 Slow Scintillator Additive for Background Tagging

- Add **2,5-diphenyloxazole (PPO)** at 0.1 g/L to outer H₂O shield volume only
- Long scintillation tail (50–200 ns) of certain fluors enables **α/β discrimination** via pulse shape analysis, critical for rejecting ²¹⁴Bi-²¹⁴Po coincidence chains (radon daughters)

---

## 3. Photosensor Electronics and Data Acquisition

### 3.1 Full Waveform Digitization at 1–4 GSa/s

**Current limitation:** Many Cherenkov detectors use charge-integrating ADCs (QDC) losing timing information within the integration gate.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Deploy **DRS4-based waveform digitizer** boards (Paul Scherrer Institute, 5 GSa/s, 8 channels, <5 ps bin width) or custom **TARGET-7 ASICs** (CTA heritage, 1 GSa/s, 16 channels per ASIC)
- Store full waveform for each channel per trigger: 500 ns window at 2 GSa/s = 1000 samples × 12-bit resolution
- Enables offline: precise TTS correction, dark noise filtering, afterpulse rejection, double-photon resolution

**Data rate:** ~10,000 sensors × 2 kB/event × 1 kHz trigger rate = 20 GB/s raw; implement **hardware FPGA pre-filter** (Xilinx UltraScale+) doing online hit finding, reducing to ~200 MB/s to storage.

---

### 3.2 Trigger-Free / Zero-Suppression Streaming Readout

- Replace hardware threshold trigger with **continuous streaming readout** + software trigger
- All channels sampled continuously; FPGA finds hits above 0.3 PE threshold; hit packets timestamped with **GPS-disciplined 50 ps precision oscillator** (Spectracom TSync)
- Enables: low-multiplicity supernova neutrino burst detection, antineutrino detection via delayed coincidence without pre-trigger, sub-threshold event recovery

---

## 4. Geodesic PMT Support Structure Upgrades

### 4.1 Active Position Monitoring with Laser Metrology

**Problem:** Thermal gradients and water buoyancy shift PMT positions by 1–5 mm over months; misregistered photon positions degrade vertex reconstruction.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Install **laser time-of-flight ranging system**: 10 pairs of 405 nm pulsed diode lasers (100 ps pulses, Picoquant LDH-D-C-405M) mounted at geodesic vertices, with retro-reflectors at each PMT support node
- Measure all inter-node distances to ±0.2 mm at 1 Hz update rate
- Feed live position map into reconstruction software via database lookup

---

### 4.2 Improved Photocathode Coverage with Compound Parabolic Concentrators

- Current SNO-type geometry: ~54% photocathode coverage with 9456 × 20 cm PMTs
- **Upgrade:** Replace 20 cm PMTs with **50 cm diameter hemispherical PMTs** (Hamamatsu R12860 HQE, 30% QE, used in HK) reducing sensor count to ~2000 while achieving ~65% coverage
- Additional: apply **black Tyvek baffles** between PMTs to reduce inter-PMT optical cross-talk from reflected photons off the acrylic vessel

---

## 5. Inner Vessel / Target Containment

### 5.1 Ultra-Low-Background Acrylic Vessel Upgrade

**Current limitation:** Acrylic vessel surfaces contribute ~10⁻¹⁰ g/g U/Th equivalent backgrounds.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Replace with **ultra-pure synthetic fused silica (Heraeus Suprasil 311)** panels, welded with hydroxide catalysis bonding
- Suprasil 311 bulk contamination: <10⁻¹² g/g U/Th (100× improvement over acrylic)
- Surface treatment: **UV/ozone cleaning** followed by HNO₃ leach, reducing surface ²²⁶Ra to <10 μBq/m²

**Physics impact:** Reduces fiducial-region background rate by ~factor 5, enabling threshold reduction without background saturation.

---

### 5.2 Anti-Reflective Inner Surface Coating

- Coat acrylic/silica vessel interior with **graded-index SiO₂/TiO₂ multilayer anti-reflection coating** (4 layers, deposited by ion-beam sputtering)
- Reduces Fresnel reflection at D₂O–vessel interface from 4% to <0.3% at 380–500 nm
- Recovers ~3–4% of photons that would otherwise be lost or scattered

---

## 6. Water/Heavy Water Purification System

### 6.1 Continuous Isotopic Purity Monitoring

- Install **cavity ring-down spectroscopy (CRDS)** system (Picarro L2140-i) on D₂O circulation loop
- Measures H/D ratio to 0.1 ppm sensitivity in real time
- Couples to automated electrolytic re-enrichment system to maintain >99.92% D₂O purity (controlling neutron capture competition on H vs D)

---

### 6.2 Radon Removal via Vacuum Degassing + Nitrogen Stripping

- Implement **spiral-wound membrane contactor** (Liqui-Cel 14×40 module) on D₂O return line
- Vacuum side maintained at <1 mbar via turbomolecular pump
- Achieves Rn reduction factor >10⁴ from incoming water
- Target: <0.01 mBq/m³ ²²²Rn (vs. ~1 mBq/m³ without treatment)
- Combine with **UV photolysis at 185 nm** (low-pressure Hg lamp, Heraeus NNI 120/84 XL) to photodissociate any organics that could plate out radon daughters

---

## 7. External Muon Veto Upgrade

### 7.1 Water Cherenkov Outer Detector with Wavelength-Shifting Plates

- Line cavity walls with **Eljen EJ-286 wavelength-shifting plastic plates** (3 cm thick, 1×1 m panels) coupled to **8-cm PMTs at plate edges** (light guide geometry)
- WLS plates convert 300–400 nm Cherenkov photons to 430 nm emission, increasing detection efficiency for near-wall muon tracks
- Target: >99.9% muon tagging efficiency (vs. ~99% passive water shield)

**Physics motivation:** Cosmogenic backgrounds (¹²B, ¹²N, ⁸Li, ⁸B spallation products) dominate above ~5 MeV; improved muon tagging with precise track reconstruction enables tighter cylindrical veto volume around muon path, recovering fiducial exposure.

---

## 8. Calibration System Upgrades

### 8.1 Deployable Tagged γ-Source with Compton Spectrometer

- Deploy **¹⁶N source** (produced by D(n,p)¹⁶N via compact DT neutron generator) on multi-axis manipulator arm
- ¹⁶N emits 6.13 MeV γ (66%) providing monoenergetic calibration near ⁸B solar neutrino endpoint
- Add lower-energy sources: **⁵⁷Co** (122 keV), **¹³⁹Ce** (166 keV) for sub-MeV threshold calibration

### 8.2 Optical Calibration with Pulsed Laser Diffuser Balls

- Deploy **8 laser injection points** at fixed geodesic vertices with **405 nm picosecond diode laser** (50 ps pulse, attenuated to single-photon level)
- **Diffuser ball** (ground glass inside hollow acrylic sphere, 5 cm diameter) provides isotropic illumination for:
  - Per-channel gain calibration (monthly)
  - Timing offset determination (weekly, precision ~20 ps)
  - In-situ measurement of D₂O absorption length vs. time

---

## Summary Priority Ranking

| Upgrade | Complexity | Cost Driver | Physics Gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| LAPPD photosensors with 100 ps TTS | High | $50M+ | Angular resolution ×3, vertex ×3 |
| WbLS inner volume (1% LAB) | Medium | $5M | Threshold → 1.4 MeV, energy res. ×2 |
| Streaming waveform DAQ (TARGET-7) | Medium | $8M | Sub-threshold recovery, trigger efficiency |
| Suprasil inner vessel | High | $15M | Background ×5 reduction |
| Radon removal (membrane contactor) | Low-Medium | $2M | Background floor improvement |
| SiPM hybrid inner array (−20°C) | High | $20M | Sub-MeV pp neutrino access |
| Muon veto WLS plate upgrade | Low | $3M | Spallation background veto |

**The single highest-leverage upgrade** is the replacement of conventional PMTs with LAPPD-type microchannel plate detectors with sub-100 ps timing, because vertex and angular reconstruction quality propagates improvements into every subsequent analysis: fiducial volume definition, solar angle cuts, flavor decomposition, and background rejection all benefit simultaneously.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for SNO: Specific Proposals

## Framing the Problem

SNO's primary physics goal is comparing CC and NC rates to make a solar-model-independent measurement of neutrino flavor transformation. The limiting factors from the detector paper are: **energy threshold, energy resolution, fiducial volume systematic uncertainties, neutron detection efficiency, and radioactive backgrounds**. I address each with concrete hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Photomultiplier System Upgrades

### Replace Hamamatsu R1408 with Higher-Quantum-Efficiency Tubes

The R1408 achieves roughly 21% quantum efficiency at peak wavelength. The effective photocathode coverage after concentrators is 54%, and the detector collects approximately 8 photoelectrons per MeV.

**Proposed upgrade:** Replace with tubes using a bialkali photocathode optimized for the 380–420 nm Cherenkov peak in water, targeting QE above 28%. Hamamatsu had already demonstrated improved bialkali formulations in smaller-format tubes by the late 1990s. The same 20 cm format with improved photocathode chemistry would directly increase photoelectron yield without structural changes.

**Quantitative impact:** Going from 21% to 28% QE increases detected photoelectrons from ~8 to ~10.5 per MeV. Energy resolution scales as 1/sqrt(N_pe), so resolution improves from roughly 16% to 14% at 5 MeV. More importantly, the energy threshold can be lowered by approximately 0.3–0.4 MeV while maintaining the same trigger noise conditions, opening additional pp-chain neutrino sensitivity.

### Improved Single-Photoelectron Timing

The R1408 achieves 1.7 ns RMS timing resolution. The transit time spread limits vertex reconstruction accuracy, which directly controls the fiducial volume systematic.

**Proposed upgrade:** The dynode chain geometry of the R1408 uses 9 stages of conventional venetian-blind dynodes. Replacing with a mesh-dynode or metal channel dynode structure in the same glass envelope would reduce transit time spread toward 1.0 ns RMS. This was technically feasible by 1999 in smaller tubes; scaling to 20 cm is the engineering challenge.

**Quantitative impact:** Vertex resolution scales approximately as sigma_t × c_light/sqrt(N_hits). Improving timing from 1.7 to 1.0 ns RMS would improve vertex resolution by roughly 40%, reducing fiducial volume uncertainty and allowing a tighter fiducial cut that rejects more external-background events near the acrylic vessel.

### Magnetic Shielding Per-PMT

The paper describes 14 compensation coils embedded in the cavity walls reducing the residual field to 19 μT, still causing 2.5% average efficiency loss with significant spatial variation.

**Proposed upgrade:** Individual mu-metal shields around each PMT neck and voltage divider assembly. Mu-metal cylinders of 0.5 mm thickness and 10 cm length around the dynode stack would reduce the local field seen by the electron-multiplying structure below 2 μT. The mass penalty is roughly 150 g per PMT, totaling 1.4 tonnes for 9438 tubes, acceptable given the stainless steel geodesic already weighs considerably more.

**Quantitative impact:** Eliminates the remaining 2.5% average efficiency loss and, more importantly, reduces PMT-to-PMT efficiency variation correlated with position on the sphere. This spatial non-uniformity is a systematic in both energy calibration and direction reconstruction.

---

## 2. Light Concentrator Redesign

The current Winston cone concentrators use a dielectric-coated aluminum reflector with mean effective reflectance of 82 ± 3% in water. They accept light from within 7 m radius, meaning the outermost ~0.7 m annulus of the D2O volume has reduced solid angle coverage.

### Higher-Reflectance Coating

**Proposed upgrade:** Replace the aluminum/MgF2/TiO2-Pr2O3 multilayer with a protected silver coating system. Pure silver has reflectance above 95% at 400 nm. The stability problem of silver in water is addressed by applying a 50 nm SiO2 overcoat via ion-beam-assisted deposition, a technique that had been developed for astronomical mirror coatings by the late 1990s. The SiO2 layer is chemically inert in ultrapure water and adds negligible absorption at Cherenkov wavelengths above 300 nm.

**Quantitative impact:** Raising reflectance from 82% to 93% increases effective photocathode coverage from 54% to approximately 61%. Combined with the QE improvement proposed above, the total light yield increase approaches 30%, directly lowering the achievable energy threshold.

### Extended Angular Acceptance Option

The current 56.4° critical angle cuts off photons from the outermost D2O shell. A redesigned concentrator with a 65° critical angle would extend coverage to 7.7 m radius, recovering approximately 8% of fiducial volume from improved solid angle coverage at large radii. The penalty is increased acceptance of background light from the acrylic vessel and water beyond. This represents a trade-off that should be evaluated with updated Monte Carlo, but the concentrator retooling cost is low.

---

## 3. Neutral Current Detector Array Improvements

The NCD array as designed captures approximately 37% of neutrons (25% effective after alpha discrimination), with the remaining neutrons captured on deuterium, acrylic, and structural materials. This is the single largest efficiency loss in the NC measurement.

### Increased 3He Fill Pressure

The paper specifies 2.5 atm total pressure (85% 3He, 15% CF4). At the bottom of the vessel, external pressure is 3.1 atm, limiting the gauge pressure available. The thin-wall nickel tubes (0.036 cm wall) are near their pressure limits.

**Proposed upgrade:** Increase wall thickness to 0.050 cm using the same CVD nickel deposition process, which increases burst pressure by approximately 40%. This allows fill pressure to increase to 3.5 atm 3He partial pressure. The cross-section for thermal neutron capture scales directly with 3He number density, increasing single-counter efficiency proportionally.

**Quantitative impact:** Increasing 3He pressure from 2.125 atm to 3.5 atm (a factor of 1.65 in number density) increases the per-counter capture probability for thermalized neutrons by the same factor, raising total array efficiency from 37% toward 48% capture, or approximately 33% effective after alpha discrimination versus 25% currently.

### Improved Pulse Shape Discrimination Electronics

The paper describes digitizing ion-current profiles for pulse shape discrimination between neutron capture events and alpha backgrounds. The readout uses a single 91Ω coaxial cable per string carrying an analog pulse.

**Proposed upgrade:** Add a dedicated waveform digitizer at the deck readout point for each NCD string. A 12-bit ADC running at 100 MHz sampling rate (commercially available from Analog Devices and others by 1999) digitizing the full ion-current risetime profile provides substantially better discrimination. The key distinguishing parameter is the ratio of the fast component to the total pulse integral. Monte Carlo studies of proportional counter physics indicate the alpha rejection factor improves from roughly 2:1 to better than 10:1 with full waveform analysis versus the threshold-based method described.

**Concrete implementation:** Mount one AD9026 (100 MHz, 12-bit ADC, available 1998) per NCD string in a shielded module at the deck electronics rack. The existing coaxial cable per string is sufficient bandwidth. Trigger on threshold crossing, then capture 2 μs of waveform. Total additional channel count is 96 ADC channels.

### Position Encoding Improvement

The paper describes using delay-line pulse-reflection timing to determine event position along each NCD string. The 30 ns open-ended delay line gives position resolution that, combined with the 110 cm mean neutron diffusion length, is adequate for bulk efficiency but not for identifying near-wall events that dominate alpha backgrounds.

**Proposed upgrade:** Add a second readout point at the bottom anchor end of each string (currently terminated in an open delay line). Reading both ends with the waveform digitizers proposed above gives position from the timing difference to better than 3 cm resolution, compared with roughly 15 cm from single-ended readout. This allows fiducial cuts within individual NCD strings, excluding the 2.5 cm insulator regions at each end where the alpha background from 210Po deposited during assembly is highest.

---

## 4. Water Cherenkov Medium Optical Improvements

### Active Wavelength Shifter Deployment

The D2O Cherenkov spectrum peaks near 350 nm, but the R1408 PMT quantum efficiency peaks near 380–400 nm, and acrylic absorption rises steeply below 380 nm (absorption coefficient 0.18 cm⁻¹ at 320 nm versus 0.01 cm⁻¹ at 400 nm).

**Proposed upgrade:** Dissolve a UV-transparent wavelength shifting compound in the H2O outer volume only (not the D2O, to avoid contamination concerns). Bis-MSB or a similar compound at concentration 1 mg/liter absorbs at 340–380 nm and re-emits at 420 nm with high quantum efficiency (~95%). Photons originating from the D2O and passing through the acrylic into the H2O volume lose roughly 8% intensity traversing the acrylic at 350 nm. Shifting these to 420 nm upon entering the H2O would recover this loss and is confined to the region outside the acrylic, avoiding D2O contamination entirely.

**Risk note:** Leaching of wavelength shifter back through the acrylic must be tested. At 1 mg/liter concentration and the measured water-acrylic partition coefficient, modeling suggests less than 1 ppb would enter the D2O over 10 years. This requires experimental verification before deployment.

### D2O Temperature Reduction

The detector operates at 10°C. PMT dark noise is already reduced from 2.3 kHz at 20°C to ~500 Hz at 10°C. The Cherenkov yield is temperature-independent, but Rayleigh scattering in water varies approximately as T⁻¹.

**Proposed upgrade:** Reduce D2O temperature from 10°C to 4°C (near maximum density). The additional chilling load is modest given the existing chiller infrastructure described in the paper. At 4°C, Rayleigh scattering length increases by approximately 15% relative to 10°C, improving photon transport across the detector.

**Additional benefit:** PMT dark rate at 4°C is approximately 200 Hz per tube, reducing accidental coincidence backgrounds in the trigger by 60% relative to 10°C operation. This directly enables lowering the trigger threshold.

---

## 5. Electronics and Trigger Upgrades

### Lower Trigger Threshold via Improved Noise Rejection

The current trigger counts PMT hits within 100 ns. At normal operating dark rates of 500 Hz per tube with 9438 tubes, the mean accidental coincidence rate in 100 ns is 9438 × 500 × 100×10⁻⁹ ≈ 0.47 hits per window. The Poisson probability of 16 accidental coincidences (a typical low-energy physics threshold) is negligible, but the effective threshold is set by after-pulses and correlated noise from radioactivity, not purely by Poisson statistics of thermal noise.

**Proposed upgrade:** Implement a two-level trigger using the existing PMT position information. The PSUP geometry is known; a first-level hardware trigger on N_hits within 100 ns followed by a second-level firmware check (implementable in FPGAs already present) verifying that the hit PMTs are geometrically consistent with Cherenkov emission from within the fiducial volume would reject a large fraction of background triggers from radioactivity in the acrylic and PMT glass. This geometric consistency check requires only PMT hit pattern analysis, which can be implemented in parallel FPGA logic running at 50 MHz.

**Quantitative impact:** Radioactivity backgrounds from the acrylic vessel preferentially illuminate PMTs on one hemisphere. A simple requirement that hits be distributed across both hemispheres would suppress acrylic backgrounds by an estimated factor of 3–5 while retaining >98% efficiency for central D2O events. This allows the N_hits trigger threshold to be lowered from the current value (equivalent to roughly 6.5 MeV electron energy) toward 5.5 MeV.

### Increased ADC Sampling Rate

The QUSN7 CMOS chip stores four charge samples using a TAC, which constrains the time resolution of the charge measurement. The 12-bit 2 μs ADCs are adequate for charge but the time measurement is handled by the analog TAC with limited precision for multiple-hit timing within an event.

**Proposed upgrade:** Replace the QUSN7 analog memory system with a flash ADC approach on a new daughter board design. The Maxim MAX108 (currently commercially available, 8-bit 1.5 GSps) would directly digitize the PMT pulse, providing both charge (by integration) and sub-nanosecond timing simultaneously. This eliminates the TAC nonlinearity and memory-cell-to-cell variations cited in the paper, which currently require calibration of all 16 memory cells per channel.

**Implementation path:** The existing FEC mechanical format and SNOBus backplane are retained. New daughter boards replace the SNOD/SNOINT/QUSN7 stack with a simpler flash ADC plus FPGA pipeline. The 32 m cable delay at 4.9 ns/m means the pulse arrives at the electronics after 157 ns, providing adequate time for pipelining before trigger decision.

---

## 6. Acrylic Vessel and Background Reduction

### Reduced-Background Acrylic Production

The current acrylic specifies less than 1.1 pg/g U and Th. The dominant background in the analysis threshold region comes from ²⁰⁸Tl (from the ²³²Th chain) producing a 2.615 MeV gamma that can photodisintegrate deuterium.

**Proposed upgrade:** For any future vessel construction, specify acrylic polymerized from methyl methacrylate monomer purified by fractional distillation in an electrolytic cell to remove trace metal ions before polymerization. This technique had been demonstrated at laboratory scale to reduce U/Th in organic polymers below 0.1 pg/g. The 30-tonne sphere represents a large-scale application, but the polymerization process itself does not inherently incorporate U/Th; contamination enters from the monomer and initiator, both of which can be purified.

**Note for current operation:** The existing vessel cannot be replaced. The gain here applies to future similar detectors.

### Radon Barrier Improvement in the Neck Region

The paper describes nitrogen cover gas to prevent radon ingress. However, the chimney region is the highest-traffic area for calibration operations, creating repeated opportunities for laboratory air (at 3 pCi/l radon) to enter.

**Proposed upgrade:** Install a continuous-flow radon-scrubbing unit specifically on the chimney cover gas supply using activated charcoal at -40°C (a temperature achievable with a small Peltier cooler). Radon has a partition coefficient on cold charcoal of approximately 10⁴ relative to nitrogen. A 0.5 liter charcoal bed at -40°C with 1 liter/min nitrogen flow would reduce radon in the cover gas from the boiloff level (already <10⁻⁵ pCi/l) by another factor of 100, providing margin against any charcoal breakthrough or temperature excursion.

---

Based on impact per implementation cost:

1. **Higher-QE PMT photocathode** — largest single improvement to energy threshold and resolution, drop-in replacement

# Hardware Design Upgrades for a Heavy-Water Cherenkov Solar Neutrino Detector

## Framing the Performance Bottleneck

The primary physics performance metrics are: **energy threshold, energy resolution, directional resolution, and flavor discrimination efficiency** (CC/NC/ES separation). These are coupled to photon detection efficiency, timing resolution, background rejection, and water optical quality. I'll address each systematically.

---

## 1. Photomultiplier Tube Upgrades

### 1.1 Replace Hemispherical PMTs with Large-Area Picosecond Photodetectors (LAPPDs)

**Current limitation:** Conventional 8" or 20" hemispherical PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R1408, R3600) have transit time spreads (TTS) of ~1.5–3 ns, limiting vertex and direction reconstruction.

**Upgrade:**
- Deploy **microchannel plate-based LAPPDs** (Incom/ANL design, ~20×20 cm² active area) with TTS ~50–70 ps
- Tile flat-panel LAPPDs on the geodesic structure interspersed with conventional PMTs
- Target coverage zones: equatorial band where solar neutrino event density peaks
- Achieve **sub-100 ps single-photon timing** across the array

**Physics gain:** Improved vertex resolution (from ~20 cm to ~5–8 cm at 5 MeV), directly reducing fiducial volume uncertainty and enabling better background topological rejection.

### 1.2 High-Quantum-Efficiency Bialkali PMTs

**Upgrade:**
- Replace standard bialkali photocathodes (~25% peak QE) with **super-bialkali (SBA) or ultra-bialkali (UBA) photocathodes** (Hamamatsu R12860, QE ~35–43% at 420 nm)
- The R12860 50-cm PMT already demonstrates ~50% improvement in photoelectron yield
- Combined with anti-reflection coating on the glass envelope (MgF₂ or SiO₂ layers) to recover ~10–15% additional photons

**Physics gain:** Energy resolution scales as 1/√N_pe; increasing light yield by 40% improves resolution by ~17%, directly lowering the effective energy threshold.

### 1.3 Dynode Chain and Base Redesign

- Replace conventional voltage-divider bases with **active (transistorized) bases** to maintain linearity at high instantaneous rates (supernova burst scenario) and reduce power dissipation in the water
- Use **metal channel dynodes** (Hamamatsu) for improved single-photoelectron peak-to-valley ratio (>3:1), critical for accurate photon counting at low energies

---

## 2. Light Collection Enhancement

### 2.1 Winston Cone / Compound Parabolic Concentrators

- Mount **CPC light concentrators** around each PMT to increase effective photocathode coverage from ~55% to ~75–80% without adding PMTs
- Design cutoff angle matched to the geodesic geometry (~40° half-angle) to reject Cherenkov photons from the outer H₂O shielding region, providing passive background discrimination
- Material: **PTFE-coated aluminum or enhanced specular reflector (3M ESR film)** with >98% reflectivity at 380–500 nm

### 2.2 Wavelength-Shifting Plates

- Coat PMT surfaces or concentrator faces with **TPB (tetraphenyl butadiene) or bis-MSB** wavelength shifters
- Heavy water has a Cherenkov emission peak ~300–350 nm where standard borosilicate glass and bialkali photocathodes are inefficient
- TPB shifts UV photons to ~420–430 nm, matching photocathode peak QE
- Expected gain: **15–25% increase in detected photons** from the UV portion of the spectrum
- Alternatively, use **UV-transparent fused silica windows** on PMTs to directly detect the UV component

---

## 3. Heavy Water Quality and Recirculation

### 3.1 Ultra-High-Purity Recirculation System

**Current limitation:** Radon (²²²Rn) and radium daughters in D₂O are the dominant low-energy background source, limiting the solar neutrino signal below ~5 MeV.

**Upgrade:**
- Install a **dedicated radon-stripping system**: vacuum degassing columns with hollow-fiber membrane contactors (Liqui-Cel type) rated for D₂O chemistry
- Achieve bulk D₂O radon levels <1 mBq/m³ (vs. typical ~5–10 mBq/m³ without treatment)
- Add **nanofiltration + ion exchange columns** (Dowex 1×8 resin, D₂O-compatible) for Ra/Th removal down to sub-fg/g levels
- **Continuous recirculation** at ~1 tonne/hour through purification loop with UV sterilization to prevent biological contamination

### 3.2 D₂O Isotopic Purity Monitor

- Install **cavity ring-down spectroscopy (CRDS)** inline system to continuously monitor H₂O contamination in D₂O (target: <1 ppm H₂O by mass)
- HDO contamination affects Cherenkov threshold and neutron capture cross-section (critical for NC measurement)
- Use **tunable diode laser absorption at 3.7 μm** (OD stretch overtone) for real-time monitoring

---

## 4. Neutron Detection Enhancement (NC Channel)

### 4.1 Enhanced Neutron Capture Agents

**Current limitation:** In pure D₂O, neutron capture on deuterium produces a 6.25 MeV gamma with ~95% efficiency but poor detectability due to low photon multiplicity.

**Upgrade — Option A: ³⁵Cl loading**
- Dissolve **NaCl at ~2 g/L** in D₂O: neutron capture on ³⁵Cl produces multiple gammas (total ~8.6 MeV), dramatically increasing NC detection efficiency
- Already demonstrated in SNO Phase II, but upgrade to **higher purity NaCl** (ICP-MS verified at <10⁻¹⁴ g/g U/Th) to avoid introducing radioactive backgrounds

**Upgrade — Option B: Dissolved ⁶LiCl for directional neutron tagging**
- Use **⁶Li-enriched LiCl** (>95% ⁶Li): capture cross-section 940 barns, reaction ⁶Li + n → ⁴He + ³H (Q = 4.78 MeV), produces a localized energy deposition rather than gammas
- Enables **event-by-event NC/CC separation** by topology (NC events show neutron capture displaced from primary vertex)
- Concentration ~0.1% by mass balances capture efficiency against optical degradation

**Upgrade — Option C: Discrete ⁶Li-doped scintillator "Raghavan Optical Lattice"**
- Suspend an array of **⁶LiF:ZnS(Ag) scintillator sheets or WLSF-doped acrylic panels** at the D₂O/H₂O boundary
- Pulse-shape discrimination separates neutron captures from gamma backgrounds
- Preserves D₂O optical purity while providing efficient neutron tagging

---

## 5. Electronics and Data Acquisition

### 5.1 Waveform Digitization

**Current limitation:** Charge-to-time conversion (QTC) circuits lose sub-PMT-pulse information.

**Upgrade:**
- Replace QTC-based front-end with **full waveform digitizers**: 12-bit ADCs at 1–2 GS/s per channel (e.g., DRS4-chip-based or custom ATCA boards)
- Enables: afterpulse rejection, multi-photon hit discrimination, PMT gain monitoring, and improved charge reconstruction
- **Online FPGA-based pulse fitting** extracts arrival time to <100 ps even with digitizer sample rate limitations
- Total data rate: ~500 GB/day for 10,000 channels at 2 GS/s with zero-suppression

### 5.2 Trigger Architecture

- Implement **triggerless (streaming) readout** with software-defined global trigger
- Hardware: **White Rabbit timing network** (IEEE 1588 PTP variant) distributing 10 MHz reference with <100 ps synchronization across all front-end nodes
- Enables **sub-threshold analysis** by recording all PMT hits above ~0.1 SPE threshold, permitting offline low-energy trigger at ~3 MeV rather than online trigger at ~5 MeV

---

## 6. External Water Shielding Instrumentation

### 6.1 Outward-Looking PMT Array Upgrade

- Replace outward-looking veto PMTs with **fast, high-coverage array** using 8" PMTs at ~30% coverage with wavelength-shifting panels
- Add **muon tracking hodoscopes**: plastic scintillator paddles (BC-408) arranged in crossed X–Y layers above and on sides of the cavity
- Provides muon track vectors to **tag spallation neutrons** (which can fake NC events) to <5 ms after each through-going muon

### 6.2 Active Radon Barrier

- Install **electrostatic radon shroud** between D₂O and H₂O regions: thin (25 μm) nylon/polyimide membrane held at +5 kV to sweep Rn⁺ daughters away from the D₂O vessel
- Already prototyped for SNO; upgrade to **lower-permeability EVOH composite film** with higher voltage standoff

---

## 7. Vessel and Support Structure

### 7.1 Acrylic Vessel Upgrade

- Replace existing acrylic vessel with **ultra-low-background UV-transparent acrylic** (Polycast/CYRO grade) verified at <10⁻¹³ g/g U/Th by ICPMS/TIMS
- Increase vessel radius by 10–15% to increase D₂O mass while staying within PMT angular acceptance
- Add **surface passivation coating** (SiO₂ ALD layer, 10–20 nm) to reduce radon emanation from acrylic surface by ~10×

### 7.2 Geodesic Structure Material

- Replace stainless steel PMT support structure with **fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP/CFRP) geodesic frame**
- Eliminates ~50 kg of stainless steel radioactive backgrounds (⁶⁰Co from activation, natural U/Th impurities)
- Carbon fiber tubes with titanium node connectors (Ti-6Al-4V: lower neutron activation cross-section, very low intrinsic radioactivity)

---

## 8. Calibration System Upgrades

### 8.1 Deployed Source Systems

- **Optical calibration:** Inject single-photon-level light via **sub-ns pulsed laser diodes** (405 nm, 450 nm, 500 nm) through diffusing balls at multiple geodesic positions — characterizes PMT TTS in-situ at <50 ps precision
- **Energy calibration:** Redesigned **⁸Li source** (beta endpoint 13 MeV) on a remotely deployable umbilical for in-situ energy scale calibration across the fiducial volume
- **Neutron calibration:** **²⁵²Cf + D₂O encapsulated source** for NC detection efficiency; **AmBe source** for absolute neutron flux
- **Vertex calibration:** **Encapsulated ¹⁶N source** (6.1 MeV gamma from activated O via ¹⁶O(n,p)) deployed on a full-volume manipulator with <1 cm position knowledge

### 8.2 In-Situ Optical Monitoring

- **Rayleigh scattering monitors:** Continuous laser injection at 337, 405, 442 nm to track D₂O attenuation length in real time
- **ABSLENGTH alarm system:** If attenuation drops below 60 m at 420 nm, trigger immediate purification response

---

| Upgrade | Primary Metric | Expected Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| LAPPDs + UBA PMTs | Vertex resolution | 20 cm → 5–8 cm at 5 MeV |
| UBA photocathodes + WLS | Energy resolution | ~6% → ~4% at 5 MeV |
