# Hardware Design Upgrades for IceCube Physics Performance

## Framing the Problem

The primary physics performance limitations identifiable from the paper are: photon detection efficiency (~25% QE with substantial angular dead zones), timing resolution (~1.2 ns array-level), waveform digitization dynamic range and deadtime, dark noise rates (~560 Hz dominated by glass scintillation), DOM angular acceptance (downward-facing single PMT), and hole ice optical uncertainty. I address each with specific hardware proposals.

---

## 1. Photon Detection: Replace PMT with Multi-PMT Configuration

### Problem
The Hamamatsu R7081-02 provides 25% peak QE (34% HQE), faces downward only, and loses ~4% of light to the mu-metal mesh. Angular acceptance is severely limited — the paper notes position-dependent efficiency dropping sharply away from the PMT axis (figure 19 shows efficiency falling from ~16% at center to near zero at edges). The single downward-facing geometry creates a known asymmetry in reconstruction of upgoing versus downgoing events.

### Proposed Upgrade: Multi-PMT Module

Replace the single 10" PMT with an array of 24–31 3" PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R12199-02 or equivalent) arranged to provide near-4π solid angle coverage within the same 13" pressure sphere. Specific implementation:

- **PMT type:** 3" metal channel dynode tubes, chosen because they have substantially higher QE (approaching 35% bialkali or higher with super-bialkali photocathodes), lower dark noise per unit photocathode area, and are operable without magnetic shielding at the 550 mG South Pole field due to their compact dynode geometry
- **Arrangement:** Geodesic tiling of the sphere interior, approximately 24 PMTs covering upper hemisphere and equatorial band plus 7 covering lower hemisphere — similar to the KM3NeT multi-PMT DOM design philosophy but adapted to the IceCube pressure sphere diameter
- **Total photocathode area:** 24 × π(3.8 cm)² ≈ 1,085 cm², compared to π(12.7 cm)² ≈ 507 cm² for the 10" tube, giving roughly 2× geometric area increase even before QE improvement
- **Effective photocathode area gain:** Combined with super-bialkali QE of ~35% versus 25% standard, yields approximately 2.8× improvement in detected photon rate for isotropic light
- **Magnetic shielding:** Eliminate the mu-metal cage entirely; the 3" PMTs tolerate 550 mG without measurable efficiency loss, recovering the ~4% photon loss and removing a mechanical complication

### Physics Impact
Isotropic angular response eliminates the dominant systematic uncertainty in shower energy reconstruction. The paper states 10% normalization uncertainty on DOM efficiency is the leading systematic in many analyses; improved and more uniform angular response directly reduces this. Cascade direction reconstruction, currently poor compared to tracks, benefits most because shower light is emitted quasi-isotropically.

---

## 2. Digitization: Replace ATWD with High-Speed ADC Architecture

### Problem
The ATWD architecture, while clever, has fundamental limitations the paper explicitly quantifies:
- Deadtime: median 6.6×10⁻⁵ for in-ice DOMs, rising to 3.2×10⁻³ for IceTop high-gain DOMs
- Two-chip alternation leaves a 50 ns re-arm gap during which a second pulse can launch the second chip but creates complex timing sequences
- 427 ns recording window misses extended pulses requiring fADC fallback
- 10-bit resolution at 300 Msps with only 128 samples per channel
- Separate fADC at 40 Msps with coarser amplitude resolution creates calibration seams visible in waveform reconstruction

### Proposed Upgrade: Continuous High-Speed ADC with Deep Buffer

Replace the ATWD+fADC combination with a single pipeline ADC architecture:

- **ADC chip:** 12-bit, 250 Msps pipeline ADC (e.g., Texas Instruments ADS5400 class or equivalent available in radiation-tolerant versions), continuously sampling
- **Buffer depth:** 16k samples deep circular buffer in FPGA BRAM, providing 64 µs of continuous recording at 250 Msps — 10× longer than the current fADC window without any mode switching
- **Gain ranging:** Two parallel ADC channels at different fixed gains (×16 and ×0.5) operating simultaneously and continuously, replacing the sequential ATWD channel scheme. A fast analog switch or resistive splitter feeds both channels; the higher-gain channel saturates on large pulses but the lower-gain channel remains linear. Waveform merging occurs in the FPGA rather than being an artifact of multi-launch deadtime
- **Zero deadtime:** Continuous sampling means no re-arm delays, no launch inhibit periods, and no missed pulses between back-to-back events. The paper's figure 7 showing 29.4 µs digitization deadtime per HLC hit is eliminated entirely
- **FPGA implementation:** A Xilinx Artix-7 or equivalent (low power, radiation-tested in similar environments) implements continuous data compression using lossless delta encoding identical to the current scheme, plus threshold-based windowed readout replacing the discriminator-launch architecture

### Calibration Simplification
Eliminating the ATWD removes the sample-dependent pedestal pattern correction (128 independent pedestals per chip per channel), the ATWD speed calibration quadratic fit, the inter-chip timing offset calibration, and the ATWD/fADC seam correction. The paper devotes significant discussion to droop correction and baseline instability propagated through these calibrations; a pipeline ADC with DC coupling (eliminating the toroid transformer) removes droop correction entirely.

### DC Coupling and Transformer Elimination
The toroid transformer (both old and new variants) is identified in the paper as a significant calibration complication, with temperature-dependent time constants and baseline shifts of up to 0.6 counts causing >2× charge measurement errors. Replace the AC-coupled toroid output stage with a DC-coupled transimpedance amplifier (TIA) front end:

- **Implementation:** A low-noise TIA with ~50 Ω input impedance, 1 GHz bandwidth, implemented with a GaAs or SiGe BJT input stage (e.g., similar to designs used in ATLAS pixel detector readout ASICs adapted for lower radiation environment)
- **Temperature compensation:** A single temperature coefficient resistor in the feedback network, calibrated once, replaces the complex two-time-constant droop model with its empirically determined parameters A, B, C, N, f
- **Linearity:** DC coupling extends linear dynamic range to DC, eliminating the undershoot artifact that makes charge integration unreliable for long pulses

---

## 3. Glass Pressure Sphere: Reduce Dark Noise at Source

### Problem
The paper identifies the glass pressure sphere as the dominant noise source, with ~250 Hz Poissonian component and ~280–340 Hz correlated component attributed to glass scintillation from ⁴⁰K decay and luminescence. At 560 Hz total, dark noise is ~22× the HLC hit rate from muons at depth and dominates trigger decisions for low-energy analyses.

The paper notes K₂O concentration of 0.03% by weight (~100 Bq per sphere) and suggests cerium as the active scintillator excited by radioactive decay.

### Proposed Upgrade: Ultra-Low-Background Synthetic Fused Silica Hemispheres

Replace borosilicate glass (Kopp Glass) with synthetic fused silica (SiO₂) hemispheres:

- **Material:** Synthetic fused silica such as Heraeus Suprasil 3001 or equivalent ultra-pure grade, which achieves U/Th concentrations below 0.1 ppb and K concentrations below detection limits (<10 ppb), compared to the ~0.03% K₂O (= 300 ppm K) in the current borosilicate glass
- **Expected noise reduction:** ⁴⁰K activity scales directly with potassium concentration. Reducing K from ~300 ppm to <0.01 ppm reduces this noise component by >4 orders of magnitude. The correlated luminescence component, if cerium-activated, is also eliminated as synthetic fused silica contains no rare earth impurities
- **Optical properties:** Synthetic fused silica transmits to 160 nm, far exceeding the current 315 nm cutoff of borosilicate glass. At 340 nm the current glass transmits only 50%; fused silica transmits >95%, recovering a spectral range where Cherenkov emission is significant and where the wavelength-shifting properties of the ice matter
- **Mechanical qualification:** Fused silica has been used in deep-ocean pressure housings; pressure rating to 690 bar is achievable with appropriate wall thickness (~12–14 mm versus current ~12.7 mm). Hermeticity is equivalent to borosilicate. The thermal expansion coefficient (0.55×10⁻⁶/K) is lower than borosilicate (~3.3×10⁻⁶/K), reducing thermal stress during freeze-in
- **Cost consideration:** Synthetic fused silica hemispheres at 13" diameter are expensive (~$3,000–5,000 per hemisphere versus ~$500 for borosilicate) but this cost is modest relative to total DOM production cost and deployment

### Physics Impact
Reducing dark noise from 560 Hz to an estimated ~50 Hz (residual from PMT thermionic emission alone) dramatically improves sensitivity to low-energy physics. The supernova detection sensitivity scales approximately as 1/√(noise rate) in the photon-counting regime; a 10× noise reduction improves supernova sensitivity by ~3×, extending detection range or improving significance at fixed distance. Low-energy neutrino oscillation studies in DeepCore, which are limited by noise-induced fake coincidences, benefit directly.

---

## 4. Timing System: Replace RAPCal with White Rabbit Protocol

### Problem
The paper reports RAPCal achieves 1.2 ns array-level timing accuracy, with individual measurements having 0.6 ns standard deviation (figure 17) and a 10 ns outlier rejection cut. RAPCal runs once per second per DOM, meaning DOM clock drift between calibrations is interpolated linearly. The 40 MHz DOM oscillator has stability of ~1×10⁻¹¹ over 5 seconds, which over 1 second gives a drift contribution of ~0.01 ns — not the limiting factor. The limiting factor is the bipolar pulse shape distortion in the dispersive cable (figure 16) and the 20 MHz sampling rate of the communications ADC used for fine-delay interpolation.

### Proposed Upgrade: White Rabbit Timing Protocol on Existing Copper Infrastructure

- **White Rabbit (WR):** A CERN-developed deterministic Ethernet-based timing protocol achieving sub-nanosecond synchronization, now commercially available in FPGA IP cores (Seven Solutions, CERN BE-CO). It uses Synchronous Ethernet (SyncE) for frequency distribution and a modified IEEE 1588 PTPv2 for phase alignment, with hardware timestamping at the physical layer
- **Implementation:** Replace the DOR card timing circuitry with a WR-capable interface. The existing twisted-pair copper infrastructure carries the WR protocol; the 720 kbps current bandwidth limit is a modulation choice, not a cable limitation — the cable supports frequencies well above 1 MHz (table 4 shows ≤20 dB attenuation at 1 MHz). Replacing the on-off keying modulation with OFDM or VDSL2-class modulation increases bandwidth to ~10 Mbps while maintaining signal integrity
- **DOM-side:** Replace the 40 MHz TCXO with a 125 MHz VCTXO phase-locked via WR to the surface master clock. WR achieves <100 ps synchronization on fiber; on copper with appropriate dispersion compensation, <500 ps is realistic, and the current RAPCal fine-delay interpolation concept is preserved but executed at 125 MHz (8 ns sample period) rather than 50 ns
- **GPS master clock:** Upgrade the Symmetricom ET6000 to a CSAC (Chip-Scale Atomic Clock, e.g., Microsemi SA.45s) disciplined GPS receiver. The CSAC provides holdover stability of <1 µs/day versus typical TCXO holdover of ~1 ms/day, important during GPS outage periods

### Physics Impact
Improving timing from 1.2 ns to <0.5 ns improves angular resolution for muon tracks. The paper states 0.6° angular resolution for muon tracks; since angular resolution scales roughly as σ_t / L where L is lever arm, halving timing uncertainty directly halves the contribution of timing to angular error. For point source searches, angular resolution improvement translates quadratically into sensitivity improvement at fixed event rate.

---

## 5. High Voltage Supply: Eliminate Gain Instability

### Problem
The paper reports ~12 DOMs showing abrupt SPE peak shifts of ≥0.05 PE, ~1% of DOMs showing >10% gain shift over 5 years, and gain calibration corrections of 3–5% needed between DOMCal runs. The high voltage generator (EMCO #9730A) has specified ripple <1 mV and stability <1 V_RMS, but the paper's identification of gain shifts correlated with MPE scaler rate changes suggests HV stability is not the only factor.

### Proposed Upgrade: Integrated ASIC High-Voltage Generator with On-DOM Feedback

- **Architecture:** Replace the discrete EMCO module with a custom HV ASIC implementing a charge-pump topology with on-chip bandgap reference and direct anode current feedback
- **Feedback bandwidth:** Current EMCO design has open-loop output regulation. A closed-loop design with 10 kHz feedback bandwidth maintains HV to ±0.1 V against load current changes (changing PMT gain in correlated noise bursts causes transient load changes that the slow EMCO regulation cannot follow)
- **PMT current monitoring:** Add a transimpedance integrator on the base board that measures instantaneous anode current and feeds back to the HV control loop on a 1 µs timescale. This eliminates the gain variation seen during high-rate correlated noise bursts
- **Digital control:** 16-bit DAC (versus implied 12-bit from the 0.5 V step size over 2047 V range) improves gain-setting resolution from 500 mV steps to ~30 mV steps, enabling finer operating point adjustment
- **Technology:** 0.35 µm HV CMOS process (e.g., AMS H35B) allows integration of both the HV generator (rated to 350V per stage, cascaded for 2000V output) and control logic on a single die. Total die area for this function is approximately 4 mm², fitting within the existing High Voltage Control Board footprint

---

## 6. Local Coincidence: Optical Fiber LC Signaling

### Problem
The paper describes LC signaling via dedicated wire pairs with configurable span (currently set to 2, i.e., nearest and next-to-nearest neighbor). The LC time window is ±1 µs. Failed DOMs break the LC chain; the paper lists 158 DOMs in non-standard LC configuration as a consequence. Wire pair failures also take out both DOMs sharing a communications pair.

### Proposed Upgrade: Optical Fiber Local Coincidence Bus

- **Implementation:** Add a thin (0.9 mm diameter) duplex optical fiber running alongside the main copper cable, terminated at each DOM breakout with a fiber optic transceiver (e.g., HFBR-1521Z transmitter / HFBR-2521Z receiver class, adapted for −40°C operation)
- **Protocol:** Replace pulse-code LC signaling with a simple serial packet (8-bit DOM address + timestamp, transmitted at 10 Mbps) allowing any DOM to signal any other DOM within reach of the fiber bus, not just nearest neighbors. This makes the LC span software-configurable to any distance without hardware changes
- **Failure isolation:** Optical coupling at each breakout uses passive tap couplers; a failed DOM does not interrupt the fiber bus because the fiber continues through the DOM breakout without an active relay. LC signaling continues along the full string regardless of individual DOM failures
- **Bandwidth for physics:** 10 Mbps fiber capacity supports not just LC flags but preliminary charge estimates, enabling a smarter hardware-level trigger that could perform a rough energy cut before full digitization, reducing unnecessary ATWD launches at high-rate periods

---

## Priority Ranking by Physics Impact

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Estimated Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-PMT module | 2.8× photon yield, isotropic response | Largest single improvement to all analyses |
| Ultra-pure fused silica sphere | ~10× dark noise reduction | Transformative for low-energy / supernova physics |
| Continuous ADC, DC coupling | Zero deadtime, eliminates droop calibration | Critical for high-rate IceTop and energetic events |
| WR timing | ~2× timing resolution improvement | Direct angular resolution gain for point sources |
| Integrated HV ASIC | Eliminates ~1% gain-unstable DOMs | Systematic reduction in energy calibration |
| Optical fiber LC | Topology-independent LC, failure-tolerant | Operational reliability, enables smarter triggering |

The multi-PMT module and fused silica sphere upgrades address the two largest physics-limiting factors identified directly in the paper — photon collection efficiency and dark noise — and should be prioritized for any next-generation deployment within the existing IceCube infrastructure or for IceCube-Gen2 string design.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for Advanced LIGO

## Framework for Evaluation

The paper identifies the fundamental noise floor as dominated by: quantum noise (shot noise and radiation pressure noise), coating Brownian thermal noise, suspension thermal noise, and seismic/gravity gradient noise. Upgrades must target these specifically. I will address each with concrete hardware proposals, constrained to technology credibly available or in late-stage development by 2015.

---

## 1. Quantum Noise Reduction

### 1.1 Squeezed Light Injection

The paper explicitly acknowledges DC readout compatibility with squeezed light (section 2.3, reference [10]) but does not implement it in the baseline design. This is the most immediately actionable upgrade.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Insert a squeezed vacuum source at the output Faraday isolator, injecting into the antisymmetric port
- Use a periodically-poled potassium titanyl phosphate (PPKTP) optical parametric oscillator (OPO) pumped at 532 nm as the squeezing source, achieving 10–15 dB of squeezing at the source
- The OPO cavity should be a bow-tie geometry with waist approximately 25 µm at the crystal, with the crystal temperature stabilized to millikelvin precision to maintain phase-matching
- Implement a filter cavity (approximately 16 m round-trip length, finesse ~5000) between the OPO and the output Faraday isolator to rotate the squeezing ellipse from amplitude squeezing to frequency-dependent squeezing, transitioning at the SQL frequency near 50 Hz
- The filter cavity mirrors require reflection losses below 5 ppm to preserve squeezing; this demands the same LMA-class coating quality as the test masses
- Use homodyne angle control via a feedback loop sensing the back-action noise floor to lock the squeezing angle optimally

**Expected gain:** 3 dB of broadband improvement is realistic given optical losses; 6 dB is achievable with sub-percent total loss budget. This directly improves the shot-noise-limited sensitivity above ~100 Hz and the radiation-pressure-limited region below, when frequency-dependent squeezing is applied.

### 1.2 Increased Arm Cavity Power

The design calls for 125 W input and 750 kW circulating, but parametric instabilities and thermal compensation limitations constrain full-power operation. The following addresses this:

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the current ITM anti-reflection coatings (specified at 50 ppm but delivered at 100–150 ppm per section 4.3) with coatings meeting the original 50 ppm specification; this directly reduces ghost beam power and scattered light coupling
- Upgrade the thermal compensation CO2 laser projectors to higher power (30 W instead of 15 W) with better spatial mode quality, using a CO2 fiber laser rather than a bulk CO2 system for improved pointing stability and noise
- Deploy electrostatic actuators on the end reaction masses with tighter (3 mm rather than 5 mm) gap uniformity tolerance, enabling more precise mode-by-mode parametric instability damping via feedback at acoustic frequencies (50–100 kHz)
- Install a ring of piezoelectric acoustic dampers directly on each test mass barrel surface, tuned to the 6–10 most dangerous parametric instability modes calculated for the as-built mirror geometry; use a lossy epoxy-free bonding technique compatible with ultra-high vacuum

---

## 2. Coating Thermal Noise Reduction

This is identified as the dominant noise source in the 30–300 Hz band. The coating mechanical loss of tantala (2.3×10⁻⁴) is the critical parameter.

### 2.1 Amorphous Silicon / Silica Coating Stack

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the Ti:Ta₂O₅ high-index layers with amorphous silicon (a-Si) deposited by ion-beam sputtering; a-Si has a refractive index of approximately 3.5 at 1064 nm, dramatically reducing the number of layers needed for a given reflectivity
- A quarter-wave stack with a-Si/SiO₂ requires approximately 8 layer pairs versus 19 for Ti:Ta₂O₅/SiO₂ to achieve the same reflectivity, reducing total coating thickness by more than a factor of 2
- The mechanical loss of a-Si is approximately 4×10⁻⁵ at room temperature, comparable to silica, giving a factor of ~5 reduction in coating Brownian noise power spectral density relative to the current tantala-based design
- Ion-beam sputtering deposition must be performed at elevated substrate temperature (200–300°C) to reduce absorption in the a-Si layers below 10 ppm, which is achievable in an upgraded LMA deposition system
- The coating design requires careful management of thermo-optic noise: a-Si has a large dn/dT (~1.5×10⁻⁴/K), so layer thicknesses must be optimized to achieve cancellation between thermoelastic and thermorefractive contributions, following the coherent noise calculation method of reference [16] in the paper
- Post-deposition annealing at 300°C for 24 hours in vacuum reduces absorption further and improves mechanical loss

**Expected gain:** Factor of 2–3 reduction in coating thermal noise amplitude, translating directly to sensitivity improvement in the 50–200 Hz band.

### 2.2 Larger Test Mass Beams

The paper notes the beam sizes are limited by aperture loss and mode stability. An incremental improvement is achievable:

**Concrete implementation:**
- Repolish the ETM substrates to increase the radius of curvature from 2245 m to approximately 2400 m, enlarging the ETM beam radius from 6.2 cm to 6.7 cm while keeping the g-parameter product within the nearly-concentric stability region (g₁g₂ < 1)
- This requires new ETM substrates (fused silica blanks are available from Heraeus) with the same Suprasil 312 specification, polished by the same super-polish plus ion-beam-figuring process described in section 4.3
- The ITM radius of curvature should be adjusted correspondingly to approximately 2050 m to maintain the arm cavity eigenmode
- Arm cavity baffle apertures must be enlarged from the current diameter (slightly larger than 34 cm test mass diameter) to accommodate the larger beam while maintaining scattered light trapping geometry

**Expected gain:** Coating thermal noise scales as 1/w (beam radius), so a 8% beam size increase gives approximately 8% reduction in coating noise amplitude.

---

## 3. Suspension Thermal Noise Reduction

### 3.1 Improved Fused Silica Fiber Geometry and Bonding

The paper reports violin mode Q of 1.1–1.6×10⁹ at the installed fibers; thermal noise improvement requires reducing the loss at the fiber-ear bond points, which dominate the suspension noise budget.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Redesign the fiber-to-ear weld profile using a CO2 laser with adaptive beam shaping (a spatial light modulator controlling the CO2 beam profile) to produce a more gradual taper at the neck, reducing the stress concentration at the weld by approximately 30%
- Increase fiber diameter in the central section from 400 µm to 420 µm to reduce thermoelastic noise contribution while keeping violin mode frequency above 500 Hz and vertical bounce mode below 10 Hz; this requires recalculation of the dilution factor
- Use hydroxide-catalysis bonding with a modified stoichiometry (higher KOH concentration, approximately 0.1 N) for the ear-to-test-mass bond to reduce the bond layer thickness from approximately 50 nm to 30 nm, directly reducing the mechanical loss contribution from this interface
- Implement annealing of the complete monolithic stage assembly (test mass plus penultimate mass with fibers attached) in a custom vacuum oven at 700°C for 12 hours to relieve residual stress introduced during fiber welding; this has been shown in prototype work to improve Q by factors of 1.5–2

**Expected gain:** Factor of 1.3–1.5 improvement in suspension thermal noise amplitude below 30 Hz.

### 3.2 Higher-Performance Blade Springs

The maraging steel blade springs in the suspension provide vertical isolation. Their creep noise is mentioned as a concern (reference [31]).

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace maraging steel blades with titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) blades of the same geometry; titanium has lower internal friction at the relevant stress levels and essentially zero magnetic susceptibility, eliminating a potential coupling path for magnetic field noise to suspension motion
- Apply a surface chemical treatment (electropolishing followed by anodization) to create a 2 µm oxide layer that reduces surface loss contribution
- Add a thin (0.5 mm) layer of silica aerogel acoustic damping material between the blade spring and its clamping structure to reduce resonant amplification of high-frequency (>100 Hz) blade modes without introducing noise in the gravitational wave band

---

## 4. Seismic and Gravity Gradient Noise

### 4.1 Improved Inertial Sensors for ISI Stage 2

The paper notes that the stage 2 GS13 geophones limit ISI performance at low frequencies. The GS13 self-noise floor is approximately 10⁻¹¹ m/√Hz at 1 Hz, which becomes the limiting factor for active isolation.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the six GS13 geophones on each BSC stage 2 platform with six custom-built, compact superconducting gravimeters or, more practically, with Nanometric Trillium Compact seismometers (already used at stage 1) — these have self-noise approximately 30 dB lower than GS13 at 0.1–1 Hz
- Alternatively, design a compact tiltmeter for each horizontal stage-2 sensor position to directly measure and subtract tilt-to-horizontal coupling, which the paper identifies as contaminating horizontal inertial sensors below 30 mHz; a suitable design uses a 1 m horizontal pendulum with optical lever readout achieving 10⁻¹⁰ rad/√Hz tilt sensitivity
- Upgrade the stage 1-to-stage 2 electromagnetic actuators from the current custom design to voice-coil actuators with 40 dB lower electrical noise floor, using ultra-low-noise current drivers based on precision resistor networks rather than op-amp-based designs

### 4.2 Gravity Gradient Noise Cancellation

The paper identifies Newtonian noise (gravity gradients) as a fundamental floor at low frequencies, potentially several times above the design curve during poor seismic conditions (reference [21]).

**Concrete implementation:**
- Install an array of 12 Streckeisen STS-2 broadband seismometers per test mass station, arranged in a 3D configuration: 4 on the surface at 3 m radius from the vacuum chamber, 4 at 1 m depth in boreholes, and 4 at 3 m depth in boreholes
- Use Wiener filter techniques to construct a real-time feedforward signal from the seismometer array that estimates the Newtonian force on each test mass; inject this signal as a feedforward correction to the test mass electrostatic actuators
- The physical borehole infrastructure requires core drilling at each test mass location; concrete-grouted borehole casings maintain coupling between sensor and ground
- Digital implementation requires low-latency (< 1 ms) signal processing; an FPGA-based Wiener filter computation running in parallel with the existing RCG system is suitable
- Achievable cancellation is 10–30 dB depending on seismic field homogeneity, pushing the effective Newtonian noise floor below the suspension thermal noise curve above 10 Hz

---

## 5. Output Optics and Readout

### 5.1 Higher Quantum Efficiency Photodetectors

The paper assumes 90% detection efficiency, with losses split among the output Faraday isolator, output mode cleaner, and photodetector quantum efficiency.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Replace the current InGaAs photodiodes at the OMC output with custom-grown, back-illuminated InGaAs photodiodes with anti-reflection coating optimized for 1064 nm, achieving quantum efficiency above 99% (compared to the 95–97% of standard devices); these are available from Laser Components GmbH and similar specialty suppliers
- Reduce OMC round-trip loss by replacing the current curved mirror coatings with a new coating run using the same a-Si/SiO₂ process proposed for the test masses (section 2.1 above), targeting loss below 20 ppm per mirror versus the current approximately 50 ppm
- Replace the output Faraday isolator TGG crystals with improved TGG crystals grown by the Czochralski method with lower iron contamination (< 0.1 ppm Fe), reducing absorption and thermal lensing by approximately 50% at 125 W; this is available from CASIX and similar suppliers

**Expected gain:** Improving total detection efficiency from 90% to 95% is equivalent to a 5% improvement in shot-noise-limited sensitivity, or equivalently allows 10% reduction in required circulating power for the same sensitivity.

### 5.2 Signal Recycling Mirror Transmission Optimization

The paper discusses the trade-off in SRM transmission (section 3.6) and notes the BNS-optimized mode requires different parameters.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Fabricate a second SRM substrate with transmission of 10% (versus the current 20%), allowing in-situ exchange during planned maintenance periods; this requires only a new coating run on an existing substrate geometry
- Design a motorized, in-vacuum SRM exchange mechanism using a translation stage with a maraging steel leadscrew and a stepper motor with magnetic shielding, allowing SRM replacement without breaking vacuum; the mechanism must achieve repositioning to within 1 µrad angular tolerance

---

## 6. Vacuum System Improvements

### 6.1 Lower Residual Gas Pressure

The paper quotes arm tube pressure of 4×10⁻⁹ Pa of hydrogen; further reduction directly reduces residual gas phase noise.

**Concrete implementation:**
- Install non-evaporable getter (NEG) strips (St707 alloy, Saes Getters) along the interior of the 4 km beam tubes; these can be activated by resistive heating to 350°C and provide distributed pumping speed of approximately 100 L/s per meter for hydrogen
- The NEG strips are mounted on ceramic standoffs at the tube inner wall outside the beam path, requiring internal access through the existing flanged sections; approximately 2000 m of NEG strip per arm is needed
- This can reduce hydrogen partial pressure by a factor of 10–100, pushing residual gas noise entirely below other noise floors

---

|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency-dependent squeezing | Quantum noise | 10–5000 Hz | Factor 1.5–2 broadband |
| a-Si/SiO₂ coatings | Coating thermal | 30–300 Hz | Factor 2–3 |
| Gravity gradient cancellation | Newtonian noise | 10–30 Hz | Factor 3–10 |
| Improved ISI inertial sensors | Seismic noise | 5–30 Hz | Factor 2–5 |

# Hardware Design Upgrades for SNO: Specific Proposals

## Framing the Problem

SNO's primary physics goal is measuring the CC/NC ratio to test neutrino flavor transformation. The limiting factors derivable from the paper are: photon detection efficiency (31% bare coverage, ~54% effective), energy threshold and resolution (~8 pe/MeV), radioactive backgrounds constraining fiducial volume, and neutron detection efficiency (37% with NCD array, or relying on chlorine capture). Upgrades should target these specific bottlenecks.

---

## 1. Photomultiplier Tubes

### Current Limitation
The Hamamatsu R1408 has 20 cm diameter with 1.7 ns RMS timing resolution. Bare photocathode coverage is 31%, boosted to ~54% effective with reflective concentrators that introduce 82% mean reflectance losses and restrict angular acceptance to a 7 m radius fiducial cone. Each PMT contains roughly 100 µg of Th+U in 850 g of glass.

### Proposed Upgrade: Large-Area Low-Radioactivity PMTs with Improved Timing

Replace R1408 tubes with a custom 25 cm hemispherical PMT built on a borosilicate formulation specifically optimized for lower radioactivity than Schott 8246. The specific target would be Th and U below 10 ppb rather than the 40 ppb achieved in 8246, requiring collaboration with Schott or Hamamatsu to reformulate the glass melt using higher-purity silica sand feedstock and a dedicated low-radioactivity furnace lining. This is technically achievable because the paper already demonstrates Schott retrofitted a furnace for SNO; a second generation would apply lessons learned.

The dynode structure should switch from the venetian-blind configuration implied by the R1408's nine-dynode design to a metal channel dynode stack as developed by Hamamatsu in their R5912 series work during the late 1990s. Metal channel dynodes provide sub-nanosecond single-photoelectron timing (approximately 0.8 ns RMS versus 1.7 ns) and significantly better peak-to-valley ratio (above 3:1 versus the 1.25 minimum specified) by reducing secondary emission spread. This directly improves vertex reconstruction precision, which sets the fiducial volume cut accuracy and hence the effective signal statistics.

The waterproof enclosure redesign should eliminate the TNC connector that caused breakdown problems in degassed water. A direct overmolded polyethylene boot with integral strain relief, as used in oceanographic instrumentation of the period, removes the connector geometry that concentrates electric fields. The silicone gel fill (GE RTV6196) is retained but the connector void is eliminated.

**Quantified benefit**: Improving timing from 1.7 ns to 0.8 ns RMS reduces vertex reconstruction uncertainty by roughly a factor of two, allowing a tighter fiducial volume cut or equivalently recovering signal events currently cut for background rejection. The radioactivity reduction from 40 ppb to 10 ppb in the glass reduces photodisintegration neutron background from PMT glass by approximately a factor of four, which the paper identifies as a dominant background source given 9438 tubes × 850 g × 40 ppb Th each.

---

## 2. Light Concentrators

### Current Limitation
The 18-piece aluminum reflector with MgF₂/TiO₂-PrO₂ dielectric coating achieves 82 ± 3% mean reflectance in water. The three-dimensional critical angle of 56.4° restricts the viewed fiducial radius to 7 m. The ABS plastic housing introduces material near the photocathode with limited documented radioactivity control.

### Proposed Upgrade: Winston Cone Geometry with Enhanced Dielectric Stack

Replace the current 18-piece approximated geometry with a single-piece spun aluminum Winston cone. Spinning rather than bending eliminates the 18 seams where coating adhesion is weakest and where the current geometry introduces angular acceptance discontinuities. The Winston cone profile is defined mathematically and can be machined on a CNC lathe to better than 50 µm surface figure, allowing the dielectric coating to be applied uniformly across a continuous surface.

The coating stack should be redesigned using four alternating quarter-wave layers of SiO₂ and TiO₂ rather than the current MgF₂/mixed oxide design. SiO₂/TiO₂ stacks were being optimized during this period for astronomical mirror coatings and achieve reflectance above 94% across 300–550 nm in air, translating to approximately 91% in water after accounting for the refractive index matching. This is achievable with standard physical vapor deposition equipment. The improvement from 82% to 91% in reflectance corresponds to a 11% increase in detected photons per event.

The ABS housing should be replaced with injection-molded PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene). PTFE has lower measured U and Th leaching than ABS, documented resistance to ultrapure water far exceeding ABS, and negligible biological growth support. The paper notes extensive accelerated aging was required for ABS precisely because its ultrapure water history was limited; PTFE has a 30-year history in ultrapure water semiconductor applications.

**Quantified benefit**: Going from 54% to approximately 60% effective coverage (conservative, accounting for geometry changes) increases detected photons per event proportionally, improving energy resolution as approximately 1/√N_pe. The current ~8 pe/MeV would increase to ~9 pe/MeV, reducing the energy threshold from roughly 5 MeV to below 4.5 MeV and increasing the detectable ⁸B neutrino flux by approximately 15% based on the shape of the ⁸B spectrum above 2 MeV.

---

## 3. Front-End Electronics and ASIC Chipset

### Current Limitation
The SNOD discriminator and SNOINT integrator chips are fabricated in AT&T's CBICU-2 bipolar process. The QUSN7 analog memory chip is in Northern Telecom CMOS4S. The 16-deep analog memory, 12-bit ADCs sampling at 2 µs cycle time, and the 400 ns per-channel deadtime are the binding constraints on timing precision and high-rate performance.

### Proposed Upgrade: Deep Analog Pipeline with Waveform Digitization

Replace the three-chip ASIC set with a two-chip solution: a fast discriminator-timer chip and a switched capacitor array (SCA) waveform sampler.

The SCA chip should be implemented in a 0.5 µm CMOS process (available commercially through MOSIS by the late 1990s) with 128 capacitor cells per channel sampling at 500 MHz (2 ns per cell), providing a 256 ns capture window. This replaces the single time measurement and three charge samples with a complete waveform from which time, charge, and pulse shape are all extractable offline. Switched capacitor arrays of this type were being developed for other HEP applications (the ORCA detector electronics program and several CERN R&D projects) during exactly this period, and the circuit topology was well understood.

The critical advantage beyond improved time precision is pulse-shape discrimination capability on every channel without dedicated hardware. The current NCD array requires separate signal cables and dedicated electronics to do pulse-shape discrimination against alpha backgrounds. With waveform digitization at the PMT level, the same capability is applied to the Cherenkov signal, enabling improved separation of single-electron Cherenkov events from multi-photon pile-up and from PMT after-pulsing, which the paper lists as a concern below 1.5%.

The 12-bit ADC on the FEC should be replaced with a 14-bit successive approximation ADC at the same 2 µs conversion speed, improving charge resolution and extending the dynamic range. The paper notes 49 PMTs have dynode taps for low-gain channels extending dynamic range by factor 100 for supernova bursts; with 14-bit charge measurement the number of special low-gain channels could be reduced.

The per-channel deadtime should be reduced from 400 ns to 200 ns by implementing a faster reset in the SCA readout state machine. The 400 ns figure was set to allow for light reflection across the detector volume (66 ns direct path maximum plus reflections). With improved vertex reconstruction from better timing, software rejection of reflected-light hits can substitute for the hardware deadtime margin, and 200 ns is adequate for direct-path photons.

**Quantified benefit**: Waveform digitization enables offline pulse-shape discrimination that the paper identifies as essential for the NCD array but which would also benefit PMT-level background rejection. Reducing per-channel deadtime from 400 ns to 200 ns halves the probability of missing a second photon hit in a high-multiplicity event, improving energy linearity at the upper end of the solar neutrino spectrum.

---

## 4. Neutral Current Detector Array

### Current Limitation
The nickel CVD tube proportional counters filled with 85% ³He/15% CF₄ at 2.5 atm achieve approximately 25% usable neutron detection efficiency (nominal 45% capture, reduced by alpha/neutron discrimination limitations). The 50 µm copper anode wire at gas gain 100 requires 1650 V. The 770 m total length deployed in 96 strings represents a substantial optical obscuration (~15% of uniformly generated photons absorbed).

### Proposed Upgrade: Increased ³He Pressure with Position-Sensitive Anode

Increase the ³He fill pressure from 2.5 atm to 4.0 atm while maintaining the same tube diameter. At 4 atm the ³He column stopping power for the 764 keV proton-triton pair from neutron capture increases, reducing the wall effect (wherein a reaction product strikes the tube wall before depositing its full energy). The paper specifically identifies the wall effect as forcing the operational efficiency down from 45% capture to 25% usable events. At 4 atm, the proton range in 85% ³He (approximately 5 cm at 2.5 atm for 573 keV proton) decreases proportionally to roughly 3 cm, and for a 5.08 cm diameter tube this substantially reduces wall-effect events. Monte Carlo calculations for similar tube geometries published in the NIM literature of the period suggest efficiency recovery to above 35% usable events is achievable.

The single 50 µm anode wire should be replaced with a resistive anode wire of approximately 1 MΩ/m impedance, fabricated from Ni-Cr alloy by Luma Metall or equivalent manufacturer. With a resistive anode, the position of a neutron capture event along the tube length is encoded in the charge division ratio between the two ends, measured by the existing delay-line technique but with improved resolution. The current design uses a 30 ns open-ended 415 Ω delay line at the tube bottom for pulse-reflection timing; resistive charge division provides continuous position measurement with approximately 1 cm resolution along the tube axis without any additional hardware beyond a second preamplifier per string. This position information enables fiducial volume cuts on the NCD data that are currently impossible, rejecting captures near the tube ends where the radioactivity from the nickel-to-fused-silica seals is concentrated.

The 91 Ω readout cable of specific gravity 0.955 (copper/polyethylene, South Bay Cable) should be replaced with a cable of specific gravity closer to 1.0 to reduce the buoyancy restoring force on the strings. The current cable specific gravity means the cable provides upward buoyancy, adding tension to the Vectran anchor cord and affecting string verticality. A coaxial design with a copper-clad steel center conductor and a foamed polyethylene dielectric achieves approximately 0.98 specific gravity while maintaining the electrical characteristics needed for the analog signal.

**Quantified benefit**: Increasing usable neutron detection efficiency from 25% to 35% represents a 40% improvement in NC event statistics. Given that the entire physics case of SNO depends on comparing the NC rate to the CC rate, and both rates have statistical uncertainties that propagate into the CC/NC ratio measurement, this improvement directly reduces the uncertainty on the primary result. For the expected rate of 13 NC neutrons per day, the improvement from 25% to 35% efficiency increases detected NC events from approximately 3.25/day to 4.55/day, reducing statistical uncertainty on the NC rate by approximately 16% for a given running time.

---

## 5. Water Purification: Radon Removal

### Current Limitation
The Process Degasser reduces radon by a factor of approximately 50. The paper identifies radon from laboratory air (3 pCi/L) and from the cavity liner as a potentially serious background, requiring the nitrogen cover gas system. The design maximum of 12 radon atoms/m²/hour from the cavity walls represents a continuing ingress that the cover gas system manages but does not eliminate.

### Proposed Upgrade: Online Radon Extraction Loop with Activated Charcoal Cold Trap

Add a dedicated radon extraction circuit to the D₂O recirculation loop consisting of a membrane degasser optimized for radon (higher membrane surface area per unit volume than the current PD design) followed by a two-stage activated charcoal trap at -40°C (achievable with a compact Peltier cooled unit rather than liquid nitrogen). The two-stage design uses a first charcoal stage to capture radon with high efficiency (charcoal at -40°C has radon partition coefficient approximately 10³ versus the liquid, compared with approximately 10 at room temperature) and a second stage as a guard column monitored with a ZnS scintillation cell to verify performance.

The membrane degasser should use hollow fiber membranes of polypropylene with 0.2 µm pores in a counter-current gas flow configuration, of the type manufactured by Membrana GmbH (the Liqui-Cel series was commercially available by the late 1990s). This geometry achieves radon removal efficiency above 99.5% in a single pass through a unit of manageable physical size (approximately 30 cm diameter, 60 cm length for the required flow rate) compared with the shower-head PD design that achieves approximately 98% removal.

**Quantified benefit**: Radon is a dominant source of photodisintegration background in the D₂O (²²²Rn decays to ²¹⁴Bi which emits a 2.45 MeV gamma above the 2.22 MeV deuteron photodisintegration threshold). Each factor of two improvement in radon removal directly reduces this neutron background, improving the NC signal-to-background ratio. Given the design requirement that photodisintegration not exceed 10% of the solar neutrino NC rate (500/year), any background reduction directly extends the useful running period before systematic limits are reached.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Component Replaced | Key Technology | Primary Benefit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low-radioactivity 25 cm PMT | Hamamatsu R1408 | Metal channel dynodes, 10 ppb glass | 4× reduction in PMT glass background; 2× better timing |
| Winston cone reflector | 18-piece Al concentrator | Spun Al, SiO₂/TiO₂ coating | 11% more detected photons; better coverage uniformity |
| SCA waveform digitizer | SNOD/SNOINT/QUSN7 chipset | 500 MHz switched capacitor, 0.5 µm CMOS | Pulse-shape discrimination; 200 ns deadtime |
| High-pressure resistive anode NCD | 2.5 atm Cu wire counter | 4 atm ³He, Ni-Cr resistive wire | 40% improvement in NC detection efficiency |
| Hollow-fiber radon extractor | Process degasser | Membrana Liqui-Cel + charcoal cold trap | >99.5% radon removal vs ~98% current |

# Hardware Design Upgrades for IceCube Physics Performance

## Framing the Problem

The paper identifies specific, quantified limitations that constrain physics performance. I will target each with concrete hardware proposals, grounded in technologies available by 2017 and the detector's documented failure modes.

---

## 1. Photon Detection: Replace the Single Large PMT with Multi-PMT Modules

### The Problem
The Hamamatsu R7081-02 has several documented weaknesses:
- Peak quantum efficiency of only **25%** (34% for HQE variant)
- A single downward-facing 10" PMT provides no directional information per DOM
- The photocathode non-uniformity is significant enough to require dedicated angular efficiency mapping for 135 bare PMTs
- The mu-metal cage blocks ~4% of incident light
- Single-PMT failure terminates the entire DOM's optical function

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace each DOM's single PMT with an array of **24–31 smaller-diameter (3") PMTs** arranged to provide near-4π solid angle coverage, following the multi-PMT module (mDOM) concept being studied for KM3NeT by 2016–2017.

**Specific components:**
- **Hamamatsu R12199-02** 3" PMTs with ~35% peak quantum efficiency at 390 nm, which were characterized and commercially available by 2016
- Mount PMTs in a geodesic arrangement on an internal support structure inside the existing 13" glass sphere, which has sufficient volume
- Each PMT operates with its own small **EMCO-style miniaturized HV module** (~0.5 W each), eliminating the single-point HV failure mode documented in the paper
- Use **mu-metal discs** behind each individual PMT rather than a cage, improving shielding efficiency while eliminating the 4% light blockage

**Physics gains:**
- Quantum efficiency improvement from 25% to ~35% increases photon yield by ~40% for the standard array, directly improving angular resolution for tracks and energy resolution for cascades
- Per-DOM directional sensitivity from coincident sub-PMT timing (photons hitting specific PMTs constrain arrival direction to ~30° within a single module) provides local event direction seed without cross-DOM reconstruction
- The 15% deposited energy resolution cited in the paper scales roughly as $1/\sqrt{N_\text{photons}}$; a 40% photon yield increase improves this by ~17%
- Redundancy: loss of one sub-PMT degrades rather than eliminates DOM performance

---

## 2. Waveform Digitization: Replace ATWD with Higher-Speed Continuous ADC

### The Problem
The ATWD architecture has several specific documented problems:
- **Deadtime**: after two back-to-back HLC hits, significant deadtime accumulates; high-gain IceTop DOMs show fractional deadtime of $3.2 \times 10^{-3}$
- **Fixed 427 ns recording window**: insufficient for photons from distant DOMs, forcing reliance on the lower-resolution 40 Msps fADC for extended waveforms
- **Two-ATWD alternating scheme** adds complexity, and DOMs with single functional ATWD (12 units documented) have permanently elevated deadtime
- ATWD uses switched capacitor arrays with **sample-dependent gain calibration** required — the per-sample ATWD calibration is identified as a significant calibration burden
- The **droop correction** from the transformer is temperature-dependent and requires a two-time-constant model; errors here directly distort energy reconstruction

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace the ATWD + fADC combination with a **single continuously-sampling pipeline ADC** operating at **250–500 Msps** with **12-bit resolution**.

**Specific components:**
- **Texas Instruments ADS5400** or equivalent: 12-bit, 1 Gsps pipeline ADC with power consumption ~1.5 W, available by 2016 in commercial instrumentation
- For lower power, the **AD9230** (12-bit, 250 Msps, ~0.9 W) provides adequate sampling for IceCube's signal bandwidth
- **Deep circular buffer in FPGA BRAM**: store 25–50 µs of continuous data (6,250–12,500 samples at 250 Msps), replacing both the 427 ns ATWD capture and the 6.4 µs fADC capture with a single unified waveform
- **Xilinx Artix-7** or **Spartan-7** FPGA (available 2016) provides sufficient logic for real-time hit detection, local coincidence processing, and compression within ~2 W

**Physics gains:**
- Eliminates the deadtime problem entirely for all hit rates below ~1 MHz
- The 12-bit resolution (vs. current effective ~10-bit from ATWD) reduces charge quantization error, improving the documented 15% energy resolution
- Removes the need for the per-sample ATWD pedestal calibration that the paper identifies as requiring dedicated "200 forced-readout waveforms" per run and is susceptible to baseline shifts of up to 0.6 counts affecting charge reconstruction
- Eliminates the transformer droop correction entirely if the AC-coupling transformer is replaced with a **DC-coupled front-end** using a bootstrapped cathode follower — the toroid transformer and its temperature-dependent two-time-constant correction model is the single most complex calibration element in section 3.2

---

## 3. Front-End Electronics: Redesign the Discriminator and Trigger Threshold System

### The Problem
The paper documents two specific discriminator-related issues:
- **SPE discriminator set at 0.25 PE** is a hard threshold; photons below this are permanently lost regardless of local coincidence
- **Discriminator threshold changes cause fADC baseline shifts** of up to 0.6 counts, requiring re-measurement of baselines and causing charge distortion in old-toroid DOMs where 1 PE can be measured as >2 PE
- The 0.25 PE threshold means the detection efficiency for dim events (relevant for DeepCore and PINGU physics) is limited by threshold effects rather than quantum efficiency

### Proposed Upgrade
Implement a **zero-suppression scheme with a lower effective threshold** using:

**Specific components:**
- Replace the single SPE discriminator with a **dual-threshold scheme**: a low threshold at ~0.1 PE for local coincidence checking only, and the existing 0.25 PE threshold for standalone SLC readout
- Use a **fully differential input stage** with an **AD8138** or similar precision differential amplifier driving the ADC, eliminating DC-coupling issues that cause the baseline-discriminator coupling problem entirely
- Add a **per-channel programmable baseline DAC** with 14-bit resolution (vs. the current scheme where baselines are set via software configuration and drift by up to 0.2 counts/year) — specifically, an **AD5370** 40-channel 16-bit DAC could serve multiple DOMs in a single string hub

**Physics gains:**
- A 0.1 PE effective threshold for local coincidence detection increases photon detection efficiency for dim pulses by ~15–20% based on typical PMT SPE charge distributions shown in Figure 12 of the paper
- Elimination of the discriminator-baseline coupling removes the dominant source of systematic baseline error identified in section 3.5, directly improving charge reconstruction for the ~1204 old-toroid DOMs where the effect is worst
- More stable baselines reduce the calibration overhead currently requiring monthly IceTop recalibration and annual in-ice recalibration

---

## 4. Timing: Upgrade RAPCal to Sub-Nanosecond Precision

### The Problem
The paper documents RAPCal timing precision of **1.2 ns** (from flasher verification), with individual RAPCal measurements showing 0.6 ns standard deviation from cable delay tracking. The 20 MHz communications ADC limits the fine-delay interpolation precision. The current angular resolution for muon tracks of **0.6°** is partially limited by timing precision — for a track crossing two DOMs 125 m apart, 1 ns timing error corresponds to ~0.04° uncertainty in reconstructed angle, but systematic effects accumulate across the array.

### Proposed Upgrade
**Upgrade the RAPCal digitization from 20 MHz to 200 MHz** using a dedicated timing ADC, and implement **time-to-digital converter (TDC) interpolation** for sub-100 ps resolution.

**Specific components:**
- **CAEN V1290** TDC chip or equivalent provides 25 ps bin size and was well-established by 2016; a custom ASIC equivalent could be integrated into the DOR card
- Replace the 20 MHz communications ADC on the DOR card with a **200 Msps ADC** (e.g., **AD9608**, 8-bit, 200 Msps, <100 mW) dedicated to RAPCal pulse digitization
- Implement **digital constant fraction discrimination** in FPGA firmware on the DOR card to extract pulse crossing times with ~100 ps precision from the higher-resolution waveform
- The **cable dispersion** distorts the received RAPCal pulse shape (visible in Figure 16 of the paper); implement a **matched filter** in FPGA using the known cable transfer function to correct for this before timing extraction

**Physics gains:**
- Improving RAPCal from 1.2 ns to ~300 ps precision would reduce the dominant systematic in track angular reconstruction, potentially improving the 0.6° angular resolution toward the ~0.2° level achievable with perfect timing given the 17 m DOM spacing and 125 m string spacing geometry
- Sub-degree angular resolution improvement directly benefits point source searches, where sensitivity scales roughly as $\sigma^{-2}$ for the angular resolution $\sigma$
- Better timing reduces the rate of false local coincidences from dark noise, allowing the LC window to be tightened from ±1 µs

---

## 5. Local Coincidence: Replace Analog LC Pulses with Digital Fiber Links

### The Problem
The current LC system uses **dedicated copper wire pairs** carrying digital pulses to nearest and next-to-nearest neighbor DOMs. The paper notes:
- LC settings must be modified around dead DOMs
- A malfunctioning DOM can sometimes still forward LC signals even when not taking data (used as a workaround)
- The LC signal is a simple digital pulse with no amplitude or timing information — it signals only that a neighbor fired, not when or how strongly

### Proposed Upgrade
Add **short-range optical fiber links** between adjacent DOMs on a string for LC signaling, carrying a **timestamped digital packet** rather than a simple logic pulse.

**Specific components:**
- Add a **low-power optical transceiver** (e.g., **Avago AFBR-57E6APZ** or similar 650 nm plastic fiber transceiver, <50 mW, < $5 per unit by 2016) to the penetrator assembly
- Plastic optical fiber (POF) running alongside the existing copper pairs in the breakout cable — POF is mechanically robust under the freeze-in stresses the paper describes
- The digital LC packet includes a **10-bit timestamp** (sub-microsecond precision) and a **4-bit charge estimate**, transmitted in a 14-bit packet at 10 Mbps — well within the capability of these transceivers
- The FPGA on the Main Board handles packet encode/decode in firmware, requiring no new ASICs

**Physics gains:**
- The timestamp in the LC packet allows surface reconstruction software to use the LC timing itself as a physics observable, adding ~1 hit's worth of timing information per DOM pair without full waveform readout — directly relevant for SLC-dominated low-energy events in DeepCore
- Charge information in the LC signal allows threshold-free coincidence logic: instead of "did neighbor fire above 0.25 PE?", the question becomes "did neighbor see charge consistent with a real photon?" This reduces false LC triggers from dark noise by a factor estimated at ~3 based on the 230–250 Hz uncorrelated noise rates vs. the ~10 Hz muon HLC rate at depth
- Fiber LC eliminates the LC cross-talk issues around failed DOMs entirely — failed optical transceivers simply produce no packet, and the surface software handles the absence cleanly

---

## 6. Glass Sphere and Pressure Housing: Reduce Dark Noise at the Source

### The Problem
Section 3.8 documents that **the majority of dark noise originates from the glass pressure sphere itself**, with:
- Correlated noise rate of 280–340 Hz attributed to luminescence (likely from cerium scintillation triggered by $^{40}$K decays)
- $^{40}$K contributing to uncorrelated noise at 230–250 Hz
- K₂O concentration of 0.03% by weight (~100 Bq per sphere)
- The correlated noise directly complicates supernova detection and low-energy analyses in DeepCore

### Proposed Upgrade
Replace the borosilicate glass spheres with **synthetic fused silica (Suprasil-grade) glass spheres** with intrinsically lower radioactive trace element concentrations.

**Specific components:**
- **Heraeus Suprasil 311** or **Corning HPFS 7980** fused silica: K content below 1 ppb by weight (vs. 0.03% = 300,000 ppb for current glass), reducing $^{40}$K activity by a factor of ~$3 \times 10^5$
- Fused silica also has **better UV transmission** (>90% at 300 nm vs. ~10% at 315 nm for current borosilicate), extending the effective photon detection range and increasing total photon yield by ~5–10% when folded with the PMT quantum efficiency curve at shorter wavelengths
- The pressure rating of fused silica is comparable to borosilicate at the required 690 bar overpressure rating
- The primary manufacturing challenge is producing hemispherical shells at 13" diameter — this is within the capability of precision optical fabrication companies (e.g., **Zygo Corporation**, **SCHOTT AG**) that routinely produce large fused silica optics

**Physics gains:**
- Reducing dark noise by even a factor of 2–5 (through lower K content) would improve the supernova detection sensitivity, since the SNDAQ system monitors summed DOM rates and its significance threshold is set by Poisson fluctuations in the dark noise sum
- The paper documents that correlated noise (280–340 Hz) dominates the total noise budget after the Poissonian component; even if correlated noise from cerium scintillation is only partially reduced, the 25% decay in noise standard deviation over 3 years (from triboluminescence) suggests the steady-state noise level is partially environmental rather than intrinsic to the glass — lower-activity glass reduces the intrinsic floor
- Better UV transmission provides additional ~5% effective photon yield with no other changes, for no additional power or complexity cost

---

## 7. Cable System: Add Per-DOM Power Monitoring with Higher Resolution

### The Problem
The paper describes DOM failures as "challenging to diagnose beyond identifying electrical shorts." 87 DOMs have failed, the majority during deployment/freeze-in. The DOR card monitors current and voltage per twisted pair (serving **two DOMs**), meaning individual DOM power draw is not measured. The paper notes a "firmware fuse" can disable power based on pair-level current deviations.

### Proposed Upgrade
Add **per-DOM current sensing** at the breakout connector level using a dedicated low-power monitoring IC.

**Specific components:**
- **Texas Instruments INA226** precision current/voltage monitor: I²C interface, 16-bit resolution, 0.1% accuracy, 330 µW power consumption — could be integrated into the breakout connector housing at each DOM attachment point
- The INA226 connects across the DOM's power input and reports via I²C back to the DOR card over one of the existing spare quads in the in-ice cable (the paper notes 5 spare quads per cable)
- Implement **anomaly detection firmware** in the DOR card FPGA: track each DOM's power signature over time, flag gradual resistance changes that precede failures (resistive degradation in connectors or penetrator assembly)

**Physics gains:**
- Early failure detection allows scheduled DOM power cycling or reconfiguration before complete failure, potentially recovering some fraction of the 55 deployment/freeze-in failures
- Per-DOM power data enables **thermal modeling** of the string: DOM power dissipation into the ice affects hole ice refreezing and long-term optical coupling, currently not measurable
- Improves diagnostic capability for the "challenging" failure modes noted in section 2.4, reducing the information gap that currently prevents distinguishing cable failures from water leaks from freeze-in damage

---

## Priority Ranking and Implementation Notes

| Upgrade | Physics Impact | Implementation Risk | Cost Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multi-PMT module | Very High | Medium | PMT cost × 24–31 per DOM |
| Continuous ADC + FPGA | High | Low | FPGA NRE cost |
| Fused silica sphere | High | Medium | Fabrication cost |
| RAPCal TDC upgrade | Medium | Low | DOR card redesign |
| Digital fiber LC | Medium | Medium | Fiber integration in penetrator |
| Discriminator redesign | Medium | Low | Main Board spin |
| Per-DOM power monitor | Low (operational) | Low | Marginal |

The **multi-PMT module** combined with the **continuous ADC digitization** represent the highest-leverage single change to physics performance, as they address the two fundamental detection limitations simultaneously: photon collection efficiency and waveform capture fidelity. The **fused silica sphere** addresses the dark noise floor that limits low-energy physics independently of all other upgrades.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for ProtoDUNE-SP / DUNE-SP

## Framing the Problem

The primary physics performance limitations identifiable from this paper are:

1. **Photon detection efficiency** is very low (0.08–2% depending on module type)
2. **HV instability** causing uptime loss and field non-uniformity
3. **Cold electronics noise** still significant at room temperature and non-negligible at cryogenic temperatures
4. **Wire-based charge readout** with inherent ambiguities and dead regions
5. **LAr purity monitoring** limited in spatial coverage inside the TPC volume

---

## 1. Photon Detection System Overhaul (Highest Priority)

### Problem
The paper reports photon detection efficiencies of 0.08% for dip-coated bars, 0.21% for double-shift bars, and only 2% for the single-cell ARAPUCA. The minimum DUNE requirement is 0.5 PE/MeV at 3.6 m drift distance. The paper notes that an all-ARAPUCA system would yield ~1.9 photons/MeV, exceeding specs by roughly 4×, but the single-cell ARAPUCA demonstrated here covers only 1223 cm² active area per module versus 1744 cm² for light guides.

### Proposed Upgrade: X-ARAPUCA with Larger Supercell Arrays

**Replace all 60 PD modules with X-ARAPUCA supercells:**

- The X-ARAPUCA design (known from DUNE development work as of 2021) extends the dichroic filter window area by tiling multiple cells into a single elongated supercell spanning the full 209.7 cm bar length
- Use **p-bis-(o-methylstyryl)-benzene (bis-MSB)** as the external WLS instead of PTP, which has better quantum yield and emission spectrum match to the dichroic filter cutoff at 400 nm
- Replace the **Omega Optical 400 nm dichroic filters** with custom interference filters optimized for the specific TPB/bis-MSB emission spectrum, targeting steeper cutoff slopes to reduce photon loss at the filter boundary
- Internal reflector upgrade: replace VIKUITI 3M ESR (>98% reflectivity) with **Lumirror E60L** or **3M ESR-2** which achieves >99.5% reflectivity in the 420-500 nm range, reducing absorption probability per bounce from ~2% to ~0.5%, compounding significantly over multiple reflections

**Photosensor upgrade within ARAPUCA cells:**

- Replace the **Hamamatsu S13360-6050 CQ/VE MPPCs (50 μm pixel, 6×6 mm²)** with **SiPM arrays using 35 μm pixel pitch** to reduce saturation at high photon flux (relevant for supernova burst detection)
- Tile **four 6×6 mm² SiPMs in a 2×2 arrangement per cell** with individual readout rather than passive ganging, using **NUV-HD SiPMs** (as developed by FBK, characterized pre-2021) which show ~40% photon detection efficiency at 420 nm at 77 K versus ~25% for the SensL C-Series used here
- The NUV-HD devices exhibit lower dark count rate at cryogenic temperatures (~10 Hz/mm² at 77 K versus ~100 Hz/mm² at 300 K), directly reducing self-trigger noise

**Active ganging electronics in cold:**

- The paper explicitly states "no front-end electronics are necessary in the cold volume" and uses passive ganging, which limits signal-to-noise. Install **cold active transimpedance amplifier (TIA) ASICs** at each SiPM group, fabricated in the same 0.18 μm CMOS process used for the TPC FE ASICs (already validated at 77 K)
- Each TIA serves 4 SiPMs, providing ~20 dB gain before the 20 m Cat6 cable run, recovering the signal degradation from cable capacitance (~100 pF for Cat6 at this length)
- Estimated improvement: SNR increases from 6-12 (reported) to >30 for single photoelectrons, enabling reliable single-PE threshold operation

**Quantitative impact:** Full X-ARAPUCA coverage with NUV-HD SiPMs and active ganging is estimated to push photon yield to 5-10 PE/MeV at maximum drift distance, enabling calorimetric energy reconstruction from scintillation alone and sub-microsecond event timing for supernova neutrino pointing.

---

## 2. High Voltage System Redesign

### Problem
The paper documents persistent current streamers at 4-6/day rate, requiring automated recovery that still causes HV interruptions. The root cause is identified as charge accumulation on FRP insulating surfaces in high-field regions, enhanced by high LAr purity. HV uptime was 96-98% during beam running but degraded during long stable-purity periods.

### Upgrade A: Surface Resistivity Treatment of FRP Components

**Apply a controlled resistive coating to all FRP structural elements:**

- The instability mechanism (charging of insulating FRP under high field) is well understood. FRP surfaces in the field cage support structure should be coated with **carbon-loaded PEEK (polyether ether ketone)** or a **graphite-loaded epoxy** to achieve a surface resistivity of 10⁹–10¹¹ Ω/square
- This resistivity range is high enough to not perturb the field cage voltage distribution appreciably (resistor chain is 0.5 GΩ/stage) but low enough to drain accumulated charge on timescales of seconds to minutes rather than hours
- Coating thickness: 50-100 μm applied by spray deposition before installation; must be validated for cryogenic thermal cycling (FRP contracts ~0.3%, carbon-loaded coatings must match or be elastically compliant)
- Specifically target the **FRP I-beams and box beams** of the top/bottom FC modules and the endwall FRP box beams, which are the structural elements nearest the high-field region at the APA-FC junction and CPA-FC junction

### Upgrade B: Redesigned HV Feedthrough with Inline Current Monitoring

**Replace the ICARUS-heritage feedthrough with an instrumented design:**

- Add **12 toroidal current transformers** (one per ground plane connection point) with **10 nA sensitivity** and **1 MHz bandwidth**, replacing the single cable-mounted toroid currently used
- The paper notes the existing toroid identifies streamer location only coarsely (upstream/downstream of toroid position). Fine-grained GP current monitoring exists but the feedthrough itself is uninstrumented for fast transients
- Integrate a **piezoelectric acoustic sensor array** (4 sensors) bonded to the HV feedthrough outer tube to detect microdischarges before they develop into full streamers, providing 10-100 ms early warning to the auto-recovery system
- This changes the recovery strategy from reactive (respond to high current) to predictive (pre-emptively reduce voltage at first acoustic signature)

### Upgrade C: Active Field Cage Termination

**Replace the passive termination boards with actively regulated termination:**

- Currently, FC termination boards use a default passive resistance, with an SHV cable available for external voltage setting
- Install **precision HV DACs** (16-bit, ±0.01% stability) at the warm end of each termination SHV connection, individually addressable via the DCS
- This allows real-time trimming of the termination voltage on each of the 8 FC chains (4 top/bottom per drift volume × 2 drift volumes) to compensate for any resistor aging or thermal coefficient mismatch
- Also enables deliberate field shaping to correct for measured space charge distortions, which at ProtoDUNE-SP surface operation reach several cm of track displacement

---

## 3. Cold Electronics: ASIC Redesign

### Problem
The paper reports ENC of ~400 e⁻ at cryogenic temperatures for the FE ASIC, dropping from ~1100 e⁻ at room temperature. The ADC ASIC is noted as problematic (320,000 transistors, known instability issues in the 35-ton prototype context). The system achieves SNR of ~16-13 for MIPs on collection wires, adequate but with room for improvement especially for low-energy physics (Michel electrons, supernova neutrinos).

### Upgrade A: Next-Generation FE ASIC in 65 nm CMOS

**Redesign the 16-channel FE ASIC in TSMC 65 nm LP CMOS:**

- The current design uses 0.18 μm CMOS. Moving to 65 nm reduces gate capacitance by ~7× and allows higher transistor density for improved differential pair matching
- The input MOSFET (currently p-channel, L/W = 0.27/10 μm) should be replaced with a **folded cascode topology** using a 65 nm device with L/W = 0.06/20 μm, reducing input-referred noise current spectral density by ~3× while maintaining 1.8 V compatibility through thick-oxide transistors at the input stage
- Target ENC: <200 e⁻ at 77 K with 150 pF input capacitance, compared to <600 e⁻ currently demonstrated
- Add a **baseline restoration circuit** implemented in digital logic to suppress low-frequency noise from LAr fluid motion coupling to wires, which is currently a significant noise source not fully addressed by shaping

### Upgrade B: Integrated 16-bit ADC ASIC

**Replace the separate ADC ASIC with an integrated 16-bit, 2 MSPS ADC:**

- The current 12-bit ADC provides 4096 levels over the ~300 fC full-scale range, giving ~73 fC/bit at maximum gain. For the 25 mV/fC gain setting, this is adequate for MIP signals but limits dynamic range for high-energy showers
- A 16-bit ADC (65,536 levels) extends the dynamic range by 12 dB, equivalent to improving sensitivity to signals ~16× smaller or extending the unsaturated range for large energy depositions
- Use a **successive approximation register (SAR) ADC** topology at 65 nm, which achieves better power efficiency than the pipeline ADC approach likely used in the current design. Target: <2 mW/channel at 1.2 V supply versus 5 mW/channel at 1.8 V currently
- Integrate the ADC and FE functions on a single die to eliminate the inter-chip connection (currently 16 lines per FE-ADC pair), reducing board area by ~40% and enabling simpler FEMB layout

### Upgrade C: On-FEMB Trigger Primitive Generation

**Add a dedicated trigger primitive ASIC or FPGA to each FEMB:**

- The paper describes self-triggering as a 2019 demonstration milestone, requiring data transmission to servers for hit-finding. This creates latency and bandwidth pressure
- Add a small **FPGA (e.g., Xilinx Spartan-7 XC7S15, validated for cryogenic operation by 2020)** to each FEMB that performs hit-finding in firmware, producing only trigger primitives (hit time, integrated charge, wire number) rather than raw waveforms for the trigger path
- Raw waveforms still transmitted on a separate path for physics reconstruction; trigger primitives transmitted on a low-bandwidth (100 Mbps) dedicated link
- Power budget: Spartan-7 XC7S15 consumes ~50 mW static at 77 K (validated behavior of CMOS FPGAs at cryogenic temperature), acceptable given the FEMB thermal budget

---

## 4. Charge Readout: Transition to Pixel or Strip Readout for Reduced Ambiguity

### Problem
The paper describes wire planes at ±35.7° producing reconstruction ambiguities when multiple tracks overlap. The 960 collection wires per APA provide 4.79 mm pitch, and the 800 induction wires per plane at each angle create combinatorial ambiguities for complex events (multi-particle final states, high-multiplicity hadronic showers).

### Upgrade: Charge Pixel Readout on One APA

**Instrument one APA with a pixelated charge readout plane using LArPix:**

- The LArPix ASIC (developed at LBNL, reported in literature by 2020) provides self-triggering pixel readout with 4.434 mm pitch pixels, fully eliminating wire ambiguity by providing inherent 3D hit reconstruction
- Replace one of the six APAs with a **LArPix-based pixel plane**: a tiled array of LArPix tiles, each containing 64 pixels with individual charge-sensitive amplifiers operating at 77 K
- Pixel-level power: ~1 μW/pixel at 77 K (self-triggered operation), totaling ~150 mW for one full APA face (7500 pixels at 4.434 mm pitch over 6×2.3 m²), well within thermal budget
- Data readout via the same FELIX infrastructure already validated in ProtoDUNE-SP, using the LArPix UART protocol adapted to the WIB interface
- This provides direct comparison of wire vs. pixel reconstruction efficiency for the same beam particles, quantifying the ambiguity penalty in wire readout for DUNE physics cases

---

## 5. Purity Monitoring: Distributed Inline Monitors

### Problem
The three purity monitors are located **outside the TPC volume** at fixed heights, providing only a 1D vertical profile of electron lifetime. The paper notes spatial non-uniformity in temperature (20 mK horizontal gradients observed), implying potential purity gradients that the monitors cannot resolve. Space charge from cosmics further complicates in-situ TPC-based lifetime measurements.

### Upgrade: Miniaturized In-Situ Purity Monitors

**Deploy a grid of 12 miniaturized purity monitors within the TPC active volume:**

- Design a purity monitor with <5 cm diameter cathode-anode gap of 10 cm (versus the current ICARUS-heritage design with ~30 cm gap), using a **UV LED at 175 nm** (available from Roithner Lasertechnik, demonstrated operation at 77 K by 2020) instead of the external Xe lamp and quartz fiber delivery system
- Twelve such monitors arranged in a 3×2×2 grid (3 heights × 2 drift volumes × 2 horizontal positions) provide a 3D electron lifetime map of the TPC
- Each monitor requires only two HV lines (cathode, anode bias) and two signal lines, routed along existing cable trays
- The UV LED power consumption is <1 mW per monitor, negligible thermal contribution
- Sampling rate: one measurement per 40 seconds (same as current monitors), providing 3D purity maps updated every minute
- The 10 cm drift distance covers electron drift times of ~65 μs at 500 V/cm, sufficient to measure electron lifetimes from 100 μs to >100 ms with the same signal ratio technique described in the paper

---

## 6. Cryogenics: Active LAr Flow Control with Inline Sensors

### Problem
The paper reports a 20 mK horizontal temperature gradient and evidence that the LAr recirculation creates thermal non-uniformity correlated with purity variations. The CFD models do not fully reproduce the measured temperature profiles ("bump at 6.2 m" unexplained). The diaphragm pump failed during operations, demonstrating single-point-of-failure vulnerability.

### Upgrade: Multi-Point Flow Metering and Adaptive Recirculation

**Install Coriolis mass flow meters on individual LAr distribution pipes:**

- The current system monitors total recirculation flow (7.0 t/h nominal) but cannot resolve distribution between the outlet pipes at the cryostat bottom
- **Micro-Coriolis sensors** (e.g., Emerson Coriolis meters adapted for cryogenic service) on each of 4 distribution pipe outlets provide real-time flow balancing, allowing the DCS to adjust individual outlet valves to achieve uniform LAr injection across the cryostat floor
- This directly addresses the observed temperature/purity gradients by controlling the source of non-uniformity rather than just measuring its effects
- Add a **redundant second LAr pump** with automatic switchover, specifically addressing the 2019 pump failure that interrupted purity monitoring and required manual intervention

---

## Priority Summary

| Upgrade | Physics Impact | Technical Readiness | Estimated Difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|
| X-ARAPUCA + NUV-HD SiPMs + cold TIA | Very High (supernova, nucleon decay timing) | High (components validated) | Medium |
| FRP resistive coating for HV stability | High (HV uptime, field uniformity) | High (known materials) | Low |
| 65 nm FE+ADC ASIC | Medium-High (low energy threshold) | Medium (requires new tape-out) | High |
| Active FC termination | Medium (field correction) | High | Low |
| LArPix pixel APA | High (reconstruction quality) | Medium (system integration) | High |
| Distributed inline purity monitors | Medium (calibration precision) | Medium | Medium |
| Multi-point flow metering | Medium (operational stability) | High | Low |

The single highest-impact upgrade is the **full replacement of light guide modules with X-ARAPUCA supercells equipped with NUV-HD SiPMs and cold active readout**, as photon detection efficiency is the most severe quantitative limitation identified in the paper, directly affecting the detector's ability to achieve its supernova burst and nucleon decay physics goals.

# Hardware Design Upgrades for ProtoDUNE-SP / DUNE-SP

## Preamble on Performance Baseline

The paper establishes several concrete performance limitations worth addressing systematically:

- Photon detection efficiency: 0.08% (dip-coated), 0.21% (double-shift), 2% (ARAPUCA) — all well below theoretical optimum
- HV instabilities: current streamers at ~1/20 hours even with auto-recovery, correlated with high LAr purity
- ENC: ~400 e⁻ at cryogenic temperature, limiting low-energy threshold
- Electron lifetime measurement range limited by purity monitor signal strength
- CRT coverage incomplete (upstream/downstream faces only)

---

## 1. Photon Detection System

This is the most significant performance gap. The paper explicitly notes the dip-coated and double-shift modules achieve 0.08% and 0.21% efficiency respectively, while ARAPUCA reaches 2% — a factor of ~10–25 improvement.
